title: A Unified Framework for Probability Estimation of Data-Dependent Events
description:
arXiv:2610.41244v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study the general problem of estimating $D(\dde(S))$, the probability that an unknown distribution $D$ assigns to an event determined by a sample $S$ of $n$ i.i.d.\ draws from $D$ through a known mapping $\dde$. The estimation algorithm knows $\dde$ and $S$ but does not have access to any additional samples from $D$. This formulation captures classical missing mass, the data-dependent targets of adaptive data analysis and post-selection inference, and the test error of a data-trained predictor, whose estimation was recently studied by \new{Gastpar et al.\ (2024a,b)}. Within this framework we examine the two classical approaches to estimation. The error of the empirical plug-in estimator is exactly a generalization gap, so generalization bounds transfer to it directly. The leave-one-out estimator, which recovers the Good--Turing estimator, is accurate for every mapping that is stable under the deletion of one sample point, including new structured examples such as neighborhoods of the sample and pierced sets.
  The main application of our framework is to error estimation for a predictor that combines a base classifier with memorized exceptions, a structure common in theory and in practice. For it, the test error is exactly the missing mass restricted to the error region of the base classifier, a region selected by the same sample. We formulate the general problem of \emph{adaptive missing mass estimation} to address such dependence and propose a natural hybrid estimator, the Good--Turing estimator restricted to the selected region. We show that the generalization of the base classifier alone does not guarantee the accuracy of this estimator, and derive two bounds on its error: the first one based on the VC dimension of possible error regions and another based on the mutual information of the selected region with the sample.

title: Part 2: I Broke Out of YouTube My Bot Now Hits Instagram & Twitter/X Too (3 Platforms, 3 Completely Different Protection Models)
description:
📖 Part 1 is here — read it first:
How I Built a Telegram Bot That Downloads YouTube Music & Videos (Up to 2 GB)

🤖 Try the live bot: (https://t.me/songsuperzxbot)
📦 Source code: github.com/chandan0000001/music-video_telegrambot

Someone sent me a message after Part 1 went live.

"Can it do Instagram Reels?"

Short answer at the time: no.

Slightly longer answer after a few weeks of work: yes, and also Twitter/X, and also Instagram Stories, profile pictures, highlights, and posts. But getting there was a completely different problem from YouTube — and I mean completely different. Three platforms. Three protection models. Three sets of rules about what you can fetch without authentication, what you can't, and what will quietly rate-limit you into oblivion if you're not careful.

This is the story of how I expanded the bot, what I learned about how Instagram and Twitter/X actually protect their content, and the architectural changes that come with supporting multiple platforms in one bot.

What the Bot Already Does (Quick Recap)

Before I get into the new stuff — if you haven't read Part 1, the short version:

The bot is a production-grade Telegram bot built with Python 3.11, aiogram 3, FFmpeg, and SQLite WAL mode. It searches YouTube, lets users pick from the top 5 results, and downloads audio in MP3/M4A/WAV up to 320kbps or video in MP4 up to 1080p. The clever parts are:

  • yt-dlp's Signature Cipher bypass — reverse-engineers YouTube's JS player to reconstruct the real stream URL
  • Smart 2 GB delivery — files under 48 MB go via HTTP Bot API instantly; larger files use native MTProto
  • Intel VAAPI hardware acceleration — FFmpeg transcodes using the GPU render node, ~10x faster than CPU
  • Full admin panel — stats, ban/unblock, broadcast, CSV export, live queue view
  • 30 automated tests — URL validation, FFmpeg pipeline, rate limiting, cancellation, database

That foundation is what Part 2 is built on. Now let's talk about why adding Instagram and Twitter/X was harder than just "swap yt-dlp's input URL."

Why Three Platforms is an Architecture Problem, Not Just a Feature

When I built the YouTube handler, it was a one-platform world. The whole flow assumed: user sends query or YouTube URL → validate → download → deliver.

The moment you add Instagram and Twitter/X, that assumption breaks. You now need:

  1. A URL router — detect which platform a URL belongs to before doing anything else
  2. Platform-specific authentication — Instagram requires a session cookie; YouTube needs cookies for age-restricted content; Twitter/X can sometimes do without
  3. Platform-specific content types — YouTube has audio or video. Instagram has reels, stories, highlights, posts, and profile pictures. Twitter/X has videos, images, and posts with mixed media
  4. Platform-specific rate limiting — YouTube is relatively forgiving. Instagram will silently downgrade your requests or temporarily block your IP if you hammer it. Twitter/X has changed its protection model more aggressively than any other platform in recent years

Here's the new routing layer that runs before any download starts:

import re
from enum import Enum

class Platform(Enum):
    YOUTUBE  = "youtube"
    INSTAGRAM = "instagram"
    TWITTER  = "twitter"
    UNKNOWN  = "unknown"

PLATFORM_PATTERNS = {
    Platform.YOUTUBE: re.compile(
        r'^https?://(www\.)?(youtube\.com/watch\?v=|youtu\.be/|youtube\.com/shorts/)[A-Za-z0-9_\-]{11}'
    ),
    Platform.INSTAGRAM: re.compile(
        r'^https?://(www\.)?instagram\.com/(p|reel|stories|tv|s)/[A-Za-z0-9_\-]+'
    ),
    Platform.TWITTER: re.compile(
        r'^https?://(www\.)?(twitter\.com|x\.com)/\w+/status/\d+'
    ),
}

def detect_platform(url: str) -> Platform:
    # SSRF guard — always first
    if re.match(r'https?://(localhost|127\.|10\.|192\.168\.|169\.254\.)', url):
        return Platform.UNKNOWN
    for platform, pattern in PLATFORM_PATTERNS.items():
        if pattern.match(url):
            return platform
    return Platform.UNKNOWN

The SSRF check runs before platform detection. An attacker sending http://192.168.1.1/admin disguised as any platform URL gets rejected at this layer, not inside any platform-specific handler.

Platform 1: YouTube (The One We Already Solved)

Covered in full in Part 1. The short summary of how YouTube protects streams:

  • Signature Cipher — stream URLs are scrambled via a JavaScript function that yt-dlp reverse-engineers from YouTube's player JS
  • n-parameter throttle — download speed is capped at ~50 KB/s unless you decrypt an "n" parameter from the same JS bundle
  • po_token — a newer proof-of-origin token embedded in browser sessions, requiring a valid cookies.txt to bypass

yt-dlp handles all three. Keep it updated and refresh cookies.txt every few weeks.

Platform 2: Instagram — Sessions, Stories, and Aggressive Rate Limiting

Instagram's protection model is fundamentally different from YouTube's. YouTube obfuscates stream URLs but serves them publicly. Instagram ties almost everything to authenticated sessions.

What's public vs what needs auth

No authentication needed:

  • Public post images and videos
  • Public Reels
  • Profile pictures (always public — served directly from Instagram's CDN)

Requires a valid Instagram session:

  • Stories (expire in 24 hours; private to logged-in users)
  • Highlights (archived stories; account-level access)
  • Content from private accounts

How Instagram serves content

When you watch a Reel in your browser, the actual video file is served from Instagram's CDN — URLs that look like:

https://scontent-iad3-1.cdninstagram.com/v/t50.2886-16/...?_nc_ht=scontent...&_nc_cat=...

These CDN URLs are time-limited and session-tied. They're embedded inside a JSON blob in the page's JavaScript bundle or fetched via an internal GraphQL endpoint. yt-dlp's Instagram extractor reverse-engineers these endpoints to pull the direct CDN URL.

For authenticated content (stories, highlights), the extractor needs a valid sessionid cookie — the same session token your browser uses when you're logged into Instagram.

Configuring Instagram in the bot 

def get_instagram_opts(content_type: str, output_path: str) -> dict:
    base_opts = {
        'outtmpl': output_path,
        'quiet': True,
        'cookiefile': 'instagram_cookies.txt',  # must contain valid sessionid
        'http_headers': {
            'User-Agent': 'Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Linux x86_64) AppleWebKit/537.36',
        },
    }

    if content_type in ('reel', 'video', 'post'):
        base_opts['format'] = 'bestvideo[ext=mp4]+bestaudio[ext=m4a]/best[ext=mp4]'
    elif content_type == 'story':
        base_opts['format'] = 'best'  # stories are single-stream
    elif content_type == 'profile_picture':
        base_opts['format'] = 'best'

    return base_opts

The rate limiting trap

Instagram rate-limits by IP and by session. If you download too many items in quick succession using the same session cookie, Instagram starts returning 401 Unauthorized errors — even for public content — or silently serves lower-quality versions.

My fix: per-platform cooldown timers. Instagram downloads enforce a 15-second minimum gap between requests from the same session. This is longer than the YouTube cooldown (10 seconds) specifically because Instagram's rate limiting is less forgiving and harder to detect when it's happening.

PLATFORM_COOLDOWNS = {
    Platform.YOUTUBE:   10,   # seconds between requests
    Platform.INSTAGRAM: 15,   # Instagram rate-limits harder
    Platform.TWITTER:   8,
}

Profile pictures — the easy one

Profile pictures are the simplest Instagram download. They're always public, always served directly from the CDN, and don't require authentication:

https://instagram.com/{username}/?__a=1

The JSON response contains graphql.user.profile_pic_url_hd — a direct image URL. No cipher, no session required, just a clean HTTP GET.

Platform 3: Twitter/X — Bearer Tokens and a Platform That Keeps Moving

Twitter's 2023 pivot to X — and the dramatic changes to API access that came with it — made this the most technically interesting platform to support.

How Twitter/X protects video content

Twitter/X video is delivered as HLS streams (HTTP Live Streaming). When you watch a video in a tweet, the player fetches an M3U8 playlist that lists the actual video segments:

#EXTM3U
#EXT-X-VERSION:3
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=2176000,RESOLUTION=1280x720
https://video.twimg.com/ext_tw_video/.../720x1280/...m3u8
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=832000,RESOLUTION=640x360
https://video.twimg.com/ext_tw_video/.../360x640/...m3u8

The M3U8 playlist URL itself is embedded in the tweet's card data, which is fetched from an internal API endpoint:

https://api.twitter.com/1.1/statuses/show.json?id=<tweet_id>

This endpoint requires a Bearer token — an authentication token that Twitter's own web client sends with every request. yt-dlp extracts this bearer token from Twitter/X's JavaScript bundle (the same approach it uses for YouTube's cipher — find the token in the JS, use it for requests).

What happened in 2023

When Elon Musk took over Twitter and rebranded it to X, free API tier access was almost entirely removed. Third-party apps that relied on Twitter's public API were killed. Nitter (the privacy-friendly Twitter frontend) started failing. Many download tools broke.

yt-dlp adapted by switching to the "guest API" — an unauthenticated path that Twitter/X still exposes for public content, using a guest token that gets issued when you visit the site without being logged in. This guest token approach still works for public tweets.

Handling tweets with multiple images

A tweet can have 1-4 images. When a user sends a tweet URL with multiple images, the bot downloads all of them and sends them as a Telegram media group:

async def handle_twitter_images(url: str, message: Message):
    with yt_dlp.YoutubeDL({'quiet': True, 'skip_download': True}) as ydl:
        info = ydl.extract_info(url, download=False)

    if 'entries' in info:
        # Multiple images — send as album
        media_group = []
        for entry in info['entries']:
            img_url = entry.get('url')
            if img_url:
                media_group.append(InputMediaPhoto(media=img_url))

        if media_group:
            await message.answer_media_group(media=media_group)
    else:
        # Single image or video
        ...

Telegram supports sending up to 10 items in a media group, which covers Twitter/X's 4-image maximum comfortably.

The Content-Type Detection System

Instagram URLs carry information about content type in the path:

URL pattern Content type
instagram.com/p/{id}/ Post (image or video)
instagram.com/reel/{id}/ Reel (short video)
instagram.com/stories/{user}/{id}/ Story
instagram.com/s/{highlight_id}/ Highlight
instagram.com/{username}/ Profile (→ profile picture)
instagram.com/tv/{id}/ IGTV (long video) 
def detect_instagram_content_type(url: str) -> str:
    if '/reel/' in url:    return 'reel'
    if '/stories/' in url: return 'story'
    if '/p/' in url:       return 'post'
    if '/s/' in url:       return 'highlight'
    if '/tv/' in url:      return 'video'
    # If it's just instagram.com/{username}/ — profile picture
    if re.match(r'https?://(www\.)?instagram\.com/[^/]+/?$', url):
        return 'profile_picture'
    return 'unknown'

The bot surfaces a different keyboard to the user depending on content type. A Reel shows "Download Video" and "Download Audio". A Story just shows "Download". A profile URL shows "Download Profile Picture". No unnecessary choices for things that have only one format.

Updated Supported Platforms

Here's where the bot stands now:

Platform Content Types Auth Required
YouTube Music search, Audio (MP3/M4A/WAV), Video (144p–1080p) cookies.txt (age-restricted only)
Instagram Reel, Video, Post, Story, Highlight, Profile Picture sessionid cookie (stories/highlights)
Twitter / X Video, Post images (up to 4), GIF None (public tweets)

All three platforms route through the same pipeline:
URL → platform detection → SSRF guard → content type detection → platform-specific yt-dlp config → FFmpeg → smart delivery (HTTP or MTProto) → cleanup.

What I Learned Building This

Instagram is the hardest platform to stay compatible with. YouTube breaks when they rotate the cipher — that's a known, predictable event that yt-dlp patches. Instagram breaks when they change their internal GraphQL schema, which happens without announcement and with no public documentation to reference. Two of my three "bot is down" incidents since adding Instagram support were Instagram schema changes, not YouTube.

Twitter/X's guest API is fragile. It works today. X has shown zero interest in maintaining compatibility with third-party tools, and the guest API could be deprecated at any point. I handle this by catching yt-dlp errors and returning a clear message to users — "this video may not be downloadable" — instead of silently failing.

Per-platform rate limiting is non-negotiable. A single rate limiter across all platforms was my first approach. It was wrong. Instagram needs longer cooldowns than YouTube. Twitter/X is somewhere in the middle. Platform-specific cooldown values aren't premature optimization — they're the difference between a bot that works reliably and one that gets session-banned after 20 minutes.

yt-dlp is genuinely impressive. One library, three completely different platform protection models, maintained by a community that ships patches sometimes within hours. The right posture when building on top of it: keep it updated, wrap all extractor calls in robust error handling, and never assume a config that works today will work in two weeks.

Try It

The bot handles all three platforms now. Drop a YouTube link, an Instagram Reel, or a Twitter/X video URL and it figures out the rest.

Try it: @songsuperzxbot

Source code: github.com/chandan0000001/music-video_telegrambot

Part 1 (YouTube deep-dive): dev.to/chandan0000001/...

Questions about Instagram's session handling, Twitter/X's HLS parsing, or anything else — drop them in the comments.

title: Migrating Monoliths to Event-Driven APIs: The Strangler-Fig Pattern
description:
Originally published on the HostingPodium Enterprise Engineering Blog.

Free SRE & Developer Diagnostics: Test your stack live with our Free Website Speed Test & Core Web Vitals Checker, Free Website Speed & Core Web Vitals Checker, or explore all 9 Free Webmaster & Cloud Engineering Tools.

A senior engineering guide to decomposing legacy PHP and Java monoliths into event-driven microservices using the Strangler-Fig pattern, Kafka CDC, and zero-downtime database refactoring.

Architectural Foundations of the Strangler-Fig Pattern

Legacy systems built on monolithic PHP and Java runtimes present significant maintenance overhead, tightly coupled database schemas, and rigid deployment pipelines. Rewriting these systems from scratch introduces catastrophic business risk and near-certain delivery failure. The Strangler-Fig pattern mitigates this by incrementally replacing specific domain capabilities with modern event-driven microservices. At HostingPodium, our engineering teams operationalize this transition via an API Gateway routing layer, Apache Kafka message buses, and CDC pipelines.

The target state moves away from synchronous, tightly coupled remote procedure calls toward asynchronous event streams. This isolation guarantees that upstream API consumers experience zero downtime while the underlying runtime transitions from legacy Apache/mod_php stacks to containerized Go or Quarkus services running on Kubernetes. Every domain boundary extracted reduces blast radius and decouples database access layers.

The API Gateway Routing Strategy

An NGINX or Envoy API Gateway sits at the edge, intercepting all inbound HTTP traffic. During the initial migration phase, the gateway functions as a deterministic reverse proxy. It inspects Uniform Resource Identifiers and header payloads, routing traffic either to the legacy PHP monolith or the new event-driven service.

http {
 upstream legacy_monolith {
 server 10.0.1.15:80 max_fails=3 fail_timeout=10s;
 keepalive 32;
 }
 upstream modern_api {
 server 10.0.2.22:8080 max_fails=3 fail_timeout=5s;
 keepalive 64;
 }
 server {
 listen 443 ssl http2;
 server_name api.hostingpodium.com;

 location /api/v1/users {
 proxy_pass http://modern_api;
 proxy_http_version 1.1;
 proxy_set_header Connection "";
 proxy_set_header Host $host;
 proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
 }

 location / {
 proxy_pass http://legacy_monolith;
 proxy_set_header Host $host;
 }
 }
}

This routing configuration allows gradual domain extraction. As soon as the user management domain is rewritten as an event-driven API, the gateway rules update dynamically without requiring client application updates. Connection pooling via proxy_http_version 1.1 and proxy_set_header Connection "" prevents socket exhaustion under high throughput.

Data Synchronization: Avoiding the Dual-Write Anti-Pattern

A primary architectural failure mode during monolith decomposition is the dual-write anti-pattern. Developers often attempt to write to both the legacy MySQL database and the new event store within application code. Network partitions, application crashes, or database timeouts inevitably lead to split-brain states and data corruption.

To guarantee consistency without distributed transactions, we deploy Change Data Capture (CDC) via Debezium connected to Apache Kafka. The legacy monolith continues writing exclusively to its native database. Debezium tails the database transaction log, capturing row-level inserts, updates, and deletes, and streams these mutations directly into Kafka topics.

Debezium Kafka Connector Configuration 

{
 "name": "legacy-mysql-connector",
 "config": {
 "connector.class": "io.debezium.connector.mysql.MySqlConnector",
 "tasks.max": "1",
 "database.hostname": "mysql.legacy.internal",
 "database.port": "3306",
 "database.user": "debezium",
 "database.password": "${file:/secrets/db.properties:password}",
 "database.server.id": "54001",
 "database.server.name": "legacy_db",
 "table.include.list": "legacy_schema.users,legacy_schema.orders",
 "database.history.kafka.bootstrap.servers": "kafka-broker-1:9092,kafka-broker-2:9092",
 "database.history.kafka.topic": "schema-changes.legacy.users",
 "include.schema.changes": "true",
 "plugin.name": "gaps"
 }
}

By leveraging the MySQL binlog, this architecture decouples data propagation from application logic. The new event-driven microservices consume these Kafka topics, updating their localized read models or operational data stores asynchronously.

Zero-Downtime Database Schema Migration

Extracting a domain from a shared monolithic database requires breaking database foreign key constraints and splitting tables. Performing these operations on production databases containing hundreds of millions of rows requires rigorous schema refactoring strategies using the expand-and-contract pattern.

  • Phase 1 (Expand): Add new columns or tables alongside legacy structures. Populate new columns using application-level triggers or CDC pipelines while primary writes still target legacy columns.

  • Phase 2 (Migrate): Backfill historical data using batch jobs with rate-limiting to prevent database CPU saturation. Validate consistency between old and new structures via checksum comparisons.

  • Phase 3 (Contract): Update application code to read and write exclusively from the new schema. Drop legacy columns and constraints only after verifying zero active queries hit them for at least two release cycles.

Migration Phase Write Target Read Target Risk Profile
Initial State Legacy Monolith DB Legacy Monolith DB High (Tightly Coupled)
Expand Legacy + CDC Sync Legacy Monolith DB Medium (Async Latency)
Dual-Read New Microservice Legacy & New (Shadow) Low (Validation Mode)
Contract New Microservice DB New Microservice DB Minimal (Isolated)

Operational Runbook: Handling Failure Modes

Transitioning production traffic introduces potential failure vectors that require automated mitigation strategies. Below is the operational runbook for managing partition lag in Kafka consumers during high-volume data migrations.

Consumer Lag Monitoring and Circuit Breaking 

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP="kafka-broker-1:9092"
CONSUMER_GROUP="user-event-processor"
MAX_ACCEPTABLE_LAG=5000

current_lag=$(kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server $KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP \
 --describe --group $CONSUMER_GROUP | awk 'NR>1 {sum += $5} END {print sum}')

if [ "$current_lag" -gt "$MAX_ACCEPTABLE_LAG" ]; then
 echo "CRITICAL: Consumer lag ($current_lag) exceeds threshold ($MAX_ACCEPTABLE_LAG). Engaging circuit breaker."
 curl -s -X POST http://api-gateway.internal/admin/circuit-breaker/open \n -d '{"service": "user-service", "reason": "kafka_lag_exceeded"}'
 exit 2
fi
echo "OK: Consumer lag is within nominal parameters ($current_lag)."
exit 0

When consumer lag spikes due to downstream database bottlenecks, the monitoring script trips the API Gateway circuit breaker. The gateway temporarily falls back to routing requests back to the legacy PHP monolith for write operations, protecting the new microservice infrastructure from cascading failures.

Observability and Distributed Tracing

Tracing requests across a hybrid architecture containing PHP, Java, and Go runtimes requires standardized propagation of W3C Trace Context headers. Every incoming request to the API Gateway generates a traceparent header containing the trace ID and parent span ID. Both legacy applications and modern event-driven services must extract these headers and inject them into outgoing database calls and Kafka message metadata.

Prometheus metrics must track error rates, latency percentiles (p99), and thread pool saturations independently for both legacy and modern components. By comparing these metrics continuously, engineering leadership can quantify the exact performance gains achieved as each domain is successfully migrated off the monolith.

Production Verification Checklist & Operational Runbook: Strangler-Fig Pattern in Practice: Migrating Legacy PHP & Java Monoliths to Event-Driven APIs

Before promoting any Strangler-Fig Pattern in Practice: Migrating Legacy PHP & Java Monoliths to Event-Driven APIs deployment into production traffic, senior platform and SRE teams validate deterministic failure handling, kernel resource ceilings, and observability telemetry across strangler fig pattern api gateway, change data capture debezium kafka, dual-write anti-pattern outbox pattern, zero-downtime schema migration. Unlike lab prototypes, production clusters must survive upstream network partitions, sudden concurrency bursts, and rolling node maintenance without dropping in-flight client transactions.

Pre-Cutover Acceptance Gates

  • Synthetic Load & Tail-Latency Benchmarking: Execute sustained concurrency tests against staging endpoints for Strangler-Fig Pattern in Practice: Migrating Legacy PHP & Java Monoliths to Event-Driven APIs, verifying that p95 and p99 response latencies remain within contractual SLO boundaries under 3x peak projected load.

  • Fault Injection & Chaos Verification: Simulate primary worker termination, AZ link degradation, and storage IOPS saturation to confirm automated failover and circuit-breaker recovery complete within sub-second thresholds.

  • Telemetry & Alert Routing Validation: Confirm Prometheus scrape targets, structured JSON log pipelines, and OpenTelemetry trace propagation emit actionable metrics for strangler-fig-pattern-migrating-legacy-monoliths-event-driven-apis before live traffic cutover.

  • Immutable Rollback Readiness: Verify that declarative GitOps manifests, database migration snapshots, and previous container image digests can restore the prior production state in under 120 seconds.

# Production Readiness Verification Probe (strangler-fig-pattern-migrating-legacy-monoliths-event-driven-apis)
systemctl is-active --quiet prometheus-node-exporter && echo "TELEMETRY_OK"
sysctl net.core.somaxconn net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse vm.swappiness
curl -fsSL -o /dev/null -w "http_code=%{http_code} ttfb=%{time_starttransfer}s
" http://127.0.0.1:8080/healthz

By enforcing these pre-cutover verification gates alongside Sub-50ms p95 API response times under high concurrency, zero-downtime blue-green deployments, and 24/7 observability, engineering teams ensure Strangler-Fig Pattern in Practice: Migrating Legacy PHP & Java Monoliths to Event-Driven APIs operates with predictable throughput, cryptographic isolation, and continuous audit compliance across OWASP Top 10 automated mitigation, OAuth2/OIDC centralized SSO, and encrypted payload transit via TLS 1.3.

title: TensorSSM: Memorizing Spatial Position in Dynamic State Space for Tensor Core Generation
description:
arXiv:2610.40871v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: High-dimensional tensors are ubiquitous in real-world applications but lead to massive storage overhead. Functional tensor decomposition addresses this by employing neural networks to map element coordinates to tensor cores, significantly reducing the parameters for data compression. However, existing functional methods typically flatten high-order tensors into 1D sequences. This folding operation causes highly overlapping local coordinate sequences and struggles to capture complex cross-mode spatial dependencies, severely limiting their expressiveness on diverse datasets. To tackle these challenges, we propose TensorSSM, a novel Implicit Neural Representation (INR) for functional decomposition method that memorizes spatial positions within a dynamic State Space Model (SSM). Specifically, TensorSSM first decomposes mode-wise coordinates into sequences spit by K-ary rule, encoding spatial tokens from coarse to fine, which effectively captures spatial variations. Furthermore, we extend the SSM's state space to explicitly map cross-mode spatial dependencies, allowing inter-mode interactions to enhance the updates of each mode. By integrating cross-mode information from previous hidden states into the current state transitions, TensorSSM effectively expands tensor representation along two dimensions: the sequence dimension for coarse-to-fine spatial tokens, and the state dimension for cross-mode memorization. This design effectively integrates spatial information into the state space and the tensor core, substantially advancing the state adaptability and enhancing the expressiveness of the data compression. Extensive experiments demonstrate that TensorSSM achieves significantly high reconstruction accuracy and storage efficiency, exhibiting robust expressiveness across diverse tensor datasets without relying on strict spatial assumptions.

title: BYOD: Build Your Own DLM - Efficient Autoregressive-to-Diffusion Language Model Conversion
description:
arXiv:2610.41574v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Unlike autoregressive (AR) models, diffusion language models (DLMs) permit parallel token updates, flexible generation, and bidirectional attention, but leading systems rely on costly pretraining or full-model fine-tuning. We present Build Your Own DLM (BYOD), a generalizable LoRA-only recipe for parameter-efficient AR-to-DLM conversion. Without architecture-specific tuning, BYOD induces diffusion generation in Gemma 2 9B, Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen2.5 7B, and Ministral 8B; to our knowledge, this is the first reported AR-to-DLM conversion of a Mistral model. The adapters comprise 4.1-5.8% of final parameters while every base-model parameter remains frozen; each 25,000-iteration conversion needs at most 102.4M tokens, processed in 3.1-4.0 hours on one Google Colab GPU. All four models generate from fully masked sequences, use bidirectional context in a controlled attention test, and retain substantial parent-model knowledge. BYOD-Gemma is the strongest BYOD conversion on our nine-task evaluation, reaching 50.6% average accuracy compared with 51.9% for LLaDA 8B Instruct in the same harness. Open-generation quality at low network function evaluation (NFE) budgets remains the principal limitation: BYOD perplexity is 8.3-11.1 versus 4.1 for LLaDA and 2.2-3.0 for the AR parents when generating 128 tokens in 64 steps. To enable further experimentation and inspection, we provide a standalone training and evaluation implementation and interactive demos for all four conversions. BYOD thus provides a practical route for extending diffusion generation to other existing model families while identifying the gap that efficient conversion must next close.

title: Dissecting the 4-Hop Cloudflare Tunnel Latency Trap & Hybrid Edge Mesh Architecture — Duong Phuc Khanh (Dương Phúc Khánh)
description:
I am Duong Phuc Khanh (Vietnamese: Dương Phúc Khánh, known across the engineering community as khanhdp or Kido, @khanhduong22, born 1995 in Da Nang, Vietnam — verified entity on Google Knowledge Graph /g/11zyg5zq1c, Wikidata Q141718572, ORCID 0009-0005-7192-2664, and featured in Báo Đà Nẵng for winning First Prize at Startup Runway 2018 and Smart Mobile Ordering Innovation).

In an effort to eliminate cloud compute bills, software engineers frequently attempt to repurpose high-core personal workstations or home servers (12–16 physical CPU threads, NVMe SSDs, residential fiber) as production hosts using Cloudflare Tunnel (cloudflared) to bypass ISP Carrier-Grade NAT (CGNAT) and dynamic WAN IPs.

However, as documented across Kido Engineering Blog and Episode 142 of Kido Chronicles, placing consumer hardware behind a standard Cloudflare Tunnel on the synchronous client request path introduces a severe architectural bottleneck: The 4-Hop Submarine Trombone Latency Trap. In this monograph, Duong Phuc Khanh (Dương Phúc Khánh) presents the transport math, WSL2 ext4.vhdx failure modes, and the Tier-1 Hybrid Edge Mesh architecture combining a regional Cloud Caddy Gateway with an encrypted Tailscale WireGuard mesh.

1. Executive Summary & Architectural Comparative Matrix

Because non-enterprise edge tiers terminate ingress tunnels at centralized regional Point-of-Presence (PoP) hubs (Singapore or Hong Kong in Southeast Asia) rather than local domestic exchange nodes, every HTTP request between an in-country user and an in-country home server is forced to traverse international submarine fiber cables twice per round-trip. This inflates Network Time To First Byte (TTFB) from ~28ms to 140ms – 220ms (a 5x–7x degradation).

The matrix below summarizes the three architectural tiers evaluated by Duong Phuc Khanh (Dương Phúc Khánh):

Architectural Tier Routing & Storage Mechanism Architectural Advantages (Pros) Critical Flaws & Failure Modes (Cons) TTFB & Availability SLA Recommendation
Option A: Naive Baseline (Cloudflare Tunnel to Home Server) Outbound QUIC tunnel via cloudflared terminated at regional edge PoPs; Docker on Windows WSL2. Zero router configuration; immune to WAN IP changes; $0 external hosting invoices. 4-Hop Submarine Trombone Loop: TTFB explodes to 140ms–220ms. High risk of ext4.vhdx corruption upon power loss; PPPoE lease resets cause downtime. • TTFB: 140ms – 220ms
• Uptime: 97.0% – 98.5%
• Data Durability: Fragile		 ❌ Premature Cost Optimization (Avoid)
Option B: Residential Router Port Forwarding + Dynamic DNS Direct ingress port 443 on residential router; automated DNS record synchronization upon IP drift. Low domestic latency (~15ms); exploits multi-core workstation CPU for zero extra cost. 1. Periodic PPPoE lease renewals yield 502 Bad Gateway for 30–60s.
2. Blocked behind ISP CGNAT.
3. Zero hardware power or dual-BGP network redundancy.		 • TTFB: 15ms – 30ms
• Uptime: 98.0% – 99.0%
• Operational Risk: High		 ⚠️ Suitable for Ephemeral Staging Only
Option C: Tier-1 Production (Hybrid Edge Mesh: Cloud Gateway + Private Tailscale) • Critical Path Tier: Regional Cloud VPS at Tier-3 Datacenter running Caddy Reverse Proxy on static IPv4 (99.99% SLA).
• Heavy Compute Tier: Residential workstation connected via private Tailscale mesh (100.x.x.x) acting as async CI runner and 3-2-1 cold backup vault.		 • Production workloads remain 100% available at deterministic 28ms TTFB.
• Eliminates idle remote VPS waste.
• Residential workstation offloads CPU-intensive workloads without risking client traffic.
• Zero router port exposure.		 Requires one low-cost regional Cloud VPS instance (~$4.5/mo) acting as entry gateway. • API TTFB: 28ms – 35ms
• Edge Cache HIT: 12ms
• Uptime SLA: 99.99% 		🏆 Tier-1 Production Standard

2. Naive Baseline & The Premature Home Server Illusion

When bootstrapping backends on local hardware, the standard docker-compose.yml pairing cloudflared with an application server and PostgreSQL looks deceptively clean:

# ❌ Naive Baseline: docker-compose.yml running production on a local workstation
version: "3.8"
services:
  cloudflared:
    image: cloudflare/cloudflared:latest
    restart: always
    command: tunnel run --token ${CLOUDFLARE_TUNNEL_TOKEN}
    network_mode: host

  app_server:
    image: enterprise/app:latest
    restart: always
    environment:
      - DATABASE_URL=postgresql://postgres:secret@127.0.0.1:5432/production
      - NODE_ENV=production
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"

  db_postgres:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    restart: always
    volumes:
      - ./pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data # Virtualized onto WSL2 ext4.vhdx
    ports:
      - "5432:5432"

While this avoids router NAT configuration and masks the residential IPv4 address, it violates physical transport locality and storage durability invariants.

3. Scale Bottlenecks & The 4-Hop Trombone Latency Breakdown

3.1. The 4-Hop Submarine Trombone Latency Loop

Cloudflare Tunnel establishes long-lived outbound-only QUIC/HTTP2 connections from cloudflared to regional PoPs (principally Singapore — SIN or Hong Kong — HKG for non-enterprise Southeast Asian routes). Every transactional HTTP request suffers a 4-hop submarine penalty:

  1. Hop 1 (Ingress): A client in Hanoi, Da Nang, or Ho Chi Minh City sends an HTTP request $\rightarrow$ Packet crosses the submarine cable to Cloudflare Singapore (~35ms).
  2. Hop 2 (Tunnel Ingress): Cloudflare Singapore encapsulates the request into the QUIC tunnel and routes it back across the submarine cable to the residential cloudflared daemon in Vietnam (~35ms).
  3. Hop 3 (Tunnel Egress): The local application queries PostgreSQL and sends the HTTP response back through the tunnel to Cloudflare Singapore (~35ms).
  4. Hop 4 (Egress Delivery): Cloudflare Singapore forwards the response back across the submarine cable to the client in Vietnam (~35ms).

The physical wire latency alone is deterministic:
$$\text{Latency}{\text{network}} = T{\text{VN}\rightarrow\text{SIN}} + T_{\text{SIN}\rightarrow\text{Home}} + T_{\text{Home}\rightarrow\text{SIN}} + T_{\text{SIN}\rightarrow\text{VN}} \approx 4 \times 35\text{ms} = 140\text{ms}$$

Adding TLS handshakes and application serialization pushes empirical API TTFB to 160ms – 240ms. By contrast, hosting the application server directly inside a Tier-3 Singapore datacenter cuts the path to a single 2-hop round-trip:
$$\text{Latency}{\text{direct}} = T{\text{VN}\rightarrow\text{SIN}} + T_{\text{SIN}\rightarrow\text{VN}} \approx 2 \times 28\text{ms} = 56\text{ms}$$

3.2. Power Instability and WSL2 Virtual Disk (ext4.vhdx) WAL Corruption

On Windows workstations, Docker executes inside a Hyper-V virtual machine (WSL2) backed by a monolithic virtual disk image (ext4.vhdx):

  • Memory Ballooning (vmmem): WSL2 dynamically claims host RAM during container spikes without promptly releasing freed pages back to the host OS.
  • Unrecoverable WAL Truncation: During sudden residential power loss or forced OS reboots, in-flight PostgreSQL fsync calls flushing Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) segments to ext4.vhdx are severed mid-write, corrupting virtual disk metadata and preventing WSL2 partition mounting on reboot.

3.3. Residential PPPoE WAN Lease Renewals

Residential fiber connections renegotiate PPPoE dynamic IPv4 leases every 24–72 hours, dropping WAN connectivity for 30–90 seconds and causing batch request failures during peak morning traffic windows.

4. Tier-1 Production Architecture: The Asian Hybrid Edge Mesh

To achieve deterministic 28ms TTFB and 99.99% uptime while still harnessing 12–16 local workstation CPU threads, Duong Phuc Khanh (Dương Phúc Khánh) architected the Hybrid Edge Mesh around strict blast-radius isolation:

  1. Critical Path Production Tier (Singapore Datacenter — 99.99% SLA):
    • Runs stateful production workloads: PostgreSQL 19 on native NVMe ext4, Valkey Cache, and Core API handlers.
    • Served via Caddy 2 Reverse Proxy on a static IPv4 address with direct BGP peering (~28ms).
  2. Heavy Compute Worker Tier (Residential Workstation — Private Mesh):
    • Completely decoupled from synchronous user requests.
    • Runs self-hosted GitHub Actions CI runners (3x faster Docker builds across 12 CPU threads), internal staging environments, and 3-2-1 encrypted cold backups.

4.1. Caddy Reverse Proxy & Encrypted Tailscale WireGuard Bridge 

# /etc/caddy/Caddyfile - Cloud VPS Gateway (Singapore) — Duong Phuc Khanh (khanhdp)
{
    email admin@khanhdp.com
    admin off
}

# 1. Production API & Core Services: Directly hosted on Singapore VPS (TTFB ~28ms)
api.example.com {
    reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:4000 {
        header_up Host {host}
        header_up X-Real-IP {remote_host}
    }
}

# 2. Heavy Staging & Operational Backends: Securely proxied via immutable Tailscale IP
staging.example.com {
    # 100.64.0.10: Tailscale mesh node address (RFC 6598) assigned to the residential workstation
    reverse_proxy 100.64.0.10:3000 {
        header_up Host {host}
        header_up X-Real-IP {remote_host}
        transport http {
            dial_timeout 3s
            response_header_timeout 30s
        }
    }
}

# 3. Static Assets: Served directly from high-speed NVMe storage with Edge Cache headers
cdn.example.com {
    root * /var/www/static
    file_server
    encode zstd gzip
    header Cache-Control "public, max-age=31536000, immutable"
}

4.2. Automated Asynchronous 3-2-1 Cold Backup Over Tailscale Mesh 

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# backup_production_to_home.sh — Duong Phuc Khanh (Dương Phúc Khánh · Kido)
set -euo pipefail

BACKUP_DATE=$(date +"%Y-%m-%d_%H%M%S")
REMOTE_HOST="edge-gateway-sgp" # SSH alias resolving over Tailscale private mesh
BACKUP_DIR="/mnt/storage/cold-backups"
ENCRYPTION_KEY_FILE="/etc/backup/encryption.key"

mkdir -p "${BACKUP_DIR}"

echo "🔄 [$(date)] Initiating PostgreSQL production backup from Singapore..."
ssh "${REMOTE_HOST}" "docker exec db_postgres pg_dump -U postgres -d enterprise_prod -Fc" \
  | openssl enc -aes-256-cbc -salt -pbkdf2 -pass "file:${ENCRYPTION_KEY_FILE}" \
  > "${BACKUP_DIR}/prod_${BACKUP_DATE}.dump.enc"

# Retain rolling 30-day snapshot history
find "${BACKUP_DIR}" -type f -name "*.dump.enc" -mtime +30 -delete
echo "✅ [$(date)] Backup completed successfully: prod_${BACKUP_DATE}.dump.enc ($(du -h "${BACKUP_DIR}/prod_${BACKUP_DATE}.dump.enc" | cut -f1))"

5. Empirical Benchmarks & Production Proof (5,000 Concurrent Requests)

title: Saidzoda-Tajik-LFM-2.6B: Adapting a 2.6B Hybrid Model to Tajik Tool Calling, and What Continued Pretraining Takes Away
description:
arXiv:2610.41576v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We release Saidzoda-Tajik-LFM-2.6B, a Tajik adaptation of the 2.6B-parameter hybrid model LFM2.5-2.6B-Base, built for tool calling in Tajik on modest hardware. The recipe has two stages: LoRA continued pretraining (CPT) on 1,485,319 cleaned Tajik web documents for 3 epochs, then one epoch of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on a mix of machine-translated Tajik tool calls, English tool calls kept as replay, and Tajik instructions. On a 174-item tool-calling test set built from BFCL v3 and machine-translated to Tajik, strict full-call accuracy on Tajik prompts rises from 20.69 for the base model to 64.14 (paired difference +43.45 points, 95% interval +35.2 to +51.7); a lenient parser that also accepts the base model's own call formats puts the base at 31.72. English shows no detectable change (76.55 and 77.24). Every CPT checkpoint scores zero: CPT removes the native tool-call format and, as the lenient re-scoring shows, part of the skill itself. Outside tool calling, accuracy on a Tajik knowledge benchmark rises from 28.0 to 35.0, Belebele Tajik shows no significant change, and English MMLU falls from 60.8 to 52.5. The model is not a general Tajik assistant. It almost never declines when no tool fits (6.9% correct on Tajik, against 31.0% for the base under the lenient parser), it is weak at multi-turn calls, and its calls should be checked before they are executed. We describe the data, the training settings and every evaluation in enough detail to repeat them.

title: AutoHebb: Self-Modifying Neural Networks that Zero-Shot Infer and Continually Learn
description:
arXiv:2610.40757v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Humans and animals have a unique capacity to generalize and learn in novel circumstances, including "0-shot" inference (ZI) and continual learning (CL) -- two powerful cognitive abilities. Despite this importance, efforts to model ZI and CL are seriously limited in several ways. First, existing models typically lack components critical to ZI and CL in the brain, namely, strong inductive biases (for ZI) and autonomous control of learning (for CL). Second, models can be less tractable to analysis if model components are overly complex (lacking simplicity), or too task-restricted if model components are overly bespoke (lacking expressivity). Here we introduce autonomous Hebbian networks ("AutoHebb"), a class of online learning feedforward neural networks that realize strong inductive biases and autonomously controlled learning, and are both simple and expressive. Unlike standard models that learn via externally controlled optimization (e.g. gradient descent), AutoHebb networks combine external feedback with internally generated activity to produce a global learning signal ('neuromodulator') fed back to the network. The neuromodulator in turn gates a biologically grounded local learning rule (3-factor Hebbian rule) that updates networks' plastic weights. Using meta-learning to search for fixed (non-plastic) weights, we find that AutoHebb networks (1) succeed on ZI tasks, (2) show emergent (untrained) ZI/CL abilities, (3) admit reverse-engineering into explicit algorithms, and (4) outperform modern learning models on ZI/CL tasks. Lastly, performance comparisons to related models implied an essential role for three model components: meta-learning, Hebbian plasticity, and autonomous control of learning. These findings indicate that AutoHebb may be useful in hypothesis generation, analysis, and discovery of biologically grounded forms of learning and generalization.

title: Your Go Fake Repository Drifts From Postgres. Run One Contract Suite Against Both
description:
• Book: Hexagonal Architecture in Go
  • Also by me: Pocket Guides for Developers — the 8-book series
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

Your checkout tests are green. One of them replays a request the way a flaky mobile client would: same order reference, sent twice. The in-memory repository stores both orders without a word, so the use case's "reference already used" branch never runs and the test passes. In production, Postgres rejects the second insert with SQLSTATE 23505, unique_violation, nothing maps it to a domain error, and the client gets a 500.

Same suite, another test. The order-history endpoint should return the newest order first. The fake appends to a slice, the test happens to insert in the order it asserts, and it passes. The Postgres adapter forgot its ORDER BY, and the Postgres docs are blunt about what that means: without sorting, "the rows will be returned in an unspecified order."

Neither bug is in the fake's code. The fake never agreed to the same rules as the database. Martin Fowler's definition of a fake already warns you: fakes "have working implementations, but usually take some shortcut." The fix he describes for doubles is a contract test, which checks that calls against your double "return the same results as a call to the external service would." In a hexagonal Go service you can do that with one exported function and a single call per adapter.

The port, with its rules written down

The contract starts as prose on the interface. If a rule isn't written here, no adapter can be held to it.

package domain

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "time"
)

var (
    ErrNotFound        = errors.New("order not found")
    ErrDuplicateRef    = errors.New("order ref already used")
    ErrVersionConflict = errors.New("order changed since read")
)

type Order struct {
    ID         string
    Ref        string
    CustomerID string
    Status     string
    CreatedAt  time.Time
    Version    int64
}

// OrderRepository is the port. Every adapter must:
//   - Create: store o with Version 1. ErrDuplicateRef if
//     another order already has o.Ref.
//   - Get: ErrNotFound if no order has that ID.
//   - ListByCustomer: newest CreatedAt first, ties broken
//     by ID in byte order.
//   - Update: write o.Status if the stored Version equals
//     o.Version, then bump it. ErrVersionConflict if not,
//     ErrNotFound if the order does not exist.
type OrderRepository interface {
    Create(ctx context.Context, o Order) error
    Get(ctx context.Context, id string) (Order, error)
    ListByCustomer(
        ctx context.Context, customerID string,
    ) ([]Order, error)
    Update(ctx context.Context, o Order) error
}

The errors live in the domain because they are business facts. "That reference is taken" means something to a checkout use case. SQLSTATE 23505 does not, and it should never cross the port.

One exported function, every adapter

The suite goes in its own package, domain/ordertest, in a normal .go file rather than a _test.go file. go build ignores files that end in _test.go, so nothing declared in one can be imported by another package, and both adapter packages need to call this. Importing testing from a non-test package has a precedent in the Go project itself: nettest.TestConn "tests that a net.Conn implementation properly satisfies the interface," and it takes a constructor the same way.


One set of checks, two implementations. Each door has to open the same way.

The constructor gives each subtest a fresh, empty repository, so subtests never see each other's rows.

package ordertest

import (
    "errors"
    "slices"
    "testing"
    "time"

    "example.com/shop/domain"
)

var t0 = time.Date(2026, 3, 1, 9, 0, 0, 0, time.UTC)

func RunOrderRepoContract(
    t *testing.T,
    newRepo func(t *testing.T) domain.OrderRepository,
) {
    t.Run("missing id", func(t *testing.T) {
        repo := newRepo(t)
        _, err := repo.Get(t.Context(), "nope")
        if !errors.Is(err, domain.ErrNotFound) {
            t.Fatalf("got %v, want ErrNotFound", err)
        }
    })

    t.Run("round trip", func(t *testing.T) {
        repo := newRepo(t)
        mustCreate(t, repo, ord("o-1", "R-1", "c-1", t0))
        got, err := repo.Get(t.Context(), "o-1")
        if err != nil {
            t.Fatal(err)
        }
        if got.Ref != "R-1" || got.Version != 1 ||
            !got.CreatedAt.Equal(t0) {
            t.Fatalf("got %+v", got)
        }
    })

    t.Run("duplicate ref", func(t *testing.T) {
        repo := newRepo(t)
        ctx := t.Context()
        mustCreate(t, repo, ord("o-1", "R-1", "c-1", t0))
        err := repo.Create(ctx, ord("o-2", "R-1", "c-2", t0))
        if !errors.Is(err, domain.ErrDuplicateRef) {
            t.Fatalf("got %v, want ErrDuplicateRef", err)
        }
        _, err = repo.Get(ctx, "o-2")
        if !errors.Is(err, domain.ErrNotFound) {
            t.Fatalf("o-2 was stored anyway: %v", err)
        }
    })

t.Context() needs Go 1.24 or later. Timestamps are compared with Equal, because the time docs note that == "compares not just the time instant but also the Location," and a database adapter is free to hand back the same instant in a different location.

The function continues with the ordering rule:

    t.Run("list order", func(t *testing.T) {
        repo := newRepo(t)
        later := t0.Add(time.Hour)
        mustCreate(t, repo, ord("o-a", "R-1", "c-1", t0))
        mustCreate(t, repo, ord("o-c", "R-2", "c-1", later))
        mustCreate(t, repo, ord("o-B", "R-3", "c-1", t0))
        mustCreate(t, repo, ord("o-x", "R-4", "c-2", later))
        got, err := repo.ListByCustomer(t.Context(), "c-1")
        if err != nil {
            t.Fatal(err)
        }
        var ids []string
        for _, o := range got {
            ids = append(ids, o.ID)
        }
        want := []string{"o-c", "o-B", "o-a"}
        if !slices.Equal(ids, want) {
            t.Fatalf("got %v, want %v", ids, want)
        }
    })

The list order subtest is built to fail a lazy fake. Insertion order is o-a, o-c, o-B, and neither that order nor its reverse matches the expected o-c, o-B, o-a. A fake that returns map iteration order fails too, at least some of the time, since the Go spec says map iteration order "is not specified and is not guaranteed to be the same from one iteration to the next." The uppercase B is there on purpose, and it comes back in the Postgres section.

The last two subtests cover updates, followed by the helpers:

    t.Run("stale version", func(t *testing.T) {
        repo := newRepo(t)
        ctx := t.Context()
        mustCreate(t, repo, ord("o-1", "R-1", "c-1", t0))
        a, err := repo.Get(ctx, "o-1")
        if err != nil {
            t.Fatal(err)
        }
        b := a
        a.Status = "paid"
        if err := repo.Update(ctx, a); err != nil {
            t.Fatal(err)
        }
        b.Status = "cancelled"
        err = repo.Update(ctx, b)
        if !errors.Is(err, domain.ErrVersionConflict) {
            t.Fatalf("got %v, want ErrVersionConflict", err)
        }
        got, err := repo.Get(ctx, "o-1")
        if err != nil {
            t.Fatal(err)
        }
        if got.Status != "paid" || got.Version != 2 {
            t.Fatalf("got %+v", got)
        }
    })

    t.Run("update missing", func(t *testing.T) {
        repo := newRepo(t)
        o := ord("nope", "R-9", "c-1", t0)
        o.Version = 1
        err := repo.Update(t.Context(), o)
        if !errors.Is(err, domain.ErrNotFound) {
            t.Fatalf("got %v, want ErrNotFound", err)
        }
    })
}

func ord(id, ref, cust string, at time.Time) domain.Order {
    return domain.Order{
        ID: id, Ref: ref, CustomerID: cust,
        Status: "pending", CreatedAt: at,
    }
}

func mustCreate(
    t *testing.T, r domain.OrderRepository, o domain.Order,
) {
    t.Helper()
    if err := r.Create(t.Context(), o); err != nil {
        t.Fatalf("create %s: %v", o.ID, err)
    }
}

The stale version subtest is the optimistic-locking rule from an earlier post on version conflicts in a Go repository adapter, folded into the shared suite instead of standing alone.

The fake, held to it

This map-backed fake passes the suite, and it is still small.

package memory

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "slices"
    "strings"
    "sync"

    "example.com/shop/domain"
)

type OrderRepo struct {
    mu    sync.Mutex
    byID  map[string]domain.Order
    byRef map[string]string
}

func NewOrderRepo() *OrderRepo {
    return &OrderRepo{
        byID:  map[string]domain.Order{},
        byRef: map[string]string{},
    }
}

func (r *OrderRepo) Create(
    _ context.Context, o domain.Order,
) error {
    r.mu.Lock()
    defer r.mu.Unlock()
    if _, ok := r.byRef[o.Ref]; ok {
        return domain.ErrDuplicateRef
    }
    if _, ok := r.byID[o.ID]; ok {
        return fmt.Errorf("memory: id %s exists", o.ID)
    }
    o.Version = 1
    r.byID[o.ID] = o
    r.byRef[o.Ref] = o.ID
    return nil
}

func (r *OrderRepo) Get(
    _ context.Context, id string,
) (domain.Order, error) {
    r.mu.Lock()
    defer r.mu.Unlock()
    o, ok := r.byID[id]
    if !ok {
        return domain.Order{}, domain.ErrNotFound
    }
    return o, nil
}

func (r *OrderRepo) ListByCustomer(
    _ context.Context, customerID string,
) ([]domain.Order, error) {
    r.mu.Lock()
    defer r.mu.Unlock()
    var out []domain.Order
    for _, o := range r.byID {
        if o.CustomerID == customerID {
            out = append(out, o)
        }
    }
    slices.SortFunc(out, func(a, b domain.Order) int {
        if c := b.CreatedAt.Compare(a.CreatedAt); c != 0 {
            return c
        }
        return strings.Compare(a.ID, b.ID)
    })
    return out, nil
}

func (r *OrderRepo) Update(
    _ context.Context, o domain.Order,
) error {
    r.mu.Lock()
    defer r.mu.Unlock()
    cur, ok := r.byID[o.ID]
    if !ok {
        return domain.ErrNotFound
    }
    if cur.Version != o.Version {
        return domain.ErrVersionConflict
    }
    cur.Status = o.Status
    cur.Version++
    r.byID[o.ID] = cur
    return nil
}

The byRef index is the fake's version of a unique constraint, and the sort is its version of ORDER BY. Without those two pieces, the duplicate and ordering bugs from the opening are exactly what you would have shipped.

Wiring it to the suite is one call:

package memory_test

import (
    "testing"

    "example.com/shop/adapter/memory"
    "example.com/shop/domain"
    "example.com/shop/domain/ordertest"
)

func TestOrderRepoContract(t *testing.T) {
    ordertest.RunOrderRepoContract(t,
        func(*testing.T) domain.OrderRepository {
            return memory.NewOrderRepo()
        })
}

The pgx adapter, mapping SQLSTATE 23505

The real adapter uses pgx v5. A failed insert carries a *pgconn.PgError with a Code (the SQLSTATE) and a ConstraintName. Checking both matters: a primary-key collision is also 23505, and it is not the same domain fact as a reused reference.

package postgres

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "fmt"

    "github.com/jackc/pgx/v5"
    "github.com/jackc/pgx/v5/pgconn"
    "github.com/jackc/pgx/v5/pgxpool"

    "example.com/shop/domain"
)

const cols = `id, ref, customer_id, status, created_at, version`

type OrderRepo struct{ pool *pgxpool.Pool }

func NewOrderRepo(p *pgxpool.Pool) *OrderRepo {
    return &OrderRepo{pool: p}
}

func (r *OrderRepo) Create(
    ctx context.Context, o domain.Order,
) error {
    _, err := r.pool.Exec(ctx, `
        INSERT INTO orders (`+cols+`)
        VALUES ($1, $2, $3, $4, $5, 1)`,
        o.ID, o.Ref, o.CustomerID, o.Status, o.CreatedAt)
    var pgErr *pgconn.PgError
    if errors.As(err, &pgErr) && pgErr.Code == "23505" &&
        pgErr.ConstraintName == "orders_ref_key" {
        return domain.ErrDuplicateRef
    }
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("create order %s: %w", o.ID, err)
    }
    return nil
}

func (r *OrderRepo) Get(
    ctx context.Context, id string,
) (domain.Order, error) {
    rows, err := r.pool.Query(ctx,
        `SELECT `+cols+` FROM orders WHERE id = $1`, id)
    if err != nil {
        return domain.Order{}, fmt.Errorf("get %s: %w", id, err)
    }
    o, err := pgx.CollectExactlyOneRow(rows, scanOrder)
    if errors.Is(err, pgx.ErrNoRows) {
        return domain.Order{}, domain.ErrNotFound
    }
    if err != nil {
        return domain.Order{}, fmt.Errorf("get %s: %w", id, err)
    }
    return o, nil
}

func (r *OrderRepo) ListByCustomer(
    ctx context.Context, customerID string,
) ([]domain.Order, error) {
    rows, err := r.pool.Query(ctx, `
        SELECT `+cols+` FROM orders
         WHERE customer_id = $1
         ORDER BY created_at DESC, id COLLATE "C"`,
        customerID)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("list %s: %w", customerID, err)
    }
    return pgx.CollectRows(rows, scanOrder)
}

func (r *OrderRepo) Update(
    ctx context.Context, o domain.Order,
) error {
    tag, err := r.pool.Exec(ctx, `
        UPDATE orders SET status = $3, version = version + 1
         WHERE id = $1 AND version = $2`,
        o.ID, o.Version, o.Status)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("update %s: %w", o.ID, err)
    }
    if tag.RowsAffected() == 1 {
        return nil
    }
    if _, err := r.Get(ctx, o.ID); err != nil {
        return err // ErrNotFound, or a real failure
    }
    return domain.ErrVersionConflict
}

func scanOrder(row pgx.CollectableRow) (domain.Order, error) {
    var o domain.Order
    err := row.Scan(&o.ID, &o.Ref, &o.CustomerID,
        &o.Status, &o.CreatedAt, &o.Version)
    return o, err
}

CollectExactlyOneRow returns an error matching pgx.ErrNoRows when the query finds nothing, which is the one place the adapter translates to ErrNotFound. CollectRows closes the rows for you.

Now the uppercase B. The fake breaks ties with strings.Compare, and the Go spec says strings "are compared lexically byte-wise." Postgres sorts text by the column's collation, and a linguistic collation such as en_US.utf8 does not have to put o-B before o-a the way byte order does. The C collation sorts "by byte values rather than natural language order," so COLLATE "C" on the tiebreak makes both adapters agree no matter what the database default is. Drop it, and the list order subtest is where you find out.

Real Postgres, behind a build tag

The integration test starts Postgres with the testcontainers-go Postgres module, runs the schema, and hands the suite a constructor that truncates the table. A //go:build line keeps it out of the default run.


The model and the real engine go on the same gauge. Only one of them needs Docker.

//go:build integration

package postgres_test

import (
    "testing"

    "github.com/jackc/pgx/v5/pgxpool"
    "github.com/testcontainers/testcontainers-go"
    tcpg "github.com/testcontainers/testcontainers-go/modules/postgres"

    "example.com/shop/adapter/postgres"
    "example.com/shop/domain"
    "example.com/shop/domain/ordertest"
)

const schema = `
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id          text        PRIMARY KEY,
  ref         text        NOT NULL,
  customer_id text        NOT NULL,
  status      text        NOT NULL,
  created_at  timestamptz NOT NULL,
  version     bigint      NOT NULL,
  CONSTRAINT orders_ref_key UNIQUE (ref)
)`

func TestOrderRepoContract(t *testing.T) {
    ctx := t.Context()
    ctr, err := tcpg.Run(ctx, "postgres:16-alpine",
        tcpg.WithDatabase("shop"),
        tcpg.WithUsername("shop"),
        tcpg.WithPassword("shop"),
        tcpg.BasicWaitStrategies(),
    )
    testcontainers.CleanupContainer(t, ctr)
    if err != nil {
        t.Fatal(err)
    }
    dsn, err := ctr.ConnectionString(ctx, "sslmode=disable")
    if err != nil {
        t.Fatal(err)
    }
    pool, err := pgxpool.New(ctx, dsn)
    if err != nil {
        t.Fatal(err)
    }
    t.Cleanup(pool.Close)
    if _, err := pool.Exec(ctx, schema); err != nil {
        t.Fatal(err)
    }

    ordertest.RunOrderRepoContract(t,
        func(t *testing.T) domain.OrderRepository {
            _, err := pool.Exec(t.Context(), "TRUNCATE orders")
            if err != nil {
                t.Fatal(err)
            }
            return postgres.NewOrderRepo(pool)
        })
}

CleanupContainer goes before the error check because its docs say a nil container is a no-op, so a half-started container still gets removed. The module page also says it supplies no default wait strategy, which is why BasicWaitStrategies() is there. One container serves all six subtests, and TRUNCATE gives each one an empty table, which keeps the run to a single container start.

The constraint is named explicitly, orders_ref_key, because the adapter matches on that name. In a real service, replace the inline schema with your migration runner, so the test checks the constraint names your migrations actually create.

Two commands now cover both worlds:

go test -race ./...                    # fake only, no Docker
go test -race -tags integration ./...  # fake and Postgres

What the suite catches next

The suite only knows the rules you gave it, and Postgres has more. Two worth adding as subtests before they bite:

Timestamp precision. Go's time.Time holds nanoseconds, and Postgres timestamptz resolution is 1 microsecond. The suite uses whole-second timestamps, so it can't see this. A subtest that creates an order with time.Now() and compares CreatedAt after a round trip will pass on the fake and, whenever the clock reading has sub-microsecond digits, fail on Postgres. Decide in the port whether the repository truncates, then make the fake do the same.

Empty results. The two adapters in this post already disagree here. The fake above returns a nil slice for a customer with no orders. The pgx adapter does not: CollectRows is return AppendRows([]T{}, rows, fn), so it starts from an empty, non-nil slice. Marshal both and the encoding/json docs say "a nil slice encodes as the null JSON value," so one adapter gives the client null and the other [], and the suite as written passes both. Add a subtest that pins the shape, or normalise it in the handler.

When a third adapter shows up (a read-through cache wrapping the Postgres repo, a SQLite build for a CLI), its test is one RunOrderRepoContract call with a different constructor. If it disagrees with the other two, the suite names the rule.

If this was useful

A contract suite only works if the port says what the rules are and database errors stay in the adapter. Hexagonal Architecture in Go is the book I wrote about that layer: where repositories, adapters and their tests sit in a Go service, and how to test both sides of a port without a pile of mocks. It is part of the Thinking in Go series, with a companion book on the language itself.

title: CAP: Learning to Optimize from Sparse Observations of Related Tasks
description:
arXiv:2610.41173v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In experiment-driven black-box optimization, each evaluation can consume materials, equipment time, and other resources, limiting the number of experiments available for a new task. Records from completed related optimization campaigns could help, but learning a sequential query policy remains challenging when task-specific experience consists of only a few sparse histories. We propose CAP (Candidate Acquisition Policy), which models shared structure and task-specific variation in fixed historical records to sample interactive practice functions. On these functions, CAP learns a feedback-conditioned query policy aimed at final optimization performance under a fixed evaluation budget. At deployment, its parameters remain fixed while each new observation informs the next query. Across five synthetic task families spanning 6 and 20 dimensions and two engineering simulation benchmarks, BOPTEST and SU2, CAP attains the lowest median final-budget value among the reported methods on four synthetic families and both engineering benchmarks. These results indicate that sparse records from completed related tasks can support adaptive query decisions on new tasks, making more effective use of limited, costly experimental evaluations.

title: STAR-FER: Adaptive Selective Restoration for Edge-Based Low-Resolution Facial Expression Recognition
description:
arXiv:2610.41310v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Variable interaction distances continuously degrade facial resolution in edge-based affective interaction, making low-resolution facial expression recognition (FER) difficult under limited computation. Full-face image or feature restoration incurs substantial overhead, whereas lightweight recognition pipelines may miss local cues that remain discriminative after degradation. We propose STAR-FER, a scale-and-task-adaptive selective restoration framework that balances recognition performance and resource constraints. A lightweight image-scale conditioned Gate jointly predicts a pixel-wise spatial ranking and a continuous restoration budget, then applies exact-support projection to obtain an input-dependent free-form mask. The mask-conditioned restorer retains complete facial context while concentrating sparse restoration and residual insertion on the selected support. Across seven degradation scales from x2 to x8 on the complete RAF-DB test set, STAR-FER achieves 80.92% mean accuracy and 71.64% Macro-F1, improving the low-resolution ResNet-18 baseline by 2.25 and 2.71 percentage points, respectively. It surpasses SR-FER by 1.04 accuracy points while requiring 8.84 GFLOPs, a 54.29% reduction, with 28.01% mean mask coverage, and maintains effective recognition at unseen non-integer scales. These results show that spatial-ranking and continuous-budget driven selective restoration reduces spatial modification and computation while maintaining low-resolution FER performance, offering an efficient path to resource-constrained affective interaction.
