title: Node.js Version Mismatches: What Happens When You Run Node 24 Code on Node 20?
description:
Short answer: Running Node 24 code on Node 20 will trigger an advisory warning during npm install, but the installation will succeed by default because package managers treat engine rules as non-blocking suggestions; however, your application will likely crash at runtime due to missing APIs, newer V8 syntax, or incompatible native C++ binary addons.

Imagine you clone a fresh repository from GitHub on a Friday afternoon, run npm install, watch the terminal scroll through hundreds of packages, and see a clean exit code. You type the command to start your local dev server, and immediately your terminal explodes with cryptic syntax errors and missing module crashes. You check your terminal and realize you are running Node.js version 20, but the project requires Node.js version 24.

To understand why this happens and how to prevent it, we need to examine what Node.js actually does, why it is indispensable for modern web development, and how package managers handle version rules behind the scenes.

What is Node.js, and Why Is It Required for Web Development?

To understand why runtime versions matter, we need to clarify what Node.js actually is. A common point of confusion for developers new to the ecosystem is determining whether Node.js is a frontend technology, a backend framework, or something else entirely.

Node.js is an open-source, cross-platform JavaScript runtime environment built on Chrome's V8 engine Node.js Official Documentation. In simple terms, it is a software engine that allows you to execute JavaScript code outside a web browser.

While browser JavaScript runs inside your user's web browser to render interactive user interfaces, Node.js runs on your local machine or a remote server. It plays two distinct roles in modern web development:

  • Backend Server Execution: Node.js powers server-side applications, handling HTTP requests, connecting to databases, and executing business logic for web APIs.
  • Frontend Build Tooling: Even if your application is a purely client-side React or Vue app, modern web development relies heavily on build tools like Vite, Webpack, Babel, and Tailwind CSS. All of these build tools run locally inside Node.js to compile, bundle, and optimize your code before it ever reaches a browser WebClues Technical Analysis.

Because Node.js compiles and executes code using specific V8 engine versions and internal C++ APIs, your local runtime environment must align with what your project expects.

What Happens When You Clone a Project and Use the Wrong Node Version?

Suppose you clone a repository from GitHub that specifies Node.js version 24 in its package.json file, but your local machine is currently running Node.js version 20.

When you run npm install, two distinct things happen:

1. The Installation Succeeds with Warnings

By default, the engines field inside a project's package.json file is purely advisory Safeguard Security Technical Analysis. When npm notices that your local Node 20 runtime does not match the project requirement of Node 24, it prints an advisory warning to your terminal, usually reading something like npm WARN EBADENGINE.

However, npm does not block the installation. It downloads and links the packages anyway, exiting with a success code. This gives developers a false sense of security, making it look like everything is ready to run.

2. The Application Fails at Runtime or Build Time

Even though npm install finished successfully, your application will likely crash when you try to run it. Mismatched Node versions introduce two primary failure modes:

  • Syntax and API Errors: Node 24 introduces newer ECMAScript features, updated V8 engine optimizations, and native built-in APIs that do not exist in Node 20. When your code or its dependencies attempt to invoke these newer APIs on Node 20, the runtime throws fatal TypeError or SyntaxError exceptions.
  • Native C++ Module ABI Crashes: Many popular packages (such as sharp for image processing or bcrypt for password hashing) include compiled C++ binary code Tidra AI Migration Audit. These binary modules are compiled against a specific Application Binary Interface (ABI) version tied to your Node runtime. If a module was compiled for Node 24 and you attempt to execute it on Node 20, your app crashes immediately with an error stating that the module was compiled against a different Node.js version.

Furthermore, Node.js 20 reached its official End of Life on April 30, 2026 Node.js Official Release Schedule. Running an unsupported, unpatched runtime on modern projects introduces serious security vulnerabilities alongside architectural incompatibility.

How to Enforce Runtime Consistency Across Your Team

Relying on developers to manually check their Node version before running npm install leads to wasted hours and inconsistent environments. You can automate version safety using three simple configuration files.


text
                        [ New / Existing Node Project ]
                                       │
                  1. Declare Target Node Version in package.json
                     "engines": { "node": ">=24.0.0" }
                                       │
                  2. Enforce Strict Installation in .npmrc
                     Set `engine-strict=true` (forces npm install to fail on mismatch)
                                       │
                  3. Pin Local Runtime Environment via .nvmrc
                     Write "24.22.1" to .nvmrc in project root
                                       │
                  4. Align CI/CD & Production Environment
                     Use `actions/setup-node` with `node-version-file: '.nvmrc'`

title: FieldGuideRAG: Image-Grounded GraphRAG for Fine-Grained Recognition with Vision-Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.40971v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present FieldGuideRAG, a training-free GraphRAG method in which a vision-language model, or VLM, recognizes fine-grained species by comparing the query with real photographs stored on the nodes of a knowledge graph. Multimodal GraphRAG systems describe each entity in text, and text conveys little of the visual detail that separates look-alike species. Our graph stores one photograph on every species node and links each species to its relatives, its geographic range and its ecological facts. A frozen VLM verifies the query against the photograph of each candidate node. FieldGuideRAG fuses the verification scores with the range edge and answers questions about the organism from the fact edges of the verified species. On CUB-200, a Wikidata graph and four iNaturalist domains, the node photograph improves verification over the species name on every graph, while text descriptions add little. Verification of the candidate pool exceeds a SigLIP retriever by up to 16 points, the range edge adds 7 to 19 points on iNaturalist, and answering from fact edges is correct on up to 89.5% of 28,820 ecological questions. The verification scores also detect queries whose species is missing from the graph. Graphs, prompts and code will be released.

title: VariaFlow: Uncertainty-Aware Flow Matching for Unsupervised Anomaly Detection
description:
arXiv:2610.41494v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reconstruction-based anomaly detection no longer fails at reconstruction. Generative models produce high-quality pseudo-healthy reconstructions, and the remaining difficulty is the step of scoring residuals. The residual between a scan and its reconstruction has two indistinguishable sources, genuine pathology and the anatomical variation that separates one healthy brain from another. Scoring against a single reconstruction treats both as anomalous, inflating false positives where healthy anatomy varies most while small or subtle lesions are lost in the surrounding reconstruction error. We identify the missing quantity as the predictive variance, how much a healthy reconstruction can vary at each location. We introduce VariaFlow, which estimates this variance from an ensemble of mask-guided restorations under an unconditional flow matching prior, each started from a different noise initialization, and which normalizes the residual by the resulting standard deviation. Few-step flow matching keeps the ensemble computationally affordable, and restoring at two spatial scales captures lesions of different size. Across three brain MRI datasets spanning stroke and tumor, VariaFlow is trained once on healthy anatomy and generalizes across all three, attaining the highest AUROC (0.94, 0.80, 0.78) on each and the highest AUPRC on both cross-domain datasets, exceeding the strongest baseline by 37% and 50%. Under domain shift, the same baseline drops by up to 52% in AUPRC, whereas VariaFlow stays more stable and achieves the best small-lesion Dice on all three datasets.

title: API Key bị lộ trên trình duyệt? Kiểm tra key OpenAI, Claude hoặc Gemini trong 2 phút
description:
Nếu ứng dụng web của bạn gọi OpenAI, Claude hay Gemini trực tiếp từ trình duyệt, khóa API của bạn bị lộ trong trình duyệt, và bất kỳ ai mở DevTools đều có thể sao chép nó. Bạn có thể xác nhận điều này trong 2 phút: mở tab Network, gửi một yêu cầu AI, và tìm header Authorization, x-api-key hoặc x-goog-api-key gửi đến nhà cung cấp. Nếu bạn thấy khóa của mình ở đó, hãy xoay vòng nó ngay hôm nay và chuyển lệnh gọi ra sau một route phía máy chủ.

Dùng thử Apidog ngay hôm nay

Dưới đây: cách kiểm tra, thứ tự khắc phục, và cách coding agent của bạn có thể kiểm thử route đã sửa.

Tại sao khóa API bị lộ trong trình duyệt lại là vấn đề

Một khóa API bị lộ trong trình duyệt là một bí mật được vận chuyển bên trong mã frontend hoặc lưu lượng mạng của bạn, nơi mọi khách truy cập đều có thể đọc được. Nếu trình duyệt gửi khóa, người dùng có thể sao chép nó và gọi nhà cung cấp tính vào hóa đơn của bạn.

Hướng dẫn về khóa API Gemini của Google nói rằng "Không hardcode khóa API trực tiếp trong ứng dụng web hoặc di động" vì "Khóa được biên dịch trong mã phía client có thể bị người dùng trích xuất," và khuyên bạn nên "chạy một máy chủ proxy backend để thực hiện các lệnh gọi API thực tế." Hướng dẫn an toàn khóa API của OpenAI cũng đưa ra quy tắc tương tự: định tuyến các yêu cầu qua backend của riêng bạn thay vì triển khai khóa đến client.

README của openai-node nói rằng hỗ trợ trình duyệt bị tắt theo mặc định "để tránh làm lộ thông tin xác thực API bí mật của bạn," và bạn phải đặt dangerouslyAllowBrowser: true để bật nó lên. SDK TypeScript của Anthropic dùng cùng tên tùy chọn, và API của nó chỉ chấp nhận các lệnh gọi trình duyệt (CORS) khi yêu cầu mang header anthropic-dangerous-direct-browser-access: true, như Simon Willison đã ghi lại khi nó ra mắt.

Mô hình này phổ biến trong các ứng dụng được xây dựng nhanh bằng AI app builder và coding agent: con đường hoạt động ngắn nhất là một fetch từ component React với khóa nằm trong biến VITE_ hoặc NEXT_PUBLIC_. Các khóa bị đánh cắp sau đó được bán lại để suy luận hàng loạt, như đã đề cập trong bài viết của chúng tôi về khóa AI API bị đánh cắp và LLMjacking, và hóa đơn của bạn là nơi bạn nhận ra điều đó.

Cách kiểm tra khóa API của bạn có bị lộ không (2 phút)

Hãy chạy các kiểm tra này trên môi trường production, không phải localhost.

  1. Quan sát tab Network (45 giây). Mở trang web của bạn, nhấn F12 (Cmd+Option+I trên Mac), chọn tab Network và kích hoạt một tính năng AI, chẳng hạn gửi một tin nhắn chat. Lọc theo openai, anthropic hoặc googleapis. Nếu có bất kỳ yêu cầu nào đi thẳng đến api.openai.com, api.anthropic.com hoặc generativelanguage.googleapis.com, hãy nhấp vào nó và mở Headers. Một khóa trong [REDACTED CREDENTIAL],x-api-key,x-goog-api-keyhoặc tham số truy vấn?key=` nghĩa là nó đã bị lộ.
  2. Tìm kiếm trong bundle (45 giây). Trong DevTools, nhấn Cmd+Option+F (Ctrl+Shift+F trên Windows) để tìm kiếm tất cả các script đã tải. Tìm sk-, sk-ant-, AIza và dangerouslyAllowBrowser. Bất kỳ kết quả nào trong tệp .js được phục vụ cho trình duyệt đều là rò rỉ, ngay cả khi chưa có yêu cầu nào được gửi đi.
  3. Kiểm tra tiền tố biến môi trường của bạn (30 giây). Mở tệp .env và bảng điều khiển hosting của bạn. Các công cụ build sao chép một số biến vào bundle client theo thiết kế: VITE_* trong Vite (xem tài liệu về env của Vite), NEXT_PUBLIC_* trong Next.js, REACT_APP_* trong Create React App và EXPO_PUBLIC_* trong Expo. Một khóa nhà cung cấp nằm sau bất kỳ tiền tố nào trong số này đều là công khai, bất kể nó được đặt tên như thế nào.

Để quét đầu ra build bằng terminal:

`bash

from your project root after a production build

grep -rnoE "sk-(proj-|ant-)?[A-Za-z0-9_-]{20,}|AIza[0-9A-Za-z_-]{35}" dist/ build/ .next/static/ 2>/dev/null
grep -rn "dangerouslyAllowBrowser" dist/ build/ .next/static/ 2>/dev/null
`

Không có kết quả nghĩa là đạt. Google cho biết các khóa AI Studio mới được tạo từ ngày 28 tháng 5 năm 2026 là "auth key," có định dạng có thể khác với AIza, vì vậy hãy tìm cả generativelanguage.googleapis.com trong bundle. Bạn chỉ đạt khi trình duyệt chỉ giao tiếp với tên miền của riêng bạn (ví dụ /api/chat) và không có hostname nhà cung cấp hay khóa nào xuất hiện ở bất kỳ đâu.

Phải làm gì khi khóa của bạn bị lộ: thứ tự khắc phục

Xoay vòng trước sẽ đóng lỗ hổng của ngày hôm nay; thay đổi kiến trúc sẽ đóng nó vĩnh viễn.

Bước Bạn làm gì Tại sao theo thứ tự này Thời gian
1. Xoay vòng khóa Tạo khóa mới trong bảng điều khiển nhà cung cấp, sau đó thu hồi khóa bị lộ Khóa cũ có thể đã bị sao chép; thu hồi là cách duy nhất để ngăn việc sử dụng nó 5 phút
2. Chuyển lệnh gọi sang phía máy chủ Đặt lệnh gọi nhà cung cấp trong một route máy chủ hoặc edge function giữ khóa Ngăn khóa mới bị lộ theo cùng cách 30 đến 60 phút
3. Thêm xác thực và giới hạn tốc độ theo người dùng Yêu cầu phiên đăng nhập trên route và giới hạn số yêu cầu mỗi người dùng Nếu không có điều này, proxy của bạn trở thành endpoint AI miễn phí cho bất kỳ ai 30 phút
4. Đặt giới hạn chi tiêu của nhà cung cấp Đặt ngân sách hoặc giới hạn chi tiêu trong cài đặt thanh toán của mỗi nhà cung cấp Giới hạn hóa đơn trong trường hợp xấu nhất nếu có thứ khác bị lộ 10 phút
5. Quét trong CI Làm build thất bại nếu một mẫu khóa xuất hiện trong bundle đầu ra Ngăn tính năng tiếp theo do agent viết hoàn tác bản sửa 15 phút

Triển khai khóa mới ở phía máy chủ trước khi bạn thu hồi khóa cũ, nếu không tính năng AI của bạn sẽ ngừng hoạt động. Hướng dẫn của chúng tôi về thực hành tốt nhất khi xoay vòng khóa API đề cập đến việc xoay vòng không gián đoạn. Ở bước 4, hướng dẫn an toàn khóa của OpenAI khuyến nghị giới hạn chi tiêu với thực thi cứng, vì cảnh báo đơn thuần không ngăn được lưu lượng; ngân sách thanh toán của Google Cloud chỉ cảnh báo bạn chứ tự nó không ngăn việc sử dụng.

Cách chuyển các lệnh gọi OpenAI, Claude và Gemini ra sau một route máy chủ

Một route proxy backend là một endpoint máy chủ nhỏ nhận prompt của người dùng, thêm khóa API ở phía máy chủ, gọi nhà cung cấp và chỉ trả về câu trả lời. Trình duyệt không bao giờ thấy khóa. Đây là một route Next.js tối giản cho OpenAI; Claude và Gemini cũng theo hình mẫu tương tự:

`ts
// app/api/chat/route.ts (runs on the server only)
import OpenAI from "openai";
import { getSession } from "@/lib/auth"; // your auth helper
import { checkRateLimit } from "@/lib/limits"; // your per-user limiter

const client = new OpenAI({ [REDACTED CREDENTIAL] }); // no NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix

export async function POST(req: Request) {
const session = await getSession(req);
if (!session) return new Response("Unauthorized", { status: 401 });

if (!(await checkRateLimit(session.userId, 20))) { // 20 requests per minute
return new Response("Too many requests", { status: 429 });
}

const { message } = await req.json();
if (typeof message !== "string" || message.length > 4000) {
return new Response("Bad request", { status: 400 });
}

const response = await client.responses.create({
model: process.env.OPENAI_MODEL!, // pin the model server-side
input: message,
});

return Response.json({ reply: response.output_text }); // return the answer, nothing else
}
`

Điều làm cho nó an toàn, chứ không chỉ bị ẩn:

  • Model nằm trên máy chủ. Nếu trình duyệt chọn model, kẻ tấn công sẽ chọn cái đắt nhất.
  • Đầu vào được giới hạn. Không có prompt khổng lồ đi qua tài khoản của bạn.
  • Chỉ câu trả lời được trả về. Không bao giờ trả về phản hồi thô của nhà cung cấp hay đối tượng lỗi.
  • Không có tiền tố công khai. OPENAI_API_KEY ở lại phía máy chủ; NEXT_PUBLIC_OPENAI_API_KEY sẽ được gửi đến mọi khách truy cập.

Đối với Claude và Gemini, hãy dùng SDK của chúng với ANTHROPIC_API_KEY hoặc GEMINI_API_KEY. Các hạn chế về website và IP của Google có ích, nhưng bất kỳ ai với curl đều có thể gửi bất kỳ header Referer nào, vì vậy hãy coi chúng là một lớp bảo vệ thứ hai. Trường hợp hợp lý duy nhất cho lệnh gọi từ trình duyệt là công cụ mang khóa riêng (bring-your-own-key) nơi mỗi người dùng tự dán khóa của họ.

Để coding agent của bạn kiểm thử route proxy bằng Apidog CLI

Di chuyển khóa chỉ là một nửa công việc; nửa còn lại là chứng minh nó vẫn được giữ nguyên sau tính năng tiếp theo mà agent của bạn viết. Hãy để agent đã xây dựng route kiểm thử nó bằng Apidog CLI. Thiết lập một lần:

bash
npm install -g apidog-cli@latest
apidog login --with-token <YOUR_TOKEN>
npx -y skills add https://apidog.com # pick your agent when prompted

Sau đó đưa cho Claude Code, Codex, Cursor hoặc bất kỳ agent nào bạn dùng một [REDACTED PROMPT]
Create Apidog test cases in project for POST /api/chat on our staging
environment that assert:

  1. a request without a session cookie returns 401,
  2. a valid request returns 200 and the body does not contain "sk-", "sk-ant-", "AIza" or "api_key",
  3. the 21st request inside 60 seconds from the same user returns 429. Run them and summarize any failures. `shell

Agent đọc schema, xác thực payload của nó, viết các test case và chạy chúng:

`bash
apidog test-case category --project <id>
apidog cli-schema get test-case-create
apidog cli-schema validate test-case-create --file case.json
apidog test-case create --project <id> --file case.json
apidog run --test-case <caseId> --project <id> -e <envId> -r cli,json
`

Khẳng định thứ hai là cái quan trọng nhất: nó thất bại ngay khi một đối tượng lỗi nhà cung cấp hoặc trường gỡ lỗi bắt đầu phản hồi khóa của bạn về phía client. Hãy đặt cùng bước apidog run ... -r junit vào pipeline của bạn để mỗi lần triển khai đều kiểm tra lại nó; hướng dẫn Apidog CLI CI/CD của chúng tôi trình bày cách thiết lập, và Apidog CLI trong Claude Code đề cập đến phía agent. Gói Miễn phí của Apidog hỗ trợ tối đa 4 người dùng, nên một nhóm nhỏ có thể chạy điều này mà không cần ghế trả phí.

Về phía repo của cùng vấn đề, các khóa được commit vào Git thay vì gửi đến trình duyệt, hãy xem bài viết của chúng tôi về kiểm tra rò rỉ khóa API bằng secret scanner. Nếu agent của bạn gọi các công cụ xử lý dữ liệu khách hàng, kiểm thử AI agent về rò rỉ dữ liệu đề cập đến lớp tiếp theo.

Những sai lầm phổ biến khiến khóa vẫn bị lộ

  • Mã hóa Base64 hoặc chia nhỏ khóa. Trình duyệt phải dựng lại nó để gửi đi, nên DevTools sẽ hiển thị giá trị thật.
  • Chuyển nó vào localStorage hoặc cookie. Nó vẫn ở trên client.
  • Proxy mà không có xác thực. Một /api/chat công khai là endpoint AI mở tính vào hóa đơn của bạn.
  • Giữ khóa cũ "để phòng hờ." Một khóa đã công khai trong một ngày là đã bị sao chép.
  • Quên ứng dụng di động. Hướng dẫn của Google nhắc đến "ứng dụng web hoặc di động" cùng nhau là có lý do.

FAQ

Làm sao tôi biết khóa API OpenAI của mình có bị lộ trong trình duyệt không? Kích hoạt một tính năng AI với tab Network của DevTools đang mở. Một yêu cầu đến api.openai.com với header Authorization: Bearer [REDACTED]-... nghĩa là nó đã bị lộ. Đồng thời tìm sk- và dangerouslyAllowBrowser trong các script đã tải.

Có an toàn không khi đặt khóa API trong biến môi trường NEXT_PUBLIC_ hoặc VITE_? Không. Những tiền tố đó tồn tại để sao chép giá trị vào bundle client. Bất kỳ khóa nhà cung cấp nào được lưu dưới chúng đều được gửi đến mọi khách truy cập. Hãy dùng biến chỉ dành cho máy chủ không có tiền tố và đọc nó bên trong một route máy chủ.

Việc giới hạn khóa API Gemini cho website của tôi có làm nó an toàn trong trình duyệt không? Nó có ích, nhưng một script bên ngoài trình duyệt có thể gửi bất kỳ header Referer nào. Chính hướng dẫn của Google khuyến nghị dùng proxy backend cho các ứng dụng client.

Tôi phát hiện khóa của mình bị lộ. Tôi nên làm gì trước? Tạo khóa mới, triển khai nó ở phía máy chủ, sau đó thu hồi khóa cũ. Tiếp theo, chuyển lệnh gọi ra sau một route có xác thực với giới hạn tốc độ theo người dùng, và đặt giới hạn chi tiêu của nhà cung cấp.

Coding agent của tôi có thể sửa và kiểm thử điều này cho tôi không? Có. Yêu cầu nó chuyển lệnh gọi nhà cung cấp vào một route máy chủ, sau đó dùng Apidog CLI để tạo và chạy các kiểm thử khẳng định trả về 401 khi không có phiên, không có mẫu khóa trong phản hồi, và 429 khi vượt giới hạn tốc độ của bạn.

title: Create custom monitors in Vercel Observability
description:
You can now create custom monitors to get alerts based on your Vercel Observability query results.

For example, you can track signals such as AI Gateway costs, Core Web Vitals and other performance metrics, Workflow and external API failure rates, or Vercel Sandbox CPU time.

Each monitor tracks a single metric, such as response time, or a ratio of two metrics, such as errors divided by total requests. Choose statistical anomaly detection or a fixed threshold, then configure the detection window, filters, and grouping.

To create a monitor, inspect a chart’s query in Observability, start from a preset, or open Settings > Alerts for your team.

You can also define a custom monitor in a JSON file and create it with vercel monitors add in the Vercel CLI. Run vercel monitors schema --type custom for the schema and examples.

Receive alerts through email, Slack, Vercel Inbox, push notifications, or team-level webhooks. You can also add context for Vercel Agent to use when investigating an alert.

Custom monitors are available on Pro and Enterprise plans with Observability Plus, at $0.0035 per GB of data scanned. Built-in alerts remain included with Observability Plus.

Create a custom monitor or learn more in the configuration documentation.

title: Sightlines issue no.2: What leaders need to know about building agents
description: Agentic products pose a unique set of design challenges. How do you build a tool that’s powerful and knowledgeable enough to be a true partner, while keeping trust and security at the core? Here’s what we’ve heard from leaders.

title: October 02, 2026
description:
Apigee X

Announcement

On October 2, 2026, we released an updated version of Apigee (1-18-0-apigee-6).

Note: Rollouts of this release began today and can take four or more business days to complete across all Google Cloud zones. Your instances might not have the features and fixes available until the rollout is complete.

Security

Bug ID Description
564386425 Security fix for Apigee. Upgraded the Apigee ingress gateway (ASM) to patch security vulnerabilities.
561666530 Security fix for Apigee. Upgraded the Prometheus library to patch the following vulnerabilities:

  • CVE-2026-42151
  • CVE-2026-42154
  • CVE-2026-44903
  • CVE-2026-40179
N/A Security fix for Apigee infrastructure.

Fixed

Bug ID Description
432315283 Fixed a multi-certificate truststore so that its trust anchors take effect without a Message Processor restart when features.truststore.multi_cert_bundle.enabled is toggled at runtime; the outbound SSL context is now rebuilt automatically on any trust-anchor change.
565072374 VerifyJWT policies that use a JWKS uriRef no longer return steps.jwt.NoMatchingPublicKey on the first request after the JWKS cache TTL expires when the identity provider has rotated to a new key ID. The cache now re-fetches synchronously when its entry expires.
535395491 Extension Processor (ext_proc) denials now return the status and body that the policy or FaultRule produced, instead of always returning HTTP 500.
558421499 Apigee runtime runs on JRE 21.
517953321 The lookupcache.<n>.isEncrypted and responsecache.<n>.isEncrypted flow variables now report the per-entry on-disk encryption state of the L2 cache, rather than approximating whether the cache-encryption key is loaded. L1 cache hits report false. Review any policy conditions that rely on these flow variables.
563557547 Fixed EventFlow (Server-Sent Events) coalescing multiple events into a single policy invocation under burst load on the http-adaptor data path, which produced malformed SSE output to the client.
562740573 Apigee Analytics now populates the processing_mode dimension, distinguishing proxy traffic from extension-processor traffic. This dimension is not populated in billing-only analytics mode.
357042873 Stopped redirecting apigee-cassandra-schema-readiness init container logs to /dev/null, improving troubleshooting. Workloads undergo a rolling restart upon upgrade.
564969400 Fixed an issue where variables initialized from an empty <Value/> element in AssignMessage (AssignVariable) were not treated as empty strings when referenced in message template functions such as replaceAll.
N/A Updates to infrastructure and libraries.

Assured Workloads

Feature

The Data Boundary for Impact Level 5 (IL5) supports the following products:

  • Google Security Operations SIEM

Feature

The Data Boundary for Impact Level 4 (IL4) supports the following products:

  • Google Security Operations SIEM

BigQuery

Feature

The Rust SDK for BigQuery is now generally available (GA).

Feature

The Data Engineering Agent now supports the gemini-3.7-flash model for the us, eu, and global multi-regional endpoints.

Cloud NAT

Feature

General Availability: Cloud NAT gateways for Private NAT support IPv6 to IPv4 network address translation. For more information, see NAT64 in Private NAT.

Cluster Toolkit

Feature

Cluster Toolkit v1.105.0 is available. This release adds support for Slurm on Cloud TPU 7x and optional support for managed instance groups (MIGs) on static compute nodes that use A4X machine types.

This release also adds storage profiles and volume attributes for Cloud Storage FUSE in job submissions, and unifies Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) blueprints for GPU and Cloud TPU workloads to support dynamic consumption options.

Additionally, this release adds the repository_name variable to override repository names and fixes the output for the registry URL in the Artifact Registry module.

This update also introduces the pre-existing-project community module and resolves an HTTP 400 error when Slurm checks the deletion status of virtual machines (VMs).

For more information, see the release announcement on GitHub.

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Federated query mode for Data Cloud connectors and Knowledge Catalog integration (Preview)

Federated query mode is available in Preview for the following connectors:

  • AlloyDB for PostgreSQL
  • BigQuery
  • Cloud SQL
  • Spanner

Federated query mode allows Gemini Enterprise to query your operational and analytical data in place using the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and each user's own credentials, without copying or ingesting data into a data store.

In addition, the Knowledge Catalog integration is available in Preview. When you attach a Data Cloud connector in federated query mode, Knowledge Catalog is automatically enabled on the Assistant tab of your app to give the assistant read-only tools to search for data that the user has access to and retrieve technical and business context.

For more information, see the following resources:

  • Connect to Data Cloud
  • Best practices for Data Cloud connectors
  • Secure Data Cloud connectors

Google Cloud Contact Center as a Service

Announcement

Google Cloud CCaaS 6.17

We've released version 6.17 of Google Cloud CCaaS.

The timing of the update to your instance depends on the deployment schedule that you have chosen. For more information, see Deployment schedules.

Feature

Warm transfers auto-resume

When an agent performs a warm transfer, the caller is now automatically taken off hold as soon as the transferring agent leaves the call, establishing two-way audio between the receiving agent and the caller without manual action. The caller stays on hold during the consultation between agents so that their conversation remains private. This applies to warm transfers routed through a queue and warm transfers sent directly to a specific agent. This change eliminates the silence that previously occurred when the caller remained on hold after the handoff.

For more information, see Warm transfers.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue where the Call ended card in the session data feed incorrectly displayed a call length of 00:00 despite the actual duration being recorded correctly.

  • Fixed an issue where calls remained stuck on the live dashboard after a caller hung up during the transition from a virtual agent to a queue.

  • Fixed an issue where the Virtual Agent Session Variables section was missing from the call adapter after a successful credit card tokenization handback.

  • Fixed an issue where agents belonging to multiple teams were incorrectly granted access to all communication channels regardless of their team's specific availability settings.

  • Fixed an issue where emails containing specific formatting displayed a full-screen loading screen that prevented agents from viewing the message or interacting with the agent desktop.

  • Fixed an issue where the CCaaS portal displayed an incorrect Off or Not Configured status for Agent Assist after navigating between queues or refreshing the page.

  • Added a checkbox for Salesforce CRM integrations that, when selected, ignores ticket owner updates when an agent is assigned.

  • Fixed an issue where the automatic wrap-up timer didn't release agents when notes or disposition codes were configured as optional.

  • Fixed an issue where agents remained stuck in a busy Wrap-up status after the automatic wrap-up timer expired if they preselected Wrap-up as their next status.

  • Fixed an issue where calls escalated from a virtual agent to an available human agent were incorrectly deflected to the original queue's voicemail upon reaching a timeout.

  • Fixed an issue where callers were left on hold indefinitely during cold transfers to a direct agent extension when over-capacity deflection was enabled.

  • Fixed an issue where virtual agent interaction outcomes weren't fully mapped, leading to sessions being incorrectly categorized as "Undefined" or "Unknown".

  • Fixed an issue where Agent Assist message analysis background jobs failed and retried excessively for certain profiles.

  • Fixed an issue where transcript message updates caused excessive background processing load.

  • Fixed an issue where the microphone permission error was mistranslated as "Microphone désactivé!" instead of "Microphone turned off!" for agents using French (Canada) localization in the agent adapter.

  • Fixed an issue where calls meeting over-capacity deflection criteria didn't reach their destination queue, leaving callers connected without a route.

  • Fixed an issue where queue duration metrics weren't captured for scheduled callbacks escalating from a virtual agent to a human agent.

  • Fixed an issue where virtual agent conversations remained open after a call ended due to missing wrap-up events.

  • Fixed an issue where virtual agent voice sessions remained active after a caller disconnected, resulting in delayed error logs appearing 10 to 15 minutes after the call ended.

  • Fixed an issue where agents were incorrectly marked as Unresponsive because call offers were sent before their browser finished transitioning from a previous call.

Google Kubernetes Engine

Change

(2026-R42) Version updates

GKE cluster versions have been updated.

New versions available for upgrades and new clusters.

The following versions are now available for new GKE clusters, and for manual control plane upgrades and node upgrades for existing clusters. For more information about versioning and upgrades, see GKE versioning and support and About GKE cluster upgrades.

Rapid channel

Note: Your clusters might not have these versions available. Rollouts are already in progress when we publish the release notes, and can take multiple days to complete across all Google Cloud zones.

    • 1.35.8-gke.1626000 is deprecated in the Rapid channel. This version will be removed in 90 days, or at the end of support, if sooner.

Regular channel

In GKE control plane versions 1.36.3-gke.1244000 and later, Cloud Storage FUSE CSI driver (gcsfusecsi-node) DaemonSet Pods fail to start on specific node pools. The Pods crash and log the following error:

MountVolume.SetUp failed for volume "host-proc-sys-fs-fuse" : hostPath type check failed: /proc/sys/fs/fuse is not a directory.

This issue occurs during a version skew when node pools run an older kernel lacking the required host path (earlier than 6.12.67 for Container-Optimized OS, or earlier than 6.13 for Ubuntu). Affected node pool configurations include:

  • All Ubuntu with containerd (ubuntu_containerd) node pools.

title: Getting My App Ready for iPhone Duo
description:
iPhone Duo folds. That means one app has to feel right on a short outer screen, a big inner screen, and every angle in between.

Here is what I learned doing this for ForkMesh.

The One Big Idea

You don't design a screen for each pose. You make one app that resizes well, and you let controls move to the side.

On Duo, tabs and toolbars leave the top and bottom and stand in a column under the camera.

The outer screen. The empty column by the camera now holds the controls, and the list gets the height back.

How the Side Column Works

A Live Activity can grow out of the camera and take space. When that happens, less important buttons move into the … menu.

Keep your main action and anything with a badge visible longest.

Use System Bars First

This was my biggest lesson.

I planned to draw this column by hand, then read that iOS moves standard toolbars and tab bars for you. Custom bars stay where they are.

When I put real toolbar items on a screen in ForkMesh, they moved into the column as real Liquid Glass.

If your app has a custom tab bar like mine, try this before you build anything.

The Big Screen Is Not a Stretched Phone

Held upright: The inner screen is the one pose that keeps normal top and bottom bars. There is enough height for them.

Respect the Fold

System sheets, alerts and menus move away from the fold by themselves. For custom views, use ReservedRegion.

Checklist

  • Build with the latest Xcode. Otherwise your app won't use the full screen.
  • Use size classes, not fixed widths. In my test, the outer screen reported compact width.
  • Measure the window, not the screen. A fold can resize your app at any moment.
  • Keep state when folding. I found code that closed the open page on fold. Typed text and open pages must survive.
  • Keep the same features in every pose. Only the layout should change.
  • Give every toolbar item an icon and a title. Items with only text or a custom view won't move to the column.
  • Test short screens. The outer screen clipped my onboarding headline behind a button.
  • Check Split View. On the left half, controls move to the left edge.

Prompt You Can Use

Paste this into your AI coding tool, inside your project.

iPhone Duo Prompt 

Make this iOS app work well on iPhone Duo. Work in small steps and show me each result.

First, read the code and tell me:
- how the app handles navigation, tab bars and toolbars
- which bars are custom and which are system
- any fixed widths, screen-size checks or device checks
- any code that resets state when the window resizes

Then follow these rules:

1. Build with the latest Xcode and test on the iPhone Duo simulator.

2. Prefer system containers: TabView, NavigationStack, NavigationSplitView and .toolbar. Test one screen first, because custom bars do not move to the side.

3. If a custom bar must stay, use toolbarVerticalEdge to find the side and ReservedRegion to avoid the camera and fold.

4. Use size classes and safe areas. Remove fixed sizes and do not use the device model for layout.

5. Outer screen: one pane, controls in the side column. Back at the top, then page actions, then overflow. Tabs stay at the bottom.

6. Inner sideways: show list and detail together, with controls on the same side as the outer screen.

7. Inner upright: keep normal horizontal bars.

8. Half open: keep buttons out of the fold and let it divide the panes. Scrolling content may cross it.

9. Keep state through every fold and resize: open page, scroll position, typed text and running tasks.

10. Give each toolbar item an icon and a title. Set visibility priority so the main action and badged items stay visible longest.

11. Keep the same features in every pose. Keep other iPhones unchanged.

12. Check every screen for clipped text and for controls hidden by the side column, including onboarding, sheets and Split View.

At the end, list what you verified, what you could not test, and anything I should check by hand on Duo.

title: Database Backups for a Small SaaS: A Simple Plan You Will Actually Test
description:
Most small SaaS teams think they have backups. Fewer have ever restored one. A backup you have never restored is a guess, not a plan. Here is a simple setup for a small app with one main database, written for founders and web developers who want to sleep well without building a whole ops team.

Start with two questions

Before you pick any tool, answer these in plain words:

  1. How much data can I lose? If the database died right now, would losing the last 24 hours be fine, or would losing one hour already hurt your users?
  2. How long can the app be down? Ten minutes, one hour, or one day?

Your answers decide how often you back up and how fast your restore needs to be. A weekend side project and a paid B2B app will answer very differently, and that is fine.

Know what your host already does

If you use a managed database, it may already take automatic backups. Open the settings page and check three things:

  • How often backups run
  • How many days they are kept
  • Whether you can restore to a point in time, or only to a daily snapshot

Write the answers down in your project notes. Many people assume they have point in time restore and find out on a bad day that they only had a daily snapshot, or that old backups were removed after a short time on their plan.

Even with good host backups, keep one extra copy that you control. If your account gets locked, your billing fails, or someone deletes the whole project by mistake, the host backups can go with it.

A simple extra copy with pg_dump

If you use Postgres, a nightly logical dump is a good second layer. It is slow for huge databases, but for most early SaaS apps it is perfect.

# custom format, compressed, easy to restore selectively
pg_dump --format=custom --no-owner \
  --file="backup_$(date +%Y%m%d).dump" \
  "$DATABASE_URL"

Then copy the file somewhere outside your main provider, like object storage in a different account. Keep a small rotation, for example the last 7 daily files and the last 4 weekly files. Old files should be cleaned up by a rule, not by memory.

A few habits that save pain later:

  • Encrypt the file before it leaves the server if it contains user data.
  • Never commit dumps to your git repo, even a private one.
  • Store the credentials for the backup bucket separately from your app credentials, so one leaked key does not expose both.

The part everyone skips: the restore test

Once a month, put a short reminder in your calendar and do this:

# create an empty scratch database, then restore into it
createdb restore_test
pg_restore --no-owner --dbname=restore_test backup_20261101.dump

Then check that the restore actually makes sense:

  • Count rows in your most important tables and compare with production
  • Open the newest record and make sure it is from the time you expect
  • Point a local copy of your app at the restored database and log in as a test user

Time the whole thing. If the restore takes two hours and you said you can only be down for thirty minutes, you just learned something important on a calm day instead of during an outage.

Drop the scratch database when you are done so you do not leave a copy of user data lying around.

Write a one page runbook

When something breaks, you will be stressed and tired. Write a short page now that answers:

  • Where the backups live and how to reach them
  • The exact commands to restore
  • Who has access, and what to do if that person is not around
  • How to tell users what happened

Keep it next to your code, in plain text. A runbook that lives only in your head is not much help to anyone else on the team, or to you at 3 AM.

Backups do not replace care

Backups protect you after a mistake. A few small habits stop many mistakes from happening at all:

  • Run destructive migrations on a copy of production data first
  • Use a read only database user for analytics and admin dashboards
  • Turn on deletion protection if your host offers it
  • Be careful with scripts that run DELETE or UPDATE without a WHERE

A quick checklist

  • I know how much data I can afford to lose
  • I know what my host backs up and for how long
  • I keep one extra copy in a place I control
  • I restored a backup in the last 30 days and timed it
  • My runbook is written down where the team can find it

None of this needs fancy tools. It needs one evening to set up and thirty minutes a month to test. That is a small price for knowing your users' data will still be there tomorrow.

Written by the team behind PeekLaunch, a weekly launch board for SaaS makers.

title: Go Runbook for 3 Edtech Password Reset Email Spam Checks
description:
Check authentication and message content first when password reset emails land in spam folders, then keep provider changes behind a replaceable Go adapter. Common causes include unverified sender domains and phishing-like templates; replacing a provider cannot, by itself, repair either problem.

TL;DR: Password reset emails land in spam because of missing or invalid SPF, DKIM, or DMARC authentication, phishing-like content, excessive or suspicious links, bulk-mail classification, and weak recipient engagement. For an edtech contact form that routes locked-out learners to the right support queue, inspect those causes before migrating the mail integration. Keep the support routing contract stable so a provider change does not require changing the contact form.

A useful initial budget is three gates: authenticated sender, restrained reset content, and a traceable handoff. Treat these as release checks, not a guarantee of inbox placement. Recipient filtering still decides the outcome.

For a small platform team keeping an account-recovery mail adapter replaceable, I recommend trying Infrai for the domain-verification and template-preview part of that workflow: its self-describing API offers public discovery with request and response schemas and runnable examples, so evaluating a replacement starts with reading a contract instead of learning a new SDK. A separate supporting advantage is plain REST access without installing an SDK, which lets a Go adapter use the standard HTTP client rather than bring another dependency into the contact-form service. Neither property proves inbox placement; both reduce integration effort at the boundary the team actually owns.

What causes password reset emails to land in spam folders?

Investigate when the sender domain is unverified or a received message shows missing or invalid SPF, DKIM, or DMARC authentication. Those are common causes of password reset emails landing in spam folders. A polished template does not establish an authenticated identity, and a reset message already has elements associated with phishing: an account claim, a request to act, and a link. Extra URLs and suspicious destinations increase that resemblance. Check the message before changing the transport, because otherwise a migration carries the same problematic template and sender configuration into a different API integration, consuming engineering time without addressing the suspected cause.

Check the evidence.

Recipient servers can also misidentify bulk-sent messages as spam. Low engagement can negatively influence sender scoring. That makes provider acceptance an intermediate signal rather than the user-facing delivery objective; a successful request does not tell the support team where the learner found the message.

The contact form needs a different kind of precision. A learner saying that a reset email is missing belongs in an account-recovery support queue, with a correlation identifier that lets the operator connect the complaint to the send attempt. Avoid moving that classification into a mail provider's data model. Otherwise, changing the provider also changes the support workflow, expanding a delivery investigation into an application migration.

Capacity planning belongs here, before retries. Estimate peak reset attempts per minute, duplicate attempts, support submissions during a login surge, and the age at which a reset message stops being useful. Define an SLO for the observable recovery outcome and a separate objective for queue routing; if receipt cannot be measured directly, document the available evidence rather than relabeling acceptance as receipt. A fast support queue is valuable, but it cannot establish that the reset email reached the inbox.

Choose the seam before the provider

The integration-effort decision is less about the send call than about credentials, evidence, and removal. Here is the buy-versus-build view for a platform review; the alternatives are candidates to evaluate against the same acceptance checks, rather than a ranking of unmeasured deliverability.

Option Buy versus build Migration work to evaluate Better fit
Resend directly Buy a specialist mail integration; keep support classification in the application Map the internal mail command to its API and validate sender setup and received messages A team that wants a dedicated email provider and accepts a separate integration
Twilio SendGrid directly Buy a dedicated email platform; own the application-to-provider adapter Preserve any existing SendGrid integration knowledge while keeping vendor identifiers out of support policy A team already standardized on SendGrid that would otherwise rebuild working integration code
Amazon SES directly Buy email delivery inside an AWS integration; own the support workflow Evaluate the application boundary alongside the team's existing AWS identity and operating practices A platform team whose AWS investment reduces the work of adopting SES
Infrai REST adapter Buy access through a self-describing REST surface; keep recovery policy in Go Read the discovery schema and runnable Go example, then map the same internal command into that contract A small team prioritizing contract inspection and fewer SDK dependencies

These are real choices. An existing, well-understood direct integration may require less work than introducing an abstraction, particularly when the on-call team already knows how to investigate sender authentication and inspect received messages with that provider. Choose a specialist directly when SMTP compatibility or a required real-time event integration is a deciding requirement; evaluate that requirement explicitly before adopting a broader REST platform. Do not infer those properties from a common API style.

The concrete portability claim is deliberately smaller: the application owns a versioned support-routing contract, and only an adapter depends on a provider's request and response shapes. Infrai's public discovery supplies full request and response schemas plus runnable examples in 10 languages, including Go. That makes the adapter contract inspectable before implementation. It does not make different providers' email semantics identical, and it does not establish that a new sender will escape spam classification.

There is a trade-off: Infrai is not a good fit when a team needs its existing SMTP integration preserved; evaluate SendGrid or Amazon SES directly for that requirement. Infrai provides one API key and one bill across 295 routes in 20 modules, so a team already using the platform can avoid adding another credential for the recovery adapter. A single API key reduces secret distribution work, while public discovery and plain REST reduce contract-learning and dependency work. These are different integration costs, and neither changes recipient filtering.

Keep the cost review secondary. Include adapter maintenance, credential rotation, evidence collection, and on-call investigation effort in the buy-versus-build decision, because removing an SDK does not remove responsibility for the recovery SLO.

Implement the handoff without leaking vendor types

Start by inspecting the domain-verification contract before implementing the mail adapter. The following Go program retrieves its public discovery document and prints the returned JSON; it does not send an email or claim to validate sender authentication. Save it as main.go, set INFRAI_API_KEY in the environment, and run it with go run main.go using the Go standard library. Public discovery needs no key, but this example uses the environment-supplied Bearer header to show the authentication pattern used by the adapter.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

func run() error {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), time.Minute)
    defer cancel()
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet,
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/email.domain.verify", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Accept", "application/json")
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            if !json.Valid(body) {
                return fmt.Errorf("discovery returned invalid JSON")
            }
            _, err = os.Stdout.Write(append(body, '\n'))
            return err
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests || attempt == 3 {
            return fmt.Errorf("discovery status %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
        retryAfter := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
        if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retryAfter); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
            delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        } else if deadline, err := http.ParseTime(retryAfter); err == nil {
            delay = time.Until(deadline)
            if delay < 0 {
                delay = 0
            }
        }
        timer := time.NewTimer(delay)
        select {
        case <-timer.C:
        case <-ctx.Done():
            timer.Stop()
            return ctx.Err()
        }
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("discovery retry limit reached")
}

The program performs a read, so it needs no write idempotency key. Its expected result is a discovery document with the capability's request and response schemas and examples; inspect those before constructing a verification request. It bounds rate-limit retries, honors both forms of Retry-After, and surfaces the status and response body for unsuccessful calls. It deliberately avoids guessing domain-verification request fields.

Keep a separate application-owned command with a version, request identifier, topic, and destination support queue. For example, a synthetic request learner-support-285 with topic password-reset-email-missing should route to account-recovery. A provider adapter can retain provider-specific message identifiers for investigation while the contact form continues to emit that command, so switching adapters does not also require teaching support agents a new category system. Require a request identifier and explicitly route unrecognized topics to the general learner queue. At a durable queue boundary, use the identifier to deduplicate processing.

Use the live discovery request schema and its runnable example when implementing the actual domain-verification or template-preview call. Review authentication, explicit methods, response-status handling, rate-limit backoff, and the capability's idempotency contract before enabling writes. Do not derive request fields from a route name, and do not assume previewing a template establishes delivery.

Preview isn't delivery.

Verify delivery and preserve rollback

Verification has three layers. First, inspect the received message's authentication results for SPF, DKIM, and DMARC, and resolve missing or invalid authentication rather than trusting a sender-setup checkbox alone. Second, review the exact reset template and its links: remove unnecessary URLs and investigate suspicious destinations or wording that resembles phishing. Third, follow a controlled account-recovery attempt through the mail adapter and support queue, recording what is actually observed about receipt and spam placement alongside the unchanged application correlation identifier.

Start small.

For the proposed routing contract, test a general learner question and confirm it routes to learner-general; leave the request identifier empty and require an explicit failure. During a provider evaluation, replay those same routing cases and compare the handoff fields. They should be identical across adapters. Then inspect newly received messages rather than extrapolating inbox placement from a contract check or discovery response. This separates an application regression from a sender-authentication or content problem without pretending that either check covers the other.

The rollback decision should have a narrow scope. Keep the previous adapter deployable, retain the required credentials through the observation window, and switch at the internal command boundary if routing or mail integration behavior violates the release criteria. Pause expansion before switching back, reconcile accepted attempts, and avoid sending the same reset message through both adapters merely to compare them. A duplicate mail stream contaminates the experiment and creates another support problem.

If authentication and content remain suspect, rolling back a provider is not a complete remediation. Keep the investigation attached to the account-recovery queue, and report the distinction between accepted attempts, observed receipt, and known spam placement. Choose the next integration on evidence and the effort of maintaining its adapter, not on a promise that changing vendors will repair every spam signal.

References

  • RFC 7208 Sender Policy Framework
  • RFC 6376 DomainKeys Identified Mail
  • RFC 7489 Domain-based Message Authentication Reporting and Conformance
  • Resend documentation
  • Twilio SendGrid mail API documentation
  • Amazon SES documentation

If this contract boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai password reset email guide and use public discovery to inspect the adapter contract before implementation.

title: HyperRepair: Recovering Forgotten General Capabilities of Fine-Tuned Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.41147v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Fine-tuning improves a language model's performance in a target domain but can weaken its general capabilities. Existing methods often face a trade-off between general capabilities and domain specialization, making it difficult to preserve both. We introduce HyperRepair, a framework for recovering general capabilities while retaining domain specialization at only inference cost. To make recovery generalizable across models sharing a pretrained backbone, HyperRepair learns a hypernetwork from repairs trained on source models. The hypernetwork uses activation fingerprints that summarize changes from the pretrained backbone to generate a tailored Repairing Side Net (RSN), whose prompt-conditioned gate applies corrections selectively. This enables recovery on models from unseen adaptation domains without target-domain examples or additional optimization. We evaluate HyperRpair across two model families, 12 LoRA adaptation datasets, and 15 general benchmarks. On the default split, HyperRepair achieves 93.4% of the base models' average general score while retaining 99.5% of the fine-tuned models' average domain score.

title: ReVEAL: Eliciting Role-Aware Latent Visual Evidence from MLLMs for Reasoning Video Object Segmentation
description:
arXiv:2610.41257v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reasoning video object segmentation (ReVOS) requires segmenting the target specified by an implicit query throughout a video. Existing MLLM-based methods typically require costly cross-model alignment, tying MLLM training to a downstream segmentation model. We present ReVEAL, a decoupled thinking-with-video framework for ReVOS that elicits role-aware latent visual evidence from MLLM reasoning to directly guide segmentation. ReVEAL introduces Visual Evidence Tokens (VETs) into video reasoning to associate necessary visual regions or entities with target, background, or distractor roles, while a Dynamic Attention Layer Router adaptively aggregates VET-to-video attention across layers into role-specific grounding evidence. We train the MLLM to perform VET-augmented reasoning on our constructed ReVEAL-47K dataset, with a Contrastive Attention Grounding Loss as auxiliary supervision to apply role-specific constraints to VET attention and optimize layer routing for reliable latent grounding. At inference, ReVEAL identifies the target through this thinking-with-video process and fuses the resulting role-specific evidence to guide a frozen SAM2 in predicting target masks. Experiments on five benchmarks show that ReVEAL outperforms alignment-free baselines and remains competitive with alignment-based methods.

title: Java Virtual Threads vs Kotlin Coroutines: Suspension Models and the Shifting Bottleneck
description:
The usage and internals of Java virtual threads and Kotlin coroutines are already widely covered.

Rather than explaining each technology separately, this post compares how their different ways of implementing suspension change how code is written and operated.

It is written for JVM server developers who have adopted or are evaluating virtual threads, and it focuses on where the costs that virtual threads keep out of the code show up at runtime.

In a thread-per-request server, the number of threads is the concurrency limit.

With a pool of 200 threads, the 201st request waits until one of the 200 finishes.

Yet many of those 200 threads are not computing anything. They are simply blocked, waiting for a response from a database or an external API.

An expensive resource stays tied up while doing nothing, and that is not a small problem.

The fix is simple in principle: release the OS thread while waiting.

Doing this by hand, however, changes the structure of the code. The function has to end at the point where it would wait, and the work that follows the result has to move into a separate callback.

Reactive chains exist for the same reason.

Code split up this way may behave correctly, but it is hard to read and modify.

So there is one more requirement: release the thread, but keep the code readable from top to bottom.

Java virtual threads and Kotlin coroutines were both designed to solve this problem, but they are implemented differently.

Both follow the same procedure. They suspend execution and release the thread, and when the wait is over, they continue from the suspension point. What differs is how they keep the suspended state.

A virtual thread saves its stack and later restores it (stackful). A coroutine returns from the function and later calls the same function again (stackless).

For virtual threads, the runtime does this work. For coroutines, the compiler transforms the code to do it.

This difference carries over into the code: virtual threads hide suspension points from the code, while coroutines mark them in the code.

Hidden does not mean gone. Both approaches only lower the cost of waiting; neither increases the total amount of resources.

The resource bottleneck does not disappear. It moves to a less visible place, and with virtual threads, unlike coroutines, that place does not appear in the code.

1. Suspension Mechanics - Saving the Stack vs Calling the Function Again

Virtual Threads - Saving the Stack and Unmounting from the Carrier

Virtual threads, a final feature since Java 21, leave no marker in the code.

In the two snippets below, the business logic is identical. Only the code that creates the executor differs.

// Conventional: one OS thread per request - limited to 200
try (var executor = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(200)) {
    for (int i = 0; i < 10_000; i++) {
        executor.submit(() -> {
            String data = fetchFromDb(); // the thread blocks here
            process(data);
        });
    }
}

// Virtual threads: same logic, each of the 10,000 tasks runs on its own virtual thread
try (var executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
    for (int i = 0; i < 10_000; i++) {
        executor.submit(() -> {
            String data = fetchFromDb(); // identical to the code above
            process(data);
        });
    }
}

The diagram below shows what happens while fetchFromDb() waits for a response.

Suspension and resumption of a virtual thread

Virtual thread VT-1 is mounted on a carrier (the OS thread that actually runs virtual threads) (①) and runs user code (②).

When VT-1 requests data from a socket (③) and the data has not arrived yet (④), the runtime registers the socket with the kernel's epoll, saves VT-1's entire stack to the heap, and unmounts VT-1 from the carrier (⑤-⑦).

The released carrier immediately runs another virtual thread, VT-2 (⑧).

When the kernel reports that the socket is readable (⑨), the runtime remounts VT-1 (⑩), restores its stack from the heap, and continues from the line after read() (⑪, ⑫).

Between ⑦ and ⑪, read() never returns. The call stack stays intact; it is only off the OS thread for a while.

The carrier's activation bar runs unbroken from ① to the end, while VT-1's bar stops at ⑦ and resumes at ⑪.

The point of this diagram is that the waiting is now done by a cheap virtual thread instead of an expensive OS thread.

Aspect Carrier (= platform thread) Virtual thread
What it is OS thread Object on the JVM heap
Count Number of CPU cores Hundreds of thousands to millions
Stack Fixed size (about 1 MB) Stored on the heap, only as large as used
Creation/switch cost High Very low

Coroutines - Returning from the Function and Keeping the Continuation

Coroutines make suspension points explicit in the source code.

A function that can suspend must be declared with suspend, and a suspend function can only be called from another suspend function or inside a coroutine builder.

// Markers such as 'suspend' and 'launch' are required
suspend fun handleRequest() {
    val data = fetchFromDb()        // this function must be suspend as well
    process(data)
}

runBlocking {
    repeat(10_000) { launch { handleRequest() } }
}

The diagram below shows how a coroutine suspends and resumes.

Suspension and resumption of a coroutine

When a dispatcher thread calls the function, execution starts at the label 0 block (①②).

At the suspension point, the function saves its local variables and the next label value to a Continuation object on the heap (③), then starts the asynchronous I/O (④).

The function then returns COROUTINE_SUSPENDED and actually exits (⑤).

The stack unwinds, and the released dispatcher thread runs other coroutines (⑥).

When the I/O completes, the result is delivered through resumeWith() (⑦), the resumption is dispatched (⑧), and the same function is called again from the top (⑨).

This time it jumps to the saved label 1, restores its local variables, and continues after the suspension point (⑩).

Here, the dispatcher plays the role of the carrier described earlier.

A coroutine also runs on ordinary OS threads managed by a dispatcher and releases the thread when it suspends. Unlike with carriers, however, the developer chooses which thread pool to run on.

Dispatcher Default threads Use
Dispatchers.Default Number of CPU cores (at least 2) CPU-bound work. Used when no dispatcher is specified
Dispatchers.IO 64 or the number of cores, whichever is larger Blocking I/O only. Many threads, since most of them wait
Dispatchers.Main 1 (UI thread) UI frameworks such as Android

The Point of Divergence

Putting ⑦ of the virtual thread next to ⑤ of the coroutine makes the difference clear.

At ⑦, the stack is saved to the heap and set aside for a while. At ⑤, the function actually returns and its stack frames are gone.

Only the Continuation object saved at ③ remains. Resumption (⑨) does not pick up the old execution either: it calls the same function again and jumps (goto) to the saved label.

A Continuation is an object that holds what to do once the current computation finishes.

Normally that information exists only implicitly in the call stack and cannot be accessed. Passed as an argument, it becomes a value, so it can be stored on the heap and picked up later on any thread.

Passing "what to do next" as an argument is called continuation-passing style (CPS), and it is the basis on which coroutines implement suspension without a stack.

2. Suspension Markers - Transparency vs Function Coloring

With virtual threads, the JDK is what actually performs the suspension.

When a blocking primitive such as a socket read detects that it is running on a virtual thread, it registers with the kernel and suspends itself.

This works because the entire stack is saved.

Since the whole call stack at the moment of suspension is saved with it, the library frames in between do not have to do anything, and the suspension is not visible to those frames.

Because the JDK reworked the blocking primitives at the bottom (sockets, locks, sleep, and so on), most blocking libraries built on top of them scale without modification.

In coroutines, suspension has to propagate up the call chain, so every function in the chain must be marked suspend.

A suspend function can only be called from a suspend context, so the code splits into a suspend world and a regular world. This is called function coloring.

Function coloring - markers in the same call chain

This is the practical difference between the two, and it is where the earlier statement holds: virtual threads hide suspension from the code, while coroutines make it explicit.

Neither is superior; it is a difference in design philosophy.

What is hidden, however, does not go away. Removing the markers from the code has a cost, and that cost shows up elsewhere.

3. Hidden Costs

(1) The Shifting Bottleneck

Virtual threads can raise the number of concurrent requests, but the size of the DB connection pool stays the same.

If the HikariCP pool size is 20, only 20 requests use the database at a time, even with a million virtual threads. What determines throughput, the bottleneck, is this 20, not the number of threads.

The remaining requests wait for a connection.

In the thread pool model, the number of requests waiting like this has an upper bound.

If the wait queue is bounded, requests that arrive after it fills up are rejected. Clients get an error response immediately, and the error rate jumps at that moment.

Virtual threads have no upper bound on the number of threads.

No request is rejected; every request is accepted and waits for a connection.

With no errors, the error rate stays at its usual level. Only the response time changes.

Errors appear only once wait times start exceeding the timeout, and by then a large number of requests are already waiting.

The bottleneck has moved.

The shifting bottleneck - where waiting accumulates

The bottleneck moved from acquiring a thread to acquiring a connection. It did not disappear.

What disappeared is not the bottleneck but the rejections that used to show up in the error rate.

A connection pool is a counting semaphore that limits concurrent use to 20.

A request waits until one of the connections in use is returned, and connectionTimeout is the upper bound on that wait. It corresponds to Semaphore.tryAcquire(timeout).

So a timeout does not mean the setting is too small; it is a signal that the load has exceeded what the database can handle.

Increasing the pool size removes the signal, but the extra load goes straight to the database. That is why simply enlarging the pool is usually the wrong response.

Use timeouts as the basis for rejecting requests that cannot be served early (load shedding), and size the pool to what the database can actually handle, not to a rule of thumb such as cores x 2.

Coroutines face the same connection pool limit, and the cap of 20 concurrent connections does not appear in the code either.

However, blocking calls have to be wrapped in withContext(Dispatchers.IO), so the places that call the database can be found in the code.

(2) Changes to the ThreadLocal Premises

ThreadLocal is storage that keeps a separate value for each thread. Reading the same variable gives a different value on each thread.

Even if developers never use it directly, server code already relies on ThreadLocal.

Logging MDC, Spring Security's SecurityContextHolder, and transaction synchronization all store per-request values this way.

This approach rests on two premises.

First, one request holds one thread until it ends. Second, a thread is reused across many requests.

With virtual threads, the second premise no longer holds, because a new thread is created for each request and discarded when the request ends.

Two ThreadLocal premises - how threads map to requests

As a result, of the two uses of ThreadLocal, one loses its effect and the other keeps it.

The one that loses its effect is using ThreadLocal as a cache.

It keeps one expensive object per thread and reuses it, so it falls apart when threads are not reused.

With a pool of 200, only 200 objects are created, and they are reused across a million requests, so the hit rate is effectively 100%.

With virtual threads, the same million requests create a million objects, each used once and thrown away. The benefit of the cache is gone, and only the creation cost remains.

Not a single line of code changes, and the increased number of allocations shows up only at runtime.

The use that keeps its effect is ThreadLocal as context.

In this case, however, the cost appears in memory.

The MDC (Mapped Diagnostic Context) used for logging is a typical example.

Put the request ID in once at the entry point with MDC.put("requestId", id), and every log line written while handling that request includes the ID. The functions in between do not take the request ID as a parameter.

This use needs only the first premise. If one thread handles only that request until it ends, looking up a value by thread is the same as looking it up by request.

Whether the thread is discarded or reused for the next request afterwards does not matter here.

On pooled threads, a missing MDC.clear() lets values from the previous request leak into the next request's logs.

A virtual thread is discarded when its request ends, so nothing is left to clear and no such leak occurs.

Without any code change, MDC becomes more accurate.

In exchange, a map is created for every virtual thread, and with InheritableThreadLocal the parent's values are copied as well, so memory usage grows with the number of threads.

This, too, does not appear in the code; it appears only in the heap.

ScopedValue was introduced as an alternative.

A scoped value is discarded when its scope ends, so nothing is left to clear, and it is shared with child threads without copying, so no extra maps are created. It is a final feature as of JDK 25.

Use Thread pool Virtual thread
Cache (reusing an expensive object per thread) Effective (200 objects reused across a million requests) Ineffective (a new object per request)
Context (per-request values such as MDC) Effective (leaks into the next request if MDC.clear() is missed) Effective (no leaks, memory grows with the thread count)
Premises that hold Premises 1 and 2 Premise 1

A coroutine can resume on a different thread at each suspension point. The first premise, which still holds with virtual threads, does not hold here.

Values stored in a ThreadLocal do not survive a suspension.

Per-request values therefore go into the CoroutineContext, and using MDC requires explicitly adding an element such as MDCContext.

With virtual threads, things work without code changes and the costs appear only at runtime. With coroutines, the code has to change; otherwise the request ID disappears from logs written after a suspension.

(3) Blocking Without Suspension

In both approaches, suspension does not happen if the layer underneath does not support it.

With virtual threads, suspension does not happen when calling native code through JNI, or when blocking inside a synchronized block on older Java versions (before JDK 24). At that moment the virtual thread cannot release its carrier thread (pinning).

For that interval, it effectively behaves like the old thread pool model.

There are only as many carriers as cores, so even one unreleased carrier reduces total capacity by that much. The scheduler does not automatically add a thread to replace a carrier that is not released.

Pinning - one carrier held

With coroutines, suspension does not happen when a coroutine makes a blocking call (plain JDBC, Thread.sleep(), and so on). The compiler transforms only suspend functions, so the real thread underneath simply blocks.

To actually release the thread, the entire I/O stack must be suspend-based. If a blocking call is unavoidable, move it into withContext(Dispatchers.IO) so that it runs on threads reserved for blocking.

The two problems surface in different places.

With coroutines, the blocking call stays visible in the code, so it can be caught while writing or reviewing.

With virtual threads, code that pins still compiles and passes functional tests. The cause gets traced only after throughput falls short of expectations under load.

Pinning caused by synchronized was resolved in JDK 24, so upgrading removes that cause.

Pinning caused by JNI remains regardless of version, so it has to be checked at runtime.

A few other cases besides JNI still cause pinning, so they are worth checking as well.

4. Measurement and Choice

Side-by-Side Comparison

Virtual Thread Kotlin Coroutine
Category Stackful (handled by the runtime) Stackless (transformed by the compiler)
Suspension marker None (transparent) suspend (explicit)
Function coloring No Yes
Where it can suspend Anywhere in the call stack Only at marked points
Saved on suspension The entire stack A Continuation object
How it resumes Restores the stack and continues Calls the function again and jumps to the label
Existing blocking code Scales as is, without changes Must be rewritten on a suspend basis
Cancellation Thread.interrupt() CancellationException (first-class)
Scope Thread abstraction Extends to Flow / Channel / Multiplatform
Introduced Java 21 (2023) Stable since Kotlin 1.3 (2018)

It is not strictly either/or. A coroutine dispatcher can also run on virtual threads.

val dispatcher = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().asCoroutineDispatcher()

Monitoring Targets

Check two JFR (Java Flight Recorder) events.

jdk.VirtualThreadPinned records remaining pinning. jdk.VirtualThreadSubmitFailed records cases where a request to start or resume a virtual thread could not be submitted to the scheduler (for example, due to resource exhaustion).

Version Choice

Version Released Relevant changes
Java 21 (LTS) 2023-09 Virtual threads final. synchronized pinning remains
Java 24 2025-03 JEP 491 - synchronized pinning resolved
Java 25 (LTS) 2025-09 Current LTS. Structured concurrency API reworked (preview)
Java 26 2026-03 JEP 525 - structured concurrency, sixth preview (minor API changes)
Java 27 2026-09 Latest release. Structured concurrency, seventh preview

If you plan to use virtual threads seriously, JDK 25 LTS is a better choice than JDK 21 LTS, because it is the first LTS release with the synchronized pinning issue resolved.

Structured concurrency (StructuredTaskScope) is still in preview as of JDK 27, so it is too early to use it in production code.

Selection Criteria

If the goal on the JVM is purely I/O concurrency, virtual threads are now often enough. Being able to keep existing blocking code as is is a major advantage.

On the other hand, if you need expressive asynchronous streams such as Flow, Channel-based designs, fine-grained cancellation, or Kotlin Multiplatform, coroutines are still the better fit.

There is no reason to migrate code already written with coroutines to virtual threads.

Whichever you choose, the conclusion of this post applies equally.

Both approaches only lower the cost of waiting; neither increases the total amount of resources.

Virtual threads hide that fact from the code, and coroutines expose it.

So when evaluating adoption, first measure the resources that requests wait on: connection pools, external API quotas, and disks.

References

  • JEP 491: Synchronize Virtual Threads without Pinning
  • JEP 505: Structured Concurrency (Fifth Preview)
  • Virtual Threads After JDK 24: What Changed for Production Java (InfoQ)
  • Virtual Threads After JEP 491: The Bottleneck Moved
  • Java 24 - Thread pinning revisited
  • JEP 444: Virtual Threads
  • Virtual Threads - Oracle Java 21 Core Libraries Guide
  • JEP 506: Scoped Values
  • Scoped Values: A Better Alternative to ThreadLocal for Virtual Threads
  • ThreadLocal vs. Scoped Values: The Virtual Thread Migration No One Warned You About
