title: The Generative Gap Between Speculative Drafter and Continuous Diffusion Language Model
description:
arXiv:2610.40847v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Continuous diffusion language models (CDLMs) and speculative drafters offer efficient language generation but are typically evaluated differently: CDLMs generate independently through iterative refinement, whereas drafters propose text for target-model verification and correction. We compare their architectures without verification, using LangFlow for CDLMs and adapting DSpark's Markov and recurrent-head architectures for standalone generation. All models are trained from scratch for unconditional, single-block OpenWebText generation at lengths 16, 128, and 1024, without target features or verification, using common preprocessing, backbone dimensions, and training-update budgets. We evaluate generation perplexity (GenPPL) with an external language model and distributional similarity to reference text with MAUVE. With default denoising steps equal to sequence length, LangFlow outperforms both DSpark variants on both metrics at lengths 128 and 1024, while DSpark-RNN leads at 16. A conditional KL analysis characterizes dependencies excluded by the Markov head's previous-token conditioning. Recurrent memory removes this restriction and improves both metrics, but the longer-sequence gap persists. Teacher probability matching further lowers Markov GenPPL without observed MAUVE gains. Increasing LangFlow's denoising steps at fixed weights improves both metrics at lengths 16 and 128, changing the length-128 ordering relative to DSpark-RNN. These results establish LangFlow's longer-sequence advantage under the evaluated budgets and highlight iterative full-sequence refinement as a route to improving standalone generation beyond gains from recurrent head memory.

title: Where, When, and How Many Bits? Scaling Laws for SGD with Stochastic Rounding
description:
arXiv:2610.41074v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Low-precision training reduces computation but introduces additional rounding error. We theoretically study how stochastic rounding (SR) affects prediction risk as model size, training time, and precision change. We consider a two-layer linear network with a fixed random first layer, trained by mini-batch SGD on fresh Gaussian data with power-law spectra. At each SGD step, the features used in forward and backward computations are rounded independently. We prove matched upper and lower bounds on prediction error for the final model and for uniform parameter averaging, with general learning-rate and precision schedules chosen before training. For fixed precisions and constant learning rates with parameter averaging, we derive how the smallest prediction error decreases with compute, and we identify model sizes and training times that achieve this optimal-compute scaling. Rounding only the forward features preserves the compute scaling of exact arithmetic, while rounding backward features changes it. Averaging parameters can change which computation needs higher precision and when higher precision is useful. Our results also give bit requirements for a given accuracy tolerance and show how backward rounding can change learning-rate schedule design. At a fixed compute budget, lower precision can improve prediction when the benefit of a larger model or longer training outweighs the additional SR-induced error. Model simulations illustrate these tradeoffs, and experiments with an MLP and a small transformer examine rounding choices beyond the theoretical model.

title: Inside the Block: How Solana Validators Actually Order Transactions Post-Alpenglow (Empirical Study)
description:
Why "Higher Priority Fee = Earlier Block Position" Is Only Half True on Solana

Most Solana developers assume that setting a higher SetComputeUnitPrice guarantees an earlier position inside a block. When we measured live post-Alpenglow Solana Mainnet blocks across Agave CentralScheduler, Agave UnifiedScheduler, Jito-Solana Block Engine, and Frankendancer/Firedancer Pack tiles, we found a much more nuanced reality.

Full reproducible code & dataset (docker compose up --build): https://github.com/duongynhi000005-oss/solana-inside-the-block-scheduler-analyzer

1. The Priority Score Formula Inside Agave's Scheduler

In Agave (prio_graph_scheduler.rs), transactions are not ranked by raw priority fee. They are ranked by reward per requested Compute Unit (CU):

Priority_Score = (ComputeUnitPrice_MicroLamports * Requested_CU_Limit + Base_Fee)
                 / (Requested_CU_Limit + Signature_And_Account_Lock_Overhead_CU)

If your swap only consumes 22,000 CU but you leave the default 200,000 CU limit without calling SetComputeUnitLimit(25_000), your effective scheduler priority is diluted by up to 6x during write-lock contention.

2. Write-Lock Contention vs. Multi-Thread BankingStage Racing

Across our Mainnet sample (slots 464182838–464182886):

  1. Uncontended Transactions: Packed in parallel across 4 non-vote banking threads, achieving a Spearman rank correlation of 0.74 to 0.89 between CU price and intra-slot entry index.
  2. Multi-Thread Flush Inversions (18% of pairs): When two non-conflicting transactions arrive in the same 50ms window on different worker threads, the thread executing a lighter batch frequently flushes to the PoH Recorder 1–3 entries ahead of a higher-fee transaction whose thread was finishing a heavy CPI instruction.
  3. Hot Writable Account Chains: Transactions writing to the same AMM pool state account are chained sequentially inside PrioGraph, delaying lower-priority writers while non-conflicting low-fee transfers sail through on adjacent threads.

3. Reproducing the Measurements in One Command

We packaged our entire telemetry collector and analyzer into a read-only Docker Compose suite (zero private keys required, dry-run by default):

git clone https://github.com/duongynhi000005-oss/solana-inside-the-block-scheduler-analyzer.git
cd solana-inside-the-block-scheduler-analyzer
docker compose up --build

title: RangeSWA: Training-Free Length Extrapolation for Continuous Diffusion Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.42084v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Continuous diffusion language models show promising potential in text generation tasks, but are prone to problems such as text repetition, semantic drift, and generation quality degradation when the generation length exceeds the training length. To address these challenges, we propose RangeSWA, a training-free length extrapolation method. The method combines local sliding-window attention, remote block summaries, and dynamic content retrieval to preserve local details and support long-range context access. In addition, generation degradation caused by length extrapolation is mitigated through positional remapping, conditioning attention correction, and denoising-stage-adaptive window scheduling. We conducted experiments on multiple continuous diffusion language models, and the results show that RangeSWA can effectively reduce generative perplexity and text repetition rates in long-text generation.

title: What an AI Rap Video Generator Taught Me About Crawlable React Pages (2026)
description:
Disclosure: I build MyAIRap.video, a photo-to-Rap tool. This is a development case study from that project, written with AI assistance and checked against our local release records. It is not a claim that server rendering alone produces rankings.

The first useful SEO question for a React product is surprisingly practical: what does a reader get before JavaScript runs?

Our redesigned interface looked complete in a browser. It had examples, pricing and a clear path to the creator. A raw HTML check told a different story: the initial response was a small shell. The words people could see after rendering were missing from the first response.

For an AI rap video generator, that is a product problem as much as a search problem. A visitor needs to understand the input, the resulting video and the purchase model before signing in.

Render the public explanation, keep the private app private

We reused the same React marketing components for pre-rendered public HTML. The homepage, pricing, tutorial and articles now have meaningful headings, paragraphs and links in the first response. Their client-side counterparts use the same route metadata rather than inventing a second title after navigation.

The account and checkout are different. We did not turn private balances or orders into indexable pages. Public explanation and authenticated actions share a design, but they do not share an indexing policy.

This distinction is easy to lose when every URL looks like “just another React route.”

A small acceptance check catches the important failures

For a public route, we check:

  • The raw response contains exactly one meaningful H1.
  • Title, description, canonical and language correspond to that route.
  • Prices visible in HTML come from the retained product catalogue.
  • Tutorial, examples and article links are real anchors.
  • The browser does not replace the correct server title with a generic default.
  • The narrow layout has no document-wide horizontal overflow.

A response-size threshold helped detect the old empty shell, but size alone is not the goal. A large response with duplicated filler would still be a bad page. We check for actual useful content and correct links.

Product claims are part of the rendering contract

Our creator has Mini and Standard, two durations and two resolutions. Existing showcase videos were made with Standard. A marketing page that implies the least expensive option always matches the showcase would create the wrong expectation, however well it rendered.

The same applies to a template button. Today it records interest in an unreleased format; it should not look like a working purchase for exact recreation.

That is why we keep pricing, availability and model caveats in the same acceptance review as headings and metadata. The page is an explanation of the application, not a separate brochure allowed to drift away from it.

What we can and cannot conclude

Raw HTML and browser checks can show that content is available. They cannot show that Google has indexed the latest version, that a keyword will rank, or that an AI assistant will cite it. Those need separate observation windows and real search or referral evidence.

If you are building a similar tool, inspect the response before writing another SEO article. Then check a client-side navigation into pricing and back. The second step catches metadata regressions that a single homepage request misses.

The MyAIRap tutorial shows the actual photo, lyric and video workflow behind this case. The main lesson is portable: make the public explanation readable, and keep the private transaction private.

title: My First Merged PR in Zalando Logbook: What I Built and What the Review Taught Me
description:
In my last post I wrote about why I started open source. This post is about the first PR that got merged for me in a big project: Zalando Logbook.

What is Logbook?

Logbook is a Java library from Zalando that logs HTTP requests and responses. If you work with REST APIs, you know why this matters. When something breaks in production, the first thing you want to see is what request came in and what response went out.

What I worked on

My PR added two things to Logbook:

  • StatusCodeBasedSink: a sink that makes decisions based on the HTTP status code of the response.
  • LevelBasedHttpLogWriter: a log writer that uses the status code to pick the log level.

The simple idea behind both: a 200 response and a 500 response should not be treated the same. Errors should stand out, and normal traffic should not fill your logs with noise.

It got merged in May 2026. You can see the full PR, the code and the review here: zalando/logbook #2301

How I approached it

I did not start by writing code. I started by talking to the maintainers on the issue, so I knew what they wanted before I built anything. Then I kept the change small and focused, wrote tests, and signed my commits.

Looking back, that order saved me a lot of pain. Writing code first and asking later is how PRs get stuck.

What the review taught me

Maintainers read very carefully. They do not only check if your code works. They ask:

  • Does this fit the style of the project?
  • Will this break anyone who is already using the library?
  • Is the naming clear for someone who has never seen this code?

Answering those questions made my code better than my first version. Reviews are slow sometimes, but they are free teaching from people who know the codebase far better than I do.

The part I did not expect

After my PR was merged, another contributor found a gap in my own work. The ECS sink did not follow the same status code behavior, so he opened an issue and then a PR to fix it.

My first feeling was a little embarrassing. But then I thought about it properly: this is exactly how open source works. Nobody ships perfect code. So instead of rushing to send a competing PR, I reviewed his one and left comments on the threshold behavior and on the docs checklist. You can read that discussion here: zalando/logbook #2379

That was a good lesson for me: reviewing someone else's PR is also a contribution, and it teaches you how others think.

What I would tell someone starting out

  1. Read the issue and talk to the maintainer first.
  2. Keep your PR small. A small diff gets reviewed faster.
  3. Take every review comment seriously, even when it feels strict.
  4. If someone finds a gap in your work later, treat it as part of the process, not as a failure.

What is next

In the next post I will write about my PR in the Adyen Java API Library, which shipped in SDK v42.0.0, and how it felt to see my change in a real release.

Proof of my work

Everything I write about here is public, so you can check it yourself:

  • zalando/logbook #2301: StatusCodeBasedSink and LevelBasedHttpLogWriter (merged)
  • adyen/adyen-java-api-library #1952: shipped in SDK v42.0.0 (merged)
  • PicnicSupermarket/error-prone-support #2275: merged after review
  • Sionna Visualizer: my side project, a 6G + AI dashboard (live demo)
  • My GitHub: all my repos and contributions

If you are a maintainer, a recruiter or a team looking for someone who learns in public and likes to collaborate, my DMs are open. Tell me in the comments if you work with Logbook or want to contribute to it, I am happy to share what I learned.

title: EgoHSI3R: Online 4D Hand-Scene Interaction Reconstruction from Egocentric Video
description:
arXiv:2610.40832v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Egocentric videos offer an abundant source of hand-scene interactions for embodied learning, which requires recovering hands, camera, and scene consistently in a shared 3D world. Existing methods focus on either camera-frame hands or world-space hand trajectories, without jointly recovering the scene pointmaps or interaction information. Building a complete reconstruction from such specialized predictions therefore typically requires per-sequence optimization. We propose EgoHSI3R, a unified feed-forward framework for online 4D hand-scene interaction reconstruction from egocentric monocular video. To jointly recover these components, it maintains a recurrent scene representation that accumulates geometric evidence over time and provides a shared world space and scale. We introduce hand-centric prompts that fuse pretrained hand priors and local scene context, while MANO vertex queries attend to scene features to predict dense per-vertex contact. These designs enable a single network to jointly estimate camera motion, dense scene geometry, world-space bilateral MANO hands, and per-vertex hand contact. Despite operating causally, EgoHSI3R achieves the lowest world-space hand joint error on ARCTIC among the evaluated methods, while offering faster inference than existing world-space hand reconstruction pipelines and competitive camera and scene reconstruction accuracy.

title: MUON-RT Reusing the Teacher's Trajectory for Momentum-Free Muon for LLM Self-Distillation
description:
arXiv:2610.41104v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Self-distillation methods for large language models with an exponential moving average (EMA) teacher already retain a history of student updates. Muon nevertheless stores a separate momentum buffer, increasing persistent training memory. We propose Muon with Reused Teacher (Muon-RT), which reuses the teacher-student displacement to eliminate momentum buffers for hidden weight matrices. We show that this displacement encodes an exponentially weighted history of applied updates and smooths temporally uncorrelated noise under a local model. Muon-RT removes its radial component, normalizes it spectrally, and mixes it with the current gradient after Newton-Schulz (NS) orthogonalization. Under explicit regularity and alignment assumptions, we establish linear contraction of an expected objective-gap bound toward a residual error level. With Self-Distillation Fine-Tuning (SDFT) on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Muon-RT improves average accuracy over AdamW by 2.6 points with 42% less persistent memory, and over momentum Muon by 5.4 points with 27% less persistent memory. With Self-Distillation Policy Optimization (SDPO) on Olmo-3-7B-Instruct, it improves average accuracy over AdamW by 2.0 points.

title: New Windows program uses artificial intelligence to evaluate victims' stolen data
description:
Security researchers have discovered VOLTA-AUTODOXER, a new Windows infostealer that uses large language models to analyze stolen data.

The malware harvests credentials, session tokens, and crypto keys, then employs models via OpenRouter to rank the victim's financial worth before exfiltration.

The program, known as VOLTA, infiltrates computers and collects massive amounts of personal data. Specifically, it can steal saved passwords, digital browsing traces, payment details, digital cryptocurrency wallets, and login profiles from various applications.

How stolen data is organized

After collecting the data, the program searches the victim's emails for receipts from orders and purchases to confirm their home address. It then creates a folder with information that includes location, address, employer, card details, and an estimate of the value of the bills.

To process this data, the program connects to artificial intelligence services. It primarily uses the Claude system, while it has a mechanism for automatically switching to other systems, such as Kimi and Gemini, in case the first system refuses to respond. A special instruction text asks the artificial intelligence to act as an analyst, assessing the value of the victim and how careful he was with his safety.

How the data reaches the perpetrators

All data and analysis results are sent to the perpetrators via the Telegram application at three different stages of the process.

title: Implementing 2026 Seller Compliance Practices for Retrying Failed Email API Calls
description:
TL;DR: Retry a failed email API call only when the response is plausibly transient, use capped exponential backoff with jitter, and write an immutable attempt record before each sleep. For a B2B marketplace order, the useful artifact is not merely sent=true; it is a chain showing which order was notified, which policy decision was made, what the transport returned, and when the next attempt became eligible.

The decision rule is deliberately boring: classify first, schedule second, send third, and record every transition. A 429 or a temporary 5xx can justify a later attempt. A malformed request, an authentication failure, or a permanent recipient rejection should go to review or a dead-letter path instead. Replaying every error at increasing intervals creates duplicate messages, obscures the real failure, and makes compliance evidence harder to defend.

That is the failure boundary.

What evidence does a seller notification actually need?

The scenario is a marketplace seller receiving notice of a new order. The notification service owns delivery attempts; the order service owns the order itself. Keep those responsibilities separate. The attempt record should contain an order identifier, notification identifier, recipient address or a privacy-preserving reference to it, policy version, attempt number, decision, response class, and UTC timestamps. Store the provider response body only under a retention rule reviewed for personal data.

A useful record distinguishes accepted, retry_scheduled, permanent_failure, and cancelled. It should preserve the idempotency key used for the request. That key does not make an arbitrary remote API idempotent by magic, but it gives a compatible transport a way to suppress an accidental replay and gives an investigator something concrete to correlate.

Record it.

Email has several layers. An HTTP API may accept a submission while later mail processing produces a bounce or delivery event. SPF is an authorization mechanism for hosts sending mail for a domain; it is not proof that a mailbox accepted a message. Record API acceptance as one fact, and downstream delivery or bounce evidence as another.

What are sound practices for retrying failed email API calls?

Start with the response class, not the number of attempts. A 429 Too Many Requests response is a rate signal; honor Retry-After when present and parseable, while still applying an operational maximum. A 5xx response generally indicates a server-side problem, but the remote contract is the authority. Transport timeouts and connection resets are ambiguous: the request may have reached the remote system before the client lost the response, so retry them only with an idempotency strategy and a bounded budget.

Do not retry a 400 caused by invalid payload data, a 401 or 403 caused by credentials or policy, or a confirmed permanent recipient rejection. A retry loop cannot repair bad data. It can multiply traffic and delay the queue behind a message that should have been quarantined.

Bound it.

For attempt n, a common schedule is base * 2^n, capped at a maximum, then randomized with jitter so a fleet does not wake every worker on the same boundary. The base and cap belong in capacity planning: model worst-case retry volume against API quota, queue depth, worker concurrency, and the notification SLO. As concrete policy inputs, a 30-second request deadline and a 15-minute retry horizon can be useful starting values for review, but they are not universal constants; measure queue age and dependency behavior before adopting them.

The queue math is easy to underestimate. Suppose 500 workers each hold one retryable job and the dependency returns 429 for two minutes. If every worker wakes at the same second, the second wave recreates the rate-limit event, and a queue that looked healthy before the incident can become a second source of load. Full jitter turns that synchronized wave into a distribution, while a cap prevents a single seller notification from consuming capacity indefinitely. Capacity planning should include the initial send plus every eligible retry, the number of workers that can become runnable during the same interval, the API quota's refill behavior, and the delay introduced by a database lease. The operational record should show the chosen delay, the cap, and the policy version so an auditor can reproduce the decision without guessing what the worker knew at the time.

Here is the policy boundary in Go. It has no vendor-specific endpoint, so the decision can be tested without network I/O.

package retry

import (
    "math/rand"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

type Decision struct {
    Retry  bool
    Delay  time.Duration
    Reason string
}

func Next(status int, retryAfter string, attempt int, base, cap time.Duration, r *rand.Rand) Decision {
    if attempt < 0 || base <= 0 || cap < base {
        return Decision{Reason: "invalid retry policy"}
    }
    if status != 429 && status < 500 {
        return Decision{Reason: "non-retryable response"}
    }
    delay := base
    for i := 0; i < attempt && delay < cap; i++ {
        if delay > cap/2 {
            delay = cap
            break
        }
        delay *= 2
    }
    if parsed, ok := parseRetryAfter(retryAfter); ok && parsed < cap {
        delay = parsed
    }
    if r != nil && delay > 0 {
        delay = time.Duration(r.Int63n(int64(delay) + 1))
    }
    return Decision{Retry: true, Delay: delay, Reason: "transient response"}
}

func parseRetryAfter(value string) (time.Duration, bool) {
    seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(strings.TrimSpace(value))
    if err != nil || seconds < 0 {
        return 0, false
    }
    return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second, true
}

This treats Retry-After as a scheduling input, not permission to wait forever. A production implementation should accept an HTTP-date if its contract requires it, reject values above the policy cap, and record that a malformed header was ignored. The policy is only one part of the design; the evidence model and queue transaction matter just as much.

Where should the attempt record sit in the send path?

Persist the notification job before a worker can claim it. A worker claims one job with a lease, creates an attempt record with a monotonically increasing attempt number, sends with the stable idempotency key, then records the result and next state. The lease timeout must exceed the expected request deadline but remain short enough to recover a crashed worker without creating overlapping sends.

The awkward case is the important one: the remote service accepts the request, then the worker dies before recording the response. On lease expiry, the next worker cannot know whether the message was accepted. That is why the idempotency key, the remote event history when available, and a bounded reconciliation state are more valuable than an aggressive retry count. Marking the job unknown_delivery is honest evidence; pretending it failed is not.

type Attempt struct {
    NotificationID string
    OrderID        string
    Attempt        int
    IdempotencyKey string
    StartedAt      time.Time
    FinishedAt     time.Time
    HTTPStatus     int
    Decision       string
    NextAttemptAt  *time.Time
    PolicyVersion  string
}

Write the attempt and job transition in one database transaction when both live in the same store. Publish a wake-up message after commit, or use an outbox table so a crash cannot leave the database saying retry_scheduled while the queue knows nothing about it. The outbox is easy to inspect, replay, and explain during an audit.

Buy or build the delivery boundary?

The decision is about control and operational load, not a race to the smallest invoice. A managed transport can remove SMTP operations and expose delivery events, while a self-hosted boundary brings deeper routing control at the cost of reputation management, patching, feedback loops, and on-call work.

Boundary Evidence you can usually own Capacity and SLO concern Main trade-off
Managed email API Request IDs, submission status, event callbacks, policy records Quota behavior and callback lag must be measured Less transport toil, more dependency on contract and retention limits
Self-hosted SMTP relay Local queue, logs, configuration, delivery attempts IP reputation, queue growth, and receiving-domain behavior become SLO inputs More control, much larger operations surface
Hybrid boundary Application audit trail plus selected transport events Two failure domains require reconciliation and alerting Stable application evidence with limited transport ownership

Define minimum evidence before selecting an implementation. Ask how long request and event records remain available, whether callbacks are signed, how rate limits are communicated, and how deletion requests affect immutable audit records. A buy decision that cannot answer those questions is an unpriced compliance dependency.

How do you verify and roll back safely?

Unit-test every response class, malformed Retry-After, cap boundary, attempt limit, and clock conversion. Use a fake transport that can return a timeout after accepting the request; the expected result is an explicit unknown-delivery path, not an unbounded replay. Then run a small canary with synthetic seller addresses and a separate mailbox, checking that attempt record, queue state, and downstream event agree.

Watch retry rate by status class, age of the oldest queued notification, queue depth, lease expiry count, duplicate-suppression count, callback lag, and the percentage of jobs ending in unknown delivery. Set an SLO for notification freshness and another for evidence completeness. A system can meet a send-latency target while quietly losing the records needed to prove what happened.

Rollback should disable new retries through a configuration flag while leaving in-flight records readable. Drain or quarantine scheduled jobs according to their policy version; do not rewrite history to make a dashboard look healthy. Keep the previous classifier available until no remaining jobs use its rules.

The practical endpoint is modest: a retry policy that is bounded, observable, and explainable. Exponential backoff protects a struggling dependency, but the audit trail protects the business decision around a marketplace order. Treat both as part of delivery design.

References

  • RFC 7208, Sender Policy Framework (SPF): https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7208
  • RFC 9110, HTTP Semantics, including status codes and Retry-After: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110
  • RFC 5321, Simple Mail Transfer Protocol: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5321
  • RFC 3463, Enhanced Mail System Status Codes: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3463
  • RFC 6585, Additional HTTP Status Codes, including 429: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6585

title: Coarse3D: Controllable and Faithful Sparse Structure Generation for Image-to-3D
description:
arXiv:2610.41231v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Coarse-to-fine 3D-native generation relies heavily on the first-stage sparse structure, which determines the global orientation and overall geometry for subsequent refinement. However, existing coarse generators suffer from two key limitations: their orientation is difficult to control due to ambiguous semantic canonicalization, and their structures are often inconsistent with input images due to weak 2D-3D grounding. We propose Coarse3D, a sparse-structure generation model that produces orientation-controllable and structurally faithful voxel geometry from arbitrary unposed images. Coarse3D introduces three designs: a first-frame anchored canonical space that aligns generation with the first input view while preserving object-centric normalization; a dual-tower DiT that couples generation with auxiliary feed-forward reconstruction to learn spatially grounded features; and spatial-prior guided attention that regularizes cross-attention with pixel-to-voxel correspondence. Coarse3D can directly replace the coarse stage of existing pipelines. Experiments show that it substantially improves sparse structure quality and consistently enhances final 3D generation, achieving state-of-the-art performance.

title: GRIT: Gradient Masking for Visually Misgrounded Tokens in Text-Rich Reasoning
description:
arXiv:2610.41629v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has recently been extended to vision-language models (VLMs), yet its effectiveness remains limited for text-rich reasoning tasks. We highlight a key factor contributing to this limitation: models frequently arrive at correct final answers despite misperceiving visual information during intermediate steps. We define this phenomenon as Correct-but-Visually-Misgrounded Reasoning (CVMR). Because standard RLVR rewards only final-answer correctness, it fails to differentiate between properly grounded and misgrounded reasoning, reinforcing both equally. Through token-level analysis, we reveal that CVMR tokens exhibit distinct attention patterns that differ systematically from well-grounded ones. Based on this observation, we propose GRIT, a training framework that incorporates visual grounding into RLVR to mitigate the impact of CVMR. Furthermore, to address the lack of text-rich reasoning benchmarks that allow for systematic evaluation across text length and reasoning depth, we introduce GRIT-Bench. Experiments demonstrate that GRIT significantly improves both reasoning accuracy and grounding fidelity over existing RLVR methods.

title: A Positional Realizability Theory of Length Generalization in Single-Head Attention
description:
arXiv:2610.41218v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Why does length generalization (LG) depend so sharply on the positional encoding (PE)? Relative schemes extrapolate fixed offsets, absolute schemes fix positions, and neither handles growing offsets. We give a realizability theory for a deliberately controlled abstraction, a single positional-only attention head, that derives this well-documented empirical pattern and says precisely where it holds and breaks. The device is a simulation transfer operator $T_L$ that re-evaluates a selected length-$L_0$-realizing positional kernel on the longer grid, with a scalar $\alpha_L \in [0,1]$ read off before any training from $(\Phi, t_n)$ alone. Here $\alpha_L$ serves as the computable witness of that taxonomy's derivation, not as a stronger empirical predictor. Our results are a relative-head deep-row characterization for kernels with a strict unique global maximizer (Theorem 2), an absolute/relative duality that derives the pattern (Proposition 4), a learned-absolute underdetermination result, and a static expressivity bound; a sufficiency theorem (Theorem 1) bridges $\alpha_L$ to LG, and the general deterministic case is a precise open conjecture (correcting a tempting but invalid "outside-colspan" argument). Experiments confirm the structure: in the controlled single-head regime $\alpha_L$ exactly separates the taxonomy's generalizing and non-generalizing (PE, task) cells (2625 trained-model measurements; stable at vocab 64/d=128). Together, these results turn the received PE taxonomy into a positional-kernel transfer theorem, and identify the content and depth mechanisms that escape it. The theory concerns the positional channel alone: tasks whose targets depend on token content, including the standard length-generalization suite such as addition and sorting, fall outside Theorem 2.

title: MOSAIC: Addressing Disproportionate Task-Modality Dependencies via Modality-Partitioned Gradient Routing
description:
arXiv:2610.41004v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In multi-task settings, combining multiple modalities allows task representations to draw on signals that a single modality alone would not capture. However, individual tasks may depend disproportionately on particular modalities, a structure that conventional fusion-based architectures do not model explicitly, instead enforcing a unified representation space. Consequently, a task's gradients can affect parameters tied to modalities it barely relies on, leaving features that compromise between competing demands. Although prior work has explored task-weighting and loss-balancing strategies, their effectiveness is limited by the absence of explicit modality separation, preventing models from optimising each modality according to its task-specific importance. To address these limitations, we propose MOSAIC (MOdality-Separated Architecture with Inter-modal Cross-attention), which preserves unimodal representations while enabling controlled interaction between them, and uses modality-specific losses to route gradients to their corresponding partitions. On the Corpus of Everyday Japanese Conversation (CEJC), MOSAIC improves average macro-F1 by 7.4 points across four tasks with a 72% reduction in backbone parameters relative to a fusion-based baseline. Our results demonstrate that modality partitioning yields consistent gains across tasks while requiring far fewer backbone parameters than a fusion-based design.

title: From Transcription to Reformulation: Defining and Benchmarking Grounded Generative Speech Recognition
description:
arXiv:2610.41292v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Speech language models have expanded automatic speech recognition (ASR) from transcription to general speech-to-text generation. Yet existing benchmarks still assume a single ground-truth transcript per utterance, an assumption that struggles when models produce readable, formatted, or structured outputs. In this work, we introduce Grounded Generative Speech Recognition (GSR), reformulating speech recognition as generating semantically grounded text instead of a single transcript. We define a grounded reformulation space that characterizes all valid textual realizations supported by the input speech, and establish a four-level hierarchy of reformulation capabilities, including literal transcription, canonical reformulation, semantic reformulation and speech-grounded structuring. Based on this formulation, we present GSR-Bench, the first comprehensive benchmark designed to evaluate generative speech recognition systems beyond exact transcript matching. GSR-Bench covers diverse scenarios including refined meeting transcription, cross-dialect translation, context-aware speech understanding, and robustness under silent or noisy acoustic conditions. To address the limitations of word-level evaluation metrics, we develop a multi-dimensional evaluation framework combining speech grounding assessment and LLM-based semantic judgment, whose reliability is validated through human preference studies. Extensive experiments across representative architectures, ranging from conventional ASR systems to end-to-end Speech-LLMs, reveal fundamental trade-offs between transcription fidelity and generative reformulation ability. Our analysis further identifies critical failure modes, including acoustic hallucination, unsupported generation, and instruction drift, providing insights into the design and evaluation of future grounded generative speech systems.

title: DecisionRank: On-Policy Distillation for Decision-Model Rerankers
description:
arXiv:2610.42128v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Decision models target structured tasks by directly predicting choices or scores, avoiding autoregressive decoding latency. However, transferring a generative LLM's ranking knowledge to a decision model remains challenging: the teacher expresses preferences through a ranked list of document ID sequences, while the student determines the ranking using scores from the first-token position. To bridge this gap, we introduce DecisionRank, a decision model trained through item-space on-policy distillation (OPD). Item-space OPD constructs the student's rollout by sorting its document scores into a ranked sequence. A generative teacher takes the resulting ranking list as inputs and provides conditional feedback to directly supervise those scores. Combined with offline ranking supervision, DecisionRank achieves state-of-the-art performance on both general and reasoning-intensive retrieval benchmarks such as TREC DL, BEIR, and BRIGHT. Across four benchmarks, item-space OPD consistently outperforms alternative training objectives. Even at 1.7B parameters, DecisionRank surpasses its 27B generative teacher on TREC DL19--23. At 8B, it outperforms its generative listwise counterpart while running $24.5\times$ faster on TREC DL and $16.7\times$ faster on BRIGHT.

title: How to Learn React: A Simple Beginner Roadmap (Step by Step)
description:
Originally published on CodingCush.

To learn React as a beginner, follow this order: be comfortable with HTML, CSS and modern JavaScript first, then learn components and JSX, then props and state, then events and forms, then fetching data, and finally routing and a framework such as Next.js — building one small project at each step instead of only watching tutorials. Most beginners who follow this sequence can build real React apps within two to three months of steady practice.

Step 0: The Skills React Assumes You Already Have

React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces, so it stands on three legs: HTML for structure, CSS for appearance, and JavaScript for behaviour. You do not need to be an expert in any of them, but three JavaScript ideas must feel friendly before React will make sense: arrow functions, array methods such as map and filter, and destructuring. These three appear in almost every React component ever written, and struggling with them inside React feels twice as hard as learning them in plain JavaScript first.

Give this foundation two honest weeks if it is new. Build one small static page, then make one tiny JavaScript app — a counter, a to-do list without a framework — so variables, functions and DOM updates are familiar territory. Skipping this step is the single most common reason beginners conclude that React is "too hard", when really the missing piece was never React at all. The official React Learn course itself opens by assuming this background, which tells you how universal the advice is.

Step 1: Components and JSX — Thinking in Pieces

React's central idea is the component: a small, reusable piece of interface written as a JavaScript function. A button, a card, a whole page — each is a component, and big interfaces are assembled from small ones the way a wall is assembled from bricks. Your first milestone is writing a component, displaying it inside another component, and passing it simple content.

Inside components you will write JSX, the HTML-like syntax that lives inside JavaScript. If JSX still feels like a stranger, our explainer on what JSX is in React walks through it with small examples before you go further. The screenshot in this article, from the official React Learn quick start, shows the pattern in its purest form: a MyButton component defined once and then nested inside MyApp with a single tag. That nesting — components inside components — is the entire architecture of every React app you will ever open, from a practice counter to the dashboard of a company you have heard of.

The official React Learn "Quick Start" page on react.dev — a component nested inside another component.

Step 2: Props and State — Data That Flows and Data That Changes

With static components under your fingers, learn the two words that run every React app. Props are data a parent hands down to a child — the title and price given to a product card. State is data a component remembers and changes itself — the count in a counter, the text in a search box — using the useState hook. When state changes, React redraws the component automatically, which is the moment the library stops feeling like markup and starts feeling alive.

Our detailed guide to React components, props and state is the natural deep-dive for this step, with examples of each idea separately. Practise with a small project that needs both: a list of books or products rendered from an array, where each card receives props, and a favourite button on each card keeps its own state. If you can build that without copying, you understand the heart of React — honestly, a large fraction of professional React work is this exact step wearing better clothes.

Step 3: Events, Forms and Lists

Next, make your interfaces respond. Handling a click with onClick, reading an input with an onChange handler and controlled form fields, and rendering lists with map plus a stable key for each item: together these turn static screens into working tools. Build a small expense tracker or a notes app at this stage. It will be ugly. It will also teach you more about state than a week of videos, because every bug in a form is a state lesson arriving exactly on schedule.

While building, adopt the habit that separates calm developers from frustrated ones: when something does not update, ask "which state should have changed?" before changing any code. In React, the screen is a reflection of state, so a wrong screen almost always means wrong or stale state — a debugging compass that will serve you in every project on this roadmap and beyond it.

Step 4: Fetching Data and Talking to APIs

Real apps display data they do not own, so step four is loading data from an API with fetch inside the useEffect hook, showing a loading message while waiting, and handling the bad day when the request fails. Public practice APIs offer free data about weather, movies, products and countries, so you can build a respectable little app without writing any backend at all.

The React installation guide is worth a visit around this stage too, because it explains how real projects are set up with modern tooling, instead of the single-file practice pages most beginners start with. Set your practice project up the proper way once — folders, components in separate files, a sensible structure — and later steps, especially sharing your work with employers, become dramatically easier.

Step 5: Routing, Next.js and the Road Beyond

Stage Learn Project to build
Foundation HTML, CSS, modern JavaScript A static page and a plain-JavaScript to-do list
Basics Components, JSX A personal profile page made of components
Core Props, state, useState A product list with favourite buttons
Interactive Events, forms, lists and keys An expense tracker or notes app
Real data useEffect and fetch A weather or movie search app
Beyond Routing, then Next.js basics A small multi-page blog or portfolio

Once single-page apps feel comfortable, learn routing — how an app shows different pages without reloading — and then meet Next.js, the framework built on React that adds routing, server rendering and structure out of the box. Our comparison of React vs Next.js explains what the framework adds and why learning plain React first makes Next.js feel like a helpful upgrade instead of a second mountain. After that, the road branches by taste: styling libraries, testing, TypeScript, or deeper state tools — all optional side quests once the main path is walked.

The Habits That Make the Roadmap Work

A roadmap is only paper without habits. Build something at every step, however small, because projects expose the gaps that tutorials politely hide. Type code yourself instead of copying it, and when an error appears, read it before searching it — React's error messages are unusually honest by industry standards. Finally, keep every project, even the embarrassing early ones, in Git repositories: six months from now, that visible trail from counter app to data-fetching app is the most convincing portfolio a beginner can show.

Frequently Asked Questions

How long does it take to learn React?

With the JavaScript foundation in place and steady practice of an hour or two a day, most beginners build comfortable, real projects in two to three months. Reaching job-ready depth takes longer, but the first working apps come quickly.

Should I learn React or JavaScript first?

JavaScript first — at least arrow functions, array methods and destructuring. React is written in JavaScript, so every gap in the language becomes a gap in React, only harder to see.

Is React hard for beginners?

The core ideas — components, props, state — are genuinely simple. Beginners struggle mainly when the JavaScript foundation is missing, or when they try to learn React, routing and a framework all in the same week.

Do I need Next.js to get a React job?

Not at the start. Employers expect strong React fundamentals first; Next.js is a valuable second skill that builds directly on them, which is why it sits at the end of this roadmap.

Conclusion

Learn React in the order it builds on itself: JavaScript foundations, components and JSX, props and state, events and forms, fetching data, then routing and Next.js — with a small, finished project proving each step. Follow that sequence patiently and React stops being a wall of new words, and becomes what it really is: a simple idea, applied one component at a time.

title: Every typed GraphQL error came back as "Internal server error" because graphql was loaded twice
description:
I had six integration tests for error codes on a small GraphQL + Postgres backend: UNAUTHENTICATED, FORBIDDEN, NOT_FOUND, BAD_USER_INPUT and friends. The resolvers threw the right errors. CI still failed the tests, and every error came back the same:

{ "errors": [{ "message": "Unexpected error.", "extensions": { "code": "INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR" } }] }

Nothing was wrong with the resolvers. The server's error masking had decided our errors weren't GraphQL errors at all.

The setup

Expected failures are typed. Everything else gets masked so stack traces and SQL never reach the client:

export class AppError extends GraphQLError {
  constructor(code: ErrorCode, message: string, extra: Record<string, unknown> = {}) {
    super(message, { extensions: { code, ...extra } });
  }
}

// resolver
if (!canEdit) throw new AppError('FORBIDDEN', 'Not allowed');

The masking rule is the usual one: if the thrown error is a GraphQLError (or wraps one), pass it through; otherwise replace it with INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR. In GraphQL Yoga that's maskedErrors: true; in Apollo it's a formatError with an instanceof check.

The cause: two GraphQLError classes

instanceof compares against one specific class object. If the module that defines GraphQLError is loaded twice, there are two classes with the same name, and an error built from one is not an instanceof the other.

graphql v16 ships both a CommonJS build (index.js) and an ES module build (index.mjs). Your code can get one while your server library gets the other, depending on how each is imported and how your test runner or bundler resolves them. Vitest, Jest and some bundlers are common places for this to happen. A monorepo with two graphql versions in node_modules does the same thing more obviously.

So the chain was:

  1. The resolver throws AppError, which extends copy A of GraphQLError.
  2. The server checks it against copy B.
  3. instanceof is false, so the error counts as unexpected.
  4. The client gets INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR, and the real code is only in the server log.

In production this looks like "the frontend can't tell a wrong password from an outage." It's easy to ship, because a manual test of the happy path never sees it.

How to check if you have it

Throw an AppError from any resolver and log this where your server handles errors:

import { GraphQLError } from 'graphql';

console.log(
  err.originalError?.constructor?.name,          // "AppError"
  err.originalError instanceof GraphQLError,     // false means two copies
);

Then look for duplicates:

npm ls graphql

More than one version listed is the obvious case. One version but false above means the CJS/ESM split.

The fix: recognize your errors by a brand, not by class identity

Give your error class a property that survives any number of module copies, and check that instead:

export class AppError extends GraphQLError {
  readonly isAppError = true;
  constructor(code: ErrorCode, message: string, extra: Record<string, unknown> = {}) {
    super(message, { extensions: { code, ...extra } });
  }
}

export function isAppError(err: unknown): err is AppError {
  return typeof err === 'object' && err !== null && (err as { isAppError?: unknown }).isAppError === true;
}

Then do the masking yourself, so the decision uses the brand:

export function maskError(error: unknown, message: string): Error {
  const e = error as { originalError?: unknown; nodes?: any; path?: readonly (string | number)[] };
  const app = isAppError(e) ? e : isAppError(e?.originalError) ? e.originalError : null;
  if (app) {
    return new GraphQLError(app.message, { nodes: e.nodes, path: e.path, extensions: app.extensions });
  }
  console.error(error);
  return new GraphQLError(message, { nodes: e?.nodes, path: e?.path, extensions: { code: 'INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR' } });
}

// GraphQL Yoga
createYoga({ schema, maskedErrors: { maskError } });

For Apollo Server, use the same isAppError check inside formatError.

Deduplicating graphql (one version, one import style) is worth doing too. But the brand check keeps working when a future dependency upgrade brings the second copy back, and that's the failure you won't be watching for.

The test that caught it

One assertion per error code, against a real server and a real Postgres:

it('forbids viewers from creating issues', async () => {
  const res = await gql(
    'mutation($i: CreateIssueInput!) { createIssue(input: $i) { id } }',
    { i: { projectId: ids.alpha, title: 'Pour slab' } },
    ids.bo, // a member with the viewer role
  );
  expect(res.errors?.[0]?.extensions?.code).toBe('FORBIDDEN');
});

If your error-code tests only call resolver functions directly, they skip the masking layer and pass while clients get 500s. Send the request through the server.

Checklist

  • Typed errors carry a brand property; masking checks the brand, not instanceof.
  • Masking runs in one function you own, with the same rule for every server.
  • npm ls graphql shows one version.
  • Each error code has a test that goes through the HTTP layer and asserts extensions.code.

Making Claude Code write it this way

This is one of the rules in the typed-errors skill of my Claude Code skills pack for TypeScript + GraphQL + Postgres backends. The starter backend in the pack is where CI caught this bug.

  • Two skills are free (GraphQL N+1 fixes and safe Postgres migrations): github.com/adnan909/free-sample
  • The full pack, with the typed-errors skill, 6 more skills and the tested starter backend: Backend Skills Pack on Gumroad

title: BDNet: Fast-slow thinking is all you need
description:
arXiv:2610.41485v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present BDNet, a hierarchical image-classification backbone built around fast image features and slow statistical references. Its baseline deformation operator (BDO) transforms the deviation of a feature from a stage-specific reference through a low-rank projection and a learned channel scale. Rather than computing pairwise token similarity, the branch operates directly on baseline-relative residuals with complexity linear in the token count. Each of four reference buffers accumulates detached stage statistics during training and remains frozen at inference. A four-stage pyramid with depths $(2,2,6,2)$ and widths $(96,192,384,768)$ yields a 20.70M-parameter classifier at $224\times224$ resolution. We organize an ImageNet-1K study around clean classification, eight controlled ablations, and Gaussian-noise, contrast, and brightness perturbations. The central hypothesis is that a slow reference can improve the robustness of a compact representation while retaining a simple tensor implementation. We distinguish this training-time statistical mechanism from input-dependent attention and make its linear inference behavior explicit.

title: Parley: A Private Messenger Template You Can Brand
description:
Plenty of organizations want their own messenger and can't use WhatsApp for it. A hospital that needs staff chat it controls. A company that wants messaging inside its product, under its brand, with no third party reading along. A community that doesn't want to live on someone else's platform. Building a secure messenger from scratch is a long project: the encryption protocol, multi-device sync, push, calls, media, groups and moderation are each a project of their own.

What is Codename One? Codename One is an open-source framework for building native iOS, Android, desktop, and web apps from a single Java or Kotlin codebase. Learn more at codenameone.com.

Parley is that messenger, finished. It's the second of this week's templates, after Skirmish, and like the others it comes as one Java project with the app, the server and the admin console. Pick the messaging template in the Initializr and you have it. The source is under MIT-0: brand it, sell it and keep your changes private.

Chats, groups and channels.
An encrypted conversation.
Voice and video calls.

What you get

Part What's in it
Messaging One-to-one chats, groups of up to 256 with invite links, broadcast channels, replies, forwards, edits and delete for everyone
Media Photos, video and voice notes, encrypted on the device before upload
Calls Voice and video calls over WebRTC, peer to peer
Privacy Disappearing messages, safety numbers, app lock, screen security, and controls for last seen, profile photo, read receipts and typing
Devices Linked devices, including a browser as another device
Bridges Optional Telegram and WhatsApp bridges, clearly marked in every conversation that uses them
Operations An admin console with a dashboard, users, reports and bridges
Reach iOS, Android, desktop and the browser from one project, in five languages including right-to-left Hebrew

The server can't read your users' messages

Parley uses the same design as Signal: X3DH to agree on keys and the Double Ratchet to rotate them with every message. It uses P-256 ECDH, which every platform's native crypto supports, with HKDF-SHA-256 and AES-256-GCM. Each message has its own key, and a key that leaks doesn't expose earlier messages.

The server stores and forwards envelopes: sender, target device, header, and ciphertext. It never sees the payload, so a breach of your server is a breach of ciphertext. Attachments are encrypted on the device with a fresh key before upload. On the phone, the history is sealed with a key held in the platform keystore.

The code that does this is short and readable, because the primitives are part of Codename One. This is the start of a session, from Ratchet.java:

```java {class="cn1-no-try"}
KeyPair ephemeral = KeyGenerator.ec(256);
PrivateKey me = Identity.privateKey();
byte[] dh1 = KeyAgreement.ecdh(me, pub(signedKey));
byte[] dh2 = KeyAgreement.ecdh(ephemeral.getPrivateKey(), pub(identity));
byte[] dh3 = KeyAgreement.ecdh(ephemeral.getPrivateKey(), pub(signedKey));
byte[] secret = x3dh(dh1, dh2, dh3,
oneTime == null ? null : KeyAgreement.ecdh(ephemeral.getPrivateKey(), pub(oneTime)));




`KeyAgreement`, `KeyGenerator` and `Hkdf` are new in `com.codename1.security`, added for Parley. They work on every platform, on the backend too, and Thursday's post covers them along with the WebRTC API.

## Calls that never touch your server

Calls use WebRTC with DTLS-SRTP, directly between the two devices. The Parley server rings the other side, relays the offer, answer and ICE candidates over the live WebSocket channel and hands out STUN and TURN credentials. The audio and video never pass through it, so a call costs your server almost nothing and stays private.

## Make it yours

The look starts at the top of `theme.css`:



```css
--brand: #0a7d6b;  /* White on the teal reads at 5:1. */
--brand-contrast: #ffffff;

Change the brand color and every screen follows, with dark mode variants beside it. The name, icon, languages, push and SMS providers, database and hosting work the same way they do in Wayline. A few directions to take it:

  • An internal company messenger: run your own TURN relay for calls (parley.ice.turn) and leave the bridges out, so nothing leaves your infrastructure.
  • Messaging inside your product: a marketplace that lets buyers and sellers talk, a clinic that talks to patients, a coaching app that talks to clients. The chat screens are ordinary Codename One forms, so they fit into another app.
  • A community app: channels for announcements, groups for members and the admin console for moderation.
  • Your own crypto choices: the curve and the cipher are in one class, Ratchet, if your compliance team has opinions.

Privacy settings.
Dark mode.
The admin dashboard.

Moderation without reading messages

An encrypted messenger still needs moderation. The admin console only sees what the server sees: accounts, message counts, conversation types and busy hours. When a user reports a conversation, their phone attaches the messages they chose to report, so content reaches an admin only through the people in that conversation. That keeps the privacy promise while still letting you handle abuse.

Try it

The development profile runs with nothing installed. Start the server, open two simulators, sign in as alice@parley.example and bob@parley.example, and message yourself. The server can also host the browser build, so a laptop browser becomes a linked device. The Parley page has the overview, and the user's guide and implementor's guide cover the rest.
