title: TADP: Dual-Branch Temporally Adaptive Differential Privacy for Expression-Aware Video Anonymization
description:
arXiv:2610.41642v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present TADP, a temporally adaptive differential privacy (DP) framework for inference-time privacy-preserving video generation under fixed-length clip-replacement adjacency. TADP uses a dual-branch design to extract identity and expression representations, clips and privatizes both branches with temporally adaptive Gaussian mechanisms whose noise scales depend only on preceding privatized releases within the same clip and are bounded below by history-uniform calibrated minima, and accounts for their joint release via adaptive R\'{e}nyi Differential Privacy (RDP) composition. The clip-level RDP guarantee is converted to $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-differential privacy, while soft quantization and subsequent temporal processing are applied only after privatization as DP post-processing. Experiments on facial expression datasets show reduced identity leakage under evaluated attacks, usable perceptual quality and temporal stability, and high facial expression recognition utility relative to the evaluated privacy-preserving baselines. TADP formally satisfies clip-level DP and empirically provides a favorable privacy--utility trade-off under the evaluated threat models and datasets.

title: Why Does Python Fail to Verify SSL Certificates? Common Causes and Practical Fixes
description:
Have you ever run a Python script that works perfectly on your local machine but fails when it tries to connect to an HTTPS API?

You might see an error similar to this:

requests.exceptions.SSLError:
HTTPSConnectionPool(host='example.com', port=443):
Max retries exceeded with url: /
(Caused by SSLError(
SSLCertVerificationError:
certificate verify failed
))

This error can be frustrating, especially when the website opens normally in your browser.

But why does Python reject an SSL certificate that your browser appears to trust?

The answer usually comes down to how Python verifies certificate chains and which Certificate Authorities (CAs) its environment trusts.

Let's look at the common causes and how to troubleshoot them.

1. Why Does Python Reject an SSL Certificate?

When Python connects to an HTTPS website, it checks the server's TLS certificate to establish that it is connecting to the intended server and that the certificate chains back to a trusted CA.

Several things can cause this verification to fail:

The certificate has expired.

The server isn't providing the complete certificate chain.

The local CA certificate bundle is outdated.

The certificate was issued by a private or untrusted CA.

A corporate proxy is intercepting HTTPS connections.

The application is using an incorrect or incomplete CA bundle.

The important thing to understand is that a browser and a Python application may use different certificate trust stores.

Therefore, a website working in Chrome doesn't necessarily mean that a Python script will trust its certificate.

2. Check Whether the Problem Is With Python or the Server

Before changing your Python configuration, check the certificate presented by the server.

You can use OpenSSL:

openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com -showcerts

Replace example.com with the hostname you're trying to access.

Look for the verification result near the bottom of the output.

For example:

Verify return code: 0 (ok)

This indicates that OpenSSL successfully verified the certificate chain using its configured trust store.

If you see a verification error, investigate the certificate chain, hostname, expiry, and trusted CA configuration.

Note: OpenSSL and Python may use different CA bundles, so a successful OpenSSL check doesn't automatically prove that Python will succeed.

3. Update Python's Certificate Bundle

One common cause is an outdated CA certificate bundle.

The Python requests library uses trusted CA certificates to verify HTTPS connections. It commonly uses the certifi package to provide a CA bundle.

First, update the relevant packages:

python -m pip install --upgrade requests certifi

Next, check which CA bundle certifi is using:

import certifi

print(certifi.where())

This prints the path to the CA certificate bundle.

You can also explicitly tell Requests to use it:

import requests
import certifi

response = requests.get(
"https://example.com",
verify=certifi.where(),
timeout=15
)

print(response.status_code)

If the request succeeds, the issue may have been related to the previous CA bundle configuration.

4. Check Whether Your Server Is Sending the Complete Certificate Chain

Another common problem occurs when a web server doesn't provide the required intermediate certificates.

A TLS certificate chain generally contains:

The server certificate.

One or more intermediate CA certificates.

A trusted root CA certificate, which is generally already present in the client's trust store.

If the server fails to provide a required intermediate certificate, some clients may be unable to build a trusted chain.

You can inspect the certificate chain using:

openssl s_client \
-connect example.com:443 \
-servername example.com \
-showcerts \
-verify_return_error

Check whether the expected intermediate certificates are being presented and whether chain verification succeeds.

If the chain is incomplete, correct the server's certificate-chain configuration rather than disabling verification in Python.

5. Configure a Custom CA Bundle When Necessary

Sometimes the problem isn't an outdated public CA bundle.

For example, your organization might use:

An internal Certificate Authority.

A private PKI environment.

A corporate HTTPS inspection proxy.

Custom certificates for internal APIs.

In these situations, Python may need to trust an additional CA certificate.

Requests supports specifying a custom CA bundle through the verify parameter:

import requests

response = requests.get(
"https://internal.example.com",
verify="/path/to/company-ca-bundle.pem",
timeout=15
)

print(response.status_code)

You can also configure the REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE environment variable:

Linux/macOS:

export REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE=/path/to/company-ca-bundle.pem

Windows PowerShell:

$env:REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE = "C:\certs\company-ca-bundle.pem"

Make sure the file contains the appropriate trusted CA certificates and is maintained securely.

If you need both public and private CA trust, use a properly constructed combined CA bundle rather than accidentally replacing public trust with an incomplete private bundle.

6. Check for HTTPS Inspection by a Corporate Proxy

If your Python application works on your home network but fails on an office network, check whether a corporate proxy is inspecting HTTPS traffic.

Some organizations intercept encrypted connections and issue replacement certificates signed by an internal CA.

Your browser may already trust that internal CA because it was installed through your organization's device-management policy.

Python may not automatically use the same trust configuration.

To investigate:

Compare the certificate issuer on your office and home networks.

Check whether your organization uses HTTPS inspection.

Ask your IT administrator for the approved CA certificate bundle.

Configure your Python application to trust the appropriate CA.

Never install an unknown CA certificate simply to make an SSL error disappear. Verify its authenticity with your IT or security team.

7. Why You Shouldn't Disable SSL Verification

You may find examples online that suggest using:

requests.get(
"https://example.com",
verify=False
)

This disables certificate verification for that request.

Although it might make the connection work, it also removes an important security check. Your application could accept an untrusted or impersonated server certificate.

This increases the risk of man-in-the-middle attacks.

Instead of disabling verification, identify why the certificate cannot be trusted and fix the underlying problem.

A Quick Troubleshooting Checklist

If your Python application still cannot verify an SSL certificate, work through this checklist:

Check whether the server certificate has expired.

Verify that the hostname matches the certificate.

Check whether the server sends the required intermediate certificates.

Update Requests and Certifi.

Check which CA bundle your application uses.

Investigate corporate proxies or private CAs.

Test the connection again without disabling certificate verification.

Final Thoughts

Python SSL certificate verification errors aren't always caused by an invalid website certificate. Sometimes the issue is with the local CA bundle, missing intermediate certificates, or a network environment that uses its own trusted CA.

The best approach is to identify where certificate verification fails before changing your application's security settings.

If you regularly work with APIs, backend services, or automated deployments, keeping CA bundles updated and monitoring certificate chains can help prevent unexpected connection failures.

Have you encountered an SSL certificate verification error in Python? Was it caused by an outdated CA bundle, a missing intermediate certificate, or something else? Share your experience in the comments.

title: Rounding is a promise when you show a player their odds
description:
Development covered 23 Sep 2026 to 24 Sep 2026 (commit dates).

A player in Myriad Immortal Sect read "Tribulation success chance: 100.0%", pressed the button, and failed. The underlying chance was 99.96 percent. Nothing was wrong with the roll. The number on the screen had been rounded to the nearest tenth, and 99.96 rounds to 100.0.

To a programmer that is a formatting detail. To the player it is the game lying and then punishing them for believing it. This window turned into a small campaign about how odds are displayed, and the rules that came out of it are short enough to steal.

Round towards the outcome you cannot promise

The first rule is about direction. Rounding to nearest is the default everywhere, and for odds it is wrong at both ends.

Near the top, anything below certainty must never display as certainty. The odds card, the result card and the chronicle line now all round down, so 99.96 reads 99.9 and only a true certainty shows 100.0. Near the bottom, the mirror case: a chance that is possible but tiny used to print "0.0%", which says impossible. It now reads "<0.1%". The dispatch board's chip, which shows whole percentages, keeps anything uncertain inside 1 to 99, so a 99.7 percent errand shows 99 and a 0.3 percent one shows 1.

The principle is that the display should never claim more certainty than the roll has, in either direction. A player can live with "99.9% and I failed". They will not forgive "100% and I failed".

One number, one formatter, everywhere

The second rule is about agreement. The same probability appeared on three surfaces: the odds panel, the result card, and the guidance card on the main screen. The guidance card rounded to a whole number, so it said "The Tribulation is open at 100%" directly beside a panel showing 99.6.

Two screens showing different numbers for the same fact are worse than either number alone, because the player now has to decide which one the game believes. Every place that shows a tribulation chance now goes through one display function. The chronicle also writes odds in the player's own number format, since a decimal comma and a decimal point are not interchangeable to someone reading in their language.

If you are preparing for a crossing yourself, the codex entry for the Transcendence Pill covers one of the items made for that moment.

Bonuses cannot pass the ceiling

The third rule came from the list of ways to improve your odds. A talisman adds fifteen points. At 88 percent it was still advertised as plus fifteen, which would make 103. Now each lever is capped at the headroom left under 100, so at 88 the talisman says plus twelve. That is a tiny change and it removes a whole class of "the numbers do not add up" confusion.

The dispatch board got the same scrutiny from the other side, since its chip was only recently relabelled after it turned out to be a power ratio rather than a probability. The guide to dispatching disciples on errands explains what that board is for.

The third question a return screen should answer

A different kind of number from the same window. When you come back after time away, the summary used to answer two questions: what happened while you were gone, and what changed. It never answered the one players act on, which is what they can now afford.

Time away pays levels, levels pay insight, and insight buys skill tree nodes. So after a gap that paid levels, the return toast and the panel now say how many nodes are within reach, using the same check the tree itself uses to decide whether a node can be bought. "You can now learn four nodes" is a reason to open the game's most important screen. A list of totals is not.

A smaller promise in the text

One more broken promise, of a different sort. Onboarding lets you pick a name and a face, several of the faces are women, and it never asks your gender. Eighteen quest strings still called the player a woodcutter's son, a village boy, him. They now say child, youth, novice, them. The Chinese text keeps its own narrator idiom, which reads differently there. The keystone nodes guide is a good next read if those newly affordable nodes made you curious.

The short version

Round odds towards uncertainty at both ends. Format them in exactly one place. Cap every bonus at the ceiling it can actually reach. And when a screen reports what happened, end with what the player can do about it now.

Check the odds yourself before your first storm: it is free to play in the browser.

title: RC Prediction: A Python Package for Parameter-Aware Reservoir Computing
description:
arXiv:2610.40984v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A nonlinear dynamical system can be characterized by the autonomous evolution of its state in time and its dependence on system parameters. As a parameter varies, the dynamics can change quantitatively and, at bifurcation points, qualitatively. When the governing equations are unknown, a data-driven model should therefore capture both elements from observational data, rather than reproduce the dynamics at a single operating condition only. Parameter-aware reservoir computing (PARC) is a model-free framework for this purpose, where the parameter is supplied to a reservoir computer through an additional input channel. PARC is trained on time series recorded at several parameter values, and the trained reservoir, run in closed loop as an autonomous dynamical system, generates trajectories at parameter values that were never observed. rc_prediction is an open-source Python package that implements this workflow. It provides multi-parameter training of a reservoir, autonomous closed-loop prediction at user-specified parameter values, parameter scans, and a standard echo state network for forecasting at a fixed parameter. Hyperparameter optimization and optional GPU acceleration through PyTorch are also provided. We use three benchmark dynamical systems as examples to demonstrate its usage. As one of the featured applications, here we illustrate the prediction of critical transitions and system collapse: trained only on pre-critical data, the model is queried beyond the training range to predict whether the system collapses, to estimate the critical parameter $p_c^{*}$, and to characterize transient lifetimes.

title: Task-Performance Routing for Multi-Teacher Distillation in CT Medical Image Segmentation
description:
arXiv:2610.41362v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Pre-trained models offer complementary strengths in CT organ segmentation, but their relative accuracy varies across organs and spatial regions. Multi-teacher knowledge distillation can combine these strengths in a single student, yet global or instance-level teacher weights overlook variation within a 3D volume. We propose Task-Performance Routing (TPR), which uses region-wise segmentation errors to determine teacher weights during training without learned routing parameters. In hard regions, TPR favors teachers with lower prediction errors; in easy regions, it uses uniform weights to combine their knowledge. A hierarchical spatial partition provides fine-grained routing in shallow encoder stages and coarse-grained routing in deep stages. Experiments on BTCV, MSD-Liver, and MSD-Pancreas with two teacher pairs and two backbone architectures show higher Dice scores than the individual teachers, adaptive ensembles, and evaluated multi-teacher distillation baselines. On MSD-Pancreas, TPR achieves Dice scores of 65.40% with SwinUNETR and 68.25% with U-Net, compared with 64.38% and 67.45% for the corresponding adaptive ensembles. Inference uses the student alone, with no routing or teacher overhead. Code is available at https://github.com/EdvinCecilia/TPR_MultiTeacher.

title: Before We Adapt: The Zero-Shot Generalization Bottleneck in Continual World Models
description:
arXiv:2610.41041v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Continual reinforcement learning (CRL) requires agents to operate under environmental changes while reusing prior knowledge whenever possible. We argue that model-based reinforcement learning provides a promising framework for this setting because learned world models (WMs) can, in principle, support change detection, knowledge reuse, adaptation, and acquisition of new knowledge. However, such benefits depend heavily on whether the learned model can generalize beyond the contexts in which it was trained. In this work, we propose to formulate this problem with a contextual Markov decision process in which context is decomposed into behavioral and physical components. This view organizes continual WM learning into reuse, adaptation, and acquisition of new knowledge. As a first step, we study direct reuse when behavioral rules remain unchanged. Using Dyna-Q and TD-MPC in controlled FourRooms tasks, we find that zero-shot reuse can degrade substantially under physical-context changes and that this behavior depends strongly on the observation representation used by the WM. Additional ablation studies and latent-space diagnostics suggest that learned representations do not automatically provide the invariances needed for reuse. These results identify representation generalization as an important bottleneck for reliable world-model reuse in CRL.

title: Announcing MCP support in Apigee hybrid: agentic tools that run in your own cluster
description: Apigee hybrid 1.17.0 introduces native Model Context Protocol (MCP) support, enabling the MCP data plane to run directly within your own Kubernetes cluster. This architecture ensures that AI agent request traffic and tool execution remain entirely inside your infrastructure while pulling configuration updates from the control plane. Developers can expose OpenAPI 3.0.x specifications as discoverable MCP tools, leverage existing security policies and API products, and trace end-to-end requests using W3C trace context headers.

title: Glyph Cluster is now available in stealth for free on AI Gateway
description:
Early access to Glyph Cluster is now available on AI Gateway for teams on a Pro or Enterprise plan with purchased AI Gateway credits. Usage is free during the stealth period.

Glyph Cluster is a reasoning model for coding and long-context analysis, with a 256K-token context window. Use it to review code, debug failures, plan implementation changes, solve quantitative problems, or compare information across long inputs.

It accepts text only and supports streaming and function calling with tools you define. Image and file inputs and structured outputs are not supported.

This model doesn't support Zero Data Retention. Prompts and responses may be retained and used for training and model improvement.

Use stealth/glyph-cluster as the model ID in the AI SDK, Chat Completions, or Responses API, or select it in a connected coding agent. Set AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY for the API examples below.

Try Glyph Cluster in the model playground.

title: La meilleure alternative à Fiddler
description:
Fiddler a gagné deux décennies de bonne volonté en tant que proxy de débogage Windows gratuit : il montrait chaque requête émise par votre machine, depuis n'importe quelle application, déchiffrée. Ce Fiddler s'appelle désormais Fiddler Classic, et la page de Telerik décrit son état sans détour : Windows uniquement, usage non commercial uniquement, mode maintenance, avec « aucun engagement pour les versions, correctifs ou support technique ». Le successeur pris en charge, Fiddler Everywhere, est multiplateforme et actif, mais c'est un abonnement : selon la page de tarification Telerik, Lite est à 7 $ par utilisateur et par mois en facturation annuelle (10 $ en mensuel), Pro à 13 $ (19 $ en mensuel) et Enterprise à 37 $, annuel uniquement. Il y a un essai de 10 jours et aucun niveau gratuit.

Essayez Apidog dès aujourd'hui

Le « Fiddler gratuit » a donc disparu pour quiconque l'utilise au travail, et la question honnête du remplacement se divise en deux. Fiddler est un proxy MITM à l'échelle du système, et Apidog n'en est pas un — cet article ne prétendra pas le contraire. Mais regardez comment la plupart des développeurs utilisaient réellement Fiddler : composer des requêtes contre leur propre API, inspecter les réponses, simuler un backend avec des règles AutoResponder. C'est du travail de client API déguisé en proxy, et pour cette part du travail, Apidog est l'outil conçu pour cela : un client de requêtes complet, un serveur mock intelligent à la place des règles AutoResponder, des points de terminaison documentés, des tests automatisés, gratuit jusqu'à 4 utilisateurs. Pour une véritable capture de trafic, les bonnes réponses sont les outils de capture comme mitmproxy, nommés honnêtement plus bas.

Qu'est-il arrivé à Fiddler

Deux produits partagent maintenant ce nom, et aucun n'est l'ancien contrat.

Fiddler Classic reste un téléchargement gratuit, mais lisez les petits caractères : usage non commercial uniquement, Windows uniquement, mode maintenance sans versions, correctifs ou support promis. Il est antérieur à HTTP/2 et à gRPC. Si vous déboguez des API d'entreprise avec, vous êtes hors licence ; si vous êtes sur Mac ou Linux, vous n'avez jamais fait partie du club.

Fiddler Everywhere est la version sur laquelle Telerik veut les professionnels : macOS, Linux et Windows, avec support HTTP/2, WebSockets, gRPC et SSE. Il a conservé les deux moitiés de l'ancien flux de travail : Compose Requests pour créer et enregistrer des appels API, et un moteur de règles (le successeur d'AutoResponder) pour modifier le trafic et simuler des réponses. Le piège, c'est le compteur. Les règles de modification du trafic et la collaboration d'équipe sont sur Pro à 13 $ par utilisateur et par mois ; Lite à 7 $ couvre la capture et l'inspection ; les contrôles Enterprise coûtent 37 $. Dix jours d'essai, puis la facture commence.

Rien de tout cela n'est un scandale ; maintenir un proxy de déchiffrement multiplateforme est un vrai travail. Mais cela change le calcul : vous ne décidez plus si vous gardez un outil gratuit, vous décidez quel outil payant mérite la place — et cela dépend du travail Fiddler que vous faisiez réellement.

Les deux tâches cachées dans Fiddler

Soyez précis sur votre propre usage avant de choisir un remplacement, car Fiddler regroupait deux tâches différentes :

Tâche 1 : capture de trafic. Vous devez voir les requêtes que vous ne contrôlez pas : les appels d'une application de bureau, l'API non documentée d'une application mobile, une session de navigateur déchiffrée. Cela nécessite un proxy MITM à l'échelle du système, avec installation de certificat. Apidog ne fait pas ce travail, et aucun client API ne le fait.

Tâche 2 : travail sur API. Vous construisez ou consommez une API que vous contrôlez. Vous composiez des requêtes, inspectiez les réponses, écriviez des règles AutoResponder pour que le front-end puisse se développer contre de fausses réponses, et rejouiez des sessions pour reproduire des bugs. Rien de tout cela n'a besoin d'un proxy ; cela a besoin d'une plateforme API. C'est là que la plupart des heures quotidiennes de Fiddler étaient réellement consacrées, et c'est pourquoi l'abonnement Everywhere pique : vous payez des prix de proxy pour du travail de client.

Si votre usage est principalement la Tâche 1, passez à la section des outils de capture. Si c'est principalement la Tâche 2, continuez à lire ; c'est le travail pour lequel Apidog a été conçu. (Pour le paysage plus large, voir outils de capture de paquets et Apidog.)

La réponse : Apidog

Apidog est une plateforme de développement API utilisée par plus de 500 000 développeurs : conception, débogage, test, simulation et documentation dans une seule application, pilotée par une seule spécification. Pour un ancien utilisateur de Fiddler, quatre choses comptent :

  1. Le Composer, adulte. Les Compose Requests de Fiddler construisent des appels ponctuels. Le client de requêtes d'Apidog couvre HTTP, WebSocket, SSE, gRPC et GraphQL, avec des environnements, des assistants d'authentification, des cookies, du scripting et de la génération de code — et chaque requête que vous enregistrez peut devenir un point de terminaison documenté avec un schéma, au lieu d'une ligne dans un journal de session.
  2. Les règles AutoResponder deviennent un serveur mock. C'est l'histoire de migration la plus solide, cartographiée concrètement ci-dessous. Au lieu d'une liste de règles locale faisant correspondre des URL et renvoyant des fichiers préenregistrés, le mock intelligent d'Apidog sert des réponses fausses conscientes du schéma depuis une URL réelle que toute votre équipe et la CI peuvent atteindre, sans aucune règle à écrire pour le cas par défaut.
  3. Le replay devient des tests de régression. Réémettre manuellement une session enregistrée se transforme en scénarios de test visuels : requêtes enchaînées, assertions, validation de schéma, exécutions pilotées par les données, lancées selon un calendrier ou en CI via l'Apidog CLI.
  4. Le prix est nul pour les petites équipes. Le plan gratuit couvre jusqu'à 4 utilisateurs, avec des exécutions illimitées, la simulation et des documents publiés. Les plans payants commencent à 9 $ par utilisateur et par mois, dans la même fourchette qu'un seul siège Fiddler Everywhere Pro.

À quoi ressemble le changement, fonctionnalité par fonctionnalité

Composer et inspecter des requêtes

Le travail quotidien sur les requêtes se traduit directement : construisez la requête, envoyez-la, inspectez le statut, les en-têtes, le corps et le timing. Apidog ajoute ce qu'une session proxy n'a jamais eu : des dossiers et des environnements au lieu d'un journal de capture, une validation de schéma pour qu'une charge utile erronée échoue bruyamment, et un historique que vous pouvez transformer en documentation. Ce que vous perdez, c'est la capture passive du trafic d'autres applications ; c'est la Tâche 1, et cela reste avec un proxy. Si votre habitude de capture était « regarder mon propre front-end appeler ma propre API », les DevTools du navigateur plus un client de requêtes est le chemin le plus léger — le même modèle que nous décrivons dans comment installer et utiliser Postman Interceptor.

Des règles AutoResponder aux mocks intelligents

Voici la cartographie concrète. Une configuration typique d'AutoResponder Fiddler pour le travail front-end :

EXACT:https://api.example.com~ (fichier local sur disque)

Puis une règle par point de terminaison, Fiddler à garder en cours d'exécution, et l'espoir que personne d'autre n'ait besoin du même backend factice sur sa machine.

Dans Apidog : définissez le point de terminaison GET ~, sans règle écrite. Besoin d'une charge utile fixe ? Attachezusers-42.json` comme exemple de réponse. Besoin que l'id 42 renvoie 200 et que l'id 99 renvoie 404 ? Ajoutez des attentes qui correspondent aux paramètres. Cela couvre chaque modèle AutoResponder (fichier statique, faux par point de terminaison, réponse conditionnelle) avec trois améliorations : le mock est partagé par URL au lieu d'être piégé dans le proxy d'une seule machine, il reste synchronisé avec la spécification, et il ne fait pas passer tout le trafic de votre système par un intercepteur juste pour simuler une API.

Tests, documentation et spécification

C'est un saut de catégorie plutôt qu'une traduction. Les sessions Fiddler meurent avec la fenêtre ; les points de terminaison Apidog s'accumulent dans une définition d'API qui génère des documents interactifs sur votre domaine, des mocks pour les consommateurs et des scénarios de test pour la CI. Si l'ensemble de comparaison réel de votre équipe est Postman ou Insomnia plutôt que Fiddler, nous avons fait ces face-à-face dans la meilleure alternative à Postman et la meilleure alternative à Insomnia.

Fiddler vs Apidog en un coup d'œil

Fiddler Classic Fiddler Everywhere Apidog
Prix Gratuit, non commercial uniquement 7 $/13 $/37 $ par utilisateur/mois (annuel) Gratuit jusqu'à 4 utilisateurs ; payant à partir de 9 $
Plateformes Windows uniquement Windows, macOS, Linux Windows, macOS, Linux, web
Statut Mode maintenance Actif Actif
Capture de trafic à l'échelle du système Oui Oui Non
Composer des requêtes API Composer de base Compose Requests Client complet : HTTP, WebSocket, SSE, gRPC, GraphQL
Simulation de réponse Règles AutoResponder, local Moteur de règles (niveau Pro), local Serveur mock intelligent conscient du schéma, URL partagée, gratuit
Points de terminaison enregistrés et documentés Non Sessions et requêtes enregistrées Points de terminaison basés sur une spécification avec documents publiés
Tests automatisés Non Basé sur le replay Scénarios visuels, assertions, pilotés par les données, CI
Exécutions CLI / CI Non Non Gratuit via Apidog CLI
Collaboration d'équipe Non Niveau Pro Plan gratuit, 4 utilisateurs

Le calcul des sièges, honnêtement

Une équipe de 5 personnes qui veut des règles de trafic et de la collaboration a besoin de Fiddler Everywhere Pro : 13 $ × 5 × 12 = 780 $ par an. La même équipe faisant du travail API dans Apidog paie 0 $ pour 4 sièges, plus 108 $ pour le cinquième à 9 $ par mois — soit 540 $ par an dans le scénario où tout le monde paie, toujours en dessous de la facture Fiddler. Mais le cadre plus juste est l'adéquation, pas le prix : ces sièges Fiddler achètent une capture de trafic dont le travail API n'a pas besoin, et n'achètent pas la spécification, la documentation, les mocks partagés ou les tests CI dont il a besoin. Payez des prix de proxy uniquement pour les personnes qui déboguent réellement du trafic étranger.

Pour une véritable capture de trafic, utilisez un outil de capture

Quand la tâche est l'interception MITM, choisissez un proxy ; ne forcez pas un client API dans ce rôle :

  • mitmproxy : gratuit, open source, multiplateforme ; console, interface web et scripting Python ; la réponse par défaut quand « remplacement gratuit de Fiddler » signifie la partie proxy.
  • Charles Proxy : licence payante unique ; choix de longue date pour le débogage d'applications mobiles, avec limitation et règles de réécriture. Il a ses propres questions d'outil vieillissant, que nous couvrons dans la meilleure alternative à Charles Proxy.
  • HTTP Toolkit : open core, interception en un clic de navigateurs, terminaux et conteneurs Docker spécifiques plutôt que du système entier ; la configuration la plus douce du groupe.
  • Proxyman : macOS natif (avec support des appareils iOS) ; le choix poli pour les équipes centrées Apple.

Un proxy de capture plus Apidog est une pile cohérente : le proxy pour la rare chasse au trafic étranger, Apidog pour le travail API quotidien. Pour démêler les proxys de débogage de l'autre type, voir Proxy API vs passerelle API expliqué.

Quand Fiddler a encore du sens

Fiddler Everywhere est le bon outil si la capture déchiffrée à l'échelle du système est votre travail quotidien et que vous voulez un produit commercial pris en charge derrière ; 13 $ par mois est raisonnable pour cela. Fiddler Classic reste défendable pour le débogage de loisir sur une machine Windows personnelle, licence et tout. Et les vétérans de FiddlerScript, avec des années de règles personnalisées, ont des coûts de changement qu'aucun bouton d'importation n'efface. Le passage à Apidog porte ses fruits dès que votre usage de Fiddler est principalement le Composer et AutoResponder : lorsque vous simulez votre propre backend via un proxy système, un serveur mock avec une URL est simplement la meilleure forme.

Questions fréquemment posées

Fiddler est-il encore gratuit ?

Fiddler Classic est gratuit mais restreint : usage non commercial uniquement, Windows uniquement, mode maintenance. Fiddler Everywhere n'a pas de niveau gratuit, seulement un essai de 10 jours, puis de 7 $ à 37 $ par utilisateur et par mois. Pour le travail API commercial sur un plan gratuit, voir le paysage des meilleures alternatives à Postman ou commencez avec le plan gratuit 4 utilisateurs d'Apidog.

Apidog peut-il capturer tout le trafic HTTP de mon système comme Fiddler ?

Non. Apidog est une plateforme de développement API, pas un proxy MITM à l'échelle du système, et nous ne prétendrons pas le contraire. Pour déchiffrer le trafic arbitraire d'applications ou mobiles, utilisez mitmproxy, Charles, HTTP Toolkit ou Proxyman ; notre guide des outils de capture de paquets les compare et montre où chacun s'intègre aux côtés d'Apidog.

Qu'est-ce qui remplace l'AutoResponder de Fiddler dans Apidog ?

Le serveur mock intelligent. Définissez ou importez un point de terminaison et Apidog sert immédiatement des réponses fausses basées sur un schéma à une URL mock partagée ; attachez des exemples pour des charges utiles fixes et des attentes pour des cas conditionnels. Contrairement aux règles AutoResponder, les mocks vivent avec la spécification et fonctionnent pour les coéquipiers et la CI sans que personne n'exécute un proxy, et ils s'exécutent dans votre pipeline via l'Apidog CLI.

Comment déplacer mon flux de travail Fiddler dans Apidog ?

Importez le fichier OpenAPI de votre API pour que chaque point de terminaison arrive avec schémas, documents et mocks en direct en une fois, puis portez les règles AutoResponder comme exemples de réponse et attentes. Les archives de session SAZ de Fiddler ne sont pas un format de collection : traitez donc le déménagement comme l'importation de votre spécification, pas de votre historique de capture.

Fiddler Everywhere est-il identique à Fiddler Classic ?

Non. Everywhere est un produit d'abonnement multiplateforme réécrit ; Classic est le freeware Windows figé, et Telerik oriente les utilisateurs commerciaux vers Everywhere. Pour la même bifurcation dans l'outil voisin, voir la meilleure alternative à Charles Proxy.

Arrêtez de payer des prix de proxy pour le travail API

Si Fiddler était votre composeur de requêtes et votre faux backend, déplacez ce travail vers l'outil conçu pour cela. Importez votre spécification OpenAPI, obtenez des points de terminaison documentés avec des mocks intelligents en direct en quelques minutes, et câblez les tests dans la CI. Téléchargez Apidog ou commencez dans le navigateur ; une équipe de 4 ne paie rien, et les règles AutoResponder que vous avez surveillées deviennent des URL mock que vous pouvez partager.

title: Beyond Response Scoring: An AI-aware Cognitive Supervision Framework for Automated Mathematical Short Answer Grading
description:
arXiv:2610.41215v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Transformer-based language models have achieved remarkable success in automated short answer grading (ASAG). However, current methods in ASAG struggle to comprehend, reason about and evaluate complex mathematical answers involving symbols and formulas. These score-only methods fail to generalize across diverse responses and skill states associated with identical scores. Moreover, they ignore the potential upward bias introduced by generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) usage in assessing students' performance and knowledge mastery. To address these limitations, we propose AICG (AI-aware Cognitive-supervised Grading), a two-branch multi-task framework. The first branch combines RoBERTa-based regression, ordinal, and classification heads for individual-answer grading. The second branch uses an expert-designed Q-matrix to associate responses with assessed skills and jointly predicts G-DINA-derived skill mastery and learning gain. Through the shared encoder, these skill-level targets provide cognitive supervision for answer grading beyond score labels. AICG further uses a Gen-AI detector, trained through supervised contrastive pretraining followed by linear classification, to estimate assistance probabilities and convert them into reliability weights, attenuating unreliable cognitive evidence during learning assessment. We conduct experiments on 49,402 instructor-graded responses spanning 19 academic semesters. Relative to RoBERTa regression, AICG reduces mean absolute error (MAE) by 50.3% and improves quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) from 0.798 to 0.927. Ablations identify Q-matrix-guided cognitive supervision as the primary source of improvement, while AI-aware weighting further reduces overall MAE by 4.2% over the unweighted cognitive model and consistently improves MAE and QWK across the four most recent post-Gen-AI semesters.

title: How Rillet ships 3× faster with AI agents on Vercel
description:
Rillet on Vercel

  • Tripled shipping rate in three months with eve agents deployed on Vercel

  • Two-person team closed 800+ Linear tickets in its first 4 months

  • Builder access via Enterprise Managed Users, SSO, and Directory Sync

  • Ships customer-requested changes to production in as little as two hours

  • Gives every builder access to models through AI Gateway

Rillet is an AI-native enterprise resource planning (ERP) platform. Their AI agents do accounting work inside a real-time general ledger, with human approval and a full audit trail. Rillet serves more than 600 customers working toward a zero-day close, reducing the time needed to close their books at month-end.

A product that helps customers close their books in near real time needs a team that can respond quickly to their requests. Anthony Liang heads Rillet’s two-person frontend team, formed only a few months ago, and leads the push to put agents to work across internal workflows, from shipping customer fixes to reviewing code.

The team builds agents with eve and runs them on Vercel, using Vercel Connect to give them access to Slack and Linear, while AI Gateway routes their model requests.

Standardizing every internal agent on eve

Anthony had been building AI applications since the GPT-3.5 era and had evaluated nearly every agent framework on the market, from the major model providers' SDKs to the open-source ecosystem. Each gave him primitives for the model loop but left him to decide where instructions lived, how tools registered, and how an agent reached Slack and GitHub.

Anthony could make those choices for his own agents, but he wanted conventions everyone at Rillet could follow, including people who had never touched TypeScript.

An agent is a directory

Anthony chose eve, Vercel's open-source agent framework for building, running, and scaling agents that keeps instructions, tools, and skills together in one directory.

People who know what an agent should do can shape its behavior through markdown instructions and skills without writing code, while its tools live in TypeScript files whose names become the API. Once an agent is ready, it can move from a laptop to Vercel without changing how it behaves. Rillet manages all of these deployments in one company-controlled Vercel organization.

Rillet uses Vercel Connect to give its agents access to Slack and Linear through reusable connections the team can attach to the projects that need them. Connect supplies short-lived tokens at runtime and handles refresh through its SDK, keeping long-lived provider secrets out of each application and giving builders fewer credentials to maintain. If a runtime token leaks, its expiration limits how long it can be used.

Anthony's team built a Slack bot that picks up tickets and opens PRs, while others run agents for incident analysis and Linear board management. Shared conventions make that work easier to reuse, and agent building has spread beyond engineering.

Running customer requests through agents, end to end

Before, when a customer would ask for a change, and the request would scatter across a Linear ticket, a Slack thread, and a catch-up conversation with an engineer. By the time anyone had the full context, the fastest part of the job was writing the code.

The person closest to the customer ships the fix

Rillet's customer success team now opens a Chrome extension alongside the Rillet app, highlights what the customer is seeing, and describes the change. The extension's eve agent captures the context and, if the change is safe and well-scoped, hands it to a coding agent that writes the spec, makes the change, and opens a pull request assigned to Anthony. Agents also spin up a browser in a sandbox to test the change and attach screenshots as proof, while Anthony reviews the pull request and merges it. If he requests changes, the agent resumes its session and addresses them.

Rillet's CEO recently posted that the company shipped more in the past few weeks than in the entire first half of 2026, on top of tripling its shipping rate over the prior three months. Rillet’s CPA team ships customer requests through its in-house agent, Nebula, within two hours of the ask. As one of their customers put it, Rillet has "completely ruined my expectations" for how quickly software vendors should make changes.

Using AI Gateway to give every builder every model

As more people at Rillet started building agents, connecting directly to Anthropic and OpenAI meant configuring access to each model provider separately. AI Gateway routes model requests to both through one integration, so builders can add an agent without setting up separate provider connections.

The model is a string

In eve, builders choose the model by setting a string in the agent’s configuration:

Agents deployed on Vercel authenticate to AI Gateway automatically. Builders can try different models for a task by changing the model string, without changing the integration. Usage breakdowns show Anthony which models the team uses and what they cost, helping him track spending and choose models as more people build autonomous agents.

Managing builder access through Enterprise Managed Users

As more people are building agents, Rillet also needs to manage their access to Vercel. With Enterprise Managed Users, builders sign in through Google Workspace single sign-on using company-managed accounts rather than personal ones. Directory Sync adds and removes their access based on assignments in Rillet’s identity provider, so account administration follows the company’s directory.

Rillet set up Enterprise Managed Users on its own and moved builders from personal to company-managed accounts in one transition, bringing their Vercel sign-in and account access under Rillet’s identity provider.

What's next

Anthony is building what Rillet thinks of as its agent factory, so bigger features can follow the same pipeline as small fixes. One agent writes PRDs and technical specs, while another connects to Rillet's Linear boards, Miro diagrams, and knowledge base to give other agents the context they need. With subagents and delegation built into eve, Anthony can add these specialized agents as directories within the same framework.

For a company whose mission is collapsing month-long processes into zero days, building agents in eve and running them on Vercel brings that same focus on speed to its internal tooling.

About Rillet: Rillet is the AI-native ERP built for the era of agentic finance. By combining a real-time general ledger, continuous close architecture, and AI agents in one system, Rillet enables humans and agents to run finance together with full context, controls, and auditability.

  • Fixed an issue where audit-proxy retried audit log exports indefinitely on permanent errors, generating excessive audit logging traffic.
  • Fixed an issue where the Kubernetes preflight health check scanned all namespaces in the admin cluster instead of the target cluster's namespace, causing cluster upgrades to fail if an unrelated cluster had stale reconciling resources.

If you use a third-party storage vendor, check the listing of our previously-qualified storage partners.

Fixed

The following issues were fixed in 1.35.600-gke.140:

  • Fixed vulnerabilities listed in Vulnerability fixes.
  • Improved containerd resilience against state corruption if a node reboots while unpacking container images.
  • Fixed an issue where the periodic configuration drift health check failed with a version not supported error while a cluster upgrade or rollback was in progress.
  • Fixed an issue where audit-proxy retried audit log exports indefinitely on permanent errors, generating excessive audit logging traffic.
  • Fixed an issue where the Kubernetes preflight health check scanned all namespaces in the admin cluster instead of the target cluster's namespace, causing cluster upgrades to fail if an unrelated cluster had stale reconciling resources.
  • Fixed an issue where upgrading or recreating a node during maintenance mode could proceed before storage volumes finished detaching, resulting in orphaned CSI VolumeAttachment resources or I/O errors. After the fix, node drain verifies that kubelet unmounts all host volumes and that CSI VolumeAttachment resources detach before completing the drain.
  • Fixed an issue where Certificate Authority (CA) rotation failed for self-managing clusters (admin, hybrid, and standalone). The failure occurs during the final phase of the rotation when attempting to move management resources back from the temporary bootstrap cluster to the self-managing cluster, which can leave the cluster in an unmanageable state. You must upgrade your clusters to version 1.35.600-gke.140 before you rotate your CAs.
  • Fixed an issue where BareMetalMachine status conditions prematurely reported nodes as ready and available during maintenance mode transitions.
  • Fixed an issue in clusters using bundled BGP load balancing where control plane upgrades or configuration updates could cause up to 20 seconds of API server connection failures while a control plane node restarted. title: Corroborative Learning: Mutual Enhancement through Task-Response Reconstruction
description:
arXiv:2610.41222v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In pattern analysis, models trained independently for the same task often develop complementary capabilities through differences in architecture, data, and optimization. Exploiting complementarity while retaining independent deployment is central to collaborative learning. Most methods establish transfer by reducing differences in predictions, relations, or representations between target and collaborator, although these differences also underlie complementarity. This creates a structural trade-off between reducing differences for knowledge exchange and preserving them for complementarity. We therefore propose Corroborative Learning (CL). Each model forms task-driven responses, with cross-group support from its collaborator. Source-excluded reconstruction of response increments from collaborator representations separates fitting and evaluation across disjoint groups and selectively constrains directions by cross-group reconstructability. The process requires no direct output or feature matching or additional inference dependency. Furthermore, with linear reconstruction and fixed collaborator representations, the loss equals a positive semidefinite directional regularizer, constraining less reconstructable directions more strongly. Signal and noise conditions characterize when directional shrinkage reduces response-estimation error. Across six language tasks, 24 models, and 36 pairs, CL improves over capacity-matched independent adaptation on every task, with positive gains across most directed model combinations. Pairwise comparisons show broad advantages over transfer and mutual-learning methods and different gains from complementarity across collaboration rules. Low-label language and vision results support cross-domain applicability. Task-relevant differences can support mutual enhancement without eliminating disagreement.

title: Safin-1.5: Safety-Native Architecture and Verifiable Reasoning for Recursive Safety Improvement
description:
arXiv:2610.40751v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) enables large language models to advance their capabilities through successive updates, but these updates can also introduce new risks and weaken existing safeguards. In line with the AI-45{\deg} Law, we pursue Safety RSI, in which safety develops as an intrinsic capability alongside general model capabilities through continual risk discovery and repair, while preserving utility and limiting over-refusal. We introduce Safin-1.5, a model built on a safety architecture and trained through recursive safety improvement, with an inference-time harness that extends its capabilities to formal reasoning. Our approach comprises three components: i) The safety architecture combines persistent safety states with hazardous-knowledge disentanglement. The former retains and selectively invokes safety knowledge, while the latter relocates targeted hazardous knowledge into removable experts, enabling its removal with minimal impact on general capabilities. ii) Recursive safety improvement establishes a discovery-evaluation-repair loop. The loop identifies new vulnerabilities and uses experimental feedback to develop repair strategies. It accepts updates only when they improve safety while preserving general capabilities and limiting over-refusal. iii) The formal reasoning harness combines the model's language understanding with symbolic inference and verification. Proof-obligation-guided semantic bridging recovers missing relations in formal representations, enabling symbolic solvers to construct checkable proofs under formalized premises and accepted semantic bridges. Experimental results demonstrate that Safin-1.5 achieves safety and reasoning performance, outperforming frontier models.

title: SQL Server'da yavaş sorgu nasıl hızlandırılır?
description:
POS hareketlerini listeleyen bir endpoint'imiz vardı. Tabloya her gün milyonlarca satır ekleniyordu ve ekranın en sık kullanılan hâli gün bazlı sorguydu: bir işyerinin belli günlerdeki hareketleri, sayfa sayfa. Bu sorgu dakikalar sürüyordu. CreatedDate kolonunda indeks vardı, ama sorgu onu kullanmıyor gibiydi.

Dört değişiklikle sorgu dakikalardan saniyelere indi. Bu yazı için o dört adımı 10 milyon satırlık sentetik bir tabloda yeniden ölçtüm. Ölçümlerden biri, o gün suçladığımız şeyin asıl suçlu olmadığını gösterdi.

Kısa cevap: SQL Server'da yavaş bir listeleme sorgusunu hızlandırırken önce indeksin gerçekten kullanılıp kullanılmadığına bak. Kolona uygulanan fonksiyonlar (CONVERT, DATEDIFF) indeksi devre dışı bırakır; filtrelediğin kolonlar için bileşik indeks gerekir. Derin sayfalarda OFFSET atlanan her satırı okur; cursor (keyset) sayfalama her sayfada aynı maliyettedir. Geniş listelerde önce yalnızca Id'leri seç, kolonları sonra getir. Join'deki bir CTE her satır için yeniden çalışabilir; ara sonucu temp tabloya almak bunu bir kez çalışır hâle getirir.

Ölçüm düzeneği

Gerçek tabloyu ve verisini kullanamam, o yüzden benzerini kurdum. PosHareketleri tablosunda 10 milyon satır var: 30 gün, günde yaklaşık 330 bin hareket. Yanında işyerleri (20 bin), terminaller (60 bin) ve iadeler (200 bin) duruyor. CreatedDate kolonunda tek kolonlu bir indeks var. Bizim tablomuz 30-40 kolondu; buradaki 10 kolon, yani gerçekte farklar daha da büyür.

Ortam SQL Server 2022 Express. Sorgular uygulamanın göndereceği gibi parametreli (sp_executesql), her biri iki kez çalışıyor ve ikincisi sayılıyor; yani önbellek sıcak.

Süreyi raporluyorum ama asıl baktığım sayı mantıksal okuma (logical reads): sorgunun okuduğu 8 KB'lık sayfa sayısı. Süre makineye, önbelleğe ve o anki yüke göre oynar; okuma sayısı oynamaz. İkisini de şöyle açarsın:

SET STATISTICS IO, TIME ON;
-- sorgu
SET STATISTICS IO, TIME OFF;

Messages sekmesinde her tablo için logical reads ve sorgunun CPU ve geçen süresi görünür. Yanına gerçek çalışma planını (actual execution plan, SSMS'te Ctrl+M) açarsan hangi operatörün bu okumaları yaptığını da görürsün.

Tarih filtresi: kolona fonksiyon uygulamak

Gün bazlı sorguda tarih filtresi CreatedDate'i güne çeviriyordu:

WHERE IsyeriId = @isyeri
  AND CAST(CreatedDate AS date) BETWEEN @bas AND @bit

Bir kolona fonksiyon uyguladığında veritabanı genellikle o kolonun indeksinde arama (seek) yapamaz. İndeks CreatedDate'in kendisine göre sıralı; CAST(CreatedDate AS date) ya da CONVERT(char(8), CreatedDate, 112) sonucuna göre değil. Bu durumda her satır için fonksiyonu hesaplayıp sonucu karşılaştırmak zorunda kalır. Bu tür koşullara sargable olmayan (non-sargable) koşul denir.

Biz bunu düzelttik: gelen tarihleri bir gün kaydırıp aralık olarak yazdık.

WHERE IsyeriId = @isyeri
  AND CreatedDate >= @bas
  AND CreatedDate <  DATEADD(day, 1, @bit)

Bu yazı için ölçerken şunu gördüm: SQL Server CAST(... AS date) için bir istisna yapıyor. Kolonu date'e çevirmeyi tanıyor ve indekste yine aralık araması yapabiliyor. Tek günlük, ilk 50 satırlık sorguda dört farklı yazımın sonucu:

Filtre Okuma Süre
CAST(CreatedDate AS date) = @gun 203 ~1 ms
CreatedDate >= @gun AND CreatedDate < @gun + 1 gün 215 ~0 ms
DATEDIFF(day, CreatedDate, @gun) = 0 14.112 1.038 ms
CONVERT(char(8), CreatedDate, 112) = ... 169.934 2.066 ms

DATEDIFF indeksi baştan sona tarıyor, CONVERT bütün tabloyu okuyor. CAST ise aralıkla neredeyse aynı. Yani bizim sorgudaki asıl yük CAST değildi.

Aralıkla yazmak yine de doğru alışkanlık. CAST istisnası SQL Server'a özgü ve yalnızca date'e çevirmede geçerli; aynı kod başka bir veritabanında ya da başka bir fonksiyonla aynı şansı bulamaz. Aralık her yerde indeksi kullanır.

Asıl fark işyeri filtresinde çıktı. Aynı sorguyu bir işyeri ve yedi gün için üç farklı indeks durumunda çalıştırdım:

İndeks Okuma Süre
Yalnızca CreatedDate 169.934 454-611 ms
CreatedDate + ayrıca IsyeriId 2.044 2 ms
Bileşik (IsyeriId, CreatedDate) 215 1-2 ms

Yalnızca tarih indeksi varken yedi günlük aralık 2,3 milyon satıra denk geliyor. Optimizer bu kadar satır için indeksten tek tek tabloya gitmektense bütün tabloyu taramayı seçiyor; CAST'lı ve aralıklı yazımın ikisi de aynı taramaya düşüyor. Bileşik indekste önce işyerine, sonra o işyerinin tarih aralığına iniliyor ve sorgu yalnızca gösterilecek satırları okuyor.

Bileşik indekste kolon sırası önemli: eşitlikle filtrelenen kolon (IsyeriId) önce, aralıkla filtrelenen kolon (CreatedDate) sonra. Ters sırada indeks yine tarih aralığını tarar, işyerini her satırda ayrıca kontrol eder.

Derin sayfada OFFSET neden yavaşlar

Listede sayfalama vardı, ama yetersizdi. Klasik OFFSET ... FETCH sayfalaması şöyle görünür:

SELECT h.Id, h.CreatedDate, h.Tutar, h.KartMaskeli, i.Ad, t.SeriNo
FROM PosHareketleri h
JOIN Isyerleri i ON i.Id = h.IsyeriId
JOIN Terminaller t ON t.Id = h.TerminalId
WHERE h.CreatedDate >= @bas AND h.CreatedDate < @bit
ORDER BY h.CreatedDate DESC, h.Id DESC
OFFSET @atla ROWS FETCH NEXT 50 ROWS ONLY;

OFFSET 50000 "50 bininci satırdan başla" demek değil, "50 bin satırı oku, at, sonra 50 satır ver" demek. Veritabanının atlanacak satırların yerini bilmesinin başka yolu yok. Sayfa ilerledikçe okunan ve atılan satır sayısı artar.

Bir günün hareketlerinde (yaklaşık 330 bin satır) 50'lik sayfalarla ölçünce:

Sayfa Okuma Süre
1 215 2 ms
100 20.339 21 ms
1.000 203.269 176 ms
6.000 169.934 (tablo taraması) 918 ms

1.000. sayfada işyeri ve terminal tablolarından da 103'er bin okuma var: sorgu atlanacak satırlar için de join yapıyor. 6.000. sayfada optimizer indeksi bırakıp tabloyu taramaya geçiyor. Bizim tablomuz 30-40 kolon olduğu için atılan her satır daha pahalıydı.

Geçici çözümümüz cursor sayfalama oldu. Fikir, "kaçıncı sayfadayım" yerine "en son hangi satırda kaldım" bilgisini taşımak. İstemci bir sonraki sayfayı isterken önceki sayfanın son satırının CreatedDate'ini ve Id'sini gönderir; sorgu oradan devam eder:

SELECT TOP (50) h.Id, h.CreatedDate, h.Tutar, h.KartMaskeli, i.Ad, t.SeriNo
FROM PosHareketleri h
JOIN Isyerleri i ON i.Id = h.IsyeriId
JOIN Terminaller t ON t.Id = h.TerminalId
WHERE h.CreatedDate >= @bas AND h.CreatedDate < @bit
  AND (h.CreatedDate < @sonTarih
       OR (h.CreatedDate = @sonTarih AND h.Id < @sonId))
ORDER BY h.CreatedDate DESC, h.Id DESC;

Bu sorgu indekste doğrudan kaldığı yere iner ve 50 satır okur. Ölçümde her sayfa 220 civarı okuma ve 2-3 ms; 1. sayfayla 6.000. sayfa arasında fark yok.

Bedeli de var: kullanıcı "47. sayfaya git" diyemez, yalnızca ileri ve geri gidebilir. Listede toplam sayfa sayısı gösteriliyorsa onu ayrı bir COUNT ile hesaplamak gerekir. Hareket listesi gibi kullanıcının genellikle baştan aşağı kaydırdığı ekranlarda bu kayıp küçük.

GUID'li tenant'larda cursor

Bizde bazı tenant'ların Id'leri long, bazılarınınki GUID'di. GUID'li tenant'larda Id üzerinden büyüktür/küçüktür yapamıyorduk, o yüzden cursor'dan yalnızca long Id'li tenant'lar yararlanabildi. Aslında sıralama zaten CreatedDate'e göre; Id yalnızca aynı tarihli satırları ayırmaya yarıyor. Bu iş için Id'nin sıralı olması değil, tekil olması ve her seferinde aynı sırayı vermesi yeterli. SQL Server'da GUID'ler de kendi (tuhaf ama tutarlı) sıralarıyla karşılaştırılabildiği için yukarıdaki sorgu GUID'le de çalışır. Tek dikkat: son Id'yi uygulamada karşılaştırma, olduğu gibi SQL'e geri gönder; .NET'teki Guid sıralaması SQL Server'ınkiyle aynı değil.

Önce Id'leri seç, kolonları sonra getir

Cursor'ın kullanılamadığı tenant'lar için başka bir yol bulduk: önce olabildiğince filtreleyip yalnızca Id'leri seçmek, join'leri ve kolonları ikinci adımda yapmak.

WITH sayfa AS (
    SELECT Id, CreatedDate
    FROM PosHareketleri
    WHERE CreatedDate >= @bas AND CreatedDate < @bit
    ORDER BY CreatedDate DESC, Id DESC
    OFFSET @atla ROWS FETCH NEXT 50 ROWS ONLY
)
SELECT h.Id, h.CreatedDate, h.Tutar, h.KartMaskeli, i.Ad, t.SeriNo
FROM sayfa s
JOIN PosHareketleri h ON h.Id = s.Id
JOIN Isyerleri i ON i.Id = h.IsyeriId
JOIN Terminaller t ON t.Id = h.TerminalId
ORDER BY s.CreatedDate DESC, s.Id DESC;

İç sorgu yine OFFSET kullanıyor ve yine atlanan satırları okuyor, ama bunu yalnızca CreatedDate indeksinde yapıyor. İndeks dar: içinde tarih ve Id var, 30-40 kolon yok. Join'ler ve geniş satırlar yalnızca seçilen 50 Id için yapılıyor. Bu kalıba deferred join de deniyor.

Grafik: bir günlük hareketlerde (yaklaşık 330 bin satır, 50 satırlık sayfa) sayfa numarasına göre süre. OFFSET: 1. sayfa 2 ms, 100. sayfa 21 ms, 1.000. sayfa 176 ms, 6.000. sayfa 918 ms. Önce Id, sonra join: 6.000. sayfa 28 ms. Cursor: her sayfa 2-3 ms.

6.000. sayfada OFFSET 918 ms'ten bu yazımla 28 ms'e iniyor, okuma 170 binden 998'e düşüyor. Cursor kadar düz değil ama sayfa numarasına göre gitme imkânını koruyor.

Join'deki CTE her satırda çalışınca

Filtrelenmiş Id'leri önce bir CTE'de toplayıp ana sorguya join'liyorduk. Planı incelediğimizde CTE'nin her satır için yeniden çalıştığını gördük ve temp tabloya geçmek zorunda kaldık.

Sebebi, SQL Server'ın CTE'yi bir ara tablo gibi saklamaması. CTE, sorguya gömülen bir alt sorgudur (inline). Optimizer onu nested loops join'in iç tarafına koyarsa, dış taraftan gelen her satır için o alt sorgu yeniden çalışır. Sentetik tabloda aynı şekli kurdum: bir işyeri aralığı ve bir haftalık hareketlerin Id'leri CTE'de, dışarıda join'ler ve iade toplamı.

WITH secilen AS (
    SELECT h.Id FROM PosHareketleri h
    WHERE h.IsyeriId BETWEEN @isyeriBas AND @isyeriBit
      AND h.CreatedDate >= @bas AND h.CreatedDate < @bit
)
SELECT h.Id, h.CreatedDate, h.Tutar, h.KartMaskeli, i.Ad, t.SeriNo,
       (SELECT SUM(r.IadeTutar) FROM Iadeler r WHERE r.HareketId = h.Id) AS IadeToplam
FROM PosHareketleri h
JOIN Isyerleri i ON i.Id = h.IsyeriId
JOIN Terminaller t ON t.Id = h.TerminalId
WHERE h.Id IN (SELECT Id FROM secilen)
ORDER BY h.CreatedDate DESC
OFFSET 0 ROWS FETCH NEXT 50 ROWS ONLY;

Gerçek planda optimizer dış tarafta tarih indeksini sondan başa tarıyor ve CTE'nin PosHareketleri aramasını her satır için bir kez çalıştırıyor. Plandaki "Number of Executions" değeri 5.002.003. Sonuç 40,6 milyon okuma ve 9 saniye.

Temp tabloyla aynı iş iki adım:

SELECT h.Id, h.CreatedDate
INTO #secilen
FROM PosHareketleri h
WHERE h.IsyeriId BETWEEN @isyeriBas AND @isyeriBit
  AND h.CreatedDate >= @bas AND h.CreatedDate < @bit;

SELECT h.Id, h.CreatedDate, h.Tutar, h.KartMaskeli, i.Ad, t.SeriNo,
       (SELECT SUM(r.IadeTutar) FROM Iadeler r WHERE r.HareketId = h.Id) AS IadeToplam
FROM #secilen s
JOIN PosHareketleri h ON h.Id = s.Id
JOIN Isyerleri i ON i.Id = h.IsyeriId
JOIN Terminaller t ON t.Id = h.TerminalId
ORDER BY h.CreatedDate DESC
OFFSET 0 ROWS FETCH NEXT 50 ROWS ONLY;

Filtre bir kez çalışıyor, sonuç #secilen'e yazılıyor. SQL Server temp tabloya istatistik de oluşturduğu için ikinci sorguda kaç satırla çalışacağını biliyor. İki adım toplam 0,85 saniye; CTE'li hâlin onda biri. Bizde de temp tablo sorguya özeldi; sorgu bitince düşüyordu, ayrıca indeks koymadık.

Temp tablonun bedeli, sorgunun artık tek bir ifade olmaması. ORM'in ürettiği tek bir SELECT ile yapılamıyor; ya ham SQL ya da stored procedure gerekiyor. Ara sonuç çok büyükse tempdb'ye yazmanın maliyeti de hesaba girer.

Kendi sisteminde nasıl fark edersin

Yavaş bir sorguyu SET STATISTICS IO ON ile çalıştır ve okuma sayısını, sorgunun döndürdüğü satır sayısıyla karşılaştır. 50 satır gösteren bir liste için yüz binlerce okuma görüyorsan sorgu ihtiyacından fazlasını okuyor.

Sonra gerçek çalışma planında iki şeye bak: indeks üzerinde Seek yerine Scan olan operatörler ve "Number of Executions" değeri 1'den çok büyük olan operatörler. İlki indeksin kullanılmadığını, ikincisi bir alt sorgunun ya da CTE'nin her satırda yeniden çalıştığını gösterir. EF Core kullanıyorsan önce üretilen SQL'i log'dan al; Include ve Select yazısında ORM tarafındaki karşılığını anlatmıştım.

Bizim sorguyu dakikalardan saniyelere indiren tek bir değişiklik olmadı. Ölçümde dört adımın ortak noktası aynı çıktı: ekranda gösterilmeyecek satırı okumamak.

Bu yazı ilk olarak huseyinbozdemir.com'da yayımlandı.
