title: What AI code reviewers miss, and the checks I built for it
description:
AI writes code fast now. Reviewing it has not got faster.

On the production Django backend we used as a test bed, about half of the recent commits were fixes. The same rule lived in several copies: sign-in, sign-out, password change and JSON body parsing each had more than one version, and they had drifted apart. One access bug came back a week after it was fixed.

So a colleague and I built healthkit, an open-source toolkit that checks Python code for the problems a tool can find reliably, so people (and AI reviewers) can spend their time on the ones it cannot.

The most useful thing we did was not a feature. It was measuring.

The number that shaped everything: 9 out of 45

A careful human review of one module had produced 45 findings. We replayed it: take the code from before each fix, run our rules, and see which findings a rule points at.

The first score was 29 of 45. It looked great. Then we read every hit by hand. Most were coincidences: an unused import that happened to sit inside a behaviour fix, findings inside routes the fix deleted anyway. Counting only the hits where the rule pointed at the actual problem: 9 of 45, about 20%.

That gap is the first lesson. Distrust the metric that looks good. Every automated score gets a by-hand read of its hits before we quote it.

The second lesson came from breaking the 45 down:

Kind of problem Example Caught by rules
Pattern: a shape in one place an exception's text sent back to the client 8 of 12
Knowledge: needs the project's model reading rows that were soft-deleted 0 of 13
Behaviour: does it do the right thing a reset link that works as a login; a race 1 of 15

Rules are good at patterns. They are close to useless at behaviour. Pretending otherwise is how a green check turns into a false sense of safety.

What a tool can own, and what it never can

That table became the design. A rule is a past mistake written down so a machine can spot it again. It catches known kinds of mistakes, never new ones.

  • Patterns and structure (who may import whom): healthkit owns these, using ruff, Opengrep and import-linter with rule sets we measured.
  • Project knowledge: partly, through small guards each project writes in its own .healthkit/ folder.
  • Behaviour: never by rules. That is the job of tests, QA and people.

So the README says it plainly: healthkit can never judge whether the logic is right, whether it is secure, or whether the design is right. A clean run means "nothing it knows about", never "safe".

Five design decisions

1. AI is not in the gate. The pass/fail decision uses deterministic rules and tools only. AI review is advisory and never blocks. When AI spots a recurring problem, it becomes a rule, and the rule enforces it.

2. Check the lines you changed. healthkit review --base main checks only the lines your branch changed, so an old codebase does not bury you in history. scan and baseline exist for when you want the whole module.

3. The agent writing code cannot quietly change the referee. Most runs are done by AI coding agents before they hand over work. An agent that can edit the rules, add exceptions or exclude folders can make any check pass. So any change to the .healthkit/ settings, and any # noqa that switches a check off, is flagged as needs human approval, even when everything else is clean. We found the gap by hand: the default excluded everything under migrations/, so real code placed there would never be checked. The default now matches only Django's generated migration names.

4. Weak rules warn, they don't block. One rule found real bugs but was right only about half the time on code it was never tuned on (41% and 55% on two projects). It ships as worth a look:: printed and counted, but it never fails the run. A rule moves to blocking only after reaching 70% on unseen code from at least two projects.

5. "Could not check" is never a pass. Exit codes: 0 nothing found, 1 problems, 2 could not check, 3 only a settings change that needs approval. This came from a tool that reported zero unused functions on code with known dead code. Its verification step had timed out and it quietly withheld everything. "0 findings" can mean "did not run". Every adapter now surfaces the tool's own errors next to its findings.

Catching bugs nobody wrote a rule for

Behaviour bugs need a different approach. healthkit api sends good and bad input to every route of an API (via Schemathesis) and treats any server error as a finding. On the test project it found six real crashes, none of which had a rule.

It also answers a question rules can't: can this user see that data?

  • Multiple users: you give it one token per role, for example an admin, a plain user, and a user in another organisation. Every route is tested as each of them, and it checks that one user cannot read another's objects.
  • Access policy: you write down who must be refused where, and any successful answer is a finding: 
[[api.deny]]
user = "HK_TEACHER"
routes = ["GET /people/students", "GET /finances/**"]
reason = "a teacher sees only her own class"
  • The size of a leak: a finding says how much came back (got 200 (469 records) or got 200 (empty)), so a real leak stands out from an empty list. It shows only the count, never the data.
  • Read-only by default: it sends GET requests only, unless you add --allow-writes. We learned this the hard way: a sweep that wrote data deactivated the user that one crashing input needed, so the next sweep found 4 crashes instead of 6. Neither bug had been fixed.

Building it with AI agents: the lessons

healthkit was built with AI assistance under a written working agreement, one rule for each thing research says AI-written code tends to miss. Three lessons stood out:

  • An agent's "refuted" is not evidence. A verifier agent marked a real bug as not a bug by misreading the code it quoted. It had been asked to run a test and did not. A two-minute script proved the bug. Now any claim, from any agent, counts only with output that was actually run.
  • Verifiers drift to what is easy to confirm. Asked to try new ways around the gate, a verifier agent re-tested the gaps we had already closed and skipped the new ideas. The first new idea we tried by hand was a complete bypass. Now every verification brief lists the cases that must be tried, and the report is checked case by case.
  • Measure before building, and you may build less. We planned a similarity engine to find copied code. Measuring first, it found 1 of 4 real cases. Two cheap checks of about 110 lines did better, and found a rate-limit bug and a security helper copied with the opposite behaviour, neither of which any review had named.

Try it 

uv tool install git+https://github.com/paudelbaibhav/healthkit
healthkit review --base main

It works on any Python project, with extra checks for Django and web APIs. Output comes as text, JSON for agents, Markdown for pull-request comments, or GitHub annotations.

Code, decisions and every lesson we wrote down: github.com/paudelbaibhav/healthkit. It's MIT licensed, with about 220 tests.

What does your team rely on to review AI-written code: rules, AI reviewers, or people? I'd like to know what has actually worked for you.

title: October 15, 2026
description:
Apigee Edge for Private Cloud

Announcement

Released Apigee Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00.

Designated Apigee Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00.00 a long-term support (LTS) release: 18 months of full support ending April 2028, then 18 months of maintenance ending October 2029. After October 2029, 4.54.00.00 receives no software updates, security mitigations, or technical support.

Installing a later 4.54 minor release or patch does not change those dates. To extend the support lifecycle, upgrade to the next LTS release.

For the support lifecycle phases, release cadences, and version numbering, see Apigee Edge for Private Cloud release and lifecycle policy.

Announcement

This release replaces Java 8 with Java 17 and Java 21, removes the Classic UI and the apigee-sso component, and updates the bundled Cassandra, Postgres, OpenLDAP, ZooKeeper, Qpid Broker-J, Nginx, and Consul versions. These changes are not backward-compatible.

For the 4.54.00 versions and the 4.53.01 versions they replace, see Supported software and supported versions.

Before upgrading, read Changes in Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00, then Update Apigee Edge 4.53.00 or 4.53.01 to 4.54.00 or New installation overview. For known issues, see Known issues with Edge for Private Cloud.

Announcement

Replaced the Classic UI (edge-ui) with the New Edge UI (edge-management-ui).

The New Edge UI is the only management UI in 4.54.00 and is installed by default. Deployments running the Classic UI must transition to it before upgrading. Custom Classic UI properties do not carry over automatically. The default port also changes from 9000 to 3001, configurable with conf_uebe_port, so firewall rules and load balancer target ports that point at 9000 fail until they are updated.

For the migration steps and the supported feature list, see Migrate to the New Edge UI and What features are supported?.

Breaking

In deployments with Apigee SSO enabled, an integrated OIDC identity broker in apigee-openldap replaces the standalone apigee-sso component and Apache Tomcat 9.0.x. Before upgrading, take a complete and validated LDAP backup; existing apigee-sso configurations do not migrate automatically. Deployments not using Apigee SSO require no action.

For migration prerequisites, validation checks, and rollback constraints, see Option 2: Upgrade UI (with Apigee SSO).

Breaking

4.54.00 runs Java in mixed mode: Java 17 for Cassandra and ZooKeeper, Java 21 for the Management Server, Message Processor, Router, and Qpid Broker-J. Both Oracle JDK and OpenJDK are supported at those versions.

Oracle JDK 8 and OpenJDK 8 are no longer supported.

API proxies with custom JavaCallout policies or custom resource JARs can break on Java 21. For details, see Changes in Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00.

Change

Upgraded Nginx on the Edge Router to 1.30.0.

If you are upgrading from Nginx 1.20.x, see Nginx 1.30 changes in Apigee Edge 4.54.00 for the full list of changes.

Change

Changed the TLS defaults on Message Processors to the Java 21 cryptographic baseline.

Message Processors run on Java 21, which enables TLS 1.3 by default (JEP 332) and prefers it for outbound backend connections, falling back to TLS 1.2. No configuration change is required if your target servers and load balancers negotiate TLS 1.3, or negotiate TLS 1.2 with forward-secret (ECDHE) cipher suites.

Java 21 also disables the non-forward-secret static RSA key-exchange suites (TLS_RSA_*). If you have overridden conf_http_HTTPTransport.ssl.cipher.suites.whitelist or conf_message-processor-communication_local.http.ssl.ciphers with static RSA suites only, backend calls fail with no cipher suites in common and the Router cannot complete a TLS handshake with the Message Processor. Replace the TLS_RSA_* entries with modern cipher suites and restart the Message Processor.

For the remediation path, see Legacy backend requirements and remediation.

Feature

Added Basic authentication to the New Edge UI, which lets you sign in without configuring an identity provider.

The New Edge UI supports Basic authentication without additional configuration. You can also configure Apigee SSO, or an external identity provider such as SAML or OIDC. This feature is generally available in 4.54.00.

Feature

Added automated pre-flight validation checks to apigee-setup and apigee-service, which surface environment configuration problems before a component is installed.

This feature is generally available in 4.54.00.

Security

Fixed multiple security vulnerabilities in Apigee Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00.

These fixes ship as part of the component upgrades in this release; see Changes in Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00.

Change

Changed the default garbage collector on Message Processors to the Garbage-First garbage collector.

Message Processors set useG1GC=true and useStringDeduplication=true by default in 4.54.00. In 4.53.01 neither was set by default. To configure garbage collection, see Configure the garbage collector for Message Processors.

Apigee Edge for Public Cloud

Announcement

On October 15, 2026, we began releasing Single Sign-On (SSO) updates for Apigee Edge for Public Cloud.

Fixed

Bug ID Component Description
560310696 SSO Fixed an issue where the Portal SSO endpoint inadvertently accepted deprecated TLS 1.1 connections. The endpoint now strictly enforces TLS 1.2+.

Apigee Integrated Portal

Announcement

On October 15, 2026, we released a new version of the Apigee integrated portal.

Fixed

Bug ID Description
560310696 Fixed an issue where the Portal SSO endpoint inadvertently accepted deprecated TLS 1.1 connections. The endpoint now strictly enforces TLS 1.2+.

Apigee X

Fixed

Bug ID Description
466116259 Updated the startup script for the managed instance group (MIG) that routes external traffic to Apigee. net.ipv4.ip_forward is now written to /etc/sysctl.d/, so an instance no longer stops forwarding traffic when a reboot or an OS update resets it. The script does not change unrelated iptables NAT rules. Instances pick up the change the next time they are restarted or recreated.

BigQuery

Feature

You can copy tables across regions. This feature is now generally available (GA).

Feature

You can now use reusable column aliases in GoogleSQL. This feature lets you define an alias for an expression in the SELECT clause of a SQL query and immediately reference that alias within the same SELECT list or in the WHERE clause of the same query block.

Reusable column aliases also streamline the migration of workloads from other data warehouses such as Snowflake and Teradata, by supporting their syntax.

This feature is generally available, and is opt-in only. To use reusable column aliases, you must first enable the feature.

Feature

You can export a conversational analytics agent's answer, including text, visualizations, tables, and citations, to a PDF or CSV file. This feature is generally available (GA).

Cloud Vision

Deprecated

Face detection model update

The emotion label response in the Cloud Vision API is deprecated. Going forward, the Cloud Vision API face detection (FACE_DETECTION feature) will return UNKNOWN for all emotion-related labels.

Compute Engine

Feature

Preview: You can create regional disks, including Hyperdisk Balanced High Availability volumes, by cloning a zonal boot disk.

For more information, see Duplicate a disk with clones.

Change

If you try to create an on-demand reservation or increase the number of reserved Compute Engine instances in a reservation when the zone has reached its reservation capacity limit for your requested machine family, then the request fails with a RESERVATION_CAPACITY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED error. For more information, see Reservation capacity limit exceeded.

Feature

Generally available: The storage-optimized Z4M machine series is generally available for Compute Engine. Powered by fifth generation Intel Emerald Rapids Xeon Scalable processors and Titanium offload processors, Z4M instances are purpose-built for workloads that require larger storage capacity, such as:

  • Parallel file systems to support AI/ML workloads
  • I/O intensive workloads such as SQL, NoSQL, and vector databases
  • AI/ML training and inference workloads such as checkpointing and distributed Key-Value (KV) cache

The Z4M machine series delivers up to 1,536 GB of memory and 168,000 GiB of local Titanium SSD capacity. Z4M also supports up to 400 Gbps of network bandwidth using two physical NICs. Z4M instances use Titanium and Cloud RDMA to help enable higher levels of networking performance, isolation, and security.

For more information, see Storage-optimized machine family.

Dataflow

Feature

Dataflow Auto VM Selection now supports 4th generation Compute Engine machine series. When Auto VM Selection is enabled, the service prioritizes these newer generation VMs for improved performance. If 4th generation VMs are unavailable at startup, the service automatically falls back to widely available 2nd generation machine families to ensure that your jobs can start without unnecessary delays.

For more information, see Auto VM Selection.

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Anthropic models are available in the Gemini Enterprise app

Administrators can make Anthropic models—Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5—available to users in the Gemini Enterprise app. After an administrator turns on a model in the Enable third-party models section of the Feature Management tab, users can select the model in the model selector. Claude models are available in the global location and the us and eu multi-regions, and are charged on a pay-as-you-go basis.

This feature is generally available. For more information, see Enable third-party models.

Looker

Announcement

The latest versions in the Looker (Google Cloud core) release channels are beginning deployment as follows:

  • Latest version in the Rapid channel: Looker 26.20
  • Latest version in the No Channel channel: Looker 26.20

The latest version in the Regular channel remains Looker 26.18.

Note: This item was added on October 23, 2026.

Feature

The Looker 26.18 features have begun to be enabled for Looker (Google Cloud core) instances.

NetApp Volumes

Announcement

Google Cloud NetApp Volumes now supports the Flex Unified service level, including custom performance, in the following region:

  • europe-west8 (Milan)

For more information about available regions, see Supported regions.

Security Command Center

Feature

To increase the precision of attack path analysis and provide attack exposure scores that help you prioritize confirmed internet exposures, Risk Engine attack path simulations support the EXTERNALLY_EXPOSED_VM_INSTANCE External Exposure finding category (Preview). This finding category identifies Compute Engine or Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) resources with a direct public IP address that allows host OS access.

For more information, see Detect exposed resources, Risk Engine feature support, and Overview of attack exposure scores and attack paths.

Video Intelligence API

Deprecated

We are deprecating the emotion label response in the API. Going forward, the API will return UNKNOWN for all emotion related labels.

title: TalentRL: Strategy-Guided Reinforcement Learning for Hierarchical Skill Routing
description:
arXiv:2610.41143v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Natural-language skills enable large language model (LLM) agents to reuse procedures across tasks, yet most systems retrieve individual skills from a flat SkillBank without explicitly modeling the high-level strategy that governs their selection and use. We introduce TalentRL, a strategy-guided reinforcement learning framework for hierarchical routing over procedural memory. Coarse-grained talents represent recurring strategies for skill use, while fine-grained skills provide executable procedures. For each task, the policy model selects a talent that guides execution and softly prioritizes its associated skills during similarity-based retrieval. However, since task outcomes depend jointly on talent selection, retrieved skill context, and downstream execution, terminal rewards alone cannot isolate the contribution of the routing decision. TalentRL therefore trains talent routing with reward contrasts between rollouts of the same task under matched interventions on the talent-conditioned context, and optimizes downstream execution with group-relative advantages. Across seven open-domain and multi-hop question-answering benchmarks, talent-aware supervised fine-tuning improves average success rate by 7.53%, 6.71%, and 9.21% over the corresponding zero-shot baselines for Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen3-8B, and Llama-3.1-8B, respectively. Reinforcement learning further improves these SFT checkpoints by 7.58% to 9.32%, and TalentRL achieves the highest average success rate among all compared methods on all three backbones. On the agentic benchmarks ALFWorld and WebShop, TalentRL achieves the highest ALFWorld success rate (99.3%) and the highest WebShop score (90.7) among all compared methods.

title: Drone-PUR: From Visual Clue Discovery to Understanding and Reasoning in UAV Scenes
description:
arXiv:2610.40801v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The reasoning capabilities of vision-language models (VLMs) can be limited by incomplete or inaccurate visual observations in the general domain. In unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) scenes, small targets, subtle attributes, and changing viewpoints further complicate perception and understanding. Therefore, we introduce Drone-PUR, a dataset and benchmark organized around visual clue discovery, interpretation, and integration, corresponding to the three capability dimensions of perception, understanding, and reasoning. Reasoning samples are designed to require models to combine multiple visual clues to derive visually grounded conclusions. Its 11 tasks provide 175k training and 20k test samples spanning single images, image sequences, cross-modal images, and multiple viewpoints. All test samples undergo human review. Evaluating 22 general-purpose VLMs reveals persistent limitations in spatial judgment and cross-modal and cross-view reasoning. Across models, stronger perception is associated with better reasoning, while single-task fine-tuning further reveals selective bidirectional transfer between these capabilities. To examine domain adaptation, we develop UAV-PUR from Qwen3-VL through staged fine-tuning with auxiliary supervision. Its 4B and 8B variants improve overall multiple-choice accuracy by 18.33 and 17.52 percentage points over their pretrained counterparts, respectively. The dataset and project resources are available at https://drone-pur.github.io.

title: KEEPER: Learning Control-Sufficient Textual Memory for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.41482v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recursive textual memory can carry earlier errors into later updates, yet task performance alone does not establish memory reliability. We define self-consistency bias as the persistence of incorrect claims already present in the incoming memory. We present KEEPER, a comparative analysis of four auxiliary objectives along information-content and update-sensitivity axes within a shared recursive interface, examining how supervision targets relate to agent performance. Among evaluated conditions, reward-related prediction achieve the highest task performance before and after offline reinforcement learning, outperforming joint supervision. A claim-level analysis of one baseline trajectory documents error persistence despite corrective observations. Together, these analyses motivate evaluating error persistence and valid-information retention alongside task outcomes.

title: Prevented is Not Protected: What Attack Success Rate Hides about RAG
description:
arXiv:2610.40742v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is vulnerable to knowledge poisoning, where adversaries manipulate retrieved evidence to influence model outputs. Existing defenses are primarily evaluated using attack success rate (ASR), which obscures defense-induced failures and the mechanisms behind apparent attack prevention. To address this issue, this work introduces \textbf{Aligned RAG Evaluation}, a matched-query protocol that jointly examines clean and poisoned responses, with and without defense. By combining matched conditions analysis, LLM-judge endorsement, and retrieval dependence controls, the proposed framework distinguishes prevented from introduced failures, target mentions from LLM endorsement, and single-passage influence from evidence composition. Experiments on HotpotQA and Natural Questions reveal that existing defenses can introduce unexpected target-positive answers, although they can prevent some attacks, while evaluation criteria can also change defense rankings. Our findings expose critical blind spots in ASR-based evaluation and motivate a more comprehensive assessment of RAG poisoning defenses. The code and the evaluation artifact are available at https://github.com/chxhana/aligned-rag-eval.

title: How to Boot into rescue mode in RHEL 7 / CENTOS 7
description:
Rescue mode provides a convenient single-user environment and allows you to repair your system in situations when it is unable to complete a normal booting process. In rescue mode, the system attempts to mount all local file systems and start some important system services, but it does not activate network interfaces or allow more users to be logged into the system at the same time. In Red Hat Enterprise Linux 7, rescue mode is equivalent to single user mode and requires the root password.

If you are already logged in as root at a local console, you can enter emergency mode directly. Use the console rather than SSH because emergency mode deactivates network interfaces:

[root@linuxlab01 ~]# systemctl emergency

To enter rescue mode during boot instead, select a kernel on the GRUB 2 screen and press e to edit. Find the line starting with linux16 and append systemd.unit=rescue.target, then press Ctrl+X to boot.

When prompted, enter the root password. You can then perform maintenance tasks such as inspecting disks, editing files with vi, or checking an unmounted filesystem.

Rescue mode vs emergency mode vs single-user mode

These three get mixed up constantly, so it helps to know which one you actually want before you are staring at a broken boot:

  • Rescue mode (rescue.target) mounts your filesystems and starts basic services, but no networking. Use this when the system boots partially and you need to repair config files, reset a password, or run fsck.
  • Emergency mode (emergency.target) is even more minimal: only the root filesystem is mounted, and read-only at that. Use this when rescue mode itself will not start — for example when a bad fstab entry stops the boot.
  • Single-user mode is the older SysV term; on RHEL 7 and later, rescue mode is its systemd equivalent.

Booting into rescue mode from GRUB, step by step

  1. Reboot and wait for the GRUB menu. If it does not appear, hold Shift (BIOS) or tap Esc (UEFI) during boot.
  2. Highlight your normal kernel and press e to edit — this does not change anything permanently, only this one boot.
  3. Find the line starting with linux16 (or linux on newer releases) and add systemd.unit=rescue.target at the end, separated by a space.
  4. Press Ctrl+X to boot with that temporary parameter.

When prompted, enter the root password. You land in a root shell where you can edit files, check logs with journalctl -xb, or run filesystem checks.

The mistakes that cost people an hour

Forgetting to remount read-write. In emergency mode the root filesystem is read-only, so every edit fails until you run:

mount -o remount,rw /

A broken fstab is the most common reason you are here. If boot fails right after you edited mounts, comment out the new line in /etc/fstab instead of debugging anything else first. Adding nofail to non-essential mounts (USB drives, secondary disks) prevents this entire class of boot failure.

No networking in rescue mode is normal. ping will not work, and that is expected, not a new problem. If you need the network to download a package, boot normally with a working kernel instead.

Inspect the failure before changing anything

Start with evidence instead of running several repair commands and hoping one works:

systemctl --failed
journalctl -xb --no-pager
lsblk -f
findmnt

The first two commands show failed units and detailed boot messages. lsblk -f identifies block devices and filesystem types, while findmnt shows what is actually mounted. Before editing a configuration file, keep a backup, for example cp -a /etc/fstab /etc/fstab.before-rescue.

After changing /etc/fstab, run systemctl daemon-reload, then mount -a to test the entries. Read any error carefully; do not assume the repair worked just because a prompt returned.

Check filesystems safely

Never run a repair utility on a mounted filesystem. For a non-root ext4 filesystem, unmount it first and substitute the device name shown by lsblk:

umount /dev/sdb1
fsck /dev/sdb1

RHEL 7 and CentOS 7 commonly use XFS. For an unmounted XFS filesystem, use xfs_repair /dev/sdb1 instead of fsck. Do not use xfs_repair -L merely to bypass a log-related error; zeroing the log can cause data loss and should be a last resort after exhausting safer options.

You cannot unmount the root filesystem while running from it. To repair root, boot the matching installation media and enter its rescue shell without mounting the installed system. This installer rescue environment is separate from systemd's rescue.target.

Rebuild initramfs only when it is relevant

If boot messages point to missing storage drivers or LVM support after a kernel or storage change, regenerate the image for the kernel currently running in rescue mode:

dracut --force /boot/initramfs-$(uname -r).img $(uname -r)

This overwrites that kernel's image, so verify the version first and retain a backup when possible. It does not repair every installed kernel.

A rescue shell has unrestricted root privileges. Use trusted consoles and boot media, and do not treat disabling SELinux or running chmod -R 777 as a repair. Those actions can create a second, security-sensitive problem while hiding the original one.

Getting back out

When repairs are done, simply:

exit
# or, to force a full restart:
reboot

Because the GRUB edit was temporary, the next boot uses your normal kernel parameters automatically. If the system comes up clean, consider making the fix permanent where appropriate (correcting fstab, rebuilding initramfs with dracut, or restoring a config you changed) — and take a snapshot or backup before the next experiment.

title: 三丰云免费云服务器实测：7天手动续期，稳如老狗
description:
上一版提到“零事故”，这个表述确实太绝对了。严格来说，我是每7天登录控制台手动点一次续期，累计三十多次，中间靠手机日历提醒才没断过。修正后的事实更平淡，但更真实：不是平台自动兜底，而是你愿意为它花30秒点一下按钮，它就真的给你稳稳跑着。这种“主动维系”的使用方式，反而让我对稳定性有了更清晰的体感。

从第一次开通到现在，配置一直是1核1G、5M带宽。跑的项目也没变：FastAPI + PostgreSQL后端、Nuxt3 SSR前端、Redis缓存。CPU偶尔冲到75%~80%，内存常驻600MB左右，5M带宽扛日常访问绰绰有余。它不会因为你是免费用户就在高峰期限速或降权——流量统计和nginx日志始终对得上，没有暗扣。

真实使用节奏：7天一续，断断续续

很多人问为什么不能“一次开通管半年”。答案很简单：规则写得很明白，免费资源是有有效期的，到期不续就回收。我设了每周六上午10点的日历提醒，雷打不动。每次点完续期，有效期立刻刷新，IP不变、数据不丢、服务不中断，连SSH会话都不用重连。

这种“可预期的确定性”，比那些号称“随时可能改规则”的平台踏实太多。中间确实有过一次忘记设置提醒，晚了一整天才续上，虽然没被回收，但那种心跳感让我立刻改回了强制提醒。对于个人开发者来说，这点时间成本几乎可以忽略不计，换来的是长期的稳定可用。

配置方面，Docker、Node.js、Python环境照常可用。我之前在另一台机器上用免费虚拟主机托管静态页面，体验也不错；但既然要跑PostgreSQL和Redis，云服务器才是正解。系统日志、磁盘使用率、网络吞吐都在监控面板里实时可见，数据透明，没有隐藏指标。

为什么愿意每7天点一次续期？

  • 成本为零，心理负担也为零：不用绑卡、不用签到、不用发帖，纯手动点击，30秒搞定
  • 续期机制透明可靠：没有隐藏条件，没有“连续登录X天才可续”之类的套路
  • 服务与续期解耦：即使某次晚了几小时续期，也不会立即删机，有缓冲余地
  • 数据始终安全：三十多次续期，数据库、配置文件、Docker卷从未丢失或损坏
  • 运维体验一致：无论第1次还是第30次续期，控制台响应速度、功能完整性完全一样
  • 信任是攒出来的：正是这一次次成功的续期，让我敢把笔记同步、代码托管这类日常任务放上去
  • 比“自动续费”更让人安心：主动操作意味着掌控感，知道服务还在、自己还能用
  • 适合轻量长期项目：不适合高可用生产环境，但作为个人技术栈的实验场+备用基础设施，完美匹配
  • 客服依然在线：期间提过两次工单（一次VNC黑屏、一次防火墙规则疑问），都在两小时内解决
  • 生态没缩水：文档更新及时，社区问答也有回应，FAQ能覆盖大部分常见问题

实测细节：负载与故障自救

说实话，75%~80%的CPU占用并不是平时维持的，而是在特定场景下出现的。比如我写了个定时任务，每天凌晨用cron触发一个数据同步脚本，同时后端在处理批量写入，这时候CPU会短暂冲高。内存方面，PostgreSQL和Redis常驻一起，600MB是个比较稳定的区间；如果偶尔飙升到800MB，通常是因为我在调试接口，开了几个后台进程。

5M带宽在这个场景下绰绰有余。Nuxt3 SSR出来的HTML体积不大，图片都走CDN或本地存储，所以流量曲线很平滑。没有遇到过因为带宽打满导致的服务不可用，这一点比很多同类产品要实在。

有一次遇到个小麻烦：SSH连上去发现某个容器状态异常，日志里全是OOM Killed。排查后发现是Redis配置里maxmemory-policy设错了，导致大Key加载时内存瞬间撑爆。重启容器、修正配置后恢复正常。这次经历让我意识到，免费资源虽好，但监控告警还是得自己搭，不能全靠平台盯着。好在三丰云的控制台给了基础的监控图表，足以发现异常。

适合谁这样用

如果你能接受每7天花30秒点一下续期，并且用途是学生课设、Linux学习、博客/简历托管、API调试、个人网盘、笔记同步、跑点小脚本这类轻量场景——那三丰云的免费云服务器就是目前最稳妥的选择之一。它不承诺“永久”，但兑现了“只要你愿意续，我就一直给”。

想试的自己搜“三丰云”官网，实名后创建实例。新手建议先从虚拟主机上手，再过渡到云服务器，体验更平滑。记住，这是实验场，不是生产环境；心态放平，折腾起来才从容。

title: DNS Propagation: What Actually Happens After You Change a Record
description:
You change an A record, and your phone loads the new server while your laptop keeps loading the old one. DNS has no mechanism for pushing a change out to resolvers. What people call propagation is resolvers everywhere holding cached copies of the old answer until each copy's TTL runs out. This guide shows where those copies live, how to inspect each one with dig, and a migration order that keeps the switchover short and reversible.

How a lookup actually works

When a program on Linux resolves a name, it calls the stub resolver in the C library. The stub follows /etc/nsswitch.conf, which normally checks /etc/hosts first and then asks the DNS server listed in /etc/resolv.conf. On Ubuntu 24.04 that is systemd-resolved at 127.0.0.53, which keeps its own cache and forwards to an upstream server.

The upstream is a recursive resolver: your router, your ISP, Pi-hole, or a public service such as 1.1.1.1, 8.8.8.8, or 9.9.9.9. With an empty cache, it walks the hierarchy:

  1. It asks a root server, which refers it to the servers for the TLD (for .com, the gtld-servers.net set).
  2. It asks a TLD server, which refers it to the authoritative nameservers for example.com.
  3. It asks an authoritative server, which returns the record and its TTL.

The resolver caches every step: the list of TLD servers, the delegation for your domain, and the final answer. Until those entries expire, it answers from cache without contacting anyone.

You can do the walk yourself, skipping the resolver's cache for everything below the root:

dig +trace www.example.com

com.            172800  IN  NS  a.gtld-servers.net.
;; Received 1170 bytes from 198.41.0.4#53(a.root-servers.net) in 20 ms
example.com.    172800  IN  NS  ns1.example-dns.net.
;; Received 180 bytes from 192.5.6.30#53(a.gtld-servers.net) in 30 ms
www.example.com. 300    IN  A   203.0.113.10
;; Received 60 bytes from 198.51.100.53#53(ns1.example-dns.net) in 40 ms

That output is trimmed and your servers will differ. The Received ... from lines show which server gave each answer, which is useful when a delegation points somewhere unexpected. On Debian and Ubuntu, dig comes from the dnsutils package (bind-utils on RHEL and Fedora).

TTL decides how long old answers live

Every record carries a TTL in seconds. A resolver that fetched the record at 10:00 with a TTL of 3600 can serve that copy until 11:00 without checking again. Resolver operators can also configure minimum and maximum cache times, so a few resolvers keep answers for more or less time than the TTL says.

This is why lowering the TTL right before a change does not help. Resolvers only learn the new, lower TTL when they refetch the record, and they refetch when the old TTL expires. If a record had a TTL of 86400 (one day), lower it to 300 at least a day before you change the value. After that day, every cache holds a copy that expires within five minutes.

Negative answers are cached too

When a name does not exist, the resolver caches that as well (RFC 2308). The authoritative server includes the zone's SOA record with an NXDOMAIN answer (or a NODATA answer, when the name exists without that record type), and the negative result may be cached for the lesser of the SOA record's own TTL and the SOA MINIMUM field. If you query new.example.com before creating it, or a monitoring check does, resolvers can keep saying it does not exist after you add it.

dig example.com SOA +noall +answer

example.com.  3600  IN  SOA  ns1.example-dns.net. hostmaster.example.com. 2026091701 7200 3600 1209600 300

The fields after the contact address are serial, refresh, retry, expire, and minimum. Here the minimum is 300 and the SOA TTL is 3600, so negative answers live for up to 300 seconds. Querying a missing name typically shows that value on the SOA in the authority section, counting down if the answer came from a cache.

Why nameserver changes take longer

Moving to a new DNS provider means changing the nameservers at your registrar. The registrar sends the change to the registry, which updates the delegation (the NS records) in the TLD zone. Those delegation records have their own TTL set by the registry, and resolvers that cached the old delegation keep asking your old provider until it expires.

The value varies by TLD, so check yours. Find the TLD's servers, then ask one of them directly:

dig com NS +short

dig @a.gtld-servers.net example.com NS +norecurse

;; AUTHORITY SECTION:
example.com.  172800  IN  NS  ns1.example-dns.net.
example.com.  172800  IN  NS  ns2.example-dns.net.

For .com the delegation TTL is 172800 seconds (48 hours). The zone's own NS records at your provider carry another TTL that resolvers may also use. The practical rule is to keep the old provider serving a correct copy of the zone for at least the delegation TTL after the switch, and preferably longer.

Checking what resolvers actually see

Start with the source of truth. Ask the authoritative server directly, with recursion turned off:

dig @ns1.example-dns.net www.example.com A +norecurse

Look for aa (authoritative answer) in the flags line. The TTL in this answer is the configured value and never counts down. If this answer is wrong, fix the zone at your provider first, because waiting will not change it.

Providers run several authoritative servers, and they can briefly disagree after an edit. dig +nssearch prints the SOA serial from each one:

dig +nssearch example.com

Matching serials mean the servers have the same version of the zone. Next, compare public resolvers:

for r in 1.1.1.1 8.8.8.8 9.9.9.9; do dig @"$r" www.example.com A +noall +answer; done

www.example.com.  187   IN  A  203.0.113.10
www.example.com.  300   IN  A  203.0.113.10
www.example.com.  2451  IN  A  198.51.100.20

The first two have the new address. The third still has the old one, cached with 2451 seconds left. Run the loop again a minute later and cached TTLs will have dropped by about 60. A TTL equal to the configured value usually means a fresh fetch. A large public resolver is many separate caches behind one address, so repeated queries can return different TTLs.

To see answers from resolvers in many regions at once, use the DNS lookup tool, which includes a global propagation map.

Caches on your own machine

dig sends queries straight to a DNS server. It ignores /etc/hosts and nsswitch.conf, so it can show the new address while your browser and curl still use the old one. To see what applications get, ask the system resolver:

getent hosts www.example.com

If that disagrees with dig, check /etc/hosts first. A test entry added during an earlier migration overrides DNS until someone removes it:

grep -n example.com /etc/hosts

Then check whether systemd-resolved is in use. It is the default on Ubuntu 24.04, while a default Debian 12 install does not include it:

resolvectl status

If the command is missing or fails with an error, there is usually no local cache to clear, unless you installed something like dnsmasq or nscd. If resolved is active, query through it and flush its cache:

resolvectl query www.example.com
sudo resolvectl flush-caches

Browsers keep their own short-lived host cache, and a browser with DNS over HTTPS enabled uses a different resolver from the operating system. Restarting the browser clears the cache. Also check its secure DNS setting when it disagrees with the rest of the machine. Your router or Pi-hole caches answers as well, and restarting its DNS service clears that layer. If you run split-horizon DNS at home, as in the home lab networking guide, your LAN will see different answers from the internet on purpose.

Why different locations see different answers

Answers vary by location for a few reasons. Public resolvers such as 1.1.1.1 and 8.8.8.8 use anycast: the same address is served from many sites, and each site has its own cache, filled at different times and expiring at different times. Some DNS providers use GeoDNS or latency-based routing, returning different records depending on where the query comes from, so a "wrong" answer in one region may be intended. And ISP resolvers fetched the record whenever their users happened to ask, so their copies expire on their own schedule.

When regions disagree, check the authoritative answer first, then check whether your provider has location-based rules on that record.

A safe migration playbook

This order works for moving a site or service to a new IP address.

  1. At least one old TTL ahead (a day is typical), lower the TTL on every record you will change to 300. Confirm with dig @ns1.example-dns.net www.example.com A +norecurse +noall +answer.
  2. Wait out the old TTL. Changing the record earlier leaves long-lived stale copies in caches.
  3. Change the record. Confirm the authoritative server returns the new value.
  4. Keep the old server running and serving correct content. Some resolvers enforce minimum cache times, and long-running programs may have resolved the name once at startup. Watch its access log (for example sudo tail -f /var/log/nginx/access.log) until traffic stops.
  5. Verify from the public resolvers above, from the DNS lookup tool, and with getent hosts on a client.
  6. Once everything is stable, raise the TTL back to your normal value, such as 3600.

If something goes wrong in step 5, revert the record. With a 300-second TTL, the rollback reaches most resolvers as quickly as the change did.

Common mistakes

Start with names that were never changed. The apex, www, mail, and API subdomains are separate records, and changing one does not change the others. Export or list the whole zone before a migration and check each name afterwards.

A CNAME at the zone apex is not allowed in standard DNS. A CNAME cannot coexist with other records at the same name, and the apex always has SOA and NS records. Providers work around this with ALIAS or ANAME records or CNAME flattening, which answer with A and AAAA records.

In zone files, a name without a trailing dot is relative to the zone origin:

www  IN  CNAME  example.com     ; becomes example.com.example.com.
www  IN  CNAME  example.com.    ; what you meant

If dig returns example.com.example.com., a missing dot is the cause.

Changing nameservers and records at the same time makes failures ambiguous, because you cannot tell whether a resolver is asking the old provider or the new one. Copy the zone unchanged to the new provider, confirm dig @old-ns and dig @new-ns return the same answers, switch the nameservers, wait out the delegation TTL, and only then edit records.

A DNSSEC DS record left at the registrar breaks resolution when you change providers. The DS record points at the old provider's signing key, so validating resolvers (including 1.1.1.1, 8.8.8.8, and 9.9.9.9) return SERVFAIL while non-validating ones still work. Diagnose it by comparing a normal query with one that disables validation:

dig example.com DS +short
dig @1.1.1.1 example.com A
dig @1.1.1.1 example.com A +cd

A SERVFAIL on the second query and an answer on the third points at DNSSEC. The safe order is to remove the DS record at the registrar, wait for its TTL to pass (check it at the TLD servers as shown earlier), switch providers, then enable DNSSEC at the new provider and add its DS record.

Before and after a DNS change

  • Note the current TTL of every record you will touch and lower it at least that far ahead.
  • Check the authoritative answer and dig +nssearch right after each edit.
  • Compare public resolvers and the DNS lookup tool map.
  • Look at /etc/hosts, the local resolver cache, and the browser before blaming DNS.
  • For provider moves, handle DS records first and change nameservers separately from records.

title: E-commerce checkout: technical fixes that reduce drop-off
description:
Some people will always leave a checkout. They were comparing prices, or the shipping cost surprised them, or they got distracted. That part is about pricing and policy.

But a share of abandoned orders comes from things developers can fix: a slow page, a forced sign-up, a payment error nobody understands, a form that fights the customer. These are the cheapest sales to win back, because the customer had already decided to buy.

Here are the four areas I'd check first.

1. Load time on the checkout itself

Teams optimise the home page and product pages, then forget the checkout. It's often the heaviest page on the site, because it loads payment scripts, address lookups, fraud checks and every tracking tag marketing ever added.

  • Measure the checkout separately, on a mid-range phone over mobile data.
  • Remove scripts that don't belong. Chat widgets, heatmaps and review widgets rarely need to run on payment steps.
  • Load payment and address scripts when needed, not on page load if the customer won't reach that step for a while.
  • Never block the page on a slow third party. 
<!-- Load non-critical scripts without blocking the page -->
<script src="/js/address-lookup.js" defer></script>

2. Guest checkout

Forcing account creation before payment is one of the most common reasons people give up. They came to buy something, not to start a relationship with a password.

  • Offer guest checkout by default. Ask for an email for the receipt, nothing more.
  • Offer an account after the order, on the confirmation page: "Save your details for next time?" At that point it's a convenience, not a barrier.
  • Let returning customers sign in, but don't make it the first thing they see.

If your platform links guest orders to an account later by email, make sure that only happens after the customer verifies the address, so nobody can see someone else's orders.

3. Payment errors

A declined card is stressful. A declined card with the message "Error 402" or "Something went wrong" loses the sale.

  • Map payment provider error codes to plain messages that tell the customer what to do next.
  • Keep everything they typed when a payment fails. Don't make them re-enter their address.
  • Prevent double charges. Disable the pay button while the request is in flight, and use the provider's idempotency key feature so a retry doesn't create a second charge.
  • Log failures with the reason code so you can see whether a pattern is a customer issue or a configuration issue. Log the reason code and order ID, never card numbers or the security code. 
// Map provider decline codes to messages a customer can act on.
// Check the exact codes against your payment provider's documentation.
const DECLINE_MESSAGES = {
  card_declined: "Your bank declined this card. Try another card or contact your bank.",
  insufficient_funds: "Your card was declined for insufficient funds. Try another card.",
  expired_card: "This card has expired. Please check the date or use another card.",
  incorrect_cvc: "The security code doesn't match. Please check the 3 or 4 digits on your card.",
  processing_error: "We couldn't reach your bank just now. Please try again in a moment.",
};

function paymentErrorMessage(code) {
  return DECLINE_MESSAGES[code]
    || "Your payment didn't go through. Please try again or use a different card.";
}

const payButton = document.querySelector("#pay-button");

async function submitPayment(submitFn) {
  payButton.disabled = true;          // prevent double clicks
  payButton.textContent = "Processing…";
  try {
    const result = await submitFn();  // your provider's confirm call
    if (result && result.error) throw result.error; // some providers return errors instead of throwing
    // success: leave the button disabled and move to the confirmation page
  } catch (err) {
    showError(paymentErrorMessage(err.decline_code || err.code)); // showError: your own UI helper
    payButton.disabled = false;       // re-enable only after a failure
    payButton.textContent = "Pay now";
  }
}

4. Form validation

Checkout forms ask for a lot, so every bit of friction adds up.

  • Validate as people go, when they leave a field, not only when they press the final button.
  • Accept input the way people type it. Strip spaces from phone numbers instead of rejecting them, and use your payment provider's hosted card fields (they handle card formatting for you and keep card data off your servers). Don't force one postcode format for every country.
  • Use the right input types and autocomplete attributes so phones show the right keyboard and browsers can fill saved details.
  • Show errors next to the field, in plain words, and move focus to the first error. Put payment errors in a role="alert" area, and set aria-invalid="true" on fields with errors.
  • Don't ask twice. Default the billing address to the shipping address. 
<label for="ship-name">Full name</label>
<input id="ship-name" name="name" autocomplete="shipping name" required>

<label for="ship-postcode">Postcode</label>
<input id="ship-postcode" name="postcode" autocomplete="shipping postal-code" required>

<label for="ship-phone">Phone (for delivery updates)</label>
<input id="ship-phone" name="phone" type="tel" autocomplete="tel" aria-describedby="ship-phone-error">
<p id="ship-phone-error" class="field-error" hidden></p>

<div id="payment-error" role="alert"></div>

<label><input type="checkbox" id="same-billing" checked> Billing address is the same</label>

// Tidy spaces, dashes and brackets when the customer leaves the field
const phoneInput = document.querySelector("#ship-phone");
phoneInput.addEventListener("blur", () => {
  phoneInput.value = phoneInput.value.replace(/[\s()-]/g, "");
});

How to know it worked

Before changing anything, set up a simple funnel in your analytics: cart, checkout start, shipping, payment, order complete. Note where people drop off. Then ship one fix at a time and watch the step it should affect. Combined with your payment failure logs, that tells you which fixes are paying for themselves and where to look next.

Checkout work isn't glamorous. But it's the one place on the site where every improvement lands on customers who'd already decided to pay.

Ahmed Vaseer is Founder & CEO - Ingenious Concepts. 80+ projects, ISO 27001 certified via Global CB.

title: Language Models Show a "Women-Are-Wonderful" Effect in Blame Attribution That is Not Just Leniency
description:
arXiv:2610.41116v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: This paper investigates the Women-Are-Wonderful (WaW) effect in language-model blame attribution: a favorable bias in which women receive more positive evaluations than men. Using 11,270 interpersonal conflicts from r/AmItheAsshole, we construct matched counterfactuals that vary the gender of the person being judged (the original poster) and the person affected (the counter-party). Across four language models, gender changes a minority of verdicts, but those changes consistently favor women. The effect is strongly role-dependent. Making the original poster a woman reduces the odds of blame by 9--52%, while making the counter-party a woman multiplies them by 2.7--9.2X. Counter-party WaW also varies across conflict types, strengthening in communication and relationship conflicts and weakening in family conflicts. Exploratory probes suggest that counter-party gender can shift judgments of sympathy, reasonableness, harm and protection. WaW is therefore not just leniency toward women being judged: models also judge conduct more harshly when it affects a woman.

title: Making every harness durable
description:
Developers are familiar with running coding agents locally through harnesses like Pi, Claude Code, and others. They are reliable daily drivers for generating code, but keeping agents running around the clock requires your computer to be on and awake, which led to the laptop lid memes and Mac mini demand spike.

Running harnesses in the cloud

Harness workloads are moving to the cloud. Individual developers are deploying always-on coding agent workflows, projects like OpenWork and HanaAgent use open-source harnesses as the engines behind the apps, and engineers are building their own harness products.

These harnesses are designed for long-lived processes that keep the session in memory, and agent tasks commonly run for minutes or hours. Locally, a harness has direct, continuous access to the workspace and session history on the same disk, so resuming interrupted work only requires a simple prompt.

In the cloud, you can replicate that setup with a VM and persistent storage, but the VM doesn't automatically record which model and tool calls completed or resume interrupted turns after a crash. A failed turn or network error means lost work.

Also, not every agent task executed through a harness needs a sandbox. Database queries and API calls can run securely in functions, and that also means required credentials never have to enter the sandbox.

Making every harness durable

We built eve and fx to run durably in the cloud out of the box, and today we are introducing durable-harness, which extends that durability to any harness, including Pi, OpenCode, Codex, and Claude Code. It uses the same machinery that powers Workflow SDK to survive crashes and function timeouts.

With durable-harness, you can:

  • Run any of these harnesses durably on Vercel

  • Self-host a harness with your own Postgres instance

  • Make your local harness workflow durable

  • Build your own durable harness

Sessions that survive a crash mid-turn

Take the example of a coding agent adding a pricing page to an existing app. The agent reads the existing page, writes a new one, opens a pull request, and waits for CI to finish before reporting back.

What happens if its function times out while CI is still running?

Kill the function or drop the connection in the demo below to compare how the two agents recover and which work is repeated.

Without durability, the agent stops work until it is manually restarted, and completed work is repeated unnecessarily.

With durable-harness, a new function reads completed results from the log and resumes the turn. If the browser disconnects, the agent keeps running, and reconnecting catches up from the log.

Logs and queues

durable-harness is the newest package in our open source portfolio. It’s a set of adapters and utilities that let the harnesses you already use keep their sessions in a World, the Workflow SDK’s durable backend.

It writes each step of a turn to a durable log. Before a model call or tool call runs, it records an intent, and when the call finishes, it records the outcome. The turn itself is backstopped with a queue message, so if its function dies, the queue hands the turn to a new function that reads the log and continues where it left off.

After a crash, the log says what finished, what was running, and what never started:

  • Completed calls never run again because their results are read from the log, so you’re never billed twice for a finished model call’s tokens.

  • Models remember their previous calls rather than repeating them.

  • Interrupted tools marked replay: 'safe' run again. Any other tool comes back to the model as possibly run, and the model decides whether to check.

Harnesses that keep their own session files, like Claude Code's transcript, Codex's rollout, and OpenCode's event store, have every record mirrored into the log, so a new function or Sandbox rebuilds them from it.

Pick your harness

fx and eve are durable on their own. For the rest, durable-harness adds durability from the outside, without changing the harness.

For the full setup guide for each harness, check the docs.

Runs everywhere

Durable agents need a log of each step, a way to resume a turn when its process dies, and a stream for whoever is watching.

Workflow SDK ships all three behind one interface, a World.

durable-harness writes to that interface, so you can move the same agent from one World to another without changing its code:

  • On Vercel, it uses the Vercel World.

  • In development, it uses files on your machine.

  • On your own servers, it uses Postgres, MongoDB, Redis, or Turso.

Two variables move every agent using durable-harness to Postgres.

For more control, such as setting a namespace or recovering sessions when your server starts, create the World in code and pass it to your agent:

Check the self-hosting docs for more details.

See every session in Agent Runs

Agent Runs on Vercel shows the trace for every session, including each model call and tool call. Turns that resumed after a crash appear in the same trace, so you can see exactly where a turn stopped and picked back up.

Tools

An agent has only the tools you give it, and they run in your function. Each tool says what should happen if a crash interrupts it. A 'safe' tool, such as a lookup, can run again. A 'never' tool, such as a refund, never runs twice: the model is told the call may have happened, so it can check before it tries again.

Here’s how the coding agent from the demo above might define its tools:

  • A tool that reads a file or checks CI status is marked as 'safe' so it can run again automatically.

  • A tool that posts a PR comment is marked as 'never' so that comments aren't posted twice.

The following example defines a tool for each policy using the example of an agent processing a refund:

For each harness’s built-in tools, like its shell and file editing, read on.

Files

When a harness needs a shell and files, it’s not safe to run them directly on a shared serverless function host. Many sessions can share the same function, and its filesystem isn’t guaranteed to persist between invocations.

To address this, durable-harness gives you a few options:

  • virtual() keeps the files in the session’s log, with a bash-compatible shell that can’t reach your function’s files or the network. It suits short tasks and small workspaces without starting an entire sandbox.

  • virtual({ durable: false }) keeps the files in memory for scratch work and clears them at the end of every turn.

  • sandbox() gives the session its own Vercel Sandbox, with /workspace on a Drive that outlives every sandbox and every function. It suits real projects and long-running work.

Compare the three side by side in the docs.

Each harness’s built-in tools run on the workspace you choose. With Pi, CodingTools installs Pi’s own read, write, edit, and bash, and virtualEnv() or sandboxEnv() gives them a workspace:

For OpenCode, pass the workspace as workspace, and for fx, pass it to fxTools(). Claude Code and Codex always run in a Vercel Sandbox, since they expect a real shell and filesystem, and aren’t safe for multi-tenant use. Their built-in tools work on the session’s Drive once you turn them on with builtins: true. Each harness guide lists its built-in tools.

Documents

Some state belongs with the session but isn’t part of the conversation, such as a to-do list, a plan, or a form the agent fills in. A document is typed JSON that lives in the session’s log, so it survives a crash and moves with the session.

Tools can edit documents through io.docs, and each edit commits to the log alongside the tool’s result, so the document’s durable state stays consistent with the tool calls themselves:

Your app can read and edit the same document without a database of its own, and the chat route can even stream every change to your UI:

In fact, the virtual() workspace from earlier is built on documents: its file tree is a document in the session’s log, and each tool call’s changes commit with its result.

Learn more about tools, files, and documents and how to keep your agent secure.

Wrapping up

Developers choose a harness for the choices it makes about prompts, tools, and context. How it survives a crash shouldn’t be one of them. With durable-harness, a turn that loses its function partway through continues from the log on a new one, without a manual retry and without repeating what already finished. Self-hosting and portability work out of the box by building on top of the Workflow SDK’s World interface.

durable-harness is open source on GitHub.

title: A 100% AI Eval Score Is a Red Flag, Not a Win
description:
A 100% AI Eval Score Is a Red Flag, Not a Win

📖 Read the full version with charts and embedded sources on ComputeLeap →

In April 2026, a team at UC Berkeley's RDI lab ran an automated scanning agent against eight of the most-cited AI benchmarks in the industry — SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Pro, Terminal-Bench, WebArena, FieldWorkArena, CAR-bench, GAIA, and OSWorld. The agent scored 100% on six of them. It didn't solve a single task. On SWE-bench Verified — the benchmark OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google have used to compare their coding agents — the exploit was a pytest conftest.py hook that marks every test as "passed." The entire attack surface: the agent and the evaluator ran in the same container.

This is not a theoretical vulnerability. This is the evaluation infrastructure the AI industry currently relies on to compare billion-dollar models. And it's broken.

The demand signal for this piece came from three directions this week: an AI Engineer conference talk titled "If Your AI Scores 100%, Your Eval Is Wrong," OpenAI's own decision to retire SWE-bench Verified after finding 59.4% of audited tasks had flawed test cases, and Epoch AI's independent review rating the benchmark as "Flawed." When the benchmark creators, the benchmark users, and the benchmark auditors all agree the system is broken, it's not a controversy — it's a consensus.

The Berkeley Exploit: A Masterclass in Why Evals Fail

The UC Berkeley team — Hao Wang, Qiuyang Mang, Alvin Cheung, Koushik Sen, and Dawn Song — did not build a better AI model. They built an AI agent whose sole job was to find and exploit weaknesses in evaluation pipelines. The results are staggering:

Benchmark Tasks Exploit Score Method
Terminal-Bench 89 100% Replaced binaries with wrappers that fake pytest output
SWE-bench Verified 500 100% Pytest hook (conftest.py) marks all tests as passing
SWE-bench Pro 731 100% Container parser overwrite
WebArena 812 ~100% Read gold answers via file:// URLs; prompt injection against LLM judge
FieldWorkArena 890 100% Validator only checks if last message is from assistant — {} scores 100%
CAR-bench — 100% Hidden instructions injected into judge prompt
GAIA 165 ~98% Used publicly available answers
OSWorld 369 73% Downloaded gold files into evaluator paths

View the full Berkeley RDI research post →

The Hacker News thread on this research hit 588 points and 143 comments — the AI engineering community's reaction was immediate and pointed:

View the full HN discussion →

The root cause is simple and damning: most agent benchmarks run the agent and the evaluator in the same sandbox. The agent can tamper with the grader. It can overwrite the test harness. It can inject answers into the scoring pipeline. This is the evaluation equivalent of giving a student the answer key and a red pen.

⚠️ Contrarian Corner: Some benchmark maintainers argue these exploits don't reflect real-world model usage — no commercial lab would ship a conftest.py hack. That misses the point. The Berkeley team explicitly said they weren't accusing current leaders of cheating. Their point is that the loopholes are easy enough that an optimizer could stumble into them. When your gradient descent process is optimizing against a broken eval, you don't need malicious intent to get inflated scores.

The team also released BenchJack, an automated vulnerability scanner for benchmarks — essentially a penetration-testing agent for evaluation pipelines. If your benchmark can't survive BenchJack, it can't be trusted.

OpenAI Walks Away From Its Own Benchmark

In February 2026, OpenAI published a post announcing it would no longer report SWE-bench Verified scores. The reasoning was blunt: the benchmark's tasks come from public repositories that model providers train on. Gains increasingly reflect training exposure — memorization — rather than genuine coding capability. OpenAI's internal audit found that at least 59.4% of frequently-failed tasks had flawed test cases that reject functionally correct patches.

View the OpenAI post →

The Hacker News discussion hit 343 points and 208 comments, with one of SWE-bench's co-creators arguing the benchmark could still be trusted if contamination was accounted for — a position that found little support in the thread:

View the full HN discussion →

That's not a rounding error. More than half of the "hard" problems were hard for the wrong reasons — not because they tested real engineering skill, but because the test harness itself was broken. When your test suite penalizes correct answers, the benchmark isn't measuring what you think it's measuring.

OpenAI now recommends SWE-bench Pro as its successor, which uses rotating held-out problems and addresses some of the contamination issues. But the deeper problem remains: any public benchmark with a static task set will eventually be contaminated. The training data for frontier models now includes most of the internet, including the benchmark's problems and solutions. The half-life of a public eval is shrinking.

View the Epoch AI benchmark review →

Epoch AI, an independent research organization, rated SWE-bench Verified as "Flawed" in their benchmark review, concluding that its static task set means current and future models are likely contaminated. They join a growing chorus of voices arguing that the benchmark has outlived its usefulness.

Goodhart's Law Has Entered the Chat

"When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure." — Charles Goodhart, 1975

The AI industry is living through one of the most expensive demonstrations of Goodhart's Law in history. Contrary Research reports that over $225 million has traded on Polymarket markets that are settled by Arena (formerly LMArena) leaderboard rankings. When that much money rides on a leaderboard position, the incentive to optimize for the metric — rather than the underlying capability — becomes overwhelming.

View the Contrary Research report →

Nick Heiner of Surge AI laid this out in his AI Engineer World's Fair talk, "When Will The Benchmaxxing Plague End?": AI benchmarking has drifted from real-world value because of weak methodology and poor incentives. The cost of building a rigorous large agentic coding benchmark runs into the millions — but the cost of gaming an existing one is near zero.

The benchmaxxing playbook is well-documented at this point:

  1. Data contamination: Train on the benchmark's problems. A January 2026 study measured contamination rates between 1% and 45% across popular benchmarks.
  2. Cherry-picking: Submit only your best-performing configuration. Report numbers from runs that happened to land high.
  3. Saturation: Top models now max out MMLU and SWE-bench while scoring near zero on ARC-AGI-3. The benchmark no longer discriminates between frontier models — it's a ceiling test, not a measure.
  4. Grader manipulation: As Berkeley showed, if your agent can touch the evaluator, it can fake the result.

Alex Duffy of Every.to captured this perfectly in "Benchmarks Are Memes": benchmarks spread like cultural memes, directing which capabilities labs invest in. When the meme is wrong — when it measures memorization instead of reasoning, or gaming instead of capability — the entire field optimizes in the wrong direction.

Andrej Karpathy has been vocal about the state of AI evaluation. His tweet about moving past toy LLM evals — "svg of a pelican on a bicycle" — toward generalized testing garnered 29K likes:

View original post on X →

His separate "Land or Water?" experiment — asking an LLM to classify 16,200 lat/long coordinates — demonstrates what creative, hard-to-game evaluation actually looks like. The models know the answer because they've compressed the internet. That's the point: a novel eval reveals what the model actually learned, not what it memorized from a test bank.

View original post on X →

ℹ️ The self-reported scores problem: When Moonshot AI published Kimi K2 with a roughly 50% score on Humanity's Last Exam, independent testers re-ran it and got 29.4%. Self-reported benchmark numbers from labs have a conflict of interest that's so obvious it would be disqualifying in any other field.

The Verification Crisis

Princeton's Sayash Kapoor has been documenting what he calls "The Missing Science of AI Evaluation" — a thesis presented at Princeton's Center for Information Technology Policy. His core finding: flawed evaluation practices have produced overoptimistic accuracy claims in hundreds of published papers across fields from medicine to political science. Evaluation methods have failed to keep pace with deployment, creating a gap where lab performance fails to predict real-world utility.

View the evaluation crisis analysis →

This is the verification crisis. We have:

  • Models that score 100% on benchmarks they can trivially game (Berkeley RDI)
  • Benchmark creators who admit their own benchmarks are contaminated (OpenAI on SWE-bench)
  • Independent auditors who rate major benchmarks as "Flawed" (Epoch AI)
  • Financial markets that settle on leaderboard positions ($225M+ on Polymarket/Arena)
  • Self-reported scores that drop 20+ points under independent testing (Kimi K2)
  • An entire doctoral thesis arguing evaluation science is broken (Kapoor, Princeton)

And yet, companies are making million-dollar procurement decisions — which model to build on, which API to commit to, which vendor to trust — based on these numbers.

💡 The harness matters more than the model. We wrote about this when Dirac took Gemini 3 Flash from 47.8% to 65.2% on TerminalBench — a +17pp swing from harness engineering alone. If the wrapping around the model matters more than the model itself, then the eval's job is to test the system, not the weights. Most evals are still testing the weights.

What Actually Works: Building Evals That Survive Contact With Reality

The Berkeley team's recommendations read like a security audit checklist, because that's exactly what they are:

1. Isolate the evaluator from the agent. Never run them in the same container. Extract artifacts through a controlled channel. If your agent can import the grader, your eval is a theater prop.

2. Keep reference answers secret. Don't publish ground truth for leaderboard splits. Rotate instances. Consider held-out evaluation where the test set changes faster than models can train on it.

3. Test adversarially. Run a null agent (one that does nothing), a random agent, and a prompt-injection agent against your benchmark. A zero-capability agent should score at baseline. If it doesn't, your eval is measuring something other than capability.

4. Treat LLM judge inputs as untrusted. If your eval uses an LLM as a grader — and increasingly they all do — delimit agent content, strip injected instructions, and prefer extracted features over subjective judgments. The arXiv paper "Benchmarking is Broken" makes this case in detail.

5. Build private, held-out eval sets from your own traffic. This is the practitioner takeaway. Public benchmarks are useful for directional signal — they tell you roughly which tier a model is in. But for the ship decision — which model to deploy in production — you need an eval that no model has ever seen, built from your actual use cases, on your actual data distribution.

David Manheim of AI Evaluation Consensus made this point on the Future of Life Institute podcast: the path to reliable evaluation is the same path the security industry has already walked. Red-team your evals. Assume adversarial conditions. Build systems that fail gracefully when assumptions are violated.

What This Means for You

If you're an engineering leader choosing an AI model for production, here's the revised playbook:

Stop trusting single-number leaderboard scores. They are marketing assets, not engineering metrics. The gap between a self-reported 50% and an independent 29.4% should destroy your confidence in any number that hasn't been independently reproduced.

Triangulate across 3-4 diverse benchmarks, then build your own. Use public benchmarks to narrow the field to 2-3 candidates. Then build a private eval from 50-100 real examples from your production traffic. This eval is your actual moat — it reflects your use case, your edge cases, your data distribution. No lab can optimize against it because no lab has seen it.

Evaluate the system, not the model. If harness engineering can swing a score by 17 points on the same model, then model benchmarks are measuring the wrong thing. Evaluate your full stack — model + prompt + retrieval + tools + error handling — against real tasks. This is what the shift to harness leaderboards is about.

Treat "100%" as a bug report. Any eval where your system scores perfectly is testing the wrong thing. If your pass rate is 100%, your eval isn't challenging your system — it's congratulating it. As Ramakrishnan Lokanathan argued in his AI Engineer talk, a 70% pass rate is more informative than 100%, because it means the eval is actually stress-testing the boundaries of what your system can do.

Budget for eval maintenance. Evals rot. As models improve and train on more data, yesterday's held-out set becomes today's training example. Plan to refresh your eval set quarterly, just like you'd rotate encryption keys or update dependency versions.

The Moat Is Verification

The AI industry spent 2024-2025 racing to build the best model. It spent 2026 discovering that we can't agree on what "best" means. The next phase — and the real competitive advantage — is verification: proving that your system actually works on real problems, in production, under adversarial conditions.

The companies that build rigorous, private, continuously-refreshed evaluation infrastructure will make better model choices, catch regressions faster, and ship more reliable products. The companies that keep chasing leaderboard positions will keep getting surprised when their 100%-scoring model fails on the first real-world query.

Berkeley showed us what 100% looks like when the test is broken. The question is what your eval shows you when it's working.

Originally published at ComputeLeap

title: Building Mawared: An Egypt-Focused HR and Payroll Platform
description:
I recently completed Mawared, a cloud-based HR platform designed around the day-to-day needs of companies in Egypt.

The idea came from a common operational challenge: employee records, attendance, leave requests, approvals, expenses, and payroll calculations can easily end up spread across spreadsheets and disconnected processes. When information is separated, it becomes harder for HR teams and managers to track what is happening and understand how one process affects another.

Mawared brings these workflows together in one connected system.
A connected view of HR operations
The platform is designed around several core areas:

  • Command Center: A dashboard for tracking attendance, payroll readiness, and operational exceptions.
  • Employee profiles: A central employee record connected to the company’s branches, departments, job titles, financial details, and documents.
  • Attendance and shifts: Attendance tracking with shift rules, grace periods, and GPS-based geofencing.
  • Approvals and leave management: A unified workflow for leave requests and other employee approvals.
  • Finance and expenses: Tools for managing advances, installments, expenses, and company custody items.
  • Governance and audit history: Role-based permissions and an audit trail to make actions and changes traceable. The goal is to make these modules work together instead of treating each one as a separate tool. Payroll designed for the Egyptian context Payroll was one of the most important parts of the project. The system’s payroll workflow accounts for items such as salary components, attendance-related deductions, advances, insurance, and income tax.

A payroll simulation helps make the calculation easier to follow by showing how the final net salary is reached. The design also includes a payroll readiness check to help identify missing or unresolved data before processing a payroll run.

Once a payroll period is locked, its records are protected from direct changes. Later adjustments can be handled as recorded settlements, keeping a clear history of what changed and when.

The platform also includes export formats for salary transfers to Egyptian banks, including CIB, QNB, National Bank of Egypt, and Banque Misr.
What I learned
Building Mawared pushed me to think beyond individual screens and features. The bigger challenge was connecting the workflows:

  • How can attendance exceptions affect payroll?
  • How can an HR manager spot missing information before payroll is processed?
  • How can approvals, expenses, and employee records remain traceable?
  • How should the product support companies with multiple branches? Working through these questions helped me think about the product from the perspectives of employees, HR teams, finance teams, and company managers.

Mawared is a project about bringing everyday HR operations into one clearer workflow, with the needs of the Egyptian market in mind.
