title: Keep the HTTP status and JSON error code separate in your AI API adapter
description:
An adapter label such as provider_rejected_402 leaves an important question unanswered: did the server send HTTP 402, or did the adapter find 402 inside a JSON body?

Those are different observations. If the adapter merges them, the next person debugging the request has to guess what actually happened.

Save a small diagnostic record before choosing a remedy

For an error response, start with four fields:

  • The HTTP status returned by your HTTP client.
  • A numeric error code found in the JSON, if present.
  • A server request ID, when available.
  • Whether the response body was a JSON object, another JSON value, invalid JSON, or too large for this example to parse.

RouterBase's error reference documents both nested and top-level JSON error shapes, along with x-request-id for correlating a request. Keep the transport status in its own field rather than replacing it with a value from the body.

A Python example you can run without calling a model

This function summarizes response data you supply. It makes no network requests and needs no API key. The example response is synthetic.

"""Offline example: summarize a supplied error response; never call an API."""

import json
from uuid import UUID


def summarize_error(http_status, headers, body):
    payload = {}
    body_kind = "too_large"
    if len(body) <= 65536:
        try:
            value = json.loads(body)
            body_kind = "object" if isinstance(value, dict) else "non_object"
            if isinstance(value, dict):
                payload = value
        except (ValueError, RecursionError):
            body_kind = "invalid_json"

    error = payload.get("error")
    fields = error if isinstance(error, dict) else payload
    code = fields.get("code")
    if isinstance(code, str) and code.isascii() and code.isdigit() and len(code) == 3:
        code = int(code)
    if type(code) is not int or not 100 <= code <= 599:
        code = None

    normalized = {name.lower(): value for name, value in headers.items()}
    request_id = normalized.get("x-request-id") or payload.get("request_id")
    try:
        request_id = str(UUID(request_id)) if isinstance(request_id, str) else None
    except ValueError:
        request_id = None

    return {
        "http_status": http_status,
        "json_numeric_code": code,
        "request_id": request_id,
        "body_kind": body_kind,
    }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(summarize_error(
        402,
        {"X-Request-ID": "00000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000001"},
        '{"error":{"code":402,"message":"Synthetic example"}}',
    ))

The output keeps http_status and json_numeric_code as separate values. In the synthetic example both are 402. If you supply HTTP 200 and a body containing {"code":402}, it preserves both values; that is an adapter test case, not a claim that RouterBase returns that combination.

The function deliberately omits error messages, prompts, request bodies, and authorization headers. It accepts only numeric codes in the 100–599 range and UUID-shaped request IDs. String error categories are left out of this small example. A missing value remains None; it is not replaced with a guessed cause.

This is a limited diagnostic summary, not a general redaction system or a complete response validator. Pass the actual integer status from your HTTP client, string header names and a text body. Bound the response read in your HTTP client too: the length check here happens after the body has reached the function.

A status is a starting point

For RouterBase organization requests, the organization guide describes 402 responses for an insufficient organization wallet and for member spending limits. The HTTP status alone does not distinguish those cases. Read the specific error in a protected debugging context, then check the relevant account scope and limits.

Avoid making automatic changes to spending caps just because an adapter emitted a generic billing label. Likewise, a successful catalog lookup does not validate a later generation request.

When escalating an issue, include the timestamp with its time zone, endpoint path, HTTP status, and request ID. Review any error text separately before sharing it. Keep credentials and private inputs out of a public support message.

Check the adapter with fixtures first

Use a nested error object, a top-level numeric code, an HTML error page, a JSON array, and an oversized body. Verify that a mismatch between transport status and body code stays visible.

We checked this example locally with synthetic inputs, including malformed JSON and an invalid request ID. No inference request was sent, and no model performance or billing behavior was tested.

We are the RouterBase team. Explore RouterBase for an OpenAI-compatible API for AI models.

title: Bayesian Distribution System State Estimation with Flow Matching
description:
arXiv:2610.40728v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Medium-voltage feeders have few real-time measurements, so distribution system state estimation (DSSE) rests on pseudo-measurements of the secondary substations, a prior in Bayesian terms. Weighted least squares keeps the power flow exact but reduces this prior to a mean and variance, while supervised deep learning estimators also learn the power flow and are tied to one measurement set. We propose PoSE (posterior sampling for state estimation), which keeps the Bayesian structure of DSSE and learns only what the distribution system operator does not know, namely the distribution of substation injections, modelled by a neural network trained with flow matching on historical data. The power flow equations, grid topology and measurements enter only at sampling, through a noise-aware Kalman-type correction. The neural network therefore never approximates the power flow, but every posterior sample is a physically consistent operating point, and one trained prior serves any measurement set, noise level and topology. On the IEEE 33-bus feeder, PoSE lowers the probabilistic injection error (CRPS) by 6.7-7.5% against a full-covariance Gaussian prior in all 12 tested settings. It provides reliable uncertainty: the 90% intervals contain the true injection almost exactly as often as exact posterior samples would, whereas those of supervised estimators contain it in only 37-78% of cases. On the 240-bus unbalanced three-phase Iowa feeder, it gives the lowest injection, voltage and branch-current errors of all estimators. A fast variant matches this accuracy at 0.2-0.6s per snapshot and, without retraining, beats Gaussian priors and retrained supervised estimators on seven reconfigured topologies.

title: State Explorer: A Zoomable Timeline for React
description:
I turned an old Azure visualization idea into an open-source React component. The useful part is the little window at the bottom.

Imagine an API that was healthy all morning, degraded for five minutes, then healthy again. On a chart showing six hours, that five-minute interval is easy to skim past. A table gives you the exact timestamps, but makes it harder to see how that incident fits into the rest of the day.

I wanted both views at once: the whole story and a close look at the interesting bit.

The lower timeline keeps the full history in view. Drag its blue window to move through time, or resize an edge to zoom into the detail chart above.

Try the live demo — move the window, pull its left or right edge, and hover an interval. The demo has service health, build pipelines, and device states, all using the same component.

The zoom window

The bottom overview shows the full time range. The blue window inside it selects the period shown in the larger chart above. Drag the middle to move to another period without changing its duration. Drag either edge to widen or narrow the period. The upper chart updates so you can inspect state changes that were hard to make out at full scale.

It feels a little like sliding a magnifying glass over the timeline. Except the magnifying glass has handles, and thankfully doesn’t roll off your desk.

Hover or focus a state interval to see its state and original start and end times. Reset view takes you back to the starting range. The window also has keyboard controls, so dragging isn’t the only way to navigate.

An idea from 2015

In 2015, I joined an internal Azure project that collected logs, metrics, and errors from resources such as virtual machines. We needed an availability page, and I kept coming back to the same question: how do you show a full day of history and still let someone investigate a brief outage?

I spent a lot of time on that question. I even missed a Thanksgiving trip to California with friends while working through the design. Eventually I built a two-level timeline with jQuery and D3.js: full history below, selected detail above. The project later moved to Angular, and I rebuilt the component for it.

The earlier Availability Explorer. I kept a simplified standalone version and its demo on GitHub.

In 2021, I heard that the component was still being used. That was a lovely surprise. The code had changed, but the interaction had proved useful for years.

State Explorer is a new implementation of that idea, built for more than availability data. Its TypeScript core handles time intervals and projection; its React package renders the SVG timeline and overview navigator. Your app supplies the entities, state intervals, and colors.

Try it

Install the two packages in a React 18 or 19 application:

npm install @state-explorer/core @state-explorer/react

Here is a small example with one five-minute degraded interval:

import { useState } from "react";
import { StateTimeline } from "@state-explorer/react";
import type { Entity, StateInterval, TimeRange } from "@state-explorer/core";

const at = (time: string) => Date.parse(`2026-09-10T${time}:00Z`);
const domain: TimeRange = { start: at("08:00"), end: at("14:00") };
const entities: Entity[] = [{ id: "api", label: "API" }];
const intervals: StateInterval<"healthy" | "degraded">[] = [
  { entityId: "api", start: at("08:00"), end: at("10:20"), state: "healthy" },
  { entityId: "api", start: at("10:20"), end: at("10:25"), state: "degraded" },
  { entityId: "api", start: at("10:25"), end: at("14:00"), state: "healthy" },
];

export function Example() {
  const [viewport, setViewport] = useState<TimeRange>({
    start: at("10:00"), end: at("12:00"),
  });
  return (
    <StateTimeline
      entities={entities}
      intervals={intervals}
      domain={domain}
      viewport={viewport}
      onViewportChange={setViewport}
      label="API state history"
      getStateAppearance={interval => interval.state === "healthy"
        ? { fill: "#167d73", label: "Healthy" }
        : { fill: "#b87916", label: "Degraded" }}
    />
  );
}

The overview covers 08:00–14:00 UTC; the detail chart starts at 10:00–12:00. The five-minute change is at 10:20. The viewport is controlled by your app: moving or resizing the window calls onViewportChange, and the chart follows the range you pass back. You can also constrain or reject a proposed range. See the checked Quick Start for a larger two-entity example.

Scope and limits

State Explorer is useful when several entities move through discrete states over time: healthy/degraded/down, queued/building/deployed, online/offline, and similar histories. It doesn’t fetch data or decide what a gap means. You provide the intervals; it shows them on a shared time axis. There is no aggregation or virtualization yet, and the 0.1.x API is experimental. Large-data performance, physical touch devices, other browser engines, and real screen readers still need broader validation.

I would love to hear where a view like this helps, and where it gets in the way. Play with the demo, explore the source and docs, or open an issue with a real use case.

title: Density-Guided Bootstrap Boundaries for Latent World-Model Reinforcement Learning
description:
arXiv:2610.41022v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Latent world models allow reinforcement learning agents to learn policies from imagined trajectories, yet determining the optimal depth of model reliance remains a fundamental challenge. Fixed imagination horizons apply uniform prediction depths regardless of trajectory reliability, exposing target values to compounding model error or over-relying on critic approximations. We introduce density-guided bootstrap boundaries, a trajectory-dependent mechanism that adapts the depth of imagined returns using a score-informed relative density proxy. The proxy accumulates the estimated divergence of a score-corrected auxiliary field formed by a feature displacement network and a noise-conditioned score estimator along imagined paths. We propose two gating mechanisms: a hard boundary that halts return expansion at a discrete state, and a soft boundary that continuously shifts the return recursion toward critic bootstrapping. Both variants preserve boundary value estimates and apply corresponding survival weights to actor and critic losses. Formulated independently of specific dynamics models and instantiated within Dreamer V3, we prove that the resulting gated Bellman operator is a strict contraction mapping and that early bootstrapping monotonically reduces conditional target variance. We clarify the theoretical assumptions distinguishing our expansion proxy from exact path likelihoods. Across continuous-control tasks and Atari Pong, empirical evaluations show that dynamic boundary selection enhances sample efficiency and late-training performance over fixed-horizon and auxiliary-enabled baselines.

title: Vercel Connect adds webhook triggers for more providers

Vercel Connect now supports webhook triggers for Resend, X, Twilio, Notion, and Telegram.

Connect receives webhook events, such as Telegram bot messages or emails received by your Resend domain, and forwards them to an endpoint in your Vercel project. It verifies incoming requests and handles provider heartbeats and verification challenges for you.

These connectors join existing trigger support for Slack, Discord, Microsoft Teams, GitHub, and Linear.

title: Mage-VL-Cowork: A Full Training Recipe to Learn Hybrid Computer Use From Evolved Harnesses
description:
arXiv:2610.40747v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Effective computer-use agents (CUAs) should seamlessly combine visual GUI interaction with code and terminal execution within a single policy. We present Mage-VL-Cowork, a 4B hybrid CUA trained from a general multimodally aligned checkpoint through an end-to-end, progressive five-stage curriculum across midtraining, SFT, and RL. To power this curriculum at scale, Mage-CUA-Forge replaces per-task agent construction with reusable, skill-conditioned generation workflows and application-specific preparers, synthesizing 293,806 desktop and web tasks across 6,915 skills while reducing recurring per-task expenditure by 82.6%. Rather than directly distilling a default teacher, we evolve the teacher harness and instantiate specialized CUA harnesses to yield high-quality trajectories alongside stage-specific supervision. Mage-VL-Cowork-4B finally climbs to 66.0% on OSWorld-Verified through different training stages with more efficient reasoning cost, achieving state-of-the-art performance at its parameter size and pushing forward the frontier of on-device intelligence.

title: axum vs actix-web vs Rocket on 1 CPU and 1 GB RAM
description:
TL;DR: I wrote the same Todo API in axum, actix-web and Rocket, then load tested each one in Docker with 1 or 2 CPU cores and 1 GB of RAM. On one core, actix served about 67k requests per second, axum 47k and Rocket 34k. Each server idled at about 1 MB of RAM. I then re-ran it on two AWS spot instances in Mumbai, a c7i.xlarge for the server and a c7i.2xlarge for the load generator, and got the same ranking over a real network. Before any of that, review found a bug in my axum version that let one bad request take the whole server down, and two settings that would have made the benchmark unfair. Code and full results: github.com/2u841r/actix-vs-axum-vs-rocket.

Why

Every "Rust web framework benchmark" I find runs on a 64-core machine and reports millions of requests per second. That tells me nothing. The servers I actually pay for have 1 or 2 vCPUs and 1 GB of RAM. I wanted to know how much each framework can handle on that.

The API

Five routes, identical in all three projects:

Method Path Does
GET /health returns OK
GET /todos lists all todos
GET /todos/{id} one todo, or 404
POST /todos creates a todo
DELETE /todos/{id} deletes, 204

State is a Mutex<HashMap<u64, Todo>> plus an AtomicU64 for ids. Nothing clever, and the same in all three, so I compare the frameworks and not my data structures.

The axum version is the shortest of the three:

let app = Router::new()
    .route("/health", get(|| async { "OK" }))
    .route("/todos", get(list_todos).post(create_todo))
    .route("/todos/{id}", get(get_todo).delete(delete_todo))
    .with_state(state);

The bug that killed the server

My first axum get_todo looked like this:

let todo = state.todos.lock().unwrap().get(&id).cloned().unwrap();

It compiles and passes clippy pedantic, and it works for every id that exists. Ask for one that doesn't and the last unwrap() panics.

The panic alone wouldn't be fatal, since axum only drops that connection. The problem is when it panics. The MutexGuard from lock() is a temporary, and temporaries live until the end of the statement. So the panic happens while the lock is still held, which poisons the mutex. From then on, every lock().unwrap() in every handler panics too.

One GET /todos/999 and the server is effectively dead.

The fix is to return a 404 instead of panicking:

async fn get_todo(
    State(state): State<Arc<AppState>>,
    Path(id): Path<u64>,
) -> Result<Json<Todo>, StatusCode> {
    state.todos.lock().unwrap().get(&id).cloned().map(Json).ok_or(StatusCode::NOT_FOUND)
}

I first tried returning Option<Json<Todo>>, which Rocket handles as a 404. axum 0.8 no longer implements IntoResponse for Option, so it doesn't compile there. Result with a status code works.

Making the comparison fair

Two settings would have skewed the results before I ran anything:

  1. Rocket logged every request. I had built its config from Config::debug_default(), which logs at the normal level. Printing a line per request at 30k req/s costs a lot, and the other two log nothing. I switched to release_default() with log_level: LogLevel::Off.
  2. actix had a hardcoded .workers(8). Tokio and Rocket size their thread pools from the CPU count. With 1 CPU, actix would have run 8 workers against everyone else's 1. I removed it.

All three frameworks call std::thread::available_parallelism(), which respects both the container's cgroup limit and its CPU pinning. Inside a container pinned to one core, nproc prints 1 and each framework starts one worker. That is what makes the comparison equal.

The setup

One shared multi-stage Dockerfile builds all three:

FROM rust:1-bookworm AS build
ARG APP
WORKDIR /src
COPY ${APP}/ ./
RUN cargo build --release && cp target/release/${APP} /app

FROM debian:bookworm-slim
COPY --from=build /app /app
ENTRYPOINT ["/app"]

Each server runs like this:

docker run --rm --network host \
  --cpuset-cpus=0 --memory=1g --memory-swap=1g \
  axum-api
  • --cpuset-cpus=0 pins it to one physical core (0,1 for the two-core test).
  • --memory-swap equal to --memory turns swap off, so going over 1 GB gets the server killed instead of slowly swapping.
  • --network host skips docker-proxy, which would otherwise add its own overhead to every request.

My laptop has a Ryzen 5 8645HS with 6 cores and 12 threads. lscpu -e=CPU,CORE shows that CPUs 6 and 7 are the hyperthread siblings of 0 and 1. I left them idle and pinned the load generator, oha, to the remaining cores:

taskset -c 2-5,8-11 oha -z 10s -c 1000 --no-tui http://localhost:3001/todos

If the load generator shares cores with the server, you end up measuring the load generator.

For each framework, bench.sh adds 100 todos, warms up for 3 seconds, then runs GET /todos at 50, 100, 500 and 1000 connections and finally POST /todos, 10 seconds each. After every run it reads memory.peak from the container's cgroup.

Results

1 CPU, 1 GB RAM

actix-web axum Rocket
GET req/s, 100 connections 67,205 47,328 33,792
GET req/s, 1000 connections 58,279 44,788 31,459
GET p99, 1000 connections 19 ms 156 ms 172 ms
POST req/s, 100 connections 123,745 113,489 70,511
Idle RAM 1.4 MB 0.9 MB 1.0 MB
Peak RAM, 1000 connections 28 MB 37 MB 38 MB

2 CPUs, 1 GB RAM

actix-web axum Rocket
GET req/s, 100 connections 128,872 80,511 63,736
GET req/s, 1000 connections 109,103 65,114 57,171
GET p99, 1000 connections 11 ms 56 ms 77 ms
POST req/s, 100 connections 236,629 217,888 133,975

No errors and no out-of-memory kills in any run. The full table, including p50 latency for every run, is in the repo README.

What the numbers say

actix wins on throughput. It did about 1.4x what axum did and about 2x Rocket. It also scaled best from one core to two.

The latency story is more interesting. At 1000 connections on one core, axum's median was 5 ms against actix's 17 ms, but axum's p99 was 156 ms against actix's 19 ms. axum and Rocket serve most requests quickly and make a few wait a long time. actix serves everyone at about the same speed. If you care about the slowest 1% of your users, that matters more than the req/s number.

RAM doesn't matter at this scale. All three idle at about 1 MB and stay under 50 MB holding 1000 open connections. A 1 GB server runs out of CPU long before it runs out of memory. The POST runs did reach 180 to 360 MB, but that was the HashMap holding over a million todos after 10 seconds, not framework overhead.

Rocket is "slow" only next to the other two. 31k requests per second on a single core is about 2.7 billion requests a day. No app I run gets anywhere near that.

Round two: AWS, over a real network

The laptop run had one obvious hole: the load generator and the server shared a machine and talked over localhost. So I ran it again on AWS in ap-south-1 (Mumbai), with two spot instances:

Role Instance vCPU RAM
Server c7i.xlarge 4 (2 physical cores) 8 GB
Load generator c7i.2xlarge 8 16 GB

Both ran Amazon Linux 2023, in the same AZ and a cluster placement group, talking over private IPs. I didn't pick c7i.large for the server, because its 2 vCPUs are two hyperthreads of one core, and the 2 CPU test would have meant something different from the laptop. On the c7i.xlarge, vCPUs 0/2 and 1/3 are hyperthread pairs, so the server got 0 or 0,1, with 2 and 3 left idle. The container still had the same 1 GB cap.

There was no SSH. Both boxes were driven with SSM Run Command, and the security group only let the load generator reach ports 3001 to 3003. The whole thing, Docker builds included, took about 20 minutes and cost well under a dollar at spot prices.

1 CPU, 1 GB RAM, on AWS

actix-web axum Rocket
GET req/s, 100 connections 66,252 47,784 40,390
GET req/s, 1000 connections 63,885 42,090 36,304
GET p99, 1000 connections 16 ms 142 ms 165 ms
POST req/s, 100 connections 171,394 150,572 73,327

2 CPUs, 1 GB RAM, on AWS

actix-web axum Rocket
GET req/s, 100 connections 111,959 79,327 61,285
GET req/s, 1000 connections 107,731 43,867 58,774
GET p99, 1000 connections 10 ms 65 ms 75 ms
POST req/s, 100 connections 286,742 228,708 113,680

On one core, the cloud matched the laptop almost exactly: actix 66k vs 67k, axum 48k vs 47k. Rocket did a bit better on AWS, 40k vs 34k. POST was faster across the board, likely because the load generator had a whole machine to itself.

The surprise was axum on 2 CPUs at high connection counts. In the main run it fell to about 44k req/s at 1000 connections, below Rocket. I didn't trust that, so I ran it twice more while the instances were still up:

axum, 2 CPUs c=100 c=500 c=1000
Run 1 79,327 44,231 43,867
Run 2 80,642 76,913 43,217
Run 3 80,250 81,166 76,492

It lands at either about 44k or about 78k, never in between. actix and Rocket stayed within a few percent in every run. I haven't found the cause yet, but it's a good reminder that one run can lie, and that a stable framework is worth something on its own.

Caveats

  • The laptop numbers are a single run. CPU boost and heat move numbers by 5 to 10%, so don't read anything into small gaps.
  • The laptop run is over localhost. The AWS run below fixes that.
  • GET /todos returns 100 todos, about 8 KB of JSON. That measures cloning and serde as much as routing.
  • The AWS run is one region and one instance family. Graviton (Arm) or AMD instances may rank differently.
  • A real app talks to a database. As I found in latency is geography, the database round trip will cost far more than any difference between these three frameworks.

So which one?

On raw numbers, actix-web, both on my laptop and on AWS. In practice, any of them will handle far more than a 1 CPU server will ever be asked to do. I would pick axum for its ecosystem (tower middleware, tokio everywhere) and how little code it takes, and reach for actix when tail latency under heavy load really matters.

Whichever you pick, don't unwrap() while holding a lock.

The code, the Dockerfile and the benchmark script are on GitHub: 2u841r/actix-vs-axum-vs-rocket. Run ./bench.sh on your own machine and see whether your numbers match mine.

title: Comparative Evaluation of LLM-Based Review Paradigms for Academic Paper Quality Assessment
description:
arXiv:2610.41391v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Growing submission volumes have renewed interest in using large language models (LLMs) to support peer review. It remains unclear how such evaluation should be structured, how much the model matters, and whether LLM scores predict research impact. We evaluate five paradigms across three input representations and three LLMs on 232 stratified ICLR 2025 submissions. Direct absolute rating matches comparative ranking on rank correlation with human scores, yet compresses most predictions above the accept threshold, flagging almost none of the papers reviewers scored below it. A base-rate-matched recalibration control locates the cause: comparative ranking supplies placement, not better ordering, and after recalibration Direct Rating reaches higher agreement than Elo while making 24% as many API calls. Abstract-only input beats full-paper summarization, and model choice matters as much as paradigm choice. Replicating on all 11,513 scored submissions reproduces these patterns, shows absolute agreement depends on the evaluated set's score spread, and finds none beating an always-reject baseline in accuracy. Human scores track citations better than any paradigm, with one exception: Group Rating retains its citation correlation after controlling for human scores, and alone ranks within the accepted pool. Ranking quality alone cannot assess review quality; calibration, thresholds, model, and target outcome all matter.

title: Scraping IKEA Data with Python: the Same Products Cost 37% More in France Than in the Netherlands
description:
The white LACK side table, article 30449908, costs €9.99 in Germany, France, Spain, Austria and Belgium. In Portugal the same article number costs €12.99. Same product, same currency, a 30% gap, and no exchange rate to blame.

I wanted to know whether that was a quirk of one cheap table or a pattern, so I built a small IKEA price index in Python: the same article numbers, priced in nine euro-zone countries on the same day. It is a pattern. Not one of the 72 articles I could match had the same price in all nine countries, and on average the French site charges 37% more than the Dutch one for identical items.

The data

I used the IKEA Pro API, which returns IKEA's catalogue as JSON for a given countryCode. Everything here comes from one endpoint, /product-search-by-keyword: five IKEA families (BILLY, KALLAX, POÄNG, MALM, LACK) searched in nine euro-zone countries (Germany, France, Italy, Spain, the Netherlands, Austria, Belgium, Ireland, Portugal), first page of results only, all collected on 24 October 2026. That is 45 requests.

Each result carries an id (IKEA's article number), name, typeName, details.designText (the colour or finish), price.currentPrice, and a variants list where every colour variant has its own id and price. Counting the variants, those 45 searches returned 1,220 distinct article numbers. Only 72 of them showed up in all nine countries, and those 72 are the basket.

Sticking to the euro zone was deliberate. Once you compare euros with kronor or dollars, half of any gap you find is the exchange rate on the day you picked. Within the euro zone, a price difference is a price difference.

The code

You need a RapidAPI key (the API's RapidAPI page has a free tier) in the RAPIDAPI_KEY environment variable, plus requests and pandas. The script caches every response on disk, so it spends 45 calls once and nothing after that.

import json
import os
from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd
import requests

HOST = "ikea-api-pro.p.rapidapi.com"
CACHE = Path("ikea_cache")
COUNTRIES = {"de": "en", "fr": "fr", "it": "it", "es": "en", "nl": "en",  # code: language
             "at": "de", "be": "en", "ie": "en", "pt": "en"}  # language changes text, not prices
KEYWORDS = ["billy", "kallax", "poang", "malm", "lack"]


def search(keyword, country):
    """Page 1 of a keyword search, cached on disk so a re-run costs no calls."""
    file = CACHE / f"{country}-{keyword}.json"
    if file.exists():
        return json.loads(file.read_text())
    r = requests.get(
        f"https://{HOST}/product-search-by-keyword",
        params={"keyword": keyword, "countryCode": country,
                "languageCode": COUNTRIES[country]},
        headers={"x-rapidapi-host": HOST,
                 "x-rapidapi-key": os.environ["RAPIDAPI_KEY"]},
        timeout=60,
    )
    r.raise_for_status()
    CACHE.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    file.write_text(r.text)
    return r.json()


rows = []
for keyword in KEYWORDS:
    for country in COUNTRIES:
        for p in search(keyword, country)["data"]["products"]:
            # The listed product plus its colour variants, each with its own article number
            items = [(p["id"], p["details"]["designText"], p["price"])]
            items += [(v["id"], v["designText"], v["price"]) for v in p.get("variants") or []]
            for article, colour, price in items:
                rows.append({"country": country, "id": article, "name": p["name"],
                             "type": p["typeName"], "colour": colour,
                             "price": price["currentPrice"]})

df = pd.DataFrame(rows).drop_duplicates(["country", "id"])
wide = df.pivot_table(index="id", columns="country", values="price", aggfunc="first")
basket = wide.dropna()  # article numbers priced in all nine countries
rel = basket.div(basket.median(axis=1), axis=0)  # 1.0 = that article's median price
index = (rel.mean() * 100).round(1).sort_values()

print(f"{len(wide)} article numbers seen, {len(basket)} priced in all 9 countries")
print(index.to_string())
print("Cheapest (or tied) for this many articles:")
print(basket.eq(basket.min(axis=1), axis=0).sum().sort_values(ascending=False).to_string())

Two decisions in there matter more than the rest. The join key is the article number, never the name, for reasons the pitfalls section makes painfully clear. And the index treats every article equally: each price is divided by that article's median across the nine countries, then averaged per country, so a €179 shelving unit does not drown out a €4.99 wall shelf. An index of 100 means "typical euro-zone price".

The first lines it prints:

1220 article numbers seen, 72 priced in all 9 countries
country
nl     84.2
de     91.6
pt     97.2

France is the dearest IKEA in the euro zone, the Netherlands the cheapest

The Netherlands comes out at 84.2 and France at 115.2. Germany is the second cheapest at 91.6, and the other six countries sit within about five points of 100. Buying one of each of the 72 articles would cost €2,779.89 on the Dutch site and €3,835.46 on the French one, 38% more.

The ranking is not driven by a few outliers. The Netherlands was the cheapest country, or tied for cheapest, on 51 of the 72 articles and the dearest on none. France was the dearest, or tied, on 34. Ireland was never the cheapest country for a single article.

Country Index Index without VAT One of each (72) Cheapest or tied Dearest or tied
Netherlands 84.2 84.5 €2,779.89 51 0
Germany 91.6 93.4 €2,945.44 29 5
Portugal 97.2 95.8 €3,255.74 12 8
Italy 102.3 101.7 €3,341.20 2 6
Spain 103.6 103.9 €3,325.39 8 13
Belgium 104.0 104.3 €3,443.39 5 6
Ireland 104.2 102.8 €3,334.00 0 10
Austria 105.3 106.5 €3,542.43 3 14
France 115.2 116.6 €3,835.46 1 34

The family matters too. France's premium is mostly KALLAX: on the 34 KALLAX articles in the basket its index is 125.1, against 105.3 on LACK. LACK is where Spain looks expensive (111.9) and Germany cheap (84.7). The Netherlands is the cheapest country on BILLY and KALLAX; on LACK, Germany edges it, 84.7 to 85.6.

Almost nothing has one euro-zone price

For each article I compared the dearest country with the cheapest. The median gap is 50.7%. Only 2 of the 72 articles stay within 25%, 43 differ by more than 50%, and 13 by 100% or more. The widest is a KALLAX insert with door: €7.50 in Portugal, €20 in France.

The LACK side table from the opening is a good example of how small these numbers can look while still being large in percentage terms: €8.99 in the Netherlands, €9.95 in Italy, €9.99 in five countries, €12 in Ireland and €12.99 in Portugal.

VAT does not explain it

The obvious objection is tax. EU shelf prices for consumers include VAT (the price indication directive defines the selling price as the final price including VAT), and the standard rates in these nine countries run from 19% in Germany to 23% in Ireland and Portugal (standard rates on the EU's Your Europe site).

So I divided every price by one plus its country's standard rate and rebuilt the index. Nothing important moved. France goes from 115.2 to 116.6 and the Netherlands from 84.2 to 84.5. The largest shift is Germany's, from 91.6 to 93.4, because it has the lowest VAT of the nine. A spread of 19% to 23% in tax cannot produce a 37% gap in prices, and France's 20% rate is in the middle of the range anyway.

What tripped me up in the data

The most famous bookcase is not in the basket. You would expect the white BILLY to be the anchor of any IKEA price index. It never made the 72, because Europe sells it under two sets of article numbers. Germany, the Netherlands, Austria, Belgium and Ireland list 00263850 (from €42.49 in the Netherlands to €65 in Ireland) and its siblings. France, Italy, Spain and Portugal list 50522040 (€44.99 to €49.99) and three siblings, the same four numbers the US site lists. This is not page-one noise: searching the exact article number 00263850 returns one result in Germany and zero in France, and 50522040 returns zero in Germany. The search response has no dimensions field, so I cannot tell from the data whether the two white bookcases are identical apart from the number; you can compare the German and French product pages yourself. Either way, joining on the number quietly drops BILLY white, and joining on the name compares two different articles.

Names are not keys. In Germany, page one of the KALLAX search has eight different article numbers that are all "KALLAX, Shelving unit, white", priced from €16.99 to €129. They are different sizes. Across the nine countries there were 101 such groups where name, type and colour were identical but the article numbers were not. Anything that matches on text will happily compare a small shelf with a large one.

Combinations have their own numbers, and they are local. IDs starting with s are combinations: a POÄNG armchair is a frame plus a cushion sold as one number. Of the 1,220 numbers I saw, 724 were combinations, and only 5 survived into the basket. The same POÄNG armchair and footstool in walnut effect with a Kelinge beige cushion is s29617733 in Germany, the Netherlands and Portugal (€149, €168 and €170) and s59617736 in Ireland (€199). POÄNG contributed nothing to the index for that reason.

Search is not a name filter. Page one of the "malm" search in Germany had 22 results: 5 named MALM and 10 named STORKLINTA. In Belgium only 2 of 22 were MALM. The total result count for the same keyword ranged from 75 in France to 615 in Germany. MALM contributed nothing either. If you want a specific article, search its number.

currentPrice is all you get, so promotions look like prices. The search response has a current price and no regular price. Seven of the nine Dutch BILLY prices in the basket end in .49 (€25.49, €42.49), and €42.49 is exactly 85% of €49.99, which looks like a 15% markdown. Portugal lists KALLAX door inserts at €7.50 where five other countries charge €15. I cannot prove either is a promotion from these fields, so I re-ran the index without BILLY and without the KALLAX inserts, 54 articles in all. The ends held: the Netherlands at 85.2, Germany 88.4, France 113.7. Austria moved up to 110.0.

formattedPrice is localised. Spain returns "44,99", Germany "59.99", the US "$79.00". Parse currentPrice, which is always a number. Badges are localised as well: the same idea arrives as "Top seller", "Best seller", "Bestseller", "Top ventes" and "Il più venduto", so filtering on one string misses most of them.

One page is a sample, not a catalogue. 615 of the 1,220 article numbers appeared in just one country. Most of that is ranking: I read page one of each search, and each country orders its results differently. Absence from page one does not mean IKEA does not sell it there, which is why I checked the white BILLY with exact-number searches before writing that paragraph.

What I would do next

Three things. Paginate with the page parameter, so the basket covers whole families instead of whatever ranked on page one. Run the same basket weekly, which is the only honest way to tell a 15% promotion from a list price. And add Sweden, Switzerland, the UK and the US with ECB reference rates for a stated date, accepting that the gaps then include currency.

The data came from the IKEA Pro API. If you want a full catalogue as a file instead, there is an IKEA US product dataset, and for anything custom, get in touch.

title: Inside hex: A Deep Dive into Local Voice Dictation
description:
Hex

Hex is local voice dictation for Mac, Windows and Linux. Hold a key, speak, and it pastes.

The Core Engineering Challenge

Hex addresses the need for local voice dictation solutions across multiple operating systems while ensuring user privacy and responsiveness. By processing speech entirely on the device, it eliminates the latency and privacy concerns associated with cloud-based alternatives.

Architectural Blueprint & System Internals

Hex's architecture is built on Rust, leveraging its performance and safety features. The application operates by holding a shortcut, speaking, and releasing the key, which triggers transcription that is pasted into the active application. Notably, the first run downloads a speech model, and subsequent uses do not require internet access. Experimental features are available in a dedicated Labs section.

Recent Changes and Trending Status

The latest release, tagged @kitlangton/hex@0.3.1, published on 2026-09-26, introduced significant performance improvements. The update optimized the handling of model progress and dictation levels using shared bounded SSE framing. This enhancement prevents failures when processing large transport chunks and improves the responsiveness of event dispatching.

Developer Experience (DX) & Implementation

Installation is straightforward across platforms:

  • Homebrew: brew install --cask anomalyco/tap/hex
  • AUR: yay -S hex-bin
  • Linux Install Script: curl -fsSL https://anoma.ly/hex/install-linux.sh | sh
  • Nix: nix profile install github:anomalyco/hex

Further documentation is available in the docs/ directory, which provides insights into usage and contribution guidelines. However, the project does not accept pull requests, encouraging users to open issues instead.

Technical Trade-offs & Performance Bounds

While Hex offers robust local processing and privacy, there are limitations. For instance, community feedback highlights the challenge of integrating custom speech models, as the current design restricts dictation to verified models. Additionally, users have reported issues with shortcut changes in Gnome that require manual resets, indicating potential friction in usability.

Community Pulse: What Developers Are Saying

Real-world feedback indicates both appreciation for Hex's capabilities and areas for improvement. For example, users have expressed a desire for support for custom speech models (see Issue #648). Furthermore, concerns about shortcut management on Linux have been raised, showcasing the importance of user-friendly design in cross-platform applications.

The Verdict

Hex provides a compelling option for developers seeking a local voice dictation tool that prioritizes privacy and performance. Its architecture, built on Rust, ensures efficient processing, while community feedback continues to shape its development path.

title: SketchDirector: Complex Scene Sketching via Agentic Layout Reasoning and Detail Refinement
description:
arXiv:2610.41260v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Existing sketch generation methods often rely on image guidance and are largely limited to individual objects or simplified scenes, leaving text-guided complex scene sketching underexplored. We present SketchDirector, an agentic framework that mimics the human sketching workflow for automatic multi-concept scene sketching. Given a scene-level text prompt, SketchDirector first employs a large language model~(LLM) to decompose the scene into multiple draft assets, where each is represented by a set of B\'ezier curves. Then, an agentic reasoning loop iteratively plans and executes their spatial arrangement, guided by self-evolving memory. Finally, a detail refinement module leverages diffusion priors to enhance sketch quality while preserving geometric structure. To support future research and applications in multi-concept scene sketch generation, we further introduce the \textit{MCSketch8K} dataset, comprising editable vector assets, compositional layouts, and object-level manipulation annotations. Extensive experiments show that SketchDirector outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in semantic and compositional quality while effectively preserving overall contour organization during refinement. The project page is: \href{https://yiki77.github.io/SketchDirector/}{https://yiki77.github.io/SketchDirector/}.

title: No Channels Left Behind: Understanding Diffusion Acceleration through Residual Gates
description:
arXiv:2610.40914v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Training acceleration methods for diffusion transformers, such as REPA and dispersive regularization, are commonly explained by additional supervision, spatial-structure priors, or improved feature geometry. We revisit this view and uncover a striking internal change: the AdaLN-Zero residual gate $\alpha$, which directly controls how conditioned updates enter the residual stream, is substantially reorganized by these methods. This observation motivates our hypothesis that acceleration arises, at least in part, from reshaping the residual gating pathway rather than solely from the feature structures explicitly imposed by auxiliary objectives. Supporting this view, accelerated models are markedly more sensitive to perturbations of $\alpha$, and their gate geometry reflects semantic relationships among classes. We further introduce the normalized participation ratio (nPR) to characterize the channel-wise organization of the gates and find that, across REPA teachers, projector architectures, and radial-objective targets, broader gate participation accompanies better generation quality. Guided by this insight, we propose a simple teacher-free radial objective that promotes broader gate participation through feature-norm regularization, without pairwise feature comparisons. On ImageNet $256\times256$ with SiT-B/2, our method improves FID over dispersive loss while increasing mean gate participation over timesteps and classes, further supporting the link between gate organization and training acceleration. Our results identify residual-gate reorganization as a measurable axis of diffusion training acceleration and suggest a simple direction for further acceleration.

title: CRoS: Causality Reward on Scrambled CoTs Improves Accuracy and Reasoning Faithfulness
description:
arXiv:2610.42054v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become the standard method for training language models to reason. However, RLVR typically relies solely on outcome correctness, which does not guarantee that the CoT causally contributes to the final answer. Without this connection, outcome rewards may fail to reinforce high-quality reasoning. Existing causality metrics assess CoT causality by perturbing the CoT, such as deleting reasoning steps or injecting errors, and measuring changes in the final answer. However, these perturbations inevitably alter information in each step. Consequently, high causality scores may reflect sensitivity to information changes introduced by perturbation rather than true causality. Such confounding effects further induce undesirable reasoning behaviors when these metrics are used as training rewards, including generating less informative CoTs and reducing exploration and self-correction. To address this problem, we propose CRoS (Causality Reward on Scrambled CoTs), a novel CoT causality metric that perturbs the order of reasoning steps without altering content, thereby preserving information within each step. On Reasoning Gym with Gemma-3-4B, CRoS outperforms existing causality and outcome rewards in out-of-domain accuracy, CoT quality, and CoT faithfulness. Specifically, CRoS achieves 46.8% accuracy on five unseen logic and games datasets, outperforming the strongest baseline (43.8%). It also achieves better CoT quality, consistently outperforming baselines in CoT-Pass@K from K=1 to 128, averaging 43.4% vs. 41.4%. For CoT faithfulness, CRoS achieves a hint acknowledgment score of 34.0% vs. 20.2%.

title: Sparse Text Diffusion under Dual Budgets: Context Connectivity and Expert Activation
description:
arXiv:2610.41487v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Long-context diffusion repeatedly pays for both token interaction and feed-forward computation. We formulate these costs as two separate budgets: the edges available to an attention graph and the experts activated for each token. This view connects local, dilated, and global attention with conditional expert computation without assuming that sparsity alone preserves document-level information. We specify normalized masked attention, distinguish denoising depth from sampling iterations, and derive graph and compute bounds. A reported sparse-expert configuration, denoted DualBudget, is analyzed across scientific summarization, multi-hop question answering, dialogue, and sentence-pair prediction. All supplied table measurements are retained. The length study shows gains over the listed baselines through 16K, together with measurable degradation as length increases. Ablations reveal mixed changes across the three reported scores, while the cost record indicates a 20% reduction relative to DiffuSeq under an unspecified timing convention. The analysis separates these observations from unmeasured claims about training speed, absorbing states, global coherence, and deployment memory.

title: AVID: A Weakly Aligned RGB-Infrared Dataset and Perturbation Benchmark for Tiny Aerial Targets
description:
arXiv:2610.40949v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Long-range detection of small drones is complicated by their visual similarity to birds and by the limited detail available from ground-based cameras. Combining visible and infrared observations offers complementary information, but their usefulness depends on target size, cross-modal alignment, and image quality. We present AVID, a benchmark for studying these factors using real RGB-infrared bird-drone surveillance footage originating from the Drone Detection Dataset and curated for the IEEE ICIP 2025 Video and Image Processing Cup. AVID comprises 32,040 corresponding frame pairs from 115 videos, with 35,952 existing bird and drone annotations at $320\times256$ resolution. Targets occupy an unusually narrow size range: 68.1\% have a geometric-mean bounding-box side of 8--16 pixels, and 99.0\% meet the COCO small-object criterion. To characterize the geometric difficulty of combining the modalities, we introduce an object-relative alignment ratio and an alignment burden curve. In a sample of 300 frame pairs, 32.3\% have estimated global translations greater than 5 pixels; among the 264 pairs with matching annotations, 16.3\% exceed one median target side. We further introduce AVID-C, which simulates seven families of image degradation at five severity levels independently in RGB, infrared, or both. A fixed-feature analysis examines how scale, degradation, and added cross-modal shifts affect fitted bird-drone class overlap. At 12--16 pixels, the Bhattacharyya error bounds are 0.148 for RGB, 0.198 for infrared, and 0.046 for their combined features. These values describe separation in the specified feature and density models, not detector accuracy. Together, AVID and AVID-C support scale-aware, alignment-aware, and sensor-specific studies of tiny aerial targets.

title: Do Language Models Know What Compelling Scientific Evidence Looks Like?
description:
arXiv:2610.41015v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Expert scientists excel at weighing empirical findings from multiple sources that vary in both statistical reliability and epistemic relevance. To what extent are language models, which are increasingly driving autonomous discovery systems, capable of such evidence deliberation? We introduce EDB-Bio, a scientific reasoning benchmark curated from real-world data in three biological domains: drug-perturbation transcriptomics, CRISPR screens, and human genome-wide association studies (GWAS). Each of EDB-Bio's 96k episodes presents a sequence of experimental results from published studies and asks the model to predict the probability that a target hypothesis is true. Out-of-the-box, open-weight and frontier models alike demonstrate systematic underconfidence and attain Brier scores comparable to a trivial base-rate forecaster. Post-training against strictly proper scoring rules significantly improves both calibration and discrimination. This calibration pays off downstream: in a sequential experiment selection task, our Ibis0 model is 2.5 times more efficient than the best frontier model. Throughout, quantifying evidence weights as Bayes factors reveals how models update their beliefs over time, whether they agree with expert biologists on relevance, and where they exhibit inconsistencies and biases. Our work extends calibration training and uncertainty analysis to a realistic scientific forecasting setting with applications to human cancer biology. We release all code, data, and trained models.

title: Dreams Are Cheaper Than Flights: Curated World-Model Data Improves Aerial Detection
description:
arXiv:2610.41030v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Robot perception is increasingly data driven, yet field data is slow, costly, and sometimes disruptive to collect. Video world models offer a cheaper source: seeded with real frames, they extend a recorded scene into new footage with the deployment's sensor, altitude, and environment. We ask whether such synthetic data matches the utility of real field data and whether detectors trained with it perform in the field. Seeding a 7B-parameter world model with wildlife drone video, we more than double the training set with curated frames. On held-out videos from the same drones, mAP@50--95 rises 4.3\% when these frames are added to real data and 10.3\% when they replace it, and up to 33.5\% on an urban benchmark. Although an expert rejects an estimated 87.5\% of generated clips, the data costs about \$1,100 of GPU time, against more than \$3,200 of field labor alone for a less useful real training set. Synthetic data thus shifts data costs from fieldwork to compute.

title: FlowMoDE: Coarse-to-fine Flow Matching for Detail-aware Sim-to-Real Monocular Depth Estimation
description:
arXiv:2610.41190v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Monocular depth estimation is a fundamental capability for 3D spatial perception in robotic and intelligent systems. While data-driven discriminative methods have achieved compelling performance for monocular depth estimation, generative approaches can reconstruct fine structural details with stronger generalization. However, most existing generative diffusion models suffer from low inference efficiency caused by multi-step sampling, whereas single-step diffusion models struggle to recover high-fidelity depth maps. To mitigate these drawbacks, this paper presents FlowMoDE, a coarse-to-fine flow-matching-based framework for efficient, structure-aware monocular depth estimation supporting sim-to-real and cross-scene generalization. The core architecture first conducts coarse-level decoding conditioned on diffused features extracted from a pre-trained semantic encoder, and subsequently restores fine-grained structural patterns via expanded decoding layers. Trained exclusively on a single synthetic indoor dataset, our proposed method outperforms prior methods across five real-world indoor and outdoor datasets, yielding an average 14.1% reduction in relative error against state-of-the-art works as well as 9.9\% reduction in chamfer distance for point cloud reconstruction. We further validate the generalization capability of FlowMoDE on realistic robotic scenes, with qualitative comparisons against state-of-the-art methods. The project page is https://flowmode-shao.netlify.app/

title: Nonlinear Maps Between Irreducible Representations in Graph Neural Networks
description:
arXiv:2610.41059v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Equivariant linear maps cannot mix non-isomorphic irreducible representations, whereas nonlinear activations can. We develop a degree-resolved version of this nonlinear interaction picture and use the resulting block inventory to construct Specht Triple, a residual on unordered graph triples. On a synthetic structural benchmark with a frozen GIN backbone, Specht Triple reduces aggregate standardised test MSE by 11.05% relative to a parameter-matched Projector Control using the same irreducible projectors and complete linear equivariant space. The results support irreducible decomposition as an inductive bias for nonlinear higher-order equivariant processing.

title: TurnTurk-GPT: Text-Based Turn-Taking Prediction for Turkish
description:
arXiv:2610.42010v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: This paper presents TurnTurk-GPT, a text-based turn-taking predictor for Turkish obtained by fine-tuning a Turkish GPT-2 model with the TurnGPT objective on synthetic and real dialogue, and evaluates it on real Turkish conversation against rule baselines, a zero-shot Turkish language model and a widely used multilingual end-of-turn detector. Evaluation uses word-level decision points on unpunctuated, lower-cased text approximating the output of streaming speech recognisers, recording-disjoint and speaker-disjoint folds, nested threshold selection and paired cluster bootstrap tests. TurnTurk-GPT outperforms the multilingual detector under both recording-disjoint and speaker-disjoint evaluation. It outperforms the zero-shot language model only when the test speakers occur in training; on unseen speakers the two are statistically indistinguishable. Removing the suffixes of the turn-final word reduces AP by up to 44%, against 2% for a sentence-internal word, locating the Turkish end-of-turn cue in verb-final morphology. Synthetic dialogue alone yields the weakest trained model, and when a speaker pauses the zero-shot and multilingual baselines remain close to chance. The model and the evaluation protocol are publicly released.

title: SimXAI: A Simple Drop-in Layer Increases Interaction Quality and Understanding in Conversational XAI
description:
arXiv:2610.41856v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Conversational explainable AI (ConvXAI) agents often use GUS-style architectures with separate modules for intent recognition, dialogue management, and template-based response generation. While faithful to the underlying XAI methods, these pipelines are hard to adapt and often struggle with context-dependent follow-up questions. We present SimXAI, a lightweight LLM-centric conversational layer that replaces these modules with a single tool-calling LLM that bridges access to existing XAI resources. Rather than a standalone agent, SimXAI serves as a modular interface that enables conversational access to external XAI resources. We further introduce an evaluation suite for single- and multi-turn parsing, faithfulness, and contextualization. Across existing and new datasets, SimXAI achieves strong function-selection accuracy and high faithfulness while better handling context-dependent requests. In a user study replacing only the conversational layer of TalkToModel, a representative GUS-based agent, users completed tasks more accurately and in fewer turn. Overall, SimXAI improves GUS-based design while preserving faithfulness and improving conversational quality.

title: Coupled or Independent? Fault Coupling in Agentic Medical Vision Systems
description:
arXiv:2610.40913v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Vision-language agents equipped with tools expose intermediate outputs for inspection and comparison with the model's reasoning, which may offer safety benefits over single-shot models. This paper tests that potential benefit when the sensor reading itself is untrusted, so that the tool and reasoning channels share a common visual fault. We consider a dermatology agent based on segmentation, contrastive retrieval, and an iterative vision-language reasoner and define a coupling taxonomy that distinguishes single-channel errors from joint errors that agree or disagree. On PAD-UFES-20, we show that typographic injection produces detectable directional retrieval capture, whereas physical corruption does not. Crop-first retrieval preserves the payload at a readable scale and produces 55% joint wrong agreement across all cases (71% of faulty cases); full-image retrieval produces 35% (43%). Under a binary decision, if both channels are wrong, their predictions must agree, so hard-label channel comparison cannot detect joint failures, limiting disagreement recall to 0.29 (crop-first) versus 0.57 (full-image). The direction of the order effect is reproduced on the independent HIBA test set.

title: Single Page Application (SPA) WorkFlow
description:
Let’s explain how we'd build the same todo application as a Single Page Application (SPA) using React.js, focusing on data and state management. Let's start
with a high-level overview and then dive into the details.

First, let's visualize the structure of our React SPA todo app:

graph TD
    A[App Component] --> B[TodoList Component]
    A --> C[AddTodo Component]
    B --> D[TodoItem Component]
    D --> E[Edit Todo]
    D --> F[Delete Todo]
    D --> G[Toggle Complete]

    H[State Management] --> A
    H --> B
    H --> C
    H --> D

In this React SPA structure, we have a main App component that contains child components for different parts of our application. The key difference from the MPA
version is that all of these components exist within a single page, and React manages the rendering and updating of these components based on user interactions
and state changes.

Now, let's talk about data flow and state management in this React SPA:

  1. State Management: In React, we typically keep the state at the highest necessary level and pass it down to child components as props. For a simple app, we might keep all state in the App component. For more complex apps, we might use a state management library like Redux or Recoil.
  2. Data Storage: Unlike the MPA where data was primarily stored on the server, in an SPA we keep a copy of the data in the client-side state. We still persist data to a server via API calls, but the immediate source of truth for the UI is the client-side state.
  3. CRUD Operations: These are typically handled by updating the client-side state and making asynchronous API calls to sync with the server.

Let's walk through a typical workflow:

  1. Initial Load:
    • React app loads and mounts the App component
    • App component fetches todos from the server (e.g., via a REST API)
    • State is updated with the fetched todos, causing a re-render
  2. Add Todo:
    • User inputs new todo in AddTodo component
    • On submit, state is updated with new todo
    • An API call is made to add the todo on the server
  3. Edit Todo:
    • User clicks edit on a TodoItem
    • TodoItem switches to edit mode (managed by local state)
    • On save, parent state is updated and an API call is made
  4. Delete Todo:
    • User clicks delete on a TodoItem
    • Todo is removed from state, causing an immediate UI update
    • An API call is made to delete the todo on the server
  5. Toggle Complete:
    • User clicks to toggle todo status
    • State is immediately updated, reflecting the change in the UI
    • An API call is made to update the status on the server

Now, let's look at a simplified code example for our main App component:

import React, { useState, useEffect } from "react";
import TodoList from "./TodoList";
import AddTodo from "./AddTodo";
import { fetchTodos, addTodo, updateTodo, deleteTodo } from "./api";

function App() {
    const [todos, setTodos] = useState([]);

    useEffect(() => {
        fetchTodos().then(setTodos);
    }, []);

    const handleAddTodo = (title) => {
        const newTodo = { id: Date.now(), title, completed: false };
        setTodos([...todos, newTodo]);
        addTodo(newTodo);
    };

    const handleToggle = (id) => {
        setTodos(todos.map((todo) => (todo.id === id ? { ...todo, completed: !todo.completed } : todo)));
        const todoToUpdate = todos.find((todo) => todo.id === id);
        updateTodo({ ...todoToUpdate, completed: !todoToUpdate.completed });
    };

    const handleDelete = (id) => {
        setTodos(todos.filter((todo) => todo.id !== id));
        deleteTodo(id);
    };

    return (
        <div>
            <h1>My Todos</h1>
            <AddTodo onAdd={handleAddTodo} />
            <TodoList todos={todos} onToggle={handleToggle} onDelete={handleDelete} />
        </div>
    );
}

export default App;

In this React example:

  1. We use the useState hook to manage our todos state.
  2. useEffect is used to fetch todos when the component mounts.
  3. CRUD operations are handled by functions that update the state and make API calls.
  4. The UI automatically updates when the state changes, thanks to React's reactivity.

The key differences from the MPA approach are:

  1. Single Page: Everything happens within a single page load. React handles updating the UI.
  2. Client-Side State: The immediate source of truth is the client-side state, not the server.
  3. Asynchronous Updates: API calls happen asynchronously, allowing for immediate UI updates.
  4. Component Structure: The UI is broken down into reusable components.

This approach provides a more fluid user experience, as most interactions don't require a full page reload. However, it also means we need to carefully manage
state and keep it in sync with the server.

Is this helpful in understanding the SPA approach? Would you like me to elaborate on any specific part of this workflow or dive deeper into how React manages
updates?

title: I built a terminal multiplexer for coding agents that works on my phone
description:
Disclosure: drafted with AI help from my own notes and posts, and checked against the repo.

I run a lot of coding agents at once, mostly Claude Code and Codex, across several projects. Running them was never the problem. The problems were everything around them: too many windows, agents leaving hung processes behind, no way to tell which one was waiting on me, and having to remote into my desktop or SSH into a single shell to deal with any of it from my phone. Even then, a terminal on a phone couldn't show me the frontend I needed to check.

I tried Orca and herdr. Both were better than what I had. Neither had a real markdown notes editor, and neither had a phone interface I could actually work in. So I built swe-mux.

What it is

A terminal multiplexer. It runs any shell or CLI in real terminals on your own machine and serves the same live sessions to your desktop and your phone. Claude Code, Codex, opencode, pi and oh-my-pi get a live status (working, done, or waiting on you), searchable history and resume. Anything else runs as an ordinary terminal with everything except the status.

It's the actual terminal, not a UI wrapped around the agent. You can use it as a plain terminal, or start claude in a shell and that pane becomes an agent session.

On the desktop it's tabs and panes of sessions, notes, files and dev-server previews. Shift+Enter, Ctrl+Backspace, paste and click-to-position behave the same in every agent, shortcuts come from tmux, VS Code, Vim or Emacs presets, and images paste straight from the clipboard.

Status

Status comes from three places: the CLI's hooks, its transcript, and the terminal itself. No single one of them reliably tells "waiting on you" apart from "busy in the background", so it uses all three. You pick which events alert you and how, a sound on the desktop and a push notification on the phone, with quiet hours and separate desktop and mobile settings.

The phone

The same sessions, over your own Tailscale network, installed as a PWA. The terminal with a usable keyboard and a key rail for the keys a phone keyboard doesn't have, git diff review, files, notes, and a push notification when an agent needs a decision.

A dev server bound to 127.0.0.1 on the host is proxied through swe-mux, so the phone opens it without another port being exposed. Being able to play-test and check a frontend on the phone is what closed the development loop there for a lot of my projects. I can work from anywhere now, and I do.

Your tailnet policy is the access control. There's no separate swe-mux login, so any device your tailnet admits gets a terminal on your machine. Treat it like SSH.

Two things I use constantly

A prompt queue, so the thing I think of mid-turn waits until the agent is actually done instead of interrupting it.

Messages between sessions, so a Codex session can ask a Claude session something. I don't want my workflow tied to one provider.

Notes

Notes, and any markdown file in a project, open in the same WYSIWYG editor on desktop and phone, and they autosave. No more notes scattered across different places.

Sessions survive updates

A separate supervisor process owns the terminals, so the daemon can restart and the app can update underneath them without killing anything. I update it several times a day. My own daemon started 615 times across the 98 days its log covers, so this was never optional.

It has limits. A reboot, a power loss or the supervisor itself crashing still ends the live processes. What survives those is the transcript and enough state to resume each agent.

Limits

It was built on Windows, which is where I use it every day and the only platform with a packaged desktop app. The installer is unsigned, so SmartScreen warns on first run; the PyPI install avoids that. macOS and Linux run the daemon and use a browser. CI runs all three, and I've tested Linux myself, but I haven't lived on macOS.

There's no swe-mux account, no server of mine in the path, and no telemetry. The agents still talk to their own providers, and there's a once-a-day update check you can turn off in Settings.

Try it

The demo is the real interface with simulated agents, nothing to install.

Install with uv tool install swe-mux (or pipx install swe-mux), then run swe-mux on Windows or swemux start elsewhere. It's Apache-2.0: github.com/jatoran/swe-mux.

I've put a lot of work into the first run. Where the install or the first hour goes wrong is the feedback I want most.

title: Vercel Agent sessions now cost 67% less
description:
Vercel Agent sessions in the dashboard and Slack now cost 67% less on average. We rebuilt how Agent manages context, reducing the tokens needed per session and improving prompt-cache reuse. These improvements are live and require no action.

What changed:

  • Workflow-based CLI skills: Updated Vercel CLI skills give agents clearer guidance for common workflows and error recovery. Other agents using these skills also benefit.

  • Incremental context management: Agent manages context more efficiently as conversations grow, including long Slack threads.

  • Improved prompt caching: Agent preserves more reusable context across turns so more of it can be read from the cache.

title: Transform Logs with Vector By DataDog
description:
Introduction

Managed platforms make deployment easy, but they decide where your logs can go. If the destination you need is a custom HTTP endpoint, that decision can leave you stuck.

This article shows how to get past it with Vector, an open-source data pipeline maintained by Datadog. The example is DigitalOcean App Platform forwarding its logs to a custom HTTP endpoint, App Platform sends logs the way it would to Datadog, Vector reshapes them, and your endpoint receives them in the format it expects.

The same idea applies well beyond App Platform. Wherever a managed service exports logs in a fixed format or to a fixed set of destinations, Vector can sit in the middle and reshape them:

  • AWS: CloudWatch Logs can stream through Amazon Data Firehose, which delivers to an HTTP endpoint in its own wrapper format. Vector has a Firehose source that unpacks it.
  • Google Cloud: Cloud Logging sinks can export to Pub/Sub, and Vector can read from a subscription.
  • Azure: Azure Monitor can stream logs to Event Hubs, which exposes a Kafka-compatible endpoint that Vector can read.
  • Heroku, Render, and Vercel: their log drains and log streams send to an endpoint you choose, and Vector can receive them.

Check each provider's current documentation for the exact format. The rest of this article follows the App Platform example.

The limitation: a fixed list of log destinations

App Platform can forward runtime logs only to a fixed list of providers, and a custom HTTP URL is not one of them. According to DigitalOcean's "How to Forward Logs in App Platform" documentation (last updated 13 Jul 2026), the supported destinations are:

  • DigitalOcean Managed OpenSearch
  • OpenSearch
  • Datadog
  • Better Stack (formerly Logtail)

The same page notes that dedicated egress IP addresses cannot be used for log forwarding, so you cannot allowlist the sender by IP.

The usual workarounds each have a cost. Running OpenSearch just to relay logs means operating a stateful service as a pass-through. Shipping logs from the application itself means handling batching and retries yourself and missing anything outside the logger. There is a better option, and it hinges on one detail: the Datadog and OpenSearch destinations both let you supply your own endpoint URL.

What Vector is

Vector is a single long-running process that moves logs, metrics, and traces from one place to another and reshapes them on the way. You describe a pipeline in YAML using three kinds of component:

  • Source: where data comes in, such as a port Vector listens on.
  • Transform: code that reshapes each event, written in VRL, the Vector Remap Language.
  • Sink: where processed data goes out, such as another HTTP endpoint.

Vector can also buffer events to disk, so a short outage downstream does not mean lost logs.

The idea: Let App Platform believe it is talking to Datadog

Configure a Datadog log destination in App Platform, but point its endpoint at a server you control. App Platform POSTs its logs there, with the api_key value in a DD-API-KEY header, and never checks who is on the other end.

That server runs Vector, which accepts the request and translates it into whatever your real endpoint expects. The api_key becomes a shared secret between App Platform and your relay, so App Platform keeps using a supported destination while the translation lives in one small config file you own.

Architecture overview 

App Platform (Datadog log destination)
   |  HTTPS POST, api_key in the DD-API-KEY header
   v
+-- Your server -------------------------------------------------------+
| Nginx: TLS and shared-secret check (401 if the secret is wrong)      |
|    |  proxy to 127.0.0.1:8282                                        |
|    v                                                                 |
|   +-- Vector (systemd service) ----------------------------------+   |
|   | Source: http_server   accepts the JSON, no schema check      |   |
|   |    v                                                         |   |
|   | Transform: remap      VRL builds a new event                 |   |
|   |    v                                                         |   |
|   | Sink: http            one event per POST, disk buffer        |   |
|   +--------------------------------------------------------------+   |
+----------------------------------------------------------------------+
   |  POST to your endpoint URL
   v
Custom HTTP endpoint (any URL that accepts JSON)

Nginx authenticates the request, Vector reshapes it, and your endpoint receives an ordinary log POST.

Building the relay, step by step

These steps assume a Linux server with Nginx and a TLS certificate already working for a domain such as logs.example.com. Vector slots in as one extra Nginx route.

1. Generate a secret and install Vector

App Platform cannot be allowlisted by IP, so a shared secret is the only authentication between it and your relay. Generate one, then install Vector:

openssl rand -hex 32
curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSfL https://sh.vector.dev | bash
cp ~/.vector/bin/vector /usr/local/bin/vector
mkdir -p /etc/vector

2. Configure Vector

Create /etc/vector/vector.yaml. The transform is where you match your endpoint's schema, so adapt its output fields.

sources:
  app_platform:
    type: http_server
    address: 127.0.0.1:8282
    path: /api/v2/logs
    decoding:
      codec: json

transforms:
  reshape:
    type: remap
    inputs: [app_platform]
    source: |
      level = "info"
      if exists(.status) {
        level = downcase(to_string!(.status))
      }

      . = {
        "level": level,
        "message": .message,
        "service": .service,
        "raw": .
      }

sinks:
  custom_endpoint:
    type: http
    inputs: [reshape]
    uri: https://your-endpoint.example.com/logs
    method: post
    request:
      headers:
        authorization: "Bearer YOUR_ENDPOINT_TOKEN"
        content-type: "application/json"
    encoding:
      codec: json
    framing:
      method: newline_delimited
    batch:
      max_events: 1
      timeout_secs: 1
    buffer:
      type: disk
      max_size: 536870912

Two choices matter here: the plain http_server source rather than datadog_agent, and . = { ... }, which replaces the whole event. The first avoids the extra date field that App Platform sends, which the Datadog-specific source rejects. The second stops the original fields travelling alongside the new ones. The framing and content-type lines make each request a single bare JSON object, which many endpoints expect. Because the file holds a credential, run chmod 600 /etc/vector/vector.yaml.

3. Add the Nginx route

Inside the existing TLS server block, check the secret and proxy to Vector:

location /api/v2/logs {
    if ($http_dd_api_key != "YOUR_SHARED_SECRET") {
        return 401;
    }
    client_max_body_size 10m;
    proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8282;
}

Reload with nginx -t && systemctl reload nginx.

4. Run Vector under systemd 

cat > /etc/systemd/system/vector.service << 'EOF'
[Unit]
Description=Vector
After=network-online.target

[Service]
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/vector --config /etc/vector/vector.yaml
Restart=on-failure

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
EOF

systemctl daemon-reload && systemctl enable --now vector

Pointing App Platform at the relay

Add a log_destinations block to the app component in the spec:

log_destinations:
  - name: custom-endpoint
    datadog:
      endpoint: https://logs.example.com/api/v2/logs
      api_key: YOUR_SHARED_SECRET

Or set the same values in the console: open the app, go to Settings, click Edit under Log Forwarding, choose Datadog, and fill in the destination name, endpoint, and API key. Make sure the right components are selected, then save. No redeploy is needed, and the same screen is where you rotate the secret later.

To test, deploy any app that writes to stdout, since App Platform forwards whatever the process prints, then watch the relay with journalctl -u vector -f. Events should reach your endpoint within seconds, along with health checks and request logs.

Reusing the relay for other apps

A second app can use the same relay without touching the server: add the same destination in its settings. All its logs then reach the same endpoint, which is fine unless you need to tell apps apart.

To keep them separate, give each app its own Nginx location with its own secret and its own Vector instance. Alternatively, keep one instance and have Nginx tag each request with a header that the transform uses to choose the target.

Conclusion

App Platform's log forwarding is limited to four named providers, but its Datadog destination accepts any endpoint you give it. Putting Vector behind that endpoint turns the limitation into a small translation problem: accept the payload, reshape it with a few lines of VRL, and forward it to the system you actually use. The same pattern fits any managed service that offers a configurable Datadog or HTTP destination.

Sources

  • DigitalOcean, How to Forward Logs in App Platform, the source for the supported destinations and the egress IP constraint.
  • Vector documentation, for sources, transforms, sinks, and VRL.

title: Agentic Systems for Calibrating Cosmological Simulations
description:
arXiv:2610.40685v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Calibrating a cosmological simulation is an expensive, high-dimensional parameter optimization task. Previous works employ Bayesian optimization for automation, which treats the simulator as a black box and precludes the incorporation of human domain knowledge or workflow into the selection policy. We propose AgenticTuner, an agentic calibration pipeline with a present-day large language model serving as the optimizer who proposes the next parameter trial. We show that these agents can achieve competitive calibration performance at a fraction of the CPU cost when they are given informal, human-readable priors (such as codebase, documentation, and heuristic guides that seasoned scientists may possess). We hope this work serves as an early step toward AI scientists that can carry out complex, long-horizon scientific tasks.
