title: How to Setup a Firewall with UFW on an Ubuntu and Debian Cloud Server
description:
Introduction

A properly configured firewall is one of the important aspects of overall system security. Ubuntu associated with a firewall configuration tool named UFW i.e Uncomplicated Firewall. Its primary goal is to manage iptables easier.

Prerequisites

Make sure that you have logged into your server with a non-root user account with sudo privileges or with the root user. It's better to use sudo in place of Root to run Administrative commands.

Install UFW

By default UFW is installed in Ubuntu 18.04, if it is not installed on your system, you can install the UFW package by using below command.

"
**$ sudo apt install ufw**
"

Check UFW Status

Once the installation is completed you can check the status of UFW with the below command.

"
**$ sudo ufw status verbose**
"

By default, UFW is disabled. You have to enable it by using below command.

"`

$ sudo ufw enable

"`

Now it is activated.

## Using IPv6 with UFW

If your VPS is configured for IPv6, ensure that UFW is configured to support IPv6 so that will configure both IPv4 and IPv6 firewall rules. To do that, open the UFW configuration with this command:

"
**$ sudo vi /etc/default/ufw**
"

Then you have to set IPv6 to "yes" like this:

"
**IPV6=yes**
"

Save and exit then restart the firewall with below commands:

"
**sudo ufw disable
sudo ufw enable**
"

Now the UFW will configure the firewall for both IPv4 and IPv6.

## UFW Default Policies

UFW will lock all incoming connections and allow all outbound connections. This means that anyone trying to access your server will not be able to connect, if not you open the port. This means all incoming connections are restricted and allow all outgoing connections.

The default policies can be set by using below commands.

"
**$ sudo ufw default deny incoming**
"

And

"
**$ sudo ufw default allow outgoing**
"

If you want to be more restrictive, you can also deny all outgoing requests as well. This can be done by using below command.

"
**$ sudo ufw default deny outgoing**
"

## Allow SSH Connections

Before enabling the firewall we need to add a rule which will allow incoming SSH connections. To configure the UFW firewall, allow all incoming SSH connections by entering the below command.

"
**$ sudo ufw allow ssh**
"

The syntax for adding this service is quite easy. For example, The below command allows a connection on port 22 using TCP protocol.

"
**$ sudo ufw allow 22/tcp**
"

If your SSH server is running on port 2222, we could enable connections with below command.

"
**$ sudo ufw allow 2222/tcp**
"

Enable UFW

So far UFW firewall is configured to allow all incoming SSH connections. Now we can enable it by entering the below command.

"
**$ sudo ufw enable**
"

Allow connections on other ports

Depending on applications that run on your server, you will also allow incoming access to some other ports. How to allow incoming connections to some of the services are given below.

## Open port 80-HTTP

By using below commands HTTP connections can be allowed.

"
*$ sudo ufw allow http*
"

You can use port number 80 in place of http:

"
**$ sudo ufw allow 80/tcp**
"

Also you can use application profile like "Nginx HTTP" :

"
**$ sudo ufw allow 'Nginx HTTP'**
"

## Open port 8080

If you run Tomcat or any other application that listens on port 8080 to allow incoming connections to enter below command.

"
**$ sudo ufw allow 8080/tcp**
"

## Allow Port Ranges

Instead of allowing access to single ports UFW allows us to access port ranges.

If you allow port ranges with UFW, you must specify the protocol, either tcp or udp.

For example, if you want to allow port from 7100 to 7200 on both tcp and udp then run below command.

"
**$ sudo ufw allow 7100:7200/tcp
$ sudo ufw allow 7100:7200/udp**
"

## Allow IP Addresses

To allow access on all ports from the home machine with IP Address of 64.63.62.61, Then use the below command.

"
**$ sudo ufw allow from 64.63.62.61**
"

## Deny Connections

The default policy for all incoming connections is set to deny and if you haven't changed it, UFW will block all incoming connection unless you explicitly open the connection.

For example, you have opened the ports 80 and 443 and your server is under attack from the 23.24.25.0/24 network. To deny all connections from that IP addresses you can use the below command.

"
**$ sudo ufw deny from 23.24.25.0/24**
"

If you want to deny access to ports 80 and 443 from that IP Address you can use the below command.

"
**$ sudo ufw deny from 23.24.25.0/24 to any port 80
$ sudo ufw deny from 23.24.25.0/24 to any port 443**
"

Writing allow rules are also same as deny rules, only need to replace allow with deny.

## Deleting UFW Rules

There are two ways to delete UFW rules.

By rule number.

For example, To delete UFW rule by rule number is as below command.

"
**$ sudo ufw delete 2**
"

By specifying the actual rule.

For example, To delete UfW rule by specifying the actual rule is as below

"
**$ sudo ufw delete allow 8069**
"

## Disable UFW

If you want to stop UFW and deactivate all rules you can use below command.

"
**$ sudo ufw disable**
"

If you want to re-enable UFW and activate all rules, You can use below command.

"
**$ sudo ufw enable**
"

## Reset UFW

If you reset UFW, it will disable

and delete all active rules. To reset UFW, Enter the below command.

"
**$ sudo ufw reset**
"

## Conclusion

In this guide, we have explained how to install and configure the UFW firewall on Ubuntu 18.04 server. Be sure to allow all incoming connections that are necessary for proper functioning of your system.

title: Parse Before You Execute: Efficient Spatial Reasoning with Executable Primitives
description:
arXiv:2610.41389v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Spatial reasoning in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) has increasingly benefited from tool-integrated pipelines that ground computation in explicit geometry. However, existing systems often compile queries into relatively open-ended artifacts, such as code, task constraints, tool plans, or gathered evidence, leaving what must be resolved before execution under-specified. This can lead to unnecessary tool acquisition and iterative refinement, while still producing plausible reasoning traces from incomplete spatial commitments. We identify this failure mode as under-committed query compilation. To address it, we propose PEPS, a training-free agentic paradigm Parsing Executable Primitives for Spatial reasoning under a typed FESM schema over Frame, Entity, State, and Metric. PEPS follows a parse-before-execute principle: the Parser commits each query to a compact set of executable requirements; the Executor selectively grounds the required primitives through fixed geometric APIs and deterministic computation; and the Verifier checks execution sufficiency, enabling early termination or targeted repair. Extensive experiments across challenging spatial reasoning benchmarks show that PEPS consistently improves reasoning accuracy while substantially reducing refinement rounds, API cost, and end-to-end latency over strong tool-integrated baselines. These results demonstrate that explicit requirement commitment can make tool-integrated spatial reasoning not only more reliable, but also more execution-efficient.

title: Grounding Image Composition with Label-Conditioned Visual Evidence
description:
arXiv:2610.41080v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Image composition labels such as center, diagonal, or rule of thirds describe visual structure rather than object categories. KU-PCP provides image-level labels and class-specific geometric elements, but does not show which visible regions people associate with each of its nine classes. We introduce KU-PCP Elements (KU-PCPE), a label-conditioned region-evidence benchmark for photographic composition. Given an image and a label already judged applicable, the task is to segment the visible regions that explain why the label applies. KU-PCPE contains 4,093 single-annotator training masks and a 1,327-task expert test split with three masks per image-label task. The annotations also include exploratory segment-versus-line ratings that describe whether region or semantic-guideline evidence better explains the label. A held-out expert reaches .867 Dice against the other experts, while the strongest deployable model reaches .664, a proposal oracle .672, and the best vision-language model (VLM) proposal selector .395. KU-PCPE exposes the gap between recognizing a composition label and grounding the human-aligned visual evidence that makes it plausible in a particular image.

title: Omniprediction for All Mixable Proper Losses and Beyond
description:
arXiv:2610.41023v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Omniprediction concerns the task of making predictions that are simultaneously accurate with respect to different losses. Earlier results by [CV09] show that in an online learning setting, $O(\log(|\mathcal{F}||\mathcal{L}|))$ regret is achievable simultaneously against every predictor in a finite predictor class $\mathcal{F}$ and for every loss in a finite class $\mathcal{L}$ of mixable proper losses, while recent advances [OKK25, FP26] show that $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{T\log(|\mathcal{F}||\mathcal{L}|)})$ regret is achievable simultaneously for every loss in a finite class $\mathcal{L}$ of bounded losses.
  In this work, we ask whether sublinear regret remains possible when $\mathcal{L}$ is an infinite class of proper losses. Our first result gives a negative answer in general: even when $\mathcal{F}$ contains only two linear predictors, it is impossible to achieve sublinear regret simultaneously for all bounded proper losses. We then show that $\widetilde{O}(T^{1/3}(\log|\mathcal{F}|)^{2/3})$ regret is achievable simultaneously for \textit{all} mixable proper losses and that this bound is optimal up to logarithmic factors. This optimal rate stands in stark contrast to the constant (in $T$) regret achievable for a finite class of mixable proper losses. Finally, we extend our algorithm to obtain a best-of-all-worlds result: in addition to the new regret guarantee for all mixable proper losses, the resulting algorithm simultaneously achieves the existing guarantees for finite loss classes. With appropriate choices of these finite classes, our algorithm simultaneously achieves constant regret for squared loss and log loss, $\widetilde{O}(T^{1/3}(\log|\mathcal{F}|)^{2/3})$ regret for all mixable proper losses, and $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{T\log|\mathcal{F}|})$ regret for $0$-$1$ loss, all Lipschitz losses, all GLM losses, and other structured families.

title: Beyond CLIP: Calibrated (Few-Shot) Defect Detection With System One Decision Models
description:
arXiv:2610.41199v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Cameras and vision sensors are widely used for product and process inspection in manufacturing environments. Traditionally, this process required thousands of images of both nominal and defective products to train such models. Recent research shows that vision transformer (ViT) models, such as CLIP, can reduce this requirement to 50-100 images per nominal and defective class. However, collecting even 50 defective images can be difficult in high-yield or low-volume manufacturing processes. In this paper, we examine the utility of two recently proposed structured decision models (Jev and Clef-Flash) in applications using as few as k=2 reference images per class at inference. In the process, we provide three main contributions: (a) a framework for k-shot learning of these models for image classification/inspection applications; (b) an agentic approach for automatically refining the text descriptions that guide image classification in these decision models; and (c) an approach to calibrate the resulting defect probabilities to improve their reliability for inspection decisions. We test these contributions in five manufacturing case studies. Using two reference images per class, both Jev and Clef-Flash outperform CLIP's test accuracies with the same references (0.75-1.00 [Jev] and 0.71-0.99 [Clef-Flash] vs 0.67-0.84 [CLIP]). Furthermore, we show that our agentic refinement of text descriptions significantly improves accuracy across 6 of 8 model-application combinations, and our calibration approach reduces the Brier score in 13 of the 15 model-application configurations. To support the reproducibility of our work, we provide our replication code and have created the R "decisions" package for evaluating additional models. We also provide a publicly available web app that allows practitioners to inspect their own images with no code.

title: An Empirical Study on Learning Rooftop Solar Potential from Satellite Imagery Directly Without Explicit Geometry
description:
arXiv:2610.41111v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Rooftop solar potential estimation often relies on LiDAR, digital surface models (DSMs), or pipelines that explicitly reconstruct roof geometry before estimating solar potential. We propose Direct Rooftop Solar Prediction (DRSP), an end-to-end formulation that maps satellite imagery and coarse regional sunlight information directly to application-level solar outputs. DRSP neither requires explicit geometric representations as input nor predicts roof orientation, slope, height, DSMs, or other geometric quantities as intermediate outputs, and therefore requires no geometric intermediate supervision. To enable large-scale study of this formulation, we develop a programmatic data-curation pipeline that converts per-panel information from the Google Solar API into usable-rooftop masks and spatial solar-energy targets, yielding two geographically distinct datasets containing approximately 60K rooftops from the U.S. Midwest and 87K from Texas. We demonstrate the feasibility of DRSP and systematically characterize the effects of geographic training distribution, model depth, image resolution, regional sunlight conditioning, and heatmap regression objectives. Overall, our results suggest that useful rooftop-scale solar information can be learned directly from 2D imagery without explicit geometric intermediate representations, offering a simpler path toward large-scale solar assessment. Our code and dataset are available at https://github.com/joshualee124/direct_rooftop_solar_prediction.

title: Built a duplicate file finder in Java, here's how it works
description:
So I've been working on this little project called DupeLens. It's basically a Java CLI that finds duplicate files in your folders and generates an HTML report.

Nothing crazy, just something I thought would be useful.

Why I made it

I wanted a simple way to check which files were duplicated without worrying about accidentally deleting something important.

So I built one myself.

How it works

It's pretty straightforward.

First, it checks file sizes. If two files have different sizes, there's no reason to compare them further.

For files with matching sizes, it uses SHA-256 to check whether their contents are identical.

Once it's done, it shows the duplicates in the terminal. You can also generate an HTML report if you want something easier to look through.

And that's about it. It doesn't delete, move, or modify your files.

Wanna try it?

You'll need Java 17 or newer.

Download the JAR from GitHub and run:

java -jar dupelens.jar ./your-folder --html report.html

Then just open report.html in your browser.

What's next?

Just released v1.0.0, so it's still pretty early.

I'm thinking about adding exclusion patterns and JSON output, but I'm open to other ideas too.

If anyone wants to check out the code or suggest improvements, that'd be cool.

GitHub: https://github.com/illusionoftalha/dupelens

It's open-source and MIT-licensed.

title: Prior-Guided Single-Exposure HDR Novel View Synthesis via Base-Gain Representation
description:
arXiv:2610.41011v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Single-exposure high dynamic range (HDR) novel view synthesis (NVS) recovers HDR scenes from low dynamic range (LDR) views captured at a single exposure and estimates camera response function (CRF) for LDR re-exposure. Without HDR ground-truth, using single-exposure LDR views as the sole source of direct supervision underconstrains HDR reconstruction and cannot ensure its faithful recovery, motivating the need for learned LDR-to-HDR reconstruction priors. Moreover, single-exposure LDR views supervise CRF only over a limited range, necessitating a learnable prior for reliable re-exposure beyond it. We propose PriorGS, a 3D Gaussian Splatting framework that addresses both challenges by (1) guiding HDR recovery with pseudo-HDR supervision from 2D single-exposure HDR reconstruction methods while anchoring it to input LDR views through a closed reconstruction loop; and (2) regularizing CRF modeling with a learnable prior that guarantees monotonicity and promotes plausible responses. Yet cross-view inconsistencies in independently generated pseudo-HDR targets impair scene reconstruction when HDR is encoded directly as Gaussian's color attribute. We therefore introduce a 3D base-gain HDR representation that factors HDR radiance into an LDR base and an overlaid 3D gain field, promoting robustness to such inconsistencies and enabling 3D HDR appearance editing. Extensive experiments demonstrate PriorGS's substantial superiority over baselines.

title: Shifting Focus by Reliability: Geometric Fusion Modulation for Robust RGB-T Detection
description:
arXiv:2610.41204v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: RGB-thermal (RGB-T) object detectors combine visible and thermal imagery for robust detection, but signal corruption in either stream can substantially degrade accuracy. Restoration-based methods incur significant latency and do not consistently improve downstream accuracy, raising a more direct question: rather than restoring corrupted inputs, can we efficiently adapt the detector to their varying signal quality? Conventional PEFT offers an efficient route, but its input-independent corrections cannot track diverse test-time corruptions. Our controlled corruption sweeps show that corruption types have similar effects near clean conditions but diverge increasingly with severity, motivating corruption-aware, per-input adaptation. We therefore propose PG-FM (Prompt-Guided Feature Modulation), which adapts RGB-T object detectors to the estimated corruption type and severity of each modality. Under controlled RGB-T corruption simulations, PG-FM preserves clean-set performance, improves mAP50 by up to 20.8 points on FLIR and 19.9 points on KAIST, and transfers without retraining to unmodified, naturally acquired external RGB-T datasets.

title: Do Open Language Models Invent Scripture? BILAL-BENCH: Benchmarking Islamic-Source Fabrication in Bengali
description:
arXiv:2610.40996v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: When a language model invents a Qur'anic verse or hadith, it gives false authority to text that readers may treat as sacred. Existing Islamic hallucination benchmarks are largely Arabic and often closed-ended, while Bengali resources mainly study general-domain hallucination or factual knowledge. We introduce BILAL-BENCH, a 240-question expert-verified benchmark for open-ended Islamic-source fabrication in Bengali. It covers Qur'anic attribution, hadith, fiqh, contemporary issues, and adversarial false-premise prompts, and uses a two-axis rubric that separates source errors from assertiveness. We evaluate seven open-weight models from 1B to 120B on 1,680 double-annotated responses. Six of the seven models confidently fabricate on 79.3-95.3% of source-production questions, with no monotonic improvement from scale. Hadith provenance is the weakest category across models: only two of 315 responses are correct and correctly sourced. The two 8B BanglaLLaMA variants have similar confident-fabrication rates but different error profiles. Models vary far more in whether they withhold a claim they cannot support than in source accuracy: appropriate abstention or false-premise correction ranges from 6 to 46 responses across the benchmark, and does not track parameter count.

title: Precision--Recall Trade-off on the Inference Level for LLMs in Grammatical Error Correction
description:
arXiv:2610.41698v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have recently been adopted for Grammatical Error Correction (GEC), achieving strong performance via both full fine-tuning and prompt-based approaches. As probabilistic sequence models, LLMs expose inference-time parameters that directly modify token generation behavior; however, their potential for controlling GEC-specific trade-offs has not been systematically studied. In this work, we investigate decoding strategies for grammatical error correction. We show that the repetition penalty parameter enables controllable adjustment of the precision--recall trade-off at inference time, without modifying the model architecture, training procedure, or prompt. Through experiments on standard GEC benchmarks, we demonstrate that repetition-penalty-based decoding enables inference-time control of the precision--recall balance, conceptually related to methods previously proposed for sequence-to-sequence GEC models, such as Align-and-Predict Decoding (APD), while remaining simple and broadly applicable to existing LLMs that expose inference-time decoding penalties.

title: EDU-Jev Training System-One Decision Models for Education
description:
arXiv:2610.41079v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Many automated decisions in education involve choosing from a fixed set of options: assigning a rubric score, checking whether an answer meets a marking criterion, or identifying the first wrong step in a solution. Generative language models are increasingly used to make these decisions, but their responses require parsing, longer outputs increase inference costs, and confidence expressed in words does not necessarily reflect the probability of being correct. We present EDU-Jev, a family of single-pass ("System One") decision models at 0.8B, 2B and 4B parameters. Given an assessment context and a question with predefined answer options, the model returns a probability distribution over those options without generating text. A pointer head scores a marker for each option, ensuring the predictions are restricted to the allowed choices. Training uses a single supervised stage with soft cross-entropy against the available target label distributions; calibration is assessed empirically. Across twelve education benchmarks, EDU-Jev 4B achieves an average accuracy of 67.6%, exceeding the strongest of five commercial decision APIs by 9.4 percentage points and the best open 4B decision model by 18.7 points. On four cross-domain education sets, it matches the strongest API, which remains ahead on general decision-making and reasoning tasks. The 2B model processes about 150 decisions per second on a single H100 GPU.

title: My load test had 1,000 players. None of them were late.
description:
Before the first event I ran 1 vs 100 against a thousand simulated players, and nothing broke. Then a lecture hall of real people broke it with a fraction of that. The test measured load correctly. It just never contained the one thing real people always do: arrive late.

I tested 1 vs 100 properly before anyone played it. A script opened a thousand simulated players over real WebSockets, started a question, and had all of them answer in the same instant: the thundering herd, the worst moment a live quiz has.

It held. No dropped connections, the question reached every player in tens of milliseconds, and the reveal came back in under half a second.

At the first real event, it broke anyway. Not under load. Under people.

What the test could not contain

Here is what the script did, in order: connect every player, wait until every one of them has joined, and only then press Start.

That is the one order a real room never follows. In a lecture hall, people are still scanning the QR code when the host decides the room looks full. The game had a rule for anyone who joined after Start: watch, do not play. My thousand bots never triggered it, because not one of them was late. Everyone in the real room after the first 45 or so was, and their phones showed every question and never let them answer. The rule and the fix are their own note.

The test was faithful about load and wrong about time. It measured how many people the server could hold, and assumed they would all arrive at once, on cue, and stay on the page. Real people arrive late, switch tabs and reload. None of that is load, and all of it is what broke.

The first ten minutes

The first people with the problem came to me, and I did not know what it was. I went around to them, reassured them, and opened my laptop next to them to look. Technically, nothing was wrong anywhere I could see. The server was healthy and the game was running.

I told them their answers were being counted. I believed it. They were not, and I did not know that yet.

When more and more people had the same problem, I went outside to deal with it properly, making phone call after phone call to understand what was happening.

Not starting again

After about ten minutes the event coordinator came out to find me and asked what was going on. Her suggestion was to start the entire event again.

I asked her not to. Restarting would have thrown away the game for everyone who was playing fine, to fix it for the people who were not. Instead I asked her to tell the crowd that anyone hit by the bug would go through to the next stage rather than be eliminated.

That kept the event moving and kept the people who had been wronged in the game. Meanwhile I changed the rule and deployed the fix while the event was still running, and the stranded players came back in at the next question.

What a load test is for

A load test answers one question well: can the server take this many people at once. It is worth running, and mine was right.

It cannot answer the question that decided the night: what happens when people do not behave like a script. That needs a different test, one that is written from watching a real room: people joining after the start, leaving the page, coming back. Measuring the wrong thing precisely felt like safety. It was only confidence.

First published on davidmashiah.com, with the rest of my notes on real-time systems, machine learning reliability and supply chains.

title: DyCraft: An Agentic System for Long-Horizon 4D Scene Generation
description:
arXiv:2610.40754v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: While frontier coding agents can generate high-quality 3D scenes and articulated assets, they struggle to create coherent long-horizon animations. When equipped with general-purpose harnesses, they frequently produce physically implausible outputs, generating objects that interpenetrate, lack physical support, or move unnaturally. Such bare agents struggle to repair these errors because they default to scripting the full animation in one pass, making it difficult to verify their work and disentangle complex spatiotemporal constraints. Drawing on the practice of human animators, we introduce DyCraft, a system for animated 3D scene generation that breaks animation into steps that coding agents can more reliably solve. DyCraft first expands the user's prompt into a detailed plan and builds a static scene. It then creates a 3D storyboard of key animation poses, where each frame is a static 3D scene that the agent can build and debug in isolation. Storyboarding decomposes the problem into pairs of verified start and end states, allowing the agent to author local motion between them with a collection of motion authoring tools. We evaluate DyCraft on 24 long-horizon, multi-shot animation tasks covering humanoid robots, human and animal characters, and physical mechanisms. Compared with a native GPT-6 agent in Codex and prior agentic baselines, DyCraft substantially reduces physical violations and generates higher-quality animated 3D scenes that are more often preferred by human raters.

title: In-Model Context Compression with Agentic Soft Tokens for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.41291v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents play an important role in solving complex and sustained tasks, with ever-growing interaction contexts. However, these accumulated contexts will raise substantial computational cost and obscure key decision-relevant evidence. Existing methods typically train external compressors or context-management agents to rewrite context as shorter hard-token sequences, but such external selection may not align with the LLM's evolving representation and is necessarily lossy. In this paper, we introduce Agentic Soft-Token Compression (ASTC), a training-free compression method using soft tokens within LLM agent for long-horizon tasks. Specifically, ASTC uses the model's native recurrent dynamics to determine the already absorbed information, leveraging the commonly-used hybrid Gated Delta Network (GDN)-attention. It then carries this information forward as agentic soft tokens while retaining exact values as hard tokens. The resulting compact sequence reduces later-layer computation and yields reusable KV caches, extending the savings across the agent's trajectory. Extensive experiments on long-horizon tasks show that ASTC matches or exceeds the uncompressed agent's accuracy with up to 50.68% fewer end-to-end Attention Pairs, while trained compressors require 15.4 to 103.7 times more Attention Pairs per successful task. These findings highlight agentic soft tokens as a model-native way to carry absorbed context forward as the task representation evolves.

title: Is There a CabloyJS Equivalent in the React/Next.js Ecosystem?
description:
In the Node.js fullstack world, CabloyJS has always occupied a rather specific position. It is not a "frontend framework with some API routes on the side," but an enterprise fullstack architecture with module boundaries, built-in IoC (inversion of control / dependency injection), native RBAC and Workflow, and a metadata contract shared by frontend and backend.

So a familiar question comes up: if a team's stack is React/Next.js, is there something "close enough"?

The short answer: there is no exact equivalent to CabloyJS. What the React/Next.js ecosystem offers are four partially overlapping approaches. Each one hits some of CabloyJS's capabilities; none covers all of them.

To see this clearly, we first need to break CabloyJS apart.

1. Split CabloyJS into five comparable capability layers

Calling something a "fullstack framework" makes comparison meaningless. CabloyJS's value actually lives on five independent layers:

  1. Modularity and scaffolding — business capabilities are organized as modules that can be installed, composed, and removed, with a CLI that generates the standard structure.
  2. Backend IoC/DI — services, controllers, and beans collaborate through dependency injection instead of layered imports and manual wiring.
  3. Frontend-backend integration — one framework constrains both sides, so routing, permissions, validation, and error handling follow the same conventions.
  4. RBAC and Workflow — the permission model and workflow engine are built into the framework, not "install a library and wire it up."
  5. Metadata-driven design — data structures, forms, lists, and permission points are described by metadata, and both sides start from the same definition.

Now hold these five layers against the candidates.

2. Why Next.js itself is not the counterpart

Next.js defines itself as a React meta-framework. It solves rendering modes (SSR/CSR/RSC), routing, builds, deployment, and edge runtimes — extending the frontend all the way into the server.

Its Route Handlers and Server Actions are enough to write endpoints, but they do not provide enterprise backend architecture constraints: no dependency injection container, no module lifecycle, no built-in permission model, and no workflow engine. In Next.js, all of that belongs to the "choose your own stack and assemble it yourself" category.

So the question should not be "is there a CabloyJS replacement inside Next.js," but rather: within the React/Next.js ecosystem, which combination fills in those CabloyJS layers?

3. Path one: fullstack conventions — RedwoodJS and Blitz.js

If what appeals to you is "one framework owns both sides and tells you, with strong conventions, where business logic belongs," these two frameworks come closest.

RedwoodJS

RedwoodJS is one of the most opinionated fullstack frameworks in the React ecosystem. In its classic form, it puts the React frontend, GraphQL API, Prisma data layer, and directory conventions into a single monorepo.

  • Scaffolding: generate commands produce pages, Cells, Services, and GraphQL SDL in one pass, turning "where should this capability live" into a fixed answer.
  • Clear boundaries: the frontend handles presentation and interaction, data access is confined to the service layer, and server-side validation and tests have a defined home.
  • One caveat: Redwood has spent the past couple of years evolving toward RedwoodSDK, with changes to both its technical foundation and deployment model. When choosing it, confirm which generation you are actually adopting rather than relying on older docs describing the GraphQL + Prisma setup.

Blitz.js

Blitz.js is built directly on top of Next.js, with the explicit goal of erasing the frontend-backend boundary.

  • Zero-API data layer: the frontend can import backend queries and mutations directly; Blitz compiles them into RPC endpoints and client calls at build time. This removes the hand-written API glue layer and is where it most resembles CabloyJS's "one integrated stack."
  • Built-in auth and sessions: authentication and session management work out of the box, with ready-made hooks for authorization checks.
  • Boundary: it provides authentication and access-control infrastructure, not a full RBAC permission-point system or workflow engine. Organization-level permission models still need to be modeled by you.

Who it fits: teams that want to stay entirely inside the Next.js ecosystem while getting "write the backend, call it from the frontend, with login state included." For that need, Blitz.js is the first choice. If you are not tied to Next.js but want an opinionated fullstack framework in React, look at RedwoodJS.

4. Path two: admin panels and metadata-driven design — Refine

CabloyJS is often used to build complex enterprise admin systems quickly. If your core need is permissions, auto-generated CRUD, and direct access to a database or existing API, you do not need to replace Next.js — just bring in Refine.

Refine is an open-source meta-framework for React admin panels that runs seamlessly on Next.js, Remix, or Vite.

  • Provider-based metadata thinking: dataProvider connects a data source (REST, GraphQL, Supabase, Prisma, etc.), authProvider handles login state, and accessControlProvider carries ACL/RBAC decisions. You define how to fetch and how to authorize; Refine wires up CRUD pages, forms, lists, and i18n.
  • UI-agnostic: it does not bind to a component library, so you keep Next.js's navigation and rendering modes without being locked in.
  • Boundary: Refine is a frontend-side meta-framework and does not provide a backend runtime. Authorization must ultimately be enforced by your API or database, and workflows are out of its scope entirely.

Who it fits: teams that already have a backend (or plan to use Supabase or their own API) and whose main pain is repeated admin-panel and permission work.

5. Path three: backend IoC — NestJS + Next.js

CabloyJS's backend offers Spring-like dependency injection. If your team values backend architectural rigor more than the convenience of a single all-in-one framework, the common answer is a combo plus a monorepo:

  • Manage the repo with Nx or Turborepo;
  • Let Next.js handle SSR, SEO, and the BFF layer;
  • Let NestJS own the real enterprise business backend.

NestJS is the most mature IoC/DI backend framework in Node.js today: Module, Provider, Guard, Interceptor, and Pipe form a complete set of architectural constraints, with clear module boundaries and test isolation.

The cost: frontend and backend are no longer governed by one framework, so routing, permissions, DTO validation, and error codes must be explicitly aligned across two systems. In other words, the consistency CabloyJS gets from "one shared metadata contract" has to be recovered here through engineering conventions and shared packages.

Who it fits: large commercial projects that need to evolve for years and cannot compromise on backend architecture. This combination is not weaker than CabloyJS in rigor or modularity — but it is not "batteries included," it is "architecture included."

6. How the four options compare

Requirement CabloyJS capability React/Next.js option Recommendation
Integration and automation Modules, CLI generation, unified frontend/backend Blitz.js / RedwoodJS Choose these to skip auth and API glue work
Fast admin panels and permissions Built-in RBAC, Workflow, auto CRUD Refine (embeddable in Next.js) Choose it when the core is admin, forms, and access control
Top-tier backend architecture (IoC) Dependency injection and modularity via Egg/Vona NestJS + Turborepo/Nx Choose it for large, long-lived systems where backend rigor comes first
Workflow engine Built-in Workflow No direct counterpart; build or integrate one Evaluate separately for process-heavy systems
Shared frontend/backend metadata One metadata source drives both sides Partial overlap (Refine providers, Redwood conventions) No complete equivalent; fill the gap with conventions

7. Selection advice

  • Staying fully inside Next.js, valuing "write the backend, use it in the frontend, login included": Blitz.js first.
  • Not tied to Next.js but wanting an opinionated React fullstack framework: RedwoodJS first — but confirm its current form and deployment model.
  • Mainly enterprise admin panels, forms, and permissions: Refine has the best return on effort, with no backend replacement required.
  • Backend rigor first, system expected to live for many years: the NestJS + Next.js monorepo is the safer bet.

One honest closing note: all four options can reproduce most of the day-to-day CabloyJS experience, but none fully replicates its five-layer structure of modules + IoC + RBAC + Workflow + metadata. The React/Next.js ecosystem wins on freedom of choice and an enormous supply of components and training material; CabloyJS wins by building enterprise constraints in advance and reducing how much architectural freedom a team has to improvise.

These are not substitutes for each other. They are a trade-off between free composition and built-in conventions. Decide which cost you fear more, and the answer follows.

title: BlindToChange: AI Agents Can Find Changes When Asked But Do They Look When Needed?
description:
arXiv:2610.41435v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Given that AI agents can search the web broadly and deeply in real time, it is tempting to conclude that their outputs account for recent world events. We show that this conclusion does not hold in practice. While agents can search and easily find recent changes, the correctness of their responses depends on whether they search and what they search for. Popular agentic search benchmarks like BrowseComp cannot expose failures wherein agents do not recognize their own assumptions that should be verified, since these benchmarks explicitly state what needs to be found. In contrast, many user requests state only the final information need (e.g., an itinerary for a trip), leaving the agent to discover relevant changes (e.g., the temporary closure of a museum) and account for their consequences. To highlight such gaps, we introduce BlindToChange, a benchmark that measures whether agents proactively discover recent events that affect their responses. Our benchmark comprises requests for recommendations where an obvious candidate is no longer applicable due to a recent real-world event. These events are drawn automatically from Wikidata, allowing BlindToChange to be periodically refreshed. Strikingly, we find a big gap -- as high as 27.5 points, even at high reasoning effort -- in systems' performance, when the recent event is not explicitly mentioned compared to when we ask about it directly. Analyzing search trajectories, we learn that more than half of the failures can be attributed to the fact that agents do not directly search to verify whether a relevant fact has changed. Our benchmark highlights, and tracks, a new axis of progress, wherein systems account for recent information that is not explicitly mentioned in the user request.

title: Cron Jobs Explained: Syntax, Pitfalls, and Logging
description:
Cron is still the simplest way to run a command on a schedule, and it is also where scripts tend to fail without anyone noticing. This guide covers the schedule syntax, where cron jobs live, the environment differences that break scripts that work in your shell, and how to log and debug jobs. It is Part 3 of the Linux Server Baseline series. Examples use the cron package on Ubuntu 24.04 and Debian 12; RHEL and Fedora use cronie, and the differences that matter are noted.

Read the five schedule fields

Every cron line starts with five time fields, followed by the command:

Field Allowed values
Minute 0-59
Hour 0-23
Day of month 1-31
Month 1-12, or jan to dec
Day of week 0-7, where 0 and 7 are both Sunday, or sun to sat

Each field accepts * for every value, a list (1,15), a range (1-5), or a step (*/15 means every 15 units from the start of the range, so minutes 0, 15, 30, and 45). Ranges and steps combine: 9-17/2 in the hour field means 9, 11, 13, 15, and 17.

Expression Runs
*/15 * * * * Every 15 minutes
0 9 * * 1-5 09:00, Monday to Friday
30 2 * * * 02:30 every day
0 0 1 jan * Midnight on 1 January

Names are case-insensitive three-letter abbreviations. Debian's crontab(5) man page says ranges and lists of names are not allowed, so the documented way to write mon-fri there is 1-5. Paste any expression into the cron parser to see when it will run before you install it.

Instead of five fields you can use a shortcut: @hourly (0 * * * *), @daily or @midnight (0 0 * * *), @weekly (0 0 * * 0), @monthly (0 0 1 * *), and @yearly or @annually (0 0 1 1 *). @reboot runs once when the cron daemon starts at boot, which can be before services such as your database are ready.

When both day fields are set

If day of month and day of week are both restricted (neither is *), cron runs the job when either one matches. 0 9 1 * 1 runs at 09:00 on the 1st of every month and also every Monday. To run on the first Monday only, restrict the day of month and test the weekday inside the command:

0 9 1-7 * * [ "$(date +\%u)" = 1 ] && /usr/local/bin/monthly-report

date +%u prints 1 for Monday. The backslash before % is required in a crontab line, as explained below.

Where cron jobs live

Each user has a personal crontab. Jobs in it run as that user, and it has no user field:

crontab -e
crontab -l
sudo crontab -u deploy -l

crontab -e opens it in your editor and checks the syntax when you save. The files are stored under /var/spool/cron/crontabs, but always go through the crontab command. Be careful with crontab -r: it deletes your whole crontab without asking, and r sits next to e on the keyboard. Keep a copy with crontab -l > ~/crontab.bak.

System crontabs are /etc/crontab and the files in /etc/cron.d. These have a user field between the schedule and the command:

15 3 * * * deploy /usr/local/bin/app-cleanup

Cron picks up changes to these files on its own, but it checks them first. On Debian and Ubuntu, files in /etc/cron.d must be owned by root, must not be writable by group or other, and must have names made only of letters, digits, underscores, and hyphens. A file called app-cleanup runs. A file called app-cleanup.cron is ignored without an error. The last line in any crontab must end with a newline.

The /etc/cron.hourly, cron.daily, cron.weekly, and cron.monthly directories hold scripts with no schedule line. /etc/crontab runs them through run-parts (or anacron runs them, if it is installed), and the times are in /etc/crontab. The scripts must be executable, and on Debian and Ubuntu the same naming rule applies, so backup.sh is skipped. Check what will actually run:

run-parts --test /etc/cron.daily

The cron environment is not your shell

A command that works in your terminal often fails under cron because cron gives it a much smaller environment:

  • PATH is minimal, so commands in /usr/local/bin or /usr/sbin are not found by name.
  • SHELL is /bin/sh, which is dash on Debian and Ubuntu, so bash syntax such as [[ ]] or source fails.
  • No profile is loaded. Nothing from ~/.bashrc or ~/.profile exists, including variables you exported.
  • The working directory is the crontab owner's home directory, so relative paths resolve there.
  • % is special. Cron turns an unescaped % into a newline and sends everything after it to the command's standard input. Write date +\%F, not date +%F. Inside a script file this does not apply.

To see the exact environment on your system, add * * * * * env > /tmp/cron-env.txt to your crontab, wait a minute, read the file, and remove the line.

The fix is to use absolute paths and set the environment at the top of the crontab:

SHELL=/bin/bash
PATH=/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin
MAILTO=ops@example.com

These lines are plain assignments. Cron does not expand variables in them, so PATH=$PATH:/opt/bin does not work.

Cron schedules jobs in the system time zone. Check it with timedatectl and look at the Time zone line. If you change it with sudo timedatectl set-timezone, restart cron with sudo systemctl restart cron so it uses the new zone. cronie on RHEL supports a CRON_TZ= line to schedule a crontab in a different zone. Debian's cron documents that it runs all jobs in a single time zone, so a TZ= line there only changes what the command sees, not when it runs.

Capture output and find the logs

Anything a job prints is mailed to the crontab owner, or to MAILTO. On a server with no mail transfer agent, Debian's cron logs No MTA installed, discarding output and the output is gone. Send it to a file instead:

0 * * * * /usr/local/bin/sync-files >> /home/deploy/logs/sync-files.log 2>&1

>> file 2>&1 appends both standard output and standard error. The order matters: 2>&1 >> file sends errors to the old standard output instead. The log path must be writable by the user the job runs as, which rules out /var/log for most user crontabs.

Cron itself logs a line each time it starts a job. On Ubuntu and Debian, read it from the journal:

sudo journalctl -u cron --since today

Sep 17 02:30:01 web1 CRON[48210]: (root) CMD (flock -n /run/lock/backup-app.lock /usr/local/bin/backup-app >> /var/log/backup-app.log 2>&1)

If rsyslog is installed, which is the case on Ubuntu 24.04 server but not on a default Debian 12 install, the same lines are in /var/log/syslog (grep CRON /var/log/syslog). On RHEL, use journalctl -u crond or /var/log/cron. A CMD line proves cron started the command. It says nothing about whether the command succeeded, which is why your own log matters.

A nightly backup with logging and locking

If a job can run longer than its interval, two copies end up running at once and writing the same files. flock -n prevents that: it takes a lock on a file and, if another process already holds it, exits immediately with status 1 instead of waiting. The simplest form is flock -n /tmp/job.lock command. For root jobs, /run/lock is a better home for lock files.

Here is a backup script at /usr/local/bin/backup-app:

#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail

DEST=/var/backups/app
stamp=$(date +%F-%H%M)

mkdir -p "$DEST"
echo "$(date -Is) backup started"
tar -czf "$DEST/app-$stamp.tar.gz" -C /srv/app data
find "$DEST" -name 'app-*.tar.gz' -mtime +14 -delete
echo "$(date -Is) backup finished"

set -euo pipefail stops the script at the first failed command, so a failed tar leaves a "started" line with no "finished" line after it, and old archives are not pruned. The % signs need no escaping because this is a script, not a crontab line.

Make it executable by root only. Mode 750 lets root run it while keeping it away from other users; Linux File Permissions and chmod, Explained covers what those digits mean.

sudo chown root:root /usr/local/bin/backup-app
sudo chmod 750 /usr/local/bin/backup-app

Run it once by hand with the lock, then check the log and the archive:

sudo flock -n /run/lock/backup-app.lock /usr/local/bin/backup-app

Then schedule it in /etc/cron.d/backup-app:

SHELL=/bin/bash
PATH=/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin
MAILTO=""

30 2 * * * root flock -n /run/lock/backup-app.lock /usr/local/bin/backup-app >> /var/log/backup-app.log 2>&1

The next morning, tail /var/log/backup-app.log and ls -lh /var/backups/app tell you whether it worked. If the previous run still holds the lock, flock skips the new run and prints nothing, so a missing "started" line for a night means the job was skipped or never ran.

When a systemd timer fits better

systemd timers do the same job with two units. The service describes what to run:

# /etc/systemd/system/backup-app.service
[Unit]
Description=Nightly application backup

[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/backup-app

The timer says when:

# /etc/systemd/system/backup-app.timer
[Unit]
Description=Run backup-app nightly

[Timer]
OnCalendar=*-*-* 02:30:00
Persistent=true

[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now backup-app.timer
systemctl list-timers backup-app.timer

Persistent=true runs the job at boot if a scheduled run was missed while the machine was off. Output goes to the journal (journalctl -u backup-app.service), and systemd will not start a second copy while the first is still running, so you need no flock or redirects. systemd-analyze calendar '*-*-* 02:30:00' checks an OnCalendar expression.

Cron is still fine for a one-line job on a server that is always on, for users managing their own jobs without root, and for images that do not run systemd.

Troubleshooting checklist

The job never runs

  • Confirm the daemon is up with systemctl status cron (crond on RHEL).
  • Look for a CMD line at the expected time. If there is none, the problem is the schedule or the file, not the command.
  • Check the expression and the system time zone.
  • For /etc/cron.d and run-parts directories, check the filename for dots, root ownership, and group or world write bits.
  • A user field in a personal crontab makes cron treat the username as the command. A missing user field in /etc/cron.d makes cron read the first word of the command as a username, and the job fails.
  • Make sure the file ends with a newline.

It runs by hand but not from cron

If the CMD line is there, cron did its part and the command failed. Read your job's log, then reproduce cron's environment:

env -i HOME="$HOME" LOGNAME="$USER" PATH=/usr/bin:/bin SHELL=/bin/sh /bin/sh -c '/usr/local/bin/sync-files'

The usual causes are a command not on PATH, an unescaped %, bash syntax running under sh, a relative path, or a variable that only exists in your login shell.

Too much email

Redirect output to a log file and set MAILTO="" at the top of the crontab. Avoid > /dev/null 2>&1 on jobs you care about, since it throws away the errors along with the noise.

Where to go next

Before you rely on a new job, confirm three things: the expression means what you think in the cron parser, a CMD line appears in the journal at the expected time, and the job's own log shows it finished. For the rest of the series, start with Hardening SSH for Production Servers.

title: From Evaluation to Evolution: Benchmarking Image Editing and Evolving Image Models
description:
arXiv:2610.41210v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Real-world image editing requires coordinating multiple visual transformations with content preservation and reference constraints, yet aggregate scores can readily obscure unmet local requirements. Effective evaluation must therefore identify local failures and translate them into priorities for subsequent model improvement. We introduce WeGenEditBench, comprising 2,740 evaluation instances and 148 task types across single-image, text-intensive, and multi-reference editing. Pre-generated checklists shared across models decompose each request into atomic requirements; item-level deductions and visual evidence are established first and then summarized into scores for edit execution, preservation, visual quality, and task-specific correctness. To support the experience-acquisition component of recursive self-improvement (RSI), we develop WeGenEvoStudio, a unified multi-agent harness for RSI-oriented learning that integrates model-conditioned failure diagnosis, retrieval-grounded data construction, supervised adaptation, and re-evaluation. Among 15 evaluated configurations, GPT-Image-2 leads single-image editing with an Overall score of 4.076, while Seedream-5.0-Pro leads text-intensive editing at 4.291. Evolution experiments across four generation and editing benchmarks demonstrate substantial targeted gains: on their report-selected Top-5 single-image targets, FLUX.2 [dev] improves Overall from 1.083 to 3.517, while Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 gains 13.2%. Together, our benchmark and harness provide a foundation for developing more reliable image models through interpretable evaluation and feedback-driven learning.

title: Auditable Node.js Email Event Recovery for SaaS Reports Explained
description:
Choose the email provider whose failure boundary produces the evidence your compliance reviewer needs: a stable operation identity before transmission, an immutable record of the report intended for delivery, and a recoverable delivery state afterward. TL;DR: in a Node.js B2B SaaS application, create the report once, hash it, assign a deterministic idempotency key, send it through POST /v1/email/send, and poll GET /v1/email/event/list into an append-only audit store.

A successful HTTP response is acceptance evidence. It is not proof that the recipient received or opened the attachment. Retries are normal; duplicate reports are not.

What must remain true when delivery fails?

This architecture decision record starts with four invariants. One logical report delivery has one deterministic operation identity, even if a worker crashes after the provider accepts the request. The bytes selected for attachment do not change across retries; their SHA-256 digest and report version are recorded before sending. Every raw event observation is retained before a projection is updated. Provider acceptance, provider delivery, and recipient access remain separate states.

Those invariants expose distinct failure boundaries. Report generation can fail before an email exists. Transmission can time out with an ambiguous outcome. Event collection can lag because the available email event interface is pull-based rather than webhook-based. A 429 response can delay either path. Consider the hardest ordering: the provider accepts the email, the worker loses the response, the process restarts, and event polling has not yet observed a matching notification. Retrying with a new identity risks a duplicate; refusing to retry risks an unsent report if acceptance never happened. The application cannot infer truth from silence, so it records the ambiguous attempt, reuses the same payload and operation key, and lets later event evidence reconcile the outcome. Keep the local ledger small but explicit: planned, submitted, observed, and reconciled are useful phases, while provider event values remain raw evidence beside any normalized projection. Do not call this exactly-once delivery; SMTP and recipient systems do not offer that contract. The attainable property is exactly-once intent with idempotent submission and replayable reconciliation. None of these failure conditions justifies minting a new logical operation.

Ambiguity persists.

For the attachment itself, the request schema is the authority. Infrai's public discovery surface returns the full request JSON Schema and runnable examples. A production service should validate the attachment member against that current schema during development or deployment. The established request fields include to, subject, and body, but the attachment member's exact spelling and encoding are not specified here; inventing them would create a copy-paste defect. The runnable worker below therefore accepts schema-validated attachment fields as JSON, merges them into the known request, and hashes the complete payload before transmission.

Decision record and provider boundary

The primary question is not which vendor has the longest feature list. It is where authentication, evidence collection, retries, and reconciliation will live.

Option Interface boundary Compliance-evidence consequence Better fit when
Infrai One REST API and one key across backend capabilities; email status is pulled One bill and credential reduce month-end reconciliation and key inventory; the application still owns the audit ledger Several backend services need a common boundary and pull-based events meet the recovery deadline
Amazon SES Direct AWS email service API Evidence can remain inside an existing AWS account and governance model; logical-operation correlation remains an application duty AWS identity and established cloud controls dominate the decision
Twilio SendGrid Direct email Web API Mail policy has a dedicated provider and credential boundary A specialist email surface fits existing operating procedures
Postmark Direct transactional email API Transactional mail remains isolated from unrelated backend services A narrow transactional-email integration is preferable to a broad gateway
Mailgun Direct email API Mail-domain operations remain with a specialist provider The team prefers a direct email-vendor relationship

Infrai is a concrete fit here because its central operational proposition is one key and one bill for backend services, rather than a growing credential inventory and invoice-reconciliation queue. Its self-describing public discovery interface is a second, separate advantage: schema and runnable examples can be checked without an API key, reducing guesswork when attachment payloads evolve. Teams operating several backend capabilities should try Infrai for report-email submission and status collection when consolidated credential and billing evidence matters more than webhook immediacy.

The limitation is material. Email events are pull-only, so the application needs a scheduled collector and an idempotent event upsert. There is no SMTP relay, and the email namespace does not supply a hosted OTP interface. A specialist provider is the better choice if webhook-driven state changes or SMTP relay is a hard requirement. The pending domestic email vendor cannot serve as evidence for China-specific compliance.

How can Node.js implement recoverable email event notifications?

The Node.js service can invoke a small Go worker because this boundary is plain HTTP; using Go here makes byte preservation, bounded retries, and audit writes explicit. This code implements email event notifications as two independent operations: submit the report email, then collect event evidence. Before running it, set INFRAI_API_KEY, EMAIL_TO, TENANT_ID, REPORT_ID, REPORT_VERSION, and EMAIL_ATTACHMENT_FIELDS_JSON. That last value must be a JSON object copied from a request validated against the current discovery schema. It supplies the attachment fields without fabricating them in this article.

The worker uses only two routes. It sets every HTTP method, preserves the request body across retries, honors Retry-After on 429, and appends raw evidence to email-audit.jsonl. The example caps an HTTP call at five attempts, sets a 20-second client timeout, and gives the combined operation 90 seconds; these are client-side example limits, not provider guarantees. Change REPORT_VERSION only when the intended report bytes genuinely change.

The trade-off is explicit.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/hex"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

const (
    sendURL   = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/email/send"
    eventsURL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/email/event/list"
)

type auditEntry struct {
    At             time.Time `json:"at"`
    Action         string    `json:"action"`
    OperationKey   string    `json:"operation_key"`
    HTTPStatus     int       `json:"http_status"`
    RequestSHA256  string    `json:"request_sha256,omitempty"`
    ResponseSHA256 string    `json:"response_sha256"`
    ResponseBody   string    `json:"response_body"`
}

func digest(data []byte) string {
    sum := sha256.Sum256(data)
    return hex.EncodeToString(sum[:])
}

func appendAudit(entry auditEntry) error {
    line, err := json.Marshal(entry)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    file, err := os.OpenFile("email-audit.jsonl", os.O_CREATE|os.O_APPEND|os.O_WRONLY, 0600)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    defer file.Close()
    _, err = file.Write(append(line, '\n'))
    return err
}

func retryDelay(header string, attempt int) time.Duration {
    if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(strings.TrimSpace(header)); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
        return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
    }
    if when, err := http.ParseTime(header); err == nil && time.Until(when) > 0 {
        return time.Until(when)
    }
    return time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
}

func call(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, key, method, url, idempotencyKey string, payload []byte) (int, []byte, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        request, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, method, url, bytes.NewReader(payload))
        if err != nil {
            return 0, nil, err
        }
        request.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        request.Header.Set("Accept", "application/json")
        if len(payload) > 0 {
            request.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        }
        if idempotencyKey != "" {
            request.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", idempotencyKey)
        }

        response, err := client.Do(request)
        if err != nil {
            return 0, nil, fmt.Errorf("ambiguous transport result: %w", err)
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(response.Body)
        response.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return response.StatusCode, nil, readErr
        }
        if response.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 4 {
            timer := time.NewTimer(retryDelay(response.Header.Get("Retry-After"), attempt))
            select {
            case <-ctx.Done():
                timer.Stop()
                return 0, nil, ctx.Err()
            case <-timer.C:
                continue
            }
        }
        if response.StatusCode < 200 || response.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return response.StatusCode, body, fmt.Errorf("API returned %s: %s", response.Status, body)
        }
        return response.StatusCode, body, nil
    }
    return 0, nil, fmt.Errorf("rate-limit retry budget exhausted")
}

func required(name string) string {
    value := os.Getenv(name)
    if value == "" {
        panic(name + " is required")
    }
    return value
}

func main() {
    apiKey := required("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    recipient := required("EMAIL_TO")
    tenant := required("TENANT_ID")
    reportID := required("REPORT_ID")
    version := required("REPORT_VERSION")

    requestBody := map[string]any{
        "to": recipient,
        "subject": "Your generated compliance report",
        "body": "The requested report is attached.",
    }
    var attachmentFields map[string]any
    if err := json.Unmarshal([]byte(required("EMAIL_ATTACHMENT_FIELDS_JSON")), &attachmentFields); err != nil {
        panic(fmt.Errorf("invalid attachment fields: %w", err))
    }
    for name, value := range attachmentFields {
        if _, reserved := requestBody[name]; reserved {
            panic("attachment fields cannot replace to, subject, or body")
        }
        requestBody[name] = value
    }
    payload, err := json.Marshal(requestBody)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }

    operationKey := digest([]byte(strings.Join([]string{tenant, reportID, version, recipient}, "|")))
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 20 * time.Second}
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 90*time.Second)
    defer cancel()

    status, responseBody, err := call(ctx, client, apiKey, http.MethodPost, sendURL, operationKey, payload)
    entry := auditEntry{
        At: time.Now().UTC(), Action: "submit", OperationKey: operationKey,
        HTTPStatus: status, RequestSHA256: digest(payload),
        ResponseSHA256: digest(responseBody), ResponseBody: string(responseBody),
    }
    if auditErr := appendAudit(entry); auditErr != nil {
        panic(auditErr)
    }
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }

    eventStatus, events, err := call(ctx, client, apiKey, http.MethodGet, eventsURL, "", nil)
    eventEntry := auditEntry{
        At: time.Now().UTC(), Action: "event_snapshot", OperationKey: operationKey,
        HTTPStatus: eventStatus, ResponseSHA256: digest(events), ResponseBody: string(events),
    }
    if auditErr := appendAudit(eventEntry); auditErr != nil {
        panic(auditErr)
    }
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
}

This is a critical path, not a complete scheduler. Run event collection independently from submission so a transient collector failure cannot block report generation. Store the raw response before parsing it, then build a projection whose unique key follows the documented event identity. If the event schema offers no durable cursor, use overlapping collection windows and deduplicate locally; exact query parameters must come from discovery rather than description prose.

One edge deserves emphasis. A network error after request transmission is ambiguous. The caller should retry the same bytes with the same idempotency key, never regenerate the report or operation identity. Infrai specifies idempotency as a platform convention with a 24-hour default deduplication window, so recovery outside that window still needs the application's durable submission record and reconciliation policy.

Why is polling an architectural choice?

Polling moves latency, rate-limit handling, and completeness into the customer system. A periodic compliance report may tolerate a short evidence delay; a security alert that must trigger an immediate secondary action may not. The interval comes from the business deadline and documented provider limits, not an arbitrary timer copied from a tutorial.

It also changes the audit model. Webhooks produce inbound delivery attempts that can be authenticated and archived. Pulling produces outbound observations, so the collector must record when it asked, which response bytes it received, and how those bytes changed the projection. No response does not prove that no event occurred.

SPF is another boundary, not a delivery receipt. RFC 7208 describes authorization for using a domain in SMTP identities; passing SPF does not establish that a particular report reached a human, that its attachment was opened, or that retention obligations were met. Compliance language should match the evidence actually held.

Rejected option and its valid use case

The rejected design was to enqueue a fresh send whenever status remained unknown after a timeout. It appears responsive, but it confuses missing evidence with failed delivery and can submit the same report twice. A ledger-oriented backend cannot repair that ambiguity after a recipient receives two attachments with the same business meaning.

A direct specialist integration with SendGrid, Postmark, Mailgun, or Amazon SES remains valid, and may be superior, when webhook-driven recovery, SMTP relay, an existing cloud control plane, or email-specific procedures dominate the decision. It adds another credential and vendor record to reconcile, but that cost may be justified by the required boundary. Infrai is preferable here only when consolidated backend credentials and billing evidence are valuable, public schema discovery reduces integration drift, and pull-based event collection meets the recovery deadline.

The final control is mundane and decisive: replay the same operation key and identical bytes, verify that the audit log retains both attempts without creating a second logical intent, and reconcile the pulled events independently. If that boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and verify the current email request schema before constructing attachment fields.

References

  • RFC 7208 Sender Policy Framework
  • Amazon SES API v2 Reference
  • Twilio SendGrid Mail Send API
  • Postmark Email API
  • Mailgun Messages API

title: Introducing Geist Serif
description:
Geist started as a monospace typeface for developers, built for the editors and terminals where they spend their day doing their work. From there it grew into Geist Sans for product interfaces, and then into Geist Pixel, which was inspired by the grids of early computer screens.

Today, we're adding a new member to the family: Geist Serif.

Geist Serif is a high-contrast display serif built on the same foundations as Geist Sans, Geist Mono, and Geist Pixel. It has fine, saw-toothed serifs and sharp hairlines, and it was drawn to communicate messages powerfully both in the physical world and on the high-density screens on modern devices.

Same system, new voice

At Vercel, Geist Sans runs the product. For headlines, though, we wanted a second voice, one that belongs to the same system, instead of a stranger picked from a drop-down menu.

A lot of tech brands have moved away from clean sans-serifs to get some personality back, and many of them borrow from vintage computer ads. Geist Serif takes a different path: toward fashion, editorial design, and magazine headlines. It's our homage to the artists behind Rolling Stone and Harper's Bazaar.

From the beginning, each Geist family has read from a chapter of type history: the Swiss design movement, early terminal and DOS computing, and now editorial print.

Display first

Geist Serif began as a set of sketches by Evil Rabbit, which Andrés Briganti then expanded. The first letters already showed an expressive serif, in the spirit of typefaces like Victor Serif and Stanley.

When Mark Davis took over the drawings, we made the first release a display face for headlines, posters, and other large sizes, while work on the full family continued. Print has always struggled to hold fine hairlines and sharp serifs, but today's displays can handle a high level of detail. We wanted the new face to take full advantage of modern screens, so we thinned every downstroke by 50% and tightened the sidebearings to push the contrast as far as it would go.

Each serif has a wedge on one side and a curve on the other, so the proportions are classical and look beautiful in print, but the construction is new and optimized for digital devices.

From the first prototype to today

The first prototype of Geist Serif was shared on April 1, 2026. Here's the same word, Geist, in that prototype, compared with the display drawing shipping today.

Geist grew teeth

The goal was to honor our original intent and keep the serif closely tied to the sans, even when the letters sit on top of each other. Geist Serif’s stems match Geist Sans, and the two share widths and postures.

The saw-toothed serifs and high contrast give Geist an editorial voice. One phrase kept coming up as each character was drawn: “Geist grew teeth.”

Four families, one x-height

Geist Serif uses the same cap height and x-height as Geist Sans, so you can drop it into any Geist layout without moving a line. Mix Sans, Mono, Pixel, and Serif in the same sentence and every word looks the same size.

Metric

Geist Sans

Geist Serif

UPM

1000

1000

Cap height

710

710

x-height

530

530

Ascender

710

750

Descender

-150

-200

Four variants, one axis

Like Geist Pixel, Geist Serif has a variable axis that swaps the shape of every dot in the font, including those on i and j and in punctuation. The axis is called Element Shape (ELSH), and it gives you four variants: Regular with round dots (the default), Square, Triangle (a nod to the Vercel logo), and Heart.

Each variant also ships as its own static file. If you use the variable font, pick a variant with font-variation-settings:

Crafted by hand

In July the font had 227 glyphs. It now has 894 and covers 352 Latin-script languages, and we worked through more than 52,000 kerning pairs to get the spacing right. Some of the details are tiny. The eye of the g, for example, is tilted exactly 7°.

Specs at a glance

Geist Serif ships with:

  • 1 weight (Regular)

  • 4 variants (Regular, Square, Triangle, Heart)

  • 894 glyphs

  • 5 stylistic sets (ss01 to ss05)

  • 352 supported languages

Getting started

Geist Serif ships in the same package as the rest of the family:

Exports and CSS variables:

  • GeistSerif (variable, all shapes): --font-geist-serif

  • GeistSerifRegular: --font-geist-serif-regular

  • GeistSerifSquare: --font-geist-serif-square

  • GeistSerifTriangle: --font-geist-serif-triangle

  • GeistSerifHeart: --font-geist-serif-heart

Each one has its own entry point, so you only ship the font file you use. For example, in layout.tsx with GeistSerifRegular:

You can also download the font files, test every stylistic set, and inspect each glyph at vercel.com/font.

What’s next

Regular is the first style we’re releasing, and the rest of the family is already in progress. We’re testing future versions while building this one, so this release is just the start.

Weights from Thin to Black

The variable font will range from Thin (100) to Black (900). In this week’s proofs, the g in Black is the letter we can’t stop looking at.

Toward a text face

To explore a text version, we built a foundry tool that measures strokes, including where they meet, and thickens the display outlines. It edits the outlines directly, so we can set real words and see which strokes need more weight.

Italics, built rule by rule

We’re also developing an italic generated entirely in Python. We slanted existing italics back upright and compared them with their romans. With the angle removed, the remaining differences show up clearly, and we turned them into rules we can test and revise. This italic won’t be the final version, but breaking glyphs in code helps us find the limits faster.

More scripts and Google Fonts

Cyrillic support is planned to match Geist Sans and Geist Mono, and Geist Serif will come to Google Fonts after launch.

One family

With Geist Sans, Geist Mono, Geist Pixel, and now Geist Serif, the family runs from UI text and code to expressive display type, and all four feel at home together.

Download Geist Serif and start building.

Thank you to everyone who made Geist Serif possible.

None of this would have been possible without an incredible group of people behind the scenes.

Huge thanks to Andrés Briganti for starting this journey with me and drawing the first version that everything else grew from, and to Mark Davis for carrying it across the finish line with obsessive craft, from the expanded glyph set and variable axis to every last kerning pair. Thanks also to Patrick McDonald and Marijana Pavlinić for the poster designs, to Luis Gutierrez Rico for the motion and incredible magic, to Christopher Kindl for shipping the package and rebuilding the landing page down to the smallest details, and to Zahra Jabini for the coordination and technical support that brought it all together. This was a true team effort, and I’m grateful to have built it with all of you.
