title: ParticleDB's Premature 'Full ACID' Claims Invalidated by Jepsen Testing Across Versions 1.1.4 to 1.1.18.11.rc-22
description:
Introduction

ParticleDB, a distributed database system, has boldly claimed "Full ACID" compliance—a promise that, if true, would ensure Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability in its data operations. However, recent testing by Jepsen across versions 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.11.rc-22 has invalidated these claims, revealing that ParticleDB’s assertions were premature. Jepsen’s investigation uncovered critical discrepancies between ParticleDB’s marketing promises and its actual performance, raising concerns about the system’s reliability in mission-critical applications.

The core issue lies in ParticleDB’s inadequate implementation of ACID properties. For instance, Jepsen’s tests exposed scenarios where atomicity—the guarantee that transactions are all-or-nothing—failed under specific workloads. This failure occurred due to race conditions in the system’s concurrency control mechanisms, where simultaneous write operations caused partial transaction commits, leading to data inconsistencies. Additionally, isolation—the property ensuring transactions execute independently—was compromised, as read operations occasionally returned stale data, a direct result of oversights in ParticleDB’s testing and validation processes.

Compounding the problem is the miscommunication or overstatement of ACID compliance in ParticleDB’s marketing materials. While the system may handle certain ACID properties under ideal conditions, Jepsen’s tests revealed that these guarantees break down under stress. For example, high-throughput workloads triggered network partitions, causing the system to prioritize availability over consistency, a trade-off that violates ACID principles. This discrepancy between marketing claims and real-world performance risks eroding trust among users and developers who rely on ACID compliance for critical applications.

The stakes are high. If ParticleDB’s claims remain unaddressed, users could face data inconsistencies and system failures in production environments. For instance, financial systems relying on ParticleDB might process duplicate transactions or lose data, leading to financial losses. To mitigate this risk, ParticleDB must re-evaluate its implementation, strengthen its testing processes, and communicate its capabilities with transparency. Only then can it regain credibility in a market where ACID compliance is non-negotiable.

Methodology

Jepsen’s investigation into ParticleDB’s “Full ACID” claims spanned versions 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.11.rc-22, employing a rigorous testing framework designed to stress-test the database’s adherence to Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability guarantees. The process involved:

  • Tooling: Jepsen utilized its proprietary testing suite, which injects controlled chaos into distributed systems to expose inconsistencies. This included network partitions, latency spikes, and concurrent transaction workloads to simulate real-world stress conditions.
  • Criteria for ACID Evaluation:
    • Atomicity: Transactions were tested for all-or-nothing execution. Jepsen observed partial commits under high concurrency, where race conditions in ParticleDB’s concurrency control mechanisms allowed incomplete transactions to persist, deforming data integrity.
    • Consistency: The system failed to maintain a valid state post-transaction, with stale data returned during read operations. This was traced to oversights in ParticleDB’s validation processes, where read-write conflicts were not adequately isolated.
    • Isolation: Jepsen detected dirty reads and non-repeatable reads, indicating compromised isolation levels. This occurred due to insufficient locking mechanisms, causing concurrent transactions to interfere with each other’s state.
    • Durability: Under network partitions, ParticleDB prioritized availability over durability, leading to data loss in certain scenarios. The system’s failure to flush writes to disk before acknowledging transactions expanded the risk of data corruption.
  • Edge-Case Analysis: Jepsen specifically targeted high-throughput workloads and network partitions, conditions under which ParticleDB’s ACID guarantees broke down. For instance, network latency exceeding 500ms triggered a consistency-availability tradeoff, forcing the system to violate ACID principles to maintain responsiveness.

The testing revealed a causal chain: inadequate implementation of ACID properties → stress-induced failures → observable data inconsistencies. ParticleDB’s claims were deemed premature due to these systemic oversights, highlighting the need for robust testing and transparent communication in distributed database systems.

Findings: Jepsen’s Investigation Exposes ParticleDB’s Premature ACID Claims

Jepsen’s rigorous testing of ParticleDB versions 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.11.rc-22 revealed systemic discrepancies between the database’s “Full ACID” claims and its actual performance under stress. Across six critical scenarios, ParticleDB failed to uphold Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability guarantees, exposing flaws in its implementation, testing processes, and marketing communications.

Scenario-Based Failures: Mechanisms and Observable Effects

  • Atomicity Failure (Race Conditions):

Under high concurrency, ParticleDB’s transaction manager failed to enforce all-or-nothing execution. Race conditions in the concurrency control mechanism allowed partial commits, where only subsets of operations were applied. This deformed transaction integrity, leading to data inconsistencies observable in financial ledger-like workloads (e.g., account balances mismatching transaction histories).

  • Consistency Failure (Stale Data Reads):

Read operations returned outdated data due to oversights in isolating read-write conflicts. ParticleDB’s validation process failed to lock shared resources during writes, allowing concurrent reads to access intermediate states. This expanded the window for stale data exposure, particularly in inventory management scenarios where stock counts fluctuated unpredictably.

  • Isolation Failure (Dirty Reads):

Insufficient locking mechanisms enabled dirty reads, where transactions observed uncommitted changes from concurrent operations. This occurred because ParticleDB’s isolation levels were not strictly enforced, allowing interference between transactions. In ticketing systems, for example, this caused phantom bookings where seats appeared available but were already reserved.

  • Durability Failure (Network Partitions):

During network partitions (>500ms latency), ParticleDB prioritized availability over durability. Writes were acknowledged before being flushed to disk, leading to data loss when nodes failed. This broke the durability guarantee, as critical updates (e.g., financial transactions) vanished post-recovery, violating ACID principles.

  • Edge-Case Breakdown (High-Throughput Workloads):

Under extreme throughput (>10,000 ops/sec), ParticleDB’s consistency-availability tradeoff mechanism heated up, forcing ACID violations to maintain responsiveness. Network partitions triggered a failover to eventual consistency, expanding the risk of stale data propagation. This was observable in real-time analytics systems, where dashboards displayed conflicting metrics.

  • Marketing Discrepancy (Overstated Compliance):

ParticleDB’s marketing materials claimed “Full ACID” without qualifying edge-case limitations. This miscommunication created a gap between user expectations and system capabilities, eroding trust. Developers relying on ACID guarantees for critical applications faced unforeseen risks, such as financial losses from inconsistent transaction processing.

Causal Chain and Optimal Remediation

The root cause of ParticleDB’s failures lies in inadequate ACID implementation, compounded by oversights in testing and validation processes. Stress-induced failures exposed systemic weaknesses, leading to observable data inconsistencies. To address these issues:

  • Re-evaluate Implementation: Strengthen concurrency control mechanisms to eliminate race conditions and enforce strict isolation levels.
  • Enhance Testing: Incorporate chaos-injection testing to simulate edge cases like network partitions and high-throughput workloads.
  • Transparent Communication: Clearly document ACID compliance limitations in marketing materials to manage user expectations.

Rule for Remediation: If stress-induced failures expose ACID violations, use chaos-injection testing to identify edge cases and re-architect concurrency control to enforce guarantees under all conditions.

Failure to address these issues risks systemic breakdowns in production environments, particularly for mission-critical applications. ParticleDB must act decisively to restore credibility and ensure data integrity.

Analysis: Why ParticleDB’s 'Full ACID' Claims Were Premature

ParticleDB’s assertion of "Full ACID" compliance crumbled under Jepsen’s scrutiny, revealing a cascade of technical oversights that rendered the claim premature. The root cause lies in the inadequate implementation of ACID properties, exacerbated by testing and validation processes that failed to simulate real-world stress conditions. This analysis dissects the causal chain, edge-case breakdowns, and practical implications for users and ParticleDB’s reputation.

Causal Chain: From Implementation Flaws to Observable Failures

The breakdown begins with ParticleDB’s concurrency control mechanisms, which failed to enforce atomicity under high-throughput workloads. Race conditions in the transaction manager allowed partial commits, violating the all-or-nothing principle of atomicity. For instance, in financial systems, this led to ledger mismatches where debits and credits failed to balance, a direct consequence of the system’s inability to handle concurrent transactions without interference.

Isolation failures further compounded the issue. Weak locking mechanisms permitted dirty reads, where transactions observed uncommitted changes from other transactions. This resulted in phantom bookings in ticketing systems, where seats appeared available but were already reserved, a clear violation of isolation guarantees.

Under stress, ParticleDB prioritized availability over consistency, a tradeoff that violated ACID principles. Network partitions exceeding 500ms latency triggered this breakdown, causing the system to acknowledge writes before flushing them to disk. This led to data loss post-recovery, as unpersisted changes were discarded during system restarts.

Edge-Case Breakdown: High Throughput and Network Partitions

ParticleDB’s claims faltered at the edges of operational capacity. At >10,000 ops/sec, the system defaulted to eventual consistency, propagating stale data in real-time analytics. This edge-case behavior was not documented in marketing materials, creating a trust gap between expectations and reality. For mission-critical applications, this discrepancy translates to unforeseen risks, such as financial losses from inconsistent transaction processing.

Practical Implications: Eroding Trust and Systemic Risks

The premature "Full ACID" claims have tangible consequences. Developers relying on ParticleDB for critical applications face data inconsistencies, system failures, and potential financial losses. For example, inventory systems experienced unpredictable stock counts due to stale data reads, while ticketing platforms suffered from overbookings. These failures stem from the misalignment between marketing promises and technical reality, a gap that erodes trust and undermines ParticleDB’s credibility.

Remediation: A Rule-Based Approach

To address these issues, ParticleDB must adopt a chaos-injection testing framework to simulate edge cases like network partitions and high-throughput workloads. This approach exposes systemic weaknesses before deployment. Additionally, re-architecting concurrency control to enforce strict isolation and eliminate race conditions is critical. A rule for remediation: If stress-induced failures expose ACID violations, apply chaos-injection testing and re-architect concurrency control to enforce guarantees under all conditions.

Transparent communication is equally vital. ParticleDB must clearly document ACID limitations in marketing materials, avoiding overstatements that create false expectations. This transparency rebuilds trust and ensures users understand the system’s capabilities and boundaries.

Conclusion: The Cost of Premature Claims

ParticleDB’s premature "Full ACID" claims highlight the dangers of overstating technical capabilities without rigorous validation. The causal chain—from implementation flaws to observable failures—underscores the need for robust testing and transparent communication. For users, the stakes are clear: unaddressed issues lead to systemic breakdowns in production, particularly for mission-critical applications. ParticleDB’s path forward requires not just technical remediation but a commitment to honesty and accountability in an era where data integrity is non-negotiable.

Conclusion and Recommendations

Jepsen’s rigorous testing of ParticleDB across versions 1.1.4 to 1.1.18.11.rc-22 has conclusively demonstrated that the database’s claims of “Full ACID” compliance are premature. The investigation uncovered systemic failures in Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability under stress, driven by flawed concurrency control and inadequate testing processes. These issues manifest as data inconsistencies, phantom reads, and durability compromises, particularly under high-throughput workloads and network partitions. The root cause lies in ParticleDB’s inability to enforce strict ACID guarantees when faced with edge cases, such as concurrent transactions exceeding 10,000 ops/sec or network latencies surpassing 500ms.

The causal chain is clear: inadequate ACID implementation leads to stress-induced failures, which in turn result in observable data inconsistencies. For instance, race conditions in the transaction manager cause partial commits, while weak locking mechanisms allow dirty reads, directly impacting mission-critical applications like financial ledgers and ticketing systems. The prioritization of availability over durability during network partitions further exacerbates the risk of data loss post-recovery.

Recommendations for ParticleDB

  • Re-evaluate Implementation: Strengthen concurrency control mechanisms to eliminate race conditions and enforce strict isolation. For example, replace weak locks with multi-version concurrency control (MVCC) to prevent dirty reads and ensure atomicity under high concurrency.
  • Enhance Testing: Adopt chaos-injection testing to simulate edge cases such as network partitions and extreme throughput. This will expose weaknesses in the system’s ACID guarantees and ensure robustness under real-world stress.
  • Transparent Communication: Clearly document ACID limitations in marketing materials. For instance, specify that the system defaults to eventual consistency above 10,000 ops/sec, avoiding overstated claims that erode trust.

Steps for Users to Ensure Data Integrity

  • Validate Claims Independently: Conduct stress tests using tools like Jepsen to verify ACID compliance under specific workloads. Focus on edge cases such as high concurrency and network partitions.
  • Implement Redundancy: For mission-critical applications, use external mechanisms like distributed locks or compensating transactions to mitigate risks of partial commits and data inconsistencies.
  • Monitor for Anomalies: Deploy monitoring systems to detect anomalies like stale reads or phantom writes, which indicate ACID violations. For example, track transaction latency spikes as early indicators of stress-induced failures.

Professional Judgment

ParticleDB’s premature “Full ACID” claims highlight a broader industry issue: the gap between marketing promises and technical reality. To rebuild trust, ParticleDB must not only address the technical shortcomings but also adopt a culture of transparency and rigorous validation. The optimal remediation strategy involves a combination of re-architecting concurrency control, chaos-injection testing, and honest communication. Failure to act will result in systemic breakdowns, particularly in production environments where ACID guarantees are non-negotiable. The rule is clear: if stress-induced failures expose ACID violations, apply chaos-injection testing and re-architect concurrency control to enforce guarantees under all conditions.

title: FlexReader: Towards Adaptive Decoding Paths for Efficient Arbitrary-Length Scene Text Recognition
description:
arXiv:2610.41426v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Existing Scene Text Recognition (STR) models are inherently coupled with a specific decoding strategy by their training paradigms, limiting their flexibility in deployment across diverse recognition scenarios. In this paper, we propose FlexReader, an STR model that supports multiple decoding strides, enabling a single model to achieve an optimal accuracy-efficiency trade-off across different datasets. Specifically, we first introduce a Sub-string Perception module to perceive the target sub-string from visual features, followed by multiple parallel decoding blocks that independently decode each character in the sub-string. During inference, FlexReader supports decoding with arbitrary strides within the perceived sub-string range. Furthermore, we propose Adaptive Prefix Decoding, which adaptively selects the decoding stride at each step based on the model's confidence in the decoded characters, thereby identifying the optimal decoding path for each input. Experimental results demonstrate that FlexReader exhibits robust recognition capability across a diverse range of benchmarks, including those featuring long text, curved text, and occlusions. It consistently outperforms existing decoding strategies in recognition accuracy while achieving up to 6-flod decoding speedup over autoregressive decoding.

title: React Fiber
description:
An Overview of Fiber Trees and Reconciliation

Unlocking the Power of Web Scraping for Data Collection and Analysis

React Fiber is a revolutionary feature in the React library that aims to significantly enhance the performance and rendering efficiency of React applications.
At the heart of Fiber lies the reconciliation process, a powerful mechanism that efficiently updates the user interface based on changes in application state.
In this blog, we will delve into the concept of Fiber trees and explore how the reconciliation process works.

Reconciliation Stack

Before the release of React 16, React employed a stack-based reconciliation algorithm known as the "stack reconciler" to compare the old and new virtual trees
and update the DOM accordingly. While suitable for simpler scenarios, the stack reconciler faced challenges as applications grew in complexity.

The synchronous nature of the stack reconciler caused updates to block the main thread, leading to janky and unresponsive user interfaces, especially with large
virtual trees or slower devices. Additionally, changes to the virtual tree were delayed until the reconciler completed its work, affecting overall performance
and responsiveness.

The Fiber Reconciler

To address these challenges and improve React's performance, React 16 introduced the Fiber reconciler, a complete rewrite of the previous stack-based algorithm
with several significant benefits.

How React Fiber Works

When a React application undergoes an update triggered by user interactions or events, the reconciliation process is initiated. Its goal is to efficiently
determine the parts of the user interface that require updating and apply these changes to the real DOM.

Fiber Trees - Current and Work in Progress

The reconciliation process involves two sets of virtual DOM trees: the "current" tree and the "work in progress" tree, also known as the Fiber tree. The
"current" tree represents the existing state of the virtual DOM, while the "work in progress" tree is a replica that incorporates the updates to be performed.

Render Phase

The reconciliation process begins with the render phase, where React traverses the component tree and creates fiber nodes, special data structures representing
different portions of the virtual DOM.

During the render phase, React compares the fiber nodes in the "current" and "work in progress" trees to identify parts of the virtual DOM requiring updates.
Leveraging a work loop, React breaks rendering work into smaller units that can be interrupted and resumed, prioritizing important updates to maintain a
responsive user interface.

Commit Phase

After completing the render phase and applying the necessary updates to the "work in progress" tree, React enters the commit phase. Here, React takes the
updates from the "work in progress" tree and applies them to the real DOM, making the changes visible to users.

React optimizes the performance by batching updates during the commit phase, reducing unnecessary reflows and repaints for a smoother user experience.

A New Horizon for Concurrency and Batching

React Fiber, the new reconciliation architecture introduced in React 16, not only improves rendering efficiency but also unlocks powerful features for
concurrency and batching. This allows React to break free from the limitations of synchronous updates and enables the library to handle complex user
interactions more intelligently.

| Concurrency and Batching

In traditional synchronous rendering, React updates the entire component tree before reflecting changes in the real DOM. This approach can lead to unnecessary
processing, causing performance bottlenecks and affecting user experience. React Fiber introduces the concept of concurrency, which enables asynchronous
rendering and prioritization of tasks.

With concurrency, React can pause, resume, or abort rendering work as needed, and even divide the rendering process into smaller, more manageable chunks. This
fine-grained control empowers React to prioritize essential updates and respond faster to user interactions, making the user interface feel more responsive and
fluid

New Functionality in React Fiber

To leverage the benefits of concurrency and batching, React introduces several new functionalities:

useDeferredValue;

The useDeferredValue hook allows developers to defer the processing of non-essential updates, optimizing performance by prioritizing high-priority work. For
example, in a search input, we may want to defer the rendering of search results until the user pauses typing. This way, React can focus on more critical tasks
like handling user input, ensuring a smoother experience.

import { useDeferredValue } from "react";

const Search = () => {
    const [query, setQuery] = useState("");

    // Defer the processing of non-essential updates
    const deferredQuery = useDeferredValue(query);

    const handleChange = (e) => {
        setQuery(e.target.value);
    };

    // Rest of the component logic
};

useTransition;

The useTransition hook allows developers to create smoother transitions during rendering updates. It helps to manage complex interactions by defining specific
points in the rendering process where React should wait for a transition to complete before displaying the changes.

import { useTransition, useEffect, useState } from "react";

const ExpensiveComponent = () => {
    const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition();

    // Simulate a time-consuming rendering process
    useEffect(() => {
        startTransition(() => {
            // Code to render the expensive component
        });
    }, []);

    if (isPending) {
        return <p>Loading...</p>;
    }

    // Return the fully rendered component
    return <div>Expensive Component Content</div>;
};

Suspense Component

The Suspense component is a powerful tool that allows developers to handle loading states and fallback UIs in an elegant and straightforward manner. It is
especially useful when dealing with asynchronous data fetching or code-splitting.

import { Suspense } from "react";

const MyComponent = () => {
    return (
        <Suspense fallback={<p>Loading...</p>}>
            {/* Asynchronously load and render the lazy component */}
            <LazyComponent />
        </Suspense>
    );
};

Conclusion

React Fiber's reconciliation process, powered by the concept of Fiber trees, plays a pivotal role in driving React's remarkable performance. By intelligently
managing virtual DOM updates and efficiently applying them to the real DOM, React ensures that user interfaces remain snappy and responsive, making React a
popular and powerful choice for building modern web applications. The introduction of React Fiber marks a significant milestone in React's evolution, paving the
way for even more efficient and responsive applications.

Thanks for reading ❤️

title: FARO: Function-Space Adaptive Return-to-Risk Optimization via Cross-Block Equal-Risk-Contribution Budget Allocation
description:
arXiv:2610.40858v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Training a large language model is compute-bound, and current recipes divide the work between optimizers by hand: orthogonalized momentum for attention and MLP matrices, Adam-style updates for the rest. This division rests on human priors about which layer type deserves which geometry, and it fixes a single global update budget that every parameter block shares. We introduce FARO, a function-space adaptive optimizer that makes the partition of parameters into blocks the unit of decision. FARO gives each block a geometry by its realized counterfactual return, then freezes the routes and reallocates the frozen per-block budget by cross-block equal risk contribution (ERC), the risk-parity principle from portfolio theory. On a GPT-style model trained on FineWeb, the framework gives two results. First, its FARO-Adaptive arm reaches 3.2780 nats at the full schedule, matching NorMuonAndAdam (3.2794), the best hand-designed recipe: it recovers the human prior without hand-setting per-layer geometry. Second, FARO-ERC improves on that arm: it lowers the clean-data loss at every one of 6 seeds, by 0.0136 nats on average, a modest but robust gain. Its sign test, paired test, and confidence interval all agree, and it exceeds the measured run-to-run noise at no added time or memory. It works by trimming the riskiest blocks rather than expanding the safest, and it holds up under a corrupted stream, still lowering the mean loss and winning the seed majority. The source code is available at https://github.com/wxj630/FARO.

title: A Practical Approach to Evaluating Airflow Visualisation in GMP Cleanrooms
description:
Pharmaceutical cleanrooms depend on controlled airflow to protect exposed products, components and critical surfaces. In aseptic manufacturing, smoke studies help teams visualise airflow behaviour under defined operating conditions.

However, capturing a video of smoke movement is not enough. The observations must be assessed against predefined acceptance criteria to determine whether the airflow pattern provides the intended protection.

This article outlines a practical approach to reviewing airflow visualisation results in GMP cleanrooms.

  1. Define the Expected Airflow Behaviour

Before conducting a smoke study, identify what the test is intended to demonstrate.

The protocol should consider:

Cleanroom layout and equipment configuration

Critical process locations and exposed products

Intended airflow direction

Relevant operating conditions

Routine interventions and operator movements

Potential contamination pathways

The expected airflow behaviour should be clear enough for reviewers to compare actual observations with the predefined criteria.

  1. Capture Representative Operating Conditions

Airflow can change when operators interact with equipment or move materials through a critical area.

A study should therefore consider relevant operating conditions, rather than relying only on observations made in an unoccupied room.

Depending on the process, the protocol may include material transfer, equipment handling, component replacement and other representative interventions.

Video recordings should clearly show the test location, the activity being performed and the resulting smoke movement.

  1. Evaluate Airflow Observations Systematically

A structured review helps teams avoid relying on subjective impressions of whether airflow looks acceptable.

The following table summarises useful observation points.

Observation

What to assess

Airflow direction

Whether air moves in the intended direction

Product protection

Whether exposed products and critical surfaces receive appropriate protection

Turbulence and eddies

Whether local disturbances affect critical locations

Operator interventions

Whether activities disrupt the intended airflow pattern

Reversal or ingress

Whether air moves from less clean areas towards higher-grade areas

Smoke clearance

Whether slow-moving or stagnant patterns require further assessment

Not every visible disturbance represents a failure. Its significance depends on its location, duration, operating conditions and potential effect on product protection.

  1. Review Interventions and Local Disturbances

Operator movements and equipment arrangements can create local airflow disturbances.

For example, an intervention near an exposed product may influence the airflow pattern around that location. Reviewers should examine the video to understand whether the disturbance affects the intended protective airflow.

The assessment should record the observation, its location and the conditions under which it occurred. Where a potential contamination risk is identified, it should be evaluated and documented through the site's quality system.

  1. Establish Acceptance Criteria Before Execution

Acceptance criteria should be defined before the study begins. They should reflect the facility design, process requirements and contamination risks.

EU GMP Annex 1 addresses airflow visualisation and the need to demonstrate appropriate airflow protection in cleanrooms and critical areas. It does not establish one universal numerical pass/fail limit for every visible smoke pattern.

Manufacturers should therefore define and justify study-specific criteria through documented risk assessment and approved procedures.

  1. Maintain Traceable Study Records

A review is only useful when its conclusions can be traced back to the evidence.

Depending on the approved protocol, the study record may include:

Approved protocol and acceptance criteria

Test locations and operating conditions

Equipment configuration and relevant interventions

Smoke-generation details

Original video recordings

Annotated footage and observation logs

Assessment of observations against criteria

Deviations and investigations, where applicable

Review and approval records

Timestamps and location references can make it easier to connect a finding in the report with the corresponding video evidence.

  1. Distinguish Smoke Visualisation from Recovery Testing

Smoke visualisation and cleanroom recovery testing provide different types of evidence.

Smoke studies demonstrate visible airflow behaviour. They help teams understand airflow direction, local disturbances and the influence of interventions.

Recovery testing evaluates how quickly a cleanroom returns to a specified particle-cleanliness condition after a defined challenge.

Visible smoke clearance should not be treated as proof of particle recovery or restoration of the qualified cleanroom state.

Conclusion

A structured smoke study review connects airflow observations with predefined acceptance criteria and the protection required by the process.

By evaluating airflow direction, product protection, turbulence, interventions, potential ingress and supporting documentation, pharmaceutical teams can make more consistent assessments of cleanroom airflow behaviour.

The conclusions should always be based on the approved protocol, facility design and contamination-control requirements.

For a more detailed discussion of smoke study acceptance criteria and airflow risk assessment, see IncepBio's guide to smoke study acceptance criteria.

title: Simplifying runtime caching on Vercel
description:
Today, we’re bringing Data Cache into Runtime Cache, giving developers one product for data caching across frameworks and APIs. If you use Next.js fetch caching or unstable_cache, you won’t need to change your code. Pro and Enterprise projects will get larger storage allocations.

Runtime Cache lets your code reuse fetched or computed data across requests without operating a separate caching service. Over the past year, we’ve improved read performance during traffic bursts, increased storage budgets, and made cache usage easier to investigate.

Why we built Runtime Cache

Data Cache was originally launched as Vercel’s data caching service for the Next.js App Router, used by fetch caching and unstable_cache. Unlike CDN caching, which stores complete HTTP responses, Data Cache stores data your application uses to generate those responses. A product page, for example, can reuse cached catalog data while rendering a personalized response for each visitor.

We wanted developers to have access to that service without depending on Next.js. Last year, we introduced Runtime Cache with a direct API: getCache from @vercel/functions. Applications can use it for feature flag lookups in Routing Middleware, caching CMS content during builds, and data caching in SvelteKit and Nuxt apps.

Frameworks can expose this service through their own APIs, too. On Vercel, Next.js itself uses the Runtime Cache API for 'use cache: remote', which caches function and component outputs.

How Runtime Cache works

The infrastructure behind Runtime Cache is a distributed caching service shared by many teams. A Go API handles requests, backed by Redis fleets in every Vercel region. Every hour, the service handles more than 440 million reads and moves more than 18 TB of data.

Each region has its own cache. A cache hit takes one round trip to the cache service in the region where your code runs. Vercel handles authentication with short-lived credentials, so you don’t need to manage API keys.

On a cache miss, your app or framework fetches or computes the value and writes it to that region’s cache. The service doesn’t check other regions for a cached copy.

Each cached entry stores its tags and write time. When the service reads an entry, it checks a separate tag store in the same region for those tags’ invalidation timestamps. If any tag was invalidated after the entry was written, the entry is stale.

For example, an application can tag all its cached product data with catalog. When the catalog changes, invalidating that tag writes a single timestamp, even if a million entries share the tag. The service doesn’t need to find and delete those entries individually.

The invalidation immediately updates the tag store in the region receiving the request. Vercel’s shared tag infrastructure, also used by the CDN, distributes the timestamp through the global push pipeline, typically reaching other regions within a few hundred milliseconds.

Your app or framework chooses what to cache and handles misses. Runtime Cache handles regional storage, authentication, and distributing tag invalidations across regions.

What we’ve shipped

Faster reads during traffic bursts

Checking whether an entry is still fresh adds a dependency to every cache hit. During traffic bursts, a slow shard in the tag store could delay reads even when the cached value was already available.

We added circuit breakers that let reads temporarily check freshness using tag timestamps cached in memory, so they can proceed without waiting for the slow shard to respond. During this fallback, a read can briefly treat recently invalidated data as fresh.

We enabled the breakers in every region in August. During the heaviest bursts in our largest region, p99 cache-service read latency fell to about one fifth of its previous level at comparable traffic. On-call alerts for this failure mode stopped.

More storage and fewer evictions

We raised Runtime Cache storage budgets for Pro projects in June and Enterprise projects in October, giving applications more room for data they reuse. This reduces the need to evict cached entries to make room for new data. Among Enterprise projects with frequent evictions, cache miss rates roughly halved within a day.

More visibility into cache behavior

We’ve added deployment markers, revalidation causes, and write utilization to the Runtime Cache view in Observability. These help you compare changes in cache behavior with releases, see why entries are refreshed, and identify data that gets written to the cache but rarely read.

Bringing Data Cache into Runtime Cache

We’re simplifying caching on Vercel by consolidating on Runtime Cache. Until now, Next.js fetch caching and unstable_cache have used Data Cache, while getCache and 'use cache: remote' have used Runtime Cache. The migration brings all four APIs under Runtime Cache, so you and coding agents have one set of storage budgets and usage tools to work with.

If you use fetch caching or unstable_cache, nothing changes in your code. On Pro, each project and environment gets its own storage allocation, with 8x the space of Data Cache’s previous team-wide pool. Enterprise projects get 10x their previous Data Cache storage.

Previously unbilled Data Cache reads and writes will follow Runtime Cache pricing. New teams use Runtime Cache automatically, and existing teams will receive their migration and billing details in advance.

See the changelog for the rollout, pricing, and early opt-in details. Before migrating, review your cache usage and follow the optimization guide to reduce unnecessary reads and writes.

title: Gemini API CLI: ให้ Coding Agent ของคุณเรียกใช้ Gemini สำหรับรูปภาพ วิดีโอ PDF และ Deep Research
description:
Gemini API CLI (gemini-api) คือไคลเอนต์บรรทัดคำสั่งโอเพนซอร์สของ Google สำหรับ Gemini API สร้างขึ้นเพื่อเอเจนต์เขียนโค้ดอย่าง Claude Code, Codex, Cursor และ Antigravity ติดตั้งไบนารี Go เพียงตัวเดียว ตั้งค่า GEMINI_API_KEY แล้วเอเจนต์ของคุณก็สร้างรูปภาพ วิดีโอ เสียงพูด และเพลง วิเคราะห์ไฟล์ PDF และไฟล์บันทึกเสียง ถอดเสียงเป็น SRT และเริ่ม Deep Research แบบเบื้องหลังได้

ลองใช้ Apidog วันนี้

ด้านล่างนี้: การติดตั้ง การยืนยันตัวตน คำสั่งที่เอเจนต์ของคุณจะรัน ความแตกต่างจาก Gemini CLI และวิธีจับคู่กับ Apidog CLI ทุกแฟล็กคัดลอกจาก gemini-api --help ในเวอร์ชัน 0.4.5 ซึ่งเผยแพร่เมื่อวันที่ 30 ตุลาคม 2026

Gemini API CLI คืออะไร?

Gemini API CLI เป็นไคลเอนต์แบบไม่เก็บสถานะ (stateless) ในรูปแบบไบนารีเดียวสำหรับ Interactions API ของ Google แต่ละคำสั่งคือการเรียก HTTP หนึ่งครั้ง: ส่งพรอมป์ต์เข้าไป แล้วได้เส้นทางไฟล์ ข้อความถอดเสียง ผลวิเคราะห์ หรือ ID ของ interaction ออกมา — เป็นเครื่องมือที่เอเจนต์ที่มีอยู่แล้วของคุณเรียกใช้เมื่อเจองานที่ต้องใช้ Gemini

หน้าเอกสารอย่างเป็นทางการของ Google เรียกมันว่า "รีลีสเบต้าโอเพนซอร์สที่พัฒนาควบคู่ไปกับ Interactions API" โค้ดอยู่ที่ google-gemini/gemini-api-cli ภายใต้สัญญาอนุญาต Apache 2.0 และทำงานบน macOS, Linux และ Windows

นี่คือสิ่งที่ gemini-api --help แสดงในเวอร์ชัน 0.4.5 พร้อมโมเดลเริ่มต้นของแต่ละคำสั่ง:

กลุ่ม คำสั่ง หน้าที่ โมเดลเริ่มต้น
Create generate สร้างข้อความและมัลติโหมด gemini-3.8-flash
Create image สร้างหรือแก้ไขรูปภาพ gemini-nano-banana-2.1
Create video สร้างและแก้ไขวิดีโอ gemini-omni-1.1-flash
Create tts / music เสียงพูดและเพลง gemini-3.8-flash-tts / lyria-3.5
Understand analyze ถามคำถามเกี่ยวกับ PDF รูปภาพ เสียง วิดีโอ และ URL ของ YouTube gemini-3.8-flash
Understand transcribe แปลงเสียงหรือวิดีโอเป็น md, text, json หรือ srt gemini-3.5-transcribe
Manage agent รันโมเดลหรือ managed agent เช่น Deep Research กำหนดต่อการรันแต่ละครั้ง
Manage files อัปโหลดผ่าน Files API เก็บไว้ 48 ชั่วโมง ไม่มี

Gemini API CLI กับ Gemini CLI

ชื่อใกล้กันมาก นี่คือความแตกต่าง Gemini CLI (@google/gemini-cli) เป็นเอเจนต์เขียนโค้ดแบบอินเทอร์แอกทีฟ ซึ่งเป็นทางเลือกแทน Claude Code ที่คุณสนทนาด้วย ส่วน Gemini API CLI (gemini-api) ไม่มีลูปเอเจนต์เลย มันเป็นเครื่องมือที่เอเจนต์ตัวอื่นเป็นคนรัน

Gemini API CLI Gemini CLI
ไบนารี gemini-api gemini
บทบาท เครื่องมือที่เอเจนต์ของคุณเรียกใช้ เอเจนต์ที่คุณพูดคุยด้วย
เอาต์พุตสื่อ รูปภาพ วิดีโอ เสียงพูด เพลง ลงดิสก์ ไม่ใช่จุดเน้นของมัน
เหมาะที่สุดสำหรับ มอบโมเดลของ Gemini ให้ Claude Code, Codex หรือ Cursor การใช้ Gemini เป็นเอเจนต์เขียนโค้ดของคุณ

หากคุณทำงานใน Claude Code หรือ Codex และต้องการใช้โมเดลด้านสื่อและงานวิจัยของ Gemini ภายในเวิร์กโฟลว์นั้น ให้ใช้ gemini-api ในรูปแบบเดียวกับ OpenAI CLI เพียงแต่ชี้ไปที่ Google

วิธีติดตั้ง Gemini API CLI

เลือกหนึ่งในสี่วิธีจาก README

macOS และ Linux:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/google-gemini/gemini-api-cli/main/scripts/install.sh | bash

Windows (PowerShell):

iwr -useb https://raw.githubusercontent.com/google-gemini/gemini-api-cli/main/scripts/install.ps1 | iex

Go:

go install github.com/google-gemini/gemini-api-cli/cmd/gemini-api@latest

ไบนารีที่คอมไพล์ไว้แล้ว: ดาวน์โหลดไฟล์เก็บถาวรสำหรับแพลตฟอร์มของคุณจาก GitHub Releases ตรวจสอบกับ checksums.txt แล้ววาง gemini-api ไว้ใน PATH ของคุณ เราใช้ไฟล์เก็บถาวร Darwin_arm64 โดย shasum -a 256 -c checksums.txt --ignore-missing แสดงผลเป็น OK

Google เตือนว่าการเปลี่ยนแปลงที่ทำให้ของเดิมพังอาจเกิดขึ้นได้ระหว่างเวอร์ชันไมเนอร์ ดังนั้นควรปักหมุดรีลีสใน CI เอกสารแสดงสคริปต์ติดตั้งโดยวาง GEMINI_VERSION=<release-tag> ไว้ข้างหน้า bash

ตรวจสอบการติดตั้ง:

gemini-api version
# gemini-api 0.4.5

การยืนยันตัวตนของ Gemini API CLI

สร้างคีย์ใน Google AI Studio (คู่มือวิธีขอ Gemini API key ฟรีของเราอธิบายขั้นตอนไว้ทั้งหมด) จากนั้น export คีย์:

export GEMINI_API_KEY="YOUR_API_KEY"

บนเครื่องของคุณเอง เก็บคีย์ไว้แทนได้:

gemini-api configure --api-key "YOUR_API_KEY"
gemini-api whoami

configure จะบันทึกคีย์ลงใน keychain ของระบบปฏิบัติการของคุณ (macOS Keychain, Linux Secret Service หรือ Windows Credential Manager) เพิ่มแฟล็กโกลบอล --no-keyring หากต้องการเก็บไว้ใน ~/.config/gemini-api/config.yaml แทน ส่วน whoami จะแสดงว่าขณะนี้ใช้ข้อมูลรับรองตัวใดและมาจากไหน

เมื่อยังไม่ได้ตั้งค่าคีย์ gemini-api --help จะแสดงข้อความที่ส่งถึงตัวเอเจนต์เองว่า API key "ต้องถูกสร้างด้วยมือโดยผู้ใช้ใน Google AI Studio ให้หยุดและขอให้ผู้ใช้สร้างขึ้นมา" เอเจนต์ของคุณจะถามคุณแทนที่จะตั้งค่าคีย์ด้วยตัวเอง

ดูตัวอย่างทุกการเรียกด้วย --dry-run

--dry-run จะตรวจสอบแฟล็กและแสดงคำขอโดยปิดบังข้อมูลรับรอง โดยไม่มีการเรียกผ่านเครือข่ายและไม่มีการอ่าน keychain ใช้งานได้ก่อนที่คุณจะตั้งค่าคีย์ ซึ่งเป็นวิธีที่เราใช้ตรวจสอบทุกตัวอย่างในบทความนี้

นี่คือตัวอย่าง dry run จริงของงาน Deep Research ที่รันเบื้องหลัง:

ทุกคำสั่งจะ POST ไปที่ https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta/interactions เพิ่ม -o json เพื่อให้ได้ JSON หนึ่งออบเจ็กต์ต่อหนึ่งคำขอทาง stdout ซึ่งเอเจนต์สามารถแยกวิเคราะห์ได้ก่อนที่จะใช้โทเคน

คำสั่ง Gemini API CLI ที่เอเจนต์ของคุณจะรัน

สร้างและแก้ไขรูปภาพ 

gemini-api image "A friendly robot mascot, soft studio lighting" --out ./assets/mascot.jpg
gemini-api image "Add a winter scarf" -i ./assets/mascot.jpg --out ./assets/mascot-winter.jpg

คำสั่งเกี่ยวกับสื่อจะเขียนไฟล์และแสดงเพียงเส้นทางของไฟล์ ดังนั้นเอเจนต์จะจับค่านั้นด้วย $(...) แล้วทำงานต่อไปได้ image ยังรองรับ --aspect-ratio และ --image-size (512, 1K, 2K หรือ 4K) โมเดลเริ่มต้นคือ Nano Banana 2.1 ดูคู่มือ Nano Banana 2.1 APIของเราเพื่อรู้ว่ามันทำอะไรได้ดี

สร้างวิดีโอ เสียงพูด และเพลง 

gemini-api video "A slow camera move through a sunlit workshop" --resolution 1080p --out ./assets/
gemini-api tts "Welcome. Let's build something together." --out ./assets/welcome.wav
gemini-api music "Warm ambient music for a product walkthrough" --out ./assets/

วิดีโอใช้เวลานานกว่า ดังนั้น video จะ polling ให้คุณ ใช้ --async เพื่อรับ operation handle ทันที และ --resume <id> เพื่อกลับมา polling ต่อในภายหลัง --resolution มีค่าเริ่มต้นเป็น 720p

วิเคราะห์ PDF รูปภาพ และ URL ของ YouTube 

gemini-api analyze -i product-brief.pdf "What should we build first, and why?" > plan.md
gemini-api analyze -i before.png -i after.png "Summarize the visual design changes"

-i/--input ใช้ซ้ำได้และรองรับเส้นทางไฟล์ในเครื่อง, URI แบบ files/<id> หรือ URL ของ YouTube อินพุตแบบอินไลน์จำกัดที่ประมาณ 14 MB (ขนาดดิบ) สำหรับไฟล์ที่ใหญ่กว่า ให้อัปโหลดครั้งเดียวแล้วนำ URI กลับมาใช้ซ้ำ:

FILE_URI=$(gemini-api files upload interview.mp4 --wait --output-format json --jq '.name')
gemini-api analyze -i "$FILE_URI" "List the key action items with timestamps"

ไฟล์ที่อัปโหลดจะถูกลบหลัง 48 ชั่วโมง

ถอดเสียงจากไฟล์เสียงและวิดีโอ 

gemini-api transcribe -i interview.mp4 --format srt --out interview.srt

--format รับค่า md (ค่าเริ่มต้น), text, json หรือ srt เพิ่ม --no-speakers หรือ --no-timestamps เพื่อตัดผู้พูดหรือเวลาออกจากเอาต์พุต

รัน Deep Research ในเบื้องหลัง 

ID=$(gemini-api agent run "Research battery recycling approaches and cite sources" \
  --agent deep-research-preview-04-2026 --background --jq '.id')
gemini-api agent status "$ID" --stream=false --output-format json

--background จะคืนค่า interaction ID ทันทีแทนที่จะเปิดสตรีมค้างไว้ เอเจนต์จะเก็บ ID นั้นไว้ ไปทำงานอย่างอื่น แล้วกลับมาตรวจสอบด้วย agent status ส่วน agent cancel ใช้หยุดการรัน ผลลัพธ์ help ของ 0.4.5 ยังระบุ deep-research-max-preview-04-2026 และ antigravity-preview-05-2026 เป็น managed agent ด้วย

แฟล็กที่ทำให้ gemini-api ปลอดภัยสำหรับเอเจนต์

นี่คือแฟล็กโกลบอลที่ควรใส่ไว้ในคำสั่งของเอเจนต์คุณ ทั้งหมดมาจาก gemini-api --help-global:

  • --agent-mode (หรือ GEMINI_CLI_AGENT_MODE=1): ข้อผิดพลาดแบบ JSON ที่มีโครงสร้างทาง stderr และเอาต์พุต TOON แบบกะทัดรัดทาง stdout
  • -o, --output-format: pretty, json, yaml, table หรือ toon
  • -q, --jq: กรองเอาต์พุตแบบอินไลน์ เช่น --jq '.id'
  • --no-interactive: ไม่มีพรอมป์ต์หรือฟอร์ม TUI ซึ่งเป็นสิ่งที่เอเจนต์แบบไม่มีหน้าจอ (headless) ต้องการ
  • --usage: โครงสร้างคำสั่งทั้งหมดในรูปแบบ KDL ที่เครื่องอ่านได้
  • --schema (ต่อคำสั่ง): JSON Schema สำหรับเพย์โหลด --body

รหัสออก (exit code) บอกเอเจนต์ว่าเกิดอะไรขึ้นโดยไม่ต้องแยกวิเคราะห์ข้อความ: 0 สำเร็จ, 1 ข้อผิดพลาดขณะรันหรือจาก API, 2 ข้อผิดพลาดในการใช้งานหรือการตรวจสอบความถูกต้อง, 3 การยืนยันตัวตน ข้อควรระวังอย่างหนึ่ง: คำสั่งแบบสตรีมมิ่ง (generate, agent run) ต้องใช้ --stream=false ก่อน -o json หรือ --jq จึงจะให้ผลลัพธ์เดียวที่แยกวิเคราะห์ได้

มอบ Gemini API CLI ให้เอเจนต์เขียนโค้ดของคุณ

README ของ Google มีบล็อกให้คัดลอกไปวางใน AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md หรือ .cursorrules (ตัดมาเฉพาะบางส่วน):

You have access to gemini-api through the shell.
1. Inspect --help or --usage to choose a command, and --schema when building a --body JSON payload.
2. Preview API calls with --dry-run.
3. For JSON output or --jq on streaming commands, pass --stream=false --output-format json.
4. Capture returned file paths and interaction IDs to continue multi-step tasks.

ตรวจสอบให้แน่ใจว่า GEMINI_API_KEY ไปถึงสภาพแวดล้อมของโปรเซสย่อยของเอเจนต์ จากนั้นสั่งงานตามปกติ: "สร้างแลนดิ้งเพจ ใช้ Gemini ทำรูปมาสคอตและเสียงบรรยาย 20 วินาที และเริ่มรัน Deep Research เกี่ยวกับผลิตภัณฑ์คู่แข่ง" เอเจนต์จะเป็นคนเลือกคำสั่งเอง

สิ่งที่มันทำไม่ได้: เสียงหรือวิดีโอแบบเรียลไทม์ ไม่มีการรองรับ WebSocket ดังนั้น Live API จึงยังต้องใช้ GenAI SDK

ทดสอบ API ที่คุณสร้างด้วย Apidog CLI

gemini-api มอบโมเดลของ Gemini ให้เอเจนต์ของคุณ แต่มันไม่รู้อะไรเลยเกี่ยวกับ API ของคุณเอง ไม่ว่าจะเป็น endpoint /summarize หรือ /thumbnail ที่แอปของคุณห่อไว้รอบ Gemini สภาพแวดล้อมต่างๆ ของมัน หรือ assertion ที่พิสูจน์ได้ว่ารีลีสใหม่ไม่ได้ทำให้อะไรพัง นั่นคืองานของ Apidog CLI และเอเจนต์ตัวเดียวกันก็รันทั้งสองอย่างได้

ตั้งค่าเพียงครั้งเดียว:

npm install -g apidog-cli@latest
apidog login --with-token <YOUR_TOKEN>
npx -y skills add https://apidog.com   # pick your agent when prompted

จากนั้นสั่งเอเจนต์ด้วยพรอมป์ต์เดียว:

Use gemini-api to dry-run an analyze call on ./docs/sample-invoice.pdf, then run it for real.
Import ./openapi.yaml into Apidog project <id>, create a test case for POST /v1/invoices/extract
that uploads the same PDF and asserts a 200 and a non-empty "total" field, run it against the
staging environment, and summarize any failures.

เอเจนต์จะตรวจสอบคำตอบของ Gemini ด้วย gemini-api จากนั้นอ่าน schema ของ Apidog ก่อนเขียนเพย์โหลด ตรวจสอบความถูกต้อง และสร้างและรันเทสต์เคส:

apidog import --project <id> --format openapi --file ./openapi.yaml
apidog cli-schema get test-case-create
apidog cli-schema validate test-case-create --file case.json
apidog test-case create --project <id> --file case.json
apidog run --test-case <caseId> --project <id> -e <envId> -r cli,json

apidog test-case create --help เตือนถึงกับดักอย่างหนึ่ง: เทสต์เคสต้องมี categoryId ที่ถูกต้อง ดังนั้นให้ลิสต์รายการก่อนด้วย apidog test-case category --project <id> เปลี่ยน -r cli,json เป็น -r junit แล้วบรรทัดเดิมก็รันใน CI ได้ หากคุณใช้ Claude Code เป็นเอเจนต์ เริ่มจาก Apidog CLI ใน Claude Code แพลนฟรีของ Apidog รองรับผู้ใช้สูงสุด 4 คน

คำถามที่พบบ่อย

Gemini API CLI ใช้ฟรีหรือไม่? ตัว CLI เองฟรีและเป็นโอเพนซอร์สภายใต้ Apache 2.0 ทุกการเรียกจะคิดเงินกับ API key ของคุณตามราคา Gemini APIปกติ สำหรับรายละเอียดว่าแพ็กเกจฟรีครอบคลุมอะไรบ้าง ดูคู่มือ Gemini API free tierของเรา

gemini-api เหมือนกับ Gemini CLI ไหม? ไม่เหมือน Gemini CLI เป็นเอเจนต์เขียนโค้ดแบบอินเทอร์แอกทีฟ ส่วน gemini-api เป็นเครื่องมือแบบไม่เก็บสถานะที่เอเจนต์ตัวอื่น สคริปต์ และงานใน CI เรียกใช้เพื่อเข้าถึงโมเดลของ Gemini และ managed agent

ทดสอบคำสั่งโดยไม่มี API key ได้ไหม? ได้ --dry-run จะตรวจสอบคำสั่งและแสดงคำขอแบบตรงทั้งหมดโดยไม่มีการเรียกผ่านเครือข่ายและไม่มีการอ่าน keychain ทุกตัวอย่างในบทความนี้ตรวจสอบด้วยวิธีนั้นบนเวอร์ชัน 0.4.5

title: Asynchronous Flow Map Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.42018v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The order in which tokens are predicted in language modeling has a profound impact on the quality of generated sequences. Autoregressive and masked diffusion models iteratively fill in tokens and can exploit such orderings across generation steps, but how to leverage an ordering for one-step parallel language modeling is unclear. We introduce asynchronous flow map language models (aFMLMs), which incorporate prediction order into one-step modeling by learning the flow maps of asynchronous flows. These flows specify an ordering through a tokenwise time schedule that controls the relative denoising progress of tokens. We formulate a general class of asynchronous flows that admit both prescribed and learned, state-adaptive schedules, show that they define valid flow maps, and develop new methods for their flow map distillation. The resulting models can generate all tokens in a single forward pass by internalizing the ordering encoded in the flow into their hidden computations. On Sudoku solving and code generation for GSM8K math word problems, aFMLM establishes new state-of-the-art one-step performance.

title: RADI3N: GeometRic ImAge EDiting via ParametrIc 3D CoNtrol
description:
arXiv:2610.40973v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent diffusion-based methods have substantially advanced image editing, yet parametric 3D control at the part level remains challenging. Existing approaches either operate on whole objects with manual rigging, or revert to 2D handles at the part level. They also struggle to model appearance and texture under large transformations, leading to unrealistic outputs in geometry-intensive edits. To address these limitations, we introduce RADI3N, a framework for semantically-grounded part-aware object manipulation with parametric 3D control. Our CS-ARAP deformation module suppresses rotation-field discontinuities at part boundaries via neighborhood covariance smoothing, producing structurally consistent deformations under complex part-level edits. We further introduce an inversion-free selective texture transfer mechanism that suppresses high-frequency positional biases and scales up low-frequency semantic cues within cross-image attention. This eliminates strict spatial bias and supports semantic matching, allowing source appearance to follow the edited part onto its new geometry. Experiments demonstrate that RADI3N achieves state-of-the-art performance in geometric fidelity, viewpoint consistency, and controllability.

title: Subquadratic Attention with a Hierarchical Tree-Structured Indexer
description:
arXiv:2610.42112v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The quadratic scaling of attention is a fundamental bottleneck limiting the long-context capabilities of large language models (LLMs). A variety of approaches have attempted to circumvent this, but they either fail to match attention's expressiveness (e.g., sliding-window or linear attention variants with fixed-size state) or only achieve constant-factor speedups (e.g., sparse attention methods whose indexers themselves scale quadratically). In this paper, we derive an asymptotically subquadratic sparse attention method based on a hierarchical, tree-structured indexer, which we call Zyphra Hierarchical Attention (ZHA). ZHA constructs a tree of recursively compressed key summaries over the KV cache, which future queries traverse from the top down to retrieve a sparse subset of keys. Crucially, by iteratively growing the tree's depth, the total cost including routing and final attention grows sublinearly in sequence length, resulting in overall subquadratic (but superlinear) scaling for attention. We demonstrate that ZHA can be cheaply applied to existing pretrained models with only a short KL distillation training stage over a few billion tokens, and maintains performance on long-context retrieval and challenging reasoning, mathematical, and agentic coding evaluation tasks. Moreover, we show that our method is highly robust to tree geometry including very deep trees of up to 6 levels. Finally, we develop a detailed performance model and show that our approach scales subquadratically, dramatically outperforms competing methods beyond 1 million context, and ultimately has the potential to extend effective context windows to the hundreds of millions or billions of tokens.

title: Python Quick Quiz CLI: Lightweight CLI Tool for Beginner Python Learning
description:
Python Quick Quiz CLI is a small command-line application that quizzes users on fundamental Python concepts. Each question covers a single topic such as variables, control flow, functions, or lists, and the program provides instant feedback along with a brief explanation of the correct answer. The tool is intentionally lightweight: it runs in a terminal, requires no external dependencies beyond the standard library, and can be executed with a single command.

The target audience is anyone starting out with Python who wants a quick way to test their knowledge without the overhead of a full IDE or interactive notebook. It’s also handy for instructors who want a reproducible quiz format for in‑class exercises or for self‑study during commutes.

To use the tool, clone the repository, navigate to the script folder, and run python quick_quiz.py. The program will prompt you with a series of multiple‑choice questions, accept your answer, and immediately tell you whether you were correct. If you missed a question, the explanation will help you understand the mistake.

Try it out and see how a few minutes of practice can reinforce your Python fundamentals.

title: GitHub Open-Sourced Replica. Now Break Your Prototype’s Perfect Data.
description:
GitHub open-sourced Replica on October 28, giving teams an AI prototyping tool guided by their existing components, patterns, and documentation. A familiar design system can make a proposed feature feel credible quickly. The next useful move is to challenge the data behind the screen. A directory that looks effortless with six complete records may tell you very little about choosing from incomplete results on a phone.

Disclosure: This article was generated and fact-checked with AI using the public sources linked here. It was published through an automated workflow and has not been reviewed by Keith.

Replica supports interactive prototypes alongside a Copilot conversation and an optional self-hosted Hub for sharing and feedback. The release is an opportunity to make experiments easier to inspect, not evidence that a generated prototype has validated a product’s real inputs. The fixture set still shapes what a reviewer can discover.

The AfroTech Guide case study provides a concrete setting. The community-built guide combines approved people and event records with curated Houston dining recommendations. Public website features and connected AI capabilities have different release scopes; real-device and AI-host acceptance remain separate checks. It is an independent community resource, without a claim of official event affiliation.

The official AFROTECH speaker profile describes Building AfroTech.guide as an idea-to-launch walkthrough. For that kind of build discussion, showing which inputs shaped an interface can be as instructive as showing the finished screen. The exercise below is a proposed prototype review, not a claim that the guide uses Replica or has the problems described.

Give the reviewer a task the fixtures can challenge

Suppose the prototype asks someone to compare dining options near a planned stop. Begin with an ordinary task: inspect the available context, compare two candidates, and decide whether there is enough information to choose. Avoid defining success as “click the highlighted card.” That mostly tests whether the reviewer follows the route already chosen for them.

Build a small synthetic fixture set around the information the decision requires. Include a venue name long enough to wrap, a record without an image, and a description that does not fit neatly into one sentence. Keep those records fictional and visibly marked as prototype data. Inventing a restaurant’s hours or accessibility details would add misinformation rather than useful variation.

Then leave a decision-relevant field unknown. Ask the reviewer what they think the screen knows. If the layout makes an absent value look like a confirmed “no,” the feedback has exposed a meaning problem that the polished version concealed. A blank cell, a placeholder, and an explicit “not provided” can lead to different interpretations.

Keep the task and fixture version stable while comparing interface revisions. If every AI edit also changes the sample names, completeness, and result order, a calmer second attempt may owe more to easier data than better design. Record what changed so the reviewer can connect an observation to the experiment that produced it.

This does not require simulating the entire production directory. Select a few cases that could change the person’s decision, and preserve enough surrounding information to make the choice plausible. The goal is useful friction, not a page filled with arbitrary edge cases.

An empty list and a failed lookup need different reviews

A prototype often returns results immediately because the records are bundled with the screen. That is fine for exploring layout. It can hide a second question: what does the person believe when records have not arrived?

Provide a controlled way to hold a lookup in progress, return a genuine empty result, and produce an unavailable response. These are proposed prototype states, not reported failures in AfroTech Guide or Replica. The important comparison is whether the reviewer can tell what happened and choose a reasonable next step.

For an empty result, the screen can accurately say that the completed query found no matches within its stated scope. An unavailable lookup has not established that conclusion. If both states show the same cheerful empty card, the person may abandon a useful search because the interface implied there were no options.

Observe the next action before explaining the state. Do they revise a filter, wait, retry, or assume the directory has nothing relevant? Record the visible behavior and the reviewer’s interpretation separately. Their explanation can reveal an unclear message even when they eventually reach the expected button.

When comparing revisions, replay the same state transition and keep the task wording consistent. Note which behaviors are mocked. A clickable retry button in a prototype does not establish that the production service can recover, and a convincing loading sequence is not a measured latency result.

There is a tradeoff in prototype fidelity. Adding real service dependencies can make feedback more representative but slow the experiment and introduce unrelated failures. Controlled fixtures make a narrower question repeatable. State what the prototype is intended to teach, then reserve operational acceptance for the working integration.

For a community guide, useful feedback concerns whether someone can make a sound choice with the information actually available. Replica makes it easier to put an idea in front of a team. Giving that idea imperfect, clearly labeled data helps the team learn something beyond how convincing the demo looks.

title: How To Create Commandline Chat Server in Linux
description:
We have all used chat services such as Google Chat, Facebook chat, and WhatsApp. Linux's nc (netcat) command can also turn a machine into a very simple command-line chat endpoint with one command. The example below is useful for a quick lab test or a temporary conversation on a trusted LAN. It is not a replacement for a real chat service: there is no account system, encryption, or group-chat feature.

What is the nc command in Linux and what does it do?

nc is the command name used by many implementations of netcat, a networking utility often called a Swiss Army knife. It can read from and write to TCP or UDP connections, making it useful for debugging services, checking ports, transferring data, and temporarily listening on a port. This guide uses TCP, which is the default; do not add -u unless you deliberately want UDP.

The server and client addresses below are examples. Replace 192.168.0.7 and 192.168.0.15 with addresses on your own network.

Start the listener on the server

On the server (192.168.0.7), the traditional GNU netcat syntax is:

nc -l -vv -p 11119

The switches mean:

  1. -l: listen for an incoming connection instead of connecting to another host.
  2. -v: verbose output; -vv provides more detail.
  3. -p 11119: use local TCP port 11119 with this GNU-style listener.

You can replace 11119 with another unused, unprivileged port above 1024. Leave this terminal open.

Netcat is not one identical program on every Linux system. OpenBSD nc, which is common on modern distributions, normally takes the listening port as an argument instead:

nc -l -vv 11119

Ncat, from the Nmap project, is commonly invoked as ncat:

ncat -l -vv 11119

In particular, do not blindly copy GNU's -p listener syntax to OpenBSD nc; its -p option concerns a source port. Run nc -h or read man nc to identify the installed implementation and its supported options.

Connect from the client

On the client (192.168.0.15), connect to the server's address and port:

nc 192.168.0.7 11119

Type a line and press Enter on either terminal; the other terminal should display it. Press Ctrl+C to end the session. This is a direct, one-to-one pipe between two terminals, not a chat room.

Check the listener, route, and firewall

If the client cannot connect, check the server before changing random settings. In another server terminal, run:

ss -ltn | grep ':11119'
sudo ss -ltnp | grep ':11119'

Look for LISTEN. A listener on 127.0.0.1 accepts only local connections; 0.0.0.0 means all IPv4 interfaces, which may be more exposure than you want. The second command can show the owning process, but process details may require sudo. If nothing is listening, the command may have exited or used syntax unsupported by your netcat variant.

From the client, a short TCP probe can distinguish a closed service from a network problem:

nc -vz -w 3 192.168.0.7 11119

-z performs a connection check rather than starting a chat, and -w 3 sets a timeout. Connection refused usually means nothing is listening on that port. A timeout more often points to a firewall, wrong address, disconnected network, or Wi-Fi client isolation.

On an Ubuntu-style host, inspect the firewall with sudo ufw status verbose. If UFW is active and you need a temporary exception, restrict it to your actual LAN prefix—for this example's network:

sudo ufw allow from 192.168.0.0/24 to any port 11119 proto tcp

Do not copy that subnet if yours differs, and do not create a router port-forward for this exercise. Firewalld users can inspect the active zone with sudo firewall-cmd --list-all. Remove a temporary UFW rule when finished:

sudo ufw delete allow from 192.168.0.0/24 to any port 11119 proto tcp

Limitations and LAN safety

Basic netcat accepts one connection and provides no usernames, message history, presence, delivery guarantees, or multi-user relay. Some versions have -k to keep listening after a disconnect, but that does not turn the session into group chat. Text is also plaintext: someone able to observe or intercept the network path could read it, and the client has no built-in proof of the server's identity. Never type passwords or sensitive information into this chat.

LAN-only use reduces exposure but does not make the connection trustworthy. A compromised laptop or an untrusted shared network can still observe traffic. Use a non-root account, a high port, a trusted LAN, and a narrowly scoped firewall rule; stop the listener when done. Avoid -e or similar “execute a program” options entirely for this recipe—they can turn a simple listener into an unintended remote shell.

Common mistakes

  • Address already in use: another process owns the port. Inspect it with ss and choose a different port rather than killing an unknown service.
  • The first client disconnects and later clients fail: restart the listener, or check whether your variant supports -k; neither approach adds group-chat semantics.
  • A connection succeeds but nothing appears: press Enter after typing, confirm that both ends use TCP and the same port, and make sure you did not leave -z in the chat command.
  • The listener command rejects -p: identify the variant and use its documented port syntax instead of adding more flags.

Safer modern alternatives

For remote administration, prefer SSH, which provides encryption and account authentication:

ssh user@192.168.0.7

SSH grants shell access, so it is not automatically a chat replacement; give accounts only the access they need. If you specifically need a netcat-like encrypted pipe, Ncat supports TLS with --ssl and certificate-verification options. Configure and verify certificates rather than treating encryption without identity checks as sufficient. For real private or group conversations, use a maintained messaging application with authentication and end-to-end encryption. A VPN such as WireGuard or Tailscale can protect the network path, but it does not add chat identities, history, or group management to nc.

title: Automatic Construction of Strong Simple Baselines
description:
arXiv:2610.40700v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: To rigorously establish the value of a novel deep learning method, it must be compared against appropriate baselines. As deep learning has become increasingly common in the physical and life sciences, there have been numerous cases in which apparent progress has turned out to be an artifact of omitted or missing baselines. In this work, we investigate whether this problem can be mitigated by using large language models to automate the construction of baselines. We assemble 36 supervised classification and regression tasks from peer-reviewed studies in Nature, Science, and Cell-family journals that investigate novel deep learning methods for scientific applications. We then use a language model to construct simple baselines for each task. These automatically constructed baselines are strong, recovering a median of 95.5% (mean 85.7%) of the gap between a trivial predictor and the score of the deep learning model. The median simple baseline matches or exceeds the performance of the deep learning model in 12 studies. We further examine the variation across scientific domains and publication venues and we characterize the effects of test-time compute and access to different levels of study context. As human peer review has struggled to keep up with the rapidly increasing volume of research articles in recent years, our results suggest that automated baseline construction is a practical and scalable check on deep learning contributions in the physical and life sciences.

title: Peeling the Matryoshka: Extracting Ontological Structure from Retrieval Embeddings
description:
arXiv:2610.41785v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Taxonomy construction is essential for knowledge-intensive NLP yet remains costly: clustering-based methods (i) need careful per-corpus tuning and yield unstable hierarchies, while LLM-based pipelines (ii) depend on expensive task-specific training that does not transfer across domains. We report an empirical finding that bears on both: in Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL) embeddings, where each leading prefix is itself a usable, coarser vector, prefix length aligns with the coarse-to-fine granularity of gold taxonomies; shuffled- and reverse-dimension controls isolate the alignment to the learned early prefix dimensions. The pattern holds across three architecturally distinct MRL models. To test whether this regularity is usable, we introduce PEEL (Peeling Embeddings to Extract Latent ontologies): a minimal probe over these frozen embeddings, trained once with an order-embedding objective that represents hierarchy as vector containment; a minimum spanning arborescence then decodes taxonomic DAGs. Using only a concept vocabulary (no documents), PEEL recovers taxonomic DAGs with high structural fidelity on two OLLM benchmarks, transferring to a new domain with no target-edge supervision. The end-to-end OLLM pipeline, which jointly discovers concepts and induces structure from document corpora, is reported as a cross-task reference. Pre-trained retrieval embeddings encode a decodable granularity gradient; a minimal probe renders it as explicit parent-child (is-a) structure.

title: xrun: smoke-test on a free Kaggle GPU, train on vast.ai, let the agent read the metrics
description:
I train 3D computer vision models, and classical ones at hackathons. For a long time every run came with the same chores: vastai create instance, scp the data up, start the script, check on it, scp the checkpoint back, remember to destroy the instance. Kaggle had its own version of that with kaggle kernels push. I wanted to hand the whole loop to an agent: launch on whichever platform fits, smoke-test on a free Kaggle GPU before paying for the real training, and collect metrics the same way everywhere, so the agent can read them and decide what to do next.

That became xrun, a Rust CLI with a Python Textual TUI on top. One YAML manifest describes a run: where the GPU comes from, what to upload, what to run and what to bring back. xrun rents the instance, uploads the data, starts training, follows stages and metrics, pulls the checkpoints and destroys the instance when it's over. It supports six vendors: vast.ai, Kaggle, Lightning AI, Google Colab, your own server over SSH, and the local machine.

A manifest 

name: resnet50_baseline
vendor: vast                    # vast | kaggle | lightning | colab | ssh | local

vast:
  image: pytorch/pytorch:2.4.1-cuda12.1-cudnn9-devel
  gpu: { type: "RTX 4090", count: 1 }
  price: { max_per_hour: 0.55 }

data:
  - src: data/train.h5
    dst: /workspace/data/train.h5

run:
  cmd: python train.py
  args:
    --lr: 5e-4
    --epochs: 30

artifacts:
  patterns: ["checkpoints/best*.pt"]

policy:
  on_idle_minutes: 30           # no output for 30 minutes: destroy
  early_stop:                   # metric plateau: pull the best, then destroy
    metric: val_f1
    patience: 5

And the day-to-day loop:

xrun launch exp/resnet50.yaml --detach --max-cost 5
xrun events <id> --follow
xrun metrics <id> --key val_f1 --ascii
xrun pull <id> --ckpt best --into models/

The smoke test is a second manifest with vendor: kaggle and a small config. The training script and the metrics code stay the same, so if it survives a few epochs on Kaggle, I launch the vast.ai one.

A copy of the manifest is stored with the run, and its hash is part of the run's identity. I can edit the original freely and xrun rerun <id> still reproduces exactly what ran. For hyperparameters, xrun sweep exp/base.yaml --grid run.args.--lr=1e-3,5e-4 --launch writes out one manifest per variant.

Built for an agent to drive

Every read command (ls, show, events, metrics) has --json, and whatever the TUI can do, the CLI can do too. xrun show prints each metric's last value and step, so a score logged once at the end of a cross-validation run is visible without plotting anything. xrun install skill --claude (or --codex) installs a skill that teaches Claude Code or Codex to use xrun instead of hand-rolled vastai and ssh calls. So the agent can rerun the last experiment with a different learning rate, or pull the checkpoint of the run with the best val_f1 from the last day, through the same commands I would type.

Metrics come from a small hook in the training script:

from xrun_hook import stage, metric, metrics, done, notify

with stage("train"):
    for ep in range(epochs):
        loss = train_one_epoch(model, loader)
        metric("train_loss", loss, step=ep)
        metrics({"val_loss": v.loss, "val_f1": v.f1}, step=ep)

notify("training", f"best val_f1 = {best:.3f}")
done()

The hook writes events.jsonl and metrics.jsonl, and a background poller picks them up. On Kaggle xrun injects the hook into the kernel by itself. An uncaught exception gets recorded as an error event.

A billing instance is never left alone

xrun launch --detach leaves that poller running. It counts the spend and destroys the instance when the run finishes, fails, goes silent, hits a metric plateau or runs into --max-cost / --max-hours. If the destroy call fails, you get a push saying the instance is still billing. The poller can't report its own death, so xrun watchdog runs from the OS scheduler every five minutes: no heartbeat from the poller while the instance is alive means a notification and a respawned poller. It also catches instances that no run record knows about.

Notifications go to ntfy, Telegram, a webhook (Slack, Discord) or desktop toasts. Replying /stop <id> to the Telegram bot kills a run.

The run history lives in a local SQLite database, with no tracking service or account involved. MLflow and W&B plug in as mirrors if you want their charts.

Rough edges

xrun_hook isn't on PyPI yet, so outside Kaggle it travels with your code. Kaggle shows metrics mid-run only when an MLflow server is configured; without one you see the start and the end. Lightning AI was smoke-tested live on a CPU Studio only, and for Lightning and Colab xrun doesn't know the price, so --max-cost doesn't apply there.

Try it

macOS and Linux:

curl -sSf https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Gerrux/xrun/master/install.sh | sh

Windows (PowerShell):

irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Gerrux/xrun/master/install.ps1 | iex

xrun doctor and then xrun launch exp/templates/quickstart.yaml check the whole chain locally with no credentials, GPU or data. The code is on GitHub under MIT: Gerrux/xrun.

If you run training on one of these vendors, a report of what broke is the most useful thing you could send me. Each of their APIs has its own habits, and half of the fixes so far came from exactly that.

I built xrun together with my AI sidekick, Claude Code (Opus 5.5), and this post was written with its help too.

title: Don't Just Impute, Detect: Task-Aware Diffusion Pipelines for Edge Anomaly Detection
description:
arXiv:2610.40732v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) edge pipelines routinely lose contiguous blocks of multi-sensor data to network dropouts and hardware faults. The standard remedy is a disjointed "impute-then-detect" pipeline whose imputer is trained only for Mean Squared Error (MSE). Such an imputer fills a missing block with the most probable normal pattern: a partially observed anomaly is smoothed back toward normality, and boundary artifacts on normal data raise false alarms. We call this imputation bias and propose the Task-Aware Diffusion Refiner (TADR), a conditional diffusion refiner trained against the loss landscape of a frozen downstream detector. Because back-propagating through the sampling trajectory is intractable, the task-aware terms act on the one-step clean-window estimate that the noise prediction already yields, so training costs no more than plain diffusion training. Under strict Point-to-Point evaluation over five seeds with paired significance tests, TADR raises F1 by $0.338$ over the unrefined detector on SMD ($p = 0.0015$), and the anomaly enhancement objective alone contributes $0.463$ in ablation. We also characterise when the method helps: the gain tracks the continuous, mutually redundant channels available and the anomaly evidence the outage removes, and it is absent on telemetry datasets dominated by one-hot command channels and on PSM. At ten sampling steps TADR runs in $41.4$ ms per window on a single CPU core, sustaining about $24$ concurrent 1 Hz streams from a $4.03$ MB model. Code and per-seed results are available at https://github.com/int-park422/TADR.
