title: CAMEL: Cross-Architecture Masked Embedding Learning for Ultra-Lightweight Retinal Foundation Models
description:
arXiv:2610.40954v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent progress in deep learning has substantially advanced automated grading of ophthalmologic pathologies, supported by large annotated datasets and improved representation learning. However, a significant gap remains between state-of-the-art performance and clinical scalability. In particular, foundation models have reshaped image-based medical screening and diagnosis. These large-scale architectures trained on extensive datasets learn rich, generalizable feature representations that can be adapted to a wide range of downstream tasks. In ophthalmology, RETFound, one of the most relevant foundation models for retinal images, performs strongly across classification, segmentation, and risk prediction tasks. Despite their effectiveness, foundation models are often computationally prohibitive, hindering their deployment in real-world clinical environments where hardware constraints and latency are critical. To bridge this gap, we introduce CAMEL (Cross-Architecture Masked Embedding Learning), a novel cross-architecture distillation framework that uses an asymmetric masking strategy during embedding learning to effectively transfer knowledge from massive teacher foundation models to compact, lightweight student models. Our experimental evaluation across four datasets shows that CAMEL preserves accuracy while drastically reducing computational complexity, enabling lightweight yet highly accurate models suitable for resource-limited clinical settings.

title: Lessons from Auditing Ethereum Fusaka (EIP-7594 PeerDAS & EIP-7825) Across 14 EL & CL Clients
description:
Why Multi-Client Differential Auditing Beats Single-Repo Code Review

Ethereum's upcoming Fusaka upgrade (combining the Osaka Execution Layer hardfork and Fulu Consensus Layer hardfork) introduces EIP-7594 (PeerDAS), EIP-7825 (Transaction Gas Limit Cap = 16,777,216), EIP-7883 (ModExp Gas Increase), and EIP-7934 (RLP Execution Block Size Limit).

When you read a single client in isolation, subtle deviations from the specification look intentional. When you compare all 7 Execution Layer clients (go-ethereum, reth, nethermind, besu, erigon, ethereumjs, ethrex) and all 7 Consensus Layer clients (lighthouse, prysm, teku, lodestar, nimbus-eth2, grandine, ethlambda) side by side against the official specification, discrepancies jump out immediately.

Case Study 1: engine_getBlobsV2 Pre-Osaka Error Code & Syncing Checks

According to execution-apis/src/engine/osaka.md#engine_getblobsv2:

  1. Clients MUST return -38005: Unsupported fork if the head block timestamp has not reached Osaka.
  2. Clients MUST return null when syncing.
  3. Clients MUST operate in all-or-nothing mode: if any requested versioned hash is missing or belongs to a v0 sidecar without 128 cell proofs, the entire response must be null.

By building a 7-client conformance matrix, we verified how each client handles > 128 hashes (-38004: Too large request), BlobSidecarVersion1 cell proof counts (CELLS_PER_EXT_BLOB = 128), and pre-Osaka fallback behavior.

Case Study 2: PeerDAS DataColumnSidecar Inclusion Proof & Custody Group Sorting

In specs/fulu/das-core.md:

  • get_custody_groups(node_id, custody_group_count) increments a uint256 counter modularly (UINT256_MAX -> 0), deduplicates group indices modulo NUMBER_OF_CUSTODY_GROUPS (128), and returns sorted(custody_groups).
  • Every DataColumnSidecar gossip message on data_column_sidecar_{subnet_id} must verify both the depth-4 Merkle inclusion proof against signed_block_header.message.body_root (generalized index 27) and the proposer signature before entering fork-choice data availability checks.

Differential matrices turn specification text into deterministic assertions across Go, Rust, C#, Java, Nim, and TypeScript.

title: Auditing Node.js code for the CVE-2026-105483 TLS identity mismatch
description:
Auditing Node.js code for the CVE-2026-105483 TLS identity mismatch

A runtime patch closes CVE-2026-105483, but an audit can still reveal applications whose architecture makes the same identity mistake easy to repeat. The bug affected Node.js 24.x and 26.x before 24.22.1 and 26.12.1. A fullwidth-digit IPv4 host normalized and resolved as an address while tls.checkServerIdentity() evaluated it as a DNS name. A trusted certificate with a matching DNS SAN could authenticate the wrong IP endpoint.

Node.js rates the issue High. The GitHub advisory lists CVSS v3.0 7.4 and CWE-295. The audit should establish where destination identity becomes security-sensitive, then confirm that those paths run on a fixed runtime and use the intended identity type.

Start with the trust decision

Search the codebase for direct use of tls.checkServerIdentity(), custom checkServerIdentity callbacks, and TLS clients that accept destination values from outside the service. Include HTTP clients built on top of the standard TLS stack and integrations that create connections from user or administrator configuration.

The direct search is only a starting point. Many applications never name checkServerIdentity; they rely on a standard client to call it. Review the path that supplies the host value. Does it come from a fixed allowlist, a generated service name, a tenant configuration object, a callback URL, or a command-line argument? Each source has a different threat model.

For each sensitive path, write down four facts:

  • The expected destination type: DNS name, IPv4 address, or both.
  • The normalization performed before the connection.
  • The validation performed after normalization.
  • The trust store and certificate profile required by the server.

If the application expects an IP address but only validates a textual DNS-like value, the identity policy is incomplete even after the runtime update.

Review normalization at the boundary

Unicode presentation can change while the underlying destination meaning stays the same. Official Node.js guidance confirms that fullwidth-digit hosts normalized and resolved as IPv4 in the vulnerable path. Code reviews should therefore avoid comparing a raw host string with a canonical host and assuming both checks describe the same value.

Prefer a small, explicit destination policy. Accept approved ASCII DNS names through an allowlist, or accept a canonical IPv4 literal after parsing and validation. Reject ambiguous mixed representations instead of trying to normalize them into a broader destination language. The application's policy should be narrower than the parser's full input grammar.

This is a mitigation, not a replacement for 24.22.1 or 26.12.1. A patched runtime is the authoritative fix. The application restriction prevents new ambiguous inputs from reaching sensitive clients and makes future regressions easier to test.

Review custom verification callbacks

A custom callback can intentionally support private names, internal addresses, or application-specific identity metadata. It can also silently remove the standard checks. Inspect whether the callback:

  • Uses the parsed destination rather than the original unnormalized string.
  • Requires an IP SAN when the intention is to contact an IP address.
  • Accepts a DNS certificate only when the destination is an approved DNS name.
  • Rejects a mismatch instead of logging it and returning success.
  • Preserves all required certificate validation steps.

Any callback that returns success based only on an application label, a hostname substring, or a certificate Common Name is a candidate for redesign. This review should not rely on a text search alone because wrappers and helper libraries can obscure the TLS call.

Prioritize credential-bearing clients

The advisory assigns high confidentiality and integrity impact, but the operational severity depends on what crosses the connection. A metadata request can disclose service behavior. A signed API request can expose credentials or modify state. A management client can carry broader authority than its destination suggests.

Rank clients by the secrecy of the request, the authority of the response, and the attacker's ability to influence the destination. A low-volume internal integration that carries an administrative token may deserve more attention than a high-volume public read-only client.

Verify deployed artifacts

The affected versions are precise enough to make inventory feasible. Node.js 24.x before 24.22.1 and 26.x before 26.12.1 need to move to a fixed release. Check runtime output, container image layers, SEA packaging, and any embedded Node.js distribution. A source repository can be clean while a release artifact remains affected.

Record the runtime version before and after rollout. If the service exposes that information internally, compare it with the deployed image digest. If it does not, use the packaging and process inspection available to the operator instead of inferring the version from a package name.

Exposure and code evidence

At 04:17 +08:00 on November 2, 2026, ZoomEye Search app="Node.js" returned 5,539,674 product matches and the CVE filter returned zero. The selected Exposure is 5,539,674 Node.js fingerprints, not confirmed vulnerable processes. Use the number to understand the technology population and internal code evidence to decide which services can reach the vulnerable path.

Completion criteria

Consider the audit complete when every sensitive TLS client has a documented expected identity type, an explicit normalization and allowlist policy, and a test that rejects a certificate with the wrong SAN class. Confirm the running runtime is 24.22.1, 26.12.1, or later, and retain the rollout evidence. A clean scan is useful only when the scanned artifact and the deployed process are the same one.

References

  • Node.js October 21, 2026 Security Releases
  • Node.js 24.22.1 release notes
  • Node.js 26.12.1 release notes
  • GitHub Advisory GHSA-8h4p-qpcq-gq24
  • ZoomEye Search

title: Fewer Heads, Fewer Memories: Pruning Redundant Attention Heads Suppresses Verbatim Memorisation
description:
arXiv:2610.40974v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models have been shown to memorise and reproduce verbatim sequences from their training data, raising concerns about privacy leakage, intellectual property exposure, and the limits of generalisation. Recent theoretical work suggests that attention heads may contribute to this behaviour by functioning as associative memory mechanisms, with memorisation capacity scaling with the number of heads. At the same time, empirical work has shown that many attention heads are redundant and can be pruned with limited impact on downstream performance. Despite these parallel findings, the effect of pruning redundant heads on memorised-sequence reproduction remains unexplored. In this work, we demonstrate that zeroing out a substantial fraction of attention heads prior to inference can significantly suppress verbatim memorisation while preserving, or even improving, language modelling performance on the benchmark used to identify redundant heads. Evaluating GPT-2-XL(1.5B) on known memorised sequences, we find that pruning 729 task-redundant heads reduces the memorisation count by 91.5%, while improving WikiText-103 perplexity by 0.92. These findings suggest that attention-head redundancy can be exploited to mitigate memorisation at inference time, without retraining or modifying the training data.

title: Navigating Multi-Cloud Complexity: Introducing CloudCompass 🧭✨
description:
As enterprise architectures scale, managing multi-cloud resources and organizing local-first development workflows can get overwhelmingly chaotic. Distributed systems demand high visibility, intuitive interfaces, and streamlined diagnostic routing.

Enter CloudCompass—an open-source, theme-aware navigation framework and modular user interface suite engineered to simplify cross-cloud resource management and modern system architecture tracking.

🎥 Watch the Demo

Get a quick visual look at the responsive layout, dynamic switching, and clean navigational interface in action:

🎬 Watch the CloudCompass Demo Video

✨ Core Features & Highlights

CloudCompass bridges the gap between complex system design and clean developer UX. Here is a breakdown of everything packed inside the repository:

1. 🌐 Unified Multi-Cloud Navigation

  • Centralizes resource tracking across diverse cloud providers and hybrid environments into a single, cohesive dashboard.
  • Eliminates context-switching fatigue by organizing services, metrics, and environment targets in one intuitive interface.

2. 🎨 Theme-Aware Modular Interface

  • Built with a modern front-end stack (Next.js, React, and Tailwind CSS), delivering fluid light/dark mode adjustments.
  • Offers adaptable layouts tailored for both high-density enterprise operations and lightweight local management.

3. 🏠 Local-First Workflow Integration

  • Fully aligned with local-first software philosophies, empowering developers to run standalone diagnostic control panels, self-hosted dashboards, or offline-capable system bridges.
  • Preserves data privacy while minimizing external API overhead.

4. 🧩 Plug-and-Play Component Architecture

  • Highly structured and modular codebase designed for rapid extension.
  • Easily customizable layout templates allow you to plug in custom API routes, metrics displays, or deployment status components without refactoring existing UI trees.

5. ⚡ Developer-First Performance

  • Engineered with optimized client-side hydration, fast route switching, and minimal bundle overhead for near-instant load times.
  • Fully open-source under the MIT license, encouraging community contributions, custom forks, and enterprise integration.

title: Qistas: A Pre-Registered, Portable Protocol for Fairness Evaluation of Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.40893v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Fairness benchmarks for large language models (LLMs) are overwhelmingly English-born and American in their social categories; translated versions carry those categories into societies where they do not apply, and almost none fix their hypotheses before the models are run. We present Qistas (Arabic qistas, "the just balance"), a protocol for evaluating how LLMs treat the social, confessional, and regional constituencies of a society, portable across countries and instantiated first for Iraq. In its pilot form it measures only what needs no verdict on contested truth: procedural symmetry across matched counterfactual pairs, differential refusal, stereotype reliance under ambiguity, and terminological framing of documented events. Every measurement is paired by construction and analysed with paired machinery (sign-flip permutation tests, exact McNemar tests, template-clustered bootstrap intervals, Holm-corrected families), with a power analysis that states, before any data exist, the smallest effect each axis can detect after the design effect of template clustering. We release the authoring apparatus (a pruned 3x5 taxonomy with four cells closed by design, per-type checklists, a cumulative rulings log, a structural audit, and a human review notebook) and report its first field test: a semantic review of a 58-item seed bank in which 24 of 25 template groups failed at least one check. The defect patterns it exposed (evaluation criteria leaking into prompts, token-level swaps that break Arabic agreement, epistemically unbalanced pairs, single-theme refusal probes, unwritten dialect twins counted as coverage) are, we argue, general hazards of counterfactual fairness benchmarks. This is a protocol paper, not a results paper: no model has been evaluated, and the accompanying pre-registration commits the hypotheses, metrics, exclusion rules, and analysis plan that the pilot will follow.

title: AWS HealthImaging: A Guide to DICOM Storage and Access
description:
Medical imaging systems generate large volumes of data, including X-rays, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), computed tomography (CT), and ultrasound studies. Managing these files requires scalable storage, reliable access, and strong data protection. AWS HealthImaging helps healthcare organizations manage medical imaging data in the cloud while supporting applications that retrieve and process Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine (DICOM) files.

In this guide, we explore how AWS HealthImaging works, how organizations can optimize DICOM storage and access, and which architectural practices support reliable imaging workflows.

What Is AWS HealthImaging?

AWS HealthImaging is a cloud-based medical imaging service from Amazon Web Services (AWS). It helps healthcare organizations store, manage, and access medical imaging data at scale.

Traditional imaging environments often rely on Picture Archiving and Communication Systems (PACS). These systems store medical images and support retrieval across clinical departments. However, growing imaging volumes can increase infrastructure, maintenance, and storage requirements.

AWS HealthImaging provides a managed cloud service for medical imaging data. Organizations can use it as part of an imaging architecture without managing every storage component themselves.

The service organizes imaging data into image sets. It also provides application programming interfaces (APIs) for importing, searching, retrieving, and managing imaging information.

Healthcare developers can use these capabilities to build applications such as:

Cloud-based medical imaging platforms.

Web-based diagnostic image viewers.

Radiology workflow applications.

Medical image research platforms.

Artificial intelligence (AI) imaging solutions.

Connected healthcare applications that use imaging records.

AWS HealthImaging can support imaging workflows across multiple facilities. Organizations should still design access, integration, and governance policies around their clinical requirements.

Understanding DICOM and Medical Imaging Workloads

Before optimizing storage and access, we need to understand the information that medical imaging systems handle.

DICOM is a standard for managing and exchanging medical imaging information. It defines how imaging systems structure, store, transmit, and identify medical images.

A DICOM study can contain multiple series, and each series can contain multiple images. For example, a CT examination may include hundreds of image slices.

DICOM files can also contain important metadata, including:

Patient and study identifiers.

Imaging modality and examination details.

Acquisition date and time.

Study and series descriptions.

Image dimensions and orientation.

Equipment and acquisition parameters.

This information helps imaging applications organize studies and retrieve relevant images.

Why DICOM Workloads Need Careful Optimization

Medical imaging workloads differ from ordinary document storage. A single examination can contain large files and thousands of individual image frames.

Radiologists may need to retrieve an entire study quickly. Other applications may request only selected frames or metadata.

Common workload patterns include:

High-volume imports: Hospitals transfer large imaging archives into centralized storage.

Frequent retrieval: Clinical applications request studies throughout the day.

Metadata searches: Users search for examinations using patient or study identifiers.

Concurrent access: Multiple clinicians may access the same imaging study.

Long-term retention: Organizations preserve imaging records according to operational and regulatory requirements.

AI processing: Algorithms retrieve image data for analysis and model inference.

An effective architecture must account for these patterns. It should balance storage requirements, retrieval performance, application needs, and operational costs.

How AWS HealthImaging Manages DICOM Storage

AWS HealthImaging provides a managed environment for storing medical imaging data. Its image set structure helps applications organize and retrieve imaging information.

Understanding this structure helps developers design efficient storage and access workflows.

Image Sets and Imaging Metadata

AWS HealthImaging organizes imported DICOM data into image sets. An image set represents a logical collection of imaging information that applications can manage.

The service provides APIs for accessing image set information and metadata. Applications can use these capabilities to identify relevant imaging records before retrieving image data.

This separation supports more targeted access patterns. For example, a viewer can search for a study before requesting its image frames.

Importing DICOM Data

Organizations often begin cloud imaging projects by transferring existing DICOM archives. AWS HealthImaging supports DICOM import workflows through its service APIs.

A typical import process involves:

Preparing the source DICOM files.

Uploading the files to an appropriate Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) location.

Starting an import job through the supported AWS HealthImaging API.

Monitoring the import job and reviewing its status.

Checking the resulting image sets and metadata.

Validating representative studies through application retrieval workflows.

Developers should validate source files before importing large datasets. This helps identify malformed files, missing metadata, and inconsistent identifiers.

They should also test import behavior with representative imaging studies. Different modalities and acquisition systems may produce different data patterns.

Managing Imaging Data at Scale

Storage planning should consider both current data volumes and future growth. Imaging archives can expand as organizations add facilities, modalities, and clinical services.

AWS HealthImaging can help reduce the operational burden of managing imaging storage infrastructure. However, organizations still need clear policies for data lifecycle management.

A practical storage strategy should address:

Expected daily and annual imaging volumes.

Historical archive migration.

Study retention requirements.

Data access frequency.

Duplicate and invalid study handling.

Backup and recovery expectations.

Regional data residency requirements.

These considerations help organizations build a storage model that supports clinical operations.

Optimizing DICOM Access and Retrieval Performance

Storage capacity alone does not determine imaging performance. Clinical applications also need predictable access to image data and metadata.

AWS HealthImaging provides APIs that allow applications to search and retrieve imaging information. Developers should design these workflows around actual user behavior.

Search Before Retrieving Image Data

A common inefficiency occurs when applications retrieve large imaging datasets before identifying the required study.

We recommend separating discovery from retrieval. Applications should first search for relevant image sets and examine their metadata.

Once users select a study, the application can request the required image data. This approach helps avoid unnecessary data transfers.

For example, a radiologist searching for a patient's previous CT scan may need only the matching study. The application should not retrieve unrelated imaging records.

Retrieve Only the Required Image Frames

Some imaging workflows require an entire study. Others need only selected images or frames.

Applications should request the smallest useful data set whenever the workflow permits. This can reduce network traffic and improve responsiveness.

A diagnostic viewer may initially load selected image frames. It can retrieve additional frames as users navigate through a study.

Developers should also consider image dimensions and rendering requirements. These factors influence how applications process and display retrieved data.

Design Efficient API Requests

Every API request adds processing and network overhead. Applications should avoid unnecessary repeated requests for identical information.

Useful optimization practices include:

Requesting only the metadata needed by the current workflow.

Reusing valid identifiers across related requests.

Avoiding repeated searches for unchanged records.

Managing concurrent requests carefully.

Applying controlled retry logic.

Monitoring API response times and error rates.

Caching can also improve application responsiveness. However, developers must define appropriate expiration and invalidation rules.

Patient information changes over time, so applications should not rely on stale metadata. They must also protect cached information through suitable access controls.

Improve Viewer Performance

Medical image viewers need to display studies efficiently. Poor retrieval design can cause delays during scrolling, zooming, and image navigation.

We recommend loading essential study information first. The viewer can then retrieve image frames according to user interactions.

Developers should test performance across different network conditions. They should also evaluate large studies and concurrent clinical sessions.

These tests help identify bottlenecks in retrieval, processing, and rendering.

Building a Scalable AWS HealthImaging Architecture

A healthcare imaging architecture usually includes more than a storage service. It connects data sources, ingestion processes, application services, viewers, and clinical workflows.

A typical architecture may include the following components:

Imaging sources: Modalities and existing PACS environments generate DICOM studies.

Ingestion layer: Import workflows transfer imaging data into the cloud environment.

AWS HealthImaging datastore: The service manages imported imaging data and image sets.

Application backend: Backend services manage authentication, application logic, and API requests.

Metadata and search services: Application components help users locate relevant studies.

Image viewer: A web or desktop application retrieves and displays imaging information.

Monitoring and security services: Operational tools track system health and access activity.

Connect Existing PACS Environments

Many healthcare organizations already operate PACS infrastructure. Replacing these systems immediately may not be practical.

A phased integration strategy can connect existing imaging environments with cloud services. Organizations can migrate selected datasets or workflows before expanding the architecture.

Developers should evaluate existing DICOM interfaces, export capabilities, and vendor restrictions. They should also define how applications handle records across cloud and on-premises environments.

Integrate with EHR and Clinical Applications

Medical images often need to appear alongside clinical records. Integrating imaging applications with Electronic Health Record (EHR) systems can help providers access relevant studies.

For example, an EHR workflow may display imaging study references within a patient's clinical record. An authorized user can then open the corresponding study in an imaging viewer.

Developers should coordinate patient identifiers and study references carefully. Incorrect mappings can associate imaging records with the wrong patient.

Support Multiple Facilities

Healthcare networks may operate hospitals, diagnostic centers, and specialist clinics across different locations.

A centralized imaging architecture can support shared access across participating facilities. However, developers must define access boundaries and organizational responsibilities.

The design should consider user identity, facility permissions, data ownership, and regional requirements. These controls help maintain appropriate access as the system grows.

Security and Compliance for Medical Imaging Data

Medical images often contain protected health information (PHI). Organizations must protect this information throughout ingestion, storage, retrieval, and sharing.

In the United States, the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) establishes requirements for protecting electronic protected health information (ePHI).

AWS provides security capabilities that organizations can configure within their cloud environments. However, using a cloud service does not automatically make an application HIPAA compliant.

Organizations must implement appropriate technical, administrative, and physical safeguards.

Encryption and Data Protection

Encryption helps protect medical imaging information against unauthorized access. Organizations should use supported encryption options for data storage and secure communication.

They should also manage encryption keys through appropriate controls. Key access should follow organizational security policies.

Identity and Access Management

AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) helps control access to AWS resources. Organizations can define permissions for users, applications, and service roles.

We recommend applying the principle of least privilege. Each application should receive only the permissions required for its specific workflow.

Healthcare applications should also enforce user-level authorization. A valid service credential should not automatically grant every user unrestricted patient access.

Audit Logging and Monitoring

Organizations need visibility into how applications access imaging records. Audit and operational logs can support security reviews and incident investigations.

Monitoring should cover:

Authentication and authorization events.

Imaging import and retrieval activity.

Failed API requests.

Permission and configuration changes.

Unusual access patterns.

Application errors and service availability.

Logs should avoid unnecessary exposure of PHI. Organizations should define retention, access, and review policies.

Network Security

Network controls help restrict communication between application components. Organizations can use suitable network isolation and access policies.

They should also review public endpoints, service permissions, and data transfer paths. Security testing should cover both application and infrastructure configurations.

Common AWS HealthImaging Implementation Challenges

Cloud imaging projects involve several technical and operational considerations. Planning for these challenges helps prevent avoidable delays.

Legacy DICOM Compatibility

Older imaging systems may produce files with inconsistent metadata or unsupported characteristics. Import validation helps identify these issues before migration.

Developers should test files from different modalities and vendors. They should also define procedures for handling failed imports.

Large-Scale Data Migration

Historical imaging archives can contain millions of files. Transferring these datasets requires careful planning around network capacity and import throughput.

Organizations should migrate data in controlled batches. They should monitor job status and validate imported studies before expanding migration.

Patient Identity and Metadata Consistency

Different systems may use different patient identifiers or metadata conventions. These differences can create duplicate records or incorrect associations.

A consistent identity-matching strategy helps reduce these risks. Teams should also establish data validation and reconciliation procedures.

Application Compatibility

Existing viewers may rely on specific DICOM interfaces or storage assumptions. They may require changes before working with a cloud-based imaging service.

Developers should review viewer capabilities early. They should also test retrieval, rendering, and clinical workflows before production deployment.

Cost Management

Cloud imaging costs depend on storage, data transfer, API usage, and other architecture choices. Organizations should evaluate expected usage before deployment.

Useful cost-management practices include:

Estimating storage growth by modality.

Reviewing data retrieval patterns.

Monitoring data transfer charges.

Avoiding unnecessary API calls.

Evaluating migration and operational costs.

Reviewing service pricing as requirements change.

Cost optimization should not compromise clinical availability or required retention policies.

Best Practices for Optimizing AWS HealthImaging Workloads

A structured implementation approach helps organizations balance performance, reliability, security, and cost.

We recommend the following practices:

Assess imaging workloads: Identify modalities, file volumes, access patterns, and retention requirements.

Validate DICOM files: Check representative datasets before large-scale imports.

Plan migration in phases: Move data in manageable batches and validate each stage.

Use targeted retrieval: Search metadata first and request only the required image data.

Optimize application requests: Reduce redundant calls and apply controlled retries.

Test real clinical workflows: Evaluate study search, image navigation, and concurrent access.

Secure every integration point: Apply encryption, identity controls, and appropriate permissions.

Monitor performance: Track import jobs, API errors, retrieval times, and application health.

Document operational procedures: Maintain integration specifications and recovery processes.

Review costs regularly: Compare actual usage with expected storage and retrieval patterns.

These practices create a foundation for reliable medical imaging applications. They also help organizations adapt as imaging workloads and clinical requirements change.

How AWS HealthImaging Supports AI and Advanced Imaging Applications

Healthcare organizations increasingly use AI to support medical image analysis and clinical research. These applications require reliable access to imaging data.

AWS HealthImaging can serve as part of an architecture that connects imaging storage with processing applications. Developers can build services that retrieve authorized image data for downstream workflows.

Potential use cases include:

AI-Assisted Image Analysis

AI models can analyze medical images to identify patterns or support clinical review. Applications can retrieve relevant imaging data and send it to authorized processing services.

Developers must validate model performance and maintain clinical oversight. AI-generated findings should not replace qualified medical judgment.

Medical Imaging Research

Research platforms often need access to large imaging datasets. Cloud-based storage can support research workflows across distributed applications.

Organizations must apply appropriate de-identification, consent, access, and governance controls. They should also follow applicable research and privacy requirements.

Connected Diagnostic Workflows

Imaging applications can connect with EHRs, reporting platforms, and clinical portals. These integrations help providers access relevant images within broader care workflows.

The architecture should maintain accurate patient and study references. It should also support appropriate access restrictions across applications.

Frequently Asked Questions

1. What is AWS HealthImaging used for?

AWS HealthImaging helps healthcare organizations store, manage, and access medical imaging data in the cloud. Developers can use its APIs to build imaging applications and retrieval workflows.

2. Does AWS HealthImaging support DICOM?

Yes. AWS HealthImaging supports workflows for importing and managing DICOM medical imaging data. Developers can use the service's APIs to access image sets and related information.

3. How does AWS HealthImaging differ from traditional PACS?

Traditional PACS platforms manage medical imaging storage and retrieval within healthcare environments. AWS HealthImaging provides a managed cloud service for medical imaging data. Organizations should compare their integration, workflow, and operational requirements before choosing an architecture.

4. Can AWS HealthImaging integrate with an EHR?

Yes. Developers can build integrations between AWS HealthImaging and EHR applications. These connections can help users access imaging studies through clinical workflows.

5. Is AWS HealthImaging HIPAA compliant?

AWS offers services and security capabilities that support eligible HIPAA workloads under applicable conditions. Organizations must configure their environments and applications appropriately. They must also meet their own HIPAA obligations.

6. How can we improve DICOM retrieval performance?

Start by optimizing metadata searches and avoiding unnecessary image transfers. Retrieve only the required data, manage API requests efficiently, and test viewer performance under realistic workloads.

7. Can AWS HealthImaging support AI medical imaging applications?

Yes. Developers can build architectures that connect AWS HealthImaging with authorized image processing and AI services. They must also address data security, model validation, and clinical oversight.

8. What should organizations consider before migrating imaging data?

Organizations should assess DICOM compatibility, archive size, network capacity, metadata quality, retention policies, and application dependencies. A phased migration with validation helps reduce operational risks.

Build Scalable Medical Imaging Solutions with Oodles

Medical imaging platforms need more than cloud storage. They require reliable data ingestion, efficient retrieval, secure access, and integration with clinical applications.

AWS HealthImaging can support these requirements within a carefully planned cloud architecture. The right implementation depends on imaging volumes, existing systems, user workflows, and long-term operational goals.

At Oodles, we work on healthcare technology solutions involving medical imaging, healthcare APIs, EHR and EMR integrations, and cloud-based application development. We help organizations evaluate technical requirements and design practical integration strategies.

title: Unsupervised Feature Selection Using Local Intrinsic Dimensionality -- Extended Version
description:
arXiv:2610.40736v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: High dimensionality degrades both the efficiency and the effectiveness of learning algorithms, and in many applications no class labels are available to guide dimensionality reduction. This paper proposes LIDFS, an unsupervised feature selection method based on Local Intrinsic Dimensionality (LID). The method builds on the formal equivalence between LID and the indiscriminability of distance measures. The data matrix is transposed so that each feature is treated as a point, and the LID of each feature is estimated by maximum likelihood from the distances to its $k$ nearest neighboring features. Features with lower LID exhibit greater local discriminability and receive higher importance scores. A refinement step then retains one representative per feature neighborhood and demotes locally redundant features. The result is a complete ranking from which any number of features can be selected without rerunning the procedure. LIDFS does not use any information about labels or the number of classes, and runs in $\mathcal{O}(d^2 n)$ time for $n$ instances and $d$ features. LIDFS is compared with classic and state-of-the-art methods and a random baseline on 23 high-dimensional datasets, the classic benchmark collection. The evaluation uses classification accuracy and AUC with five downstream classifiers, as well as clustering accuracy and normalized mutual information, over both full and aggressive selection ranges. LIDFS ranks first in the supervised evaluations and first or tied second in the clustering-based evaluations. It belongs to the top statistical group together with methods that require the number of classes, and it runs faster than its closest competitor. Several recent methods, by contrast, fail to outperform the random baseline. A sensitivity analysis shows that small neighborhood sizes yield the best results.

BigQuery

Feature

The Apache Hive catalog endpoint in the Lakehouse runtime catalog is now generally available (GA). This integration lets you use the metastore as a serverless, central metadata layer, enabling seamless data sharing and unified querying across Apache Spark, Apache Hive, and BigQuery.

For more information, see About the Hive catalog endpoint and Set up Spark and Hive with the Lakehouse runtime catalog.

Feature

Metadata migration from Dataproc Metastore to Lakehouse is now generally available (GA). You can perform a one-time backfill migration or dry run to migrate metadata from a Dataproc Metastore service to an Apache Iceberg REST catalog endpoint or a Hive catalog endpoint using the Google Cloud console, the gcloud CLI, or the REST API.

For more information, see Migrate metadata from Dataproc Metastore to Lakehouse.

Feature

Conversational analytics now lets you create a conversation with all of the data sources in multiple projects, or create a conversation with a dataset. These features are generally available (GA).

You can publish a BigQuery Conversational Analytics agent in Gemini Enterprise. This feature is now generally available (GA).

Feature

The AI.AGG function now supports the output_schema argument, which lets you specify the schema of the function output as a comma-separated list of fields. This feature is generally available (GA).

Certificate Manager

Change

Google-managed public SSL certificates signed by Google Public CA (pki.goog) are gradually transitioning from a 90-day validity period to a 45-day validity period to improve security.

To align with modern industry-wide security standards and promote shorter certificate lifespans, Google-managed public certificates now rotate more frequently. This proactive rotation enhances the overall security posture of load balancers. The transition requires no manual intervention or configuration changes as Certificate Manager automatically manages both issuance and renewal.

For more information, see Google-managed certificates and Use Google-managed certificates.

Cloud Load Balancing

Change

Google-managed public SSL certificates signed by Public Certificate Authority (pki.goog) are gradually transitioning from a 90-day validity period to a 45-day validity period to improve security.

To align with modern industry-wide security standards and promote shorter certificate lifespans, Google-managed public certificates signed by Public Certificate Authority now rotate more frequently.

This proactive rotation enhances the overall security posture of load balancers. Transition requires no manual intervention or configuration changes as Google Cloud automatically manages issuance and renewal for both Certificate Manager and Compute Engine SSL certificates.

For more information, see Renew a Google-managed SSL certificate.

Feature

Service rate limiting policies are now available in Preview for regional internal Application Load Balancers and Secure Web Proxies.

Service rate limiting policies let you maintain service availability among trusted clients that might consume an inordinate amount of resources.

For more information, see the Service rate limiting overview.

title: CompoSET: A Controlled Single-Edit Benchmark for Vision-Language Compositionality
description:
arXiv:2610.41118v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Vision-language compositionality is the ability to identify which properties, relations, quantities, and states bind to which entities in both an image and a caption, and to match those bindings across modalities. Existing benchmarks evaluate this ability through image-text matching: a model ranks candidate image-caption match similarities and succeeds when the correct match comes on top. In such datasets, paired images differ by more than a single binding: scene, layout, and content all differ, with 97% of pixels changing on average. Such pairs do not isolate compositionality: results are confounded by global image differences. We introduce Compositional Single-EdiT (CompoSET), a benchmark dataset in which each base image-caption pair has an edited counterpart, or foil, that preserves the scene but differs by a single controlled edit, such as color, count, spatial relation, or object state. Base and foil images preserve naturalistic scene complexity yet are visually near-identical: only 8% of pixels change on average. Our dataset has many foils per base scene (~22) in order to separate scene difficulty from edit difficulty, a distinction one-foil-per-base benchmarks cannot make. CompoSET contains 1,776 instances across 80 naturalistic scenes, spanning 16 edit types in 4 semantic categories, with captions at 3 verbosity levels. We test 22 dual-encoder VLMs and find that all models perform at or below chance level on CompoSET, despite scoring well on prior benchmarks. This suggests that apparent progress under prior image-text matching protocols may be an artifact arising from confounds in benchmark design, and that compositional understanding in dual-encoder VLMs is far from solved. CompoSET addresses the confounds and offers a better controlled benchmark to measure future progress.

title: Beyond Scarcity: When Encoder Adaptation Is Worthwhile
description:
arXiv:2610.41213v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Long-tailed recognition often learns a shared representation before correcting the classifier for class imbalance. Once the classifier has been rebalanced, however, final accuracy does not reveal whether further encoder adaptation remains worthwhile. Standard imbalance benchmarks obscure this question because they jointly vary the number of distinct examples available to rare classes and the frequency with which those examples shape the representation. We introduce a controlled evaluation framework that separates unique support from representation allocation and estimates the incremental value of encoder updates through matched classifier-only and full-network continuations from a common corrected model. The framework combines stage-specific controls, multiple representation and adaptation objectives, whole-distribution metrics, and hierarchical inference over class assignments, support reconstructions, and optimization runs. Across the controlled study, the same low-support regime moves from one in which classifier-only training is adequate to one in which encoder adaptation yields a practically meaningful benefit solely as representation allocation becomes more imbalanced. The transition persists across classifier corrections, representation objectives, normalization and augmentation controls, and ImageNet-scale evaluation, while preserving frequent-class accuracy. Under the prespecified one-percentage-point operating margin, the two regimes are separated by simultaneous confidence bounds. These results show that benchmark construction can alter a post-correction training decision and that support size alone does not characterize the remaining value of representation adaptation.

title: General Frequency Principle for Linear Approximation Classes
description:
arXiv:2610.41179v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In this paper, we study a general frequency principle under gradient descent training for the finite linear approximation classes. Under suitable assumptions, we prove that the learner amplitude relative to the target amplitude vanishes at high frequencies, uniformly throughout training. We also establish sufficient conditions for low-frequency priority, covering single-frequency targets trained separately and two frequency components trained in the same run. This general frequency principle does not imply that lower frequencies always converge faster. Instead, for two frequencies that satisfy certain comparison conditions, one component will take longer to learn than the other; and in common cases, the longer component has higher frequency. Numerical experiments with Legendre and trigonometric bases validate the theoretical results.

title: Frozen in Time: How a Physics Foundation Model Forgets Under Sim-to-Real Adaptation
description:
arXiv:2610.40857v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Scientific foundation models (SciFMs) have achieved remarkable performance on a wide range of PDEs, including the ability to efficiently adapt to unseen data distributions with additional finetuning. As with all neural architectures, finetuning such models comes with the risk of catastrophic forgetting, whereby adapting to new tasks degrades prior knowledge of the model. We study catastrophic forgetting in Walrus-1.3B, a SciFM for continuum dynamics, over the course of a two-stage sim-to-real adaptation: first finetuning on simulated flow around a cylinder and then adapting to experimental data of the same system. We find that finetuning on the simulations rapidly degrades rollout performance on the original pretraining datasets, with one-step errors increasing up to 35x after just 20 epochs. Subsequent adaptation to real data further erodes performance on the simulated task. We characterize the potential drivers of forgetting, such as dataset dependence and task representation similarity. We then show that replaying as little as 1% simulated data during real-data finetuning recovers most of the lost simulation performance while retaining effective adaptation to the experimental dynamics. Our results identify catastrophic forgetting as a practical obstacle to sim-to-real adaptation of SciFMs and show that lightweight replay strategies significantly improve retention.

title: Segment Anything Pancreas: A Unified MRI Segmentation Model for Pancreatic Cancer Radiotherapy
description:
arXiv:2610.41063v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Background: Limited tumor annotations and incomplete labels across MRI datasets hinder unified segmentation of pancreatic tumors and organs at risk (OARs) for MRI-guided radiotherapy. Purpose: We propose Pancreas-MedNeXt, a unified model that segments the whole pancreas, its subregions, tumors, and surrounding OARs from one MRI volume. Methods: The model uses a shared MedNeXt encoder-decoder with supervised whole-pancreas and subregion pretraining, followed by multitask fine-tuning. Three output heads predict the pancreatic subregions, tumor, and OARs (stomach, duodenum, kidneys). An annotation-aware loss allows training on partially labeled data without treating unannotated structures as background. Pancreas and tumor were evaluated by three-fold cross-validation on 142 PANTHER patients (92 diagnostic, 50 MR-Linac), subregions and OARs on Cyst-X and AMOS test sets, and pancreas and OARs on 33 external T1-weighted TotalSegmentator scans. Comparisons with nnU-Net, MedNeXt, VISTA3D, and Swin UNETR used the Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) with paired bootstrap 95% CIs. Results: Pancreas-MedNeXt achieved the highest mean pancreas and tumor DSC on diagnostic and MR-Linac MRI. Tumor DSC was 58.41% and 42.55%, exceeding task-specific MedNeXt by 4.94 (95% CI: 0.28-9.45) and 5.89 (95% CI: 2.37-9.72) percentage points, respectively. Whole-pancreas DSC was 85.73% and 70.66%. Pretraining improved head, body, and tail DSC by 2.01, 3.00, and 3.78 percentage points over training from scratch. It also achieved the highest DSC for the pancreas, duodenum, and right kidney on AMOS, and for all five organs on external MRI, exceeding the next-best method by 4.92-8.85 percentage points.Conclusion: A single Pancreas-MedNeXt model segments tumors, pancreatic subregions, and OARs on diagnostic and MR-Linac MRI, which could streamline contouring for pancreatic cancer radiotherapy.

title: Shipping Ming-Image Design: size the card by its files, and check the alpha in code
description:
Say you want an image endpoint for app mockups, slides and stickers, and Ming-Image-0.1-Design from inclusionAI looks like the right fit. It is MIT licensed and trained for layouts full of text. Its PNGs always carry an alpha channel, a fourth layer that stores the opacity of every pixel. Before you ship it, three things decide whether it behaves: which GPU you rent, how you phrase the transparency request, and what happens when a result is too big to send back.

We ran it on one NVIDIA A100 80GB on our cloud and wrote up every number in the Ming-Image Design test on one A100.

Budget memory from the component list

The model card calls it a 6B model. That figure covers only the diffusion transformer, the part that refines random noise into an image step by step, and it is 12.3 GB on disk. The repository also ships a 34 GB language model that interprets the prompt, a 6.2 GB connector between the two and a 0.25 GB decoder that produces the pixels: 52.9 GB in total.

Once loaded, the model held 46.3 GiB of GPU memory before drawing anything. A 1024 x 1024 image peaked at 50.45 GiB, and a 2048 x 2048 one reached 64.4 GiB. That lines up with the authors' GitHub README, where the smallest setup they validated is one GPU with at least 80 GiB. If your capacity planning starts from a parameter count, add up the folder sizes first.

We also planned to fake a 24 GB card by capping the A100's memory. An open bug kept the new setting from reaching the running model, so nothing under 80 GB is tested.

Treat transparency as a prompt format you have to test

inclusionAI lists ten trigger phrases for transparent output and asks you to open the prompt with a single one. There is no special code path: the decoder always emits four channels, and transparency happens only if the model draws it.

We wrote the request six different ways, and a single version produced a cutout. It started with "RGBA, 4-channel, transparent background" as a line by itself, followed by the fox sticker description: 83.2 % of pixels came out fully transparent. Put a comma after the phrase instead and the fox sat on opaque white, with a minimum alpha of 247. Yet the same newline trick on an app icon still gave a solid background. The newline helped the fox, and it guarantees nothing.

The practical rule is to stop trusting the request and measure the response:

prompt = "RGBA, 4-channel, transparent background\n" + description  # newline, not ", "
alpha = np.asarray(Image.open("out.png").getchannel("A"))
transparent = (alpha == 0).mean()  # fox with newline: 0.832, with a comma: 0.0

Retry or reject below a threshold that fits your assets. Our backend (the small server that keeps the model in memory and serves requests) returns this fraction with every image.

Quoted strings are the spec, the rest is filler

In 5 of our 7 layouts, every string we put in quotes was correct. Anything unspecified, such as chart axes or feature cards, filled up with pseudo-words that pass at a glance.

Long lists slip. A 12-line menu asked for in two columns came out in one, with two wrong prices and an invented line. If your output carries prices, someone has to read every line. inclusionAI suggests first rewriting prompts into a structured, Figma-style description with another language model; we did not try that.

Three settings that bite between the model and your client

What Why it matters
12 steps, guidance 1.0 Steps are drawing passes; guidance is how hard the prompt steers them. The authors validated these. Our panel's image tester defaults to 20 and 4.5.
1024 and 2048 only It draws at the closer level, then resizes: a 1920 x 1080 slide is drawn at 1024.
Result size Our test setup accepted answers up to 8 MB. Two busy 2048 images went over, got discarded, and the client sat until a 300-second timeout.

Resolution alone does not predict file size: other 2048 images fit. The SDK example's backend now lowers WebP quality until the file fits, tested on saved images only. The long platform wait is still open, and we did not check the hosted limit.

Speed with the authors' untuned script: 6.2 to 7.4 seconds of GPU time per 1024 image over 10 runs, 35.8 seconds per 2048 image. The vLLM-Omni serving engine reports about 2.2 seconds at 1024 on two H100s; we did not run it.

What this does not prove

These are observations, not a quality score: 15 images, one try per prompt, prompts we wrote, one seed (the random starting point), a single GPU model, and requests sent one by one. We did not call the hosted service.

On Python 3.11 the authors' pinned versions did not run as written; slightly newer numpy and torch fixed it. The dependency fixes, per-size memory figures and the full transparency table sit in the engineering appendix. To compare text rendering, our MOSS-Image hands-on test measured the same kind of layouts on one A40.

Credit where it belongs. inclusionAI made Ming-Image-0.1-Design and released it under MIT, inference code and transparency phrases included. It reuses pieces from other teams: Ling for the language model, Qwen2.5 for vision, Qwen2 for the connector, Z-Image for the transformer design and Qwen-Image for the decoder. The vLLM-Omni team contributed a serving recipe plus benchmark numbers, hugging-apps a demo Space, and the AI Search channel is where we first saw the model. We wrote the custom backend, deployed it, fixed the dependencies and took the measurements. Timings, sample images and the deploy walkthrough live in the Ming-Image Design research article on inferencekey.com.

title: Generative SDEs with Trainable Diffusion and Density-Based Losses
description:

title: SACQ: Structure-Aware Codebook Quantization for Ultra-Low-Bit Vision-Language-Action Models
description:
arXiv:2610.41408v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models enable capable robot behavior, but their large memory footprint limits deployment on resource-constrained robotic platforms. Weight quantization is a natural remedy, yet post-training quantization (PTQ) recipes inherited from large language models degrade when applied to VLAs at ultra-low precision. Existing low-bit PTQ methods often fail to explicitly account for the structure of downstream operations and allocate precision without considering its effect on the policy actions. We introduce SACQ, an ultra- low-bit weight-only vector-codebook quantization framework for VLAs. SACQ combines (1) structure-aware codebook fitting with role-specific quadratic metrics that reflect input statistics and downstream sensitivity; (2) action-aware mixed-bit allocation based on the increase in final-action error as individual layers are compressed; and (3) two-stage post-quantization refinement that reassigns codeword indices with second-order error compensation and calibrates codebooks and row-group scales against the decoded action. Using GR00T N1.7, SACQ achieves 93.85% average success across four LIBERO suites at 1.5 bits per language/action weight while reducing model memory by 4.83x. With INT8 activation quantization and low-precision attention, it retains 93.55% success while running 1.51x faster than BF16. On SimplER, SACQ further achieves 63.76% and 52.27% success under Visual Matching and Variant Aggregation at 2 bits per language/action weight, compared to 58.90% and 53.45% for BF16, respectively.

title: How to Scrape Dribbble with Go: Designer Profiles, Shots, Collections, and a Portfolio Tracker (2026)
description:
Dribbble is where a lot of designers keep their portfolio, so it's a natural data source if you're scouting talent, studying which kinds of shots get attention, or keeping an eye on your own numbers. The first thing most people search for is "Dribbble API". There is one. It just doesn't do what most people expect.

So this post covers both: what the official Dribbble API gives you, and how to build a small Dribbble scraper in Go for the public pages it doesn't cover. The scraper uses the standard library plus golang.org/x/net/html, and it will:

  1. Respect robots.txt with a tiny matcher, and stop cleanly at bot challenges
  2. Read a designer profile: name, headline, bio, location, followers, skills
  3. Page through a designer's shots with likes, views, and publish dates
  4. List a designer's collections, and read the shots inside one
  5. Snapshot a few portfolios into CSV and report what changed

Everything below was run on October 30, 2026, and the output is real.

Before you start: Dribbble's Terms of Service list "copying, distributing, or disclosing any part of the Website ... by any automated or non-automated 'scraping'" as a prohibited activity. robots.txt allows the pages used here, but robots rules and terms are different things. Read the terms and weigh the legal risk for your use case before running anything, and prefer the official API wherever it covers what you need. Treat this as a learning project or small-scale research: keep request rates low, don't republish people's work, don't resell the data, and don't use it to mass-message designers. If you only need your own data, use the official API.

Is there a Dribbble API?

Yes: the Dribbble API v2 (https://api.dribbble.com/v2/, docs at developer.dribbble.com). You register an application, do the OAuth flow, and send Authorization: Bearer <token>. The limit is 60 requests per minute and 1,440 per day per authenticated user, with X-RateLimit-* headers and Link header pagination.

The catch is in the endpoint list. v2 has GET /user, GET /user/shots, GET /shots/:id, create/update/delete shot, projects, and jobs. All of them are about the authenticated user. The docs for "Get a shot" say it plainly: "This endpoint returns only shots owned by the currently authenticated user." The old v1 endpoints for any user's shots, followers, and popular lists are gone. Without a token, GET https://api.dribbble.com/v2/user returns 401, and /v2/users/simplebits/shots is a 404.

You want Use
Your own shots, profile, projects (e.g. to show your Dribbble work on your site) Dribbble API v2
Other designers' public profiles, shots, likes/views, collections The public website, which is what this scraper reads

How dribbble.com looks from a scraper's point of view

I checked the site with curl and with Go's HTTP client first. Here is what came back:

path                                            status  notes
/robots.txt                                     200
/simplebits                                     200     ~300 KB, shots embedded as JSON
/simplebits?page=2                              200     next 24 shots
/simplebits/about                               200     bio, location, skills, counts
/simplebits/collections                         200     6 collections per page
/simplebits/collections/4582-Data-Viz           200     24 shots per page
/shots/27755136-Measure-Twice-Print             202     AWS WAF challenge, empty page
/shots/popular, /search/logo                    202     AWS WAF challenge
/shots/popular.rss                              202     AWS WAF challenge
/simplebits.rss, /shots.rss                     404     the old RSS feeds are gone

The status codes were the same with a Chrome User-Agent, curl's default, and Go's Go-http-client/1.1. So three findings shaped the code.

1. robots.txt is clear about what's off-limits. Profiles, collections, and shot pages are allowed. These are disallowed for every crawler:

Disallow: /*/followers$
Disallow: /*/following$
Disallow: /*/tags$
Disallow: /*/tags/*
Disallow: /shots/*/comments
Disallow: /shots/*/fans
Disallow: /shots/*/rebounds
Disallow: /shots/*/buckets
Disallow: /shots/week/*   (and /day/*, /month/*, /year/*)

So no follower lists, no who-liked-this lists, no comments. The scraper below checks every path against these rules before it sends a request.

2. Profile and collection pages are server-rendered, and the shots come as JSON. The profile page includes a <script> with var newestShots = [...], one object per shot in the grid:

{"id":27755136,"title":"Measure Twice Print","path":"/shots/27755136-Measure-Twice-Print",
 "published_at":"September 23, 2026","is_rebound":null,"rebounds_count":0,
 "attachments_count":0,"view_count":"23.3k","likes_count":"108","liked":null,"ga":[]}

That's easier and sturdier than scraping the grid's CSS. Logged out, the page shows a "Sign up to continue" button where infinite scroll would be, but the classic ?page=2 link is still in the HTML and works.

3. Individual shot pages, popular, and search sit behind an AWS WAF challenge. They return HTTP 202 with x-amzn-waf-action: challenge and a small JavaScript page that a real browser solves. I didn't try to get around it, and you shouldn't either. Everything in this post comes from profile and collection pages, which already show titles, likes, views, and dates for every shot. The scraper treats a 202 as "stop", not "retry".

One more detail: the page's own config included "isRobot": true for my requests. Dribbble knows exactly what you are, so be polite.

Step 1: Project setup and a polite fetch helper 

mkdir dribbblescraper && cd dribbblescraper
go mod init dribbblescraper
go get golang.org/x/net/html

getHTML checks robots.txt, keeps at least two seconds between requests, backs off on 429/5xx, and returns ErrChallenged on a WAF challenge. The User-Agent is honest. Put your own contact URL in it.

package main

import (
    "bufio"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "regexp"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

const (
    base      = "https://dribbble.com"
    userAgent = "dribbblescraper/0.1 (+https://example.com/contact)"
)

var (
    client = &http.Client{Timeout: 25 * time.Second}

    // ErrChallenged means AWS WAF answered with a JavaScript challenge
    // (HTTP 202, empty-ish body, x-amzn-waf-action: challenge). We stop
    // instead of trying to solve it.
    ErrChallenged = errors.New("blocked by AWS WAF challenge")
    ErrDisallowed = errors.New("path disallowed by robots.txt")

    lastRequest time.Time
    minGap      = 2 * time.Second
)

// getHTML fetches a dribbble.com path after checking robots.txt, waits at
// least minGap between requests, and backs off on 429/5xx.
func getHTML(path string) (string, error) {
    if !robots.Allowed(path) {
        return "", fmt.Errorf("%w: %s", ErrDisallowed, path)
    }
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        if wait := minGap - time.Since(lastRequest); wait > 0 {
            time.Sleep(wait)
        }
        lastRequest = time.Now()

        req, _ := http.NewRequest("GET", base+path, nil)
        req.Header.Set("User-Agent", userAgent)
        req.Header.Set("Accept", "text/html")
        req.Header.Set("Accept-Language", "en-US,en;q=0.9")
        res, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            time.Sleep(time.Duration(attempt+1) * 3 * time.Second)
            continue
        }
        body, err := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(res.Body, 8<<20))
        res.Body.Close()
        if err != nil {
            return "", err
        }
        switch {
        case res.Header.Get("x-amzn-waf-action") != "" || res.StatusCode == 202:
            return "", fmt.Errorf("%w: %s", ErrChallenged, path)
        case res.StatusCode == 429 || res.StatusCode >= 500:
            fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "HTTP %d on %s, backing off\n", res.StatusCode, path)
            time.Sleep(time.Duration(attempt+1) * 15 * time.Second)
            continue
        case res.StatusCode == 404:
            return "", fmt.Errorf("not found: %s", path)
        case res.StatusCode != 200:
            return "", fmt.Errorf("GET %s: HTTP %d", path, res.StatusCode)
        }
        return string(body), nil
    }
    return "", errors.New("gave up after retries: " + path)
}

The robots matcher is about 50 lines. It reads the User-agent: * group and turns each rule into a regexp, so * matches anything and a trailing $ anchors the end:

// --- a tiny robots.txt matcher (User-agent: * group, * and $ wildcards) ---

type robotsRules struct{ allow, disallow []*regexp.Regexp }

var robots = &robotsRules{}

func loadRobots() error {
    req, _ := http.NewRequest("GET", base+"/robots.txt", nil)
    req.Header.Set("User-Agent", userAgent)
    res, err := client.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    defer res.Body.Close()
    if res.StatusCode != 200 {
        return fmt.Errorf("robots.txt: HTTP %d", res.StatusCode)
    }
    inStar := false
    sc := bufio.NewScanner(res.Body)
    for sc.Scan() {
        line := strings.TrimSpace(strings.SplitN(sc.Text(), "#", 2)[0])
        k, v, ok := strings.Cut(line, ":")
        if !ok {
            continue
        }
        k, v = strings.ToLower(strings.TrimSpace(k)), strings.TrimSpace(v)
        switch {
        case k == "user-agent":
            inStar = v == "*"
        case inStar && k == "disallow" && v != "":
            robots.disallow = append(robots.disallow, robotsPattern(v))
        case inStar && k == "allow" && v != "":
            robots.allow = append(robots.allow, robotsPattern(v))
        }
    }
    return sc.Err()
}

// robotsPattern turns "/*/followers$" into ^/[^?]*?/followers$ style regexps.
func robotsPattern(p string) *regexp.Regexp {
    anchored := strings.HasSuffix(p, "$")
    p = strings.TrimSuffix(p, "$")
    parts := strings.Split(p, "*")
    for i := range parts {
        parts[i] = regexp.QuoteMeta(parts[i])
    }
    re := "^" + strings.Join(parts, ".*")
    if anchored {
        re += "$"
    }
    return regexp.MustCompile(re)
}

func (r *robotsRules) Allowed(path string) bool {
    // Match on the path without the query string for $-anchored rules.
    p, _, _ := strings.Cut(path, "?")
    for _, a := range r.allow {
        if a.MatchString(p) {
            return true
        }
    }
    for _, d := range r.disallow {
        if d.MatchString(p) {
            return false
        }
    }
    return true
}

A test pins down the rules we care about. It runs against the live robots.txt:

package main

import (
    "errors"
    "testing"
)

func TestRobots(t *testing.T) {
    if err := loadRobots(); err != nil {
        t.Skip("no network:", err)
    }
    cases := map[string]bool{
        "/simplebits":                     true,
        "/simplebits?page=2":              true,
        "/simplebits/about":               true,
        "/simplebits/collections":         true,
        "/simplebits/followers":           false,
        "/simplebits/following":           false,
        "/simplebits/tags":                false,
        "/shots/123-Foo/comments":         false,
        "/shots/123-Foo/fans":             false,
        "/shots/week/2026-10-01":          false,
        "/shots/27755136-Measure-Twice-P": true,
    }
    for path, want := range cases {
        if got := robots.Allowed(path); got != want {
            t.Errorf("Allowed(%q) = %v, want %v", path, got, want)
        }
    }
}

func TestShotPageIsChallenged(t *testing.T) {
    if err := loadRobots(); err != nil {
        t.Skip("no network:", err)
    }
    _, err := getHTML("/shots/27755136-Measure-Twice-Print")
    t.Logf("shot page: %v", err)
    if err != nil && !errors.Is(err, ErrChallenged) {
        t.Errorf("unexpected error: %v", err)
    }
}

$ go test -v ./...
=== RUN   TestRobots
--- PASS: TestRobots (0.05s)
=== RUN   TestShotPageIsChallenged
    robots_test.go:37: shot page: blocked by AWS WAF challenge: /shots/27755136-Measure-Twice-Print
--- PASS: TestShotPageIsChallenged (0.07s)

Step 2: Small HTML helpers

golang.org/x/net/html gives you a parse tree but no selectors, so a few helpers go a long way. parseCount matters more than it looks: Dribbble shows views as 23.3k, and counts on the about page as 117,603.

package main

import (
    "strconv"
    "strings"

    "golang.org/x/net/html"
)

func parseDoc(s string) (*html.Node, error) { return html.Parse(strings.NewReader(s)) }

func attr(n *html.Node, key string) string {
    for _, a := range n.Attr {
        if a.Key == key {
            return a.Val
        }
    }
    return ""
}

func hasAttr(n *html.Node, key string) bool {
    for _, a := range n.Attr {
        if a.Key == key {
            return true
        }
    }
    return false
}

func hasClass(n *html.Node, class string) bool {
    if n.Type != html.ElementNode {
        return false
    }
    for _, c := range strings.Fields(attr(n, "class")) {
        if c == class {
            return true
        }
    }
    return false
}

// findAll walks the tree and returns every node matching pred.
func findAll(n *html.Node, pred func(*html.Node) bool) []*html.Node {
    var out []*html.Node
    var walk func(*html.Node)
    walk = func(n *html.Node) {
        if pred(n) {
            out = append(out, n)
        }
        for c := n.FirstChild; c != nil; c = c.NextSibling {
            walk(c)
        }
    }
    walk(n)
    return out
}

func first(n *html.Node, pred func(*html.Node) bool) *html.Node {
    if all := findAll(n, pred); len(all) > 0 {
        return all[0]
    }
    return nil
}

func byClass(c string) func(*html.Node) bool {
    return func(n *html.Node) bool { return hasClass(n, c) }
}

func byTag(tag string) func(*html.Node) bool {
    return func(n *html.Node) bool { return n.Type == html.ElementNode && n.Data == tag }
}

// text returns the whitespace-collapsed text content of a node (nil-safe).
func text(n *html.Node) string {
    if n == nil {
        return ""
    }
    var b strings.Builder
    var walk func(*html.Node)
    walk = func(n *html.Node) {
        if n.Type == html.TextNode {
            b.WriteString(n.Data + " ")
        }
        if n.Type == html.ElementNode && (n.Data == "script" || n.Data == "style" || n.Data == "svg") {
            return
        }
        for c := n.FirstChild; c != nil; c = c.NextSibling {
            walk(c)
        }
    }
    walk(n)
    return strings.Join(strings.Fields(b.String()), " ")
}

// parseCount turns "117,603", "23.3k", "1.2m" or "381" into an int.
func parseCount(s string) int {
    s = strings.ToLower(strings.TrimSpace(strings.ReplaceAll(s, ",", "")))
    mult := 1.0
    switch {
    case strings.HasSuffix(s, "k"):
        mult, s = 1_000, strings.TrimSuffix(s, "k")
    case strings.HasSuffix(s, "m"):
        mult, s = 1_000_000, strings.TrimSuffix(s, "m")
    }
    f, err := strconv.ParseFloat(s, 64)
    if err != nil {
        return 0
    }
    return int(f*mult + 0.5)
}

// leadingCount reads the number at the start of "223 Shots" or "117,603 followers".
func leadingCount(s string) int {
    f := strings.Fields(s)
    if len(f) == 0 {
        return 0
    }
    return parseCount(f[0])
}

Step 3: A designer profile

The /about page has everything: name, headline, bio, location, "Member since", Pro badge, skills, and follower counts. The trap is that there are (at least) two profile templates. On simplebits (Dan Cederholm, a Dribbble co-founder) the masthead shows "117,603 followers / 1,820 following / 46,450 likes". On Betraydan the masthead shows location and specializations instead, and there's no likes count at all. Both templates have a .profile-stats-section with count + meta spans, so the code reads followers from there and only takes likes when they're shown.

package main

import (
    "net/url"
    "regexp"
    "strings"

    "golang.org/x/net/html"
)

type Profile struct {
    Username    string   `json:"username"`
    Name        string   `json:"name"`
    Headline    string   `json:"headline"`
    Bio         string   `json:"bio"`
    Location    string   `json:"location"`
    MemberSince string   `json:"member_since"`
    Pro         bool     `json:"pro"`
    Followers   int      `json:"followers"`
    Following   int      `json:"following"`
    Likes       int      `json:"likes"` // 0 when the template doesn't show it
    Skills      []string `json:"skills"`
}

var usernameRe = regexp.MustCompile(`^[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9_-]{0,63}$`)

// normalizeUser accepts "simplebits", "@simplebits" or "https://dribbble.com/simplebits/about".
func normalizeUser(s string) string {
    s = strings.TrimPrefix(strings.TrimSpace(s), "@")
    if u, err := url.Parse(s); err == nil && u.Host != "" {
        s = strings.Split(strings.Trim(u.Path, "/"), "/")[0]
    }
    if !usernameRe.MatchString(s) {
        return ""
    }
    return s
}

// fetchProfile reads /<user>/about, which has everything the main profile page
// has in its masthead plus bio, location, "Member since" and skills.
func fetchProfile(user string) (Profile, error) {
    p := Profile{Username: user}
    page, err := getHTML("/" + user + "/about")
    if err != nil {
        return p, err
    }
    doc, err := parseDoc(page)
    if err != nil {
        return p, err
    }
    p.Name = text(first(doc, byClass("masthead-profile-name")))
    p.Headline = text(first(doc, byClass("masthead-intro")))

    if p.Headline == "" { // the second profile template shows specializations instead
        p.Headline = text(first(doc, byClass("masthead-profile-specializations")))
    }

    // Dribbble has (at least) two profile templates. Both have a
    // ".profile-stats-section" with <span class="count"> + <span class="meta">
    // pairs; only one also has "N likes" in ".masthead-stats".
    if sec := first(doc, byClass("profile-stats-section")); sec != nil {
        for _, a := range findAll(sec, byTag("a")) {
            n := leadingCount(text(first(a, byClass("count"))))
            switch text(first(a, byClass("meta"))) {
            case "followers":
                p.Followers = n
            case "following":
                p.Following = n
            }
        }
    }
    if stats := first(doc, byClass("masthead-stats")); stats != nil {
        for _, st := range findAll(stats, byClass("stat")) {
            if t := text(st); strings.HasSuffix(t, "likes") {
                p.Likes = leadingCount(t)
            }
        }
    }

    var bio []string
    for _, b := range findAll(doc, byClass("bio-text")) {
        bio = append(bio, text(b))
    }
    p.Bio = strings.Join(bio, "\n")

    // The info section is rendered twice (small screens and large), so take the first.
    p.Location = text(first(doc, byClass("location")))
    p.MemberSince = strings.TrimPrefix(text(first(doc, byClass("created"))), "Member since ")
    p.Pro = first(doc, func(n *html.Node) bool { return hasClass(n, "info-item") && hasClass(n, "pro") }) != nil

    if sec := first(doc, byClass("profile-skills-section")); sec != nil {
        for _, a := range findAll(sec, byTag("a")) {
            if s := attr(a, "data-skill"); s != "" {
                p.Skills = append(p.Skills, s)
            }
        }
    }
    return p, nil
}
