Two things you won't get logged out: social links and email. They sit behind "Get in touch", which opens a signup dialog. That's fine. That's the designer's choice.

Step 4: Shots, page by page

extractJSONVar finds var newestShots = and hands the rest of the page to json.Decoder. The decoder stops at the end of the JSON value, so there's no need for a fragile regexp to find the closing ].

Thumbnails are lazy-loaded: the <img src> is a 1×1 GIF, and the real URL is in data-src (and in a <noscript> copy). If your scraper saves src, you get 24 transparent pixels.

package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

// Shot is what the profile page ships in `var newestShots = [...]`,
// plus the thumbnail we read from the HTML grid.
type Shot struct {
    ID          int64  `json:"id"`
    Title       string `json:"title"`
    Path        string `json:"path"`
    PublishedAt string `json:"published_at"` // "September 23, 2026"
    Rebounds    int    `json:"rebounds_count"`
    Attachments int    `json:"attachments_count"`
    ViewsRaw    string `json:"view_count"`  // "23.3k" (rounded!)
    LikesRaw    string `json:"likes_count"` // "108"
    Views       int    `json:"-"`
    Likes       int    `json:"-"`
    Thumbnail   string `json:"-"`
}

func (s Shot) URL() string { return base + s.Path }

func (s Shot) Published() time.Time {
    t, _ := time.Parse("January 2, 2006", s.PublishedAt)
    return t
}

// extractJSONVar finds `var <name> = ` in a page and decodes the JSON value
// that follows. json.Decoder stops at the end of the value, so we don't need
// to guess where the array ends.
func extractJSONVar(page, name string, out any) error {
    marker := "var " + name + " = "
    i := strings.Index(page, marker)
    if i < 0 {
        return fmt.Errorf("%q not found (markup changed?)", marker)
    }
    return json.NewDecoder(strings.NewReader(page[i+len(marker):])).Decode(out)
}

// fetchShotsPage reads one page of /<user>?page=N. Logged out, each page has 24 shots.
func fetchShotsPage(user string, page int) (shots []Shot, hasNext bool, err error) {
    body, err := getHTML(fmt.Sprintf("/%s?page=%d", user, page))
    if err != nil {
        return nil, false, err
    }
    if err := extractJSONVar(body, "newestShots", &shots); err != nil {
        return nil, false, err
    }

    // Thumbnails are lazy-loaded: src is a 1x1 GIF, the real URL is in data-src.
    thumbs := map[string]string{}
    if doc, err := parseDoc(body); err == nil {
        for _, li := range findAll(doc, byClass("shot-thumbnail")) {
            id := attr(li, "data-thumbnail-id")
            if img := first(li, byTag("img")); img != nil && id != "" {
                src := attr(img, "data-src")
                if src == "" {
                    src = attr(img, "src")
                }
                thumbs[id] = strings.Split(src, "?")[0]
            }
        }
    }
    for i := range shots {
        shots[i].Views = parseCount(shots[i].ViewsRaw)
        shots[i].Likes = parseCount(shots[i].LikesRaw)
        shots[i].Thumbnail = thumbs[fmt.Sprint(shots[i].ID)]
    }
    hasNext = strings.Contains(body, `class="next_page"`) && strings.Contains(body, `rel="next"`)
    return shots, hasNext, nil
}

// fetchShots pages through a profile until maxPages, an empty page, or no "Next" link.
func fetchShots(user string, maxPages int) ([]Shot, error) {
    var all []Shot
    seen := map[int64]bool{}
    for page := 1; page <= maxPages; page++ {
        batch, hasNext, err := fetchShotsPage(user, page)
        if err != nil {
            return all, err
        }
        added := 0
        for _, s := range batch {
            if !seen[s.ID] { // pages can overlap if a new shot is posted mid-crawl
                seen[s.ID] = true
                all = append(all, s)
                added++
            }
        }
        if added == 0 || !hasNext {
            break
        }
    }
    return all, nil
}

Step 5: Collections

Collections are curated sets of other people's shots. A designer's /collections page lists them 6 at a time, and ?page=2 gives the next 6. Each one is an li.shots-group-item with a name, a shot count, and a designer count:

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "net/url"
    "regexp"
    "strings"

    "golang.org/x/net/html"
)

type Collection struct {
    ID        string `json:"id"`
    Name      string `json:"name"`
    URL       string `json:"url"`
    Shots     int    `json:"shots"`
    Designers int    `json:"designers"`
}

// fetchCollections reads /<user>/collections?page=N (6 per page, logged out).
func fetchCollections(user string, maxPages int) ([]Collection, error) {
    var all []Collection
    for page := 1; page <= maxPages; page++ {
        body, err := getHTML(fmt.Sprintf("/%s/collections?page=%d", user, page))
        if err != nil {
            return all, err
        }
        doc, err := parseDoc(body)
        if err != nil {
            return all, err
        }
        items := findAll(doc, byClass("shots-group-item"))
        for _, li := range items {
            c := Collection{ID: attr(li, "data-id"), Name: text(first(li, byClass("collection-name")))}
            if a := first(li, byClass("shots-group")); a != nil {
                c.URL = base + attr(a, "href")
            }
            c.Shots = leadingCount(text(first(li, byClass("shots-count"))))
            c.Designers = leadingCount(text(first(li, byClass("designers-count"))))
            all = append(all, c)
        }
        if len(items) == 0 {
            break
        }
    }
    return all, nil
}

A single collection page uses newer markup (shot2-item), 24 shots per page. Here the title and path are attributes on a <drb-shot-metadata> custom element, which is nicer than digging through text. The author is the profile link inside the details block.

type CollectionShot struct {
    ID         string
    Title      string
    URL        string
    Author     string // profile path, e.g. "Betraydan"
    AuthorName string
    Likes      int
    Views      int
    Thumbnail  string
}

type CollectionPage struct {
    Name      string
    Curator   string
    Shots     int
    Designers int
    Items     []CollectionShot
}

var collectionPath = regexp.MustCompile(`^/[A-Za-z0-9_-]+/collections/\d+(-[^/]*)?$`)

// fetchCollection reads one collection (24 shots per page) from a full URL.
func fetchCollection(raw string, maxPages int) (CollectionPage, error) {
    var out CollectionPage
    u, err := url.Parse(raw)
    if err != nil || !collectionPath.MatchString(u.Path) {
        return out, fmt.Errorf("want https://dribbble.com/<user>/collections/<id>-<slug>, got %q", raw)
    }
    seen := map[string]bool{}
    for page := 1; page <= maxPages; page++ {
        body, err := getHTML(fmt.Sprintf("%s?page=%d", u.Path, page))
        if err != nil {
            return out, err
        }
        doc, err := parseDoc(body)
        if err != nil {
            return out, err
        }
        if page == 1 {
            out.Name = text(first(doc, byClass("collection-page__title")))
            out.Curator = text(first(doc, byClass("curator__name")))
            for _, v := range findAll(doc, byClass("collection-page__meta-details-value")) {
                t := text(v)
                switch {
                case strings.HasSuffix(t, "Shots"):
                    out.Shots = leadingCount(t)
                case strings.HasSuffix(t, "Designers"):
                    out.Designers = leadingCount(t)
                }
            }
        }
        added := 0
        for _, it := range findAll(doc, byClass("shot2-item")) {
            id := attr(it, "data-id")
            if id == "" || seen[id] {
                continue
            }
            seen[id] = true
            added++
            s := CollectionShot{ID: id}
            if m := first(it, byTag("drb-shot-metadata")); m != nil {
                s.Title, s.URL = attr(m, "title"), base+attr(m, "path")
            }
            if img := first(it, byTag("img")); img != nil {
                s.Thumbnail = strings.Split(attr(img, "src"), "?")[0]
            }
            if d := first(it, byClass("shot2-item-details__user-container")); d != nil {
                if a := first(d, byTag("a")); a != nil {
                    s.Author = strings.Trim(attr(a, "href"), "/")
                }
                s.AuthorName = text(first(d, byClass("shot2-item-details__user-name")))
            }
            // Stats: the like count sits in [data-shot-like-count]; views are the
            // text of the last ".shot2-item-stats__item".
            stats := findAll(it, byClass("shot2-item-stats__item"))
            if lc := first(it, func(n *html.Node) bool { return hasAttr(n, "data-shot-like-count") }); lc != nil {
                s.Likes = parseCount(text(lc))
            }
            if len(stats) > 0 {
                s.Views = parseCount(text(stats[len(stats)-1]))
            }
            out.Items = append(out.Items, s)
        }
        if added == 0 {
            break
        }
    }
    return out, nil
}

Step 6: A portfolio tracker

Point-in-time numbers aren't very interesting. Changes are. track appends one row per profile to profiles.csv and one row per shot to shots.csv, all with the same snapshot_at. report compares each designer's last two snapshots: follower change, the shots that gained the most likes, and shots that are new since the previous run.

package main

import (
    "encoding/csv"
    "fmt"
    "os"
    "path/filepath"
    "sort"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

// appendCSV appends rows to path, writing the header first if the file is new.
func appendCSV(path string, header []string, rows [][]string) error {
    _, statErr := os.Stat(path)
    f, err := os.OpenFile(path, os.O_CREATE|os.O_APPEND|os.O_WRONLY, 0o644)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    defer f.Close()
    w := csv.NewWriter(f)
    if os.IsNotExist(statErr) {
        w.Write(header)
    }
    w.WriteAll(rows)
    return w.Error()
}

// track takes one snapshot of each profile and its newest shots.
func track(dir string, users []string, pages int) error {
    if err := os.MkdirAll(dir, 0o755); err != nil {
        return err
    }
    now := time.Now().UTC().Format(time.RFC3339)
    for _, user := range users {
        p, err := fetchProfile(user)
        if err != nil {
            fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "%s: %v\n", user, err)
            continue
        }
        shots, err := fetchShots(user, pages)
        if err != nil {
            fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "%s shots: %v\n", user, err)
        }
        err = appendCSV(filepath.Join(dir, "profiles.csv"),
            []string{"snapshot_at", "username", "followers", "following", "likes", "shots_seen"},
            [][]string{{now, user, strconv.Itoa(p.Followers), strconv.Itoa(p.Following), strconv.Itoa(p.Likes), strconv.Itoa(len(shots))}})
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        var rows [][]string
        for _, s := range shots {
            rows = append(rows, []string{now, user, strconv.FormatInt(s.ID, 10), s.Title,
                s.Published().Format("2006-01-02"), strconv.Itoa(s.Likes), strconv.Itoa(s.Views), s.URL()})
        }
        if err := appendCSV(filepath.Join(dir, "shots.csv"),
            []string{"snapshot_at", "username", "shot_id", "title", "published", "likes", "views", "url"}, rows); err != nil {
            return err
        }
        fmt.Printf("%-16s followers %d · likes %d · %d shots snapshotted\n", user, p.Followers, p.Likes, len(shots))
    }
    return nil
}

report reads both CSVs back, groups rows by user and snapshot time, and diffs the last two snapshots:

func readCSV(path string) ([][]string, error) {
    f, err := os.Open(path)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    defer f.Close()
    rows, err := csv.NewReader(f).ReadAll()
    if len(rows) > 0 {
        rows = rows[1:] // drop header
    }
    return rows, err
}

// report compares the two most recent snapshots per user.
func report(dir string) error {
    profiles, err := readCSV(filepath.Join(dir, "profiles.csv"))
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    shots, err := readCSV(filepath.Join(dir, "shots.csv"))
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    snaps := map[string][]string{} // user -> snapshot times, oldest first
    follow := map[string]int{}     // user|time -> followers
    for _, r := range profiles {
        snaps[r[1]] = append(snaps[r[1]], r[0])
        follow[r[1]+"|"+r[0]], _ = strconv.Atoi(r[2])
    }
    likes := map[string]int{} // user|time|shot -> likes
    titles := map[string]string{}
    for _, r := range shots {
        likes[r[1]+"|"+r[0]+"|"+r[2]], _ = strconv.Atoi(r[5])
        titles[r[2]] = r[3]
    }
    users := make([]string, 0, len(snaps))
    for u := range snaps {
        users = append(users, u)
    }
    sort.Strings(users)
    for _, u := range users {
        ts := snaps[u]
        if len(ts) < 2 {
            fmt.Printf("%s: only one snapshot so far\n", u)
            continue
        }
        prev, cur := ts[len(ts)-2], ts[len(ts)-1]
        fmt.Printf("%s  %s → %s\n  followers %+d\n", u, prev[:16], cur[:16], follow[u+"|"+cur]-follow[u+"|"+prev])
        type gain struct {
            id string
            d  int
        }
        var gains []gain
        var fresh []string
        for k, v := range likes {
            parts := strings.SplitN(k, "|", 3)
            user, t, id := parts[0], parts[1], parts[2]
            if user != u || t != cur {
                continue
            }
            if old, ok := likes[u+"|"+prev+"|"+id]; ok {
                if v != old {
                    gains = append(gains, gain{id, v - old})
                }
            } else {
                fresh = append(fresh, titles[id]) // not in the previous snapshot
            }
        }
        sort.Slice(gains, func(i, j int) bool { return gains[i].d > gains[j].d })
        if len(gains) == 0 {
            fmt.Println("  no like changes on tracked shots")
        }
        for _, g := range gains[:min(3, len(gains))] {
            fmt.Printf("  %+5d likes  %s\n", g.d, titles[g.id])
        }
        for _, t := range fresh {
            fmt.Printf("  new shot: %s\n", t)
        }
    }
    return nil
}

package main

import (
    "encoding/csv"
    "encoding/json"
    "flag"
    "fmt"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
)

func main() {
    if len(os.Args) < 2 {
        fmt.Println("usage: dribbblescraper profile|shots|collections|collection|track|report [flags] args")
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    cmd := os.Args[1]
    fs := flag.NewFlagSet(cmd, flag.ExitOnError)
    pages := fs.Int("pages", 2, "max pages to fetch")
    out := fs.String("out", "", "CSV output file (shots) or directory (track/report)")
    fs.Parse(os.Args[2:])

    if err := loadRobots(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "can't read robots.txt, refusing to crawl:", err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    if err := run(cmd, fs.Args(), *pages, *out); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

func run(cmd string, args []string, pages int, out string) error {
    if len(args) == 0 && cmd != "report" {
        return fmt.Errorf("%s: missing argument", cmd)
    }
    if (cmd == "profile" || cmd == "shots" || cmd == "collections") && normalizeUser(args[0]) == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("%q is not a Dribbble username or profile URL", args[0])
    }
    switch cmd {
    case "profile":
        p, err := fetchProfile(normalizeUser(args[0]))
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        b, _ := json.MarshalIndent(p, "", "  ")
        fmt.Println(string(b))

    case "shots":
        user := normalizeUser(args[0])
        shots, err := fetchShots(user, pages)
        if err != nil && len(shots) == 0 {
            return err
        }
        fmt.Printf("%d shots from %d page(s) of %s\n", len(shots), pages, user)
        for _, s := range shots[:min(5, len(shots))] {
            fmt.Printf("  %s  %5d ♥ %7d views  %s\n", s.Published().Format("2006-01-02"), s.Likes, s.Views, s.Title)
        }
        if out != "" {
            return writeShotsCSV(out, shots)
        }

    case "collections":
        cs, err := fetchCollections(normalizeUser(args[0]), pages)
        if err != nil && len(cs) == 0 {
            return err
        }
        for _, c := range cs {
            fmt.Printf("  %-22s %4d shots · %4d designers  %s\n", c.Name, c.Shots, c.Designers, c.URL)
        }

    case "collection":
        c, err := fetchCollection(args[0], pages)
        if err != nil && len(c.Items) == 0 {
            return err
        }
        fmt.Printf("%s, curated by %s: %d shots by %d designers (%d fetched)\n", c.Name, c.Curator, c.Shots, c.Designers, len(c.Items))
        for _, s := range c.Items[:min(5, len(c.Items))] {
            fmt.Printf("  %5d ♥ %7d views  %-28s by %s\n", s.Likes, s.Views, s.Title, s.Author)
        }

    case "track":
        if out == "" {
            out = "portfolio"
        }
        var users []string
        for _, a := range args {
            if u := normalizeUser(a); u != "" {
                users = append(users, u)
            }
        }
        return track(out, users, pages)

    case "report":
        if out == "" {
            out = "portfolio"
        }
        return report(out)

    default:
        return fmt.Errorf("unknown command %q", cmd)
    }
    return nil
}

func writeShotsCSV(path string, shots []Shot) error {
    f, err := os.Create(path)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    defer f.Close()
    w := csv.NewWriter(f)
    w.Write([]string{"id", "published", "title", "likes", "views", "views_raw", "rebounds", "url", "thumbnail"})
    for _, s := range shots {
        w.Write([]string{strconv.FormatInt(s.ID, 10), s.Published().Format("2006-01-02"), strings.TrimSpace(s.Title),
            strconv.Itoa(s.Likes), strconv.Itoa(s.Views), s.ViewsRaw, strconv.Itoa(s.Rebounds), s.URL(), s.Thumbnail})
    }
    w.Flush()
    return w.Error()
}

Pitfalls, in one place

  • The Dribbble API is for your own account. v2 only returns the authenticated user's shots. No public endpoints for other designers.
  • Terms of Service. Dribbble's terms prohibit scraping. robots.txt allowing a page doesn't change that. Keep it small, slow, and non-commercial.
  • Shot pages, popular, and search are behind AWS WAF. You get 202 plus x-amzn-waf-action: challenge. Stop there. Profile and collection grids already have titles, likes, and views.
  • robots.txt forbids followers, following, tags, comments, fans, and rebounds. Check every path, not just the first one.
  • The old RSS feeds are gone. /<user>.rss and /shots.rss return 404, and /shots/popular.rss is challenged.
  • Two profile templates. Followers live in different places, and likes are missing on one. Test with more than one designer.
  • Lazy-loaded images. src is a 1×1 GIF; use data-src.
  • Counts are rounded. 23.3k views. Keep the raw string.
  • Dates are display strings. published_at is "September 23, 2026", with no time or time zone. Parse with "January 2, 2006" and treat it as a day.
  • Pages can shift. If a designer posts while you crawl, page 2 can repeat a shot from page 1. De-duplicate by shot ID.
  • The markup will change. The shots JSON and the custom elements (drb-shot-metadata, data-shot-like-count) are steadier than layout classes, but none of this is a contract.

When you'd rather not maintain the parsers

If you need more than a few designers, or you just don't want to fix two profile templates every time Dribbble ships a redesign, I also run ScrapeAtlas*, which has four Dribbble endpoints that return JSON for the same public pages:

Endpoint Params Returns
GET /v1/dribbble/profile username (or a profile URL) profile: name, headline, bio, location, followersCount, followingCount, likesCount, skills, languages, website, socialLinks, isPro, isTeam
GET /v1/dribbble/shots username, page (1-100) shots[] with title, thumbnailUrl, videoUrl, author, likesCount, viewsCount, plus pagination.nextPage
GET /v1/dribbble/collections username, page collections[] with name, shotsCount, designersCount, thumbnailUrls
GET /v1/dribbble/collection url (a /<user>/collections/<id>-<slug> URL), page collection (name, description, owner, counts) and one page of shots[]

Auth is an x-api-key header. Each successful request costs one credit, and failed requests cost nothing:

req, _ := http.NewRequest("GET", "https://api.scrapeatlas.com/v1/dribbble/shots?username=simplebits&page=2", nil)
req.Header.Set("x-api-key", os.Getenv("SCRAPEATLAS_API_KEY"))
res, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
// Response: {"success":true,"status":"success"|"partial", "shots":[...],
//            "pagination":{"page":2,"nextPage":3},
//            "coverage":{"complete":false,"warnings":["metrics_unavailable"]}}

Read status and coverage.warnings. When a page doesn't show likes or views, likesCount/viewsCount come back as null with a metrics_unavailable warning instead of a made-up 0. That's the same honesty you want from your own scraper. It reads the same public pages as the DIY version, so it doesn't give you follower lists, comments, or anything robots.txt rules out.

For a handful of designers you track daily, though, the DIY scraper above is enough.

Wrapping up

  • The official Dribbble API is your-account-only. Great for showing your own shots on your site, no help for research.
  • Profiles and collections are server-rendered. Shots come as embedded JSON (newestShots), and ?page=N still works logged out.
  • Respect the walls. robots.txt rules out followers, tags, comments, and fans; AWS WAF guards shot pages and search. Stop, don't bypass.
  • Expect two templates, lazy images, and rounded counts.
  • Track changes, not snapshots. A tiny daily cron job turns a scraper into a portfolio tracker.

What would you track on Dribbble: your own shots, a list of designers you'd like to hire, or which topics get the most likes? Tell me in the comments.

*I build it.

title: MotorSense: A Video-EMG Dataset of Motoric Representations for Action Understanding
description:
arXiv:2610.41127v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Computer vision models learn hand action only from its visual consequences, without access to the underlying embodied motor signals. We address this absence with MotorSense, the first large-scale paired egocentric video and surface electromyography (EMG) dataset. MotorSense pairs bimanual EMG bands with egocentric video and yields synchronized video, bimanual EMG and IMU, and audio across 100 hours of unscripted manipulation. EMG offers a powerful scalable alternative to manual annotation: it captures finger movement, hand configuration, and the forces exerted between hand and environment as a dense signal free of occlusion and labeler bias, whereas manual annotation is costly, subjective, and unreliable under occlusion. We use MotorSense to learn sensorimotor alignment, producing an organization of action that is shared across the visual and motoric spaces, through cross-modal pre-training between video and EMG. The resultant vision models are then transferred to downstream tasks that benefit from sensorimotor alignment: in this case, action recognition, 3D hand reconstruction, and 3D contact reconstruction. We further demonstrate a generative application in which EMG motor signals are used to condition a video diffusion model, yielding videos of fine-grained hand manipulation. Across four action-centric computer vision tasks and eight popular video datasets, we demonstrate that sensorimotor alignment provides a stronger foundation for visual representation learning than conventional self-supervised learning methods over video, outperforming every baseline across all tasks and datasets evaluated.

title: Apriel Voice 27B Preview: An Open Model for Speech, Reasoning, and Tool Use
description:
arXiv:2610.40738v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: A capable voice assistant must do more than recognize words; it must understand requests, reason over context, sustain conversations, and act through tools. We present Apriel Voice 27B Preview, an open speech-language model that unifies these capabilities within a shared reasoning backbone while retaining text and image input modalities. Built on the post-trained Gemma 4 26B-A4B checkpoint, Apriel Voice directly processes speech and generates both responses and tool calls without requiring a separate dialogue model. We introduce a two-stage training procedure to adapt the model to speech. The first stage establishes the speech interface, while the second jointly adapts the projector and backbone through supervised fine-tuning, text replay, and source-dependent cross-entropy and forward Kullback--Leibler divergence supervision. Automatically constructed speech-conditioned dialogues provide conversational training data, while local teacher serving, overlapping teacher and student computation, and fused full-vocabulary losses enable efficient online distillation. In thinking mode, Apriel Voice achieves a score of 98.90 on Big Bench Audio, 81.13 on Speech-BFCL, and a task success rate of 65.51% on $\tau$-Voice, with a mean latency of 1.91 seconds. It also achieves 51.27% English EVA accuracy and 74.13% experience pass@1. Finally, we deploy Apriel Voice 27B Preview on a custom serving platform to support interactive voice interactions.

title: KV-Cache Patching: Tracing How and Where Fine-Tuned Behaviors Arise
description:
arXiv:2610.41480v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Fine-tuning a language model changes how it responds, but where is this fine-tuned behavior instantiated? To better understand this, we evaluate whether the change in model behavior arises only during the generation of the answer tokens where the change manifests, or whether altered processing of previous tokens causes it via the attention mechanism. For this, we patch the KV cache from a LoRA fine-tuned model into the unmodified base model, and vice versa. Our results show that for some behaviors, like responding in German or emergent misalignment, patching the KV cache can indeed transfer them from the fine-tuned to the base model. Correspondingly, patching the KV cache from base to fine-tune can partially or fully remove fine-tuned behavior. Furthermore, we find that the effect of patching grows with how much of the KV cache is patched and concentrates at a few pivotal positions, with system-prompt and chat-template tokens having disproportionate influence.

title: CVE-2026-105483: when an IPv4 address is checked as a DNS name
description:
CVE-2026-105483: when an IPv4 address is checked as a DNS name

Node.js applications often treat an IP address as the least ambiguous destination possible. CVE-2026-105483 shows why that assumption deserves scrutiny. In affected 24.x and 26.x releases, tls.checkServerIdentity() can evaluate a host written with fullwidth digits as a DNS name even though the same host normalizes and resolves to an IPv4 address. A certificate containing a matching DNS subject alternative name can then authenticate the connection without an IP address SAN.

The Node.js project published the fix in 24.22.1 and 26.12.1 on October 21, 2026. It rates the bug High. The GitHub advisory records CVSS v3.0 7.4 with network access, high attack complexity, no privileges or user interaction, and high confidentiality and integrity impact. The weakness is CWE-295, improper certificate validation.

The identity mismatch

TLS hostname verification asks a narrower question than DNS resolution. The client must decide what kind of identity it intended to contact, then compare the peer certificate with that identity. For a name, a DNS SAN is appropriate. For an IP address, the certificate should carry a matching IP address SAN.

The vulnerable path classified a fullwidth-digit host as something other than an IP address. It still normalized and resolved the host as IPv4. Verification then checked DNS names and the certificate Common Name. An attacker who can present a trusted certificate with a numeric DNS SAN could therefore satisfy the wrong identity check.

This is a regression introduced after the fix for CVE-2026-48618. The relevant distinction isn't whether the connection eventually uses TCP over IPv4. It is whether certificate verification understands that the endpoint is an IP address at the point where identity policy is applied.

Conditions for exploitation

Several conditions must align:

  • The client runs an affected Node.js 24.x or 26.x release.
  • The application connects to a host represented with fullwidth digits.
  • The host resolves to the IPv4 endpoint controlled by, or reachable by, the attacker.
  • The server certificate chains to a CA trusted by the client.
  • The certificate contains a DNS SAN matching the normalized address, such as 127.0.0.1 or an applicable wildcard, and no matching IP SAN is required.

An internet-facing Node.js process is not automatically vulnerable. The application must place the affected hostname flow in a security-relevant path. Common examples include user-supplied callback URLs, connector configuration, proxy targets, or integrations that accept destination addresses from another system. A hard-coded DNS name with ordinary TLS handling may never exercise the bug.

Impact

Successful exploitation defeats the identity binding TLS is expected to provide. The client can establish a session with an unintended endpoint while treating the peer certificate as valid. That can expose request data, credentials carried inside the session, and response integrity. The advisory assigns high confidentiality and integrity impact, though availability impact is absent.

The existence of a trusted certificate does not imply that the attacker is a public CA or that every internal CA is affected in the same way. The practical question is whether the client trusts a certificate chain that contains the attacker's chosen identity. Internal PKI, test CAs, and delegated certificate issuance can alter that answer.

Affected scope

The official advisory limits affected versions to Node.js 24.x before 24.22.1 and 26.x before 26.12.1. The same October release also fixed issues in the 22.x line, but this CVE is not listed as affecting 22.x. Teams should read the full release notes instead of applying one version rule to every CVE from that date.

Applications that share a supported but older runtime through containers, embedded runtimes, or managed build images need the same check. A package manifest can say one version while the deployed process executes another. Record the runtime reported by the actual process and the image digest used to deploy it.

Exposure context

On November 2, 2026 at 04:17 +08:00, ZoomEye Search app="Node.js" returned 5,539,674 product-fingerprint matches. Filter vul.cve="CVE-2026-105483" returned zero. Exposure is the larger selected count and represents Node.js fingerprints, not confirmed vulnerable deployments.

That distinction matters for prioritization. The count can help identify a broad technology population, but it cannot establish the running version, the application's TLS destination policy, or the trust anchors in use. Version and code-path evidence remain necessary.

Remediation

Upgrade to Node.js 24.22.1 or 26.12.1, or a later release on a supported line. Rebuild container images and redistributed binaries so old runtimes are not reintroduced during deployment. Verify the runtime inside the running application and the build artifact, not just the source dependency declaration.

As a temporary reduction measure, reject user-controlled non-ASCII host strings and require canonical ASCII DNS names or canonical IPv4 addresses before the TLS client is invoked. This can narrow the affected input path, but it is not a substitute for the patched runtime. Review custom certificate verification callbacks because bypassing the standard check can preserve a separate identity flaw.

Assurance

Add a regression test with an isolated test CA and a certificate that contains a numeric DNS SAN but no matching IP SAN. The fixed runtime should reject that certificate when the destination is an IP endpoint. Test the deployed binary, not only application code, and retain the fixture so a future dependency rollback fails visibly.

References

  • Node.js October 21, 2026 Security Releases
  • Node.js 24.22.1 release notes
  • Node.js 26.12.1 release notes
  • GitHub Advisory GHSA-8h4p-qpcq-gq24
  • ZoomEye Search

title: Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite: Ein Vokabelquiz als erstes API-Projekt
description:
Google stellte Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite am 17. Juni 2025 als Vorschau vor. Am 22. Juli folgte die stabile Version. Innerhalb der Gemini-2.5-Familie lag der Schwerpunkt bei der Veröffentlichung auf Geschwindigkeit und Kosteneffizienz, etwa für Übersetzung und Klassifikation. [1][2]

Wer bereits eine einfache API-Anfrage senden kann, braucht als nächsten Schritt oft eine überschaubare Anwendung. Für diesen Versuch habe ich zehn vorbereitete Vokabelfragen über die Crazyrouter API an gemini-2.5-flash-lite geschickt. Daraus sollte eine einzelne HTML-Datei mit Antwortauswahl, Punkten und einer Wiederholung der falsch beantworteten Fragen entstehen.

Das Projekt hat einen klaren Übergang: Bis zur Antwort arbeite ich mit einer Modell-API, danach mit einer lokalen Webseite. Die erste Version enthielt die wesentlichen Abläufe; fehlende Details habe ich direkt in der Datei ergänzt.

Warum das mit Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite erstellte Quiz ohne API läuft

Ein Modell verarbeitet Eingaben und erzeugt Antworten. Eine Chat-App stellt dafür eine Oberfläche bereit; über eine API können andere Programme dieselbe Art von Anfrage stellen.

In diesem Projekt erzeugte Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite die HTML-Struktur, die Gestaltung und die Spiellogik. Crazyrouter war der verwendete API-Zugang. Der Browser führt die fertige Datei aus. Beim späteren Beantworten der Fragen findet keine weitere Modellanfrage statt.

Die HTML-Datei im Repository kann als index.html heruntergeladen und lokal geöffnet werden. Sie enthält einen festen Fragenkatalog. Ein Neuladen erzeugt keine neuen Aufgaben; Lernstände werden zwischen Besuchen nicht gespeichert.

Wer später Fragen bei jedem Durchlauf erzeugen lassen möchte, benötigt zusätzlich einen Aufruf auf dem Server, eine Prüfung der neuen Aufgaben und eine Begrenzung der Nutzung. Das wäre ein anderes Projekt als die hier geprüfte statische Datei.

Für die erste Version konnte ich mich deshalb auf die Datei konzentrieren: Fragen anzeigen, Antworten auswerten und eine neue Runde starten.

Laut Google kann das Modell Text, Bilder, Video, Audio und PDF als Eingaben verarbeiten. Die Ausgabe ist Text. Welche Formate und Parameter ein bestimmter Anbieter tatsächlich unterstützt, muss zusätzlich geprüft werden. Bilder verstehen zu können bedeutet bei diesem Modell also nicht, Bilder erzeugen zu können. [3]

Eine Webseite lässt sich trotzdem generieren: HTML, CSS und JavaScript bestehen aus Text. Daraus kann der Browser Fragen, Schaltflächen und eine Punkteanzeige darstellen.

Weitere mögliche Einstiegsaufgaben sind das Sortieren von Nachrichten, das Herausziehen bestimmter Angaben aus einem Dokument oder das Aufbereiten einer Mitteilung. Google nennt Klassifikation und einfache Datenextraktion als Einsatzbereiche. Diese Aufgaben wurden hier nicht mitgetestet; der konkrete Versuch betrifft nur das Vokabelquiz. [3]

Die Anfrage an Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite und die erzeugte Datei

Die Quiz-Demo enthält zehn englische Fragen mit jeweils vier Antwortmöglichkeiten. Eine richtige Antwort bringt zehn Punkte, eine falsche null. Nach einer Runde lassen sich die Antworten ansehen oder nur die Fehler wiederholen.

Die englischen Sätze üben unter anderem den Unterschied zwischen „borrow“ und „lend“. Fragen, richtige Antworten und Erklärungen standen vor der Generierung fest. Das Modell sollte diese Inhalte in eine Anwendung einbauen. Der Versuch bewertet deshalb nicht, wie gut es selbstständig neue Lernaufgaben erstellt.

Die ursprünglichen Anweisungen waren auf Chinesisch. Auch die Schaltflächen, Übersetzungen und Erklärungen der Demo sind weiterhin in vereinfachtem Chinesisch. „开始闯关“ startet das Quiz, „下一题“ führt zur nächsten Frage und „查看成绩“ zeigt das Ergebnis. Dieser Artikel ist keine zusätzliche Messung mit einem deutschen Prompt und keine deutsche Version der Spieloberfläche.

Für das Verhalten habe ich konkrete Regeln vorgegeben: Eine Frage darf nur einmal gewertet werden. Ohne Antwort darf man nicht weitergehen. Eine neue Runde muss den alten Punktestand löschen. Bei der Fehlerwiederholung sollen sich sowohl die Anzahl der Fragen als auch die maximal erreichbaren Punkte anpassen.

Aus „Baue ein Quiz“ wurde so eine Reihe prüfbarer Erwartungen. Wer drei Fragen falsch beantwortet, sollte anschließend drei Fragen mit höchstens dreißig Punkten üben können.

Am 2. November 2026 wurde eine Generierungsanfrage an die Chat-Completions-Schnittstelle von Crazyrouter gesendet. Das verwendete Modell war gemini-2.5-flash-lite. Die Antwort kam mit HTTP 200 zurück, der Abschlussgrund war stop, und die Ausgabe war nicht durch das Längenlimit abgeschnitten. Bis zur vollständigen Antwort vergingen rund 18,1 Sekunden.

Die Anfrage verwendete temperature mit dem Wert 0.3, max_tokens mit 9000 und stream mit false. Die gemessene Zeit gehört zu genau dieser einen Anfrage. Sie enthält keine anschließenden Korrekturen und ist keine Aussage über typische Antwortzeiten.

Nach dieser Antwort war die Generierung abgeschlossen. Ob der Punktestand beim Neustart verschwindet, musste sich anschließend im Verhalten der Datei zeigen.

Das Quiz von Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite: Rückmeldungen prüfen und ergänzen

Bei einem Quiz kann man den Zustand vor und nach jeder Aktion beschreiben. Vor der Antwort sind die Optionen verfügbar. Nach der Antwort ist die Entscheidung gesperrt, die Rückmeldung sichtbar und der Wechsel zur nächsten Frage möglich. Am Ende der Runde werden die gesammelten Antworten ausgewertet.

Die entscheidende Prüfung betraf danach die Anwendung. In den Skripttests ergaben zehn richtige Antworten 100 Punkte, zehn falsche null und sieben richtige siebzig. Die Wiederholung nach drei Fehlern umfasste drei Fragen mit einem Maximum von dreißig Punkten. Mehrfaches Auswählen derselben Antwort brachte keine zusätzlichen Punkte.

Die Zahlen stimmten in diesen Fällen. Bei der Rückmeldung an die Spieler fehlten jedoch noch vier Dinge:

Lücke in der ersten Version Lokale Korrektur
Die letzte Frage hatte weiterhin eine Beschriftung für „Nächste Frage“ Die Schaltfläche kündigt jetzt die Ergebnisansicht an
In der Rückschau fehlten die Erklärungen Jede Frage erhielt ihre zugehörige Erklärung
Bei einer perfekten Runde fehlte ein eindeutiger Hinweis Die Seite teilt mit, dass es keine Fehler zu wiederholen gibt
Die Rückmeldung nannte das richtige Wort nicht direkt in der Überschrift Das Lösungswort steht nun auch dort

Diese Änderungen erfolgten lokal, ohne eine weitere Modellanfrage. Zusätzlich wurden Zustandsprüfungen, die Tastaturbedienung und die Gestaltung für schmale Ansichten angepasst. Die verlinkte Demo enthält diese Korrekturen.

Danach bestanden alle elf automatisierten Prüfungen. Sie liefen mit jsdom, einer simulierten Umgebung für Seitenelemente und Skripte. Geprüft wurden unter anderem Punkte, wiederholte Eingaben, Neustart, Fehlerwiederholung und Erklärungen. Darstellung und Touch-Bedienung in echten Browsern sind damit nicht abgedeckt; diese Prüfungen sind noch offen.

Das Ergebnis zeigt eine brauchbare Grundlage für diese begrenzte Aufgabe. Es belegt weder eine fehlerfreie erste Generierung noch eine allgemeine Zuverlässigkeit bei größeren Anwendungen.

Interessant sind dabei auch Wiederholungen. Wenn ein Klick bereits gewertet wurde, darf ein zweiter Klick dieselbe Aktion nicht erneut auslösen. Wenn die Fehlerliste zu einer neuen Runde wird, muss der alte Punktestand verschwinden. Eine Funktion kann für sich betrachtet funktionieren und beim Übergang in die nächste Runde trotzdem falsche Daten übernehmen.

Das mit Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite erstellte Quiz schrittweise ändern

Für die nächste Version würde ich eine einzelne Änderung wählen und ihre Folgen beschreiben. Beim Austausch eines Wortes betrifft das die Frage, die richtige Auswahl und die Erklärung. Eine neue Spielregel kann zusätzlich den Punktestand oder den Neustart verändern.

Soll zunächst nur die Darstellung anders aussehen, können Fragen und Bewertung unverändert bleiben. Bei einer neuen Spielregel muss dagegen auch geprüft werden, ob die bisherigen Abläufe weiterhin passen.

Als kurze Kontrolle bietet sich eine Runde mit absichtlich falschen Antworten an: Sind nur diese Fragen in der Wiederholung? Passt die erreichbare Punktzahl? Beginnt eine vollständige neue Runde wieder bei null? Das sind Vorschläge für die eigene Prüfung, keine zusätzlichen Messungen dieses Versuchs.

Zugang zu Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite und Einrichtung der API

Die Verfügbarkeit hängt vom Zugangsweg ab. Am 2. November 2026 beschrieb die Dokumentation der Gemini Developer API einen Zugang für Nutzer, die die 2.5-Modelle bereits zuvor aktiv verwendet hatten. Die entsprechende Google-Cloud-Seite nannte dagegen den 20. Oktober 2026 als Einstellungsdatum und unterschied diesen Lebenszyklus ausdrücklich von dem der Gemini API. [3][5]

Für diesen Versuch wurde vor dem Aufruf geprüft, ob das Modell in der Liste des verwendeten Crazyrouter-Kontos enthalten war. Eine erfolgreiche Anfrage dieses Kontos ist keine Zusage für die Verfügbarkeit anderer Konten.

In einem Werkzeug mit frei einstellbarer OpenAI-kompatibler Verbindung werden drei Angaben benötigt: der API-Schlüssel aus der Crazyrouter-Konsole, die Basisadresse https://api.crazyrouter.com/v1 und der genaue Modellname gemini-2.5-flash-lite. [4]

Wer HTTP direkt verwendet, sendet eine POST-Anfrage an https://api.crazyrouter.com/v1/chat/completions und nutzt Bearer-Authentifizierung. Die Basisadresse eines SDK und der vollständige Endpunkt erfüllen unterschiedliche Zwecke; der Pfad sollte nicht doppelt angehängt werden. Die API-Dokumentation und das Anfrageformat beschreiben diese Verbindung. [4]

Übermittle den Fragenkatalog, die Regeln und die Anforderung einer vollständigen HTML-Datei zusammen als Nachricht in messages. Bei direkter Verarbeitung der Antwort findest du den erzeugten Text unter message.content im ersten Eintrag von choices. [4] Speichere nur den HTML-Inhalt, ohne einleitende Erläuterungen oder Markdown-Markierungen. Achte auf die Endung .html und prüfe danach die beschriebenen Abläufe.

Der Schlüssel bleibt im privaten Werkzeug oder auf dem Server. Er gehört nicht in die öffentlich geteilte Datei. Dass die Demo ohne Schlüssel spielbar ist, liegt daran, dass die Generierung bereits abgeschlossen ist.

Wenn eine Anfrage scheitert, prüfe Zugangsdaten, Endpunkt, Modellname und Kontozugang. Wenn die Anfrage erfolgreich war, aber das Spiel falsch zählt, liegt die nächste Untersuchung in der erzeugten Anwendung. Diese Trennung macht aus einem ersten API-Erfolg einen verständlichen Entwicklungsablauf.

Dieser Text wurde mit KI erstellt.

Quellen, geprüft am 2. November 2026:

[1] Google: Vorschau vom 17. Juni 2025.

[2] Google Developers Blog: Stabile Version vom 22. Juli 2025.

[3] Google AI for Developers: Dokumentation zu Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite.

[4] Crazyrouter: API-Dokumentation und Anfrage- und Antwortformat.

[5] Google Cloud: Modellspezifikation und Lebenszyklus.

title: Object-Oriented Programming: The 4 Pillars Explained
description:
Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) is one of the most widely used paradigms in software development. Instead of organizing code as a long list of functions operating on loose data, OOP organizes it around objects: bundles of data (attributes) and behavior (methods) that model things in your problem domain.

Whether you're building a web API, a data pipeline, or a game, understanding OOP helps you write code that is easier to reason about, reuse, and maintain.

In this article, we'll cover the four pillars of OOP with practical Python examples:

  1. Encapsulation
  2. Abstraction
  3. Inheritance
  4. Polymorphism

Quick Refresher: Classes and Objects

A class is a blueprint. An object is an instance created from that blueprint.

class Dog:
    def __init__(self, name: str, age: int):
        self.name = name  # attribute
        self.age = age    # attribute

    def bark(self) -> str:  # method
        return f"{self.name} says woof!"


rex = Dog("Rex", 3)
print(rex.bark())  # Rex says woof!

Dog is the class; rex is an object with its own name and age. With that in place, let's look at the pillars.

1. Encapsulation

Encapsulation means bundling data and the methods that operate on it into one unit, and restricting direct access to the internal state. Outside code interacts with the object through a controlled public interface rather than poking at its internals.

Why does this matter? It protects your object's invariants. If anyone can set balance = -1000000 directly, you can't guarantee your object is ever in a valid state.

Example: A bank account 

class BankAccount:
    def __init__(self, owner: str, balance: float = 0.0):
        self.owner = owner
        self._balance = balance  # "protected" by convention

    @property
    def balance(self) -> float:
        """Read-only access to the balance."""
        return self._balance

    def deposit(self, amount: float) -> None:
        if amount <= 0:
            raise ValueError("Deposit must be positive.")
        self._balance += amount

    def withdraw(self, amount: float) -> None:
        if amount <= 0:
            raise ValueError("Withdrawal must be positive.")
        if amount > self._balance:
            raise ValueError("Insufficient funds.")
        self._balance -= amount


account = BankAccount("Amina", 100)
account.deposit(50)
account.withdraw(30)
print(account.balance)  # 120

# account.balance = 1_000_000  -> AttributeError: can't set attribute

A few notes on Python specifically:

  • Python has no strict private keyword. A single leading underscore (_balance) is a convention that says "internal, don't touch."
  • A double underscore (__balance) triggers name mangling, which makes accidental access harder, but it is still not true privacy.
  • The @property decorator lets you expose a value as a read-only attribute, and you can add validation later without changing how callers use the class.

Takeaway: Hide the internals, expose a safe interface, and enforce rules in one place.

2. Abstraction

Abstraction means exposing what an object does while hiding how it does it. Users of your class shouldn't need to know the implementation details, only the contract.

In Python, the abc module lets you define abstract base classes that declare methods subclasses must implement.

Example: Data loaders

Imagine a program that needs to load data from different sources. The calling code shouldn't care whether the data comes from a CSV file or an API.

from abc import ABC, abstractmethod
import csv
import json


class DataLoader(ABC):
    """Contract that every loader must follow."""

    @abstractmethod
    def load(self) -> list[dict]:
        """Return the data as a list of records."""
        ...


class CSVLoader(DataLoader):
    def __init__(self, path: str):
        self.path = path

    def load(self) -> list[dict]:
        with open(self.path, newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
            return list(csv.DictReader(f))


class JSONLoader(DataLoader):
    def __init__(self, path: str):
        self.path = path

    def load(self) -> list[dict]:
        with open(self.path, encoding="utf-8") as f:
            return json.load(f)


def count_records(loader: DataLoader) -> int:
    # This function only knows about the abstraction.
    return len(loader.load())

If you try to instantiate the abstract class directly, or a subclass that forgets to implement load, Python stops you:

loader = DataLoader()
# TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class DataLoader
# with abstract method load

Takeaway: Abstraction defines a clear contract. Code that depends on the contract keeps working no matter how many new implementations you add.

Encapsulation vs. abstraction: Encapsulation is about protecting data by controlling access. Abstraction is about simplifying usage by hiding complexity. They work together but solve different problems.

3. Inheritance

Inheritance lets a class (the child or subclass) acquire the attributes and methods of another class (the parent or superclass). It promotes code reuse and models "is-a" relationships: a Manager is an Employee.

Example: Employees 

class Employee:
    def __init__(self, name: str, salary: float):
        self.name = name
        self.salary = salary

    def describe(self) -> str:
        return f"{self.name} earns {self.salary:,.2f} per month."


class Manager(Employee):
    def __init__(self, name: str, salary: float, team: list[Employee] | None = None):
        super().__init__(name, salary)  # reuse the parent's setup
        self.team = team or []

    def add_to_team(self, employee: Employee) -> None:
        self.team.append(employee)

    def describe(self) -> str:
        base = super().describe()  # extend, don't rewrite
        return f"{base} They manage {len(self.team)} people."


dev = Employee("Brian", 4000)
lead = Manager("Wanjiru", 6500)
lead.add_to_team(dev)

print(dev.describe())
print(lead.describe())

Output:

Brian earns 4,000.00 per month.
Wanjiru earns 6,500.00 per month. They manage 1 people.

Key ideas:

  • Manager(Employee) declares the inheritance.
  • super() calls the parent's implementation, so you build on it instead of duplicating it.
  • The child can override methods (like describe) to specialize behavior.

A word of caution

Inheritance is powerful but easy to overuse. Deep hierarchies become rigid and hard to change. A good rule of thumb is "favor composition over inheritance": if the relationship is "has-a" rather than "is-a," pass in another object instead of subclassing.

class Engine:
    def start(self) -> str:
        return "Engine started."


class Car:
    def __init__(self):
        self.engine = Engine()  # Car HAS an Engine (composition)

    def start(self) -> str:
        return self.engine.start()

Python also supports multiple inheritance (class C(A, B)), but use it sparingly. It can introduce confusing method resolution order (MRO) issues.

Takeaway: Use inheritance for genuine "is-a" relationships and shared behavior, and reach for composition when in doubt.

4. Polymorphism

Polymorphism means "many forms." It lets you treat different objects through the same interface, with each object responding in its own way. You write code against a general type, and the correct behavior is chosen at runtime.

Example: Shapes 

from abc import ABC, abstractmethod
import math


class Shape(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def area(self) -> float:
        ...


class Rectangle(Shape):
    def __init__(self, width: float, height: float):
        self.width = width
        self.height = height

    def area(self) -> float:
        return self.width * self.height


class Circle(Shape):
    def __init__(self, radius: float):
        self.radius = radius

    def area(self) -> float:
        return math.pi * self.radius ** 2


class Triangle(Shape):
    def __init__(self, base: float, height: float):
        self.base = base
        self.height = height

    def area(self) -> float:
        return 0.5 * self.base * self.height


shapes: list[Shape] = [Rectangle(4, 5), Circle(3), Triangle(6, 2)]

for shape in shapes:
    print(f"{type(shape).__name__}: {shape.area():.2f}")

Output:

Rectangle: 20.00
Circle: 28.27
Triangle: 6.00

The loop doesn't use if isinstance(...) checks. It just calls .area(), and each object does the right thing. Adding a new Hexagon class later requires no changes to the loop.

Duck typing

Python takes polymorphism a step further with duck typing: "If it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, it's a duck." An object doesn't need a shared parent class, it just needs the right methods.

class Duck:
    def speak(self) -> str:
        return "Quack!"


class Robot:
    def speak(self) -> str:
        return "Beep boop."


def make_it_speak(thing) -> None:
    print(thing.speak())


for item in (Duck(), Robot()):
    make_it_speak(item)

If you want duck typing with static type checking, Python's typing.Protocol lets you describe the required interface without inheritance.

Takeaway: Write code that depends on behavior, not concrete types, and new functionality becomes a matter of adding classes instead of editing existing code.

Putting It All Together

Here is a small example that uses all four pillars in one place: a notification system.

from abc import ABC, abstractmethod


class Notifier(ABC):                       # Abstraction
    def __init__(self, recipient: str):
        self._recipient = recipient        # Encapsulation (internal state)

    @abstractmethod
    def send(self, message: str) -> str:
        ...


class EmailNotifier(Notifier):             # Inheritance
    def send(self, message: str) -> str:
        return f"Emailing {self._recipient}: {message}"


class SMSNotifier(Notifier):               # Inheritance
    def send(self, message: str) -> str:
        return f"Texting {self._recipient}: {message}"


def alert_all(notifiers: list[Notifier], message: str) -> None:
    for n in notifiers:                    # Polymorphism
        print(n.send(message))


alert_all(
    [EmailNotifier("mary@example.com"), SMSNotifier("+254700000000")],
    "Your report is ready.",
)

Output:

Emailing mary@example.com: Your report is ready.
Texting +254700000000: Your report is ready.
  • Abstraction: Notifier defines what a notifier does.
  • Encapsulation: _recipient is kept internal to the object.
  • Inheritance: Both notifiers reuse the base class's structure.
  • Polymorphism: alert_all works with any notifier, treating them uniformly.

Summary

Pillar Core idea Python tools
Encapsulation Bundle data with behavior and control access _underscore convention, @property
Abstraction Expose what, hide how abc.ABC, @abstractmethod
Inheritance Reuse and specialize via "is-a" relationships class Child(Parent), super()
Polymorphism One interface, many behaviors Method overriding, duck typing, Protocol

OOP isn't about using every feature everywhere. It's about modeling your problem clearly, keeping responsibilities separated, and making code easy to extend without breaking what already works. Start small, practice by modeling real things you know, and the four pillars will start to feel natural.

title: PathoJev: Efficient Pathology Decisions from Shared Visual Context
description:
arXiv:2610.40752v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Pathology workflows require multiple visual judgments about the same slide, from identifying tumor type to assessing grade and invasion. Generating and parsing a separate textual response for each structured question adds latency between visual evidence and usable decisions. Building on the System One paradigm, we introduce PathoJev, a pathology model that directly predicts answer probabilities for whole-slide and region-level assessment. PathoJev encodes each slide once and evaluates independent question suffixes in batches over the shared visual context. Reusing the hybrid backbone's recurrent states further limits the computation that grows with slide-context length for each additional question. Across three whole-slide benchmarks, the 9B and 27B models achieve mean accuracies of 77.2% and 78.1%, exceeding SlideChat by 5.4 and 6.3 percentage points. Both scales also maintain competitive accuracy on five ROI benchmarks. On WSI-Bench, the 9B model runs 9.1x faster than SlideChat. Shared context accelerates eight-question workloads by 6.9x and 5.9x over separate prefix encoding, rising to 11.2x and 8.9x for 64 questions. These results provide a reusable probabilistic interface for combining multiple visual judgments in whole-slide and local tissue assessment. Code: https://github.com/ChyaZhang/PathoJev.

title: Spatial Atlas-Informed Loss Ensembles for Whole-Body PSMA PET/CT Metastasis Segmentation
description:
arXiv:2610.40834v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Existing whole-body PSMA PET/CT prostate metastasis segmentation methods generally rely on images alone, without explicitly incorporating where metastases tend to occur. We investigate whether a population metastasis atlas can improve lesion detection when integrated into model training. We constructed voxel-wise mean and standard deviation maps from 375 expert-annotated training scans and used them to weight the cross-entropy loss of an nnU-Net. The additional penalties for missed lesions and false positives depend on spatial atlas statistics and diminish as predictions become confidently correct. Seven configurations were compared on validation data; three were combined by majority voting into SAILS (Spatial Atlas-Informed Loss enSemble). We compared SAILS with a baseline nnU-Net and inference-time atlas fusion on AutoPET~III (110 disease-positive cases) and Deep-PSMA (100 external cases). No atlas or registration is needed at inference. Results: On AutoPET~III, SAILS improved whole-body Dice (0.531 vs. 0.520; p=0.006), reduced missed-lesion volume (9.5 vs. 12.1 cc/case; p<0.01), and increased pooled lesion sensitivity (0.857 vs. 0.843; p=0.004). On Deep-PSMA, SAILS detected 126 additional reference lesions (sensitivity 0.769 vs. 0.751; p<0.001), without a significant whole-body Dice change (-0.009; p=0.36). High-risk bone Dice improved in both cohorts (0.576 vs. 0.552 and 0.667 vs. 0.653; both p<0.01). False-positive volume increased by 2.3 and 18.2 cc/case, respectively (p<0.001). Atlas-weighted training improves lesion detection, especially in high-risk bone, without test-time atlas registration, but increases false positives.

title: Check for updates always, restart only when nobody is typing: an idle gate for a self-updating Node.js helper
description:
Disclosure: I'm the developer of the app described here, and this post was drafted and published by an AI agent from the project's source code.

Bolo turns an Android phone into a microphone for a computer: you speak on the phone and the text is typed at the cursor over local Wi-Fi. The computer side is a small Node.js helper in the tray. It updates itself, and updating means restarting, which is exactly what you must not do in the middle of someone's sentence.

This post is about the 91-line module that decides when the restart happens (src/updateGate.js), and the bug that made it necessary.

The first rule was too cautious

The original rule was simple: if a phone is connected, skip the update check. A phone mid-dictation should never see the helper vanish.

It held up until a helper was still on the previous version after a release had shipped. Its phone was simply always connected, so the check never ran. "Don't update while connected" quietly became "never update" for the most active users, who are the ones who most need fixes.

The lesson: "connected" is not "busy". A phone can sit connected for hours while nobody says a word.

Split the decision in two

The fix separates two things the old rule had glued together:

  1. Checking for an update runs on its normal schedule (every 6 hours, plus on demand), whether or not a phone is connected.
  2. Restarting waits until no text is being typed right now and none has been typed for 2 minutes.

Busy is measured where the typing happens. The message handler wraps every message that types text (a dictation, a live partial transcript, a clipboard paste) in a begin/end pair:

async function handleMessage(ws, message) {
  const typing = message.type === 'text'
    || message.type === 'realtime_text'
    || message.type === 'clipboard_paste';
  if (!typing) return handleMessageInner(ws, message);
  updateGate.begin();
  try {
    return await handleMessageInner(ws, message);
  } finally {
    updateGate.end();
  }
}

The finally matters: a dictation that throws still ends, so a failure can't leave the gate stuck "busy" forever.

The gate itself

Two pieces of state, a counter and a timestamp:

let lastActivityAt = 0;
let inFlight = 0;

function begin() { inFlight++; lastActivityAt = now(); }
function end()   { inFlight = Math.max(0, inFlight - 1); lastActivityAt = now(); }

function isIdle(idleMs = IDLE_MS) {
  return inFlight === 0 && now() - lastActivityAt >= idleMs;
}
  • A counter, not a boolean. Two messages can overlap (a partial transcript and the final text). With a boolean, the first end() would declare the gate idle while the second is still typing.
  • Math.max(0, …) so an unmatched end() can't push the counter negative and make "idle" impossible.
  • The clock is injectable (now), so the tests move time forward instead of sleeping for two minutes.

Waiting is a re-check loop that sleeps only as long as it has to:

function waitForIdle({ idleMs = IDLE_MS, pollMs = POLL_MS } = {}) {
  return new Promise((resolve) => {
    const check = () => {
      if (isIdle(idleMs)) return resolve();
      const t = setTimeout(check,
        Math.min(pollMs, Math.max(50, idleMs - idleForMs())));
      t.unref?.();
    };
    check();
  });
}

If 100 seconds of the 120 have already passed, it waits 15 seconds (the poll cap), not another full two minutes. unref() keeps a pending wait from holding the process open on its own.

One waiter at a time

The 6-hour timer keeps firing while an update waits for a quiet moment. Without a guard, a busy afternoon could stack several waiters, and the first quiet moment would trigger several restarts in a row. So there is exactly one pending update:

let pending = null;

async function runGatedUpdate({ version, check, apply, interactive, ... }) {
  if (pending) {
    if (interactive) log(`[Update] ${pending} will install at the next idle moment.`);
    return 'pending';
  }
  const result = await check(version);
  if (!result.enabled || !result.updateAvailable) return /* 'disabled' | 'current' */;
  pending = result.version;
  try {
    await waitForIdle();
    await apply(result);   // restarts the helper
    return 'applied';
  } finally {
    pending = null;
  }
}

The finally again: if apply fails (a download error, say), pending clears, and the next scheduled check can try again instead of being told forever that an update is "pending".

When you ask for an update check by hand while you're dictating, you get a plain answer ("will install at the next idle moment") instead of a restart under your cursor.

What I'd keep from this

  • Name the condition you actually care about. "Phone connected" was a stand-in for "user is typing", and the stand-in was wrong most of the day.
  • Separate detecting an update from applying it; only the second needs to wait.
  • Count in-flight work; don't flag it. Always release in finally.
  • Allow one pending action, and clear it on failure.
  • Make time injectable so a 2-minute rule is testable in milliseconds.

Bolo is on Google Play (search "Bolo AI"), and the Windows companion is on GitHub releases. The phone and the computer talk over your local Wi-Fi.

title: What Problem Does React Solve Better Than Other Alternatives
description:
Did you ever think about what problem React actually tries to solve?

So, the problem starts when you need to build a complex layout, and this layout depends on multiple states.

Now, the problem starts. How do you keep this complex UI synchronized with changing application state without manually managing every DOM change?

Before React, you needed to figure out which DOM elements were affected by a particular state change. Then, you needed to find those elements and modify them manually. You had to make sure every affected element was updated properly so the UI remained consistent with the application state.

But React took a somewhat different approach. It changes the programming model, where the current state describes what the UI should look like. Now, React determines what needs to change and updates the host environment.

1. Direct DOM Manipulation

When the UI gets complicated and you need to change the UI in multiple places, the task becomes complicated because the developer has to manually maintain the relationships between application state and the UI.

React manages DOM manipulation itself.

2. Declarative UI

In other frameworks or libraries, you need to explicitly say:

  • Do this.
  • Find that element.
  • Change its text.
  • Add the class.
  • Remove this button.
  • Show that button.
  • Hide that element.

This is imperative UI.

But React uses Declarative UI, where React takes responsibility for keeping the actual UI consistent with that declaration. This becomes the responsibility of the framework/runtime instead of the application's responsibility.

3. Change Propagation Problem

Change propagation means how you propagate this change throughout the UI.

If you do this task manually, then there might be some chances of forgetting the changes in the UI.

To eliminate this, React establishes a model where changes in state automatically re-render the relevant component tree and reconcile the result.

These are the changes that React solves perfectly, but other frameworks or libraries miss out on.

title: Findings from the $1M Vercel Sandbox challenge
description:
In August, we launched the $1M hacker challenge for Vercel Sandbox, inviting security researchers to try and escape Vercel Sandbox. We also coordinated with cybersecurity experts Trail of Bits to review the source code and security architecture.

Here is a summary of the challenge:

  • 1,285 reports over two weeks

  • $242,000 in bounties paid out

  • One Linux kernel zeroday vulnerability uncovered

No reports showed anyone accessing customer data in Vercel Sandbox. The most severe finding was the defect in the upstream Linux kernel.

The kernel zero day

The program's most important report arrived on day three.

Paulos Yibelo of pwn.ai, a HackerOne researcher working from a standard sandbox with no special access, found a defect in the Linux kernel's networking stack. Paulos discovered that specially crafted packets sent from within the microVM enabled three different attacks:

  1. Leak host memory over the network

  2. Crash the host machine

  3. Execute code on the host

Leaking host memory

In the first attack, memory from the host, the machine your sandbox shares with other tenants, shows up in packets the guest sends over the internet. This can happen continuously, for as long as the guest keeps sending.

This attack was demonstrated against Vercel production sandboxes.

Crashing the host and executing code on the host

The researcher also found that by sending specific packets, they could compromise the host.

First, by sending two packets, the researcher crashed the host machine, shutting down every sandbox running on it. Second, using the same flaw, they were able to run commands with full administrator privileges on the host, breaking out of the sandbox’s isolation boundary.

The packet-related crash and code execution attacks were demonstrated on the researcher’s own KVM and Firecracker machines matching Vercel Sandbox configuration.

Responsibly disclosing the kernel vulnerability

Almost every major cloud provider isolates customer workloads on this same layer of the Linux kernel, so any defect is shared-infrastructure risk.

Immediately after being notified, we collaborated with the researcher to understand and mitigate the vulnerability, working with AWS and other industry partners to prioritize a fix, and ensuring that Vercel customers and other developers using the kernel were safe.

The researcher also contacted the kernel maintainers and worked with them to create candidate patches. Fixes are under private review and CVEs are pending, so we are not publishing additional details until the patches are public. We are disclosing the existence of the vulnerability because it was separately disclosed in public.

Our approach to pressure-testing Vercel Sandbox

The HackerOne challenge made bounties available to any researcher, but we also extended our program to include internal evaluations and an independent investigation.

Before launching the public bounty, we performed live security assessments internally with full source access and support from the engineers who created and maintain Vercel Sandbox. We also engaged Trail of Bits, bringing on two engineers to evaluate our security architecture.

Not every finding came from the outside. Marcos Hernanz, a Vercel intern, found a cross-tenant data leak in the Linux device-mapper storage layer. This vulnerability let any sandbox read recycled disk blocks from previously deleted sandboxes.

The white-box deep dive

Trail of Bits spent four engineer-weeks inside our source code, with full access to the repositories and two enterprise test teams. They delivered 20 findings, and each was tested, confirmed, and referenced to the exact code.

They also performed an architectural review and concluded that our virtualization boundary is sound. Each sandbox runs on its own Firecracker microVM with a dedicated guest kernel, and the device model is deliberately tiny. No guest shares a running kernel with the host, or with another tenant.

On top of that foundation, they gave us three structural recommendations, which we implemented:

  • Find and eliminate all trust in the guest. Our control plane accepted values returned by software running inside the microVM, and every one of those values is tenant input. Anything that crosses the boundary should be derived server-side or signed with a key the guest cannot reach.

  • One policy, one decider. Egress enforcement was split across subsystems that each parsed the same network policy independently, and they did not always agree. We now use one canonicalization routine per data type, one component per decision, and revalidate connections when policy changes.

  • Assume the next zero day. Keep host and guest kernels up to date, reduce the kernel attack surface via build and runtime configs, disable nested virtualization, and use Firecracker’s jailer to run each microVM process with restricted permissions and isolate it from the rest of the host.

Vercel Sandbox findings

We received 1,285 reports in two weeks. This volume is only possible because researchers now hunt at AI speed.

Here is a breakdown of reports by category:

  • 877 duplicates

  • 319 not applicable

  • 57 valid

  • 32 informative

In our report triage we have validated:

  • 1 Critical finding

  • 5 High findings

  • 9 Medium findings

  • 42 Low findings

  • 32 Informative findings

We have paid out $242,000 in bug bounties.

The medium, Low, and Informative findings are small policy-boundary gaps, like a firewall rule that behaved differently than documented and a field that trusted the guest more than it should.

The most severe finding was the Linux kernel zero day defect, and no reports showed anyone reading a customer’s files, secrets, or application data.

We were most impressed with the heterogeneity of the reports. It was clear that researchers used different setups and have different obsessions. Some clearly know Linux namespaces and steered their agents straight at the kernel boundary. Others went after the network policies, and many went after areas we didn’t think to put on the menu.

That variety is what you're funding with a public challenge. Here's one of the more interesting findings it produced.

Cross-tenant disk snapshot restore (with limits)

Filed on day one of the challenge, this report is our favorite example of why we run a public bug bounty, even after internal assessments and a white-box engagement.

When you snapshot a sandbox, the control plane has to record where the snapshot data landed: {storage_url, size, checksum}. The flaw the researcher found was subtle: that answer came from software running inside the guest, and services running on the host trusted it. That is a trust-boundary violation. The guest is where our customers (and hackers) run untrusted code, so the host can never take its word as authoritative.

The researcher combined a known, documented container-escape primitive with this trust flaw. They intercepted the snapshot response inside their own sandbox and rewrote it, swapping the storage objects of two snapshots belonging to two separate accounts they owned. That meant restoring "your" snapshot materialized the other account's entire filesystem.

The researcher demonstrated that each account could read and modify the other’s files, verified the results using hashes, and preserved the test resources so we could independently reproduce the findings.

The limits of this attack matter. Aiming the swap at a specific victim required knowing that victim's internal snapshot storage key, a random 96-bit identifier the platform generates per snapshot and never exposes through the API. The only place that key appears is inside the victim's own sandbox. The researcher owned both accounts, which is what made the proof possible; there was no demonstrated path for a stranger to target another tenant. We still treated it as a priority fix, because a boundary that depends on a secret staying secret is not a boundary.

Trail of Bits independently flagged the same root cause in their assessment, which told us the finding was real, important, and discoverable from two completely different angles.

The fix shipped within a week, and the control plane now binds every snapshot object to the project that created it and rejects anything else. Snapshot creation moved out of the guest-reachable environment into a host-side service, and storage paths are project-scoped with strictly validated URLs.

Thank you to the research community

We would like to thank every researcher who filed a report, whether their finding was a zero day or a duplicate. Every technique discovered in the challenge informs how we protect the workloads running on Vercel Sandbox.

Thank you also to Trail of Bits for your comprehensive internal investigation and guidance.

Read the original challenge announcement and learn more about Vercel Sandbox in the documentation.
