title: Our mocks were lying to us for four months
description:
I want to talk about a specific kind of green build. The kind where 612 tests pass in 38 seconds, the coverage badge says 87%, and the thing is broken in production.

We had that build for most of a quarter.

The setup

We run a small logistics product. One of our TypeScript services talks to a third-party carrier API to fetch rates, book shipments, and pull tracking updates. When we built that integration, a colleague recorded a bunch of real responses, saved them as JSON fixtures, and wired them into our tests with nock. Fast, deterministic, easy to read. Everyone liked it.

That was in January.

How drift actually happens

Nobody decides to let mocks go stale. It happens in tiny steps.

The carrier added an optional surcharges array to rate responses. Our fixtures didn't have it, so our code never learned about it. Nothing broke. Yet.

Then they started returning estimated_delivery as a date-only string (2026-03-14) for some ground services instead of a full timestamp. Our code did new Date(value) and formatted it in the user's timezone. For anyone west of UTC, the delivery date showed up a day early. That one sat in prod for weeks, because who double checks whether "Thursday" should say "Friday"?

Then the big one. In April they moved tracking events behind pagination. The first call returned 20 events and a next_cursor. Our fixture had 6 events and no cursor, because the shipment we'd recorded back in January was a short one. In production, long-haul shipments stopped showing their latest status. Customers saw "In transit, Memphis" for packages that had been delivered two days earlier.

Every one of our tests passed through all of this. They were testing our code against January's API.

The afternoon I diffed everything

After the tracking complaint landed in our support channel ("customer says delivered, app says Memphis, again"), I blocked out an afternoon and did something slightly tedious. I wrote a throwaway script that sent the same requests behind each of our 34 fixtures to the carrier's sandbox, then diffed the real response shape against the saved one. Keys and types only, not values.

11 of 34 had drifted. Most trivially, a new optional field here and there. Three in ways that changed behavior.

I pasted the diff output in our team channel with no comment. Someone replied with the skull emoji, which was fair.

Where unit tests stop being useful

I don't think the lesson is "mocks bad". Our mocked unit tests were doing their actual job: given input X, does this function produce Y. The problem was that we were treating them as proof that our service worked with the carrier. They can't be that. A mock is a claim about someone else's system, and nobody was checking the claim.

That's the boring core of the whole unit testing vs integration testing argument, at least as I understand it now. A unit test isolates your code so you can trust its logic. An integration test puts your code next to the real dependency so you can trust the connection. You want both, and the trap is letting the fast, pleasant one stand in for the slow, annoying one.

We'd let the fast one stand in for everything.

What we do now

Nothing dramatic. Three changes.

A nightly drift check

That throwaway diff script became a nightly job. It hits the sandbox, compares response shapes to our fixtures, and posts to Slack if anything moved. It doesn't fail the build, because the sandbox is flaky enough that we'd be crying wolf twice a week. But we now see drift within a day instead of within a quarter.

Re-recording fixtures instead of hand-editing them

When drift showed up, we used to open the JSON and patch it by hand. That's how the January fixtures had turned into a weird hybrid of real and imagined responses. Now we re-record from the sandbox and commit the new file, so the PR diff shows exactly what changed upstream. Reviewers actually read those diffs, which surprised me.

Some teams push this further and record production traffic directly, then replay it as tests with dependencies mocked from the same recording. Keploy works roughly that way. We're not there yet, but fixtures that can't drift because they're re-captured from reality is a nice idea.

A thin layer of real calls

We added a handful of integration tests that run against the carrier sandbox on every PR that touches the carrier client. Seven of them. They book a shipment, fetch rates for three service levels, and pull tracking for a sandbox shipment with enough events to force pagination. About 40 seconds total, mostly because the sandbox is slow. We gate them on file paths so they don't run on unrelated changes.

Things I got wrong along the way

My first instinct was to replace all the nock mocks with sandbox calls. I got about halfway before the suite went from 38 seconds to just over six minutes and started failing randomly whenever the sandbox hiccuped. A teammate asked, very politely, whether I was trying to get people to stop running tests locally. I reverted most of it.

The other mistake: I assumed the carrier would loudly announce breaking changes. They did, kind of. Two of the three were on a changelog page I didn't know existed. The pagination change went out by email to an address belonging to someone who left the company last year. Go check where your vendors' notices actually land. I'll wait.

Where we ended up

612 unit tests, still mocked, still fast. Seven integration tests against the sandbox. One nightly drift check. Extra CI time on a relevant PR is under a minute.

The pagination test would have caught the tracking bug on its first run. The nightly diff would have flagged the date format the morning after it changed. Not perfect. Still a lot better than finding out from a customer whose package is apparently stuck in Memphis forever.

title: Advanced JavaScript Module Systems and Bundlers: Webpack, Rollup, and More
description:
JavaScript development has evolved tremendously with the rise of modern frameworks, large codebases, and complex dependencies. At the core of managing this complexity lie module systems and bundlers — crucial tools that help developers organize code, manage dependencies, and optimize delivery for browsers and servers.

This post dives into modern module systems, particularly CommonJS and ES Modules (ESM), and explores popular bundlers like Webpack and Rollup that bring these systems together for efficient application builds.

A Quick Recap: JavaScript Module Systems

Before bundlers, JavaScript had no native module system, leading to global namespace pollution and maintenance nightmares. Over time, these patterns emerged:

  • CommonJS: Introduced primarily for server-side with Node.js, CommonJS loads modules synchronously using require() and exports functionality with module.exports. It's simple but geared towards backend environments due to blocking behavior.
  • ES Modules (ESM): The official JavaScript module system introduced in ES6 with import and export syntax. Modules load asynchronously, support static analysis for optimization, and are natively supported on modern browsers and recent Node.js versions. ESM facilitates features like tree shaking, removing unused code for leaner bundles.
Feature CommonJS ES Modules (ESM)
Loading Synchronous Asynchronous
Syntax require, module.exports import, export
Support in Browsers No (needs bundling) Yes (native support)
Tree Shaking No Yes
Use Cases Server-side (Node.js) Client & Server

Why Do We Need Bundlers?

Modern JavaScript applications consist of hundreds or thousands of modules. Browsers historically didn’t support module semantics natively or loading numerous separate files created performance bottlenecks due to multiple HTTP requests.

Bundlers tackle this challenge by:

  • Combining all modules and dependencies into one or more optimized files
  • Supporting various module formats (CommonJS, ESM, AMD)
  • Performing code transformations (transpiling, minification)
  • Enabling advanced optimizations (code splitting, tree shaking)
  • Managing static assets (images, stylesheets) alongside JS

Popular Bundlers: Webpack and Rollup

Webpack

Webpack is a highly configurable, versatile bundler widely used in modern web development.

Strengths:
  • Supports multiple module formats.
  • Handles complex dependency graphs.
  • Rich plugin ecosystem for features like hot module replacement (HMR).
  • Integrates with loaders for CSS, images, TypeScript, etc.
  • Supports code splitting for lazy loading. Use case: Large applications requiring fine-grained control over the build process, such as React, Angular, or Vue apps.
Rollup

Rollup is designed primarily for bundling JavaScript libraries and is favored for its efficient tree shaking and smaller bundles.

Strengths:
  • Focuses on ES modules with static analysis.
  • Generates highly optimized, minimal bundles.
  • Simpler configuration compared to Webpack.
  • Ideal for library authors and smaller projects. Use case: JavaScript libraries or smaller apps where minimizing output size is critical.

How Bundlers Work: A High-Level View

  • Entry Point: The bundler starts from an entry module specified by the developer.
  • Dependency Graph: It builds a graph by recursively resolving all imported modules.
  • Transforming: The bundler applies loaders and plugins to transform code (e.g., transpiling with Babel).
  • Optimizing: Removes dead code (tree shaking), minifies output, and splits bundles if configured.
  • Output: Generates bundled file(s) for deployment or development.

Choosing Between Webpack and Rollup

Criteria Webpack Rollup
Project Size Large-scale, complex apps Libraries & smaller apps
Configuration Effort More complex, more options Simpler, more straightforward
Tree Shaking Supported but sometimes limited Excellent, ES modules based
Plugin Ecosystem Extensive Growing but smaller
Build Speed Slower on large projects Generally faster
Asset Handling Excellent (CSS, images, etc.) Basic, but extendable

Final Thoughts

Advanced module systems like ES Modules and CommonJS underpin modern JavaScript application structure. Bundlers like Webpack and Rollup bring modular code together, optimize it, and prepare it for production environments with sophisticated features. Selecting the right bundler and understanding module systems is key to efficient, scalable frontend and backend JavaScript development.

Stay tuned for more insights as you continue your journey into the world of web development!

Check out the YouTubePlaylist for great JavaScript content for basic to advanced topics.

title: Kernel-based Interpolatory Methods for Context Compression of Attention Mechanisms
description:
arXiv:2610.40943v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The bottleneck of attention mechanisms, which are the fundamental building block of modern language models, is their quadratic complexity in terms of context size. There has thus been an increasing interest in the compression of the context, also called KV-cache compression. In this article, we consider the problem of compressing the context of attention mechanisms by first formulating it in the Hilbert space associated with its kernel. In this formalism, attention can be represented as the ratio of two linear maps whose interpolant is also the ratio of interpolants, this allows us to consider the interpolation of the linear maps directly. We thus introduce two novel KV-cache compression methods which we call GAIM and Q-DAIM, based on the Generalized Empirical Interpolation Method (GEIM) and the Q-Discrete Empirical Interpolation Method (Q-DEIM), respectively. As the cost of these methods is quadratic in terms of context length, we propose surrogate models based on the Taylor series, the Performer and the Random Fourier Features method which allow the compression to be done in linear time. Finally, we extend this result to the streaming attention setting, providing new methods which allow one to penalize the selection of interpolation nodes based on the previously interpolated context and to update the previous interpolation based on new information. We then provide numerical results on the convergence of the residuals and the output error in future queries and preliminary results on the LongBench-E benchmark showing performance comparable to the state-of-the-art methods. These experiments suggest that the range revealed by our Q-DAIM method could help identify where information is concentrated in the KV cache, thus enabling an efficient compression.

title: LG CNS completes 30 MW hyperscale AI data center in Jakarta
description:
📅 2 November 2026 • The Korea Times

LG CNS has completed construction of a 30 MW hyperscale AI data center in Jakarta, with the announcement made on 2 November 2026. The project makes the Korean IT services company the first from Korea to build an AI data center outside the country for a local customer. The facility is finished, fully committed to a tenant, and marks the entry of Korean data center engineering into one of Southeast Asia's fastest-growing digital markets.

Demand arrived before construction did. 100% of the facility's capacity was contracted before the build was completed. The customer is KMG, a joint venture between Indonesia's Sinar Mas Group and Korea Investment Real Asset Management. Full pre-completion occupancy stands out in an industry where operators usually lease capacity in stages over the first years of operation, and it reflects how scarce AI-ready capacity has become in the region as training and inference workloads grow faster than new supply can come online. For KMG the arrangement secures long-term AI capacity inside Indonesia at a moment when AI workloads are competing for space across APAC.

The technical design is built around AI workloads rather than conventional hosting. The power system sustains more than 300 kW per rack, roughly 60 times the density of a typical data center rack. That level of per-rack power is what modern GPU clusters for model training draw, and it shapes most other engineering choices in the building. Cooling follows a hybrid approach: air-based cooling serves phase 1, while liquid cooling is planned for subsequent phases as rack densities climb further.

The Jakarta site is a first phase, not a finished campus. The next stage of construction will raise total capacity to 400 MW, a scale that would place the facility among the largest AI data centers in Indonesia. The project therefore doubles as a capacity plan for a market where local compute supply is being built out under pressure from demand.

LG CNS positions the project as the start of a regional 'AI factory' business — data center capacity operated as a production input for AI development rather than general-purpose hosting. The company plans expansion across APAC, naming Malaysia, Thailand, Vietnam, the Philippines and Japan as target markets. The list of target markets mirrors where digital economies in the region are scaling and where governments are pushing for in-country data infrastructure. For enterprises planning AI workloads in the region, the project adds in-country capacity options at a time when data residency requirements and local compute demand are both rising across Southeast Asia.

IMPACT: Who is affected — AI teams, cloud and infrastructure buyers planning compute in Southeast Asia, plus colocation, energy and construction partners in the region. What changes — regional buyers gain a contract-ready option for AI capacity, with 30 MW operational now and 400 MW planned, and rack densities above 300 kW push liquid-cooling readiness up the checklist for anyone building AI-grade sites. What to watch — the pace of the 400 MW expansion, contract structures around the KMG joint venture, and LG CNS entries into Malaysia, Thailand, Vietnam, the Philippines and Japan.

Cloud Billing

Feature

Spend cap budgets are now generally available for a limited set of services

For eligible services, you can configure a spend cap budget to automatically pause usage when your estimated spend exceeds the budget amount you set. You can manage spend cap budgets in the Budgets page in the Google Cloud console and using the Cloud Billing Budget API.

Spend caps are a cost control mechanism. A spend cap is enforced when usage costs exceed your budget target amount. When enforced, any new request to the eligible services, within the specified project, are paused and no further usage costs are accrued until the spend cap is lifted. You can manually lift an enforced spend cap, or wait until the start of the next month when the spend cap is automatically lifted.

Spend caps use gross, estimated costs to trigger the alerts and caps, enforcing a cap much faster than the actual costs are processed and appear on billing reports. Even though faster than reports, the enforcement of spend caps isn't instant and any cost overages are billed as normal.

More information about spend cap budgets

For managing spend cap budgets in the Google Cloud console, see:

title: Building Mintu: A Privacy-First Desktop AI Companion with Tauri 2, Rust, and Local LLMs (v0.2.1 Release)
description:
Most desktop AI tools today suffer from two fundamental problems: they rely entirely on remote cloud APIs—raising serious privacy concerns—and they require constant context-switching between separate application windows.

To address both issues, I built Mintu, an open-source, local-first desktop companion that integrates directly into your screen as a native Dynamic Island. With today's v0.2.1 release, Mintu expands its platform footprint and core capabilities.

Here is a breakdown of what Mintu is, how its architecture works, and what is new in version 0.2.1.

The Core Philosophy: Complete Local Privacy

Mintu does not send prompts, conversation logs, or telemetry to external servers. All text generation and processing happen entirely on the user's hardware.

Key architectural pillars:

Zero Telemetry: No analytics beacons, tracking cookies, or external error reporters.
Local LLM Inference: Powered by llama.cpp, running quantized GGUF models (e.g., Qwen 2.5) directly on your CPU/GPU.
Local Persistence: Conversations, settings, and memory fragments are persisted strictly within a local SQLite database (mintu.db).
Offline-First: Network access is only used when the user explicitly downloads a new model or checks for GitHub releases.
The Tech Stack

Building a persistent, low-overhead desktop island that stays reactive required a stack optimized for memory efficiency and cross-platform native execution:

Core & System Integration: Rust via Tauri 2
Inference Runtime: llama.cpp bindings for quantized GGUF models
UI / Frontend: TypeScript, Vite, Modern CSS
Database: SQLite (local embedded storage)
OCR & Vision: Windows Media OCR / native image pipeline

Tauri 2 allows the application to maintain a minimal memory footprint compared to traditional Chromium-based wrappers, while Rust provides the concurrency and safety needed for background LLM inference and system monitoring.

What is New in Version 0.2.1

The v0.2.1 release focuses on workstation flexibility, productivity tooling, and multi-platform distribution:

  1. Multi-Monitor Display Management

Users with multi-monitor workstations can now freely anchor and move the Dynamic Island across displays without layout disruption or window clipping.

  1. Quick Scratchpad

An inline, accessible note-taking interface integrated directly into the island, allowing developers to dump code snippets, thoughts, and quick tasks without leaving their IDE or current window.

  1. Dedicated Audio Engine

A lightweight, zero-dependency sound pipeline designed for subtle auditory feedback during focus timer transitions and background system alerts.

  1. Native macOS Universal Package

In addition to Windows 10 and 11 (64-bit), Mintu now officially supports macOS across both Apple Silicon (M1/M2/M3/M4) and Intel architectures, integrating with Apple Keychain and native window management.

  1. Direct Web Distribution

Users can now download both Windows installer packages (.exe) and macOS universal archives directly from the official website without relying solely on GitHub release mirrors.

Verification and Security

Because Mintu is a community-driven open-source project without commercial code-signing certificates, we publish full SHA-256 checksums for every build so users can independently verify binary integrity before execution:

Windows Installer (Mintu_0.2.1_x64-setup.exe): 670E600D8F80606C87AE949F88EB65599DFDA8825804821873F10F1D0237A5BA
macOS Universal (Mintu-v0.2.1-macOS.zip): 3C24988419EA9869AA9F76FBE2D924DA40F75C5D4F75963ED48390C2E38B5ED5
Try It Out and Contribute

Mintu is 100% free and licensed under the permissive MIT License.

Website: https://mintudev.netlify.app/
GitHub Repository: https://github.com/HuseynDeveloper/Mintu

Feedback, bug reports, and pull requests are welcomed. If you find the project interesting, consider starring the repository on GitHub.

title: VoxLution: Evolving Voxels for High-Fidelity 3D Scene Generation
description:
arXiv:2610.41501v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: High-resolution 3D indoor scene generation is crucial for immersive applications such as virtual reality, spatial computing, and robotics simulation. We introduce VoxLution, a coarse-to-fine transformer-based approach that generates high-fidelity indoor scenes with rich details, overcoming the overly smooth geometry typical of existing generative models. First, we generate a low-resolution spatial layout; then, based on this structural information, we progressively refine the scene geometry locally in chunks. Key to our approach is formulating 3D super-resolution as a sequence modeling problem over multi-resolution sparse voxel grids. To achieve this, we introduce a training-free, resolution-invariant tokenization scheme that compactly encodes the geometric information of eight octants into a single decimal number. We formulate the transformer sequence to include multiple resolutions, allowing the coarse layout to guide the generation of fine local details. To ensure coherence across local chunks, we incorporate adjacent chunk boundary information directly into the transformer sequencing. VoxLution achieves scene generation at a finer voxel resolution than existing baselines, demonstrating state-of-the-art performance on standard benchmarks with 59.6% lower FPD and 51.1% lower FID on 3D-FRONT, and 70.5% lower FPD and 73.8% lower FID on Scannet++.

title: Do not treat image complete as a successful decode result
description:
HTMLImageElement.complete can be true for a broken image. It can also be true when the element has no source, so it cannot establish that an image loaded successfully.

For an image-processing step, handle the operation you actually need. If the next step requires decoding, await decode() and handle rejection before replacing the preview. Keep the selected job identifier available when your application allows another file to be chosen during that wait.

The following is an illustrative boundary around an existing image element:

async function requireDecodedImage(image) {
  await image.decode();
  return image;
}

Handle rejection in the caller. A rejected promise should leave the previous preview intact when that is the intended interface behavior. Do not label an export ready merely because an earlier complete check returned true.

Keep load or decode status separate from the later canvas drawing and export result. Successful decoding does not establish that every subsequent operation will succeed. Name the failing stage in the interface so a missing image and a failed export are distinguishable.

Reference: MDN complete.

title: Transferring Peptide-Target Interaction Patterns to Small Molecules by Joint Guidance for Diffusion and Flow Matching
description:
arXiv:2610.41322v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generating small molecules to target protein-protein interactions (PPIs) remains one of the most challenging yet high-reward frontiers in drug discovery. Unlike traditional small-molecule drugs that bind to deep, well-defined pockets, PPI interfaces often comprise broad, shallow binding surfaces. A natural strategy is to leverage known peptide-target interactions, as peptide ligands provide rich interface-level constraints. However, a major algorithmic challenge is that rigid atom-level conditioning on peptide structures can over-constrain the generative space and exclude valid small-molecule solutions. To address this challenge, we present PIFT (Peptide InterFace Transfer), a novel framework that transfers peptide-target interaction patterns to small molecules through joint sampling-time guidance of masked discrete diffusion and continuous flow matching. PIFT first maps peptide-target and small-molecule-target interfaces into a shared, target-conditioned interaction space, capturing transferable interface information across molecular modalities. The resulting peptide-derived reference then jointly steers building-block logits and 3D coordinates toward peptide-compatible molecules while preserving a strong adapted molecular prior. Extensive experiments across diverse PPI targets show that the learned representation captures cross-modal interaction compatibility, while peptide guidance improves interface recovery and achieves strong docking performance and favorable molecular properties.

title: Idempotency Keys Under Distributed Retry Pressure: Key Scoping, Storage Contracts, and the Deduplication Boundary
description:
Idempotency Keys Under Distributed Retry Pressure: Key Scoping, Storage Contracts, and the Deduplication Boundary

Idempotency keys are a solved problem in the abstract and a continuous failure mode in production. The concept is straightforward: a caller supplies a stable key, the server uses it to detect duplicate requests, and it returns the same response without re-executing side effects. What makes idempotency hard is not the idea — it is the contract between key scoping, storage semantics, retry timing, and failure recovery. Get any one of those wrong and you either duplicate the operation or falsely deduplicate it.

This article focuses on the mechanics that matter in a Go microservice under real retry pressure: where the deduplication boundary sits, what storage backend choices actually guarantee, and where the most common scoping mistakes create silent correctness holes.

Where Idempotency Lives in the Stack

Most teams bolt idempotency onto their HTTP or gRPC handler layer as if it were a middleware concern. It is not, or at least not entirely. The deduplication boundary must sit at the boundary of the side effect, not the boundary of the network call.

Consider a payment service that charges a card, writes a ledger entry, and publishes a payment.completed event. A middleware that deduplicates at the handler boundary can short-circuit all three of those steps on a retry — which is correct. But if the payment charge succeeds and the service crashes before the ledger write, the next retry must not be deduplicated. The key must still be in an uncommitted state because the operation did not complete.

This leads to the first architectural constraint: idempotency keys must track operation state, not just request receipt.

type IdempotencyRecord struct {
    Key       string
    Status    RecordStatus // Pending | Complete | Failed
    Response  []byte       // serialized response, nil if Pending
    CreatedAt time.Time
    ExpiresAt time.Time
}

type RecordStatus int

const (
    StatusPending  RecordStatus = iota
    StatusComplete
    StatusFailed
)

A Pending record means a previous attempt started but has not committed a result. That is fundamentally different from a missing record, and your retry path must handle it differently.

Key Scoping: The Most Underspecified Part

A common mistake is treating the idempotency key as globally unique. It should be scoped to the operation type. A key like req-abc123 that a client reuses across different endpoints will produce false deduplication if your store does not namespace by operation.

More subtle is scoping across service versions. If you deploy a new version of the payment handler that changes what the response body contains, a deduplicated response from an old record may return a shape the caller cannot parse. This is not a theoretical concern — it surfaces during rolling deployments when old records are still in TTL window.

The storage key should encode at minimum: {service}.{operation}.{caller-supplied-key}. In Go:

func idempotencyStoreKey(service, operation, clientKey string) string {
    return fmt.Sprintf("%s:%s:%s", service, operation, clientKey)
}

For multi-tenant systems, tenant ID must also be part of the namespace. A key that one tenant generates is not transferable to another tenant's operation space, and failure to namespace there is a data isolation bug, not just a correctness one.

Storage Backend Contracts and What They Actually Guarantee

The storage layer for idempotency records is where most production failures originate. The two common choices are Redis and a relational or document store. Each has a distinct failure profile.

Redis is fast and TTL-native, but it offers no transactional guarantee across the idempotency write and the actual side-effect operation. The classic failure sequence:

  1. Request arrives. Redis key absent — proceed.
  2. Write Pending record to Redis.
  3. Execute payment charge.
  4. Redis crashes before writing Complete.
  5. Retry arrives. Redis key absent (evicted or lost). Operation executes again.

This is not a Redis-specific bug — it is a consequence of using a separate store for idempotency state without a two-phase commit between the side-effect store and the idempotency store. Redis also silently evicts keys under memory pressure unless you configure maxmemory-policy noeviction, which most clusters do not do for performance reasons.

The mitigation is to write the idempotency record in the same transaction as the side effect when the side-effect store supports transactions. If your ledger is in MongoDB, write the idempotency record as a document in the same database within a multi-document transaction. The idempotency record and the business record commit atomically or both roll back.

session, err := mongoClient.StartSession()
if err != nil {
    return err
}
defer session.EndSession(ctx)

_, err = session.WithTransaction(ctx, func(sc mongo.SessionContext) (interface{}, error) {
    // Check and insert idempotency record atomically
    _, err := idempotencyCol.InsertOne(sc, IdempotencyRecord{
        Key:       storeKey,
        Status:    StatusPending,
        CreatedAt: time.Now(),
        ExpiresAt: time.Now().Add(24 * time.Hour),
    })
    if mongo.IsDuplicateKeyError(err) {
        existing := &IdempotencyRecord{}
        if findErr := idempotencyCol.FindOne(sc, bson.M{"_id": storeKey}).Decode(existing); findErr != nil {
            return nil, findErr
        }
        if existing.Status == StatusComplete {
            return existing.Response, ErrAlreadyProcessed
        }
        // Pending: a concurrent attempt is in-flight or a prior attempt crashed.
        return nil, ErrConcurrentRequest
    }
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }

    // Execute the side effect
    result, err := chargeCard(sc, req)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }

    // Mark complete
    encoded, _ := json.Marshal(result)
    _, err = idempotencyCol.UpdateOne(sc,
        bson.M{"_id": storeKey},
        bson.M{"$set": bson.M{"status": StatusComplete, "response": encoded}},
    )
    return encoded, err
})

The duplicate key error on insert is the atomic check-and-set. MongoDB's unique index on _id makes this safe under concurrent retries.

The Pending State Is a Correctness Boundary, Not an Edge Case

When a record is Pending, you have two valid behaviors: wait with a timeout, or return a 409 Conflict with a Retry-After header. The wrong behavior is to let the second request proceed as if the key did not exist. That produces a concurrent execution with two threads operating on the same logical operation, which is exactly what idempotency is supposed to prevent.

A Pending record older than a plausible request timeout (say, 30 seconds beyond your p99 handler latency) can be treated as a crashed operation. At that point, the retry policy should allow the new request to claim the key and attempt the operation again — but only after the Pending record is explicitly transitioned to Failed or deleted. This requires a background reaper or a compare-and-swap transition.

In Go, that reaper is a goroutine with a ticker that scans for stale Pending records:

func (s *IdempotencyStore) ReapStale(ctx context.Context, staleness time.Duration) {
    ticker := time.NewTicker(30 * time.Second)
    defer ticker.Stop()
    for {
        select {
        case <-ctx.Done():
            return
        case <-ticker.C:
            cutoff := time.Now().Add(-staleness)
            _, _ = s.col.DeleteMany(ctx, bson.M{
                "status":     StatusPending,
                "created_at": bson.M{"$lt": cutoff},
            })
        }
    }
}

The staleness value must be calibrated against your upstream timeout chain. If your downstream payment processor has a 10-second timeout and your handler has a 15-second deadline, a 20-second staleness threshold is defensible.

TTL Contracts and the Replay Attack Boundary

Idempotency records cannot be kept forever. A 24-hour TTL is common for payment-style operations; a 7-day TTL appears in some batch processing designs. The TTL is not just an operational cleanup concern — it defines the window inside which a caller can safely retry. A caller retrying after the TTL has expired gets no deduplication guarantee.

This creates a decision: do you document the TTL as part of your API contract, or do you absorb the operational cost of longer retention? For any operation with financial consequence, the TTL window should be explicit in API documentation and enforced server-side, not left as an undocumented implementation detail.

The TTL also bounds replay attack surface. An idempotency key that lives indefinitely is a key that an attacker can replay indefinitely to get a cached successful response. This is especially relevant if your response body contains sensitive data (a charge receipt, a token). TTL expiry forces re-authentication of the operation, which is the correct security posture.

Decision Framework

When designing idempotency into a service, answer these questions in order:

  1. Where does the side effect commit? Your idempotency record must commit in the same atomic scope as the side effect, or your deduplication guarantee is probabilistic.

  2. What is your key namespace? Include service, operation, and caller-defined key at minimum. Add tenant ID for multi-tenant systems.

  3. What does Pending mean for your retry policy? Define a maximum in-flight window beyond which a Pending record is treated as failed, and implement a reaper.

  4. What is your TTL, and is it part of the API contract? Document it. Callers need to know how long their retry window is valid.

  5. What does your storage backend actually guarantee under failure? Redis is fast but requires explicit noeviction policy and does not solve the two-phase commit problem. Transactional document or relational stores give stronger guarantees at the cost of throughput.

  6. What happens when you return a cached response after a schema change? Version your response schema or scope your idempotency keys to include a version segment if your response structure evolves.

Idempotency is not middleware. It is a distributed protocol between the caller's retry logic, the service's state machine, and the storage backend's consistency guarantees. The failures that surface in production are almost always at the seams between those three — not inside any one of them.

title: Your Abandoned Carts Just Got a New Rescue Route
description:
Shopify Messaging now supports WhatsApp marketing automations. Here’s what it means and how to set it up before Black Friday.

Think about the last time you left something in an online cart. Did you get an email? Probably. Did you open it? Maybe not.

Now think about the last WhatsApp message you got. You probably read it within minutes.

That gap is what Shopify is going after with its latest update. On October 28, 2026, Shopify announced that you can now create WhatsApp marketing automations inside Shopify Messaging. You can read the official post here: Create WhatsApp marketing automations in Shopify Messaging.

Let’s break down what’s new.

Three ready-made flows, one new home

The update is short and simple. You can now send well-timed WhatsApp messages to customers automatically. Shopify gives you ready-made templates for three common moments:

  • Abandoned browse: Someone looked at your products but didn’t add anything to their cart.
  • Abandoned cart: Someone added items to their cart but never started checkout.
  • Abandoned checkout: Someone started checkout but didn’t finish paying.

You can also add WhatsApp to your own custom automations, not just the pre-built ones.

To find it, open your Shopify admin and go to Messaging > Automations.

Your emails get buried. WhatsApp messages usually don’t.

Most stores already send abandoned cart emails. That’s good, but inboxes are crowded. Your message sits next to dozens of other promotions.

WhatsApp feels more personal. It’s where people chat with friends and family, so messages tend to get noticed fast.

It matters most if your customers live in places where WhatsApp is part of daily life, like India, parts of Europe, Latin America, and the Middle East.

The other big win is convenience. Before, many stores needed a separate app to run WhatsApp flows. Now it lives in the same place where you already manage your store.

Set it up in five simple moves

You don’t need to be a tech expert. Here’s a simple path.

  1. Open Messaging > Automations. This is the home of your WhatsApp flows. Follow the setup steps to connect your WhatsApp Business account.

  2. Start with abandoned checkout. These shoppers were the closest to buying. A friendly nudge here often brings the best return, so turn this one on first.

  3. Then add abandoned cart and abandoned browse. Once checkout is running, add the other two. Each one catches shoppers at a different stage.

  4. Test before you go live. Place a test order and check that the shopper name, product name, and cart link show up correctly. A broken link in a recovery message is worse than no message at all.

  5. Collect opt-ins. This one is important. WhatsApp requires customers to say yes to marketing messages. Add a clear opt-in checkbox at checkout or sign-up. Sending messages to people who haven’t agreed can get your number restricted.

Before you press “turn on”: four quick checks

Costs may apply. The Shopify changelog doesn’t go into pricing, so check the Shopify Help Center page on marketing automations before you launch. WhatsApp usually charges per message category, and marketing messages tend to cost more than service messages.

Don’t overdo it. One helpful reminder is great. Three pushy ones in a day will annoy people. Keep your tone warm and short, like a message from a friend who works at your store.

Keep email running. WhatsApp isn’t a replacement. Use both. Some customers will respond to email, others to WhatsApp, and having both gives you more chances to win the sale.

Check your account early. If your Meta business account has any issues, it’s better to find out now than in the middle of a sale.

Black Friday won’t wait for your setup

Black Friday and Cyber Monday bring lots of traffic and lots of abandoned carts. People compare prices, get distracted, and leave. Every recovered order during this period counts.

If you set this up today, you’ll have time to test, fix small problems, and start collecting opt-ins before the rush. If you wait until the sale starts, you’ll be fixing things while customers are already slipping away.

If you only do one thing this week

Shopify didn’t invent WhatsApp marketing. It made it easier. You don’t need extra tools or complicated setups to start. You need a few minutes, a connected WhatsApp Business account, and a clear opt-in process.

Turn on the abandoned checkout flow, test it, and let it run. A small message at the right moment can bring back a sale you thought was gone.

Read the official update here: Shopify Changelog: Create WhatsApp marketing automations in Shopify Messaging

title: Steering Vectors as a Training Signal in LLM Post-Training
description:
arXiv:2610.40998v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Steering vectors (SVs) are residual-stream directions that shift the behavior of LLMs when added to hidden states at inference time. While prior work has mainly used SVs as post-hoc controls, we ask whether the same directions can also guide parameter updates during post-training. We study this question across supervised learning, including SFT and distillation, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Our framework considers two intervention regimes: a hidden-state hook during teacher-forced supervised training, and an advantage-repair mechanism on wrong rollouts in GRPO. For each regime, we analyze three design axes, which are the steering direction, its placement, and the operation used to combine it with training. In supervised settings, SV injection improves over plain SFT and distillation, with gains scaling with the off-policy gap and reaching up to a $12\%$ improvement when distilling from thinking-mode teachers. These gains hold across three random seeds. In RL settings, applying a correctness-contrast direction as advantage repair on wrong rollouts, including otherwise zero-gradient all-wrong groups, recovers a learning signal that transfers to held-out math benchmarks and acts as a composable auxiliary signal that adds to existing zero-variance remedies such as entropy-aware advantage shaping. We further identify three failure boundaries. In detail, code generation can break the direction, cross-family layer transfer can break the placement, and inference-time application on an SV-trained checkpoint can break the intervention regime. Together, these results establish steering vectors as a conditional but effective training signal for LLM post-training. Our code is available here.

title: AI Gateway logs now show session affinity
description:
AI Gateway logs now have a Sessions view that groups requests into sessions and shows how session affinity routed each one. Each row shows the coding agent or app that ran the session, such as Claude Code, Codex, or Cursor, along with its cost, models, providers, and how much of its input was cached across every turn.

Open a session to see its cache hit rate, duration, and path. The path lists each turn with its model and timing, and names the provider serving the session along with any earlier ones. Session affinity sends each turn to the provider that served the one before it, so the provider already has most of the prompt in cache. A session that stays on one provider reads more of each prompt from cache.

Filter sessions by turns, client, model, provider, authentication, or cost. Single-turn sessions are hidden until you clear the minimum turns filter.

Session affinity runs by default on text and chat requests. To group requests yourself, send the same sessionId in providerOptions.gateway, or the same x-session-id header, on every request in a conversation. Requests without one are grouped by a fingerprint of the conversation's opening and appear as fingerprinted sessions.

Read the session affinity documentation for more information on how AI Gateway identifies sessions.

title: Open Source Radar · 2026-11-02: Agent infrastructure is splitting into replaceable parts
description:
By Renchao Wu. Originally published on widechaos.cn.

For this issue I picked five projects from GitHub Trending and topic-search candidates, mostly AI agents and developer tools. I read each project's README, release notes and recent commits; I did not install them unless an entry says so. Stars and other numbers are from GitHub as of 2026-11-02.

All five point at the same thing: infrastructure for agents; retrieval, a knowledge base, a skills directory, an evolution loop, and one course that turns evaluation into a specification.

1. sahenjp/RustXNG ⭐ 471 · Rust

GitHub: https://github.com/sahenjp/RustXNG

In one line: A self-hosted search service that returns ranked results and page text in a single request, built to be an agent's retrieval layer.

What it is: Written in Rust, AGPL-3.0-or-later, a port of SearXNG with a SearXNG-compatible response shape and a browser UI on port 8888. The repository was created on 18 October 2026 and reached v0.26.0 in two weeks, with two releases on 1 November.

What stands out:

  • Text comes back with the results. With include_raw_content=1 it returns about 32,000 characters from the top five pages, so an agent can inspect extracted text without fetching every page separately. Extraction does not establish source accuracy, completeness or permission to republish it.
  • Several upstream engines with per-engine failure handling. 226 engine types, 352 settings entries, 180 enabled by default; each engine has its own timeout, failed engines are suspended with backoff, and engines that keep returning nothing are rested.
  • The project documents default SSRF checks. The documented policy restricts fetching to public addresses. I have not tested redirects, DNS changes or the full network boundary; it is not an independent security guarantee.
  • Ops surface included. /healthz, OpenMetrics /metrics, response cache, image proxy, bot rate limiting, and idle timeout for sidecars.

Compared with: The relationship to SearXNG is a port, not a fork in spirit; compatible interface, engines carried over, plus page-text fetching, SSRF protection and a ranking pass (term coverage, site authority, identifier match). Those additions are documented by the project; I did not re-check them against SearXNG item by item. Against hosted search APIs the difference is self-hosting and text volume: the README reports a 100-question comparison on one machine, hit@1 of 79–83 versus Exa 77 and Tavily 34; about 32,000 characters per request versus about 9,000 and about 1,200; 0.01 s for a repeated query versus 0.6 s and about 1 s. Those are the project's own numbers, not my tests, and it notes they move a few points between runs.

Recent updates: v0.26.0 (1 November) published a ghcr.io image and made the English README primary; v0.25.0 the same day repositioned the project as an agent retrieval layer. All three release notes are one line about checksums, so the substance is in the commit messages.

Who it's for: Anyone who wants to host an agent-search endpoint. The metasearch service still sends queries to enabled upstream engines and fetches third-party pages; self-hosting does not make retrieval offline or eliminate third-party data exposure. Two conditions apply: Google is unavailable in this build (the WML endpoint returns 403, the HTML endpoint needs JavaScript, headless browsers get detected), so replacement engines need testing; and the license is AGPL-3.0-or-later, whose exact terms should be checked for the intended deployment. The README specifically discusses source obligations for a modified network-service version; network access alone is not a complete licence analysis.

My take: ⭐⭐⭐. Collapsing "found it" and "got citable text" into one request is the right subtraction; whether it replaces an existing setup depends on results without Google.

Checked: README, three release notes, recent commits and docs/COMPARISON-EXA.md; not installed.

2. undefined-ui/second-brain-os ⭐ 1,170 · HTML

GitHub: https://github.com/undefined-ui/second-brain-os

In one line: A plain-Markdown knowledge base an agent maintains for you, plus a course and toolkit for building that agent.

What it is: 130 pages; a guide, a seven-module agents course and five handbooks; with a toolkit of 18 skills, 72 slash commands, 6 subagents, 4 scripts, a plugin and a starter vault. MIT. Obsidian is a viewer, not a dependency. It implements the llm-wiki pattern Karpathy published as a gist on 4 April 2026: the wiki is primary and raw sources are an archive; new sources get compiled into existing pages; three operations; ingest, lint, query.

What stands out:

  • Compilation, not side-by-side summaries. A concept page is rewritten and thickened by new sources instead of becoming a list of excerpts. That is a maintenance choice; I have not measured long-term accuracy or upkeep.
  • Maintenance is a command, not a reminder. 72 slash commands cover creating pages, merging, health checks and graph export; /metrics, /health and /graph-export run from scripts inside the vault.
  • Health has script-generated indicators. The health and graph-export entry points provide observable indicators. A health score or graph export does not by itself detect every contradiction or establish that stored claims are true.
  • The resource list is dated. Every entry in resources/ carries one line on why it belongs, and the README states it was checked on 1 November 2026 with stars from that day's API.

Compared with: The README compares this file-maintenance approach with memory servers and retrieval-based context assembly. This one is a methodology document plus a copyable vault plus a command set, and its bet is that an agent maintains files through fixed operations. It names Basic Memory 1.0, ai-memory 3.0 and Hindsight 1.0 and explains how it differs; that is its own account, and I did not read those repositories. The checkable dimensions are three: whether writes leave evidence, whether pages are compiled, and whether lint actually runs.

Recent updates: No releases; main-branch iteration. On 2 November the graph recommendation moved from Kuzu to Ladybug (Kuzu was archived in October 2025; the project describes Ladybug as a continuation with embedded CSV support; I have not independently verified migration compatibility), and the README was reorganised by level with a "new this month" section. A companion site went up on 14 October.

Who it's for: People already keeping file-based notes who want an agent to take over filing and linking. It assumes Claude Code's directory conventions (.claude/skills, commands, agents); another agent means changing how they load. If you want "install it and it organises itself", this is not that; it gives process and scripts, and you still feed it the first ten sources.

My take: ⭐⭐⭐. The method matters more than the tooling, and here the method is written as executable commands.

Checked: README, the llm-wiki pattern document and recent commits; not installed.

3. ant-research/AntOmniEvo ⭐ 1,221 · Python

GitHub: https://github.com/ant-research/AntOmniEvo

In one line: A framework that treats a system's tunable parts as a directory of files, has a coding agent rewrite them from failure trajectories, and keeps the loop and the audit trail.

What it is: Python, Apache-2.0. The division of labour is "you define, the framework controls, AI does the work": you supply how to run the system, an evaluator, train/val data, a directory mapping for the tunable artifacts, and a starting point; the framework handles scheduling, budgets, selection and persistence; a coding agent acts as the Proposer. Tunable artifacts can be a skill's SKILL.md plus scripts, a pipeline's pipeline.json plus node code, or a single-file algorithm plus its description. The system being optimised need not contain an LLM; the Proposer must be able to write code.

What stands out:

  • Optimisation becomes file editing. Prompts, skills, DAG topology and node implementations all go through one mechanism because they share one property: they are files.
  • The scoring rule is the objective. The evaluator returns 0 to 1, train and validation are split, and the README insists on a held-out set rather than gains on the training split.
  • The design records edits alongside failure evidence. The deliverable includes lineage linking changes to the failure material used by the proposer. This records a rationale, not proof that the edit caused an improvement.
  • Candidate state is persisted for interruption and resumption. Candidates, runs, analyses and changelogs land in a CandidateStore. I have not tested crash recovery, partial external effects or exact replay behaviour.

Compared with: OpenEvolve is another evolutionary-code-optimisation project; its reported gains are tied to its own tasks and evaluation conditions, which I did not reproduce. This project widens the object to skills, prompts, pipeline configs and node code inside a directory, restricts the editor to a coding agent reading failure trajectories, and treats the change-to-failure mapping as part of the deliverable. These descriptions do not establish that the projects have mutually exclusive optimisation targets or that either is more effective. I only read both READMEs and ran neither.

Recent updates: No releases. On 29 October the visualiser gained an English/Chinese switch; on 28 October a trajectory-model document landed along with a note that the paper's experiment scripts and datasets will be open-sourced separately. The paper is Mara Chain (arXiv 2609.35855).

Who it's for: Teams with a repeatable, reasonably cheap evaluation whose optimisation target can be expressed as a directory of files. The docs are explicit about the mismatch cases: a handful of scalar parameters, an evaluation that is not repeatable or is very expensive, or output with strict compliance requirements (it edits files in a sandbox, so audit the permissions yourself).

My take: ⭐⭐⭐. Treating auditability as a hard requirement is worth more than the evolutionary machinery itself.

Checked: README, docs/when-to-use.md, recent commits and the paper entry; not installed.

4. wanghao-SunSky/cs329z-chinese ⭐ 407 · HTML

GitHub: https://github.com/wanghao-SunSky/cs329z-chinese

In one line: A Chinese-language course on engineering AI agents, built around Stanford CS329Z's public materials: 19 lessons, four exercises, readable offline.

What it is: 19 lessons, four hands-on exercises, Markdown sources, a single-file offline HTML reader, and scripts to build and verify publication. The order follows the engineering chain: agent landscape, LLMs for builders, RAG, tool use and function calling, orchestration, context management, memory architecture, multi-agent systems, system optimisation, evaluation engineering, data selection and quality, LLM judges, safety, coding agents, proactive agents, open problems. The README states plainly that this is an independent Chinese study guide, not an official Stanford translation, and that rights to the original course and code stay with their authors; open revisions live in a separate editorial-notes file. There is no license file at the repository root.

What stands out:

  • Evaluation is written as a specification. Lesson 13 formalises agent evaluation as a four-tuple; request, environment, stopping criteria, scorer; and lists four difficulties: non-unique solution paths, stateful environments with side effects, compounded non-determinism, and cost plus safety constraints.
  • Scaffolding is called out. The same model with a different token budget or tool set cannot be compared directly; realistic scaffolding needs controlled variables. That one line is useful when reading anyone else's leaderboard.
  • Dense per lesson. A lesson runs several thousand characters with stated learning goals, not a bullet outline.
  • Offline. The single-file HTML does not depend on the site.

Compared with: Among Chinese agent courses it chose to reproduce one course lesson by lesson rather than spread a roadmap wide; the cost is narrow coverage. Against the original English course the increment is Chinese phrasing and engineering organisation, and I did not compare coverage lesson by lesson. There is a practical constraint: the text is organised from public course materials, the repository carries no license, and rights stay with the original authors; public availability does not establish permission to redistribute or use the material commercially; check the applicable rights.

Recent updates: First release on 28 October, then per-lesson descriptions and Chinese search improvements on 31 October. Five days in: 407 stars, 45 forks.

Who it's for: Python developers who want to fill in agent engineering concepts systematically, especially evaluation and safety. If you want a runnable codebase, that is not the shape here; there are exercises, but the body is lecture material.

My take: ⭐⭐. Solid as a Chinese-language evaluation text; as an engineering reference it needs code alongside.

Checked: README, lesson 13, and the repository file list; did not run the build scripts.

5. heilcheng/awesome-agent-skills ⭐ 6,332 · TypeScript

GitHub: https://github.com/heilcheng/awesome-agent-skills

In one line: A cross-vendor directory of agent skills; 388 entries; with six quality criteria attached.

What it is: An 82 KB README with 388 links in six languages, plus a companion site. Two halves: official and vendor directories (AI platforms and models, cloud and infrastructure, developer tools and frameworks, the Google ecosystem, business and marketing, security and web intelligence; six sections with 47 vendor groups), and community skills (16 groups covering vector databases, data and analytics, cloud storage, marketing and more). Its claim is to list skills real teams use rather than bulk-generated ones; the compatibility list names Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity, Gemini CLI, Cursor, GitHub Copilot and Windsurf.

What stands out:

  • Organised by who published it. Vendor-maintained skills come first, then third-party ones; a useful provenance distinction, not a substitute for inspecting the contents.
  • Six quality criteria. Unambiguous instructions, one focused task, a working example, documented trade-offs, SKILL.md under 500 lines, verified on the target agent. Usable directly as acceptance checks.
  • Translations are a pipeline. Commits show translated READMEs and site data synced from the main README rather than six hand-maintained copies.
  • Submissions pass an automated gate. Every pull request triggers a checker script: only README.md may change, changes must be additive, at most five lines per PR, a fixed line format, duplicate detection, the repository must exist and not be archived, it must contain a SKILL.md, have at least 20 stars and be at least 14 days old; failures get a needs-fixes label. Entries come from outside contributors, but code enforces the floor.

Compared with: Against a plain link list it adds two concrete things; six stated quality criteria and an automated gate that actually rejects submissions (the rules above are the script's rules); against each vendor's own marketplace it is a horizontal index, and its compatibility list names intended hosts. It does not establish that each listed skill was tested on every host or version. What the gate verifies is entry compliance and repository availability; it cannot verify a claim like "verified on the target agent", which still depends on the author or your own test.

Recent updates: On 2 November it synced multilingual READMEs and site data, tidied a triage batch, and added claude-code-skills-zh, motionboard, mobbin/skills and others (#641 to #647). Created on 29 December 2025; 6,332 stars since.

Who it's for: People looking for existing skills, or wanting acceptance criteria for their own. Start with the vendor sections; check third-party entries' maintenance yourself.

My take: ⭐⭐. Fine as an index, not as a quality endorsement.

Checked: README structure, the quality-standards section, the pull-request checker script and recent commits; installed no skills.

At a glance

Project What it is Most distinctive Who it's for Worth digging
RustXNG Self-hosted retrieval layer Results and page text in one request, SSRF-guarded Anyone wiring search for a local agent ⭐⭐⭐
second-brain-os Self-maintaining knowledge base Maintenance as 72 commands; a documented ingest/lint/query workflow People on file-based notes ⭐⭐⭐
AntOmniEvo Auto-evolution framework Every edit carries a failure trail, diffable and revertible Teams with a stable evaluation ⭐⭐⭐
cs329z-chinese Chinese agent course Evaluation taught as a four-tuple specification Anyone filling gaps in evaluation and safety ⭐⭐
awesome-agent-skills Skills directory A cross-vendor index with six stated acceptance criteria Finding skills, setting standards ⭐⭐

Notes from this issue

  • Agent infrastructure is being split into replaceable parts. Retrieval, knowledge bases, skill directories and evolution loops each have their own projects, and the interfaces look more like services an agent calls than interfaces a person uses. When choosing, ask about the interface shape before the feature list.
  • The projects make auditability part of their design. An evolution framework requires every edit to carry a failure trail; a knowledge base makes lint a mandatory operation. Those choices make changes easier to inspect; I have no evidence here about the authors' prior losses or the effectiveness of the checks.
  • Stating limits has become part of the documentation. One says outright that Google is unavailable in this build; another says the framework does not fit systems with only a few scalar parameters. Sentences like these help more than a performance table.

title: I built a CLI package manager for macOS because brew list hid 145 dependencies
description:
I ran brew list on my Mac and got 188 names.

I knew maybe 40 of them. The other 145 were libraries that arrived because
something else needed them — abseil, icu4c, isl, highway. Nothing told
me which was which, what anything did, how much space it took, or which command
would remove it safely.

That is the problem Cydia and Sileo solved on a jailbroken iPhone: one list,
searchable, with a Remove button. macOS never got that view. So I built one.

What Dronagiri does

Dronagiri is a terminal app that reads the package databases of Homebrew, npm,
pipx, Cargo, RubyGems and go install, then puts everything in one sortable
table:

  • real on-disk size, measured with one batched du
  • install date
  • one-line description and homepage
  • last-used evidence from Spotlight and timestamped shell history
  • popularity from Homebrew's public analytics
  • dependencies in their own tab, each labelled with the packages that need it
  • broken entries: packages a manager still lists whose files are gone

The part I use most is the Mine / Dependencies split. brew list treats the
40 tools I chose and the 145 libraries they dragged in as one flat list.
Dronagiri separates them.

The hard parts

Two things were harder than the UI.

Dependencies lie. Homebrew's JSON lists declared dependencies, which is wrong
surprisingly often. Dronagiri asks brew deps <formula> for the actual runtime
linkage, then inverts the graph. That is why it can say "needed by ffmpeg, mpv"
instead of guessing.

"Last used" is mostly unknowable. APFS mounts with noatime, so access
times never change. Most shells do not timestamp their history. Dronagiri uses
Spotlight's kMDItemLastUsedDate for .app bundles and timestamped shell
history for commands. When neither exists, it says never — meaning no trace,
not proof you never ran it. The detail panel spells that out.

Safety

Deletion is deliberately inconvenient. Select rows with space, press d, and
confirm twice in bordered dialogs. The first window lists every package and the
space freed; the second is a last-chance warning. Removal is delegated to the
manager that installed the package. No --force, no --ignore-dependencies, no
private APIs.

Try it 

go install github.com/MasterShivnath007/dronagiri@latest
dronagiri

Or download a binary for Apple Silicon or Intel from the releases page. It is
MIT-licensed, macOS 13+, and there is no telemetry or account.

  • Website and install guide: https://mastershivnath007.github.io/dronagiri/
  • Source: https://github.com/MasterShivnath007/dronagiri
  • The brew list comparison: https://mastershivnath007.github.io/dronagiri/#compare

If you try it, I would like to know what your Mine/Dependencies split looks
like — and which package you were surprised to find.
