title: Does PNG to ICO keep transparency? A measured alpha test at 16, 32 and 48 px
description:
Does PNG to ICO keep transparency? A measured alpha test at 16, 32 and 48 px

Yes. A PNG with an alpha channel, converted to ICO, keeps alpha = 0 in every transparent pixel at all three sizes tested. Below is the pixel-by-pixel proof.

The question

When you save an image as JPEG, the alpha channel is gone — JPEG has no transparency. If your icon source was a JPG, renaming the file extension to .ico does not bring alpha back; the pixel data simply doesn't contain it.

But if your source is a PNG with an alpha channel, does the ICO conversion preserve it? I ran a measurement to find out.

Source image

A test PNG with a gradient alpha channel: at 16×16, every row steps through alpha values 0, 64, 128, 255 — four columns of each. The image has 64 fully transparent pixels (alpha = 0), 128 partially transparent pixels (alpha 64 and 128), and 64 fully opaque pixels (alpha = 255). At 32×32 the pattern scales up to 256/512/256. At 48×48 the anti-aliasing produces a richer distribution but the transparent count is 528.

The ICO file produced from this PNG is 625 bytes total, containing three frames: 16×16 (138 bytes), 32×32 (151 bytes), 48×48 (282 bytes). Pillow independently decoded each PNG entry inside the ICO to verify the pixel data.

Method

  1. Open the PNG in the converter at icoforge.com/png-to-ico-transparency-test.
  2. Convert to ICO and download the output file.
  3. Decode each frame inside the ICO using Pillow's Image.open().
  4. Count pixels at each alpha value: 0 (transparent), 1–254 (partially transparent), 255 (opaque).

Results

Size (px) Frame bytes Alpha 0 (transparent) Alpha 1–254 (partial) Alpha 255 (opaque)
16 138 64 128 64
32 151 256 512 256
48 282 528 1,248 528

ICO total: 625 bytes. Source SHA-256: a6286835afc613468120d32d780b3d954bfb5b85e983cc0ea845617b8eb04e7a. Output ICO SHA-256: 33d026fca2ea106d6e46b51c944f20531f16105dd40797b155295b1e56715903.

Every number in this table comes from the measurements at icoforge.com/png-to-ico-transparency-test, where the source PNG and output ICO are also available for download.

Why alpha = 0 at the transparent pixels means transparency survived

The source PNG has 64 pixels at alpha = 0 in the 16×16 frame. If the ICO conversion had flattened the image — filling transparent areas with white or black — those pixels would show alpha = 255. Instead, the ICO frame contains exactly 64 pixels at alpha = 0, matching the source. The same holds at 32×32 (256 pixels at alpha 0) and 48×48 (528 pixels at alpha 0). The transparent regions are preserved.

The partially transparent pixel counts also match: 128 at 16×16, 512 at 32×32, 1,248 at 48×48. These are the pixels where the source alpha is 64 or 128 — and the ICO preserves those intermediate values exactly.

What about JPEG sources?

JPEG does not store an alpha channel. A JPG file contains only RGB data. If you convert a JPG to ICO, the result has no transparency — not because the converter dropped it, but because the source never had it. Changing a .jpg filename to .ico doesn't change the pixel data inside.

Data and sources

All measurements were taken on 2026-10-26 using Chrome's canvas rendering pipeline and verified with Pillow. The raw measurements JSON is available at:

  • /samples/png-alpha-test/measurements.json — frame byte counts, alpha value distributions, and SHA-256 hashes for source and output.

The source PNG and output ICO files are downloadable from the PNG to ICO transparency test page.

License: CC0 (public domain).

title: Three fewer graph passes, 12% more time
description:
Bounded Accord’s Speed Demon engineering notes, written on October 31, 2026 and updated after our last push on November 2. Live-board results are practice scores, separate from final judging.

The last graph-construction change in this account removed three complete reads of a five-million-edge array. It preserved the order of every adjacency list and left the shortest-path search unchanged. It passed the correctness checks. The measured program took about 12% longer.

That result came from our entry in Speed Demon, organised by Hackathon Raptors. Bounded Accord implements four tasks in Rust: log aggregation, Boolean and phrase search, a CSV join, and directed shortest paths. The entry repository contains the implementations and their performance records.

The comparisons below cover rejected changes, an officially scored storage improvement, and an input-partitioning change that reached the live board on the last day.

One graph pass can carry more expensive work

Track D stores the graph in two compressed sparse row structures: one for outgoing edges and one for incoming edges. Each row’s edges are contiguous. A forward search from the source and a reverse search from the target can then read their own adjacency arrays without searching the original edge list.

The accepted constructor first parses triples of source, destination and weight. For each direction, it counts degrees, computes row offsets, allocates edge storage, and scans the triples again to fill that storage. There are four full triple scans after parsing.

The candidate counts both degrees while parsing, then fills both adjacency arrays in one shared triple scan. Each edge still appears in its original relative order within its row. Parallel edges, exact duplicates, self-loops and zero weights remain intact. The input byte buffer is released before the edge arrays are allocated in both versions.

The following comparison includes reading, construction, all queries and writing the output:

Measurement Accepted constructor Fused constructor
Pinned-image process time 0.858853 s 0.960344 s
Peak native process RSS 192,388 KiB 185,220 KiB
Nonblank, non-comment source lines 281 286

Times are means of the middle three of five runs per version, after fixed warm-ups. Baseline and candidate runs were interleaved on the same Intel Core i5-12500H machine running Ubuntu 24.04 under WSL2. The images were pinned, six workers were used, and the published child timer excluded container startup. RSS came from separate native runs; it is not the official container-memory measurement.

The time ratio, baseline divided by candidate, was 0.894317. Memory fell by about 3.7%. Both timing spread checks passed, but the candidate missed our previously fixed efficiency requirements. We restored the accepted source and executable and checked the full output hash again.

The comparison establishes that this implementation was slower in this environment. It does not identify a cache-miss rate, a memory-bandwidth limit, or the cost of each added write. Counting loop passes supplied a hypothesis; it did not measure the cost of the resulting access pattern.

An exact small-key representation did pay

Track C joins CSV records to countries and counts distinct names per country. Splitting records at every newline would be wrong: a quoted field can contain a newline. In the officially scored pipeline, the producer carries quote parity across input blocks and dispatches only complete logical records. Six workers decode fields and accumulate numeric totals.

Distinctness spans all workers. The accepted design groups requests into 64 mutex-protected shards. Under a shard’s lock, the first occurrence of an exact (name, country) pair sets a membership bit and increments one worker’s count. Summing those counts is valid because the first-pair decision is shared.

The useful storage change was deliberately narrow. When there are at most 256 country groups, including the unmatched group, names of at most 16 bytes fit in two words plus a length. Four words hold the country-membership bits. The key contains every name byte; it is not a fingerprint used as identity. Length distinguishes a short name from a longer zero-padded value. Longer names and larger country tables keep the full-byte fallback.

Against the preceding accepted pipeline, this change reduced pinned-image time from 0.186579 to 0.152485 seconds and native peak RSS from 24,060 to 19,828 KiB. It passed its fixed adoption requirements. Its subsequent official run, run-52f0819fc621, recorded 55.455380 machine points, up from the previous best of 51.737524.

The tests targeted the representation’s boundaries: every inline-key byte position, lengths around 16 and 17 bytes, zero bytes, country-bit boundaries, tables through 513 countries, concurrent first-pair updates and reused scratch storage. Fast-path checks alone would have missed the fallback’s obligations.

A small time saving can lose the combined comparison

A later Track C candidate scanned each complete record for outside-quote commas and quote counts. That metadata let it derive decoded note lengths without visiting every note byte in the decoder. Unescaped names borrowed their input bytes; escaped names used scratch storage. Record framing and membership storage stayed unchanged.

It was correct across the tested cases, including split vector blocks, escaped quotes, embedded newlines, Unicode, BOM bytes and a two-megabyte note. It also reduced measured process time slightly:

Measurement Accepted parser Structural-metadata parser
Pinned-image process time 0.150447 s 0.147206 s
Peak native process RSS 20,060 KiB 20,016 KiB
Nonblank, non-comment source lines 393 458

The speed ratio was 1.022018, below our fixed 1.18 adoption requirement. Both timing spread checks passed. The source increase also mattered: Speed Demon’s coefficient charges for source size as well as time, memory and dependencies. Using our local RSS and line-count proxies gave a coefficient ratio of 0.988437, below our required 1.05. These counts differ from the host’s formatted-source and container-memory axes, so the ratio is an estimate, not a predicted official score.

We rejected this implementation before submission. Its shorter decoding path did not produce enough whole-program benefit to cover the measured trade-off.

Finding five boundaries without listing every record

A later input-partitioning change reached the local adoption threshold. The first version mapped the immutable CSV file read-only and divided it into six complete-record ranges. Workers borrowed those ranges directly, eliminating the producer’s owned buffers and channels. Its partitioner still scanned the entire input sequentially, collecting record-end offsets to choose just five internal cuts. That version saved memory but missed the time requirement.

The next version computes quote parity in six parallel byte ranges. A prefix XOR supplies the quote state at each proposed cut; a forward scan then finds the next newline outside a quoted field. An escaped quote contributes two quote bytes, so even a cut between them receives the correct starting state. Long quoted records may send several cuts to the same boundary, producing valid empty ranges. After partitioning finishes, six parsing workers borrow the resulting slices. The parser and shared membership tables stay unchanged.

This comparison uses a new fixed batch against the previously accepted producer pipeline:

Measurement Accepted producer pipeline Parallel-parity partitioning
Pinned-image process time 0.149709 s 0.124672 s
Container cgroup peak memory 20,582,400 B 18,612,224 B
Source-line proxy 409 491

The time reduction was 16.7%, and the measured memory reduction was 9.6%. The local coefficient ratio was 1.087865, above the fixed 1.05 requirement. That calculation uses time, memory, source size and direct runtime dependencies; image size is a separate build limit. Both implementations had a dependency-axis value of one.

Memory was read from the Docker cgroup with host data prewarmed and a common trusted holder keeping the cgroup available after the timer exited. This measures the container’s recorded peak, but it does not reproduce the host’s parent harness or isolation. The source count is also a local proxy. The baseline had one slower run; the predeclared middle-three mean excluded the fastest and slowest of five runs from each version, with all raw values retained.

Eleven Rust tests, seventeen validation groups and all fourteen image outputs passed. The checks included quote pairs split at every byte position, long records, Unicode, BOM handling and the final record without a newline. The source was frozen before fresh seeds 137 and 138 and reserved seed 139 were generated.

A separate diagnostic sampled the unchanged candidate twice. It captured 620 and 621 CPU events, with text decoding accounting for about 20% in each capture. The earlier producer pipeline also placed text decoding near 21%. These are exclusive CPU sample locations, not elapsed-time shares; they do not establish that a previously rejected parser change should be tried again.

The change's first live-board run, run-e08fc96bfae2, recorded 57.147738 machine points; the previous best was 55.455380. The board measured 0.160190 seconds instead of 0.187834, and 17,788,928 bytes of peak memory instead of 20,283,392. Formatted source grew from 401 to 483 lines. On the board the coefficient rose by a factor of 1.081, close to the local estimate of 1.088, although the two use different time, memory and source-size measurements.

The local winner that lost on the board

An earlier Track D experiment reordered vertices with breadth-first numbering. Its final local version remapped queries early enough to release the permutation before constructing the final adjacency arrays. The fixed native comparison improved from 0.849322 to 0.705578 seconds: about 16.9% less elapsed time. The RSS ratio was 0.997095, and the local coefficient proxy passed its gate.

The official trial was valid but scored 49.524627 machine points. The retained best was 50.424918. We restored the prior source.

Those official values are separate historical runs, not an interleaved experiment isolating the numbering change. The board observation was enough to reject that trial as an improvement over the retained best; it was not enough to explain the reversal. A later local diagnostic compared native and container execution contexts and still did not establish the cause.

This also changed how we described unchanged-source results. A repository push can run tracks whose source did not change. Our best recorded A and D values came from such runs. They belong in the measurement record, but their variation cannot be credited to a new algorithm. On the final day, the unchanged Track A source took 0.189345 seconds in one run and 0.146796 in the next, against its best of 0.130583.

Correctness evidence has a separate job

For the fused graph candidate, seven Rust property tests passed. One checked that parsing preserved the ordered rows in both directions. Another tested every directed three-node graph whose nine possible edges were absent, zero-weight or unit-weight: 19,683 graphs, with every source-target pair checked against Bellman–Ford.

The wider checks covered 117 adversarial and random graphs, repeated queries, large path sums, zero cycles and directed reachability. Seven host examples ran with one, two, six and twelve workers. Fresh tiny seeds 127 and 128 passed before reserved seed 129, with the source frozen. Published sample/full hashes and all fourteen measured or warm-up image outputs matched.

These checks made a performance comparison meaningful by ruling out the tested wrong-answer cases. They do not prove every possible input correct or turn a slower result into a useful optimisation. The graph invariants still have to hold: path sums remain 64-bit, reverse edges retain their own weights, and bidirectional search cannot stop merely because it found a meeting.

The entry at code freeze

Our last push before the November 2, 15:00 UTC code freeze was commit f00c64fca46bb4124462c053305a1395c596035f. It only updated the performance records; its source is the same as commit 29a57dc3752e417842e5bc2bf4796170c2ead170, which carried the parallel-parity change. The table lists the best live-board value for each track. The values come from different recorded runs, not a simultaneous four-track timing batch.

Track Process time Machine points Run
A: Ingest 0.130583 s 61.431366 run-8ed375c52049
B: Index 0.918916 s 55.479075 run-a9ce34cd1404
C: Join 0.159350 s 57.219847 run-596f68f709a3
D: Traverse 0.723518 s 50.424918 run-396084b71fdb

The A and D bests came from pushes that changed other tracks, with their own source unchanged. C's best came from the final, documentation-only push, which re-ran the parallel-parity source; its first run had scored 57.147738. These are practice-board machine results, not final judging or an award: final scoring reruns the recorded commit on a held-out dataset, and judges contribute 35% of each track total. The per-track PERF.md files retain the unsuccessful comparisons alongside the accepted changes; MEASUREMENTS.json binds the best values to run IDs and source hashes.

For the next graph-construction change, the missing evidence is where the modified access pattern spends time. For the CSV pipeline, the open question is whether the board's 8% coefficient gain holds on the held-out dataset.

The implementations, validation and this article were developed with Codex; Claude Code added the November 2 board results. Algorithm references, measurement limits and assistance disclosures are retained in the entry repository. Task definitions and the official scoring procedure are published by Hackathon Raptors.

title: Sparse Autoencoders for Expert-Assisted Interpretation of Histopathology Foundation Model Embeddings
description:
arXiv:2610.40905v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Histopathology foundation models learn rich embedding representations, but their internal structure remains difficult to inspect. Concept-level interpretability is particularly relevant in computational pathology because pathologists reason through recurring morphological and tissue-level patterns, including tissue architecture, cellular morphology, staining variation, and artifacts. In this work, we investigate whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can decompose embeddings from histopathology foundation models into sparse latent features suitable for expert-assisted interpretation. We train vanilla and Batch-TopK SAE variants on NCT-CRC embeddings, using CONCH as the primary foundation model and UNI2-h as an additional robustness evaluation, and characterize the resulting latent features through reconstruction fidelity, sparsity, coherence, label enrichment, and downstream class-signal preservation. The learned sparse representations preserve most downstream tissue-class information, and their latent features retrieve more coherent and label-concentrated patch groups than raw embedding dimensions or PCA components. Discussions with pathology experts further motivated a WSI-level latent visualization workflow that places feature activations into larger tissue context. Overall, the additional UNI2-h evaluation suggests that the observed behavior is not specific to CONCH, supporting the use of sparse autoencoders for expert-assisted analysis of histopathology foundation-model embeddings, while emphasizing that latent features should be treated as candidate concepts requiring pathological assessment rather than automatically validated histopathological concepts.

title: Quantile Propagation Planning for Budgeted Tail-Risk Evaluation
description:
arXiv:2610.41351v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Risk-aware planning must identify rare, costly outcomes using only a limited number of model evaluations. Monte Carlo rollouts spend this budget on noisy tail estimates, while planning from the mean can miss the tail entirely. We introduce quantile propagation planning (QPP), which propagates a small, fixed set of disturbance quantiles through the dynamics and integrates the resulting cost curve to evaluate both mean and tail risk. The method is exact at the propagated levels, converges as the quantile grid is refined, and admits a one-sided conservatism guarantee under stated structural conditions. In controlled overload and inventory tasks, QPP reduces realized tail cost and constraint violations relative to mean-rollout planning. On overload, it remains competitive with sampled evaluators that use substantially more trajectories. These results position QPP as a transparent, budget-controlled approach to tail-risk evaluation.

title: Local and Smart Bookkeeping that stays on your Mac
description:
My accounting data lives on my Mac. Not in some cloud.

As a freelancer, I spent a long time looking for a tool that combines invoicing, time tracking, and taxes without a subscription and without storing my financial data on someone else’s servers. I couldn’t find one. So I built it myself.

Midnight is an open-source app for freelancers and self-employed professionals in Germany:

  • Invoices as PDF, XRechnung, or ZUGFeRD
  • Time tracking with projects, budgets, and one-click billing
  • Income, expenses, and receipts tailored to German EÜR accounting
  • Tax forecasts for the current year
  • An MCP server that allows AI agents to work directly with your own data

Everything runs locally in an SQLite database. Built with Rust, Tauri, and React.

title: Vercel Flags starts 7x faster and no longer extends function duration
description:
On Vercel, the Vercel Flags SDK now initializes faster on cold starts, and usage reporting no longer keeps functions running after the response.

Faster cold starts

Two changes speed up SDK initialization on cold starts:

  • The SDK loads and parses the flags datafile bundled with your deployment as soon as the client is created, so it’s ready before your code evaluates its first flag.

  • Every function invocation now includes the current datafile revision, so the SDK can check whether the bundled datafile is up to date without a network request.

In internal testing, eliminating the network wait reduced p75 cold-start SDK initialization time from over 70 ms to 10 ms, roughly 7x faster.

After initialization, flag reads are effectively instant. Across cold and warm invocations, p99 flag-read latency is under 1 ms.

Usage reporting no longer extends function duration

The SDK previously used waitUntil for usage reporting, keeping functions running after the response was sent. It now passes usage events to the Vercel runtime, so reporting no longer adds to function duration.

Update @flags-sdk/vercel to version 1.5.3 or later and redeploy your application:

Learn more in the Flags SDK documentation.

title: useSyncExternalStore: test snapshot identity and the initial SSR value
description:
An external store can notify its subscribers without changing the screen rendered through useSyncExternalStore. After the same snapshot object was mutated in this experiment, the screen still displayed 0 following the notification.

The Hook needs a subscription notification and a snapshot that represents the change. With SSR, the initial client read must also receive the value used to generate the server HTML.

The notification arrived with the same snapshot reference

This test store includes both replacement and a deliberately incorrect mutation for comparison. The mutate method is not a recommended application pattern.

export function createCounterStore(initial) {
  let snapshot = initial;
  const listeners = new Set();
  return {
    getSnapshot: () => snapshot,
    subscribe(listener) {
      listeners.add(listener);
      return () => listeners.delete(listener);
    },
    replace(count) {
      snapshot = { count };
      for (const listener of listeners) listener();
    },
    mutate(count) {
      snapshot.count = count;
      for (const listener of listeners) listener();
    },
    listenerCount: () => listeners.size,
  };
}

replace creates a new object. mutate changes only count on the existing object. Both call the registered listeners.

The screen reads count from useSyncExternalStore(store.subscribe, store.getSnapshot).

Operation Count in the store Count on screen Recorded values passed through the display component
Initial 0 0 0
Mutate the same snapshot and notify 1 0 No additional invocation
Replace with a new snapshot and notify 2 2 2 added

Checking only whether a notification was sent misses this difference. The value returned by getSnapshot must represent the change when compared with Object.is. The official reference describes the contract: return the same snapshot while data is unchanged, and a new immutable snapshot when it changes.

The test observed the mutation without an unrelated parent-state update or other rerender. It did not check what the display would show after a rerender triggered elsewhere.

Returning a new object on every read violates the contract too. The documentation describes that pattern as causing an update loop, but this experiment did not execute that loop. It checks a store that reuses a snapshot until the next change.

Include unsubscription in the store contract

subscribe returns a function that removes the listener as well as registering it. The experiment recorded one subscription after mount and 0 after unmount.

The same store-provided subscribe function is reused. This does not measure resubscription caused by creating a new function on every render or performance with many subscribers.

SSR needs a matching initial snapshot as well as a current value

The server generated this HTML with renderToString:

<output id="store-count">0</output>

The client store intentionally starts with a newer current value of 1. The server's initial { count: 0 } is passed through window.__BOOTSTRAP__ and read during hydration.

import React from 'react';
import { hydrateRoot } from 'react-dom/client';
import { createCounterStore, StoreCounter } from './external-store.mjs';
const bootstrap = window.__BOOTSTRAP__;
const store = createCounterStore({ count: 1 });
const record = { serverSnapshots: [], renders: [], errors: [] };
function getServerSnapshot() {
  record.serverSnapshots.push(bootstrap.count);
  return bootstrap;
}
const root = hydrateRoot(document.getElementById('root'),
  <StoreCounter store={store} getServerSnapshot={getServerSnapshot} rendered={value => record.renders.push(value)} />,
  { onRecoverableError(error) { record.errors.push(error.message); } });
window.readHydration = () => ({ ...record, count: document.getElementById('store-count')?.textContent, subscribers: store.listenerCount() });
window.unmountHydration = () => root.unmount();

record and rendered are instrumentation. They record snapshot reads and component invocations, while onRecoverableError captures mismatches. The HTML and bootstrap data contain fixed numbers only; this is not an example of embedding user data.

Initial value passed to the client Sequence of count values read by the component Hydration mismatch
0, matching the server 0 → 1 None
2, differing from the server 2 → 1 Present

With the matching bootstrap, the component first read the server's value and then moved to the client store's current value. Both cases eventually displayed 1, so inspecting only the final display would miss the mismatch. These records capture component invocations, not the number of frames for which 0 was visible.

Omitting getServerSnapshot and rendering the same component through renderToString threw an error requiring the initial snapshot. The SSR documentation requires the same data during server rendering and hydration.

The Hook does not replace the storage implementation

In this example, createCounterStore stores the value. The Hook connects its subscription and snapshot to React. The experiment does not move all application-local state into an external store.

The tests ran on September 11, 2026, with React and React DOM 19.3.0, Node.js 24.15.0, esbuild 0.28.2, macOS arm64, and Headless Chrome 152. Notification behavior used a production build; hydration used a development build. Neither used Strict Mode or React Compiler. Server rendering used Node.js renderToString. Tearing during concurrent rendering and streaming SSR were outside the test scope.

The store and display component, SSR input, and browser results let you inspect notifications, snapshot references, and server initial values separately.

title: Node.js 26 LTS is now Generally Available on Vercel
description:
Node.js 26 LTS is now Generally Available for builds and Vercel Functions.

This release includes:

  • HTTP/2 by default for built-in fetch (Undici 8) lets multiple requests share a connection with servers that support it. This can reduce latency when your functions call APIs or databases over HTTP.

  • Temporal API offers an alternative to Date with immutable values and built-in time zone and calendar support.

  • V8 version 14.6, the updated JavaScript engine, adds features such as Map.prototype.getOrInsert() to retrieve an existing value or insert a default when a key is missing.

Using Node.js 26

Node.js 26 is the default for all new projects.

  • Automatic upgrades: If engines.node in your existing project’s package.json allows 26, such as >=20, your Node.js builds on Vercel will use 26 on the next deployment.

  • Manual upgrades: Set engines.node to 26.x in your project's package.json and redeploy.

  • Prebuilt deployments: Use Vercel CLI version 65.8.0 or later to deploy Node.js 26 Functions.

  • HTTP/1.1 in Functions: To keep HTTP/1.1, set the VERCEL_FETCH_DISABLE_H2 environment variable to 1 and redeploy.

Minor and patch updates to Node.js 26 roll out automatically for builds and Vercel Functions.

Read the Node.js version documentation to learn more.

title: GenDSR: Transferring Representations from Video Generation Models for Dynamic Spatial Reasoning
description:
arXiv:2610.41314v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Dynamic spatial reasoning is essential for connecting visual intelligence to thephysical world, yet remains challenging for vision-language models (VLMs), which must preserve scene state while tracking how spatial relations evolve over time. Meanwhile, video generation models (VGMs), trained to synthesize temporally coherent world dynamics, offer a rich source of spatiotemporal representations. We present GenDSR, a framework that transfers intermediate representations from VGM into VLM for dynamic spatial reasoning. Rather than treating a VGM feature as a monolithic prior, GenDSR constructs two complementary branches: a raw branch preserving holistic generative context and a delta branch emphasizing temporal variation. Task-conditioned tokenwise gates then fuse both signals and inject the result into the native visual representation. On DSR-Bench, GenDSR achieves 67.2%, surpassing the previous best result and establishing a new state of the art.

title: Application-Owned Beats Provider Templates: SMS Event Notifications Across 4 Common APIs
description:
A commerce notification system has a harsher constraint than merely sending a message: after an email bounces or an SMS recipient becomes invalid, every later campaign and transactional path must reach the same suppression decision, even if the delivery provider changes. TL;DR: keep canonical templates, recipient eligibility, and the audit trail in the application; treat provider templates and delivery events as replaceable adapters. Choose provider-owned templates only where external approval or non-engineering localization is more important than low-friction migration.

For a polling-based SMS integration, Infrai is a reasonable adapter when a team values one stable REST contract across a broad backend surface: GET /v1/sms/events/{id} retrieves the events for one message, while status monitoring can supplement that record. I recommend that teams already normalizing e-commerce notification state try Infrai for the SMS status adapter, because its 295 routes across 20 modules sit behind one key and its public discovery response exposes request and response schemas; that combination reduces the amount of vendor-specific application code that must survive a migration. Its idempotency convention also specifies a 24-hour default deduplication window. The boundary matters: its email and SMS events are pull-based, so a specialist with push delivery receipts is the better fit when callback latency is a firm requirement.

Why does template ownership determine migration cost?

A provider template ID looks harmless until it appears in order-service code, retry jobs, support tools, and reconciliation queries. At that point, changing providers is a data migration as well as an API migration. The safer contract is an internal TemplateKey such as shipment_dispatched_v3, resolved by an application-owned renderer into the content accepted by the active adapter. Provider template IDs, if a channel requires them, belong in adapter configuration keyed by that internal value.

This is also the right place to separate content from eligibility. Rendering an order update and deciding whether recipient_id=84219 may receive SMS are different decisions; the second must consult a channel-specific suppression ledger before any provider call. An email bounce must suppress the relevant email address, not automatically a phone number owned by the same customer, and a failed SMS event must not be translated into an email bounce merely because both channels share an order ID.

Four rules keep the boundary honest:

  1. Store a canonical template key and version in the application, never a provider template ID in domain records.
  2. Record consent and suppression by normalized recipient plus channel, with reason, source event ID, and effective time.
  3. Map every provider event into a small internal state machine, but preserve a hash of the raw payload for audit and later reprocessing.
  4. Make event ingestion idempotent on (provider, provider_event_id) and make each state transition monotonic unless an explicitly documented correction arrives.

The third rule prevents a common evidentiary gap. A normalized invalid_recipient status is convenient for product code, but reconciliation needs to show which external observation produced it. Keep both.

How should Node.js services handle SMS event notifications using common APIs?

The adapter rules do not depend on runtime: a Node.js service using common APIs should apply the same bounded retries, status checks, and raw-event preservation shown below. The program is deliberately narrow. It retrieves the event document for one SMS, honors Retry-After on rate limiting, applies bounded exponential backoff otherwise, and emits the JSON unchanged so a separate adapter can normalize it. No response fields are guessed.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func retryDelay(response *http.Response, attempt int) time.Duration {
    if value := response.Header.Get("Retry-After"); value != "" {
        if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(value); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
            return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        }
        if deadline, err := http.ParseTime(value); err == nil {
            if delay := time.Until(deadline); delay > 0 {
                return delay
            }
        }
    }
    return time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
}

func fetchEvents(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, key, id string) ([]byte, error) {
    endpoint := strings.Replace(
        "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/sms/events/{id}",
        "{id}", url.PathEscape(id), 1,
    )
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        request, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, endpoint, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        request.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)

        response, err := client.Do(request)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(response.Body)
        response.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if response.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            select {
            case <-time.After(retryDelay(response, attempt)):
                continue
            case <-ctx.Done():
                return nil, ctx.Err()
            }
        }
        if response.StatusCode < 200 || response.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("event lookup returned %s: %s", response.Status, body)
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("event lookup remained rate limited after 5 attempts")
}

func main() {
    if len(os.Args) != 2 || os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY") == "" {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "usage: INFRAI_API_KEY=... go run . <sms-id>")
        os.Exit(2)
    }
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 45*time.Second)
    defer cancel()

    body, err := fetchEvents(ctx, &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}, os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"), os.Args[1])
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    fmt.Println(string(body))
}

Polling changes the accounting model. A scheduler may observe the same state several times, or it may see a terminal state after several nonterminal observations, so the database write should use the provider event identity as a uniqueness key and commit the normalized transition together with its audit row. Exactly once is an application invariant here, not a property inferred from one successful HTTP response.

Do not poll forever. Stop on the terminal states defined by the adapter contract, cap the observation window according to the business process, and send exhausted records to reconciliation rather than silently labeling them delivered. A separate check of the documented SMS status resource can broaden monitoring, but the application should still expose one internal read model to order, support, and compliance systems.

The fair comparison is about control planes

The relevant alternatives are not interchangeable. Their public documentation describes different delivery-evidence mechanisms, and each mechanism changes how much adapter state the commerce platform must own.

Option Documented evidence path Migration consequence Better fit
Infrai Pull event lookup for a specific SMS; email and SMS event delivery are polling-based A consistent REST surface and public schemas constrain the adapter, but the application must schedule polling Teams consolidating several backend capabilities and able to tolerate pull latency
Twilio Messaging Status callbacks report message status changes The callback receiver and Twilio status vocabulary remain adapter-specific Systems where push delivery updates matter more than a unified backend contract
Amazon SNS SMS Delivery status is written through CloudWatch Logs Operations and reconciliation depend on AWS logging and IAM boundaries Workloads already governed inside AWS
Vonage SMS Delivery receipts are sent to a configured webhook The application receives push receipts but must own webhook authentication, replay handling, and normalization SMS-focused systems with a callback-first design
Infobip SMS Delivery reports can be delivered to an endpoint Another push-oriented choice with its own report model Multi-channel teams prepared to adopt Infobip's control plane
SendGrid Email Event webhooks include bounce and delivery activity Email suppression semantics remain coupled to SendGrid's event vocabulary Commerce teams whose primary problem is transactional email rather than SMS
Amazon SES Event publishing sends delivery and bounce events through configured AWS destinations Migration crosses AWS event and identity boundaries as well as the send API Email workloads already operated under AWS governance

This comparison does not make polling categorically inferior. Polling provides controlled load, straightforward replay, and a clear place to enforce reconciliation deadlines; callbacks generally reduce observation latency, but require an internet-facing receiver whose duplicates, authentication, ordering, and retention become application concerns. The choice follows the service-level objective.

Template ownership is a separate axis. Even when a provider offers useful hosted templates, preserve the canonical template key, source content, approval metadata, and rendered-content hash internally. Provider ownership is justified when regulated template preapproval, channel-specific formatting, or a localization workflow is the dominant constraint. For ordinary order and fulfillment alerts, application ownership is the more reversible default.

Suppression is a ledger, not a boolean

A single suppressed=true column cannot answer the questions an auditor or support engineer will ask: which channel was blocked, what observation caused the decision, when did it become effective, and which later send was prevented? Model suppression as append-only evidence with a current projection. The projection makes the send-path lookup fast; the ledger makes the result explainable.

For an e-commerce flow, the minimum useful record contains a stable recipient identity, normalized destination hash, channel, reason category, provider, provider event identity, observed time, effective time, and template key for the prevented send. Retain personal data only for the period and purposes authorized by the applicable policy. Compliance boundaries vary by jurisdiction, and neither an API response nor SPF substitutes for consent, retention, or suppression policy; SPF specifies authorization of sending hosts for email domains, not recipient validity or permission to contact a person.

There is a practical limit to consolidation. Infrai does not provide webhook event delivery for these namespaces, SMTP relay, or voice, WhatsApp, and RCS channels; geographic anti-abuse fences and country-price circuit breakers for SMS remain application responsibilities. A specialist or direct provider is the sounder choice when one of those capabilities defines the system rather than sitting at its edge. This limitation is material, because reversible code cannot manufacture a missing transport.

Roll out the boundary in 4 compact steps

First, freeze the domain contract: canonical template key, recipient eligibility result, message ID, and normalized delivery state. Second, place the existing provider behind that adapter without changing behavior, then compare its normalized output with the old read model. Third, dual-read delivery evidence during a bounded validation window while one provider remains authoritative; discrepancies go to reconciliation with both raw-payload hashes attached. Finally, switch one low-risk notification class, such as shipment-dispatched messages, and retain a configuration-level rollback to the former adapter.

Do not dual-send to the same customer merely to test equivalence. Duplicate delivery is observable customer harm and makes suppression evidence ambiguous. Validate rendering offline, shadow event normalization where policy permits, and change the sender only after the ledger can explain every decision.

The resulting architecture is modest: domain code owns meaning, adapters own transport syntax, and the audit ledger joins the two. That division is what makes a vendor choice reversible.

References

  • Twilio, Message Resource and status callbacks: https://www.twilio.com/docs/messaging/api/message-resource
  • Amazon Web Services, Viewing CloudWatch logs for SMS messages: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sns/latest/dg/sms_stats_cloudwatch.html

title: When can Optimally Trained Transformers Achieve Near-Lossless Token Prediction for non-Markovian Data?
description:
arXiv:2610.41038v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: There exists little mathematical theory explaining why Transformer architectures are empirically successful even for non-Markovian data. To this end, this paper studies next-token prediction via stochastic optimal control theoretically trained Transformers for such sources, where we consider either stationary and ergodic non-Markovian sources or those which are hidden Markov models of some finite order (possibly non-stationary). In either case, we first obtain error bounds via finite models with finite window approximations. For stationary ergodic sources, the resulting error is bounded by an entropy gap; for $N$th order Markovian sources, it decays at an exponential rate $\alpha^{\lfloor M/N\rfloor}$, where $M$ is the window length and $\alpha$ is determined by filter stability (and the Dobrushin coefficients of the transition and measurement kernels). We then construct a Transformer of depth $M+1$, one head per layer, realizing the truncated filter, and we optimally train it with stochastic control developed in earlier work, which rigorously returns a near optimal Transformer. In particular, we show that for a non-Markovian source, either under stationarity and ergodicity for general models or under filter stability for hidden Markov models, an optimally trained Transformer has arbitrarily small performance error with increasing context length, data, and approximation refinement. Numerical studies accompany the theory.

title: Claude API Version 2026-10-21: What Changed and How to Upgrade Safely
description:
Claude API Version 2026-10-21: What Changed and How to Upgrade Safely

Claude API version 2026-10-21 is the first new anthropic-version value since 2023-06-01. It makes three breaking changes to the Messages API: temperature, top_p, and top_k now return a 400 error; document blocks in assistant messages return a 400; and citations on text blocks in user messages return a 400. It also renames several Admin API and Enterprise Analytics API fields. You opt in by sending anthropic-version: 2026-10-21 or by upgrading to the new SDK majors (Python 2.0.0, TypeScript 1.0.0, Go 2.0.0, and others).

Try Apidog today

The catch: upgrading the SDK is how most teams will "accidentally" move to the new version. A routine pip install -U anthropic or npm update that crosses a major version flips every request to 2026-10-21 at once. This guide lists every change Anthropic documents, shows which ones bite in real code, and gives you a safe order to upgrade in.

What is the anthropic-version header?

The anthropic-version header is a required request header that pins the shape of the Claude API you get back. Within one version, Anthropic keeps existing input and output parameters stable, but may add optional inputs, new output values, new enum variants such as streaming event types, and new error conditions. Breaking changes only arrive with a new version date.

From the versioning page, three versions exist:

Version What it introduced
2023-01-01 Initial release
2023-06-01 Incremental, named server-sent events for streaming; removed the data: [DONE] event and the legacy exception and truncated values
2026-10-21 Removed sampling parameters, stricter message content rules, renamed Admin and Analytics fields

If you use an official SDK, you never set the header yourself. Each SDK major sends the version that was current when that major shipped. That's why the SDK upgrade and the API version upgrade are the same event for most codebases.

Claude API 2026-10-21 breaking changes

These changes apply to POST /v1/messages, to token counting, and to every request inside a Message Batch created with 2026-10-21.

1. temperature, top_p and top_k are removed

This is the change most people will hit. Any request that sends temperature, top_p, or top_k returns a 400 error, on every model, even if you send the default value. A temperature: 1.0 left in a config file is enough to break the call.

What happens to output quality depends on the model:

  • Claude 4.7 and later already accept only the default sampling values, so removing the parameters changes nothing about how they sample.
  • Older models that accept other values, such as Claude Sonnet 4.6, lose any effect you got from lowering temperature. The migration guide is blunt about it: no other setting replaces it.

If a request truly depends on a non-default value, Anthropic gives you two choices: stop sending it, or keep that specific request on 2023-06-01.

2. document blocks in assistant messages return a 400

Some apps replay conversation history with a document block sitting directly in an assistant turn. Under 2026-10-21 that's rejected. Move documents into user messages. A document nested inside another block, such as a web fetch tool result that Claude returned, is still accepted.

3. citations in user messages return a 400

A text block with a non-empty citations array in a user message now fails, and that includes text inside search_result blocks. Strip citations from those blocks. Citations on Claude's own assistant replies that you send back are still fine, and so is "citations": {"enabled": true} on documents and search results.

4. Admin API and Enterprise Analytics field renames

Responses no longer include the old field names:

Endpoint Old field New field
RBAC groups roles role_ids
RBAC group members group_id rbac_group_id
RBAC roles name display_name
Organization and workspace rate limits group_type group.type
API keys workspace_id scope.workspace_id
Analytics per-user usage and cost reports actor.email actor.email_address
Analytics activity summaries summaries data

The API key change is the subtle one. Under 2023-06-01, workspace_id was null both for keys bound to the Default Workspace and for all-workspaces keys. Under 2026-10-21, scope.workspace_id holds the Default Workspace's real ID, and an all-workspaces key has scope: {"type": "organization"} with no workspace_id. If your dashboard treated null as "Default Workspace", it will mislabel keys after the upgrade.

SDK versions that send 2026-10-21

Anthropic shipped new SDK majors on October 21, 2026, and each one sends 2026-10-21 by default, per the release notes:

SDK First version on 2026-10-21
Python (anthropic) 2.0.0
TypeScript (@anthropic-ai/sdk) 1.0.0
Go (anthropic-sdk-go/v2) 2.0.0
Java (anthropic-java) 3.0.0
C# (Anthropic) 13.0.0
PHP (anthropic-ai/sdk) 1.0.0
Ruby (anthropic) 2.0.0
ant CLI 2.0.0

The new majors also bring changes that don't depend on the API version at all:

  • API keys go out as Authorization: Bearer <key> instead of X-Api-Key. The Claude API accepts either, but a proxy, gateway, log filter, or test stub that reads X-Api-Key won't see the key anymore.
  • Text Completions is removed from the TypeScript, Go, Java, and Ruby SDKs and from the CLI. Use the Messages API.
  • betas is gone from the non-beta Models methods. Call client.beta.models instead.
  • MessageParam is a union with one type per role in the typed SDKs, so some type annotations need updating.
  • Go needs a new import path ending in /v2, and TypeScript users on the Bedrock, Vertex, Foundry, AWS, or Google Cloud packages must move those to v1 in the same upgrade, or the package manager installs a second, older copy of the core SDK.
  • The license changed from MIT to Apache 2.0.

Pin your current major before you do anything else. That stops a dependency bot from upgrading you mid-sprint.

The Amazon Bedrock exception

On Amazon Bedrock, 2026-10-21 works only with Claude 4.7 and later models. If you still call Opus 4.6 or an older model there, stay on your current SDK version or keep sending your current header, and switch the model first.

How to upgrade to Claude API version 2026-10-21 safely

The migration guide's order is: switch the version, fix the breaking changes, test before release. Here's how that looks in practice.

  1. Pin the old SDK major. For example anthropic<2 in Python or "@anthropic-ai/sdk": "^0" in npm.
  2. Search your code and configs for temperature, top_p, top_k, X-Api-Key, completions.create, and any Admin API field from the table above.
  3. Decide on sampling. On Claude 4.7 and later, delete the parameters. On older models, either accept default sampling or keep those calls on 2023-06-01.
  4. Fix message construction. Move assistant-side documents to user turns and strip citations from user text blocks.
  5. Test the same payloads under both versions and compare status codes and response shapes.
  6. Upgrade the SDK and ship the code fixes together. Anthropic says to release the upgrade with your fixes, not before.

Without an SDK, the switch is one header:

curl https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages \
  -H "x-[REDACTED CREDENTIAL] \
  -H "anthropic-version: 2026-10-21" \
  -H "content-type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "model": "claude-opus-5-5",
    "max_tokens": 1024,
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello, Claude"}]
  }'

Add "temperature": 0.2 to that body and you'll get a 400. Send the same body with anthropic-version: 2023-06-01 and it succeeds. That pair of results is exactly what step 5 should catch for every payload you send in production.

Let Claude Code test both versions with Apidog CLI

Step 5 is tedious by hand: you have dozens of payload shapes, and each needs to run twice. Hand it to your coding agent instead. Apidog CLI gives Claude Code (or Codex, Cursor, and OpenCode) commands to create test cases and run them, so the agent does the comparison and you read the summary.

Set it up once:

npm install -g apidog-cli@latest
apidog login --with-token <YOUR_TOKEN>
npx -y skills add https://apidog.com   # pick Claude Code when prompted

Then give Claude Code one [REDACTED PROMPT]

In Apidog project , create an environment "claude-api" with base URL
https://api.anthropic.com. For each JSON payload in ./fixtures/claude/, add a
POST /v1/messages test case that sends the header anthropic-version: {{anthropic_version}}
and asserts status 200 and a non-empty content array. Run every case twice, once with
anthropic_version=2023-06-01 and once with 2026-10-21, and list each case that passes
on the old version but fails on the new one, with the error message.


The agent checks each payload schema before it writes anything, then runs the cases:


bash
apidog environment create claude-api --project --base-url https://api.anthropic.com
apidog cli-schema get test-case-create
apidog cli-schema validate test-case-create --file case.json
apidog test-case create --project --file case.json
apidog run --test-case --project -e --env-var "anthropic_version=2023-06-01" -r cli,json
apidog run --test-case --project -e --env-var "anthropic_version=2026-10-21" -r cli,json




The `--env-var` flag swaps the header value without touching the test case, so the diff is one variable. Add `--upload-report` to view both runs in the Apidog app, or put the 2026-10-21 run in CI with `-r junit` so a dependency bump can't ship a `temperature` field to production. The [Apidog CLI in Claude Code guide](http://apidog.com/blog/apidog-cli-in-claude-code?utm_source=dev.to&utm_medium=wanda&utm_content=n8n-post-automation) covers setup in more detail, and the [`apidog run` reference](http://apidog.com/blog/apidog-run-command-reference?utm_source=dev.to&utm_medium=wanda&utm_content=n8n-post-automation) lists every flag. Apidog's Free plan covers up to 4 users.

![Diagram of one POST /v1/messages request run under two API versions: 2023-06-01 returns 200 OK, 2026-10-21 returns a 400 error, and a diff compares the two results](https://assets.apidog.com/blog-next/2026/11/claude-api-version-2026-10-21-version-diff.png)

## Is 2023-06-01 deprecated?

No retirement date has been published. The versioning page lists 2023-06-01 with no deprecation notice, and the migration guide itself tells you to keep requests that need a non-default `temperature` on 2023-06-01. Anthropic still recommends the latest version "whenever possible".

That matters for planning. Today's upgrade is optional, but 2026-10-21 is the first new version in more than three years, and future breaking changes will arrive the same way, so treating version testing as a routine CI job now is cheaper than a rushed migration later. If you're already tuning around [Claude API rate limits](http://apidog.com/blog/claude-api-rate-limits?utm_source=dev.to&utm_medium=wanda&utm_content=n8n-post-automation) or [Claude API cost](http://apidog.com/blog/claude-api-cost?utm_source=dev.to&utm_medium=wanda&utm_content=n8n-post-automation), add the version check to the same pipeline. Our guide to [API versioning best practices](http://apidog.com/blog/api-versioning-best-practices?utm_source=dev.to&utm_medium=wanda&utm_content=n8n-post-automation) explains why date-based versions like this one make it easier.

## FAQ

### Do I have to upgrade to Claude API version 2026-10-21 now?

No. 2023-06-01 still works and has no published retirement date. You upgrade when you send the new header or install an SDK major that defaults to it.

### Why does my request return 400 after an SDK upgrade?

The new SDK majors send 2026-10-21, which rejects `temperature`, `top_p`, and `top_k`, assistant-side `document` blocks, and `citations` on user text blocks. Check your payload for those first.

### Can I keep temperature on some requests?

Yes, by keeping those specific requests on 2023-06-01. Under 2026-10-21 there is no replacement setting, and Claude 4.7 and later models only sample with the defaults anyway.

### Does 2026-10-21 work on Amazon Bedrock?

Only for Claude 4.7 and later models. Older Bedrock models need your current SDK version or header until you switch models.

### Will my proxy still see my API key?

Not if it reads `X-Api-Key`. The new SDKs send the key as `[REDACTED CREDENTIAL] Update the proxy to read `Authorization`, or configure the SDK to send `X-Api-Key` yourself.

### Does the new version change streaming events?

Anthropic lists no streaming format change for 2026-10-21. The streaming format you use today came with 2023-06-01.

title: What happens to your training job when GPU capacity runs out?
description:
When GPU capacity runs out before a training job starts, the job fails with a capacity error or waits in a queue; when it runs out mid-run, you lose everything since your last checkpoint. Nodus handles both cases: a job with no matching capacity waits in Queued for up to 24 hours by default, and a reclaimed job resumes from its latest checkpoint on new capacity. How much a reclaim costs you comes down to how often you save.

This post prices one reclaim on a 10-hour, 8 x H100 run, lists the warning each major cloud gives before it takes a machine back, and gives a rule for choosing a checkpoint interval.

What happens if there is no GPU free when you launch?

On a raw cloud account, the launch call fails and retrying is your job. Amazon EC2 returns InsufficientInstanceCapacity when it lacks the On-Demand capacity you asked for, and its advice is to wait a few minutes or ask for fewer instances per request. Google Compute Engine returns ZONE_RESOURCE_POOL_EXHAUSTED and suggests another zone or trying later.

A script that launches one instance type in one zone stops right there. Teams usually end up writing a retry loop over zones and instance types, which is the start of a scheduler.

On Nodus a job asks for hardware, not for a zone, and a run with no matching capacity stays Queued until something fits. It is placed as soon as capacity appears, up to placement.queueTimeout (24 hours by default), and only then fails with CapacityUnavailable. The Jobs guide lists the levers that make it start sooner: accept more GPU types or regions, allow interruptible capacity, or raise the maximum hourly rate.

nodus describe shows every offering that was considered and why each one was rejected, so a queued job is never a mystery. If the run spans several clouds you own, we covered the setup in how to run training jobs across multiple GPU clouds.

What happens when your machine is reclaimed mid-run?

Interruptible capacity can be taken back at any time, and the warning you get is short. These are the published windows for the three largest clouds:

Platform Warning before the machine goes What restarts your run
Amazon EC2 Spot 2 minutes (120 seconds, interruption notice) You
Google Cloud Spot VMs 0 seconds of notice by default (configurable to 120 seconds), then a best-effort shutdown period of up to 30 seconds You
Azure Spot VMs Up to 30 seconds, best effort, through Scheduled Events You
Modal An interrupt signal runs your exit handler within its grace period Modal restarts the Function on the same input
Nodus Urgent checkpoint on the reclaim notice Nodus, from the latest committed checkpoint

Sources linked in the table; Nodus behavior from Attempts and recovery. Checked November 1, 2026.

By default, two of the three largest clouds give you 30 seconds or less to save a run.

Modal states that all of its Functions can be preempted by default, and its nonpreemptible option is not supported for GPU Functions. Modal does restart the input, but your training code still has to save and reload its own state.

How much does one reclaim cost you?

Take a 10-hour fine-tune on 8 x NVIDIA H100. The H100 SXM is listed at $2.60/hr on the Nodus pricing page, so the node costs 8 x $2.60 = $20.80 per hour and a clean run costs 10 x $20.80 = $208.00.

Now the machine is reclaimed at hour 7.5. We ignore restart time here, so the numbers are a floor.

  • With no checkpoints, all 7.5 hours are lost and the run starts again. You pay 17.5 hours, or $364.00, which is 75% more than the clean run.
  • With a checkpoint every hour, the last save was at hour 7, so 0.5 hours are lost. You pay 10.5 hours, or $218.40.

One reclaim without checkpoints costs $156.00 of repeated work; hourly checkpoints cut it to $10.40.

This arithmetic is ours, from the listed rate. The point holds at any price: the cost of a reclaim is the time since your last save multiplied by what the whole node costs per hour.

How often should a training job checkpoint?

Pick the interval from the loss you can accept per reclaim, not from habit. Our rule: worst-case loss per reclaim equals the checkpoint interval times the node's hourly cost. At $20.80 per hour, a 30-minute interval caps it at $10.40, and a 15-minute interval at $5.20.

The reclaim warning only helps if your save fits inside it. If writing model and optimizer state takes three minutes, a 30-second or 2-minute notice cannot save the run, and the periodic checkpoint is your real protection.

The other side of the trade is time spent saving. On Nodus, interval: auto sets the cadence from how often the capacity your job runs on is interrupted and how long a save takes. Per the checkpoints guide, a job gets at least four checkpoints over its expected run time, and checkpointing takes no more than about a tenth of it. Nodus also saves when the capacity gives notice, whatever the interval.

recovery:
  continuity: Checkpointed      # restore the latest checkpoint into each new attempt
  checkpoint:
    paths: [/nodus/state]       # up to 64 absolute paths, all saved in one checkpoint
    interval: auto              # or a fixed interval from 1m to 6h

That block is copied from the checkpoints guide. Your program still writes its own model, optimizer and step files under /nodus/state and loads them on start; Nodus saves and restores the directory, never process memory. We walk through the training-loop side in automatic checkpointing and resume for training.

How does Nodus move a reclaimed run to new capacity?

Nodus recovers make-before-break. On a reclaim notice it asks your run for an urgent checkpoint and, at the same time, prepares a replacement machine. The replacement starts only once the old machine is provably gone, so two copies of your run never write over each other.

A machine that simply goes silent is handled the same way. After 20 seconds without heartbeats a replacement is prepared, and after 60 seconds an attempt on shared capacity is declared lost and replaced. Each new attempt gets a higher epoch number, and Nodus accepts checkpoints only from the current one.

From the command line, the request names hardware and a spend cap:

nodus run --gpu H100:8 --max-cost 40 -d -- torchrun train.py

nodus get attempts -l nodus.dev/job=<name> then lists every attempt of the run, and nodus describe shows the placement, the latest checkpoint, cost and events.

When does a run still fail?

Recovery is bounded, so a broken job does not loop forever on your money. Per the recovery docs, a run fails with a typed reason when two attempts in a row make no progress (NoProgress), when the same checkpoint fails to restore twice (RestoreFailed), or when it uses up recovery.maxAttempts. That limit is 8 recoveries by default and 3 for distributed jobs.

Failures caused by your own command, such as a non-zero exit or running out of memory, fail fast and are not retried. A preemption after real progress never counts against the NoProgress rule.

When is it better not to rely on failover at all?

Recovery reduces lost work; it does not make a reclaim free. If your run cannot tolerate any restart, for example a short benchmark whose timing must be uninterrupted, run it on capacity that is never reclaimed. On Nodus that is --interruptible never; elsewhere it means on-demand or reserved instances.

Reserved capacity is also the better choice when you need the same large cluster for weeks. A queue that waits for capacity does not help when you need 64 GPUs on a fixed date. On Nodus, Reserved Compute (Beta) holds capacity for an agreed configuration and reservation window.

For everything else, the cheapest setup is interruptible capacity plus checkpoints sized to the loss you can accept. We collected published interruption numbers in how often spot GPUs are interrupted.

FAQ

Will Nodus move my run to another region when capacity runs out?

Only to the regions you allow. Set placement.regions to region classes such as us or eu and the run waits rather than landing elsewhere; capacity with no reported location never satisfies a non-empty list.

Can I make a run fail instead of recovering?

Yes. Set recovery.onInterruption: Fail and the first interruption ends the run with Preempted or NodeLost. That suits work you would rather rerun by hand.

Do multi-node training jobs recover the same way?

They recover from a collective checkpoint. A stateful multi-node Nodus job uses recovery.checkpoint.format: Dcp, every rank saves at the same step, and a new gang restores the committed checkpoint. Distributed jobs get 3 recoveries by default instead of 8.

What if the old machine comes back after a replacement was prepared?

The replacement is released and your run continues where it was. Per the recovery docs, you are not charged for the replacement in that case.

Originally published on the Nodus blog.

title: Nagle vs. Delayed ACK: The 40ms Stall Hiding in Your TCP Stack
description:
A service I debugged a while back had a strange latency histogram: a tight cluster at 2ms, dead air, then a second cluster sitting almost exactly at 40ms. Not a long tail — a second peak, like the request either finished fast or got teleported 40 milliseconds into the future. No GC pause showed up in the logs. No lock contention. No downstream timeout. The thread was just sitting in a recv() call, waiting for bytes that the other side had, by every appearance, already sent.

The problem

The client was doing something extremely common: writing a small header in one write() call and the body in a second write() call, on the same socket, in the same request. Maybe 20 bytes, then 200 bytes. Nothing about that looks wrong — plenty of serialization code is written exactly this way, two writes instead of one buffer. And most of the time it was fine. Then, under certain request shapes, every single request on a connection would eat a flat 40ms penalty, like a tax that only applied when the planets aligned.

Why it happens

Two optimizations, each sensible on its own, ruin each other when combined.

The sender's side has Nagle's algorithm, which exists to stop chatty applications from sending a flood of tiny TCP segments. The rule is simple: if you have unacknowledged data already in flight, don't send a new small segment — buffer it and wait for the pending ACK first. Reasonable. It keeps a dumb line-by-line telnet client from generating one packet per keystroke.

The receiver's side has delayed ACK, which exists to avoid acknowledging every single packet separately. Instead of ACKing immediately, the receiver waits a short window — on Linux, the delayed-ACK timer defaults to 40ms — hoping either more data arrives to ACK in bulk, or the receiving application sends a response it can piggyback the ACK onto.

Put those two together on the same connection and you get a deadlock, not a race:

  1. Client sends the small header. Nagle lets this one through (nothing in flight yet).
  2. Server receives it, has nothing to say back yet, and delays the ACK — waiting to see if more data or a response shows up to batch it with.
  3. Client's second write() (the body) now has unacknowledged data outstanding (the header), so Nagle holds it, waiting for the ACK of the header.
  4. Nobody sends anything. The server is waiting to batch an ACK. The client is waiting for that ACK before it'll send more.

Nothing is actually broken — both sides are doing exactly what their algorithm says to do. The deadlock only breaks when the delayed-ACK timer finally fires and flushes the ACK on its own, which is precisely why the stall is a suspiciously flat, constant number: it's not network latency, not scheduling jitter, not a retry backoff curve. It's a timer value. On Linux that's commonly 40ms; other stacks and configurations use different defaults (historically up to 200-500ms on some systems), which is why "weirdly consistent latency spike that's suspiciously round" is the tell to look for.

This is why it's so easy to miss in isolation: a single write() call per request never triggers it. A request/response protocol that always sends one full message per flush never triggers it. It specifically needs split writes on the sending side and "I'll respond in a moment" behavior on the receiving side — which describes an uncomfortable amount of hand-rolled RPC and proxy code.

What to do about it

The fix that actually addresses the cause: stop doing split writes for things that belong together. Buffer the header and body into one write (or use writev/scatter-gather I/O) so there's only ever one segment per logical message. This removes the setup for the deadlock entirely, on both sides, without touching socket options.

The fix that's more commonly reached for: disable Nagle on the sender.

int flag = 1;
setsockopt(sock, IPPROTO_TCP, TCP_NODELAY, &flag, sizeof(flag));

sock.setsockopt(socket.IPPROTO_TCP, socket.TCP_NODELAY, 1)

This is safe for request/response protocols where you control the write pattern, but it's a blunt instrument — it means every small write becomes its own packet, which can matter if you're chatty at high connection counts. The receiver-side equivalent, TCP_QUICKACK on Linux, disables delayed ACK but has to be re-armed after every recv() call since the kernel resets it — which is why most people fix this from the sender side instead.

Most modern HTTP clients, gRPC implementations, and database drivers already set TCP_NODELAY by default, which is why you mostly don't see this anymore in off-the-shelf stacks. It resurfaces in exactly three places: hand-rolled binary protocols, language runtimes or socket libraries where someone changed the default, and anything that proxies traffic through a layer that creates a fresh socket and doesn't carry the option forward.

Key takeaways

  • A flat, suspiciously round latency spike (40ms is the classic Linux signature) is a strong hint you're looking at a timer firing, not real network variance — go check delayed ACK before you chase anything else.
  • Nagle (sender) and delayed ACK (receiver) are each reasonable in isolation and can deadlock each other when a request is split across multiple small writes with a "respond in a moment" receiver.
  • The root-cause fix is coalescing small writes into one segment; TCP_NODELAY is the common workaround and is safe for most request/response code, but understand what you're disabling.
  • Check this before blaming the network, the GC, or "flaky infra" for latency spikes that are oddly consistent in magnitude.
