title: Near-Optimal First-Order Regret for Bandits with Feedback Graphs
description:
arXiv:2610.40861v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study first-order regret guarantees for adversarial bandits with a fixed, known directed feedback graph. For strongly observable graphs, [ACBDK15] establishes a minimax regret of $\widetilde{\Theta}(\sqrt{\alpha T})$, where $\alpha$ denotes the independence number of the graph and $T$ denotes the horizon. On the other hand, the best existing first-order bound scales as $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{(\kappa+1) L^\star})$ [LLZ20], where $\kappa$ denotes the clique partition number, satisfying $\kappa+1\geq\alpha$, and $L^\star$ denotes the cumulative loss of the best arm, leaving a gap between the graph dependence in worst-case and first-order guarantees. In this paper, we bridge this gap by obtaining an expected regret bound of $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{\alpha L^\star}+\alpha)$. Our first result is an algorithm for the special case of self-aware graphs, in which every vertex has a self-loop. The algorithm combines the update of EXP3 [ACBFS02] with a sampling rule inspired by exploration by optimization [LS20]. More specifically, we construct a map whose fixed points yield sampling distributions that control the one-round regret remainder in terms of the learner's loss and the graph's independence number, which is crucial in deriving optimal first-order guarantees. We further show that a sufficiently accurate fixed point can be computed in polynomial time by a geometrically convergent iteration. Finally, we extend the algorithm to general strongly observable graphs and achieve the same $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{\alpha L^\star}+\alpha)$ guarantee by adapting the two-level aggregation approach of [LLZ20].

title: Chrome Blocked 8 eMudhra CA Keys on Oct 17. A Node Release From Oct 14 Still Trusts Them.
description:
On Saturday, October 17, at 18:05 UTC, a researcher reported to the Chrome Root Program that the private keys of eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates could be recovered by anyone. The keys had been generated with weak randomness. With one of them you can sign a certificate for any domain, and clients that still trust that intermediate will accept it.

Chrome blocked the keys 100 minutes later with a CRLSet push. Firefox blocked them the same day. Microsoft followed on the 20th, Apple on the 22nd, and Chrome removed the root above them, emSign ECC Root CA - G3, from its root store on October 27.

That covers browsers. Your backend is not a browser. It calls Stripe, sends webhooks and talks to your email provider through Node, Python or Go, and a lot of those don't read CRLSets. They check against a list of roots that shipped with the runtime or the package.

So I tested it. Same Debian 13 box, with the patched system ca-certificates (20250419+deb13u1) installed. A Node binary released on October 14 still connected to a site signed by a compromised intermediate.

What actually happened, briefly

  • Eight intermediates under emSign ECC Root CA - G3 had keys that could be recovered straight from the public certificates. eMudhra says it revoked all eight on October 18, that seven were never used in production, and that the one in production had issued zero certificates.
  • No abuse has been reported. Cloudflare said it found no exploitation on its services, and the test page below says plainly that nobody knows whether non-browser clients were targeted. Browsers also enforce Certificate Transparency, so a forged cert that was never logged fails there anyway.
  • Most non-browser clients check neither revocation nor CT. For them, the only fix is a trust store that no longer includes those roots.

Dennis Jackson from Mozilla put up a test page with live endpoints signed by the compromised intermediates, plus a list of which packages have shipped fixes. If your client connects and gets the text "That's bad!", it still trusts them. The -noct hosts use leaf certs that were never logged to CT, which is the case an attacker would actually use.

The test

A 13-line script that calls fetch() on the four test hosts:

// check-emudhra.mjs
const hosts = ['dv-g3b', 'dv-g3b-aaa', 'dv-g3b-noct', 'dv-g3b-aaa-noct'];
console.log(`node ${process.version}`);
for (const h of hosts) {
  const url = `https://${h}-emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com/`;
  try {
    const res = await fetch(url, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(15000) });
    const body = (await res.text()).trim().slice(0, 40);
    console.log(`${h.padEnd(16)} TRUSTED   ${res.status} "${body}"`);
  } catch (e) {
    console.log(`${h.padEnd(16)} rejected  ${e.cause?.code ?? e.message}`);
  }
}

Real output, run this morning:

node v24.22.1
dv-g3b           rejected  CERT_REVOKED
dv-g3b-aaa       rejected  CERT_REVOKED
dv-g3b-noct      rejected  CERT_REVOKED
dv-g3b-aaa-noct  rejected  CERT_REVOKED

node v24.22.0
dv-g3b           TRUSTED   200 "Your client successfully connected to th"
dv-g3b-aaa       rejected  UNABLE_TO_GET_ISSUER_CERT_LOCALLY
dv-g3b-noct      TRUSTED   200 "Your client successfully connected to th"
dv-g3b-aaa-noct  rejected  UNABLE_TO_GET_ISSUER_CERT_LOCALLY

The full body of that 200 is "Your client successfully connected to the site. That's bad!". Node 24.22.0 came out on October 14. Node 24.22.1 is the October 21 security release, which updated the bundled roots to NSS 3.131.1 and added a check that rejects chains containing blocked public keys. That second change is most likely where the CERT_REVOKED comes from.

I ran the same thing in Python with requests, which uses certifi's bundle and not the OS:

certifi 2026.10.23
dv-g3b           rejected  unable to get local issuer certificate
dv-g3b-noct      rejected  unable to get local issuer certificate

certifi 2026.07.22
dv-g3b           TRUSTED   200 'Your client successfully connected to th'
dv-g3b-noct      TRUSTED   200 'Your client successfully connected to th'

(The two -aaa hosts, which use Sectigo cross-signs, were rejected by every client on this box, old or new, so I've left them out here.)

curl on the same machine rejected all four, because it uses the patched system bundle. So the OS was fixed and two of the three clients on it weren't.

Why patching the OS didn't help

Node ships its own copy of the Mozilla root list inside the binary. requests reads certifi's cacert.pem out of your virtualenv. Updating ca-certificates touches neither.

One trap I didn't expect: node --use-system-ca didn't help on the old binary either. It still trusted the bad host. The Node docs say that flag uses the system store "along with" the bundled one, so the old bundled root is still there. --use-openssl-ca, which swaps the bundled store for OpenSSL's system store, did reject all four on the old binary. Upgrading Node is still the real fix. The flag just tells you where the trust is coming from.

Where the old copies are hiding

For a small SaaS or a side project, I'd check these:

  • Docker images built before October 21. The Node or Python inside is whatever was current at build time. If you pin node:24-slim by digest, it doesn't move until you move it.
  • Anything on Node 20. It's end-of-life, so it doesn't get the new root list at all. Vercel's advisory says the same thing and tells people to move to 22 or newer.
  • A pinned certifi in requirements.txt, poetry.lock or uv.lock. Patched from 2026.10.19.
  • CI runners and self-hosted cron boxes, which tend to drift.
  • Your Mac. As of the test page's October 28 update, the curl, git and python3 Apple ships still trust the compromised certificates.

The project you haven't touched since summer is the most likely to still have the old list. If that's you, I wrote a list of what to check first when you restart an abandoned side project, and an expired runtime is one of the items on it.

An 18-line check for any machine or image

This prints 1 if emSign ECC Root CA - G3 is still in the system bundle, in the node you're running, or in your certifi:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# roots-check.sh: 1 = root still trusted (bad), 0 = gone
NODE=${NODE:-node}; PY=${PY:-python3}
needle='emSign ECC Root CA - G3'

count_in_bundle() {
  openssl crl2pkcs7 -nocrl -certfile "$1" | openssl pkcs7 -print_certs -noout \
    | grep '^subject=' | grep -c "$needle"
}

echo "system bundle:          $(count_in_bundle /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt)"
echo "node $($NODE -v) bundled: $($NODE -e '
  const { X509Certificate } = require("crypto");
  const hits = require("tls").rootCertificates
    .filter(pem => new X509Certificate(pem).subject.includes(process.argv[1]));
  console.log(hits.length)' "$needle")"
CF=$($PY -c 'import certifi; print(certifi.where())')
echo "certifi $($PY -c 'import certifi; print(certifi.__version__)'):     $(count_in_bundle "$CF")"

Output for the current versions and then the old ones:

system bundle:          0
node v24.22.1 bundled: 0
certifi 2026.10.23:     0

system bundle:          0
node v24.22.0 bundled: 1
certifi 2026.07.22:     1

To check a container, mount the script and run it inside, something like docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/c" your-image bash /c/roots-check.sh. Slim images often lack openssl or python, so just keep the line that applies (for a Node image, the node -e part is all you need).

Is your own site's certificate affected?

This is the other half, and for most indie sites the answer is no. If your cert comes from Let's Encrypt or Google Trust Services, like most small sites, nothing changes for you. It matters if you bought an ECC certificate that chains to emSign ECC Root CA - G3. The University of Michigan, for example, had to replace certificates issued through CERTInext with ECC keys, and its sites behind Cloudflare in Full (strict) mode started returning 526 errors on October 20.

To see which root you're on, look at the issuer line and every row of the chain, not just the expiry date. openssl s_client -connect yourdomain.com:443 -showcerts shows them, or you can paste the domain into a free SSL checker that lists the issuer and the full chain. If "emSign" shows up anywhere in that chain, get a new certificate from a different CA before your visitors start seeing warnings.

The fix list

  1. Node: 22.23.4, 24.22.1 or 26.12.1 or later. Get off Node 20.
  2. certifi 2026.10.19 or later, and update the lockfile too.
  3. Rebuild images with --pull --no-cache so you don't reuse the old layer, then redeploy. Restart long-running processes too. A Node process that's been up since September is still running the old binary with the old roots.
  4. Run check-emudhra.mjs (or curl on the test host) from inside the deployed thing, not from your laptop. Cloudflare's write-up makes the same point: a passing browser test doesn't mean your background worker is fixed.
  5. If something starts failing with certificate errors after you patch, do not "fix" it with NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0 or verify=False. That turns off the protection you just installed.

This is the second certificate change this month that only shows up when you check what's actually running instead of what the config says. The other one is Let's Encrypt moving to 64-day certificates, where the danger is hardcoded renewal thresholds.

If you pin your base image by digest (which you should for other reasons), what makes you rebuild it? A schedule, Renovate/Dependabot bumping the digest, or only when something breaks?

title: bf16 Rounding Silently Discards Most RL Policy Updates: A Hidden Training-Inference Mismatch and an Unbiased One-Line Fix
description:
arXiv:2610.41073v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training of language models keeps fp32 master weights in the optimizer and serves rollouts from a bf16 copy produced by round-to-nearest conversion. At the learning rates in common use, most per-step updates are smaller than half a bf16 spacing and the conversion discards them: on Qwen3-1.7B only 0.4-0.5% of served weights change per step, and the policy that generates the training data lags the optimizer by 50-150 steps. Existing mismatch corrections cannot see this lag because they compare two copies downstream of the same rounding. We propose Fair Cast: export the master with an unbiased rounding rule (stochastic rounding or error feedback) and compute the training loss on the served copy. The change is one line at the export call, adds no hyperparameters and costs 22-38 ms per export of 1.7B parameters. Across 25 matched seed-pairs on Qwen3-0.6B to 4B with AdamW and Muon, Fair Cast is ahead on 18, tied on 6 and behind on 1, with a mean gain of 6.1 points; on zebra puzzles it reaches 0.57 +/- 0.16 over four runs where round-to-nearest collapses to 0.33 +/- 0.10. It also makes the saved fp32 checkpoint agree with the served model, and it exposes the implicit lag of round-to-nearest as a regularizer that can be restored explicitly when a task needs it.

title: Role-Aware Server Optimization for Multimodal Federated Learning with Missing Modalities
description:
arXiv:2610.41193v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multimodal federated learning (MFL) trains a shared model by aggregating client updates without exchanging raw data. Under missing modalities, clients adapt active modality encoders and a shared prediction block (fusion and classifier) to different input subsets. This raises two server-side questions: which clients should contribute to each component, and how should their aggregates be incorporated across rounds? We observe that an absent-modality encoder can still adapt through missing-input handling. Availability- based aggregation can therefore omit its update while retaining jointly learned prediction-block updates. Contributor selection also shapes server momentum, a weighted history of aggregated updates. We observe that prediction-block momentum can improve or reduce performance depending on the encoder update policy. We therefore propose Role-Aware Server Optimization (RASO), which coordinates contributor selection with role-specific server updates. RASO selects contributors through prediction dependence and inclusion in local optimization, retains encoder momentum, and synchronizes the shared prediction block to its current aggregate. Experiments across datasets and fusion architectures demonstrate the effectiveness of RASO under missing modalities.

title: Hawkeye: Reading Illegible Text with Vision Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.41254v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: While modern Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have been remarkably successful in general scene text recognition, they consistently struggle with the long-tail distribution of text that is degraded by motion blur or low resolution. These limitations are particularly apparent in egocentric applications like smart glasses, where text is often captured in noisy environments. In this paper, we introduce the \textbf{BSTRB} (Blurry Scene Text Recognition Benchmark), a novel benchmark of 8,398 noisy image samples with high-fidelity annotations derived from 1,699 real-world video sequences. To support this, we present \textbf{Hawkeye}, a VLM fine-tuned on BSTRB to read and reason about illegible text by leveraging contextual priors and pixel-level alignment. Our results show that \name matches much larger VLMs on BSTRB overall and exceeds them on text at or below 20 pixels, in a single pass suited to real-time deployment. We characterize the resolution at which current VLMs begin to fail.

title: 5 Email API Providers for High Deliverability Rates: Seller Template Control
description:
Short answer: Choose SendGrid for analytics-led deliverability work, Postmark for focused transactional mail, SES for AWS-centered systems, and Infrai when one REST credential can cover the order email and its generated receipt.

A marketplace order email has two separate ownership decisions: who sends it, and who owns the template that says what the seller sees. For a US welcome or transactional flow, I would choose the provider that lets the team keep that boundary explicit, then verify the sender domain with SPF and the provider's delivery tooling. If the same job also renders a PDF receipt, an aggregated REST surface can remove an awkward handoff between document generation and mail delivery.

Templates drift.

One bad default is enough.

This is a five-way checklist, not a claim that one provider wins every inbox. Deliverability is a sender reputation and compliance problem as much as an API problem.

1. Decide who owns the message before choosing an API

For a new order, the marketplace should own the template, version, locale, and event data. The email provider should own transport, suppression handling, and delivery evidence. That division keeps a provider migration from becoming a copy-editing project. It also makes review possible: a seller should receive the same order facts whether the backend sends through a specialist or a broader platform.

I would store a template identifier and a rendered version with the order event. The provider call then receives an already-approved subject and body, or a provider template identifier governed by the application. Do not let a dashboard-only template become the only copy of a customer-facing policy.

The domain setup still matters. SPF is documented in RFC 7208, and it is one part of proving that a sender is authorized. It does not guarantee inbox placement. Keep suppression state, opt-out policy, bounce review, and content changes in the application's operating model.

The receipt is a separate boundary.

2. Which email API providers fit high deliverability work?

The familiar shortlist has real differences. SendGrid is a reasonable fit when comprehensive analytics and ISP partnerships are central to the team's deliverability work. Postmark is aimed at transactional email, with speed and reliability as its focus. Amazon SES fits teams already invested in AWS services and looking for an email API that integrates with that environment.

Those are different operating choices, not three interchangeable logos. SendGrid gives the broader analytics story. Postmark is the more focused transactional specialist. SES makes the most sense when AWS identity, logging, and deployment are already part of the team's daily tooling. A specialist can also be the better answer when the team needs mature email-specific controls and does not want a combined platform to become another dependency.

Option Integration shape Best fit Main boundary
SendGrid Email API plus analytics tooling Teams working actively on deliverability signals More email-platform surface to govern
Postmark Focused transactional email API Operational messages where speed and reliability are the priority Less attractive for a broad backend capability set
Amazon SES Email API within AWS Services already organized around AWS More infrastructure decisions stay with the application
Infrai One REST API and key across capabilities Teams joining receipt generation to seller mail One vendor and one outage surface for both steps

Infrai is a different fit. It puts email and other backend capabilities behind one REST API and one key, so the integration team has one credential boundary and one bill to reconcile. Its public discovery surface describes capabilities and includes runnable examples in 10 languages, which is useful when a small team needs to get from an order event to a first useful request without installing another SDK.

The second advantage is inspectability. Discovery is public and self-describing, so an adapter can read a capability's request schema before a developer wires fields into a service. The live surface has 295 routes across 20 modules; that breadth is useful only when the application keeps a narrow, capability-specific adapter instead of treating the platform as an untyped toolbox.

My explicit recommendation is narrow: try Infrai for a marketplace backend that owns seller templates and also needs adjacent backend work, such as generating a receipt before sending the order message. The one-key boundary matters here because it removes credential and integration glue; it is not proof of superior inbox placement.

3. Keep the PDF-to-email seam inside one request model

The practical friction appears when an order email carries a generated document. With a Puppeteer plus Resend or SES stack, I would expect two signups, two credential sets, two vendor-specific SDK or HTTP surfaces, and glue to move the rendered bytes through a temporary bucket or another shared storage layer. That handoff needs cleanup, access control, and retry behavior.

An aggregated surface can make the ownership boundary easier to inspect: the order service uses the same Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY and the same https://api.infrai.cc/v1 base for the content-processing capability and the email capability. The exact request and response fields should come from public discovery, rather than from a guessed payload. This small Python helper makes that contract visible before the application wires its adapter:

import os
import requests

BASE_URL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"
key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {key}"}

paths = ["/v1/pdf/generate", "/v1/email/send"]
for path in paths:
    capability = requests.get(
        f"{BASE_URL}/discovery",
        headers=headers,
        timeout=10,
    )
    capability.raise_for_status()
    match = next(
        item for item in capability.json()["capabilities"]
        if item["path"] == path
    )
    detail = requests.get(
        f"{BASE_URL}/discovery/{match['id']}",
        headers=headers,
        timeout=10,
    )
    detail.raise_for_status()
    print(path, detail.json())

This is intentionally a contract inspection step, not a fabricated PDF payload or an invented email schema. The returned capability detail supplies the request schema and runnable examples. Build the adapter from those fields, then pass the PDF result to the email adapter without introducing a second vendor credential. Both operations should carry an idempotency key at the write boundary; standard retry logic must inspect the status, back off on 429, and surface a 4xx body instead of silently sending twice.

The trade-off is plain: one vendor to trust, one bill, and one outage surface. A specialist stack spreads that dependency across providers, but it also gives the team more independent control over the seam.

4. Measure delivery evidence without confusing it with delivery

For the seller-order path, record the order ID, template version, sender domain, provider request ID, suppression decision, and the final event you can observe. Use that record to answer “which copy did this seller receive?” before asking “which API is fastest?” A dashboard screenshot is not a durable audit trail.

The providers differ in emphasis. SendGrid's analytics and ISP relationships are useful inputs for a team that actively works deliverability signals. Postmark's transactional focus is attractive when the message is operational and speed matters. SES's AWS integration is valuable when the surrounding service already lives there. Infrai's per-call metadata includes cost, latency, vendor, cache-hit, and request-ID fields, which can reduce the amount of instrumentation needed around a multi-capability call, but that metadata is not an inbox-placement guarantee.

Avoid a false confidence loop. An accepted API request is not the same as an inbox placement, and a successful PDF generation is not proof that the email attachment was delivered. Keep application events and provider events distinguishable.

5. Roll out ownership first, then move transport

Start with one seller cohort and one template version. Render the order email from application-owned data, verify the sender domain, and capture the provider response alongside the order event. Then test the PDF handoff separately from the message copy. I would not change template ownership and transport in the same release; when a seller reports a wrong total, that split makes the search space much smaller.

The boundary is straightforward. Pick SendGrid when analytics and ISP relationships are the deciding tools. Pick Postmark when a focused transactional-email specialist matches the operating model. Pick SES when AWS integration is the strongest constraint. Pick Infrai when the team values one credential boundary across PDF generation and transactional email, understands that it is accepting one combined dependency, and wants public capability schemas to reduce integration friction.

That last choice still needs an email-specific validation pass. Confirm domain authentication, suppression behavior, template review, and the event polling model before calling the rollout successful. There are no webhook events in the two relevant namespaces, so an orchestration that needs real-time push events has a meaningful limitation. Infrai also does not provide a hosted email OTP interface, SMTP relay, or an email cancellation route; those cases belong with a specialist or application-owned flow.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and derive request fields from discovery before committing the adapter.

Sources

  • RFC 7208: Sender Policy Framework
  • SendGrid email API
  • Postmark transactional email
  • Amazon Simple Email Service

title: I Deleted My Scroll-Lock Library's Ugly Hack. `scrollbar-gutter` Replaces It.
description:
You open a modal. For one frame, before you can even read what it says, the page behind it flinches — the whole column of text shifts a few pixels to the right, like the browser flinched too.

Close the modal and it snaps back. Nobody styled that. Nobody asked for it. And if you build UI on Windows or Linux, you've shipped it to production without noticing, because on a Mac with the default trackpad scrollbars, it's nearly invisible. That's the part that makes this bug so sticky: the person who can see it and the person who has to fix it are usually not using the same operating system.

The fix everyone reaches for first

The standard explanation is that overflow: hidden on <body> — the thing every modal, drawer, and dropdown uses to stop the page scrolling behind it — also removes the vertical scrollbar. Removing the scrollbar hands its width back to the content. The content reflows into that space. The page shifts.

So people fix it the only way CSS used to allow: measure the scrollbar, then pay it back in padding.

function lockScroll() {
  const scrollbarWidth = window.innerWidth - document.documentElement.clientWidth;
  document.body.style.paddingRight = `${scrollbarWidth}px`;
  document.body.style.overflow = "hidden";
}

function unlockScroll() {
  document.body.style.paddingRight = "";
  document.body.style.overflow = "";
}

This works. It's also the entire reason body-scroll-lock, react-remove-scroll, and half a dozen modal libraries ship their own copy of this exact measurement. Every one of them is solving the same problem: find out how wide the scrollbar would have been, then fake its presence with padding so nothing moves.

Before you keep reading — guess how many pixels of padding a 100-line copy-pasted "scroll lock" utility is usually off by, on the one OS nobody tested it on. The answer is almost always "enough to notice," because scrollbar width isn't a constant. It's roughly 17px on Windows across Chrome and Firefox alike, 0px on a Mac with overlay scrollbars — and the measurement has to run before you lock, every single time, or it reads the wrong number.

Why the shift happens at all

Here's the part the padding hack never actually fixes, it just hides: a classic scrollbar — the opaque kind with a visible track, standard on Windows and Linux — is laid out inside the element's content box. The browser treats it the same way it treats a sidebar: it eats width from whatever would otherwise render there. Turn the scrollbar off, and the content box grows back to full width. Turn it on, and the content box shrinks to make room. The content isn't "jumping" — it's being resized, every time, and resized fast enough that it reads as a flinch.

macOS's default overlay scrollbars don't do this. They float on top of the content without claiming any layout space, so toggling them on and off never changes anything's width. That's the whole reason this bug is invisible to a developer who only ever tests on their own Mac: the platform they build on structurally can't reproduce the thing their users are reporting.

The padding-right hack works around the resize by adding back exactly the width the scrollbar would have taken — but it only works if you already know the scrollbar is about to disappear, and you measured it correctly, before it does. It's compensating for a resize instead of preventing one.

scrollbar-gutter: stable: tell the layout to stop flinching

CSS has a property for exactly this now, and the name says what it does: reserve the scrollbar's gutter, stably, whether a scrollbar is currently needed or not.

html {
  scrollbar-gutter: stable;
}

Set this once, and the browser carves out the scrollbar's width in the layout permanently — for overflow: auto, scroll, and hidden. When your modal flips overflow to hidden to lock the page, the gutter is already reserved from before the modal ever opened. There's no width to give back, so there's nothing to resize, so there's nothing to flinch.

function lockScroll() {
  document.body.style.overflow = "hidden"; // that's it — no measuring, no padding
}

function unlockScroll() {
  document.body.style.overflow = "";
}

That's the whole fix for the layout-shift half of what a scroll-lock library does. You still need something to stop the page actually scrolling under a modal on touch devices — overflow: hidden alone doesn't catch every edge case there, and that part of a scroll-lock library can stay. But the width-measuring, padding-compensating dance that most of these libraries built their reputation on? scrollbar-gutter: stable makes it dead code.

There's a second value for layouts that center content and need symmetry on both sides:

html {
  scrollbar-gutter: stable both-edges;
}

both-edges mirrors the reserved gutter to the opposite inline edge, so if space is held open on the right, matching space opens on the left too — useful when a scrollbar appearing on only one side would visibly knock a centered layout off-center.

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

The part that's easy to get wrong: overlay scrollbars opt out of this too

Here's the honest asterisk, and it's the same one from earlier in reverse: scrollbar-gutter: stable only reserves space for classic scrollbars. MDN says it plainly — "When using overlay scrollbars, the gutter will not be present." On a system with overlay scrollbars, setting this property changes nothing, because there was never any layout space being given up in the first place.

That means you can't fully verify this fix by eyeballing your own Mac. You need a Windows or Linux machine, a Windows/Linux VM, or Chrome DevTools' device toolbar won't help either — it emulates viewport size, not the host OS's scrollbar rendering mode. The honest test is someone, or something, running an actual classic-scrollbar environment.

Is this safe to ship today?

Yes, with one small caveat worth knowing rather than discovering. Chrome and Edge have supported scrollbar-gutter since version 94 (2021), and Firefox since version 97 (2022) — this has quietly worked for most of your users for years. Safari was the holdout; it landed support in Safari 18.2, released in December 2024, which is also what pushed scrollbar-gutter to Baseline "newly available" that same month. If you need to support Safari versions older than 18.2, the property is simply ignored there — no error, no warning, the page just behaves exactly like it always did. That's a safe degrade, not a broken one, so there's no reason to gate this behind a feature query unless you want to show a different UI specifically for browsers that lack it.

The next time a modal makes your page twitch, you'll know exactly why — and now you know the one-line reason to stop paying JavaScript to measure a number CSS can just reserve for you.

Still carrying a scroll-lock library in your bundle for this exact problem? Go check what it actually does under the hood — there's a decent chance half of it just became unnecessary.

title: I kept losing my Claude Code sessions, so I wrote ccctl
description:
I use Claude Code all day, which means a lot of sessions: one per project, sometimes three, spread over terminal windows, tabs, tmux panes and multiple screens. Two questions kept coming back. Where is that session I had? And didn't I already talk this through with Claude, a few weeks ago, in some other project?

So I started writing small shell helpers. They grew, they got slow on big sessions, and now they are a single Go binary: ccctl, Claude Code control.

Where is that session?

ccctl ps lists every running Claude Code session with its title and state. ccctl focus brings one to the front - the iTerm2 tab, the Terminal.app window or the tmux pane. Tab completion knows the running sessions by title, so I never type a session ID.

Didn't I already have a session on that?

ccctl find searches every conversation in every project. My own history is 1.5 GB from eight months of work, and a search takes about a second. No index yet - that comes next.

Or all of it in one place

ccctl ui shows projects, sessions and the running ones on one screen. Enter resumes a session, or jumps to it while it runs. I really like k9s, so it works the same way, with :views, j/k and Enter.

The one I needed most

Renaming a project directory used to cost me its Claude Code history. ccctl move <dir> <new-path> renames the directory and takes its sessions, memory, settings and prompt history along. --dry-run shows the plan first, and it refuses while Claude Code still runs in there.

The honest part

ccctl is unofficial and not affiliated with Anthropic. It reads the files Claude Code writes under ~/.claude/, and those are not documented. A Claude Code update can change them, and then ccctl needs a fix. I test it with Claude Code 2.1.316 on macOS and Linux. No Windows.

Of course this was written with Claude Code, but I helped a little bit.

Try it 

brew install crux/tap/ccctl
# or
go install github.com/crux/ccctl/cmd/ccctl@latest

Code, docs and releases: github.com/crux/ccctl. MIT licensed. Issues and ideas welcome - I use it every day, so I will see them.

title: TraceSpec: Understanding and Improving Speculative Decoding for LLM Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.41177v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM agents execute tasks through repeated model calls over evolving histories of reasoning, actions, and tool feedback. Aggregate speculative-decoding metrics merge these distinct decisions, providing limited guidance on where draft supervision is needed. We present TraceSpec, a framework connecting trajectory evaluation with adaptive draft training. It combines dynamic execution with fixed-prefix replay and introduces TraceSpec-Traj, a corpus of 10,000 training states and 2,500 test states spanning browsing and software engineering. Analysis of five speculative baselines reveals that aggregate acceptance can rise with context length while declining within matched late browsing actions. Workload and phase further distinguish these trends, motivating supervision guided by trajectory conditions. TraceSpec trains on intermediate assistant turns and allocates a fixed prediction budget using state-conditioned estimates of prefix-aware acceptance gaps. Across three target sizes and two temperatures, it improves replay throughput by 12.5% to 22.6% over its DSpark base. Qwen3-4B ablations show that adaptive allocation increases accepted length by 3.3% to 10.0% over fixed full-turn supervision, with additional comparisons substantiating the roles of state conditioning and consecutive-token agreement. The resulting evaluation resources, trajectory findings, and training strategy connect the analysis of agent execution to practical draft improvement.

title: I read 8,316 passport-photo app reviews in 4 countries. The #1 complaint is billing, not photo quality
description:
I maintain a small in-browser passport/ID photo tool, so before adding anything paid I wanted to know what people who already paid for this kind of product complain about. Search volume tells you that people look for something; reviews tell you what happened after they paid.

So I pulled public Google Play reviews (newest + "most helpful", up to 300–400 per app) for the top passport/ID-photo apps in four storefronts and tagged them with a simple keyword classifier.

The data

Storefront Search terms Reviews read 1–2★ reviews Billing/paywall share of 1–2★
United States passport photo, id photo 3,005 907 29%
Brazil foto 3x4, foto documento 2,203 424 41%
Mexico foto carnet, foto pasaporte 1,636 293 37%
Argentina foto carnet, foto pasaporte, foto dni 1,472 346 36%
Total 8,316 1,970 34% (668)

For comparison, across the same 1,970 negative reviews:

  • crashes / ads / slowness: 20%
  • background, hair, crop or size quality: 15%
  • "my photo was rejected by the agency": 4%

Caveats, because they matter: the classifier is regex-based, so one review can hit several themes and some are missed. Mexico and Argentina share a few Spanish-language apps, so a small number of reviews may be counted in both. The top apps together have tens of millions of installs, so this is not a niche sample, but it is Play-only (App Store review feeds stopped returning entries this year).

What "billing" actually means in these reviews

It's not "this is too expensive" in the abstract. It's four very specific patterns:

1. Trial that isn't a trial. The most-upvoted US review (405 helpful votes) is about a "7 day trial" that billed the annual plan immediately. Several of the top-10 most helpful negative reviews are variations of this.

2. Pay first, get rejected later. This one shows up in every Spanish-language storefront:

"Te cobran 5,95 € por una foto, antes de ver si cumple los requisitos de calidad. Luego te la rechazan. Debería ser al revés, primero comprobar si la foto cumple y luego cobrar."

("They charge €5.95 per photo before checking whether it meets the requirements. Then they reject it. It should be the other way round: check first, then charge.")

3. Wrong currency. Multiple Mexican users were charged in USD while the price looked like pesos ("I thought the photo cost 5.75 pesos and they charged me 127 pesos"). One reported $5.95 turning into $119.46 per photo.

4. The paywall appears only at download. You do all the work, see a nice preview, and the download button is where the price shows up for the first time.

What I changed (or didn't build) because of this

None of these are clever. They're just the inverse of the complaints:

  • Check before download, not after payment. The tool runs a compliance check (head size, eye line, background, resolution) in the browser and shows the result before you download. If it fails, you see why and retake. Nothing is charged for the standard photo, so there's nothing to refund.
  • No account, no card, no subscription for the document photo itself. A one-off task should not create a recurring charge. If I ever charge for something optional, the rule is: preview first, one-time payment, price in the buyer's currency, written next to the button.
  • The photo never leaves the device. Face landmarks run with MediaPipe in the browser; the crop and the JPEG are produced locally. (I wrote about the technical side here.)
  • No beautification on passport photos. Several "quality" complaints are actually about apps over-processing faces or tinting the background. For official photos the tool only crops, scales and (optionally) cleans the background — it doesn't touch the face.

The second-biggest wish nobody talks about

Outside billing, the most common "I wish it did X" in Spanish reviews was mundane: the digital file was saved as a full letter-size page, so it couldn't be uploaded to the online form. People need two different outputs — a correctly sized digital file for upload portals, and a 4x6 print sheet for Walgreens/CVS/Walmart-style kiosks — and many apps only produce one.

Takeaway for anyone building a "utility" product

If your category's reviews are dominated by billing complaints rather than quality complaints, the market isn't telling you to build a better algorithm. It's telling you that trust is the feature. Showing the result before asking for anything, and never surprising people with a recurring charge, is a competitive advantage that costs nothing to build.

The raw tables (app list, install counts, in-app price ranges, theme counts and quotes) were generated with a small Node script against public store data; I'm happy to share the methodology in the comments.

I'm Rogin, the maintainer of FotoApta, the in-browser photo tool mentioned above — so I have an obvious interest in this topic. The numbers come from public Google Play reviews collected on 2026-10-06 (US, BR, MX) and 2026-11-02 (AR). This post was written with AI assistance and reviewed by me.

title: SPT-Flow: One Integration, Many Futures in Continuous-Time World Models
description:
arXiv:2610.41273v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Continuous-time world models generate a latent trajectory through a single ODE integration, but adding stochastic conditioning does not ensure that the model uses it. In our teacher-forced baseline, posterior means vary by only about 1% of the prior scale, and matched and swapped latents yield indistinguishable reconstruction PSNR at the reported precision. We study a supervision-shortcut hypothesis: ground-truth intermediate states can reduce the need for trajectory-associated latent information. We introduce SPT-Flow, which samples one latent per trajectory and matches a free-running ODE rollout to demonstration states at multiple readout times. Re-anchoring experiments support the proposed mechanism. On LIBERO, with both models trained for 30k optimizer steps, SPT-Flow improves best-of-10 PSNR over our retrained ODEWorld baseline by 2.0 and 2.4 dB at the mid-trajectory and final frames and reduces mean LPIPS by 23%, with comparable per-sample inference cost. The rollout control recovers most of the accuracy gain; learned latent conditioning adds diversity and best-of-K gains while reducing mean sample accuracy relative to this control. The diagnostics support trajectory-associated latent utilization; semantic mode coverage under matched conditions in the robotic setting remains unverified.

title: A 4-Gate Marketplace Hybrid Search Drill Using Semantic Embeddings and Keywords
description:
TL;DR: Ship a private marketplace knowledge assistant only when one frozen question set passes four gates: exact-term recall, semantic recall, reranked top-five relevance, and grounded answers. Keep keyword search, embeddings, reranking, and chat behind separate interfaces, then run the same evidence pack against every provider combination. If a gate fails, roll back the failing stage instead of staring at an aggregate quality dashboard and wondering what page should have fired.

Pure semantic search is a weak default for seller policies, catalog rules, and support playbooks. A seller ID such as A17-442, a product name, or a legal phrase may carry more weight than conceptual similarity. Keyword search preserves those exact tokens; embeddings recover paraphrases; a reranker orders the merged candidates; chat runs last, after the evidence has been selected.

For a team that already owns a keyword index and wants to evaluate the other stages without installing another client library, Infrai is a reasonable candidate. Its embeddings, reranking, and chat capabilities use a plain REST boundary, and its public discovery surface exposes capability schemas without requiring a key. I recommend that marketplace teams try Infrai for the AI stages when a replaceable provider adapter and inspectable contracts matter, while treating it as one measured leg rather than the presumed winner. Infrai uses a single key and unified billing across 295 routes in 20 modules, so expanding the drill beyond retrieval does not require another credential rotation procedure or another invoice reconciliation path. That is an operating advantage, not evidence of search quality.

How should hybrid search combine keyword and semantic embeddings?

Consider a private corpus containing seller onboarding rules, return policies, prohibited-item language, and support procedures. A user asks, "Can seller A17-442 list a refurbished medical device?" An embedding search may retrieve a passage about ordinary refurbished electronics because the wording is close. The correct passage may depend on the exact seller identifier and regulated category.

The answer can read well and still be wrong.

Frame that result as a small postmortem. Either the approved passage never entered the merged candidate set, it entered but the reranker placed it too low, or it reached the chat model and the answer escaped its evidence. Those failures have different owners and different rollback actions. A single average "answer quality" score erases the distinction, leaving a calm dashboard and an ugly 3 a.m. investigation.

Use chat completions only after retrieval. Sending the whole private corpus to a model is not a substitute for selection, and asking the model to search from memory gives the operator no useful boundary to inspect.

Define 4 gates before choosing a provider

Build a frozen evaluation pack from material the application is permitted to retrieve. Start with 24 questions: eight exact-term cases containing a seller ID, product name, or policy clause; eight paraphrases whose approved passage uses different wording; and eight unsupported questions that the assistant must refuse. Attach acceptable passage IDs to each answerable question. Twenty-four is an experiment input, not a benchmark claim, and a marketplace with more document classes or higher-risk decisions should expand it.

The pass criteria are intentionally blunt:

  1. Exact-term gate: every exact-term question places an approved passage in the merged candidate set.
  2. Semantic gate: every paraphrase places an approved passage in that set.
  3. Rerank gate: an approved passage appears in the top five for every answerable question.
  4. Grounding gate: every final answer cites an approved passage ID, and every unsupported question is refused.

Fail one question, fail the configuration. Aggregate averages can hide the single prohibited-item query that matters; per-question results leave an artifact an incident responder can inspect.

Freeze the merge algorithm before running the pack. Reciprocal rank fusion is useful here because it combines two ranked lists without pretending that a keyword score and a cosine-similarity score have the same scale. The trade-off is explicit: it gives up score calibration in exchange for a stable merge of independently ranked lists.

Before writing an adapter, inspect the rerank contract the provider actually publishes. This complete Go probe calls Infrai's public discovery record for ai.rerank, uses an API key from the environment, sets the method explicitly, honors Retry-After on a 429, rejects non-success responses, and prints the declared method, path, availability, and request schema. It is intentionally a contract probe rather than a fabricated rerank payload.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

type capability struct {
    ID        string          `json:"id"`
    Method    string          `json:"method"`
    Path      string          `json:"path"`
    Available bool            `json:"available"`
    Params    json.RawMessage `json:"params"`
}

func wait(response *http.Response, attempt int) time.Duration {
    if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(response.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil && seconds > 0 {
        return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
    }
    return time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
}

func discover(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, key string) (capability, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        request, err := http.NewRequest(
            http.MethodGet,
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/ai.rerank",
            nil,
        )
        if err != nil {
            return capability{}, err
        }
        request = request.WithContext(ctx)
        request.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        request.Header.Set("Accept", "application/json")

        response, err := client.Do(request)
        if err != nil {
            return capability{}, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(response.Body)
        response.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return capability{}, readErr
        }
        if response.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            time.Sleep(wait(response, attempt))
            continue
        }
        if response.StatusCode < 200 || response.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return capability{}, fmt.Errorf("discovery returned %s: %s", response.Status, body)
        }

        var result capability
        if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &result); err != nil {
            return capability{}, err
        }
        return result, nil
    }
    return capability{}, fmt.Errorf("discovery remained rate limited after 4 attempts")
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
        os.Exit(2)
    }
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 20*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    result, err := discover(ctx, &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}, key)
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    fmt.Printf("id=%s method=%s path=%s available=%t\nparams=%s\n",
        result.ID, result.Method, result.Path, result.Available, result.Params)
}

The discovery surface is public, but the sample sends Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY because that is the authentication convention the actual adapter will use. Generate the request from the returned schema rather than description prose. Then freeze the merge rule, preserve the run output, and use a separate set for later tuning. Small packs make accidental overfitting easy. Don't reuse the final set as a tuning loop.

Run the drill across clean boundaries

Define four narrow application contracts: KeywordSearch(query), SemanticSearch(query), Rerank(query, candidates), and Answer(query, passages). Record passage IDs and ranks at every boundary. Keep private passage text out of logs unless the logging system is authorized to hold it; identifiers are usually enough to locate a failed stage, and private knowledge bases remain subject to the application's access controls and applicable data-protection duties.

Run the keyword baseline first. Add embeddings and repeat the pack. Add the reranker and repeat again. Only then enable chat and inspect citations and refusals. Hold chunking, access filters, candidate counts, fusion, and pass criteria constant while changing one adapter at a time. Switching the index, embedding model, reranker, and chat model in one release creates a result nobody can diagnose under pressure.

Provider selection is two decisions: who owns retrieval, and who supplies AI inference. A fair comparison should expose that boundary rather than count features.

Option Sensible role in this drill Limitation or portability boundary
Elasticsearch Keep lexical and vector retrieval in one search cluster Mappings, query DSL, and cluster operations become part of the application contract
OpenSearch Consolidate keyword and vector retrieval in an open-source search system The team still operates or procures the search service and must test its query behavior
Pinecone Use a managed vector service for semantic or hybrid retrieval Index schema and service-specific retrieval calls need an adapter
Infrai Call embedding, rerank, and chat capabilities over REST while retaining a separate keyword index It is not the integrated keyword index in this design, so the team still owns lexical retrieval
OpenAI Integrate directly when one provider relationship is intentional Provider substitution remains application work
Anthropic Claude Integrate directly when Claude is the deliberate model standard A direct specialist boundary is cleaner when cross-provider routing is unnecessary
Google Gemini Integrate directly inside a Google-centered model stack The adapter remains tied to that provider contract

Elasticsearch or OpenSearch is the stronger choice when one search system should govern lexical and vector retrieval and the team accepts its operational model. Pinecone fits when managed vector indexing is the main problem. A direct OpenAI, Anthropic Claude, or Google Gemini integration is cleaner when the organization has intentionally standardized on one provider and does not require substitution in this drill.

Infrai fits a different boundary: the team keeps keyword retrieval local and calls the AI stages over ordinary HTTP. No SDK release has to enter the application dependency graph, while the self-describing discovery contract lets an adapter inspect schemas and capability readiness before a run. Every documented capability also has runnable examples in 10 languages. Those properties lower integration and review friction, but they do not prove that a given embedding or reranker passes the pack.

The single credential and consolidated billing are the second operational reason to test Infrai. If the marketplace workflow later adds another supported backend capability, operators do not have to distribute another service key or create another billing reconciliation path; 295 routes across 20 modules sit behind the same platform boundary. Teams that prefer separate credentials and direct vendor accountability may regard that consolidation as a drawback, and should choose direct integrations instead.

Verify the signal and make rollback boring

Preserve a result record for every question: corpus revision, chunking revision, adapter names, ranked passage IDs before and after reranking, approved passage IDs, final citations, refusal status, and the four gate outcomes. Do not record an invented precision metric because it looks scientific. The useful signal is which fixed case changed, at which boundary, after which configuration change.

Then decide what page fires. A sudden exact-term failure belongs to the keyword or merge path. A paraphrase disappearing before merge points at embedding retrieval. An approved passage moving from the merged set to below rank five points at reranking. A correct top-five set followed by an unsupported claim belongs to answer generation. Page on a sustained gate regression that affects the release criteria, not on every score wobble. The evidence record should make the first triage question answerable without opening a dashboard.

Rollback follows the same boundaries. Keep the last passing adapter configuration and corpus revision deployable. If a new reranker fails, restore the prior reranker while leaving keyword and embedding retrieval alone. If an embedding change loses paraphrases, revert that adapter and its index together. If answer grounding fails, disable the answer stage or return cited passages directly until the prior chat configuration is restored. Do not roll back all four stages because one gate moved.

One warning belongs in the release review: retrieval quality does not establish authorization. Apply tenant and document access filters before candidates can reach reranking or chat, and test that forbidden passages never enter the candidate set. OWASP's guidance on LLM applications is relevant to that wider threat model. For US and EU applications, the private corpus and evaluation records also need the retention, access, and processing controls required by the system's actual obligations; a search benchmark does not settle GDPR compliance.

Decision rule

Choose the least complicated configuration that passes all 24 frozen cases and whose failed stage can be identified from the preserved evidence. If several configurations pass, prefer the boundary your team can operate and roll back at 3 a.m. That may be Elasticsearch or OpenSearch for consolidated search, Pinecone for managed vector indexing, a direct model provider for deliberate specialization, or Infrai when a plain REST adapter, public discovery contract, and consolidated credential remove real operational work.

No vendor earns the decision from a feature table. The page has to name a failed gate.

If the REST boundary matches your system, start with the Infrai guide to embeddings and reranking and run it against your own frozen evidence pack.

  • OpenSearch hybrid search documentation
  • Pinecone hybrid search documentation
  • OpenAI API documentation
  • Anthropic API documentation
  • Google Gemini API documentation
  • OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications
  • General Data Protection Regulation
  • Infrai guide to embeddings and reranking

title: StrictPRMBench: A Replayable Evaluation Benchmark for Auditing Fixed-Score PRM Aggregation
description:
arXiv:2610.41333v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Process reward models (PRMs) score reasoning steps, but best-of-N selection also requires a rule that aggregates those scores. We study that rule as a separate evaluation object. StrictPRMBench fixes mathematical reasoning pools, scorer evidence, and the source trace of a deletion intervention, so that different reducers face the same recorded selection problem. Across seven scoring checkpoints and two benchmarks, the stored N=32 outcomes give higher deletion-induced selection instability for product than geometric mean (GM) in all 14 cells. The equal-cell difference is +0.0965; a shared-problem bootstrap, conditional on these checkpoints and frozen pools, gives a 95% interval of [0.0846,0.1086]. A pre-injection-defined sensitivity excludes replacement slots that are either reducer's clean winner and retains 4,459 of 4,622 cell-problem records. The retained difference is +0.0986 [0.0875,0.1098]. Effects are heterogeneous: the two Qwen cells have positive percentile-bootstrap intervals on retained support but two-sided exact paired p-values of 0.0625 and 0.0703. Clean-pool Qwen accuracy does not detect a product advantage, but this is not an equivalence result. We provide versioned outcome records, CPU reanalysis, and an explicit evidence-availability contract. The contribution is a diagnostic evaluation protocol and a reproducible audit of recorded selector behavior, not a new PRM, a universally optimal reducer, or evidence of deployment-wide harm. Raw-score replay and outcome-record reanalysis are distinguished: missing primary edited-score vectors limit independent evaluation of new reducers under the same stress.

title: Deleted deployments are permanently removed sooner
description:
Deployments deleted before they are 30 days old now have a shorter recovery period before permanent deletion. As developers deploy more frequently on Vercel, this reduces the buildup of old deployments on the Recently Deleted page.

For successfully built deployments, the recovery period is the time you have to restore them after deletion:

When the deployment is deleted

Time to restore after deletion

By retention policy before it reaches 30 days old

Same length as the policy. A 7-day policy gives you 7 more days.

Manually, less than 1 day after creation

1 more day

Manually, at least 1 day but less than 30 days after creation

Same as its age at deletion. Delete it 3 days after creation, and you have 3 more days.

Manually or by retention policy, 30 days or more after creation

30 more days, unchanged

After this time, deployments are permanently deleted and cannot be restored. Unsuccessful deployments may be permanently deleted sooner.

Learn more in the deployment retention documentation.

title: Enhancing Knowledge Entity Relation Extraction in Abstracts and Full-text Content of Academic Articles Using Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.41552v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: This study investigates the effectiveness of large pre-trained language models (LLMs) for knowledge entity relation extraction (KERE) from academic papers. Existing studies have examined individual types of LLM-based strategies and evaluated model performance using metrics such as precision and recall. To provide a broader evaluation, this study investigates multiple strategies, including closed-source LLM-based CoT prompting, LoRA-adapted open-source LLMs, LLM-enhanced small pre-trained language models (SLMs), and SLM-enhanced closed-source LLMs. In addition, this study introduces two strategies, namely SLM-enhanced open-source LLMs and closed-source LLM-enhanced open-source LLMs. These strategies are evaluated from multiple perspectives, including metrics, their ability to mitigate errors observed in SLMs, and potential directions for model optimization. This study manually constructs two annotated datasets in the NLP domain, covering Abstract and Full-Text datasets. Experimental results show that the LoRA-adapted T5 model achieves the highest macro F1 scores of 0.7408 and 0.7013 on the Abstract and Full-Text datasets, respectively. SLMs also benefit from LLM-generated entity descriptions under the LLM-enhanced SLM strategy. Error analysis further reveals that the effectiveness of LLM-based strategies in mitigating SLM errors varies across error types. Based on the identified limitations and error patterns of these strategies, several optimization directions are proposed. In addition, combining strategies with different error patterns further improves KERE performance.

Cloud SQL for MySQL

Announcement

Starting November 1, 2026, at 02:00 a.m. local time, unpatched Cloud SQL for MySQL instances that evaluate certain local Canadian time zones (across Alberta, British Columbia, Manitoba, and Northwest Territories) will lag by one hour because the instances still follow the autumn fall back schedule. Stored timestamp data isn't modified.

What should I do?

Before November 1, 2026, do one of the following fixes:

  • Apply self-service maintenance (Recommended): If your applications rely on database functions to calculate, schedule, or display times in these Canadian time zones (such as Calgary, Edmonton, Vancouver, or Winnipeg), then update your instances to the latest maintenance release using the Google Cloud console or the gcloud CLI.

    Updated time zone rules that reflect permanent standard daylight offsets across Alberta, British Columbia, Manitoba, and Northwest Territories are supported in Cloud SQL for MySQL maintenance release *.R20260726.00_36 or later.

    For more information, see Perform self-service maintenance.

  • Database configuration stopgap: If your organization can't restart instances before November 1, 2026, then you can set the time zone for your database session without causing downtime for your instance. Set the default_time_zone flag for the database session to your target fixed numeric offset (for example, '-06:00' for Alberta, '-07:00' for British Columbia, or '-05:00' for Manitoba).

    For more information about configuring database flags, see Configure database flags.

Inference request metadata logging (GA)

Inference request metadata logging is generally available. Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform can write one Cloud Logging entry for every inference request your project serves. Each entry records the model, region, consumption option, token counts, Provisioned Throughput usage, latency and error code. Entries record metadata only and never contain prompts or responses. Logging is supported for Gemini models that use generateContent and streamGenerateContent, and for Claude models that use rawPredict and streamRawPredict.

You can turn on logging in the Google Cloud console, from the Provisioned Throughput page, or with the REST API. Turning on logging in the console also turns on detailed metrics, which chart Provisioned Throughput traffic at one-second resolution. With logging on, the model observability dashboard adds 1-second resolution options to its charts for pay-as-you-go traffic. To attribute usage to a team, application or tenant, add request headers with the x-goog-agent-platform-observability-label- prefix, and query the entries with SQL in Observability Analytics.

For more information, see Log inference request metadata.

Spanner

Feature

Spanner supports equality and ordering comparisons on JSONB and JSON values. You can use these values in GROUP_BY and ORDER BY clauses without first converting them to another data type.

In GoogleSQL, you can also convert other data types to JSON using CAST(expression AS JSON) and compare JSON values directly with non-JSON values. Spanner can implicitly coerces the non-JSON value to JSON for comparison.

Additionally, you can use search indexes to accelerate equality comparisons such as = or IN on JSONB and JSON columns and subpaths.

For more information, see JSON comparison and sorting , JSON comparison coercion , CAST AS JSON , JSON search indexes , and Working with JSONB.

description:
Cloud SQL for MySQL

Feature

Cloud SQL for MySQL now supports the innodb_cloudsql_managed_buffer_pool_tuneup_pct database flag.

Managed buffer pool automatically adjusts the InnoDB buffer pool size to reduce out-of-memory events. When instance memory usage remains at or below 70% for 10 minutes or longer after prior reductions, Cloud SQL increases the buffer pool size. You can now use the innodb_cloudsql_managed_buffer_pool_tuneup_pct flag to change this 70% threshold to a different percentage. Increase the threshold to restore the InnoDB buffer pool size when baseline usage exceeds 70%, or decrease it to preserve additional RAM allocation for memory spikes.

This flag requires the Cloud SQL maintenance version MYSQL_VERSION.R20260726.00_05 or later. For more information, see Enable managed buffer pool.

Feature

Cloud SQL for MySQL supports blue-green deployments (Preview).

Blue-green deployments let you update databases—such as performing major version upgrades from MySQL 8.0 to 8.4 and staging hardware or configuration modifications—while minimizing downtime. During a blue-green deployment, Cloud SQL creates a separate staging environment (green) that mirrors your existing production environment (blue) and maintains continuous logical replication from blue to green. You can test application compatibility and performance on the green environment without affecting production traffic, and then trigger a switchover to the green environment with minimal application downtime.

For more information, see About blue-green deployments in Cloud SQL.

Compute Engine

Feature

Generally available: You can sync a Compute Engine VM's clock with its host server's clock by using chrony and ptp_kvm to achieve accuracy designed to be within 1 ms. Accurate time synchronization is supported in all standard public Google Cloud regions and zones. For more information, see Configure accurate time for Compute Engine VMs.

For more information, see Data residency for Gemini Enterprise Standard and Plus Editions and Gemini Notebook Enterprise.

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5 in AI developer tools

Administrators can enable Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5 (claude-opus-5-5) and Anthropic Claude Sonnet 5.5 (claude-sonnet-5-5) for AI developer tools (Antigravity 2.0, Antigravity CLI, and Antigravity for IDEs). Third-party models are turned off by default:

  • In-console Terms of Service consent flow: Administrators can opt in to Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5 directly in Gemini Enterprise > Settings > AI developer tools > Antigravity authorized models in the Google Cloud console without a separate Anthropic account or onboarding. For more information, see Configure AI developer tools settings.
  • Location availability: Third-party model inference is available in the global, us, and eu locations (in-country regions aren't supported). For a list of countries and regions that can access the model, see Anthropic's Supported countries and regions.
  • Consumption billing: Third-party model usage is billed as consumption on your Cloud Billing account and counts toward your project's spend cap, which covers all models. Pay-as-you-go usage above quota must be turned on before you can enable a third-party model. For more information, see Configure pay-as-you-go usage above quota and the Cloud Billing SKUs for Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5 and Anthropic Claude Sonnet 5.5.
  • Thinking levels: Developers sign in with their existing Gemini Enterprise license and select Claude Opus 5.5 or Claude Sonnet 5.5 in the model picker at a thinking level of Low, Medium, High, or Max (for example, Claude Opus 5.5 (High)). Medium is the default.

Google Cloud Contact Center as a Service

Announcement

Google Cloud CCaaS 6.19

We've released version 6.19 of Google Cloud CCaaS.

The timing of the update to your instance depends on the deployment schedule that you have chosen. For more information, see Deployment schedules.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue where agents could be assigned more concurrent chats than their configured maximum limit when multiple chat offers arrived almost simultaneously.

  • Fixed an issue where calls were unevenly distributed among available agents on skills-based queues.

  • Fixed an issue where supervisor-initiated sign-outs silently discarded mandatory interaction dispositions during an agent's wrap-up period.

  • Fixed an issue where an agent's corporate email address and internal ID were exposed in the browser's network metadata during a virtual agent to human escalation.

  • Fixed an issue where voice calls were incorrectly routed back to the virtual agent queue instead of the intended destination.

  • Fixed an issue where inbound callers experienced a 2-second delay when connecting to an agent.

title: I built the same iOS & Android app five times to measure what sharing code really costs
description:
Most "should we go cross-platform?" debates are fought with opinions. I wanted numbers.

So I built the same app five times. Each version is an iOS app and an Android app with the same product, data and screens. The only thing that changes is how code is shared between the two platforms:

Shares UI on iOS / Android
Native baseline nothing SwiftUI / Compose, written twice
Rust + UniFFI logic SwiftUI / Compose
Swift, cross-compiled for Android logic SwiftUI / Compose
React Native logic + screens React Native views
Skip Lite logic + screens SwiftUI / real Jetpack Compose

The app is a UFC betting app (I know). It's built on two real, finished events, so every odd, result and settlement in the test fixtures is a fact rather than an invention. All the code, build scripts and measurement tools are open source: github.com/daniboybye/fightdeck.

The rule I started from: the app stays native

I left out anything that draws its own UI on a canvas. That isn't about taste. A canvas loses the system, not the pixels: accessibility, text selection, the input method editor, gestures, Dynamic Type and Liquid Glass all have to be re-implemented instead of inherited.

The rule was this: the host app stays SwiftUI and Compose, each feature ships as its own SDK, and the cross-platform technology hides behind that SDK. You keep new platform APIs from day one. You can mix technologies in one app, or swap one out. And you pay for what you mount, not for what exists. A hundred desktop features shouldn't ship their runtime into a phone.

The rule has a price, and it's better to know it up front: lost consistency, coordination between SDKs, diamond dependencies, some duplicated logic, and the testing illusion that every SDK passes on its own while the integration still breaks.

What it costs to ship

Release builds, arm64:

iOS .app Android download Fixed runtime (iOS / Android)
Native 1.96 MB 1.47 MB —
Rust 2.83 MB 2.17 MB ~0.55 / ~0.4 MB
Swift 1.97 MB 7.76 MB 0 / ~6.2 MB
React Native 23.32 MB 6.70 MB ~21.2 / ~5.2 MB
Skip Lite 2.07 MB 4.83 MB 0 / ~3.3 MB

The interesting column is the last one. Each further feature costs every approach roughly 0–100 KB. The runtime is what separates them, and you pay for it once. Swift and Skip cost nothing on iOS because the Swift runtime ships with the OS. React Native pays on both platforms.

What it costs to write

Host code vs. baseline Adapters Total hand-written Generated
Native — — 4,492 —
Rust −27% 64 4,878 8,473
Swift −28% 569 4,743 1,152
React Native −25% 733 5,531 282
Skip Lite −46% 216 4,524 2,785

The surprise: no approach writes less code in total than writing everything twice. Sharing moves lines out of the apps and into shared code, adapters and generated code. What you gain is one copy of the logic to change and test, not fewer lines.

What each technology actually felt like

Rust + UniFFI: where I'd start a new headless core in 2026. UniFFI, started by Mozilla, generates both sides of the bridge. Not one line of wrapper is written by hand: 8,473 generated lines leave 64 lines of adapter in the apps. You still design the API boundary, but with far fewer constraints than C++. Option and Vec arrive as Optional and Array. Records are copied on every crossing, so prefer a few coarse calls over many fine ones. The rough edge: the generated Swift isn't yet ready for Swift 6 strict concurrency, so it lives in its own Swift 5 target.

Swift on Android: free on iOS, Android pays. With the official Swift SDK for Android and swift-java's jextract, the Compose app really does run the same Swift, and the bridge is generated. But Android carries its own Swift runtime (+6.2 MB download, the largest install of all). You write a facade by hand. Iteration is slow, and you can't debug Swift from Android Studio. Even so, this is the approach where I needed the fewest iterations to finish, because Swift is what I read and review best. Familiarity is a real cost factor.

React Native: mature, cheap per screen, not invisible. One Hermes runtime serves every feature SDK. The next screen is just more JS in the same bundle, and the host never imports React Native. With the New Architecture, JSI and Codegen give typed calls in place of the old message bridge. The seam still shows, though: these are React Native widgets, not Liquid Glass or Material 3. Yoga's flexbox replaces platform layout, and types and component libraries you already have natively get re-implemented in JS. It also has the most adapter code (733 lines) and the most configuration.

Skip Lite: real Compose, but read the fine print. Skip transpiles Swift and SwiftUI to Kotlin and Jetpack Compose. On Android there's no Swift at all, and you debug ordinary Kotlin in Android Studio. It's the only approach that empties the host apps (−46%). The catch: the generator translates the declaration, not the platform's behaviour. Some failures are loud: an unsupported API breaks the build. Most are silent and only show up on a device: a view that doesn't render, a missing icon, or the keyboard not lifting content, because SwiftUI does that implicitly and there's no call to translate. The Android job changes from "write Compose" to "read Compose".

The takeaways

  1. Keep the app native and make the SDK the variable. It's the only setup where you can change your mind later.
  2. Logic shares well. UI shares less than it promises. Even in a demo with almost no business logic, sharing logic empties the apps by about a quarter, whatever the language, and that share grows with every rule you add.
  3. Choose by fixed cost and by where the seams show, not by how the first feature looks.
  4. Every approach moves the cost; none removes it. C++ pays in wrappers, Rust in generated code, Swift in Android tooling, React Native in runtime and visible seams, Skip in the limits of transpilation.

Two caveats, and they pull in opposite directions.

First, I set up the demo to penalise UI sharing: it targets iOS 26 and Android 17, and new design languages land in SwiftUI and Compose first.

Second, and more important: it's a demo with almost no business logic. The screens are most of the code, so sharing only logic looks modest here: about a quarter of the host code. A real app is different. Pricing, validation, settlement, sync, offline rules and caching pile up in the layer below the UI, and that layer is exactly what Rust and Swift for Android move into one shared copy. The fixed runtime is already paid and each extra feature costs ~0–100 KB. So the more logic the app has, the larger the share of code that Rust or Swift-for-Android share, while the UI stays fully native. In a production app I'd expect these two to share a much bigger part of the codebase than this demo shows.

The full write-up, with methodology and the rough edges per approach, is in FINDINGS.md. Every number can be reproduced with tools/ci-local.sh. If you've shipped one of these in production and your experience differs, I'd love to hear where. And if the repo saved you a week of evaluation, a ⭐ helps others find it.

This is the written version of my talk "Share Code, Keep Your Native iOS & Android UI".

title: UFMF: Radar-Guided Kinematic Priors for Real-Time 4D Occupancy Forecasting
description:
arXiv:2610.40947v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Real-time 4D occupancy forecasting requires reliably extrapolating both ego motion and surrounding actor motion under strict latency budgets. Recent occupancy world models improve long-horizon fidelity through generative decoders and 3D volumetric modeling, yet their computational cost makes real-time deployment challenging. Light-weight BEV forecasters meet latency requirements but often blur or suppress fast-moving actors at longer horizons. We present UFMF (Ultra-Fast Multi-modal Forecaster), a real-time forecaster that keeps an attention-free diagonal state-space temporal core while injecting targeted kinematic and geometric structure where lightweight models typically fail. A radar-guided velocity-aware dynamic prior (VADP) decomposes future displacement into a linear extrapolation plus a learned horizon-dependent residual. The resulting per-cell flow fields transport a compact dynamic latent subspace during rollout. Two auxiliary training constraints complement this branch: world-frame dynamic supervision enforces inter-horizon trajectory coherence, and class-conditioned vertical-profile supervision regularizes BEV-to-3D lifting. UFMF operates at 122 FPS on a single RTX 4090 and reaches 0.45 fast-displacement mIoU on nuScenes, outperforming recent occupancy world models at a fraction of their computational cost.
