title: How I Solved the Pakistan Address & City Data Problem for MERN Developers
description:
The Problem
Developers building e-commerce or delivery apps in Pakistan usually rely on outdated, broken GitHub Gists. These flat JSON files lack relational structure, miss newly formed districts, and ignore how local courier networks actually operate.

The Solution: pakistan-address
I engineered a plug-and-play npm package to permanently solve this data headache:

Normalized Official Data: Accurately maps the structured hierarchy of Provinces → Divisions → Districts → Tehsils.

Unofficial Courier Delivery Areas: Includes distributed real-world delivery zones. Government boundaries rarely match how local logistics work on the ground; this dataset bridges that gap for realistic checkout flows.

Fully Typed: Built with TypeScript to catch data errors at compile time, not during a user's checkout.

Stop copy-pasting outdated text files and use a reliable, maintained package for your next location-based app.

title: Threat modeling the CVE-2026-105483 certificate bypass
description:
Threat modeling the CVE-2026-105483 certificate bypass

CVE-2026-105483 is best treated as an identity-binding failure. In affected Node.js 24.x and 26.x releases, tls.checkServerIdentity() could validate a fullwidth-digit IPv4 destination as a DNS identity. The connection normalized and resolved the destination to IPv4, while verification accepted a certificate with a matching DNS SAN. A client could therefore trust a server certificate for an endpoint it did not intend to contact.

The issue was fixed in Node.js 24.22.1 and 26.12.1 on October 21, 2026. Node.js rates it High. The advisory records CVSS v3.0 7.4 with high attack complexity and high confidentiality and integrity impact.

The vulnerable decision

TLS combines three operations that must remain aligned:

  1. Parse the requested destination.
  2. Establish a transport connection to the resolved endpoint.
  3. Verify that the peer certificate identifies that endpoint under the application's identity policy.

The vulnerable Node.js path separated the third step from the first two. The certificate chain could be signed by a trusted CA, yet the certificate identity could describe the endpoint as a DNS name rather than an IP address. This makes a generic statement such as "the certificate is trusted" insufficient. The relevant question is "trusted for what identity."

Build a concrete threat model

Start with the attacker's required position. The attacker needs to influence or impersonate the resolved endpoint, present a certificate trusted by the client, and supply a DNS SAN that matches the normalized address representation. High attack complexity in the CVSS vector reflects these coordinated conditions.

Next, identify where the client's destination comes from. A fixed, operator-controlled DNS name sharply limits who can select the fullwidth form. A tenant-provided callback URL, proxy setting, connector target, or imported integration can expose a wider population of potential attackers.

Then examine the data carried after the handshake. A health check may reveal little. A request with a bearer token, signed administrative operation, private file, or privileged database query can produce serious confidentiality and integrity impact.

Finally, examine certificate trust. A public trust store is only one source. Internal CAs, development roots, delegated intermediates, and application-specific trust bundles may create certificates that are valid for the client but outside the assumptions of public issuance policy.

Risk questions for each client

The following questions produce useful evidence:

  • Can any untrusted party choose a destination string?
  • Is the destination expected to be a DNS name or an IP address?
  • Does the application canonicalize the value before making a trust decision?
  • Does it require an IP SAN for an IP endpoint?
  • Which CAs can issue a certificate with an address-like DNS SAN?
  • What credentials or data are sent after the certificate check?
  • Can an operator detect a connection to an unexpected address?
  • Is the deployed Node.js runtime fixed?

A yes or no answer is less useful than an attached artifact: a code path, a certificate profile, a network policy, a runtime version, or a test result.

Separate exposure from compromise

ZoomEye Search app="Node.js" returned 5,539,674 product-fingerprint matches at 04:17 +08:00 on November 2, 2026. The CVE filter returned zero. The selected Exposure is 5,539,674, but the observable unit is a Node.js fingerprint, not a vulnerable process or a victim.

That evidence does not show that CVE-2026-105483 was exploited. It also cannot show whether an internet-facing service accepts user-controlled destinations. Use the count as background for why a Node.js estate matters, then rely on internal control evidence for incident decisions.

Prioritization

Prioritize clients that combine three properties: attacker-influenced destinations, a broad trust store, and high-value requests. Patch those systems first, then remove ambiguous destination inputs from their TLS path. Rotate credentials only if there is evidence that a connection reached an unintended endpoint; this CVE does not establish that event by itself.

For services with fixed destinations, upgrade on the normal critical-patch schedule while confirming the actual runtime. A fixed runtime is necessary even when the immediate exploit path looks narrow because configuration and integrations change over time.

Validation and response

Create an isolated test with a private CA and a certificate containing a numeric DNS SAN but no matching IP SAN. Verify that the patched client rejects the certificate for an IPv4 endpoint. Add a positive control with a matching IP SAN so the test distinguishes a correct rejection from a broken TLS client.

Monitor for failed identity checks after deployment, but do not assume silence proves safety. Existing clients may not log certificate identity details at the destination level. Combine runtime version evidence, destination-policy review, and controlled test results before closing the risk.

Remediation

Upgrade Node.js to 24.22.1, 26.12.1, or later. Rebuild packaged runtimes and redeploy images or single-executable applications that contain the old binary. Restrict user-controlled host inputs to canonical DNS names or canonical IP literals, require the matching SAN class, and avoid bypassing the standard certificate verification path.

The objective is to make one statement true across code, certificate policy, and deployment evidence: the identity being verified is the identity the application actually intended to use.

References

  • Node.js October 21, 2026 Security Releases
  • Node.js 24.22.1 release notes
  • Node.js 26.12.1 release notes
  • GitHub Advisory GHSA-8h4p-qpcq-gq24
  • ZoomEye Search

title: What makes up your AWS NAT gateway cost
description:
Your AWS NAT gateway cost is the price of the service that lets servers without a public IP address reach the internet. According to AWS pricing on 28 October 2026, a gateway in us-east-1 costs USD 0.045 an hour, or about USD 33 a month. Every gigabyte it handles adds another USD 0.045, traffic to S3 included. In Frankfurt, used in the examples below, both rates are USD 0.052, and one gateway with its public IPv4 address comes to about USD 42 a month before the first byte goes through it.

In Cost Explorer, filter to EC2-Other, group by Usage type and compare NatGateway-Hours with NatGateway-Bytes. Outside us-east-1 both names start with a Region code, EUC1- in Frankfurt. If the hours cost more, look for gateways to delete; if the bytes do, look for the server sending the most data.

A NAT gateway costs money before the first byte

AWS bills every hour a gateway is provisioned and available, and a partial hour counts as a full one. In Frankfurt that is about USD 38 a month. The gateway's public IPv4 address adds USD 3.65 a month.

For production, AWS recommends a NAT gateway in each Availability Zone whose resources need the internet. Across three zones that is about USD 125 a month before any traffic.

A gigabyte to the internet costs USD 0.142 through the gateway

AWS applies the USD 0.052 processing fee to every gigabyte that passes through the gateway, whatever its source or destination. Traffic to the internet is then charged standard data transfer on top: USD 0.09 per GB in Frankfurt once the 100 GB of free transfer each month is used up. That gigabyte ends up at USD 0.142.

A server in a different Availability Zone from its gateway pays another USD 0.01 per GB for the traffic between them. Traffic within one zone is free, so keep data-heavy servers in their gateway's zone.

The chart for this part is in the original post.

Finding what sends traffic through the gateway

To find which gateway carries the traffic, compare the gateways' CloudWatch metrics BytesOutToDestination and BytesInFromDestination with the Sum statistic.

The server behind it shows up in VPC Flow Logs. According to AWS re:Post, it is enough to send them from the gateways' network interfaces to CloudWatch Logs. They are billed and record nothing from before you enable them, so leave them on for a few working days, then switch them off.

In CloudWatch Logs Insights, run the article's query on that log group. Replace the example addresses with your gateways' private addresses, listed under NAT gateways in the VPC console, and your VPC's CIDR range.

filter (dstAddr in ["10.0.1.25", "10.0.2.25", "10.0.3.25"]
  AND isIpv4InSubnet(srcAddr, "10.0.0.0/16"))
  OR (srcAddr in ["10.0.1.25", "10.0.2.25", "10.0.3.25"]
  AND isIpv4InSubnet(dstAddr, "10.0.0.0/16"))
| stats sum(bytes) as bytesTransferred by srcAddr, dstAddr
| sort bytesTransferred desc

In the top rows, look up the address that is not a gateway under Network Interfaces in the EC2 console, which also lists ECS tasks and Lambda functions.

Traffic to S3 in the same Region can bypass the gateway through a gateway endpoint, which has no charge. My post on EC2-Other shows how to add one and what to check in bucket policies first. The same endpoint also takes most of an ECR image pull off the gateway, because according to the ECR documentation the image layers are downloaded from S3. If the endpoint has its own policy, it must allow the ECR layer bucket.

NAT gateways nobody uses

Since November 2025 Compute Optimizer has flagged NAT gateways that have had no traffic for 32 days, and since February 2026 Trusted Advisor has done the same. Trusted Advisor's cost checks, though, are not included in the Basic or Developer Support plans, so on those plans use Compute Optimizer, which you opt in to once per account.

Without those tools, check two CloudWatch metrics over the last 32 days: the maximum of ActiveConnectionCount and the sum of BytesOutToDestination. The first counts only TCP connections, so only zero on both means nobody is using the gateway.

Before you delete a gateway, point the route tables that use it at another gateway or remove those routes; otherwise they stay as blackhole routes and those subnets lose their way out to the internet. AWS also does not release the gateway's Elastic IP address from your account, so it keeps costing USD 3.65 a month as an idle address. Release it once you know nobody has it on an allowlist, for example at a payment provider.

NAT instance vs NAT gateway

An EC2 instance can do the gateway's job, but the NAT AMI from AWS runs on Amazon Linux 2018.03, unsupported since 2023, so build your own on Amazon Linux 2023 and turn off its source/destination check. AWS's comparison recommends the gateway for availability and less upkeep, but an instance is billed only by type and hours, with no per-GB processing charge. Internet and cross-zone transfer cost the same either way.

In Frankfurt, a gateway with its public address costs about USD 42 a month without traffic, and a t4g.micro instance with its address and disk about USD 11. With 1 TB a month through it, the gateway comes to about USD 95, while the instance stays at about USD 11.

A single instance has no automatic failover, so if it stops, your private servers lose internet access until someone restarts it. Small t4g instances reach full network speed only in short bursts on network credits; once those run out, they drop back to their baseline bandwidth. Patching the system is also your job, and every reboot cuts your private servers off the internet.

An instance suits test and development environments, or a few servers with little outbound traffic. If losing outbound internet access would stop orders or payments, keep the gateway in production. Either way, move S3 traffic to the free gateway endpoint first, because that needs no extra server.

What it means for a small team

Delete idle gateways together with their addresses first. When NatGateway-Bytes grows, find the source with the query above before adding an endpoint for the AWS service that receives the most data.

Instead of clicking through Cost Explorer, you can load an export of the whole bill grouped by Usage type into the CSV analysis. When NAT and transfer are a significant part of the bill, it shows gateway hours, processed data and internet transfer separately.

Every gateway that has carried nothing for 32 days is about USD 42 a month in Frankfurt that you get back by deleting it and releasing its address.

Originally published on codelevel.pl. Prices are net, for businesses. AWS, Hetzner and OVH are trademarks of their owners; CODELEVEL is not a partner, reseller or representative of any of them.

title: DUGO: Dual-Scale Gaussian Memory for Online Temporal Action Localization in Egocentric Procedural Videos
description:
arXiv:2610.41402v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Online Temporal Action Localization (OnTAL) aims to detect and localize action instances from untrimmed streaming videos in real time. Unlike offline approaches, OnTAL models have no access to future frames and cannot go back and refine earlier predictions, which makes the task considerably harder given the strict real-time constraints and narrow temporal window available. Most existing OnTAL methods lean on either brief anchor-based context or a single-scale memory of past frames, which limits how well they can capture actions unfolding across multiple time scales or requiring long-range reasoning in Procedural Videos. To address these gaps, we present DUGO (Dual-Scale Encoding and Gaussian Memory Online), a new OnTAL framework that jointly models local motion dynamics and long-range temporal dependencies. At its core, DUGO uses a Dual-Scale Temporal Encoder, pairing depth-wise local representations with global self-attention so it can pick up both fine-grained temporal patterns and broader contextual cues. We also introduce a Gaussian Memory Bank, which represents action memory as stochastic, input-conditioned Gaussian prototypes, allowing for richer temporal memory through gated cross-attention applied at both the encoder and anchor-query stages. Extensive experiments on procedural egocentric datasets (EGTEA, EPIC-Kitchens-100) demonstrate that DUGO achieves state-of-the-art performance while also providing substantial improvements on non-egocentric benchmarks such as Muses. The project page is available at: https://aman554-eq.github.io/DUGO

title: Attention Maps Know When to Think: Training-Free Difficulty-Aware Chain-of-Thought for Reasoning Segmentation
description:
arXiv:2610.41618v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting has become a standard reasoning strategy in Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs), showing strong performance in complex vision-language tasks such as reasoning segmentation. However, our analysis reveals that indiscriminate CoT usage can lead to degraded performance by inducing unnecessary reasoning, a phenomenon we term overthinking. In reasoning segmentation, overthinking often leads to misalignment between the query's intent and visual grounding. To address this, we propose Difficulty-Aware Chain-of-Thought (DA-CoT), a training-free adaptive framework that selectively triggers CoT based on the input's intrinsic difficulty. We find that the entropy of the model's attention maps reliably reflects task difficulty: low entropy indicates confident, localized grounding, while high entropy suggests uncertainty and potential benefit from CoT. DA-CoT uses this entropy signal to determine whether to apply CoT prompting. Additionally, we introduce a Bidirectional Rethinking mechanism that enables the model to automatically flip its reasoning decision when the initial output fails, enhancing robustness by recovering from failures induced by overthinking and underthinking. DA-CoT demonstrates its effectiveness by achieving state-of-the-art performance on the Reasoning Segmentation benchmarks while significantly improving inference efficiency.

title: Hardening SSH for Production Servers
description:
SSH is the gateway to your server, so it is the first service to lock down on a new machine. By the end of this guide you will have key-only logins, no direct root login, a short list of accounts allowed in, and fail2ban banning addresses that keep failing, with every change tested before you close your session. This is Part 1 of the Linux Server Baseline series (Part 2 covers file permissions, Part 3 covers cron). Commands target Ubuntu 24.04 and Debian 12, with RHEL differences noted where they matter.

Set up key-based login first

Once password logins are off, a key is the only way in over the network, so the key has to work before you touch the server config. Generate an ed25519 key on your workstation, not on the server:

ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "alice@laptop"

Accept the default path (~/.ssh/id_ed25519) and set a passphrase. Then copy the public half to the account you will log in as:

ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub deploy@203.0.113.10

ssh-copy-id uses your password one last time and appends the key to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the server. Confirm the key works on its own by telling the client not to fall back to a password:

ssh -o PreferredAuthentications=publickey deploy@203.0.113.10

If you get a shell, key authentication works. While you are logged in, run sudo whoami and confirm it prints root, because root login is about to be disabled and this account is how you will administer the box.

For the rest of this guide, keep one SSH session open and run every test from a second terminal. Reloading sshd does not drop established sessions, so the open one is your way back if a change goes wrong. Also, if your admin account has no local password (common on cloud images), set one with sudo passwd deploy so the provider's console login works if you need it.

Put your settings in a drop-in file

On Ubuntu 24.04 and Debian 12, /etc/ssh/sshd_config starts with Include /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/*.conf. For most keywords sshd keeps the first value it reads, and it reads the included files in lexical order before the rest of the main file. Cloud images often ship a file such as 50-cloud-init.conf, and it may contain PasswordAuthentication yes. If you add PasswordAuthentication no to the bottom of sshd_config, or to a file named 60-hardening.conf, the cloud-init value is read first and yours is ignored.

Check what is already there:

grep -rniE 'include|passwordauthentication' /etc/ssh/sshd_config /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/

Naming your file 00-hardening.conf puts it ahead of everything else. Create it with sudoedit /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-hardening.conf:

PubkeyAuthentication yes
PasswordAuthentication no
KbdInteractiveAuthentication no
PermitRootLogin no
MaxAuthTries 3
LoginGraceTime 30
AllowUsers deploy alice
X11Forwarding no

What each line does:

  • PasswordAuthentication no and KbdInteractiveAuthentication no together stop password prompts. With UsePAM yes (the Debian and Ubuntu default), keyboard-interactive auth can still ask for a password through PAM, so both are needed. KbdInteractiveAuthentication is the current name; older guides call it ChallengeResponseAuthentication, which is now a deprecated alias.
  • PermitRootLogin no replaces the default prohibit-password, which still allows root in with a key. Admins log in as themselves and use sudo, so the logs show who did what.
  • PubkeyAuthentication yes is already the default. Stating it keeps the file self-explanatory.
  • MaxAuthTries 3 limits authentication attempts per connection (default 6). Every key the client offers counts as one attempt.
  • LoginGraceTime 30 disconnects clients that have not authenticated within 30 seconds (default 120).
  • AllowUsers refuses every account not listed, even with a valid key. On a box with many admins, AllowGroups sshusers is easier to maintain. Pick one: if you set both, a user has to pass both checks. Make sure your own account is on the list.
  • X11Forwarding no overrides the yes in Debian and Ubuntu's stock config. Servers rarely need it.

Validate and reload without locking yourself out

Test the syntax before anything else. No output means the config parsed:

sudo sshd -t

Then ask sshd for the effective configuration, which shows the value that actually won after all files were read:

sudo sshd -T | grep -i passwordauthentication

passwordauthentication no

Repeat the grep for permitrootlogin, kbdinteractiveauthentication, maxauthtries, and allowusers. If any shows the old value, an earlier file is setting it (see troubleshooting below).

Reload the service. It is called ssh on Ubuntu and Debian and sshd on RHEL and Fedora:

sudo systemctl reload ssh

Now, from a second terminal, log in again. Then confirm passwords are refused by disabling key auth on the client:

ssh -o PubkeyAuthentication=no deploy@203.0.113.10

deploy@203.0.113.10: Permission denied (publickey).

A login as root should fail the same way. If the new login does not work, go back to the session you kept open, move the file aside with sudo mv /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-hardening.conf /root/, reload, and work out what went wrong before trying again.

Change the port for less log noise

Moving SSH off port 22 cuts the volume of automated login attempts in your logs. It is not real security: a port scan of your address still finds the new port, and key-only auth is what actually protects you. Do it if the noise bothers you, and open the firewall before you move sshd.

sudo ufw allow 2222/tcp
sudo ufw status

Add Port 2222 to 00-hardening.conf and run sudo sshd -t. How you apply it depends on whether SSH is socket-activated, which is the default on Ubuntu 23.04 and later, including 24.04:

systemctl is-enabled ssh.socket

If that prints enabled, systemd owns the listening socket and generates its port from your sshd config, so regenerate and restart the socket:

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl restart ssh.socket

If it prints anything else, such as disabled on Debian 12, restart the service with sudo systemctl restart ssh. Either way, existing sessions stay up. Confirm the new listener:

sudo ss -tln | grep -E ':(22|2222)\s'

From a second terminal, run ssh -p 2222 deploy@203.0.113.10. To confirm the port is reachable from outside your provider's network, test it with the port checker. Only then remove the old rule with sudo ufw delete allow 22/tcp (or sudo ufw delete allow OpenSSH, depending on how it was added).

On RHEL, Rocky, and Alma, SELinux only lets sshd bind ports labelled ssh_port_t, and the firewall is firewalld. Label and open the port before restarting sshd:

sudo semanage port -a -t ssh_port_t -p tcp 2222
sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-port=2222/tcp
sudo firewall-cmd --reload

semanage comes from the policycoreutils-python-utils package.

Ban repeated failures with fail2ban

MaxAuthTries limits guesses per connection. fail2ban works across connections: it watches for failed logins and adds a firewall rule that blocks an address after too many. With passwords disabled it mostly saves log space and CPU, but it is cheap to run.

sudo apt install fail2ban python3-systemd

Leave jail.conf alone so package upgrades can update it cleanly, and put your settings in /etc/fail2ban/jail.local:

[DEFAULT]
ignoreip = 127.0.0.1/8 ::1 198.51.100.7

[sshd]
enabled = true
port = 2222
backend = systemd
maxretry = 5
findtime = 10m
bantime = 1h

An address that fails maxretry times within findtime is banned for bantime. Set port to your SSH port (use ssh if you stayed on 22), or bans will block a port nobody is using. Put your office or VPN address in ignoreip so you cannot ban yourself.

backend = systemd makes fail2ban read the journal instead of a log file. Default Debian 12 installs have no /var/log/auth.log because rsyslog is not installed, and without this line the sshd jail fails to start. It works on Ubuntu 24.04 as well. Restart and check the jail:

sudo systemctl restart fail2ban
sudo fail2ban-client status sshd

The output lists currently failed and total banned counts plus the banned IP list. If an address you need gets banned, release it with sudo fail2ban-client set sshd unbanip 198.51.100.23.

Troubleshooting common lockouts

Locked out completely

Use your provider's web console, serial console, or rescue mode. These log in locally without going through sshd or the firewall, which is why the local password matters. Once in, move the drop-in aside, run sudo sshd -t, and reload. If the firewall is the problem, sudo ufw allow 22/tcp gets you back.

Permission denied (publickey)

Check the username first. Cloud images create a distro-specific default user (ubuntu on Ubuntu, for example), and any account left out of AllowUsers is refused. Next, check file permissions. sshd ignores authorized_keys if ~/.ssh or the file can be written by other users, or if the home directory is group- or world-writable. The fix for an account named deploy:

sudo chmod 700 /home/deploy/.ssh
sudo chmod 600 /home/deploy/.ssh/authorized_keys
sudo chown -R deploy:deploy /home/deploy/.ssh

If octal modes are unfamiliar, Linux File Permissions and chmod, Explained covers what these numbers mean. The server log usually names the reason, such as Authentication refused: bad ownership or modes:

sudo journalctl -u ssh -n 30

Use -u sshd on RHEL. On the client side, ssh -v shows which keys were offered.

Too many authentication failures

With MaxAuthTries 3, an agent holding several keys can use up the attempts before it reaches the right one. Offer only the key you mean:

ssh -o IdentitiesOnly=yes -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 deploy@203.0.113.10

A setting is ignored

If sshd -T shows the old value, another file sets it first. Find it with sudo grep -rni passwordauthentication /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/, then remove the line or rename your file so it sorts earlier. On Ubuntu, a port change that does not show up in ss usually means daemon-reload and the ssh.socket restart were skipped. If the old port is still listed after both, run sudo systemctl restart ssh as well.

Checklist before you log out

  • Key login works from a fresh terminal, and password login is refused.
  • Your admin account has a local password for console access.
  • sudo sshd -t is clean and sudo sshd -T shows the values you set.
  • The firewall allows your SSH port and the port checker can reach it.
  • sudo fail2ban-client status sshd shows the jail running.

Next in the series, Linux File Permissions and chmod, Explained covers the modes that decide whether sshd trusts your key files.

title: On the Origin and Evolution of Training-Inference Mismatch in LLM Reinforcement Learning
description:
arXiv:2610.40945v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: On-policy reinforcement learning for large language models assumes that training responses are sampled from the current policy. In practice, an inference engine samples the responses and a separate trainer computes the gradients, and the \textbf{training-inference mismatch} between the two makes the training data off-policy. The mismatch has two sources, the numerics of the engine and the stale weights of asynchronous sampling, and a correction that stabilizes training under one source can fail under the other. \textit{We ask which property of a mismatch source decides the correction it needs.} Evaluating the trainer at the sampler's weights splits each sampled-token error exactly into a \textit{numerical discrepancy} of the engine and a \textit{policy lag} of the trainer, and we follow both through training. The numerical discrepancy stays approximately constant, so it biases the updates by a nearly fixed amount, and centering the score at each prefix removes its leading bias. The policy lag is produced by the trainer's own updates: the bias it leaves enters the next update, which enlarges the next lag and closes a feedback loop. Importance weighting cuts this loop only while the lag ratio stays concentrated, and on Qwen3-1.7B it fails at the step where the effective sample size of the ratio falls below one half. From this account we derive the \textbf{discrepancy-lag correction} (DLC), which centers the numerical discrepancy, clips the lag ratio against the sampler's weights and resynchronizes the sampler when this effective sample size falls below one half. Under a stale sampler, DLC keeps the KL divergence from on-policy training within twice the KL between two independent on-policy trainings on Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B, and its resynchronization prevents collapses that the per-token corrections leave and that a KL measured on the sampler's prefixes does not detect.

title: rl_rob: A transparent, from-scratch Python library for teaching reinforcement learning from tabular methods to deep policy gradients
description:
arXiv:2610.41303v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: rl_rob is an open-source Python library for teaching reinforcement learning. It implements the arc of a modern course, from tabular temporal-difference learning through linear function approximation to deep value-based and policy-gradient methods, with every algorithm written from first principles so that its update rule is visible in a few lines of code. All agents share one interface, so learners can compare methods directly across stages and trace a deep reinforcement learning update from the temporal-difference error to the weight change. The library supports teaching and assessment in which students implement, modify and explain update rules, rather than only produce working code.

title: Our Capture Script Filmed the Test Harness, Not Lullwood
description:
When a video, a build or a report looks wrong, look at the artefact before you theorise about the code that made it. We relearned this on Lullwood, our free browser horror game built in three.js and Next.js. A short gameplay clip for Bluesky cost six agent working sessions and two failed reviews, and shipped nothing. Two source-cited root causes were both wrong. One frame pulled from the video showed the real problem: our capture script was recording a synthetic test scene, not the game.

The setup

Lullwood is built by Claude agents, so "a heartbeat" below means one working session of one agent. The clip was meant to be a short vertical video of a player holding still while a wolf sniffs past. A Playwright script drove headless Chromium against our own WebGL build and recorded the page. The capture tooling worked exactly as designed. The scene it was told to record was the problem.

Four takes, two failures

The first two takes were too short, and the captions we had written existed only in a text file next to the video, never in the pixels. Neither reached review.

The third take ran 23.8 seconds and opened on a flat, pale daytime gradient with no fog and no trees. That was qaWorld=micro, a test world that stands in for the night forest. The status bar had already spelled out the mechanic in text before the wolf appeared. Failed.

The fourth take ran about 23 seconds and fixed the empty world. It still opened on the full game HUD, then held a blown-out white band across the top of the frame for twenty seconds, with an untextured, motionless wolf sitting under it. Failed again. It had passed the length and resolution checks (about 23 seconds, 720x1280).

Two root causes, both wrong

Between those takes, two diagnoses went onto the ticket. Both were specific and both cited the engine source.

The first said the wolf could not see the player. At night its detection range plateaus at 6.16 units, and the staged hiding spot needed 6.3 to trigger. True as far as it went. The real culprit was a different setting, a test-world detection scalar that had nothing to do with the time of day.

The second said the hide camera was sitting inside the bush mesh, and that point-blank exposure was blowing out the picture. It came with a fix: re-stage the shot just before or after the hide beat. That would have bought a fifth take and a third failure. A single frame at the 22-second mark showed the player standing in open forest with no bush anywhere in shot, and the same white band still across the top.

Pulling that frame is one command, ffmpeg -ss 22 -i clip.webm -frames:v 1 frame.png. Our environment had no ffmpeg on the path, which did not help. Playwright ships a bundled binary.

What was actually wrong

The script called a QA hook built for engine tests. That hook throws out the real forest and rebuilds a small synthetic one from a short list of arguments: a bush, a wolf, nothing else. No argument puts real terrain, lighting or art into the frame, because it was never meant to. We were filming the test harness and calling it a shot of the game.

What nearly buried the answer was a healthy part of the pipeline. A 16:9 capture in the same folder was dark, foggy and exactly on-brand, which proved the renderer was fine. It was also filed as clip-wolf-16x9.webm, and it is the title screen. There is no wolf in it. Something that works is the best cover for something broken sitting next to it, and for most of an afternoon it argued for "this is a headless rendering limit".

Why this is not a game story

Every team that has trusted a green run over the thing the run produced has been here. The pipeline passed, the numbers matched the spec, and the artefact was still wrong. Reasoning about what a build should put on screen is still reasoning. It gave us two confident wrong answers in a row, and a wrong diagnosis costs more than no diagnosis, because it is actionable. "It's the bush" sends you to re-stage a shot that could never work. "I don't know yet" sends you to go and look.

What we changed

  • Footage for clips now comes from the live site or a production build, never the QA hook.
  • Before a root cause goes on a ticket, someone pulls the frame and looks at it. Container measurements come second.
  • The clip itself is cancelled.

We wrote the original, longer account on the Lullwood devlog. If you want the game behind the story, Lullwood is free in the browser and needs no signup.

We're one human founder plus a fleet of Claude agents building Lullwood in the open.

Application Design Center

Feature

Use the recommendeIAMroles API to identify a list of required APIs and Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles that you must configure before you deploy your application.

BigQuery

Feature

Iceberg external tables and Iceberg managed tables now support flexible column names by default. This feature is generally available (GA).

Feature

The gemini-embedding-2 model works well for embedding long strings, including multilingual and unstructured data. It supports a mix of text, images, audio, video, and PDF files. You can use this model in the AI.EMBED, AI.SIMILARITY, and AI.GENERATE_EMBEDDING functions. This model is generally available.

Cloud Load Balancing

Feature

External IPv6 addresses are now supported for Standard Tier. For more information, see IPv6 subnet ranges.

This feature is in Preview.

Cloud Workstations

Feature

Cloud Workstations supports Assured Workloads control packages to help you meet regulatory, data residency, and data sovereignty requirements.

Specifically, the Cloud Workstations API (v1, v1beta, and v1alpha) supports the following Assured Workloads control packages:

  • Data Boundary for FedRAMP High
  • Data Boundary for FedRAMP Moderate
  • Data Boundary for Impact Level 2 (IL2)
  • Data Boundary for Impact Level 4 (IL4)
  • Data Boundary for Impact Level 5 (IL5)
  • US Data Boundary and Support (AW Regional Controls - Premium)
  • EU Data Boundary with Access Justifications

For more information about compliance-supported regions for each control package and API fields that aren't intended for sensitive data, see Regulatory support in Cloud Workstations.

Compute Engine

Feature

Generally available: Z3 machine types that have 8 to 44 vCPUs can use Hyperdisk Balanced High Availability volumes to synchronously replicate data across two zones.

For more information, see About Hyperdisk Balanced High Availability.

Feature

Preview: External IPv6 addresses are now supported for Standard Tier. For more information, see IPv6 subnet ranges.

Confidential Space

Announcement

A new Confidential Space image (260900) is available.

Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

Fixed

CodeMender updates (v0.12.0)

This release introduces updates to CodeMender:

  • Hidden file scanning: Added the --include-hidden flag to cm find (or include_hidden under scan in config.yaml) to include hidden directories and files, such as .github/ and .config/, in vulnerability scans.
  • Larger file support: Raised the default file discovery size limit (max_file_size_kb) from 500 KB to 2 MiB so cm find no longer skips large source files. Existing configurations that use the previous 500 KB default are upgraded automatically, and --deep and --diff scans can now read beyond the inline preview of files larger than 64 KB.
  • Report output for every scan mode: cm find --output now writes the scan report for standard, --deep, --parallel, and --diff scans.
  • Scoped fixes: cm fix now prevents the agent from modifying CI/CD pipelines, static analysis configurations, build definitions, and repository configuration files that are outside the scope of the vulnerability being fixed.
  • Accurate session token usage: cm now reports the total token usage across all turns of a session, instead of only the final turn, so token counts in cm stats and session exports match billed usage.
  • Bug fixes:
    • Fixed duplicate findings in cm report and cm stats, and stopped merging distinct vulnerability types reported on the same line.
    • Fixed database is locked errors during cm find --deep scans with multiple workers.
    • Reduced false positives by requiring a concrete, viable exploit before reporting a finding with high confidence.
    • Included sessions from cm find --deep and cm find --diff workers in cm stats.
    • Fixed cm verify resolving relative finding and exploit artifact paths against the current working directory instead of the project root.

For more information, see the CodeMender documentation.

Google Kubernetes Engine

Deprecated

Starting on July 1, 2026, Identity Service for GKE is deprecated in GKE version 1.36 and earlier. This feature is also unavailable in organizations that were created on or after July 1, 2025. GKE version 1.37 and later don't support Identity Service for GKE. Before you upgrade clusters to 1.37 and later, disable this feature and migrate to Workforce Identity Federation.

For more information, see Identity Service for GKE deprecation.

Feature

GKE support for using the c4-standard-* machine types (up to 192 vCPUs) as Confidential GKE Nodes with Intel TDX is generally available. For more information, see the following pages:

  • To use this feature with GKE , see Encrypt workload data in-use with Confidential GKE Nodes.
  • To learn more about the feature from Compute Engine, see Confidential VM overview.
  • To see supported configurations, including machine support, see Supported configurations and its "Machine types, CPUs, and zones" section.

Google SecOps

Feature

[Spotlight Feature] Terraform and client libraries for multiple features using Chronicle API

Terraform providers and Google Cloud client libraries are now available for several Google SecOps features using Chronicle API including Feeds, Parsers, Rules, Findings Refinements, Retrohunts, Dashboards, Data Tables, Watchlists, Custom Lists, Environments, Environment Groups, Data Export, SOAR Domains, and SOAR Networks. For more information, see Terraform reference.

Terraform providers enable programmatic provisioning and management of Google SecOps resources as code, while Client Libraries enable developers to build custom integrations and automate Google SecOps workflows in their preferred programming languages. For more information, see Client libraries.

Guest Environment

Feature

Version 20260921.00 of the guest agent is now available for all supported operating systems. This version introduces the following features:

  • The managed workload identity certificate refresher is now a locally bundled extension. For more information, see Managed workload identities overview.
  • The guest telemetry extension is updated to version 1.1 and polls every 15 minutes instead of every 24 hours. However, it will only send data to the API every 24 hours, unless it detects a change in the system since the previous poll. The extension supports the following capabilities:
    • Running a command as the user associated with a discovered process.
    • Configuring regular expressions to match against the version command output.

Fixed

Version 20260921.00 of the guest agent is now available for all supported operating systems. This version introduces the following fixes:

  • The NetworkManager setup now no longer reloads the primary NIC when it applies changes to the network configuration of secondary NICs, unless necessary.
  • If the core plugin successfully rolls back any configurations, then it force-reloads the configurations to make sure that the instance re-obtains DHCP leases for secondary NICs.
  • The core plugin now respects the address-manager configuration flag and the corresponding metadata attribute.
  • The extensions manager now ignores install and remove requests from ACS for the core plugin and locally bundled extensions.
  • The extensions manager no longer logs that there are no local plugins to install when it's installing local plugins.
  • The metadata script runner now respects the sysprep_specialize configuration flag.

Knowledge Catalog

Feature

Data products in Knowledge Catalog now support Looker (Google Cloud core) assets. You can package, govern, and share Looker (Google Cloud core) dashboards, dashboard elements, Looks, Explores, and LookML projects, models, and views in a data product using Google Group mirroring and IAM access controls. This feature is generally available.

For more information, see About data products and Create data products.

Managed Service for Apache Spark

Change

Managed Service for Apache Spark (formerly Google Cloud Serverless for Apache Spark): Users may now specify short template names when creating a serverless session.

Network Intelligence Center

Feature

Flow Analyzer displays packet drops, allowing you to analyze packet loss in your traffic flows. For more information, see Display flows in packet drop mode.

Network Service Tiers

Feature

External IPv6 addresses are now supported for Standard Tier in Preview. For more information, see IPv6 subnet ranges.

Virtual Private Cloud

Feature

Preview: External IPv6 addresses are now supported for Standard Tier. For more information, see IPv6 subnet ranges.

title: Shopify Just Opened Campaign Autopilot to Every Store: What Devs and Store Builders Should Know
description:
If you build or maintain Shopify stores, your clients are about to ask you one question: "Should I turn on Autopilot?"

On October 28, 2026, Shopify made Campaign Autopilot available to all merchants. It also added more channels and a new SEO feature. Here's the official post: More channels and features now available in Campaign Autopilot.

Let's break it down in plain words, with a developer's eye on what to check first.

What Campaign Autopilot actually does

The idea is simple. A merchant sets a budget and some guardrails. Autopilot then looks at the store, the products, and the customers, and builds a marketing campaign.

It also decides which channels to run on, how much to spend on each, and moves budget toward what's working. The merchant doesn't have to build separate campaigns on every platform.

The channels it can reach

According to the changelog, Autopilot can reach shoppers across:

  • Meta Ads
  • Microsoft Advertising
  • Snapchat
  • Shop
  • Shopify Messaging
  • X Ads (coming soon)

For anyone who has juggled several ad dashboards for one client, having this in one place is a big change.

The new SEO suggestions

This part is easy to miss. Autopilot now suggests SEO optimizations. The merchant reviews and approves them, so nothing goes live on its own.

Merchants can also ask for SEO updates directly in Sidekick, Shopify's built-in assistant.

If you've ever had a client who "doesn't have time for SEO," this gives them a low-effort place to start.

Where merchants find it

Autopilot lives in the Growth tab of the Shopify admin. You can jump straight there with the Growth tab link. For the full guide, see the Shopify Help Center.

What you can do for your clients before they turn it on

Autopilot builds campaigns from what's already in the store. The changelog says it looks at the store, products, and customers. So it's reasonable to assume the quality of that data affects the quality of the campaigns. Here's a short checklist you can run through.

1. Clean up the product catalog. Check titles, descriptions, prices, and images. Fix missing alt text, empty descriptions, and broken variants. Messy data in means messy ads out.

2. Review the storefront. Ads send people to your pages. Make sure product pages load fast, look right on mobile, and have a clear path to checkout.

3. Check tracking and analytics. Before spending money, confirm that orders and traffic sources are being recorded correctly. You can't judge a campaign you can't measure.

4. Help set sensible guardrails. Talk with the client about a starting budget and limits. Start small, watch the results, and raise it later.

5. Go through the SEO suggestions together. Read each one before approving. Some may not fit the brand voice, and a quick human review catches that.

Keep your own judgment in the loop

Autopilot is a helpful tool, but it isn't magic. A few habits will save you headaches.

  • Don't set it and forget it. Check performance in the first days and weeks.
  • Give it time to learn. A Common Thread Collective post on this update suggests allowing two to three weeks of learning time before peak traffic. That's one agency's advice, not a Shopify rule, but it makes sense for systems that optimize on their own.
  • Explain the limits to clients. Autopilot can pick channels and shift budget, but it doesn't know everything about the brand. Someone still needs to review what goes out.

Why the timing matters

Black Friday and Cyber Monday are just around the corner. Ad costs often rise during busy seasons, so stores that start early have more time to learn what works.

If your clients turn this on the week of the sale, you'll be fixing small problems while customers are already shopping. Starting now gives everyone room to test.

The takeaway

Campaign Autopilot doesn't replace good products or good store work. It takes over the repetitive parts of marketing: picking channels, splitting budget, and suggesting SEO changes.

If you do one thing this week, open a test store or a client store, look at the Growth tab, and see what Autopilot suggests. Then run the checklist above before anyone spends real money.

Official update: Shopify Changelog: More channels and features now available in Campaign Autopilot

Have you tried Campaign Autopilot yet? Share your experience in the comments.

title: Navigating Multi-Cloud Complexity: Introducing CloudCompass 🧭✨
description:
As enterprise architectures scale, managing multi-cloud resources and organizing local-first development workflows can get overwhelmingly chaotic. Distributed systems demand high visibility, intuitive interfaces, and streamlined diagnostic routing.

Enter CloudCompass—an open-source, theme-aware navigation framework and modular user interface suite engineered to simplify cross-cloud resource management and modern system architecture tracking.

🎥 Watch the Demo

Get a quick visual look at the responsive layout, dynamic switching, and clean navigational interface in action:

🎬 Watch the CloudCompass Demo Video

✨ Core Features & Highlights

CloudCompass bridges the gap between complex system design and clean developer UX. Here is a breakdown of everything packed inside the repository:

1. 🌐 Unified Multi-Cloud Navigation

  • Centralizes resource tracking across diverse cloud providers and hybrid environments into a single, cohesive dashboard.
  • Eliminates context-switching fatigue by organizing services, metrics, and environment targets in one intuitive interface.

2. 🎨 Theme-Aware Modular Interface

  • Built with a modern front-end stack (Next.js, React, and Tailwind CSS), delivering fluid light/dark mode adjustments.
  • Offers adaptable layouts tailored for both high-density enterprise operations and lightweight local management.

3. 🏠 Local-First Workflow Integration

  • Fully aligned with local-first software philosophies, empowering developers to run standalone diagnostic control panels, self-hosted dashboards, or offline-capable system bridges.
  • Preserves data privacy while minimizing external API overhead.

4. 🧩 Plug-and-Play Component Architecture

  • Highly structured and modular codebase designed for rapid extension.
  • Easily customizable layout templates allow you to plug in custom API routes, metrics displays, or deployment status components without refactoring existing UI trees.

5. ⚡ Developer-First Performance

  • Engineered with optimized client-side hydration, fast route switching, and minimal bundle overhead for near-instant load times.
  • Fully open-source under the MIT license, encouraging community contributions, custom forks, and enterprise integration.

🚀 Quick Start Guide

Getting CloudCompass running locally takes only a couple of minutes:

# Clone the repository
git clone [https://github.com/kamalsoft/cloudcompass.git](https://github.com/kamalsoft/cloudcompass.git)

# Navigate into the project directory
cd cloudcompass

# Install dependencies
npm install

# Start the local development server
npm run demo

title: DrawSplat: Atlanta World-Guided Implicit Gaussian SLAM for Indoor Reconstruction
description:
arXiv:2610.41602v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: RGB-D SLAM requires accurate online tracking, high-quality rendering, and geometrically consistent reconstruction. Existing Gaussian SLAM methods mainly optimize Gaussian primitives with photometric, depth, or local frame-to-model constraints, which are often insufficient in indoor scenes with weak textures, large planar structures, noisy depth, and long trajectories. The resulting maps may suffer from pose drift, surface thickness artifacts, noisy normals, and blurred structural boundaries. We propose DrawSplat, an Atlanta World-guided implicit Gaussian SLAM framework for indoor reconstruction. DrawSplat follows a drawing-like process: explicit point-line geometry first sketches the structural layout, and implicit neural Gaussians then fill in high-fidelity appearance and continuous geometric details. It estimates camera poses, sparse geometry, and gravity direction through point-line joint tracking, infers structural planes from tracked lines using the shared-gravity component of the Atlanta World prior, and converts them into differentiable regularization terms on Gaussian centers and normals. To improve compactness and efficiency, DrawSplat further combines an anchor-based implicit neural Gaussian representation with adaptive structural sampling, which allocates Gaussian capacity to structurally informative regions. Experiments on multiple datasets show that DrawSplat achieves robust tracking, high-fidelity rendering, and strong geometric reconstruction among Gaussian-based SLAM systems, while maintaining a practical balance among quality, efficiency, and model size.

title: Aligning MLLMs with the Latent Structure of Human Cognition via Behavior-Derived Semantic Dimensions
description:
arXiv:2610.41951v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved impressive performance across a wide range of reasoning tasks, yet it remains unclear whether their internal representations and decision criteria align with the latent structure of human cognition. In this work, we propose a novel framework to align MLLMs with the multidimensional mental representations underlying human similarity judgements. We build on a previously established behavior-derived semantic embedding space, in which objects are represented along 66 interpretable dimensions derived from 4.70 million human Odd-One-Out (O1O) judgements. For each triplet, we infer the most salient decision dimension and convert it into a dimension-grounded linguistic rationale. This enables MLLMs to learn both the final choice and a justification consistent with the inferred behavioral criterion. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach improves model consistency with human similarity judgements while retaining competitive performance on standard multimodal benchmarks. Furthermore, using searchlight Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) on an independent fMRI Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD), we observe increased representational alignment between model and human. Ultimately, our findings point to a data-driven route for incorporating human cognitive structure into MLLMs alignment. The code is available \href{https://github.com/ening-open/cogalign}{here}.

title: A Theoretical Framework for Understanding and Building "Any-task inference" Capable Foundation Models
description:
arXiv:2610.40934v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In this work, we provide a formal framework and mathematical definition for the subset of foundation models focused on enabling the property of "any-task inference" (ATI) (similar to zero-shot inference), rather than those designed for pre-training fine-tuning. To achieve this mathematical definition, we formalize the notion of a "space of tasks of interest," which we include in the problem domain, then provide an interface-based formal definition for ATI foundation models as those that map samples of data $x$ and tasks $t$ to predictions over the space of labels directly. While simple, this definition allows us to show that all ATI foundation models can be decomposed through a "universal task reduction" lens into encoder, model, and decoder aspects. We can leverage this decomposition to also decompose foundation model error into terms corresponding to different aspects of this reduction, stratified into a collection of "design terms," which are theoretical properties that can inform one of whether a particular proposed ATI foundation model can achieve optimality or not due to the structure of the proposed task reduction, and "realized model excess" terms which capture interactions between learned and programmatic components of foundation model systems. Lastly, we can use this perspective to offer two "prototypical" recipes for realizing ATI foundation models in diverse domains, which we term generative and discriminative variants of ATI foundation models. This exercise is grounded throughout by 5 real-world examples of foundation models in different settings, varying greatly in how these capabilities are realized, showing the applicability of this definition to real-world settings.

title: October 2026 for React and AI Devs: Next.js 16.4, TypeScript 7.1 Beta, a Big TanStack Month, Convex 1.47 to 1.49
description:
October was busy. Next.js shipped a release and two critical security fixes in the same month, TypeScript 7.1 went to beta, TanStack put out five announcements in four weeks, and Convex shipped three minor versions. This is what I think is worth knowing from it, with a link to the release note or announcement behind every item. Dates are the publish dates on those pages.

There's one thing to put in your calendar first. Next.js has a scheduled security release on November 3 covering seven medium-severity vulnerabilities. The advisories aren't public yet, so plan an upgrade window for that day.

Next.js

Next.js 16.4 (Oct 6). The headline is that the Next.js team now recommends Cache Components for every Next.js app. New apps from create-next-app get it enabled by default, and the post says it will be the default in Next.js 17. There's also a lot of agent tooling: next upgrade --agent gives a coding agent version-specific upgrade steps, experimental.agentUpgrade nudges you during next dev and next build when a relevant upgrade exists (the default policy only covers security fixes), and experimental.agentFeedback (on by default in new apps, opt-in for existing ones) lets an agent draft bug reports that you review before anything gets sent. For everyone else: a 20 to 25% smaller Turbopack disk cache, lazy server HMR, shorter CSS Module class names in production, and React 19.3. The experimental Rust React Compiler got a fast path that skips files that don't need it, and the post reports 30% less memory and 15% faster compiles for it.

October 14 security update. This one is not optional. Two critical unauthenticated RCEs were fixed: one in use cache functions that return multiple typed arrays (no workaround, so upgrade even if you don't think you have that pattern), and one in the Image Optimization API with SVGs on glibc-based Linux, which comes from the upstream image library. If you can't upgrade right away, the workaround for that one is making sure Next.js resolves sharp 0.35.5 or later. There's also a high-severity DoS for App Router apps with at least one Server Action. The fixed versions are 16.4.1 and 15.5.28. The latest 16.4 patch is 16.4.3 on npm (Oct 23).

Two agent-focused posts. Improving navigation in v0 with Next.js 16.4 (Oct 16) walks through Partial Prefetching and the new next-partial-prefetching-optimizer skill on a real app. Ship less JavaScript with your AI agent (Oct 28) introduces the next-bundle-optimizer skill, which gives an agent Turbopack's module graph. Vercel says agents cut close to 2 MB of compressed JavaScript across v0 and vercel.com with it. It requires Turbopack.

React

There was no React blog post in October; React 19.3 is from September. On Oct 14, the same day as the Next.js security update, React published 19.3.1 along with backports 19.2.9, 19.1.10 and 19.0.9. The release notes say "Improve transport protocol" under React Server Components, and the Next.js post links two upstream React advisories. If you use RSC outside Next.js, upgrade React too.

React Hook Form shipped 7.90.0 and 7.91.0, mostly useFieldArray fixes, and v8.0.0-beta.5, which says it improves React Compiler compatibility and adds full test coverage with the compiler.

TypeScript

TypeScript 7.1 Beta (Oct 20). The language changes are small but useful. Ambient module declarations can now match on import attributes (declare module "*" with { type: "text" }). There's support for source phase imports (import source), and es2026 is now a stable --target and --lib (Map.prototype.getOrInsert, Uint8Array.fromBase64, Error.isError and more). The bigger story is the new programmatic API split into entry points like typescript/sync and typescript/async, plus "content mappers", a plugin point that lets tools for Vue, Svelte, Astro, MDX and similar formats feed TypeScript a virtual version of the file. Running them from tsc needs the new --runExternalCode flag. Microsoft's own numbers show 1.2x to 1.9x faster checks than 7.0 on five large codebases. One behavior change might add errors: distributive conditional types are stricter about constraints. The post says an RC is about a month out.

TanStack

TanStack Charts 1.0 (Oct 5). A new charting library, already at 1.0. The pitch is "charts you don't have to outgrow".

TanStack Start 1.0 is stable (Oct 13). This is the formal API commitment for the full-stack framework many people were already running in production during the RC. If you were holding off on Start until it hit 1.0, that wait is over.

TanStack AI 1.0 (Oct 23). Stable core APIs, rewritten docs, 23 provider adapters, and an experimental agent harness. The harness APIs are explicitly not covered by the stability promise.

Introducing TanStack Redact (Oct 26). A smaller replacement for React and React DOM in the browser that keeps your application code unchanged. It's early (0.2.x on npm), so check its compatibility docs before trying it on a real app.

TanStack DB 1.0 RC1 (Oct 29). The release candidate, plus a long post about the "oracle" tests used to harden it. Read the RC migration guide before upgrading. Query Collection handlers no longer refetch automatically after a mutation, and that one quietly changes app behavior.

Convex

Three minor versions landed in about two weeks, all in the convex-js changelog.

1.47 (Oct 15) added .staged() on defineTable, so a schema change can be validated in the background instead of blocking the deploy on a table scan. npx convex deploy now asks before building an index on a large table, ctx.meta.getSnapshotTs() is public, and the envList MCP tool returns only variable names by default.

1.48 (Oct 22) lets deployments sign their own JWTs with ctx.auth.signJwt in mutations (verifiable via the deployment's /.well-known/jwks.json) and makes ctx.storage.store() and ctx.storage.get() work in mutations, not just actions. Verbose deploy logs now redact env values, and npx convex env list shows only names when it detects an AI agent is running it.

1.49 (Oct 30) drops Node.js 20, so you need Node 22 or newer for the CLI. It also adds a v.function() validator for function handles and an npx convex plugins install command for the Claude Code and Codex plugin.

AI SDKs and agent tooling

Composio TypeScript SDK. 0.23.0 (Oct 12) lets a session tool ask for user input, such as an approval, instead of running, and surfaces that as a new ComposioToolInputRequiredError. 0.24.0 (Oct 14) adds session.executeMeta() for running COMPOSIO_* meta tools. 0.27.0 (Oct 22) adds session hooks, which can block a tool call before it runs or block its result before the agent sees it. 0.25 and 0.26 change how the SDK passes identity and credentials to its API client, so read those notes if you set custom headers.

Vercel AI SDK. Only patch releases on 7.0 in October (7.0.127 through 7.0.159). The one I'd note is 7.0.158, which added stat, listDirectory and deleteFile to the experimental sandbox session.

MCP TypeScript SDK 1.32.0 (Oct 2). HTTP client transports now only follow same-origin redirects. If your server endpoint redirects to another host or port, either configure the final URL or set redirectPolicy: 'follow'. On the v2 packages, @modelcontextprotocol/server 2.3.0 adds an expectedResource option to requireBearerAuth so a server only accepts tokens issued for it.

OpenAI Agents JS. 0.19 to 0.21 were mostly fixes. If you used the Runloop sandbox provider, 0.21.0 of agents-extensions removed it and links a migration guide.

What I'd do this week

Make sure you're on Next.js 16.4.1+ (or 15.5.28+) already, then upgrade again after the November 3 release. If you're on Convex and still on Node 20, sort that out before you bump to 1.49. Everything else can wait for a quiet afternoon. For me that's TypeScript 7.1's content mappers and TanStack Start 1.0.

What did I miss from October that you're actually using?

title: Digital sovereignty in professional translation workflows: a case study of migrating from Windows to Linux
description:
arXiv:2610.41561v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: This study examines digital sovereignty in professional translation through a screening of computer-assisted translation tools and translation management systems, and a case study of migrating a translator's workstation from Windows to Linux. The framework combines three principles - Control, Continuity and Exit - with three practical requirements: native Linux operation, independence from mandatory external services, and independent access to essential data and resources. Drawing on documentary evidence and the limited number of responses received from providers, the ecosystem screening distinguishes Linux accessibility from operational independence: browser-based platforms may remain dependent on provider-controlled infrastructure. The migration case demonstrates the feasibility of reconstructing one professional workflow around a locally operable Linux core, using LoopCAT, LibreOffice and locally run TranslateGemma, alongside tools for optical character recognition, communication, credential management and backup. Selected cloud services remained available where needed. The findings suggest that digital sovereignty depends on how workflow dependencies are organized, rather than on individual applications or operating systems. It does not require technological isolation, but meaningful control over essential components, continuity of work and practical exit options. The framework is tailored to the case examined here and may require adaptation to other professional workflows.

title: Gemini API CLI: 코딩 에이전트가 이미지, 동영상, PDF, Deep Research를 위해 Gemini를 호출하도록 하기
description:
Gemini API CLI: 코딩 에이전트가 이미지, 동영상, PDF, Deep Research를 위해 Gemini를 호출하도록 하기

Gemini API CLI(gemini-api)는 Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Antigravity 같은 코딩 에이전트를 위해 만들어진 Google의 오픈소스 Gemini API 명령줄 클라이언트입니다. Go 바이너리 하나를 설치하고 GEMINI_API_KEY를 설정하면, 에이전트가 이미지, 비디오, 음성, 음악을 생성하고, PDF와 녹음을 분석하며, 오디오를 SRT로 전사하고, 백그라운드에서 Deep Research를 실행할 수 있습니다.

지금 Apidog를 사용해 보세요

이 글은 설치, 인증, 에이전트가 실행할 명령, Gemini CLI와의 차이점, 그리고 Apidog CLI와 함께 사용하는 방법을 다룹니다. 모든 플래그는 2026년 10월 30일에 릴리스된 버전 0.4.5의 gemini-api --help에서 그대로 가져왔습니다.

Gemini API CLI란 무엇인가?

Gemini API CLI는 Google의 Interactions API를 위한 상태 비저장(stateless) 단일 바이너리 클라이언트입니다. 각 명령은 하나의 HTTP 호출입니다. 프롬프트가 들어가면 파일 경로, 전사본, 분석 결과 또는 인터랙션 ID가 나옵니다. 작업에 Gemini가 필요할 때 기존 에이전트가 호출하는 도구입니다.

Google의 공식 문서 페이지는 이를 "Interactions API와 함께 발전하는 오픈소스 베타 릴리스"라고 부릅니다. 코드는 Apache 2.0 라이선스로 google-gemini/gemini-api-cli에 있으며, macOS, Linux, Windows에서 실행됩니다.

다음은 0.4.5에서 gemini-api --help가 나열하는 내용과 각 명령의 기본 모델입니다:

그룹 명령 기능 기본 모델
Create generate 텍스트 및 멀티모달 생성 gemini-3.8-flash
Create image 이미지 생성 또는 편집 gemini-nano-banana-2.1
Create video 비디오 생성 및 편집 gemini-omni-1.1-flash
Create tts / music 음성 및 음악 gemini-3.8-flash-tts / lyria-3.5
Understand analyze PDF, 이미지, 오디오, 비디오, YouTube URL에 대한 질문 gemini-3.8-flash
Understand transcribe 오디오 또는 비디오를 md, text, json 또는 srt로 변환 gemini-3.5-transcribe
Manage agent 모델 또는 Deep Research 같은 관리형 에이전트 실행 실행별로 설정
Manage files Files API 업로드, 48시간 보존 해당 없음

Gemini API CLI vs Gemini CLI

이름이 비슷하니 차이를 정리하겠습니다. Gemini CLI(@google/gemini-cli)는 대화형 코딩 에이전트로, 당신이 대화하는 Claude Code 대안입니다. Gemini API CLI(gemini-api)에는 에이전트 루프가 전혀 없습니다. 다른 에이전트가 실행하는 도구입니다.

Gemini API CLI Gemini CLI
바이너리 gemini-api gemini
역할 에이전트가 호출하는 도구 당신이 대화하는 에이전트
미디어 출력 이미지, 비디오, 음성, 음악을 디스크에 저장 주요 초점 아님
최적 용도 Claude Code, Codex, Cursor에 Gemini 모델 제공 Gemini를 코딩 에이전트로 사용

Claude Code나 Codex에서 작업하며 그 워크플로 안에서 Gemini의 미디어 및 리서치 모델을 원한다면 gemini-api를 사용하세요. Google을 향해 있다는 점만 다를 뿐, OpenAI CLI와 동일한 패턴입니다.

Gemini API CLI 설치 방법

README에 있는 네 가지 방법 중 하나를 선택하세요.

macOS 및 Linux:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/google-gemini/gemini-api-cli/main/scripts/install.sh | bash

Windows (PowerShell):

iwr -useb https://raw.githubusercontent.com/google-gemini/gemini-api-cli/main/scripts/install.ps1 | iex

Go:

go install github.com/google-gemini/gemini-api-cli/cmd/gemini-api@latest

사전 빌드된 바이너리: GitHub Releases에서 자신의 플랫폼용 아카이브를 다운로드하고, checksums.txt와 대조한 뒤, gemini-api를 PATH에 넣으세요. 저희는 Darwin_arm64 아카이브를 사용했으며, shasum -a 256 -c checksums.txt --ignore-missing이 OK를 출력했습니다.

Google은 마이너 버전 간에 호환성을 깨는 변경이 발생할 수 있다고 경고하므로, CI에서는 릴리스를 고정(pin)하세요. 문서에서는 설치 스크립트에서 bash 앞에 GEMINI_VERSION=<release-tag>를 두는 방법을 보여줍니다.

설치를 확인하세요:

gemini-api version
# gemini-api 0.4.5

Gemini API CLI 인증

Google AI Studio에서 키를 생성한 다음(무료로 Gemini API 키 받기 가이드에서 자세히 다룹니다), 내보내세요:

export GEMINI_API_KEY="YOUR_API_KEY"

자신의 워크스테이션에서는 대신 저장할 수도 있습니다:

gemini-api configure --api-key "YOUR_API_KEY"
gemini-api whoami

configure는 키를 OS 키체인(macOS Keychain, Linux Secret Service 또는 Windows Credential Manager)에 저장합니다. 대신 ~/.config/gemini-api/config.yaml에 보관하려면 전역 --no-keyring 플래그를 추가하세요. whoami는 어떤 자격 증명이 활성 상태인지, 어디에서 왔는지 보여줍니다.

키가 설정되지 않은 경우, gemini-api --help는 에이전트 자체를 향한 문장을 출력합니다. API 키는 "사용자가 Google AI Studio에서 수동으로 생성해야 합니다. 중단하고 사용자에게 생성을 요청하세요."라고 나옵니다. 에이전트는 스스로 키를 구성하지 않고 당신에게 요청할 것입니다.

--dry-run으로 모든 호출 미리보기

--dry-run은 플래그를 검증하고 자격 증명을 가린 상태로 요청을 출력하며, 네트워크 호출도 키체인 읽기도 하지 않습니다. 키를 설정하기 전에도 작동하므로, 여기 있는 모든 예제를 이 방식으로 확인했습니다.

다음은 백그라운드 Deep Research 작업의 실제 dry run입니다:

모든 명령은 https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta/interactions로 POST합니다. -o json을 추가하면 요청당 하나의 JSON 객체를 stdout으로 받을 수 있어, 에이전트가 토큰을 소비하기 전에 파싱할 수 있습니다.

에이전트가 실행할 Gemini API CLI 명령

이미지 생성 및 편집 

gemini-api image "A friendly robot mascot, soft studio lighting" --out ./assets/mascot.jpg
gemini-api image "Add a winter scarf" -i ./assets/mascot.jpg --out ./assets/mascot-winter.jpg

미디어 명령은 파일을 쓰고 해당 경로만 출력하므로, 에이전트는 $(...)로 이를 캡처하여 계속 작업을 이어갑니다. image는 --aspect-ratio와 --image-size(512, 1K, 2K 또는 4K)도 받습니다. 기본 모델은 Nano Banana 2.1이며, 이 모델이 잘하는 것은 Nano Banana 2.1 API 가이드를 참고하세요.

비디오, 음성, 음악 생성 

gemini-api video "A slow camera move through a sunlit workshop" --resolution 1080p --out ./assets/
gemini-api tts "Welcome. Let's build something together." --out ./assets/welcome.wav
gemini-api music "Warm ambient music for a product walkthrough" --out ./assets/

비디오는 더 오래 걸리므로 video가 대신 폴링합니다. --async를 사용하면 작업 핸들을 즉시 받고, --resume <id>로 나중에 폴링을 다시 시작할 수 있습니다. --resolution의 기본값은 720p입니다.

PDF, 이미지, YouTube URL 분석 

gemini-api analyze -i product-brief.pdf "What should we build first, and why?" > plan.md
gemini-api analyze -i before.png -i after.png "Summarize the visual design changes"

-i/--input은 반복 지정할 수 있으며, 로컬 경로, files/<id> URI, 또는 YouTube URL을 받습니다. 인라인 입력은 원본 기준 약 14MB로 제한됩니다. 더 큰 파일의 경우 한 번 업로드하고 URI를 재사용하세요:

FILE_URI=$(gemini-api files upload interview.mp4 --wait --output-format json --jq '.name')
gemini-api analyze -i "$FILE_URI" "List the key action items with timestamps"

업로드된 파일은 48시간 후에 삭제됩니다.

오디오 및 비디오 전사 

gemini-api transcribe -i interview.mp4 --format srt --out interview.srt

--format은 md(기본값), text, json 또는 srt를 받습니다. --no-speakers 또는 --no-timestamps를 추가하면 출력에서 화자나 타임스탬프를 제거할 수 있습니다.

백그라운드에서 Deep Research 실행 

ID=$(gemini-api agent run "Research battery recycling approaches and cite sources" \
  --agent deep-research-preview-04-2026 --background --jq '.id')
gemini-api agent status "$ID" --stream=false --output-format json

--background는 스트림을 열어둔 채 유지하는 대신 인터랙션 ID를 즉시 반환합니다. 에이전트는 ID를 저장하고 다른 작업을 하다가 agent status로 다시 확인합니다. agent cancel은 실행을 중지합니다. 0.4.5 도움말에는 deep-research-max-preview-04-2026과 antigravity-preview-05-2026도 관리형 에이전트로 나열되어 있습니다.

gemini-api를 에이전트에 안전하게 만드는 플래그

다음은 에이전트 지침에 넣을 만한 전역 플래그로, 모두 gemini-api --help-global에서 가져온 것입니다:

  • --agent-mode(또는 GEMINI_CLI_AGENT_MODE=1): stderr에 구조화된 JSON 오류, stdout에 간결한 TOON 출력.
  • -o, --output-format: pretty, json, yaml, table 또는 toon.
  • -q, --jq: 출력을 인라인으로 필터링합니다. 예를 들어 --jq '.id'.
  • --no-interactive: 프롬프트나 TUI 양식이 없으며, 헤드리스 에이전트에 필요합니다.
  • --usage: 전체 명령 트리를 기계 판독 가능한 KDL로 출력.
  • --schema(명령별): --body 페이로드에 대한 JSON 스키마.

종료 코드는 텍스트를 파싱하지 않고도 에이전트에게 무엇이 잘못되었는지 알려줍니다. 0은 정상, 1은 런타임 또는 API 실패, 2는 사용법 또는 검증 오류, 3은 인증입니다. 한 가지 주의점이 있습니다. 스트리밍 명령(generate, agent run)은 -o json이나 --jq가 단일 파싱 가능한 결과를 주려면 --stream=false가 필요합니다.

코딩 에이전트에 Gemini API CLI 제공하기

Google의 README에는 AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md 또는 .cursorrules에 붙여 넣을 블록이 있습니다. 발췌하면 다음과 같습니다:

You have access to gemini-api through the shell.
1. Inspect --help or --usage to choose a command, and --schema when building a --body JSON payload.
2. Preview API calls with --dry-run.
3. For JSON output or --jq on streaming commands, pass --stream=false --output-format json.
4. Capture returned file paths and interaction IDs to continue multi-step tasks.

GEMINI_API_KEY가 에이전트의 서브프로세스 환경에 전달되는지 확인하세요. 그런 다음 평소처럼 프롬프트를 입력하세요: "랜딩 페이지를 만들고, 마스코트 이미지와 20초 보이스오버에는 Gemini를 사용하고, 경쟁 제품에 대한 Deep Research 실행을 시작해 줘." 그러면 에이전트가 명령을 선택합니다.

하지 않는 것도 있습니다. 실시간 음성이나 비디오입니다. WebSocket 지원이 없으므로 Live API는 여전히 GenAI SDK가 필요합니다.

Apidog CLI로 직접 만든 API 테스트하기

gemini-api는 에이전트에게 Gemini의 모델을 제공합니다. 하지만 당신의 자체 API — 앱이 Gemini를 감싸는 /summarize나 /thumbnail 엔드포인트, 그 환경, 또는 릴리스가 깨지지 않았음을 입증하는 검증 — 에 대해서는 아무것도 모릅니다. 그것이 Apidog CLI의 일이며, 같은 에이전트가 둘 다 실행할 수 있습니다.

한 번 설정하세요:

npm install -g apidog-cli@latest
apidog login --with-token <YOUR_TOKEN>
npx -y skills add https://apidog.com   # pick your agent when prompted

그런 다음 에이전트에게 하나의 프롬프트를 주세요:

Use gemini-api to dry-run an analyze call on ./docs/sample-invoice.pdf, then run it for real.
Import ./openapi.yaml into Apidog project <id>, create a test case for POST /v1/invoices/extract
that uploads the same PDF and asserts a 200 and a non-empty "total" field, run it against the
staging environment, and summarize any failures.

에이전트는 gemini-api로 Gemini의 답변을 확인한 다음, Apidog 스키마를 읽고 페이로드를 작성하며, 이를 검증하고 케이스를 생성하고 실행합니다:

apidog import --project <id> --format openapi --file ./openapi.yaml
apidog cli-schema get test-case-create
apidog cli-schema validate test-case-create --file case.json
apidog test-case create --project <id> --file case.json
apidog run --test-case <caseId> --project <id> -e <envId> -r cli,json

apidog test-case create --help는 한 가지 함정을 알려줍니다. 케이스에는 유효한 categoryId가 필요하므로, 먼저 apidog test-case category --project <id>로 목록을 확인하세요. -r cli,json을 -r junit으로 바꾸면 같은 줄이 CI에서 실행됩니다. Claude Code를 에이전트로 사용한다면 Claude Code에서 Apidog CLI 사용하기부터 시작하세요. Apidog의 무료 플랜은 최대 4명의 사용자까지 지원합니다.

FAQ

Gemini API CLI는 무료인가요? CLI 자체는 Apache 2.0에 따라 무료이자 오픈소스입니다. 모든 호출은 일반적인 Gemini API 가격에 따라 당신의 API 키로 청구됩니다. 무료 티어가 무엇을 포함하는지는 Gemini API 무료 티어 가이드를 참고하세요.

gemini-api는 Gemini CLI와 같은 건가요? 아닙니다. Gemini CLI는 대화형 코딩 에이전트입니다. gemini-api는 다른 에이전트, 스크립트, CI 작업이 Gemini 모델과 관리형 에이전트에 접근하기 위해 호출하는 상태 비저장 도구입니다.

API 키 없이 명령을 테스트할 수 있나요? 예. --dry-run은 명령을 검증하고 네트워크 호출이나 키체인 읽기 없이 정확한 요청을 출력합니다. 이 글의 모든 예제는 0.4.5에서 이 방식으로 확인했습니다.

14MB보다 큰 파일은 어떻게 처리하나요? gemini-api files upload <file> --wait를 실행하고, 반환된 files/<id>를 보관한 뒤, analyze, transcribe, generate, image, video 또는 agent run의 -i에 전달하세요. 업로드는 48시간 후에 만료됩니다.

버전을 고정해야 하나요? 예, CI에서는 고정하세요. Google은 CLI가 베타인 동안 마이너 버전 간에 호환성을 깨는 변경이 발생할 수 있다고 밝혔습니다.

title: Language Models Show Conformity Bias in RAG: When the Majority Endorses a Poisoned Claim
description:
arXiv:2610.41012v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can expose language models to misleading evidence in retrieved documents. We investigate whether increasing the number of mutually agreeing poisoned documents affects a model's ability to detect misinformation. We evaluate 200 randomly selected questions from SciFact (random seed 38), comparing contexts with one poisoned and six healthy documents against contexts with six mutually agreeing poisoned documents and one healthy document. For Gemma-3-12b, poison-detection rates decrease from 25% (50/200) in the minority condition to 10% (20/200) in the majority condition. Among the 38 questions with different outcomes across conditions, 34 change from detected to undetected, while only four change in the opposite direction (exact McNemar test, p = 6.04e-7). This pattern is consistent with a conformity-like response to a majority of mutually agreeing poisoned documents. Our results provide initial evidence of conformity bias in RAG-based misinformation detection: Gemma-3-12b is substantially less likely to detect poisoned claims when they dominate the retrieved evidence.
