title: Cypress Email Tests Need a Freshness Gate
description:
An email test can find a message and still be wrong. This happens when a shared inbox contains an older verification email, the test selects the newest result without checking its age, and the browser follows a link that belongs to another run.

The result is especially confusing in Cypress. The command log shows that an email was found, the link was clicked, and the test failed later on a page that looks unrelated. A freshness gate makes the ownership question explicit: did this message arrive after this test triggered the email?

I use a temp mail so inbox for experiments when a real mailbox is not appropriate, but the provider is not the reliability strategy. The strategy is to record a boundary, reject stale messages, and preserve enough evidence to explain the next check.

Why the newest email can still be the wrong email

Suppose a password-reset test does this:

cy.request("POST", "/api/password-reset", { email });
cy.get("[data-testid=inbox-message]")
  .first()
  .click();

This looks reasonable until a retry, a local manual run, or another parallel worker leaves messages in the inbox. “First” is a sorting decision, not proof that the message belongs to this test.

A stale message may contain a valid link, so the failure is not always immediate. The link can open a reset page with an expired token, a session mismatch, or a state created by another test. Increasing Cypress retries can hide the collision for a while, but it does not fix the evidence boundary. The setup is a little more work, yet the diagnosis becomes much clearer.

Define freshness as a test contract

Capture the time immediately before the action that should cause delivery. Then make freshness one of the acceptance rules, along with recipient, subject, and a unique test marker when the application supports one.

const triggeredAt = new Date();

cy.request("POST", "/api/password-reset", { email }).then(() => {
  cy.pollInbox({ email, since: triggeredAt.toISOString() }).then((message) => {
    expect(message.receivedAt, "message freshness").to.be.greaterThan(
      triggeredAt.toISOString(),
    );
    expect(message.to).to.equal(email);
    expect(message.subject).to.contain("Reset your password");
  });
});

The exact mailbox API will vary. The useful part is the contract. since should be enforced by the query when possible, and checked again after parsing. Clocks can differ between services, so allow a small documented skew rather than pretending timestamps are perfect. If that detail is ignored, failures becomes hard to reproduce.

For teams that separate test signals from application behavior, using topic scores to keep automation work focused is a useful reminder: give each signal one clear job. Freshness proves timing and ownership; the UI assertion proves the browser flow.

A Cypress helper with an evidence trail

Keep polling, filtering, and diagnostics in a custom command or helper. The spec should say what the user is doing, while the helper explains why a candidate was accepted or rejected.

Cypress.Commands.add("waitForFreshMessage", (options) => {
  const evidence = [];
  const deadline = Date.now() + 45_000;

  function check() {
    return cy.mailbox(options.inbox).then((messages) => {
      const fresh = messages.filter((message) => {
        const isFresh = new Date(message.receivedAt) >= new Date(options.since);
        const isOwned = message.to === options.email;
        const hasSubject = message.subject.includes(options.subject);

        evidence.push({
          id: message.id,
          receivedAt: message.receivedAt,
          isFresh,
          isOwned,
          hasSubject,
        });

        return isFresh && isOwned && hasSubject ? message : null;
      }).find(Boolean);

      if (fresh) return cy.wrap({ message: fresh, evidence });
      if (Date.now() >= deadline) {
        throw new Error(`No fresh message found: ${JSON.stringify(evidence)}`);
      }
      return cy.wait(1_000).then(check);
    });
  }

  return check();
});

In production code I would also validate the timestamp format and cap the evidence size. The important behavior is that an old message is visible in the failure output instead of silently discarded. A burner email address can keep test data isolated, but isolation still needs a freshness check.

If CI stores the message body or headers, keep that artifact tied to the run id. Versioning email evidence by digest gives a practical way to compare what changed between retries without copying a whole mailbox into every log.

Triage stale-message failures

When the helper fails, I inspect the evidence in this order:

  1. Only old messages appear: check inbox reuse, worker cleanup, and the since timestamp.
  2. Fresh messages have the wrong recipient: check address allocation and application routing.
  3. Fresh messages have the wrong subject: check localization, template changes, or a different notification being selected.
  4. A message passes but the link fails: inspect token lifetime, session binding, and the browser state.

This order avoids changing the polling timeout before checking whether the test is reading the correct mailbox. A phrase like tempail may appear in search notes or a manual run, but it should never become evidence that a message is owned by the current test.

A repeatable checklist

Before merging a Cypress email test, verify:

  • the trigger boundary is captured immediately before the delivery action
  • each worker has an isolated inbox or a unique test marker
  • freshness, recipient, and subject are separate acceptance checks
  • rejected messages record ids and reasons
  • the deadline and clock-skew allowance are documented
  • CI saves the evidence when polling fails
  • the browser assertion runs only after the message passes the gate

If a team needs an external disposable email address generator for short-lived test data, keep its use inside non-production environments and document the data-retention assumption. The test should still be useful if the provider changes its inbox sorting.

Q&A

Is checking the newest message enough?

No. Newest is a relative ordering, not a relationship to the current test. Compare against the trigger boundary and verify ownership.

Should Cypress retry the whole test?

Usually not as the first response. Retry the bounded inbox observation while retaining the evidence from each attempt. A whole-test retry can make a stale-message problem look intermittent.

What if the provider has coarse timestamps?

Use a small, explicit clock-skew window and add a unique marker to the address or subject when possible. If neither is available, label the weaker guarantee in the test output.

A fresh-message gate does not make delivery instant. It makes the test honest about what it observed, which is a much better starting point when QA has to repair a red run.

title: Your bank's CSV export is the messiest API you will ever consume
description:
I spent two weeks writing a bank-statement parser that runs inside the browser tab. No upload, no server, no account. Paste a CSV export from your card provider, get back the recurring charges hiding in it.

The part I underestimated was not the recurring-charge logic. It was the file format. Every bank invents its own dialect of CSV, and each dialect exists because someone in 2009 thought it was obvious. Here are the traps that broke my first parser, in the order they broke it, with the rule I ended up shipping.

1. The header is not on line one

Almost every export opens with a preamble: account holder, masked card number, statement period, a blank line, sometimes a marketing sentence. My first version assumed lines[0] was the header and produced zero rows on half of the samples.

The fix is to stop assuming and start searching. I scan the first ten lines, split each one, and ask whether it looks like a header: it needs a date-ish column, a description-ish column, and either an amount column or a debit/credit pair.

const DATE_ALIASES = ['date', 'transaction date', 'posted date', 'post date', 'trans date'];
const DESC_ALIASES = ['description', 'merchant', 'payee', 'name', 'memo', 'details'];
const AMOUNT_ALIASES = ['amount', 'transaction amount'];
const DEBIT_ALIASES = ['debit', 'withdrawal', 'withdrawals', 'charges'];
const CREDIT_ALIASES = ['credit', 'deposit', 'deposits', 'payments'];

One subtlety matters more than the aliases: a transaction line that appears above the header must be reported instead of being silently skipped with the preamble. If a row above the header parses as a date, I emit an issue pointing at that line. Quietly ignoring money is the worst possible parser behaviour.

2. The delimiter is not always a comma

European exports use semicolons. Some accounting tools use tabs. And the sample rule I first wrote, "look at the first line and count separators", fails for exactly the files that need it, because the first line is usually the preamble sentence and it contains no delimiters at all.

So the sniffing window is the first twenty lines instead of just the first one:

const sample = lines.slice(0, 20).join('\n');
for (const candidate of ['\t', ';', ',']) {
  const count = sample.split(candidate).length - 1;
  if (count > bestCount) { best = candidate; bestCount = count; }
}

Tab wins ties by virtue of being tested first. That is a deliberate choice: a tab-delimited file usually has no commas inside fields, while a comma file with a semicolon in a merchant name is common.

The splitter itself has to respect quoting, including the doubled-quote escape, or a merchant called "SMITH, J LLC" becomes two columns and the amount lands in the wrong place.

3. Negative money has at least four spellings

A charge is positive money leaving the account. Depending on the bank, the same refund looks like any of these:

  • -12.99
  • 12.99- (trailing minus, common in mainframe-era exports)
  • (12.99) (accounting parentheses)
  • a debit column and a credit column, where the sign lives in the column header

My parser normalises all four into integer cents before anything else touches the value. Integers instead of floats: 0.1 + 0.2 is a well-known way to make a totals column disagree with itself by a cent, and a subscription audit that is one cent off still fails the only test a user runs, which is whether the number matches their statement.

4. The same character means two different things

1,234.56 and 1.234,56 are the same amount. 12,50 and 1,250 are not, and they are both plausible inputs. The rule I ended up with:

  • if the string contains a comma and no dot, and exactly two digits follow the last comma, treat the comma as a decimal separator
  • otherwise strip every comma 
if (value.includes(',') && !value.includes('.')) {
  const parts = value.split(',');
  value = (parts.length === 2 && parts[1].length === 2)
    ? `${parts[0]}.${parts[1]}`
    : value.replace(/,/g, '');
} else {
  value = value.replace(/,/g, '');
}

Currency symbols, non-breaking spaces and stray letters get stripped before that check. If what remains does not match ^\d+(\.\d{1,2})?$, the amount is rejected and the line is reported as an issue. Rejecting is cheap; guessing is not, because a misread amount corrupts every downstream total silently.

5. Dates are ambiguous, and guessing is worse than refusing

03/04/2026 is March 4th or April 3rd depending on where the file was produced. Six months of a subscription billed on the 4th can look like a monthly cadence or like two weeks of chaos.

The parser accepts ISO dates and short numeric dates, and exposes a single dayFirst flag. There is no automatic detection, because automatic detection here means inferring a locale from a file that does not declare one. A user who sees garbled dates can flip one switch; a user who does not notice they are garbled now has a wrong answer they trust.

6. Merchant descriptors are a compressed format

Raw descriptors look like this:

SP *SPOTIFY USA
PAYPAL *STEAM
SQ *BLUE BOTTLE
POS DEBIT 4821 WHOLEFDS MKT

They are written for a 22-character field, so payment processors prepend their own prefixes and banks append store numbers. Grouping by the raw string produces one subscription per location.

Normalisation does three things: strip known prefixes, unify punctuation, then drop trailing pure-digit tokens (store numbers) and truncate.

The prefix list has one hard constraint that cost me an afternoon:

// the separator is required, otherwise "SP\s*" eats the first two letters of SPOTIFY
/^SP[\s*]+/i

A permissive ^SP turns every Spotify charge into OTIFY USA, and it groups correctly by accident while being wrong about the merchant name. Requiring at least one separator after the prefix fixes it, and the same pattern applies to SQ, TST and PAYPAL.

7. Turning rows into cadence: why the median wins

Once every row belongs to a normalised merchant, recurrence is a question about intervals. I collect the positive charges, compute the day gaps between consecutive ones, and take the median.

Median because a single missed month should not move the answer. If a charge lands on the 3rd, the 5th, and then the 2nd of the month after a skipped cycle, the mean interval is inflated and a monthly subscription scores as irregular; the median still says thirty.

The classification is deliberately narrow:

  • monthly: median gap 25–35 days, at least 3 charges
  • annual: median gap 350–380 days, at least 2 charges
  • weekly: median gap 6–8 days, at least 4 charges
  • anything else: one-off

The counts are not decorative. Two charges 30 days apart are as likely to be a coincidence as a subscription, so monthly needs a third observation before it earns a row.

Confidence is a separate field, and it is where the honesty lives. Monthly is high confidence at four or more charges with every interval within five days of the median; annual needs three charges within ten days; weekly needs six within two. Everything else is medium. A high-confidence row is a claim the tool is willing to defend; a medium row is a hint.

The monthly equivalent is what makes an annual bill comparable to a monthly one: annual divided by twelve, weekly multiplied by 52 and divided by 12. Sorting by that number is the whole point of the audit, because it answers one question in a fixed order: which line costs the most per month.

8. What the audit refuses to claim

Two limits are worth stating, because users find them before you document them.

The first is aggregated billers. APPLE.COM/BILL and GOOGLE *... collapse an entire ecosystem into a single descriptor. The parser flags those rows, and the audit shows them as one line, because the statement does not contain the information needed to split them. Pretending otherwise would produce a confident, wrong breakdown.

The second is the trial that converts. A subscription billed once has one observation. Until the second charge arrives, it is a one-off, and the tool says so. There is no setting that makes it guess.

What comes out

The output is a priority list sorted by monthly equivalent, each row carrying the cadence, the last charge date, the next expected date (last charge plus the median interval), the annual equivalent, and the charge count. Two exports come with it: a CSV and a Markdown table of the same list, so the audit can be pasted into whatever the user actually uses to cancel things.

And a print stylesheet, because the moment this becomes real is the moment someone holds it next to a phone call.

The parser is about 500 lines and does not need a backend. If you want to try it on your own export, it runs on the statement audit page. Paste a redacted export; nothing leaves the tab.

If you have a bank export that this parser mangles, send me the header line and one broken row (with the amounts changed). Format bugs are the ones I can actually fix.

title: Transparent Image Fallback System with Canvas API
description:
Transparent Image Fallback System with Canvas API

Understanding the Need for a Fallback System

Transparent images are essential for creating layered designs on the web. However, not all browsers or environments support full transparency, which can lead to unexpected rendering issues. A fallback system ensures that even when transparency is not supported, the image still displays correctly with a default background. When this workflow includes background removal, RemovePhotoBG can be used before export. Keep the original image and review the cutout against its intended destination background.

Building a Fallback System with Canvas API

The Canvas API allows developers to draw images and handle transparency programmatically. By using the Canvas API, we can create a fallback system that handles transparent images and provides a default background when necessary.

  1. Check Image Support: Before rendering an image, check if the browser supports transparent images. This can be done by examining the image's format and the browser's capabilities.

  2. Create a Canvas Element: Use the Canvas API to create a drawing surface where the image will be rendered. This allows for greater control over the image's display and fallback behavior.

  3. Draw the Image: Draw the image onto the canvas. If the image has transparency, it will be displayed correctly. If not, the canvas will default to a solid background.

  4. Handle Fallback: If the browser does not support transparency, the canvas will automatically fall back to a solid background. This ensures that the image is still visible and maintains the intended design.

TypeScript Example with Failure-Case Tests

Here is a TypeScript example that demonstrates how to implement a transparent image fallback system using the Canvas API:

const canvas = document.createElement('canvas');
const ctx = canvas.getContext('2d');
const img = new Image();

img.src = 'transparent-image.png';

img.onload = () => {
  if (ctx && img.complete) {
    canvas.width = img.width;
    canvas.height = img.height;
    ctx.drawImage(img, 0, 0);
    document.body.appendChild(canvas);
  }
};

img.onerror = () => {
  console.error('Failed to load image');
};

To test this system, you can simulate different browser environments and check if the fallback behavior is triggered correctly. This ensures that the system is robust and handles all edge cases.

Ensuring Robust Image Display

By implementing a fallback system with the Canvas API, developers can ensure that transparent images are displayed correctly across all browsers. This approach provides a reliable solution for handling image transparency and maintaining the intended design.

Conclusion

A transparent image fallback system with the Canvas API is an essential tool for web developers. By understanding the need for a fallback system and implementing it correctly, developers can ensure that images are displayed correctly and maintain the intended design across all browsers.

title: Let Claude Code read your production database — even a write disguised as SELECT gets refused
description:
Pointing an AI agent at a database is easy. Pointing it at production is where people stop.

dbboard is an open-source desktop database client with an MCP server that gives Claude Code read-only access to Postgres, MySQL, Turso / libSQL, Cloudflare D1, MongoDB and Firestore — enforced by the database, not by a keyword filter.

The usual guard is a keyword filter: reject anything that starts with UPDATE or DROP. It holds until the agent writes a CTE that deletes, a SELECT … FOR UPDATE, or two statements in one string. And the agent still needs the password, which now sits in its config and its transcript.

dbboard is built so that this question has a boring answer.

The one idea: the database says no, not only a filter

dbboard ships a separate MCP server, dbboard-mcp, that hands the connections you already have to Claude Code or Claude Desktop. Every read passes two checks.

First, the statement is parsed — a real SQL parser, not string matching — and anything that is not a single read-only statement is refused. Then it runs inside the database's own read-only mode, or through an adapter that cannot write at all:

Engine How a read is run
Postgres, Neon, Supabase, CockroachDB, Aurora DSQL BEGIN TRANSACTION READ ONLY
MySQL / MariaDB SET TRANSACTION READ ONLY
Turso / libSQL PRAGMA query_only
Cloudflare D1 no read-only mode exists, so the parser is the enforcement and fails closed
Cloud Firestore the adapter has no write path to reach: it implements the read endpoints and nothing else
MongoDB only six commands (find, aggregate, count, distinct, listCollections, listIndexes) and only their known options; the pipeline is walked for a $out or $merge hidden inside a $facet, $lookup or $unionWith

The second check is the one that matters. Here is dbboard-mcp against a local Postgres with fictional data, called exactly as an agent calls it:

run_read_query  DELETE FROM orders WHERE quantity = 1
→ query failed: not a single read-only statement: only read-only SELECT / WITH / EXPLAIN statements are allowed

run_read_query  WITH gone AS (DELETE FROM orders RETURNING id) SELECT count(*) FROM gone
→ query failed: not a single read-only statement: a data-modifying statement (in a CTE or set expression) is not read-only

run_read_query  SELECT nextval('orders_id_seq')
→ query failed: cannot execute nextval() in a read-only transaction

run_read_query  SELECT count(*) FROM orders
→ 180

The first two are caught by the parser. The third is a plain SELECT that still writes — it advances a sequence — so no parser flags it. Postgres refuses it, because the transaction itself is read-only. The table still has all 180 rows, and the sequence did not move.

Three more rules sit around that:

  • Passwords never reach the agent. They stay in the OS keychain. The agent sees { id, name, kind } for each connection, and no error message embeds a URL.
  • Writing is off until a person turns it on, per connection. Even then only an allowlist runs (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, CREATE TABLE, …). DROP of anything, TRUNCATE, GRANT / REVOKE and user or role changes are refused whatever the setting says.
  • Results are bounded, so one careless query cannot pour a whole table into the agent's context.

How to give Claude Code read-only access to your database

Download dbboard-mcp for your platform from the latest release (one self-contained executable), then:

# macOS
claude mcp add dbboard --scope user -- "$HOME/.local/bin/dbboard-mcp"

# Windows (PowerShell)
claude mcp add dbboard --scope user -- "$env:LOCALAPPDATA/dbboard/dbboard-mcp.exe"

The agent can then list connections and tables, describe a table, search a connection's schema by column name, follow foreign keys, and run read queries. Ask it "which orders in the last week have no shipment row?" and it finds the tables itself.

And for the person: one window

The desktop app is the same connections, for you:

  • Every database you look after in one sidebar — Postgres (Neon, Supabase, CockroachDB, Aurora DSQL), MySQL / MariaDB, Turso / libSQL, Cloudflare D1, Firestore and MongoDB. An SSH tunnel reaches the one behind a bastion; a colour and a tag on each connection show which one you are about to run against.
  • Leave the database name blank and one login lists every database it can open, with schemas and tables beneath.
  • Fix one value without writing an UPDATE: double-click the cell, type, save. Edits are keyed on the primary key, so a table without one stays read-only instead of guessing.

What it is not

Not a hosted service: nothing leaves your machine except your own queries to your own databases. Not code-signed either — a certificate is a recurring purchase this project does not make, so every release ships SHA256SUMS.txt to check instead.

Try it

  1. Download from the download page (Windows x64 / ARM64 .exe, macOS .dmg)
  2. Manage → Add connection, pick the database type, fill in the server
  3. Add dbboard-mcp to your agent as above

MIT-licensed. Bug reports and requests: Issues.

title: Why SQLite WAL Still Raises "database is locked" in Python
description:
You switch a small Python service to SQLite write-ahead logging, start two workers, and still see "database is locked." The obvious question is whether WAL is broken. Usually it is not. The mistaken assumption is that allowing readers and writers to overlap is the same as allowing multiple writers to commit simultaneously.

SQLite's WAL documentation makes the distinction explicit: readers can continue while a writer appends, but there is still only one active writer. That matters for webhook handlers, queue consumers, background jobs, and small web applications that share a single database file. A slow transaction can block a perfectly ordinary insert in another process.

This tutorial starts with a reproducible lock, then changes only the parts that actually control write contention. The examples use Python's built-in sqlite3 module, a local temporary database, and ordinary SQL. You do not need an ORM or a server installation.

WAL changes reader/writer overlap, not the single-writer rule

In the default rollback-journal mode, a reader can interfere with a writer's ability to complete a transaction. WAL stores new pages in a separate log first. A reader keeps using a consistent view of the database while the writer appends changes. That is a useful improvement for workloads that mix frequent reads with short writes.

However, the WAL still has one write stream. Two connections cannot both own the writer lock. The second writer must wait until the first transaction ends, or fail when its busy timeout expires. WAL is not a substitute for keeping transactions short.

A practical model is to separate three operations:

  • Reading a stable snapshot.
  • Owning the writer lock and committing a change.
  • Copying committed WAL content back into the main database during a checkpoint.

They have different concurrency behavior. Treating them as a single "SQLite is concurrent" setting hides the cause of most locking complaints.

Reproduce a blocked writer with two connections

Save the following as a standalone Python file and run it. It creates a temporary database, enables WAL, and opens two independent connections. Connection A deliberately keeps a write transaction open while connection B attempts another write.

from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory
import sqlite3

with TemporaryDirectory() as folder:
    db = Path(folder) / "events.db"

    setup = sqlite3.connect(db, isolation_level=None)
    mode = setup.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL").fetchone()[0]
    setup.execute(
        "CREATE TABLE events (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, message TEXT)"
    )
    setup.close()
    assert mode == "wal"

    writer_a = sqlite3.connect(db, timeout=0.2, isolation_level=None)
    writer_b = sqlite3.connect(db, timeout=0.2, isolation_level=None)

    writer_a.execute("BEGIN IMMEDIATE")
    writer_a.execute(
        "INSERT INTO events(message) VALUES (?)", ("first",)
    )
    try:
        writer_b.execute(
            "INSERT INTO events(message) VALUES (?)", ("second",)
        )
    except sqlite3.OperationalError as error:
        print(type(error).__name__, str(error))
    else:
        raise AssertionError("Second writer unexpectedly succeeded")

    writer_a.execute("COMMIT")
    writer_b.execute(
        "INSERT INTO events(message) VALUES (?)", ("second",)
    )

    print(writer_b.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM events").fetchone()[0])
    writer_a.close()
    writer_b.close()
~~~{% endraw %}

The expected observation is an OperationalError mentioning that the database is locked, followed by a row count of two. Connection B did not have corrupt data or a broken journal. It tried to write while connection A owned the writer lock. After A committed, B could proceed.

The small timeout is intentional. It makes the demonstration fast instead of leaving the program waiting. In a real service, choose a timeout from the request latency budget rather than copying this demonstration value blindly.

Notice the explicit BEGIN IMMEDIATE. It requests the write transaction at the start instead of letting the first write statement discover the contention later. That makes the critical section visible to the reader and to anyone inspecting logs.

## Set a bounded busy timeout, then measure it

Python's sqlite3.connect accepts a timeout parameter. Its documented default is five seconds. This controls how long a connection waits on a lock before raising an OperationalError; it does not promise that a lock will clear during that window.

SQLite also exposes PRAGMA busy_timeout, measured in milliseconds. You can inspect the configured value directly rather than guessing which connection settings are in effect.{% raw %}

~~~python
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect("app.db", timeout=2.0, isolation_level=None)
value = db.execute("PRAGMA busy_timeout").fetchone()[0]
print("Busy timeout in milliseconds:", value)

db.execute("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS jobs (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY)")
db.close()
~~~

The path here is illustrative; use a file inside your application's designated data directory. For tests, prefer a temporary directory. Keep a timeout small enough that one stuck worker cannot absorb an entire fleet of incoming requests. A longer timeout can smooth brief bursts, but it does not fix a writer that holds a transaction while waiting for network I/O.

A useful diagnostic log records transaction start time, time spent waiting to begin a write, commit time, and which operation ran inside the transaction. A simple error count without timing data will not tell you whether the cause is lock acquisition, a slow transaction, or a checkpoint interaction.

## Move network calls out of write transactions

This pattern causes unnecessary contention: begin a transaction, read a job, call a remote API, wait for a response, then update the row and commit. The database writer lock is now tied to unpredictable network latency.

The better boundary is usually a short claim transaction followed by the slow work outside it. A final short transaction records the result. If multiple workers may claim the same job, enforce the claim atomically with a conditional update, not a separate SELECT followed by an unconditional UPDATE.

The next example shows a claim that can be attempted by multiple connections. Each connection uses its own handle to the same local database.{% raw %}

~~~python
import sqlite3

def claim_job(db_path: str, job_id: int, worker: str) -> bool:
    conn = sqlite3.connect(
        db_path, timeout=2.0, isolation_level=None
    )
    try:
        conn.execute("BEGIN IMMEDIATE")
        changed = conn.execute(
            """
            UPDATE jobs
               SET status = 'claimed', worker = ?
             WHERE id = ? AND status = 'pending'
            """,
            (worker, job_id),
        ).rowcount
        conn.execute("COMMIT")
        return changed == 1
    except Exception:
        if conn.in_transaction:
            conn.execute("ROLLBACK")
        raise
    finally:
        conn.close()
~~~{% endraw %}

This function intentionally does not perform the job itself. Its only responsibility is to claim it. The worker can then release the connection, execute the slow external task, and store completion in another short transaction.

A conditional claim is not a complete job queue. You still need an explicit policy for abandoned claims, visibility timeouts, retryability, and side effects. In particular, a failed network response must not automatically be interpreted as a failed remote operation. The database can prevent duplicate local claims without proving whether an external action happened.

## Make transaction ownership explicit

Connection behavior changed in modern Python: the sqlite3 module has an autocommit interface, while isolation_level controls the older implicit transaction behavior. Code copied from older tutorials may therefore use different transaction assumptions than your service.

The examples here deliberately set isolation_level=None and issue SQL BEGIN, COMMIT, and ROLLBACK statements themselves. This is a simple way to make each critical section visible for teaching and testing. It is not a recommendation to mix implicit and explicit transaction models in an existing application.

If you use Python's newer autocommit parameter instead, choose a model once and test it against the exact Python version deployed. Do not assume that wrapping every operation in a with block fixes a transaction that begins too early. Confirm when the lock is actually acquired and when the database is free to accept the next writer.

A review of transaction boundaries should answer four concrete questions. Where does the transaction start? Which statement first needs the writer lock? Does any file, HTTP, model, or queue operation happen before commit? Does every exception path roll back or otherwise release the connection? If the answers are unclear, adding a timeout is only masking uncertainty.

## See what a long-lived reader does to checkpoints

A checkpoint copies content from the WAL back into the main database file. SQLite normally handles checkpointing automatically, so most small applications can begin with its defaults. That does not mean checkpoint progress is guaranteed under an endless stream of overlapping readers.

A reader holds a snapshot end mark. A checkpoint cannot advance past pages needed by that reader. If readers never finish, the WAL can grow even while new writes continue to succeed. This often appears as a growing database-wal file rather than as an immediate write failure.

You can inspect checkpoint status through PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(PASSIVE). It reports three values: whether the operation encountered a busy condition, the number of pages in the WAL, and the number of pages checkpointed.

~~~python
import sqlite3

conn = sqlite3.connect("app.db", timeout=2.0)
mode = conn.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode").fetchone()[0]
if mode != "wal":
    raise RuntimeError("Expected WAL mode")

busy, log_pages, checkpointed = conn.execute(
    "PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(PASSIVE)"
).fetchone()

print({
    "busy": busy,
    "wal_pages": log_pages,
    "checkpointed_pages": checkpointed,
})
conn.close()
~~~

This is a diagnostic probe, not an instruction to force TRUNCATE after every request. A passive checkpoint may stop before completing without disrupting active readers. More aggressive checkpoint modes have different blocking behavior, so schedule them with knowledge of your workload rather than using them as a reflexive lock repair.

Also keep the database on a local filesystem suitable for SQLite WAL. Its shared-memory design does not support the ordinary cross-machine network-filesystem scenario described in SQLite's official documentation.

## Use a small contention test before tuning production

A reliable test needs at least two independent connections to the same file. A single connection running a loop cannot reproduce writer competition by itself. The most revealing test holds a transaction open on one connection, then measures how the other behaves with a known timeout.

Run the test in both directions: first with a deliberate hold that exceeds the timeout, then with a short hold that ends before the timeout. Confirm the expected failure and expected successful wait. Log elapsed time, not just the exception text.

After that, verify the application's own transaction length. A write query may take milliseconds while the surrounding transaction stays open for seconds. Look for synchronous HTTP calls, expensive serialization, long loops, or human input inside write transactions. Those are better targets for improvement than arbitrary PRAGMA values.

Keep the test separate from production records. A temporary directory and deterministic fixtures make the result repeatable and prevent a performance experiment from altering real work.

## A practical decision rule for small Python services

Start with WAL when the application has mixed reads and writes on one local machine and the mode is appropriate for its storage. Use a finite lock timeout and short write transactions. Have each process or worker create and manage its own connection according to the application's threading model. Avoid passing one Python connection around unrelated threads.

If a lock persists, measure the actual transaction boundary and write occupancy before increasing the timeout. If the database-wal file grows, inspect long-lived readers and checkpoint progress separately. These are two different symptoms with different interventions.

If the required write throughput depends on many simultaneous long write transactions, SQLite's single-writer design may be the wrong fit. That is an architectural decision, not evidence that WAL is malfunctioning.

The key result is reproducible: WAL lets readers overlap a writer; it does not let two writers own the write lock. Fix the time spent holding that lock, and the "database is locked" exception becomes a measurable contention signal rather than a mysterious configuration failure.

## Primary references

- [SQLite: Write-Ahead Logging](https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html) — writer concurrency, checkpoints, and filesystem constraints.
- [Python: sqlite3 module](https://docs.python.org/3/library/sqlite3.html) — connection timeout and transaction-control behavior.
- [SQLite: PRAGMA statements](https://www.sqlite.org/pragma.html) — busy_timeout and wal_checkpoint semantics.

The reproducer and claim function intentionally use built-in Python and SQLite features only; adapt transaction and recovery policy to the failure modes of your application.

---

Originally published on [Dispatch](https://dispatch-blog.hashnode.dev/why-sqlite-wal-still-raises-database-is-locked-in-python).

title: CoFiBreak: A Coarse-to-Fine Diversity Reward for Effective Multi-Turn Jailbreak
description:
arXiv:2610.40926v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Automated red teaming trains an attacker large language model (LLM) to elicit harmful responses from a victim LLM, but reinforcement learning can collapse attackers onto a narrow set of prompts when attack success is the only reward. Such a collapse of attack diversity can bias safety evaluation toward repeatedly testing near-duplicate attack patterns rather than the underlying harmful intents. Existing methods often trade off attack success or inference cost for greater content or strategy diversity. We propose CoFiBreak, a coarse-to-fine diversity reward for Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) that improves attack diversity while preserving strong attack effectiveness and low inference cost. The coarse reward broadens which strategies the attacker uses by encouraging strategies underrepresented within each GRPO group, while the fine reward broadens how those strategies are realized by discouraging reuse of the same personas, framings, and output formats after harmful-intent information is removed from prompt embeddings. Diversity rewards apply only to attacks that already exceed an effectiveness threshold, so diversity cannot be gained through ineffective attacks. Since both rewards are computed only during training, CoFiBreak also retains inference efficiency. Trained with Llama3.1-8B-Instruct as the victim, CoFiBreak discovers 1.6-2.0x as many distinct successful fine-grained strategies as the strongest baseline across frontier victims on HarmBench. It reaches 98.8% ASR@10 (attack success rate with 10 generations per intent) on AdvBench with the highest diversity score among all compared methods, which is 2.1x that of the strongest-attacking baseline. The resulting attacks transfer to unseen frontier LLMs, reaching 71.0% ASR@10 on AdvBench with the unseen victim Claude-Opus-4.6. The code will be released.

title: A – Z Linux Commands – Overview with Examples
description:
There are a countless number of commands in Linux. We are bound to use a number of them on a daily routine or numerous times to perform common tasks than others. It is important to note that certain commands are "distro-based" - they can only be found in specific distros. While others are generic Unix/Linux commands that you'll find in all if not most mainstream distros.

In this article, we will introduce you a list of most frequently used Linux commands with their examples for easy learning. You can find the actual description of each Linux command in their manual page which you can access like this:

$ man command-name

adduser/addgroup Command

The adduser and addgroup commands are used to add a user and group to the system respectively according to the default configuration specified in /etc/adduser.conf file.

$ sudo adduser clinerds

agetty Command

agetty is a program which manages physical or virtual terminals and is invoked by init. Once it detects a connection, it opens a tty port, asks for a user's login name and calls up the /bin/login command. Agetty is a substitute of Linux getty:

$ agetty -L 9600 ttyS1 vt100

alias Command

alias is a useful shell built-in command for creating aliases (shortcut) to a Linux command on a system. It is helpful for creating new/custom commands from existing Shell/Linux commands (including options):

$ alias home='cd /home/clinerds/public_html'

The above command will create an alias called home for /home/clinerds/public_html directory, so whenever you type home in the terminal prompt, it will put you in the /home/clinerds*/public_html* directory.

anacron Command

anacron is a Linux facility used to run commands periodically with a frequency defined in days, weeks and months.

Unlike its sister cron; it assumes that a system will not run continuously, therefore if a scheduled job is due when the system is off, it's run once the machine is powered on.

For more information about anacron and cron read: Cron Vs Anacron: How to Schedule Jobs Using Anacron on Linux

apropos Command

apropos command is used to search and display a short man page description of a command/program as follows.

$ apropos adduser

apt Command

apt tool is a relatively new higher-level package manager for Debian/Ubuntu systems:

$ sudo apt update

apt-get Command

apt-get is a powerful and free front-end package manager for Debian/Ubuntu systems. It is used to install new software packages, remove available software packages, upgrade existing software packages as well as upgrade entire operating system.

$ sudo apt-get update

aptitude Command

aptitude is a powerful text-based interface to the Debian GNU/Linux package management system. Like apt-get and apt; it can be used to install, remove or upgrade software packages on a system.

$ sudo aptitude update

arch Command

arch is a simple command for displaying machine architecture or hardware name (similar to uname -m):

$ arch

arp Command

ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) is a protocol that maps IP network addresses of a network neighbor with the hardware (MAC) addresses in an IPv4 network.

You can use it as below to find all alive hosts on a network:

$ sudo arp-scan --interface=enp2s0 --localnet

at Command

at command is used to schedule tasks to run in a future time. It's an alternative to cron and anacron, however, it runs a task once at a given future time without editing any config files:

For example, to shutdown the system at 23:55 today, run:

$ sudo echo "shutdown -h now" | at -m 23:55

atq Command

atq command is used to view jobs in at command queue:

$ atq

atrm Command

atrm command is used to remove/deletes jobs (identified by their job number) from at command queue:

$ atrm 2

awk Command

Awk is a powerful programming language created for text processing and generally used as a data extraction and reporting tool.

$ awk '//{print}'/etc/hosts

For more Awk concepts (basic and advance) with simple and easy-to-understand, we've created a book that contains 13 chapters with a total of 41 pages, which covers all Awk basic and advance usage with practical examples: Awk Getting Started Guide for Beginners

batch Command

batch is also used to schedule tasks to run a future time, similar to the at command.

basename Command

basename command helps to print the name of a file stripping of directories in the absolute path:

$ basename bin/findhosts.sh

bc Command

bc is a simple yet powerful and arbitrary precision CLI calculator language which can be used like this:

$ echo 20.05 + 15.00 | bc

bg Command

bg is a command used to send a process to the background.

$ tar -czf home.tar.gz .
$ bg 
$ jobs

To learn more about bg command, read: Start Linux Command in Background and Detach Process in Terminal

bzip2 Command

bzip2 command is used to compress or decompress file(s).

$ bzip2 -z filename      #Compress
$ bzip2 -d filename.bz2  #Decompress

To learn more examples on bzip2, read: How to Compress and Decompress a .bz2 File in Linux

cal Command

The cal command print a calendar on the standard output.

$ cal

cat Command

cat command is used to view contents of a file or concatenate files, or data provided on standard input, and display it on the standard output.

$ cat file.txt

To learn more about cat command, read: 13 Useful Cat Command Examples on Linux

chgrp Command

chgrp command is used to change the group ownership of a file. Provide the new group name as its first argument and the name of file as the second argument like this:

$ chgrp clinerds users.txt

chmod Command

chmod command is used to change/update file access permissions like this.

$ chmod +x sysinfo.sh

chown Command

chown command changes/updates the user and group ownership of a file/directory like this.

$ chmod -R www-data:www-data /var/www/html

To learn more about chgrp, chmod and chwon commands, read: Managing Users & Groups, File Permissions & Attributes in Linux

cksum Command

cksum command is used to display the CRC checksum and byte count of an input file.

$ cksum README.txt

clear Command

clear command lets you clear the terminal screen, simply type.

$ clear

cmp Command

cmp performs a byte-by-byte comparison of two files like this.

$ cmp file1 file2

comm Command

comm command is used to compare two sorted files line-by-line as shown below.

$ comm file1 file2

cp Command

cp command is used for copying files and directories from one location to another.

$ cp /home/clinerds/file1 /home/clinerds/Personal/

date Command

date command displays/sets the system date and time like this.

$ date
$ date --set="8 JUN 2017 13:00:00"

dd Command

dd command is used for copying files, converting and formatting according to flags provided on the command line. It can strip headers, extracting parts of binary files and so on.

The example below shows creating a boot-able USB device:

$ dd if=/home/clinerds/kali-linux-1.0.4-i386.iso of=/dev/sdc1 bs=512M; sync

df Command

df command is used to show file system disk space usage as follows.

$ df -h

diff Command

diff command is used to compare two files line by line. It can also be used to find the difference between two directories in Linux like this:

$ diff file1 file2

dir Command

dir command works like Linux ls command, it lists the contents of a directory.

$ dir

dmidecode Command

dmidecode command is a tool for retrieving hardware information of any Linux system. It dumps a computer's DMI (a.k.a SMBIOS) table contents in a human-readable format for easy retrieval.

To view your system hardware info, you can type:

$ sudo dmidecode --type system

du Command

du command is used to show disk space usage of files present in a directory as well as its sub-directories as follows.

$ du /home/aaronkilik

echo Command

echo command prints a text of line provided to it.

$ echo "This is clinerds- Linux How Tos"

eject Command

eject command is used to eject removable media such as DVD/CD ROM or floppy disk from the system.

$ eject /dev/cdrom
$ eject /mnt/cdrom/
$ eject /dev/sda

env Command

env command lists all the current environment variables and used to set them as well.

$ env

exit Command

exit command is used to exit a shell like so.

$ exit

expr Command

expr command is used to calculate an expression as shown below.

$ expr 20 + 30

factor Command

factor command is used to show the prime factors of a number.

$ factor 10

find Command

find command lets you search for files in a directory as well as its sub-directories. It searches for files by attributes such as permissions, users, groups, file type, date, size and other possible criteria.

$ find /home/clinerds/ -name clinerds.txt

free Command

free command shows the system memory usage (free, used, swapped, cached, etc.) in the system including swap space. Use the-h option to display output in human friendly format.

$ free -h

grep Command

grep command searches for a specified pattern in a file (or files) and displays in output lines containing that pattern as follows.

$ grep 'clinerds' domain-list.txt

groups Command

groups command displays all the names of groups a user is a part of like this.

$ groups
$ groups clinerds

gzip Command

Gzip helps to compress a file, replaces it with one having a .gz extension as shown below:

$ gzip passwds.txt
$ cat file1 file2 | gzip > foo.gz

gunzip Command

gunzip expands or restores files compressed with gzip command like this.

$ gunzip foo.gz

head Command

head command is used to show first lines (10 lines by default) of the specified file or stdin to the screen:

# ps -eo pid,ppid,cmd,%mem,%cpu --sort=-%mem | head

history Command

history command is used to show previously used commands or to get info about command executed by a user.

$ history

hostname Command

hostname command is used to print or set system hostname in Linux.

$ hostname
$ hostname NEW_HOSTNAME

hostnamectl Command

hostnamectl command controls the system hostname under systemd. It is used to print or modify the system hostname and any related settings:

$ hostnamectl
$ sudo hostnamectl set-hostname NEW_HOSTNAME

hwclock

hwclock is a tool for managing the system hardware clock; read or set the hardware clock (RTC).

$ sudo hwclock
$ sudo hwclock --set --date 8/06/2017

hwinfo Command

hwinfo is used to probe for the hardware present in a Linux system like this.

$ hwinfo

id Command

id command shows user and group information for the current user or specified username as shown below.

$ id clinerds

ifconfig Command

ifconfig command is used to configure a Linux systems network interfaces. It is used to configure, view and control network interfaces.

$ ifconfig
$ sudo ifconfig eth0 up
$ sudo ifconfig eth0 down
$ sudo ifconfig eth0 172.16.25.125

ionice Command

ionice command is used to set or view process I/O scheduling class and priority of the specified process.

If invoked without any options, it will query the current I/O scheduling class and priority for that process:

$ ionice -c 3 rm /var/logs/syslog

iostat Command

iostat is used to show CPU and input/output statistics for devices and partitions. It produces useful reports for updating system configurations to help balance the input/output load between physical disks.

$ iostat

ip Command

ip command is used to display or manage routing, devices, policy routing and tunnels. It also works as a replacement for well known ifconfig command.

This command will assign an IP address to a specific interface (eth1 in this case).

$ sudo ip addr add 192.168.56.10 dev eth1

iptables Command

iptables is a terminal based firewall for managing incoming and outgoing traffic via a set of configurable table rules.

The command below is used to check existing rules on a system (using it may require root privileges).

$ sudo iptables -L -n -v

iw command is used to manage wireless devices and their configuration.

$ iw list

iwlist Command

iwlist command displays detailed wireless information from a wireless interface. The command below enables you to get detailed information about the wlp1s0 interface.

$ iwlist wlp1s0 scanning

kill Command

kill command is used to kill a process using its PID by sending a signal to it (default signal for kill is TERM).

$ kill -p 2300
$ kill -SIGTERM -p 2300

killall Command

killall command is used to kill a process by its name.

$ killall firefox

kmod Command

kmod command is used to manage Linux kernel modules. To list all currently loaded modules, type.

$ kmod list

last Command

last command display a listing of last logged in users.

$ last

ln Command

ln command is used to create a soft link between files using the -s flag like this.

$ ln -s /usr/bin/lscpu cpuinfo

locate Command

locate command is used to find a file by name. The locate utility works better and faster than it's find counterpart.

The command below will search for a file by its exact name (not *name*):

$ locate -b '\domain-list.txt'

login Command

login command is used to create a new session with the system. You'll be asked to provide a username and a password to login as below.

$ sudo login

ls Command

ls command is used to list contents of a directory. It works more or less like dir command.

The -l option enables long listing format like this.

$ ls -l file1

lshw Command

lshw command is a minimal tool to get detailed information on the hardware configuration of the machine, invoke it with superuser privileges to get a comprehensive information.

$ sudo lshw

lscpu Command

lscpu command displays system's CPU architecture information (such as number of CPUs, threads, cores, sockets, and more).

$ lscpu

lsof Command

lsof command displays information related to files opened by processes. Files can be of any type, including regular files, directories, block special files, character special files, executing text reference, libraries, and stream/network files.

To view files opened by a specific user's processes, type the command below.

$ lsof -u clinerds

lsusb Command

lsusb command shows information about USB buses in the system and the devices connected to them like this.

$ lsusb

man Command

man command is used to view the on-line reference manual pages for commands/programs like so.

$ man du
$ man df

md5sum Command

md5sum command is used to compute and print the MD5 message digest of a file. If run without arguments, debsums checks every file on your system against the stock md5sum files:

$ sudo debsums

mkdir Command

mkdir command is used to create single or more directories, if they do not already exist (this can be overridden with the -p option).

$ mkdir clinerds-files
OR 
$ mkdir -p clinerds-files

more Command

more command enables you to view through relatively lengthy text files one screenful at a time.

$ more file.txt

mv Command

mv command is used to rename files or directories. It also moves a file or directory to another location in the directory structure.

$ mv test.sh sysinfo.sh

nano Command

nano is a popular small, free and friendly text editor for Linux; a clone of Pico, the default editor included in the non-free Pine package.

To open a file using nano, type:

$ nano file.txt

nc/netcat Command

nc (or netcat) is used for performing any operation relating to TCP, UDP, or UNIX-domain sockets. It can handle both IPv4 and IPv6 for opening TCP connections, sending UDP packets, listening on arbitrary TCP and UDP ports, performing port scanning.

The command below will help us see if the port 22 is open on the host 192.168.56.5.

$ nc -zv 192.168.1.5 22

netstat Command

netstat command displays useful information concerning the Linux networking subsystem (network connections, routing tables, interface statistics, masquerade connections, and multicast memberships).

This command will display all open ports on the local system:

$ netstat -a | more

nice Command

nice command is used to show or change the nice value of a running program. It runs specified command with an adjusted niceness. When run without any command specified, it prints the current niceness.

The following command starts the process "tar command" setting the "nice" value to 12.

$ nice -12 tar -czf backup.tar.bz2 /home/*

nmap Command

nmap is a popular and powerful open source tool for network scanning and security auditing. It was intended to quickly scan large networks, but it also works fine against single hosts.

The command below will probe open ports on all live hosts on the specified network.

$ nmap -sV 192.168.56.0/24

nproc Command

nproc command shows the number of processing units present to the current process. It's output may be less than the number of online processors on a system.

$ nproc

openssl Command

The openssl is a command line tool for using the different cryptography operations of OpenSSL's crypto library from the shell. The command below will create an archive of all files in the current directory and encrypt the contents of the archive file:

$ tar -czf - * | openssl enc -e -aes256 -out backup.tar.gz

passwd Command

passwd command is used to create/update passwords for user accounts, it can also change the account or associated password validity period. Note that normal system users may only change the password of their own account, while root may modify the password for any account.

$ passwd clinerds

pidof Command

pidof displays the process ID of a running program/command.

$ pidof init
$ pidof cinnamon

ping Command

ping command is used to determine connectivity between hosts on a network (or the Internet):

$ ping google.com

ps Command

ps shows useful information about active processes running on a system. The example below shows the top running processes by highest memory and CPU usage.

# ps -eo pid,ppid,cmd,%mem,%cpu --sort=-%mem | head

pstree Command

pstree displays running processes as a tree which is rooted at either PID or init if PID is omitted.

$ pstree

pwd Command

pwd command displays the name of current/working directory as below.

$ pwd

rdiff-backup Command

rdiff-backup is a powerful local/remote incremental backup script written in Python. It works on any POSIX operating system such as Linux, Mac OS X.

Note that for remote backups, you must install the same version of rdiff-backup on both the local and remote machines. Below is an example of a local backup command:

$ sudo rdiff-backup /etc /media/clinerds/Backup/server_etc.backup

reboot Command

reboot command may be used to halt, power-off or reboot a system as follows.

$ reboot

rename Command

rename command is used to rename many files at once. If you've a collection of files with ".html" extension and you want to rename all of them with ".php" extension, you can type the command below.

$ rename 's/\.html$/\.php/' *.html

rm command

rm command is used to remove files or directories as shown below.

$ rm file1
$ rm -rf my-files

rmdir Command

rmdir command helps to delete/remove empty directories as follows.

$ rmdir /backup/all

scp Command

scp command enables you to securely copy files between hosts on a network, for example.

$ scp ~/names.txt root@192.168.56.10:/root/names.txt

shutdown Command

shutdown command schedules a time for the system to be powered down. It may be used to halt, power-off or reboot the machine like this.

$ shutdown --poweroff.

sleep Command

sleep command is used to delay or pause (specifically execution of a command) for a specified amount of time.

$ check.sh; sleep 5; sudo apt update

sort Command

sort command is used to sort lines of text in the specified file(s) or from stdin as shown below

$ cat words.txt

split Command

split as the name suggests, is used to split a large file into small parts.

$ tar -cvjf backup.tar.bz2 /home/clinerds/Documents/*

ssh Command

ssh (SSH client) is an application for remotely accessing and running commands on a remote machine. It is designed to offer a secure encrypted communications between two untrusted hosts over an insecure network such as the Internet.

$ ssh clinerds@192.168.56.10

stat Command

stat is used to show a file or file system status like this (-f is used to specify a filesystem).

$ stat file1

su Command

su command is used to switch to another user ID or become root during a login session. Note that when su is invoked without a username, it defaults to becoming root.

$ su 
$ su clinerds

sudo Command

sudo command allows a permitted system user to run a command as root or another user, as defined by the security policy such as sudoers.

In this case, the real (not effective) user ID of the user running sudo is used to determine the user name with which to query the security policy.

$ sudo apt update
$ sudo useradd clinerds
$ sudo passwd clinerds

sum Command

sum command is used to show the checksum and block counts for each each specified file on the command line.

$ sum output file.txt

tac Command

tac command concatenates and displays files in reverse. It simply prints each file to standard output, showing last line first.

$tac file.txt

tail Command

tail command is used to display the last lines (10 lines by default) of each file to standard output.

If there more than one file, precede each with a header giving the file name. Use it as follow (specify more lines to display using -n option).

$ tail long-file
OR
$ tail -n 15 long-file

talk Command

talk command is used to talk to another system/network user. To talk to a user on the same machine, use their login name, however, to talk to a user on another machine use 'user@host'.

$ talk person [ttyname]
OR
$ talk'user@host' [ttyname]

tar Command

tar command is a most powerful utility for archiving files in Linux.

$ tar -czf home.tar.gz .

tee Command

tee command is used to read from standard input and prints to standard output and files as shown below.

$ echo "Testing how tee command works" | tee file1

tree Command

The tree command is a tiny, cross-platform command-line program used to recursively list or display the content of a directory in a tree-like format.

$ tree

time Command

time command runs programs and summarizes system resource usage.

$ time wc /etc/hosts

top Command

top program displays all processes on a Linux system in regards to memory and CPU usage and provides a dynamic real-time view of a running system.

$ top

touch Command

touch command changes file timestamps, it can also be used to create a file as follows.

$ touch file.txt

tr Command

tr command is a useful utility used to translate (change) or delete characters from stdin, and write the result to stdout or send to a file as follows.

$ cat domain-list.txt | tr [:lower:] [:upper:]

uname Command

uname command displays system information such as operating system, network node hostname kernel name, version and release etc.

Use the -a option to show all the system information:

$ uname

uniq Command

uniq command displays or omits repeated lines from input (or standard input). To indicate the number of occurrences of a line, use the -c option.

$ cat domain-list.txt

uptime Command

uptime command shows how long the system has been running, number of logged on users and the system load averages as follows.

$ uptime

users Command

users command shows the user names of users currently logged in to the current host like this.

$ users

vim/vi Command

vim (Vi Improved) popular text editor on Unix-like operating systems. It can be used to edit all kinds of plain text and program files.

$ vim file

w Command

w command displays system uptime, load averages and information about the users currently on the machine, and what they are doing (their processes) like this.

$ w

wall Command

wall command is used to send/display a message to all users on the system as follows.

$ wall "This is CLINerds - Linux How Tos"

watch Command

watch command runs a program repeatedly while displaying its output on fullscreen. It can also be used to watch changes to a file/directory. The example below shows how to watch the contents of a directory change.

$ watch -d ls -l

wc Command

wc command is used to display newline, word, and byte counts for each file specified, and a total for many files.

$ wc filename

wget Command

wget command is a simple utility used to download files from the Web in a non-interactive (can work in the background) way.

$ wget -c http://ftp.gnu.org/gnu/wget/wget-1.5.3.tar.gz

whatis Command

whatis command searches and shows a short or one-line manual page descriptions of the provided command name(s) as follows.

$ whatis wget

which Command

which command displays the absolute path (pathnames) of the files (or possibly links) which would be executed in the current environment.

$ which who

who Command

who command shows information about users who are currently logged in like this.

$ who

whereis Command

whereis command helps us locate the binary, source and manual files for commands.

$ whereis cat

xargs Command

xargs command is a useful utility for reading items from the standard input, delimited by blanks (protected with double or single quotes or a backslash) or newlines, and executes the entered command.

The example below show xargs being used to copy a file to multiple directories in Linux.

$ echo /home/aaronkilik/test/ /home/aaronkilik/tmp | xargs -n 1 cp -v /home/aaronkilik/bin/sys_info.sh

yes Command

yes command is used to display a string repeatedly until when terminated or killed using [Ctrl + C] as follows.

$ yes "This is CLINerds- Linux HowTos"

youtube-dl Command

youtube-dl is a lightweight command-line program to download videos and also extract MP3 tracks from YouTube.com and a few more sites.

The command below will list available formats for the video in the provided link.

$ youtube-dl --list-formats https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iR

zcmp/zdiff Command

zcmp and zdiff minimal utilities used to compare compressed files as shown in the examples below.

$ zcmp domain-list.txt.zip basic_passwords.txt.zip
$ zdiff domain-list.txt.zip basic_passwords.txt.zip

zip Command

zip is a simple and easy-to-use utility used to package and compress (archive) files.

$ tar cf - . | zip | dd of=/dev/nrst0 obs=16k
$ zip inarchive.zip foo.c bar.c --out outarchive.zip
$ tar cf - .| zip backup -

zz Command

zz command is an alias of the fasd commandline tool that offers quick access to files and directories in Linux. It is used to quickly and interactively cd into a previously accessed directory by selecting the directory number from the first field as follows.

$ zz

That's it for now! As we mentioned before, there are a countless number of commands in Linux. The list is possibly longer than we can offer. Use the feedback form below to share any useful and frequently used commands missing in this list.

title: Li$^{2}$SAO: Lifting Light Singl-Rollout Asynchronous RL Optimization via Group-Relative Actor-Critic Bootstrapping
description:
arXiv:2610.40726v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Asynchronous reinforcement learning (RL) is becoming a mainstream paradigm for post-training large language models (LLMs), as it improves training efficiency by updating the model as rollouts arrive. Recent work argues that group-wise sampling in GRPO does not naturally fit asynchronous RL training because rollout lengths follow a long-tailed distribution, and proposes Single-rollout Asynchronous Optimization (SAO) to improve stability and off-policy behavior, especially on agentic tasks. However, SAO relies on a closed-source value model obtained from scaling value pretraining. In this paper, we analyze GRPO and LiSAO, our lightweight reproduction of SAO without the pretrained value model, on single-turn reasoning and multi-turn agentic tasks. We find that GRPO outperforms LiSAO on reasoning tasks, while the reverse holds on agentic tasks. Since the value model of LiSAO is not yet well trained , LiSAO lags behind GRPO substantially in early training steps. To address this issue, we propose Li$^{2}$SAO, which Lifts Light Single-rollout Asynchronous Optimization with group-relative actor-critic bootstrapping: while the critic is cold, a group-relative advantage trains the actor and a group-centered return trains the critic, after which training switches to single-rollout GAE. Experiments show that Li$^{2}$SAO catches up with or surpasses GRPO in early training and further raises the later performance ceiling. Code is available at https://github.com/jd-cc-coder/Li2SAO.

title: Better Retrievers, Worse Labels: How Incomplete Relevance Judgments Distort Abstention Evaluation in Conversational RAG
description:
arXiv:2610.40966v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Conversational RAG benchmarks such as MTRAG and RETECO evaluate retrieval and generation end to end: each system answers from its own retrieval, so abstention must be scored against whether each retrieved context is sufficient. A convenient shortcut reads sufficiency off the relevance judgments and treats a context without gold documents as unanswerable. We re-run the official baselines exactly and test this shortcut on RECOR (RETECO track~2) with four retrievers (nDCG@10 from .18 to .59) and three Qwen3 readers. Two open LLM judges and a panel of four small open models label each context by content, and a model of another family audits 250 contexts blind, with adjudication. The stronger the retriever, the larger the share of no-gold contexts that still contain the answer (28\% to 72\%) and the lower the shortcut's precision (.68 to .10; .70 to .21 under the audit). A reader agrees: Qwen3-4B answers 62--67\% of these false misses correctly, against 23--30\% of no-gold contexts judged insufficient and 1\% with no documents. In most false misses, the answer comes from a hard negative mined for the same question, another turn's gold or a neighbouring chunk of the gold page. On MTRAG, whose judgments come from annotators, precision drops from .72 to .50. Under the shortcut, answerability AUROC is up to .19 too low, and the best sufficiency detector appears to be a retrieval score that never reads the documents. We release code, runs and labels, and recommend scoring refusals against content labels, not the presence of gold.

title: Beyond Trial-and-Error: A Geospatial-Guided Active Reasoning Framework for Robust Aerial Vision-and-Language Navigation
description:
arXiv:2610.41446v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Aerial Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) requires UAVs to locate language-specified goals in large-scale urban environments, where objects often appear small and visually ambiguous from high-altitude viewpoints. Existing methods largely follow a reactive paradigm common in indoor VLN, repeatedly updating navigation states from local observations while underutilizing the geospatial structure that remains stable during navigation. As a result, visually similar distractors can cause a reactive goal search to repeatedly reinforce locally plausible goal hypotheses based on passively accumulated evidence, leading to unreliable localization. To address this, we propose GeoReasoner, a robust framework that shifts the paradigm of Aerial VLN from reactive trial-and-error to geospatial-guided active reasoning. Specifically, GeoReasoner first performs pre-search geospatial reasoning to derive region-level priors and constrain the goal hypothesis space. Building on these, it further conducts hypothesis-driven exploration to actively acquire discriminative evidence and refine competing goal hypotheses. Finally, consistency-aware goal verification adversarially assesses complementary evidence sources before stopping, hence reducing premature or erroneous goal confirmations. Experiments on the real-world CityNav benchmark demonstrate that GeoReasoner sets a new SOTA among zero-shot Aerial VLN methods while competing favorably with supervised approaches.
