title: S2TDR: Structured Multimodal Reconstruction for Sticker-Aware Dialogue Understanding
description:
arXiv:2610.41176v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Stickers are widely used in social media dialogues to express affect, stance, and intent beyond literal text. Their meanings are often non-literal and context-dependent, making them difficult to handle with generic visual fusion or standalone captioning. We propose Sticker-to-Text Dialogue Reconstruction (S2TDR), a structured multimodal reconstruction framework that converts sticker turns into contextually appropriate textual utterances. S2TDR decomposes sticker interpretation into visual cue extraction, affective-intent inference, and context-aware dialogue reconstruction, using OCR text only as an auxiliary cue when available. The reconstructed dialogue can then be consumed by existing text-based dialogue models. Experiments on sentiment analysis, intent recognition, and dialogue summarization show that S2TDR generally improves multiple downstream models over direct sticker integration methods. Further analyses on component ablations, OCR-empty stickers, and reconstruction quality indicate that structured reconstruction provides an interpretable and effective way to integrate sticker semantics into dialogue understanding.

title: Redesigning Solitaire for one thumb (and A/B testing where the deck goes)
description:
Most of the people who play Solitaire on our site do it on a phone, held in one hand, often on the sofa in the evening. Many of them are over 60. Until this week our Klondike layout on phones was simply the desktop layout squeezed into a tall screen: the deck in the top corner, the buttons in a toolbar at the top, and the cards small.

On a 6.5" phone held in one hand, the top of the screen is the hardest place to reach. And the deck is the thing you tap most in Klondike. So we rebuilt the portrait layout around the thumb.

What changed

A bottom bar instead of a top toolbar. Settings, New game, Hint and Undo now sit in a bar at the bottom, as big icon buttons with a label under each one. Undo is on the right, where a right thumb rests. Time, moves and score stay in a slim strip at the top, because you read them but never tap them.

The deck can live at the bottom. In the settings sheet you can choose Deck position: Top / Bottom. At the bottom, the deck and the waste pile sit just above the bar, so drawing a card is a short thumb move instead of a stretch. A small badge shows how many cards are left in the deck.

Left or right hand. A Hand setting mirrors the deck and Undo to the other side. It's a small thing, but without it a left-handed player has to reach across the whole screen for every card.

Draw 1 or Draw 3, from the next deal. The choice used to be buried in a menu. It's now the first row of the settings sheet, and it applies from the next deal so a game in progress never changes under you.

Columns use the whole height. In portrait there's a lot of empty felt under the columns. Long columns now fan down into that space before the cards start to overlap more, and face-down cards squeeze first so the face-up ones stay readable.

Dragging feels lighter. While you drag, the card lifts slightly around your finger, every legal drop shows a soft glow, and the one under your finger glows stronger. Tapping a card still sends it to the best place, so dragging is optional.

Landscape and desktop keep the original layout. The whole portrait mode is one class on the body, so the CSS stays scoped and nothing else moves:

portraitLayout() {
  let on = false;
  try { on = matchMedia('(orientation: portrait) and (max-width: 700px)').matches; } catch (e) {}
  document.body.classList.toggle('np-sol-portrait', on);
  this._portrait = on;
}

Top or bottom? We don't know yet, so we're testing it

My guess was that the bottom deck is better. But players who have used Solitaire for 30 years expect the deck in the top corner, and "easier to reach" doesn't always mean "feels right".

So players who never touched the setting get one of the two positions at random, once, and keep it. An explicit choice in the settings always wins over the test:

let ab = null;
try { ab = localStorage.getItem('np-sol-ab'); } catch (e) {}
if (ab !== 'top' && ab !== 'bottom') {
  ab = Math.random() < 0.5 ? 'top' : 'bottom';
  try { localStorage.setItem('np-sol-ab', ab); } catch (e) {}
}
// logged once per player as an event, so we can compare the two groups

What we'll compare per variant: how many people leave in the first 10 seconds, how many games get finished, how many are won, play time, and how many come back the next day. Finished games matter more to us than taps: if the bottom deck makes people quit fewer games, that's the answer.

The test started today, so there are no results yet. I'll post a follow-up when there's enough data to say something honest.

Small things we learned on the way

  • Put a word under every icon. A gear or a lightbulb is obvious to us; it isn't to everyone. "Settings" and "Hint" cost a few pixels and remove the guessing.
  • Don't change the rules mid-game. Draw 1 / Draw 3 applies from the next deal, so a game in progress never changes under you, and daily puzzles and duels keep the rules everyone else plays with.
  • Keep the bar out of the system gesture area. On phones with a home indicator, the bar needs env(safe-area-inset-bottom) padding, or the Undo button fights with the swipe-home gesture.

If you want to try it, it's at nitroplayer.com/games/solitaire. It works best on a phone, held in one hand. I'd love to hear where you'd put the deck.

title: Stepwise-Querying: Distilling Reasoning without Access to Teacher Chain-of-Thought
description:
arXiv:2610.41769v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reasoning distillation is widely used to transfer the reasoning capabilities of large language models to smaller students through teacher-generated supervision. In the black-box setting, however, teachers may expose only final answers and brief solutions, leaving intermediate calculations and validity conditions unavailable and thus limiting the reasoning supervision available for distillation. We propose Stepwise Querying, which elicits step-specific explanations without requiring access to the teacher's internal chain-of-thought (CoT) traces. Independent queries to the same teacher request intermediate derivations, validity checks, and corrections for individual steps, the assembled solutions are then used for standard supervised fine-tuning. Across two teachers, two students, and four mathematics and code benchmarks, our method achieves the highest score in 14 of 16 comparisons with three baselines. We further introduce Stepwise Explanation Information Gain (SEIG), a diagnostic based on the log-ratio of a frozen student's probabilities of correct step completion under stepwise and global explanations. Analyses on GSM8K show that incorrect-answer trajectories can remain useful when they preserve valid intermediate reasoning, while further decomposition yields limited additional gains.

title: Text as an Index for Zero-Shot Cross-Domain Knowledge Tracing
description:
arXiv:2610.41883v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Knowledge tracing (KT) predicts a student's next response from their history. New platforms often have question texts but no response logs for training, motivating zero-shot cross-domain KT. Existing transfer and cold-start methods use question semantics, but cross-platform semantic discrepancies limit transferability. We propose TIZSKT, which separates behavioral sequence modeling from domain-local historical evidence construction and uses text as an index rather than a directly transferable predictive representation. The Mastery-Dynamics Encoder learns correctness dynamics without question identifiers or text embeddings. Domain-Local Question Addressing builds fixed question addresses using a frozen text encoder and an unsupervised per-domain projection. The Text-Addressing Kernel uses these addresses to aggregate the current student's previous outcomes into a question-specific historical correctness summary. Cross-Segment Continuation retains access to earlier responses without extending the behavioral encoder's input sequence. Evidence-Volume Read-Out preserves the total kernel mass discarded by normalization and combines its log-compressed value with the behavioral state and historical correctness summary to predict the next response. All trainable parameters are learned from source domains; target inference uses public question texts and the current student's observed history without target-domain training. Leave-one-domain-out experiments on three public datasets show that TIZSKT achieves the highest mean AUC and accuracy among evaluated baselines on all target domains. Ablations confirm the contributions of text addressing and cross-segment continuation.

title: My backtest's worst week didn't stand out in any weekly stat. The trades showed why
description:
A max drawdown number tells you how deep the hole was. It doesn't tell you what dug it, and the fix depends on that:

  • Stops hit soon after entry. The entry or the stop size is the problem.
  • Losers that were in profit first. The exit is the problem.
  • Trades held too long against you. You need a time exit.

So I zoom into the worst stretch and look at the trades one by one. This post walks through one run, including a check I expected to explain the drawdown and that didn't.

The run

  • Strategy: moving-average cross (5/20), take profit 0.3%, stop loss 0.2%
  • Data: 30,000 synthetic 15-minute bars from a regime-switching generator. The dataset is named USDJPY_15M, but the prices and the dates (Oct 2026 to Sep 2027) are made up
  • Result: 1,863 trades, +4.6%, max drawdown -14.1%, win rate 41.5%

The UI in the screenshots is in Japanese. There is an EN switch at the top right.

The worst week

Instead of the deepest point of the drawdown, I looked for the steepest 7-day fall in equity. The deepest point often sits at the end of a long, slow slide, and a single week of that slide looks like nothing. The steepest week was Dec 13 to Dec 20: equity went from 10,303 to 9,691.

I compared the 46 trades opened that week with all 1,863:

That week Whole run
Win rate 19.6% 41.5%
Closed by the stop 70% (32 of 46) 49%
Median holding time 0.76 h 0.76 h
Losers that were in profit first (by at least half the loss) 35% 31%

The holding time didn't change, so the trades weren't held longer. The share of losers that were in profit first barely moved, so the exit wasn't giving back more than usual. What changed was the stop: 70% of the week's trades ended there, against 49% over the whole run.

The check that didn't explain it

My first guess was that the market was unusual that week. I split the 44 weeks of the run two ways and looked at the stop-out rate in each group:

Weeks grouped by Quietest / choppiest quarter Middle half Most volatile / trending quarter
Median 15-minute move 49.7% 48.9% 48.5%
Trend efficiency (net move / range) 49.4% 49.1% 48.0%

The stop-out rate is about 49% in every group. The drawdown week ranked 17th of 44 by volatility, right in the middle. It was a trending week (efficiency 0.68 against a median of 0.35), but the trending quarter as a whole made money: +33 a week on average.

A weekly label would have said "trend week, this strategy is fine in trends". That would have been wrong, and the weekly numbers couldn't show why.

What the trades showed

The zoomed chart shows it. Price rallied from 123.9 to 133.5 in three days, then moved sideways between 131 and 137, with a spike to 137.09 on Dec 16 that reversed within the day.

The stops were hit on both sides: 16 of 23 buys and 16 of 23 sells. A 0.2% stop is only about 2.5 median 15-minute moves wide. That's fine while price drifts. After a rally of nearly 8%, the swings around the new level were wide enough to reach it in both directions, while the average bar size for the week still looked normal.

The trade timeline under the charts shows the same range from the trades' side. Each bar is one trade, from open to close: green for buys, red for sells. Overlapping trades go on separate rows. The bars are short and they alternate between buys and sells, so these were quick stop-outs in both directions, not a few trades that dragged on.

This doesn't tell me the fix. It tells me where to look: at the stop size or at a filter right after large moves, not at the exit. I'd test either one on a part of the data I haven't looked at yet, because a filter tuned on one bad week fits that week and little else.

Doing this with your own backtest

  1. Find the steepest 7-day fall in equity, not the deepest point.
  2. For that week's trades, compare four numbers with the whole run: win rate, share closed by the stop, median holding time, share of losers that were in profit first.
  3. If only the stop share jumped, look at the entry and the stop. If the in-profit-first share jumped, look at the exit. If holding time jumped, add a time exit.
  4. Don't trust a weekly volatility or trend label to find it for you. In this run it pointed the wrong way.

How the zoom works

Some details on the chart side, in case you're building something similar.

The equity, drawdown, exposure and trade timeline charts are Chart.js with chartjs-plugin-zoom (Ctrl+wheel to zoom, drag to pan). When one finishes a zoom or pan, it reads its x range and applies it to the others with chart.zoomScale("x", { min, max }, "none"). The "none" animation mode matters: with animation on, each chart fires its own updates while the others are still moving.

The price chart is different. Its candles come from the server at a fixed bar budget, so on a range change it picks the finest timeframe that fits the range. In the clip, the zoomed week is drawn with 30-minute bars. It only picks timeframes the dataset actually has.

Redrawing the price chart is async. If it resets the other charts' ranges when it finishes, a Ctrl+wheel gesture that's still going gets cut off. So a flag keeps the other charts as they are while a sync redraw is in flight.

Entry and exit arrows are drawn only when 80 trades or fewer are in view. With 1,863 trades in the full view, arrows would just be noise. The two thin strips above the price chart show where opens and closes cluster, and the arrows take over once you've zoomed in far enough.

The demo runs without an account. The chart view in this post is in the app, where a free account comes with sample data to try it on: Hawk Backtester

If you find the cause of a drawdown a different way, I'd like to hear how.

title: CEFR Level Assessment across Languages and Text Granularities
description:
arXiv:2610.41553v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Automatic assessment of textual CEFR levels is an important task in educational natural language processing. However, accurate CEFR level prediction remains challenging due to the naturally imbalanced distribution of CEFR levels and the ambiguous boundaries between adjacent levels. To address these challenges, we propose a unified training objective that combines focal loss with supervised contrastive learning. Focal loss mitigates class imbalance by emphasizing underrepresented and difficult examples, while supervised contrastive learning learns more discriminative representations by encouraging intra-class compactness and inter-class separation. We evaluate the proposed method on sentence- and document-level CEFR assessment in both monolingual and multilingual settings. Experimental results demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms strong baselines across all settings, establishing new state-of-the-art performance on multiple CEFR assessment benchmarks.

title: PersonaChatBench: Evaluating Chat Assistants with Diverse Simulated Users
description:
arXiv:2610.42060v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Conversational assistants are expected to help people with diverse backgrounds, preferences, and communication styles. Yet evaluations centered on a single cooperative user provide limited insight into how reliably an assistant serves users with different personas. We introduce PersonaChatBench, a framework for evaluating task competence and responsiveness to diverse user needs. PersonaChatBench pairs the same underlying task with multiple simulated users, each guided by a private persona card that specifies distinct needs, preferences, and interaction behaviors. By holding the task fixed while varying the user, the framework examines how assistant performance changes across user conditions. We evaluate 20 language models across six domains, separately assessing native task outcomes, fulfillment of expressed persona needs, and simulator fidelity. Our results show that task performance and need fulfillment vary across personas and domains. Strong task performance does not necessarily translate into satisfying individual needs, and models' relative strengths in meeting those needs are not consistent across domains. PersonaChatBench makes these differences measurable, revealing gaps obscured by aggregate scores and helping identify which users an assistant serves well and where adaptation is needed. It provides a basis for evaluating consistency across users and guiding the development of assistants that better accommodate diverse needs in everyday applications.

title: Scout-Refine-Correct: Teaching Flow Models to Refine Their Own Samples
description:
arXiv:2610.41598v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The quality of image generation models trained with diffusion or flow matching is largely fixed by the training budget: at inference, the only available lever is the number of sampling steps, and additional steps improve quality only up to a point. We present a training recipe, Scout-Refine-Correct (SRC), that instead gives a flow-matching generator a genuine inference-time refinement capability. At each sampling step the model takes a scout rollout -- $K$ steps ahead along its own trajectory -- extrapolates a full-sample estimate, and feeds that estimate back to itself as a self-conditioning signal before taking the real step. This can be repeated for $R$ refinement rounds. Two correction losses, applied during training at states the model's own rollouts actually reach rather than only on the ground-truth path, teach the model to use this signal to reach new samples instead of collapsing to a suboptimal one. On ImageNet-256, SRC improves LightningDiT-B from FID~14.5 to FID~7.26 at NFE~550, matching a privileged best-of-$N$ baseline that uses an oracle FID verifier to choose among samples. SRC uses no external verifier, no reward signal, and, after ablation, almost no extra parameters over the base architecture. Combining SRC with best-of-$N$ improves the result further, to FID~3.81 at NFE~4400, showing that the two axes are complementary. We ablate the main design choices -- the architectural pathway for the scout signal, the scout horizon, each correction loss, and the training schedule to demonstrate key working components of training.

title: Vercel Sandbox creation now returns a ready sandbox
description:
A new Vercel Sandbox is now ready to run commands and read or write files when creation completes.

Sandbox.create() now resolves only after snapshot restoration completes, so the first command or file operation no longer waits for it. Startup errors also reject Sandbox.create() instead of surfacing during that operation.

Snapshot restoration time now counts toward creation instead of the first operation. Creation is about 50 ms longer at p50, with a larger increase possible for uncached snapshots. The total time through the first operation remains the same.

This change applies automatically, with no SDK upgrade or configuration changes required. See the Sandbox.create() documentation for details.

title: Building Browser-Only Calculators for Real-World Tasks: 6 Lessons from MendNook
description:
Building Browser-Only Calculators for Real-World Tasks: 6 Lessons from MendNook

A rectangular screen frame has a width, a height, and two diagonals. Calculating the theoretical diagonal is easy. Helping someone understand whether that number is useful for a real repair is much harder.

That's the kind of product-design problem behind MendNook, a collection of home measurement guides and browser-based calculators. The site includes tools for checking screen-frame diagonals, planning screen materials, recording blind measurements, and comparing door-bottom gaps.

This post isn't a walkthrough of our production source code. Instead, it's a practical breakdown of six design principles for small browser-based tools, with illustrative JavaScript examples.

1. Separate the calculation from the decision

A diagonal calculator can use the Pythagorean theorem:

function rectangularDiagonal(width, height) {
  if (!Number.isFinite(width) ||
      !Number.isFinite(height) ||
      width <= 0 || height <= 0) {
    return null;
  }

  return Math.hypot(width, height);
}

rectangularDiagonal(30, 24);
// Approximately 38.42 inches

But the output should say theoretical diagonal, not your frame is square.

A calculation assumes ideal rectangular geometry. It cannot detect cracked corners, bent rails, or poor installation.

The transferable lesson: don't let an accurate formula imply a conclusion it cannot support.

2. Validate the meaning of an input

JavaScript has a surprising behavior:

Number("") // 0

That is usually not what someone expects from an empty measurement field.

A better starting point:

function parsePositiveMeasurement(raw) {
  const trimmed = raw.trim();

  if (trimmed === "") return null;

  const value = Number(trimmed);

  return Number.isFinite(value) && value > 0
    ? value
    : null;
}

A production form should also display a clear field-level error, explain units, and distinguish an absent optional measurement from an invalid required one.

If the interface accepts decimal inches, say so. If users cannot enter fractions such as 35 1/8 directly, explain how to enter 35.125.

3. Don't turn a conditional guideline into a universal rule

Consider an inside-mount blind measurement helper.

A user might record widths at three positions:

const widths = [35.25, 35.125, 35.0];

const narrowestWidth = Math.min(...widths);
// 35 inches

But the correct height rule can vary depending on the product and manufacturer.

A useful interface can report the shortest and longest measured heights without incorrectly declaring either the final ordering dimension.

The calculator organizes evidence. Manufacturer-specific instructions determine the final decision.

This principle applies beyond home improvement: finance, shipping estimates, insurance, and many other domains where a single formula cannot describe every rule.

4. Make the no-JavaScript experience honest

An interactive calculator might require JavaScript, but its explanatory content should remain useful when scripts are unavailable.

A progressive-enhancement fallback can provide:

  • The formula and its assumptions
  • A clearly labeled worked example
  • Manual measurement instructions
  • An explanation of what the calculator cannot determine

Never present a static sample value as though it was calculated from the user's inputs.

5. Minimize unnecessary data collection

Most measurement calculators need only numbers and a formula, not a user account.

MendNook's public tools are browser-based and do not require registration or a paywall.

Local arithmetic can reduce friction and make it easier to explain how entered measurements are handled.

However, a browser-based calculator is not automatically private. Developers still need to examine third-party scripts, analytics, storage, and network requests before making privacy claims.

6. Test edge cases, not just the happy path

For a rectangular diagonal calculator, useful tests include:

Test Expected behavior
30 × 24 inches Approximately 38.42 inches
Empty width Ask for a measurement
Negative height Show a validation error
Invalid numeric input Reject the value
Unequal measured diagonals Show the difference without inventing a universal tolerance
JavaScript disabled Keep educational instructions available

These checks can matter more to users than sophisticated component architecture.

The wider lesson

A useful real-world calculator is not simply:

Input → Formula → Output

It's closer to:

Input → Validation → Contextual calculation → Limitations → Next action

For an example, explore the MendNook frame diagonal calculator. It explains the formula and, importantly, what the result cannot prove.

What's one UX guardrail you've added because a mathematically correct result could still mislead users?

I'd love to hear how other developers handle this challenge.

Code snippets are illustrative examples, not excerpts from the production source.

title: I added a Three.js typewriter intro to my site, and then I made it skippable
description:
My portfolio opens with a typewriter scene built in Three.js. It looks great the first time. The tenth time, it's a delay.

This post is about the rules that keep a nice-to-have animation from turning into an obstacle, with the actual mechanics so you can copy them. The short version: flair should serve the first impression and then get out of the way.

The temptation

A 3D intro is fun to build. It shows off the skills the site exists to demonstrate. And for a first-time visitor it sets a tone: a typewriter clacking out the masthead of a newspaper fits the theme.

But think about what it costs the visitor:

  • A wait before they can see anything useful.
  • Weight: Three.js and a scene mean extra JavaScript to download and run.
  • Repetition: someone who opens the site twice, or navigates away and back, sees it again.

A feature that's delightful once and irritating ten times needs rules.

Rule 1: show it once per session

I store a flag in sessionStorage. Once the intro has played in a tab, it doesn't play again in that tab.

const KEY = 'press-intro-seen';

function shouldPlayIntro(): boolean {
  try {
    if (new URLSearchParams(location.search).has('noload')) return false;
    return !sessionStorage.getItem(KEY);
  } catch {
    return false;          // storage blocked: skip the intro, don't break the page
  }
}

function markIntroSeen() {
  try { sessionStorage.setItem(KEY, '1'); } catch { /* ignore */ }
}

Two choices worth noting:

  • I used sessionStorage, not localStorage. A new session gets the intro again, which keeps the delight for returning visitors without being relentless within a visit.
  • The try/catch matters. Some browsers or privacy modes block storage; in that case the safe behaviour is to skip the intro rather than throw and break the page.

Rule 2: let people skip it

Any click or key press jumps past the intro.

function enableSkip(onSkip: () => void) {
  const handler = () => {
    window.removeEventListener('pointerdown', handler);
    window.removeEventListener('keydown', handler);
    onSkip();
  };
  window.addEventListener('pointerdown', handler, { once: true });
  window.addEventListener('keydown', handler, { once: true });
}

This is the single most important rule. An animation people can't skip is an animation for the author, not the visitor. Anyone in a hurry, anyone on a slow device, anyone who's already seen it gets an instant exit.

Rule 3: provide a URL escape hatch

?noload skips the intro entirely. It's useful for three reasons:

  1. Development. I don't want to watch the typewriter every time I refresh while styling a section.
  2. Testing. Automated browser checks can skip straight to the content.
  3. Sharing. If I send someone a link to a specific part of the site, I can send the version that doesn't make them wait.

Rule 4: lazy-load everything below the hero

The intro shouldn't block the rest of the page from being ready. Every home section below the hero is loaded lazily (React.lazy), so the heavy 3D code and the lower sections don't compete for bandwidth on first load.

const Projects = React.lazy(() => import('./sections/Projects'));
const Blog     = React.lazy(() => import('./sections/Blog'));

// ...inside the page
<Suspense fallback={null}>
  <Projects />
  <Blog />
</Suspense>

A short accessibility and performance checklist

Before shipping any intro or motion-heavy hero, check:

  • prefers-reduced-motion. Respect it. Offer a static version for people who've asked for less motion.
  • Keyboard users. Can they skip it without a mouse? (A key press does it.)
  • Screen readers. Is the real content in the DOM and reachable, not trapped behind a canvas?
  • Low-end devices. Does it hold a reasonable frame rate, or does it make the page feel broken?
  • Slow connections. Measure the added weight. A big scene can cost more than it gives.

The principle

Flair should serve the visitor's first impression and then get out of the way.

If a feature can't be skipped, it's for me, not for them. Everything else on this list is just ways of putting that sentence into code.

Honest downside

3D adds weight, and no amount of lazy loading fully hides that. If your audience is on slow connections or older devices, measure before you add it, and be ready to cut it. A beautiful intro that makes your site feel slow has made the wrong trade.

A minimal Three.js scene (about 40 lines)

If you've never used Three.js, here's the smallest useful scene: a rotating cube. Everything else is variations on this.

import * as THREE from 'three';

const canvas = document.querySelector('canvas')!;
const renderer = new THREE.WebGLRenderer({ canvas, antialias: true });
renderer.setPixelRatio(Math.min(window.devicePixelRatio, 2));   // cap cost on hi-dpi screens

const scene  = new THREE.Scene();
const camera = new THREE.PerspectiveCamera(50, 1, 0.1, 100);
camera.position.z = 4;

const cube = new THREE.Mesh(
  new THREE.BoxGeometry(1, 1, 1),
  new THREE.MeshNormalMaterial()
);
scene.add(cube);

function resize() {
  const { clientWidth: w, clientHeight: h } = canvas;
  renderer.setSize(w, h, false);
  camera.aspect = w / h;
  camera.updateProjectionMatrix();
}
window.addEventListener('resize', resize);
resize();

renderer.setAnimationLoop(() => {
  cube.rotation.x += 0.01;
  cube.rotation.y += 0.015;
  renderer.render(scene, camera);
});

Two details worth copying into any scene: cap the pixel ratio (rendering at 3× on a phone is rarely worth the battery) and handle resize.

Respecting reduced motion

Some visitors ask their device for less motion. Honour it:

const reduceMotion = window.matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)').matches;

if (reduceMotion) {
  showStaticMasthead();      // plain, instant version of the hero
} else {
  playIntro();
}

This is more than politeness. For people with vestibular disorders, large animated scenes can cause real discomfort.

Clean up after yourself

A scene that's no longer visible should stop costing CPU and GPU:

function stopIntro() {
  renderer.setAnimationLoop(null);   // stop the render loop
  scene.traverse(obj => {
    if ((obj as THREE.Mesh).geometry) (obj as THREE.Mesh).geometry.dispose();
    const m = (obj as THREE.Mesh).material;
    if (m) (Array.isArray(m) ? m : [m]).forEach(x => x.dispose());
  });
  renderer.dispose();
  canvas.remove();
}

Forgetting this is a classic cause of pages that get slower the longer you stay on them.

A performance budget

Decide limits before building, so "just one more effect" has something to bump against.

Budget item Example target
Added JavaScript for the intro As small as you can; measure it
Time until content is usable Content must not wait for the intro
Frame rate on a mid-range phone Smooth enough that it doesn't feel broken
Memory after intro ends Back to baseline (dispose everything)

I'm deliberately not giving numeric thresholds, because they depend on your audience. Pick your own and measure them with the browser's performance tools.

Questions to ask before adding a hero animation

  1. Does it help the visitor understand something, or only impress?
  2. Can it be skipped instantly?
  3. What happens on a slow phone with a bad connection?
  4. What happens with JavaScript disabled or storage blocked?
  5. Will I still like it on the fiftieth visit?

If three of the five answers are bad, simplify.

A middle path

If you love the effect but not the cost, make it optional and on demand: a "play intro" link in the footer, or show it only on the very first visit. Delight you choose beats delight you're forced through.

What flashy feature have you added to a site and later regretted? And did you cut it, or did you make it optional?

title: Communication-Efficient Private Federated Reinforcement Learning with Post-Quantum Authentication for Vehicular Networks
description:
arXiv:2610.41055v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Federated reinforcement learning supports cooperative vehicular routing without centralizing trajectory data, but model updates may reveal private information and incur communication overhead over intermittent vehicle-to-infrastructure links, particularly when post-quantum authentication is required. We study correlated private quantization, using complementary shared randomness between paired vehicles to reduce aggregation mean squared error while preserving the marginal parameter-level local differential privacy and one-bit communication cost of independent quantization. A tunable extension mixes shared and independent randomness to bound privacy leakage given paired outputs and shared-randomness side information. For this extension, R\'enyi differential privacy accounting establishes vector-level local differential privacy for one model upload even when pairings are revealed. Under matched vector-level privacy and identical local and global parameters, the extension yields 16.5% lower analytical aggregation mean squared error than independent quantization. We evaluate cooperative routing by coupling traffic simulation with packet-level simulation of post-quantum-authenticated vehicle-to-infrastructure communication. Compared to full-precision updates, one-bit uploads reduce authenticated uplink size by 92.4% and increase mean verified updates aggregated per round from 19.6 to 26.5. Under mobility-constrained communication at a parameter-level privacy budget of 1, correlated private quantization reduces mean travel time by 14.3% relative to independent quantization at the same budget and communication cost. At a parameter-level privacy budget of 0.3, a vehicle-origin inference attack trained on independent simulations reaches 30% accuracy with correlated private quantization and 22% with independent quantization after 100 rounds, versus 91% without privacy and 10% for random guessing.

title: Characterizing Recoverable Expert-Utilization Signatures in Fine-Tuned Mixture-of-Experts LLMs
description:
arXiv:2610.41039v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) large language models are increasingly deployed in distributed environments, from federated learning to edge-cloud systems, their architecture harbors an underexplored landscape of security vulnerabilities. Moving beyond textual analysis, we uncover structural memorization: a novel vulnerability where a fine-tuned model memorizes not only its training data but also the internal pathway used to process it, creating a characteristic routing fingerprint unique to the training process. We provide comprehensive empirical evidence that structural memorization emerges consistently even from a few samples, and that its intensity is directly influenced by the choice of trainable modules.
  We show that these memorized expert pathways can be stealthily recovered through the model's unconditional generation, using only routing and output logits, with no knowledge of the fine-tuning data or procedure. In distributed deployments, this vulnerability is amplified as routing information is exposed at multiple trust boundaries, including federated aggregation points, edge-cloud interfaces, and multi-tenant monitoring systems. Recovery exposes a critical blind spot: traditional membership inference metrics, viewed through the lens of expert routing, fail to identify memorized data corresponding to these structural pathways. To close this gap, we devise composite metrics combining reference model tail likelihood with complexity-aware normalization, significantly improving detection of memorized routing structures. This enables adversaries to pinpoint critical experts shaped by fine-tuning, whether dominant or dormant, and execute targeted attacks such as router manipulation or backdoor injection in realistic distributed settings where attackers lack training data but can observe routing patterns across system components.

title: Part 13: Setting up five trial environments: what you need before you build
description:
Part 13 · One Agent, Five Platforms

Nobody writes about the part before the build: accounts, entitlements, regions, model access and trial limits. It's also where a comparison can quietly go wrong, because a trial that leaves out the agent product isn't a fair test of the platform.

This part is the checklist I'm using for all five platforms. Like Part 11, it's documentation-only. Everything below comes from each vendor's own trial, pricing or getting-started pages as I read them on 1 November 2026, linked in the text. Trial terms change often, so check them on the day you sign up.

The question that matters most

For each platform, the first question isn't "is there a free trial?" It's "does the trial include the agent product?" A platform trial and an agent-product trial are often not the same thing.

That turned out to be the most useful thing to check on every platform below.

MuleSoft

The Agent Fabric getting-started page lists what you need:

  • An Anypoint Platform account, with Agent Fabric enabled for your organisation by an administrator.
  • Omni Gateway, CloudHub 2.0 (every organisation has a shared space) and Exchange.
  • Anypoint Code Builder, plus Java 17 and Maven for custom MCP servers or A2A apps.
  • API keys for your LLM providers, and an identity provider that issues JWTs for some features.

Anypoint has a free-trial sign-up. The page doesn't say whether Agent Fabric is included in a trial, and says to contact your administrator or MuleSoft account team if it isn't available. Check that first.

Boomi

The Boomi AI overview says Agentstudio is generally available to direct customers, and its Base Edition comes with every Boomi Enterprise Platform edition. The only trial it mentions is a 30-day free trial of Personal Edition. It doesn't spell out which Agentstudio features that edition includes. Use of Boomi AI is covered by Boomi's AI acceptable use policy.

SAP

SAP has two relevant trials, and they cover different things:

  • The generative AI hub trial is 30 days. It gives access to SAP AI Launchpad and SAP AI Core, with models from several providers, including Anthropic, Google and OpenAI. Prompt optimisation isn't included.
  • The SAP Build trial is a 30-day basic trial on a shared tenant with sample data. It includes a workbook for creating Joule skills with Joule Studio, but it's "a selected subset" of SAP Build, and Joule skills created there can't be deployed to production. The page doesn't name the agent builder.

For this series, the generative AI hub trial covers model access. Whether the agent-building side can be tested properly in a trial needs checking.

Azure

The Foundry Agent Service pricing page says there's no additional charge for creating or running Foundry-native agents with prompts and workflows. You pay for the models, the tools (such as file search and code interpreter) and, for hosted agents, the container compute. Azure's general free account offers $200 of credit for 30 days. That's an Azure-wide offer, not specific to Foundry.

AWS

The AWS Free Tier FAQ says new customers get up to $200 in credits on a free plan that lasts up to six months or until the credits run out. When it ends, the account is suspended, data is kept for 90 days, and the account is erased if you don't upgrade. The FAQ doesn't list Bedrock among the credit-eligible services, so confirm that on the Free Tier page.

AgentCore pricing is consumption-based, with separate charges for runtime, gateway, identity, memory, evaluations and more. There's no AgentCore-specific free trial; some features are free during preview.

The checklist I'm using

The same eight checks, for every platform:

  1. Does the trial include the agent product? Not just the platform.
  2. How long does it last, and what happens at the end? Some trials stop; AWS suspends and later deletes.
  3. Model access. Bring your own API key, or use the platform's models? Which models?
  4. Region. Pick one region and keep it for every component.
  5. MCP and A2A support in the trial. The tool contract has to be testable.
  6. Spending limits. Set a budget alert before the first model call. Credits run out faster than you'd expect with agents.
  7. Terms on publishing results. Some trial terms limit publishing benchmarks. As Part 5 said, where they do, I'll score from documentation and build experience only.
  8. Data. Only the fictional golden set from Part 10. No real invoices, no client data, ever.

Two rules on top: personal trial accounts, not employer ones, and nothing that connects to a real system of record.

What this changes

The builds stay documentation-only for now, as with MuleSoft. Where a trial does include the agent product, a hands-on build can follow, and the scores will be updated with a note saying what changed.

Boomi is next: hosting the tool contract.

Which platform was easiest to start on for you?

This series describes a reference build on a fictional company. Trial and pricing details come from vendor pages as of 1 November 2026 and change often; check current terms before you sign up.

title: Certified Behavioral Retention for Continual Adaptation with Held-Out Anchors
description:
arXiv:2610.40740v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Continual adaptation requires deciding not only how to update a model, but whether to commit an update without exceeding a declared budget for changes to protected behavior. We introduce Certified Anchor-Based Adaptation (CABA), a candidate-agnostic post-update gate that reserves historical observations from candidate optimization, compares old and candidate policies on frozen representations, and selects the largest tested interpolation coefficient whose worst-anchor forward KL divergence remains within budget. The finite check requires neither action labels nor complete trajectories. We develop a theory-led certification framework that separates measured anchor retention from conditional off-anchor guarantees. Under explicit representation-coverage and Lipschitz assumptions, an accepted update satisfies a uniform behavioral-divergence bound on protected support. The analysis gives regularity bounds for affine softmax heads, probabilistic coverage and compression guarantees, interpolation monotonicity conditions, grid-resolution bounds, and trajectory-level and sequential-composition guarantees. In a controlled UCI Human Activity Recognition study used as a non-stationary sensor-policy proxy, CABA reduces mean forgetting from 1.01 percent for unconstrained adaptation to 0.00 percent at budget epsilon = 0.05, while reducing final average accuracy from 93.04 percent to 88.48 percent. The experiment illustrates a retention-plasticity trade-off and does not establish foundation-model or robotic performance. CABA provides an auditable retention check for candidate generators exposing comparable policy distributions and a declared update path, while deployment also requires separate evidence of current-task utility.

title: Building a third-party embed that survives any host page
description:
We publish Regime Map, a country-by-country register of gambling regulation. The people who write about the subject, lawyers and journalists mostly, need the same picture we already draw: which countries license online casino and which don't. So we made the map embeddable. Paste a snippet, get the map.

The hard part of a third-party embed isn't drawing the thing. It's that you ship code into pages you will never see. Somebody's WordPress theme sets svg { max-width: 50% }. Somebody else's news site has a strict Content-Security-Policy. A third one is a React app that adds your element after your script has already run. And the reader on a cheap phone didn't ask for your 200 KB of JavaScript.

This post is the list of decisions we made so the embed survives all of that, and so it can't damage the host page in return.

The contract is the markup

What a site pastes is the whole public interface:

<div data-regimemap="map" data-lang="en" data-region="world" data-theme="light">Interactive map: online casino regulation by country.</div>
<p>Map: <a href="https://regimemap.com/gambling-regulation-map/">Regime Map</a></p>
<script async src="https://regimemap.com/embed/v1/embed.js" referrerpolicy="no-referrer"></script>

Three rules follow from treating that as an API:

  • Everything lives under /embed/v1/. Inside v1, anything may change as long as pasted code keeps working. New options arrive as new data- attributes with defaults. A breaking change would be /embed/v2/, and v1 keeps running.
  • The text inside the <div> is the no-JavaScript fallback. If the script is stripped or blocked, the reader still gets a sentence and the link below it.
  • Nothing ever goes blank. If we retire the embed, or switch it off for one site, it renders a short card instead of an empty box.

Load almost nothing up front

The script tag points at a loader of 2.4 KB gzipped. It does four things:

  1. Finds its own origin from document.currentScript, so the same file works in any environment with no configuration.
  2. Reserves each embed's height straight away, from the region's aspect ratio or a card's usual height, so the host page doesn't jump when the map arrives.
  3. Waits for an IntersectionObserver with a 200 px margin. A map in the footer of a long article costs the reader 2.4 KB until they scroll near it.
  4. Shares requests. Two maps and three cards on one page fetch each file once. Pasting the script tag twice is harmless; the second copy just rescans.

Everything else is plain ES5 with no framework, no dependencies and no web fonts. The renderers get content-hashed names and a one-year immutable cache; the loader is cached for an hour and names the current pair. Translated strings travel in the per-language data file, not in the renderer, so one renderer serves all seven languages and stays cacheable.

piece gzipped
loader 2.4 KB
map renderer, including the world geometry 33.4 KB
map data, per language 2.5–3.3 KB
map, total ≈ 39 KB
country card, total ≈ 8 KB

Single-page apps get one global, window.RegimeMapEmbed.scan(), to call after they insert an element. Each element mounts once; to change options you replace the element (in React, a new key).

Shadow DOM, but carefully

Each embed renders into an open shadow root. That stops the host's selectors from matching our elements, but it does not stop inheritance: font, color, line-height, letter-spacing and friends still flow in from the host. So the first rule is:

:host { all: initial; display: block; }

and then the stylesheet sets every property it relies on, including box-sizing. We tested against a page with deliberately hostile rules on *, div, a, table, svg and button.

Two details mattered more than we expected:

  • Styles arrive as a constructable stylesheet (adoptedStyleSheets). Where that API is missing, a <link> to a CSS file inside the shadow root takes over. Hosts with a strict style-src then only need to allow our origin.
  • There is no style="" attribute anywhere in the output. Sizes are set through the CSSOM instead. A host with style-src-attr 'none' still renders the embed. Inline style attributes are the first thing a strict policy kills, and they're easy to add without noticing.

Under a strict CSP the script form needs our origin in script-src and connect-src (plus style-src for the fallback path). The iframe form needs frame-src. That's it.

Credit without touching the host page

The embed is free. The one condition is a visible credit line under it, and that line is the host's own HTML, outside anything we render. The host may add rel="nofollow" to it, and the terms say so plainly.

The embed checks for it: a visible link to our domain in its parent element or one of the next two siblings. A hidden or zero-opacity link doesn't count. If there is none, the embed draws its own credit bar inside its own frame.

What it never does is inject a link into the host page. A widget that adds links to other people's pages from JavaScript is exactly what search engines describe as link spam, and it would also be rude. Every link the embed renders itself opens in a new tab with rel="nofollow noopener".

When scripts aren't allowed

Plenty of platforms strip <script>. For those there is an iframe form with the same options as query parameters. Two lessons:

  • Iframe height has no good answer without postMessage resizing, which we chose not to depend on. The map frame keeps a 16:10 ratio with a 420 px minimum, because at 320 px wide 16:10 alone is too short for the header, map and legend. Country cards get a fixed height that the configurator measures for that country and language at 360 px, so a phone never cuts them off.
  • Some platforms take neither scripts nor iframes, Medium and Substack among them. There the honest answer is a screenshot with a caption that credits and links the source.

Switching off one site without naming it

Sometimes an embed shows up somewhere it shouldn't. Every data file carries an off list of 32-bit FNV-1a hashes of hostnames (lower case, without www.). The embed hashes its own host, or an iframe's parent, and on a match shows "not available on this site" with no link.

Hashes, so the public file doesn't list anyone. And FNV-1a rather than SHA-256 because crypto.subtle only exists in secure contexts, and plenty of host pages are still plain http. The change reaches every embed within the hour, which is the data file's cache time.

Accessibility is part of "survives"

A map that only works with a mouse doesn't survive a keyboard user. The SVG is aria-hidden and a sentence summarises it. The map is one tab stop with a roving tabindex: arrow keys move from country to country, Home and End jump to the ends, Enter goes to the country's link, Esc closes. There's a full table view. Touch targets are 44 px, and small states are drawn as dots so they can be found and tapped at world scale. prefers-reduced-motion removes the transitions.

A checklist, if you're building one

  • Treat the pasted markup as a versioned API, with a no-JS fallback inside it.
  • Ship a tiny loader; lazy-load the rest near the viewport; reserve the height first.
  • Shadow DOM plus :host { all: initial }, then set everything you inherit.
  • No inline style attributes. Constructable stylesheets with a <link> fallback.
  • Never inject links or markup into the host page.
  • Offer an iframe form, and say honestly where neither form works.
  • Have a way to switch off one site without publishing a list of sites.
  • Make the keyboard and table views first-class, not an afterthought.

The configurator, with a live preview of the map and the country cards, is at regimemap.com/data-api. How we count where the embed appears without logging the people who read it deserves its own post; that's next.

title: CVE-2026-105483: certificate SAN policy decides the risk
description:
CVE-2026-105483: certificate SAN policy decides the risk

The Node.js bug behind CVE-2026-105483 has a simple defensive lesson: a certificate is valid only for the identity type the client intended to verify. In affected Node.js 24.x and 26.x releases, a fullwidth-digit IPv4 host could be normalized and resolved as an address while tls.checkServerIdentity() evaluated DNS names and the Common Name. The result was a certificate trust decision for the wrong identity class.

Node.js fixed the problem in 24.22.1 and 26.12.1 on October 21, 2026. The vendor rates it High. The advisory score is CVSS v3.0 7.4 with a network vector and high attack complexity. The CWE is 295, improper certificate validation.

DNS SAN and IP SAN are different promises

A DNS SAN says that the subject is identified by a DNS name. An IP address SAN says that the subject is identified by a literal IP address. Browsers and TLS libraries normally enforce that separation because an address and a name are different identities, even when DNS or an operating system resolver maps one to the other.

The affected Node.js path did not recognize the fullwidth-digit destination as an IP address. It normalized the destination to a normal IPv4 address and connected there. Verification then compared the normalized value with DNS names. A certificate carrying DNS:127.0.0.1 or an applicable DNS wildcard could satisfy that comparison.

The missing control was not a missing signature check. The chain could be trusted. The problem was that the signed identity did not describe the type of endpoint the client believed it was contacting.

Why public CAs and private PKI need separate review

High attack complexity reflects the certificate conditions. The attacker needs a chain trusted by the client and a certificate whose DNS identity matches the address representation used in verification. A public CA policy may restrict issuing DNS names that are numeric IP-looking strings, but an organization cannot assume that every CA in its trust store follows the same issuance profile.

Private PKI deserves direct attention. Internal CAs may issue certificates for test services, ephemeral hosts, or address-like names. Those certificates can be legitimate for their original scope while still becoming dangerous if they are accepted for an IP endpoint the client did not intend to contact.

Teams should inventory trust stores, intermediate authorities, and delegated issuance paths used by Node.js clients. That work is broader than this CVE, but the vulnerability provides a concrete reason to ask whether certificates with address-like DNS SANs are still necessary.

Application behavior that raises risk

The Node.js runtime flaw becomes a security incident only when an application reaches the affected verification path. Look for destinations that can be influenced by a tenant, administrator, integration, webhook, import, or configuration API. Also review connectors that accept an arbitrary endpoint and then attach credentials or sensitive data.

An application that always contacts a fixed DNS name has a smaller practical attack surface. An application that accepts a full URL, extracts its host, connects with Node.js TLS, and sends an API token has a much clearer identity dependency. The certificate certificate requirements still apply, but the attacker's ability to choose the destination representation matters.

Do not infer vulnerability from a hostname that happens to contain Unicode. Trace the exact value through URL parsing, validation, DNS resolution, and the TLS call. Record whether the application expects a DNS name, an IP address, or both, and whether the expected identity is checked after normalization.

Affected versions and deployment visibility

The official affected range is Node.js 24.x before 24.22.1 and 26.x before 26.12.1. The 22.x line received other security fixes in the same release cycle but is not listed as affected by this CVE. Check the actual process version and the container image digest. A lockfile, package manifest, or base-image tag is supporting evidence, not proof of what runs.

This matters in long-lived deployment systems. A service can inherit a patched image name while an old layer or sidecar still runs a vulnerable binary. Build attestations and runtime version reporting should agree before a team marks the deployment complete.

Exposure has a limited meaning

ZoomEye Search app="Node.js" returned 5,539,674 matches at 04:17 +08:00 on November 2, 2026. The CVE filter returned zero. Exposure is 5,539,674 because the policy selects the greater verified query count. These are product fingerprints, not vulnerable installations.

Use the figure to frame internet-scale relevance, not to assign incident status. A Node.js fingerprint cannot reveal the exact release, the trust store, the application's destination validation, or whether the vulnerable certificate path is reachable. Those facts belong in internal evidence.

Remediation

Upgrade to 24.22.1, 26.12.1, or a later maintained release. Rebuild and redeploy every artifact that embeds Node.js. Verify the running version after rollout and retain the evidence with the change record.

Review certificate profiles for address-like DNS SANs, especially in internal PKI and test environments. Require applications to canonicalize destinations before policy checks, reject inputs that are neither approved DNS names nor canonical IP addresses, and avoid custom certificate verification that skips the standard hostname check.

Finally, test with certificates that isolate the behavior: one with only a numeric DNS SAN, one with a matching IP SAN, and one with neither. A patched client should accept only the certificate whose identity matches the intended endpoint type. Keep the test local and controlled, and do not use production trust anchors.

References

  • Node.js October 21, 2026 Security Releases
  • Node.js 24.22.1 release notes
  • Node.js 26.12.1 release notes
  • GitHub Advisory GHSA-8h4p-qpcq-gq24
  • ZoomEye Search

title: React Controlled vs Uncontrolled Components
description:
React makes it easy to manipulate data using forms.

One of the most common patterns you’ll see in React when dealing with forms is that we need to make React aware of changes to the form inputs when the user
types. This means that the component containing those input elements typically needs to keep track of the text in the input elements using state.

React supports two types of components: controlled components and uncontrolled components. Let’s uncover the main differences between controlled and
uncontrolled components.

Controlled Component

Unlike the uncontrolled component, the input form element in the controlled component is handled by the component rather than the DOM. It takes its current
value through props. The changes are notified through useState Hook. Let’s consider an example to understand it in a better way.

import { useState } from "react";
export default function ControlledComponent() {
    const [name, setName] = useState("");
    const [age, setAge] = useState();
    const [hairColor, setHairColor] = useState("");
    return (
        <form>
            <label htmlFor="name">
                Name
                <input name="name" type="text" placeholder="Name" value={name} onChange={(e) => setName(e.target.value)} />
            </label>
            <label htmlFor="age">
                Age
                <input name="age" type="number" placeholder="Age" value={age} onChange={(e) => setAge(Number(e.target.value))} />
            </label>
            <label htmlFor="haircolor">
                Hair Color
                <input name="haircolor" type="text" placeholder="Hair Color" value={hairColor} onChange={(e) => setHairColor(e.target.value)} />
            </label>
            <button type="submit">Submit</button>
        </form>
    );
}

The input field is Controlled because React sets its value from the state.

<input value={value} />

Whenever we type into the input field, the onChange handler updates the state with the input’s value accessed from the event object. The value state variable is
the source of truth. When we need to access the value entered by the user into the input field, we have to read the value from the state variable. The
Controlled components can help access the value of any input field.

Uncontrolled component

Similar to the traditional HTML form inputs, the uncontrolled component can be written using a ref to get form values from the DOM. Thus there is no need to
write an event handler for every state update and the HTML elements maintain their own state that will be updated when the input value changes.

import { createRef } from "react";
export default function UncontrolledComponent() {
    const nameInput = createRef();
    const ageInput = createRef();
    const hairColorInput = createRef();
    const handleSubmit = (e) => {
        e.preventDefault();
        console.log(nameInput.current.value);
        console.log(ageInput.current.value);
        console.log(hairColorInput.current.value);
    };
    return (
        <div>
            <form onSubmit={handleSubmit}>
                <label htmlFor="name">
                    Name
                    <input name="name" type="text" placeholder="Name" ref={nameInput} />
                </label>
                <label htmlFor="age">
                    Age
                    <input name="age" type="number" placeholder="Age" ref={ageInput} />
                </label>
                <label htmlFor="haircolor">
                    Hair Color
                    <input name="haircolor" type="text" placeholder="Hair Color" ref={hairColorInput} />
                </label>
                <button type="submit">Submit</button>
            </form>
        </div>
    );
}

Conclusion

Both the controlled and uncontrolled form fields have their merit. Evaluate your specific situation and pick the approach — what works for you is good enough.
