title: Context Optimization Is Not Stream Recovery: Integrating context-mode Without Hiding Failures
description:
Your production agent fails at 3:47 AM. The on-call engineer opens the transcript: thirty-two thousand lines of test output, followed by a cheerful "I've analyzed the failures and here's my recommendation." The model never saw the actual error. It hit the context ceiling three tool calls ago and has been operating on stale summaries since.

This is not a conversation-history problem. A five-turn chat consumes maybe 8,000 tokens. A single pytest run with verbose output can return 50,000. One file search across a monorepo can yield 200 results. The agent keeps working, the streaming UI keeps typing, and nothing alerts you that the decisions being made are now based on truncated evidence.

mksglu/context-mode attacks that specific failure mode by sandboxing tool output, enforcing routing through MCP hooks, and persisting session memory outside the immediate inference context. The project reports 98% output reduction across 17 platforms. I have not reproduced those measurements.

As an external integrator, I evaluated one narrower question: Can a tool-output boundary reduce model input without making streamed responses misleading when the transport fails?

That requires keeping context management and stream delivery architecturally separate.

Put the reduction boundary before inference

The architecture splits into two paths.

The agent execution path routes tools through context-mode's supported mechanisms. Large outputs stay outside the model's immediate context; the model receives bounded, semantically selected information. Session memory maintains continuity across turns.

The presentation path takes the resulting conversation, invokes inference, and streams assistant output into React using the Vercel AI SDK.

Do not insert a generic truncator between those paths. Cutting a pytest log at 8,000 characters preserves setup noise while removing the actual failure line. Cutting serialized messages can corrupt tool-call relationships, leaving the model with a reference to a result that no longer exists in context.

Instead, enforce an application-level contract: the conversation submitted for inference must already contain bounded, relevant tool results. Preserve a reference to complete output wherever the execution environment supports later retrieval. Context-mode's configuration and retrieval semantics are deployment-specific; they are not interchangeable with AI SDK transport settings.

This matters because smaller input does not make delivery reliable. A proxy can still buffer output, a browser can disappear, and a user can cancel mid-sentence.

A bounded streaming route

The following Next.js App Router handler is the inference boundary, not a replacement for context-mode's MCP integration.

Install the compatible AI SDK 5 family: ai@5, @ai-sdk/openai@2, and @ai-sdk/react@2 for the client. Commit the lockfile. Set B_LOST_API_KEY and MODEL_ID in the server environment. The model identifier must be supported by your configured endpoint.

B-Lost's OpenAI-compatible relay at https://b-lost.com/v1 is the gateway in this topology. Whether its complete deployment path delivers unbuffered SSE is something to measure, not assume.

// app/api/chat/route.ts
import {
  convertToModelMessages,
  streamText,
  validateUIMessages,
} from "ai";
import { createOpenAI } from "@ai-sdk/openai";

export const runtime = "nodejs";
export const maxDuration = 60;

const MAX_INPUT_BYTES = 120_000;

export async function POST(request: Request) {
  const apiKey = process.env.B_LOST_API_KEY;
  const modelId = process.env.MODEL_ID;

  if (!apiKey || !modelId) {
    return Response.json(
      { error: "Inference configuration is missing." },
      { status: 503 },
    );
  }

  // Also enforce a body-size limit at the ingress proxy.
  const body = await request.text();

  if (new TextEncoder().encode(body).byteLength > MAX_INPUT_BYTES) {
    return Response.json(
      { error: "Reduce tool output before requesting inference." },
      { status: 413 },
    );
  }

  let messages;
  try {
    const payload = JSON.parse(body);
    messages = await validateUIMessages({
      messages: payload.messages,
    });
  } catch {
    return Response.json(
      { error: "Invalid UI message payload." },
      { status: 400 },
    );
  }

  const provider = createOpenAI({
    apiKey,
    baseURL: "https://b-lost.com/v1",
  });

  try {
    const result = streamText({
      model: provider.chat(modelId),
      messages: await convertToModelMessages(messages),
      abortSignal: AbortSignal.any([
        request.signal,
        AbortSignal.timeout(55_000),
      ]),
      maxRetries: 0,
      maxOutputTokens: 2048,
    });

    return result.toUIMessageStreamResponse({
      headers: {
        "Cache-Control": "no-cache, no-transform",
        "X-Accel-Buffering": "no",
      },
      onError: () => "Generation interrupted. Retry explicitly.",
    });
  } catch {
    return Response.json(
      { error: "Unable to start generation." },
      { status: 502 },
    );
  }
}

The byte limit is an admission guard, not a token budget. It runs after reading the body, so ingress must enforce its own limit. Neither this guard nor message validation constitutes authentication or tenant authorization.

The 55-second deadline leaves headroom below the route's 60-second deployment allowance. Platforms impose different limits. The abort signal requests cancellation; propagation of browser disconnects through hosting infrastructure still needs testing.

Diagnose the boundary that actually failed

Use useChat from @ai-sdk/react with its default transport pointed at /api/chat. This route emits the AI SDK UI-message stream protocol. A raw OpenAI SSE parser is the wrong consumer.

That distinction explains a common integration failure: the network tab shows incoming bytes, but the UI never updates because the client expects a different event format. Do not manually split arbitrary network chunks on newlines; chunk boundaries need not match SSE frames or UTF-8 character boundaries.

For buffering diagnostics, compare upstream first-byte time, route first-byte time, and the browser's first rendered text. Run curl -N against the deployed route with a valid message payload. If curl receives periodic events but React updates in bursts, investigate rendering pressure. With the AI SDK 5 React hook, experimental_throttle can reduce update frequency; rendering expensive Markdown on every delta can otherwise dominate the main thread.

If both curl and the browser receive one final burst, investigate the relay and hosting path. X-Accel-Buffering: no is advisory, not a universal buffering override.

Keep interruption visible

The deliberate trade-off here is rejecting oversized conversations rather than silently degrading them. The agent must return to its context-management layer and select better evidence.

Disabling automatic retries avoids treating a second generation as continuation of the first. It sacrifices some transient-error recovery for predictable UI semantics.

After cancellation or transport failure, keep partial assistant text visibly incomplete. Do not promote it into persistent session memory as a completed conclusion. Context-mode can reduce what enters inference; the application still owns whether an interrupted answer becomes durable agent history.

The hardest operational dilemma: you can reduce what enters the model, or you can retry failed streams automatically, but doing both without losing signal fidelity requires explicit session-state reconciliation that most frameworks do not provide. When your agent's context budget runs out mid-task, do you surface the failure to the user, retry with reduced context and risk nondeterministic behavior, or persist partial work and rely on the next turn to recover? How are you handling context exhaustion and stream interruption in production agent systems?

title: The Optimistic Maintainer: Why Fast Merges Beat Endless Review Cycles
description:
If you have ever contributed to open source, you probably know this feeling.

You find a bug in a tool you use every day. You clone the repo, spend a Saturday afternoon digging through unfamiliar code, write a clean 40-line fix, verify it works, and open a pull request. More recent, you ask your agent to find the fix and open the pull request. You feel great.

Then the waiting begins.

Two weeks pass. A maintainer appears, leaves three comments on variable naming and asks if you can rebase against a newly refactored branch. You make the changes. Another three weeks pass. A second reviewer asks why you didn't rewrite the surrounding function to use a different pattern. By month two, the enthusiasm that carried you through that Saturday afternoon is completely gone. You close the tab and never open a PR to that project again.

I've been on that side of the fence. Now, as the maintainer of TTT—a terminal text editor and IDE written in Go—I'm on the other side.

Over the last few months, the project has crossed 1,750 commits, 185,000 lines of code, and more than 70 unique community contributors. We ship a new stable release roughly every week.

Someone looking at our Git log recently pointed out an interesting pattern:

"The maintainer seems to merge almost everything quickly and just creates follow-up tickets for the rest."

They were spot on. That is not an accident or sloppy rubber-stamping. It is a deliberate strategy: optimistic merging. It is the single most important reason our community has grown this fast without burning me out.

Here is why it works, how we do it, and the engineering safety net that makes it possible.

The Trap of the Adversarial Gatekeeper

Most maintainers start out with good intentions. They care about their project, so they treat their repository like a fortress and themselves as the gatekeeper. Every incoming pull request is viewed with skepticism: What could this break? Did they follow all my implicit rules?

The problem is that open source contribution is discretionary effort. A contributor doesn’t work for you. When someone gives you a PR, they are giving you a gift of their free time. And even in modern times when opening a PR can be automated with an agent, they are opening the PR on your repository instead of somewhere else.

If you meet that gift with four rounds of nitpicking over inconsequential details, you aren't "maintaining high standards"—you are imposing friction. The contributor burns out, and you burn out from reading the same 30 lines of code across six weeks of back-and-forth.

Worse, when maintainers get paranoid about breaking things, they freeze. PRs pile up in the queue because the maintainer is afraid to merge them until they have a free weekend to manually test every edge case.

I wanted TTT to feel different: if you submit a working fix with tests, your code should be in main within hours, not months.

Step 1: You Need a Safety Net You Actually Trust

Here is the catch: you cannot practice optimistic merging if you don't trust your test suite. If merging a PR requires you to open the editor and manually poke at things to see if it feels right, you will inevitably become a bottleneck.

In previous posts, I wrote about how we built our --exec testing harness and how we used differential testing for our TextMate engine and Vim emulation.

Those weren't just academic exercises. They are the exact safety net that gives me the confidence to merge fast:

  1. 3,500+ Automated Tests: Across core algorithms, JSON-RPC LSP client communication, and buffer undo transactions.
  2. Deterministic UI Snapshots: Using our in-memory SimScreen and --exec scripts, CI tests actual visual layouts, tree widget expansions, and cursor goal-column math without needing a physical terminal.
  3. Automated PR Benchmark Comparisons: Every pull request runs scripts/bench-compare.mjs against main. It opens 64 MiB code files and 1 GiB logs. If a community PR introduces an accidental allocation loop or slows down rendering, CI tells us before I even open the review.
  4. Architectural Zones (ARCHITECTURE.md): Domain packages (internal/core/*) are strictly decoupled from the UI. They are forbidden from starting processes or touching terminal state.

Because the machine ruthlessly verifies that the invariants haven't broken, I don't have to spend my mental energy acting like a human compiler. Across 1,750+ commits, we have had exactly three reverts in the entire history of the project.

Step 2: The 90% Rule

When a contributor opens a pull request that solves 90% of a problem, passes CI, and includes tests, what do you do with the remaining 10%?

The gatekeeper demands that the contributor spend another week figuring out that last 10%.

The optimistic maintainer says: Merge the 90%.

Here’s what that looks like in practice:

  • The fix is solid, but missed a secondary edge case? Merge the PR, thank the contributor, and file a follow-up ticket: "Follow-up on #1284: handle ancestor tree preservation on collapsed roots."
  • The feature works, but needs a benchmark comparison? Don't make the contributor write a complex benchmark suite from scratch. Cherry-pick their commit, add the sub-benchmark alongside it, tag them with Co-Authored-By, and merge both.
  • Variable naming or a comment could be cleaner? Spend 30 seconds pushing a polish commit directly to main after merging, rather than making the contributor wait three days for another review cycle.

When contributors see their PR merged the same day they submitted it, the psychological shift is immediate. They don't feel like an outsider seeking approval; they feel like part of the team. Many of our most active contributors—people like Hao Chen, Jay Hemnani, Nandaleio, and Lzcwbcgs—started with a single small PR and kept coming back because the turnaround was fast and respectful.

Step 3: Defend Scope, Not Syntax

Optimistic merging does not mean accepting every feature anyone dreams up. If you merge every feature request into core, your binary will quickly turn into bloatware.

The distinction is: Be generous with code quality and bug fixes, but be strict about architectural scope.

Whenever a PR proposes something that doesn't belong in the core binary, I don't reject the contributor's idea—I guide it into our Lua plugin system:

  • A contributor built a great Linux desktop launcher integration into the core binary (#683). Core isn't the right place for desktop session launchers, so we agreed to package it as a featured Lua plugin (#1267).
  • A contributor submitted a port of the Catppuccin Mocha theme as a built-in Go theme. Rather than bundling dozens of themes into the core executable, we asked them to register it as a plugin manifest from ttt-plugins (#1240).

By pushing niche features into plugins, the core binary stays lean (single static Go binary, ~14 MB), while the community still gets the features they care about.

Step 4: Culture Encoded in Code

Most open source projects have a CONTRIBUTORS.md file that rots in the repository root. Almost nobody reads it, and bug reporters are never mentioned at all.

I wanted the culture of TTT to reflect that an editor is only as good as the people using it and reporting bugs. So we wrote a small script:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# scripts/update-contributors.sh
set -euo pipefail

REPO="eugenioenko/ttt"
OUTPUT="internal/app/contributors.json"

contributors=$(gh api "repos/$REPO/contributors?per_page=100" --paginate \
  -q '.[] | select(.type == "User") | .login' | jq -R . | jq -s .)

reporters=$(gh api "repos/$REPO/issues?state=all&per_page=100" --paginate \
  -q '.[] | select(.pull_request == null and .user.type == "User") | .user.login' |
  sort | uniq -c | sort -k1,1nr -k2,2 | awk '{print $2}' | jq -R . | jq -s .)

jq -n --argjson c "$contributors" --argjson r "$reporters" \
  '{contributors: $c, reporters: ($r - $c)}' > "$OUTPUT"

Before every release, this script fetches every person who contributed code and every person who opened an issue that led to a fix. It compiles them directly into contributors.json, which is embedded in the binary.

When you open Help > About inside TTT, you see this:

┌───────────────────────── About TTT Editor ─────────────────────────┐
│ Version: v1.10.0                                                   │
│ Website: https://tttedit.dev                                       │
│ GitHub:  https://github.com/eugenioenko/ttt                        │
│ ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── │
│ ttt is great because of everyone who contributes code, reports     │
│ issues, and uses it:                                               │
│                                                                    │
│ HaoChen · JayHemnani · Nandaleio · prime120 · Lzcwbcgs · ...       │
│                                                                    │
│ Thank you!                                                         │
│                                                            [Close] │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Every bug reporter and every code author is literally baked into the application they helped build. It runs offline, makes zero network calls, and permanently credits the community.

The Takeaway

If you are maintaining an open-source project and feeling overwhelmed by PRs, consider flipping the model:

  1. Invest in automated safety nets first. If you don't trust your CI, build harness tests and benchmarks until you do. You cannot be a fast maintainer if you are a fearful maintainer.
  2. Stop holding PRs hostage over formatting. If the logic works and passes tests, merge it. Fix the variable name yourself in two minutes or open a follow-up ticket.
  3. Protect your architectural boundaries, not your ego. Save your "no" for scope creep and core bloat. Say "yes" to fixes and performance wins as fast as humanly possible.

High rigor and community warmth are not mutually exclusive. When your automated testing is ruthless, your human maintainership can be optimistic.

TTT is open source at github.com/eugenioenko/ttt and available at tttedit.dev. Come open a PR—we’ll probably merge it.

title: How do you run training jobs across multiple GPU clouds?
description:
You run training across several GPU clouds by putting one scheduler in front of all of them: a job names the hardware it needs, and the scheduler decides where it runs and where it goes when a machine disappears. Nodus does this for you: it places each job on the cheapest capacity that can start it, spends the credits in the cloud accounts you connect first, and restores the run from its last checkpoint on another machine if one is reclaimed. The other two options are an open-source orchestrator you operate yourself, or a script per cloud, which works until the first preemption at 3 a.m.

Why would you spread one team's training over several clouds?

The usual reason is money you already have, not a grand multi-cloud strategy. A small AI team often holds AWS credits from an accelerator program, a GCP grant, and a prepaid balance on a GPU provider such as RunPod or Lambda. Each pile expires on its own schedule, and none of them alone has the right GPU free every time you need it.

The second reason is availability. The GPU you want is often sold out in one place and free in another, and interruptible capacity gets reclaimed. We collected the published numbers in how often spot GPUs are interrupted.

A job that can only run in one account waits or dies. A job that can run in any of five has five chances to start.

The cost of doing this by hand is coordination: five consoles, five quota limits, five ways to launch a machine, and no single place that says which run is where and what it cost.

What are the three ways to do it?

Each approach moves the same three jobs (choosing a location, falling back, recovering a run) to a different owner.

Approach Who picks where a job runs Who handles a lost machine Who runs the control plane
A launch script per cloud You, by hand You, by relaunching Nobody
Open-source orchestrator (SkyPilot, dstack) The orchestrator, from a search space you define The orchestrator, with your checkpoint code You (or a hosted tier)
Nodus Nodus, from your connected accounts and its own capacity Nodus, restoring the last committed checkpoint Nodus

Sources: SkyPilot overview, SkyPilot managed jobs, dstack docs, Nodus cloud accounts. Checked November 1, 2026.

Our decision rule: if you have one cloud and one GPU type, a script is fine. Once you have two credit balances or you use interruptible capacity, you want a scheduler, and the real question becomes whether you want to operate it.

How does Nodus decide which cloud a job runs on?

Nodus places each run on the cheapest offering that fits the request, has a machine free and stays inside your limits, according to the placement docs. If that offering cannot be used, the next cheapest takes the run. You can switch the trade-off with a placement profile: Balanced (the default), Cost for the lowest expected cost to completion including lost work, or Speed for the fastest finish within 1.5 times the cheapest expected cost.

Deadlines and money filter the list before anything is picked. Offerings whose p90 finish is later than your deadline are dropped, and so are offerings whose expected cost exceeds your remaining budget. If nothing is left, the job waits in Queued and the estimate says why, for example ExceedsRemainingBudget. nodus describe then shows the chosen offering, the fallbacks in order and every rejected offering with its reason.

From the command line, a job asks for hardware, not for a cloud:

nodus run --gpu H100:8 --max-cost 40 -d -- torchrun train.py

That example is copied from the nodus run reference, which also documents --profile and --interruptible.

How do you spend credits in your own cloud accounts first?

You connect each account once and give it a credit limit, and Nodus places your Jobs, Workspaces and other single-node work there before its own capacity. This is a Beta feature, turned on per organization, and the cloud accounts guide lists AWS, GCP, Azure, Kubernetes and API-key providers including Lambda, RunPod, Nebius and DigitalOcean.

Here is a setup for a team with AWS credits and a RunPod balance. The commands are copied from the nodus cloud connect reference, with --priority added to set the order:

nodus cloud connect aws aws-main --credit-limit 500 --priority 1
printf '%s' "$RUNPOD_API_KEY" | nodus cloud connect runpod my-runpod --credit-limit 200 --priority 2

Work goes to priority 1 first, then 2. Accounts with the same priority, or none, go to whichever has the cheapest machine for the work. The credit limit is spent at the Nodus list estimate, which can differ from what your cloud bills you, so the docs advise setting it a little below the credit you actually hold.

What happens when an account is full or out of credit is your choice, set with --burst:

--burst When the account cannot take the job
Allow (default) The job runs on Nodus capacity at Nodus rates
Approve The job waits until you approve it with nodus request approve-burst
Deny The job waits for your account

One honest limit: multi-node runs and Sandboxes use Nodus capacity, not your connected accounts. If your plan is an 8-node gang inside your own AWS account, this feature does not do that today.

What does a run cost each way?

Take one 8 x H100 run of 10 hours, which is 80 GPU-hours. In your own connected account, the job estimate shows a Nodus route fee of $0.02 per device-hour, so the Nodus charge is 80 x $0.02 = $1.60. Your cloud bills the machine and disk separately, against your credits.

If your accounts are full and the run bursts to Nodus capacity, the H100 SXM 80 GB is listed at $2.600/hr on the Nodus pricing page, so the same run costs 80 x $2.600 = $208.00, all in.


The route fee is all Nodus adds in your own account; the machine itself is paid from your cloud credits.

The two numbers are not a like-for-like price comparison, because the first excludes your cloud's bill. They show what you pay Nodus in each case, which is the number to plan around when your credits run out mid-project.

If the job bursts, these are the other rates you would see on the same page:

GPU Listed Nodus rate per GPU-hour
NVIDIA B200 180 GB $5.500
NVIDIA H200 SXM 141 GB $3.593
NVIDIA H100 SXM 80 GB $2.600
NVIDIA A100 80 GB $1.090
NVIDIA L4 24 GB $0.430

Prices checked November 1, 2026 on the Nodus pricing page.


A burst to an L4 or A100 is cheap; a burst to B200 for a long run is where a budget cap matters most.

What happens when a machine in one cloud disappears mid-run?

A run survives a lost machine only if it saves checkpoints, whichever scheduler you use. On Nodus, a machine that stops sending heartbeats gets a replacement prepared after 20 seconds, and after 60 seconds of silence an attempt on shared capacity is declared lost and replaced, per the attempts and recovery docs. The replacement starts only once the old machine is provably gone, so two copies never write the same checkpoint.

A Checkpointed run loses at most the work since its last committed checkpoint. Recovery has limits: by default 8 recoveries per run, and 3 for distributed Jobs. Failures caused by your own code, such as a non-zero exit or out of memory, fail fast and are not retried. The checkpoint guide shows the save and resume pattern in Python.

With a connected AWS account, one extra rule helps across clouds: if AWS refuses a machine because your GPU quota for that family is used up, Nodus skips that family in that region for an hour and runs the work elsewhere.

Where is an open-source orchestrator the better choice?

SkyPilot or dstack is the better choice when you need things Nodus does not do in your own accounts today, or when you want to own the control plane.

Pick SkyPilot if you run multi-node training inside your own clouds, Kubernetes clusters or Slurm, because it combines them into one pool with automatic failover across the search space you give it, per its overview. Its managed jobs recover from preemptions, GPU errors and node crashes, and clean up resources when done. It is open source, so nothing sits between you and your cloud bill.

Pick dstack if you want a self-hosted control plane across GPU clouds, Kubernetes and on-prem clusters, described in its docs as a unified interface for development, training and inference.

The trade is operating it. You configure each cloud's credentials and quotas, keep the controller running, and write the checkpoint and resume logic your jobs need. Pick Nodus when you would rather not run that layer, want one prepaid bill with per-job cost caps, and are happy for multi-node runs to use Nodus capacity.

How do you move an existing training script onto this?

Keep your script, make it write checkpoints to the checkpoint path, and launch it with a GPU request instead of a cloud name. The quickstart runs a script from your own directory with this command:

nodus run --name cli-quickstart --gpu L4 --image nodus/pytorch \
  --max-cost 1 --timeout 10m --no-warm --dry-run \
  --output metrics=/nodus/outputs/metrics.json -- python train.py

Drop --dry-run once the estimate looks right. Connect your cloud accounts afterwards; nothing in the job changes, and Attempts › Ran on on the job page shows whether each attempt ran in your account or on Nodus capacity. For multi-GPU code, our PyTorch multi-GPU training guide covers the torchrun side.

FAQ

Does connecting a cloud account let Nodus change my existing machines?

No. Viewing an account is read-only and does not create, change or delete resources. Running work is a separate, explicit upgrade, and Nodus then creates, labels and deletes only its own machines there.

Can one training run span two clouds at once?

Not by default. A multi-node run is placed with network: Colocated, which keeps every node in one location on one network. Regional and Global placement are possible, and the placement docs note that relayed paths between nodes have lower bandwidth, so most distributed training should stay in one place.

What does it cost to run CPU work in my own account?

CPU work has no Nodus routing fee; your cloud provider bills the machine and disk within your account's spending cap. The $0.02 per device-hour route fee applies to own-account GPU Jobs.

How do I stop using a connected account?

Disconnect it in Nodus first. Nodus stops placing work there, moves running work to the next source and terminates the machines it started, and only then should you remove its access on the cloud side.

Originally published on the Nodus blog.

title: GraphNIAH: A Benchmark for Long-Context Reasoning over Real-World Graphs
description:
arXiv:2610.41704v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The needle-in-a-haystack (NIAH) benchmark was introduced as a test for measuring a model's ability to find small relevant facts within a very large body of input text. However, existing NIAH benchmarks each suffer from one or more of the following limitations: (1) reliance on synthetic data, so their evaluations may not generalize to real-world settings; (2) reuse of previously published datasets, leading to the risk of benchmark contamination; (3) dependence on manual annotation, which requires human effort to create and update data and is prone to future benchmark contamination; and (4) unrealistic simplification of long-context multi-hop reasoning where each next step is trivial given previous steps, while real-world reasoning often requires planning over multiple possible proof paths. To address these limitations, we introduce \Benchmark, a dynamic benchmark built from real citation relationships among scientific papers published after the evaluated models' knowledge cutoff date, which utilizes real-world information while ensuring no benchmark contamination. The fully automated benchmark construction pipeline samples representative subgraphs of the citation graph formed by these papers and converts each subgraph into a long-context QA example with a verifiable answer. We use GraphNIAH to evaluate eight LLMs from the GPT-5.6, Gemini-3, and Qwen3.5 families. We find that accuracy falls as questions require longer reasoning paths: at question depths of 16 and 32, the GPT-5.6 and Qwen3.5 models answer YES/NO questions no better than random guessing, mostly by answering NO; four of the eight models answer no counting example correctly, and the others model get worse as the subgraph size increases. These findings suggest that current LLMs often stop searching the citation relationships in their context before they reach the answer, even though every fact they need is in the context.
